en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Essence of the Meaning of the Vinaya Piṭaka (Third Part)
5. The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) 1.
The Chapter on False Speech (Musāvādavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (Musāvādasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)
1. Regarding the phrase "of the minor rules" (*khuddakānaṃ*) in the first training rule of the Chapter on False Speech (*Musāvādavagga*):
here, they say that the word "minor" (*khuddaka*) is a synonym for "many" (*bahu*). "Because of their great number, these are called 'minor'.
In that context—meaning within those nine chapters, or within those minor rules—he says "form is impermanent," etc., in order to clarify precisely the concealment of one reason by another reason.
Having asserted that "form is impermanent," he states the reason for it as "because it is subject to being known.

When told by another, "If that is so, then even Nibbāna would fall into the state of impermanence," he states another reason— "because it is subject to birth"— in order to conceal that previous reason.

Regarding the statement, “He speaks a falsehood while being fully aware (*sampajāna*),” it should have been said “he speaks a falsehood while fully aware”; however, this is a grammatical description (*niddesa*) with the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*). Therefore, it says, “knowing, he speaks a falsehood.
“Having known, and for one who knows, speaking a falsehood” means: having known [the truth] at the prior stage, and speaking a falsehood at the moment of speech for one who is still knowing [it].
And what is called “speaking” here consists in making that which has not occurred appear as having occurred, or making that which has occurred appear as not having occurred.
It is the application of making known by means of body or speech. In the phrase "in the case of intentional lying" (*sampajānamusāvāde*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause;
therefore, for one who speaks an intentional lie, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) on account of that, with that as the cause, and with that as the condition.
In this way, the meaning should be understood here and in other similar instances.
3. It deceives by means of this, thus it is *visaṃvādanaṃ*; it is the mind that proceeds with the intention of deception. Therefore he said:
“having placed before oneself the mind of deception while speaking. It is spoken by means of this, thus it is *vācā*; it is the volition (*cetanā*) that originates speech.
Therefore he said: “false speech... [is] volition. Speech that has reached differentiation means speech divided into many different types. Thus...
By the words "by the first line, pure volition... it should be understood that [this] is stated," he illustrates this:
neither pure volition alone, nor the pure sound alone, nor pure intimation alone constitutes what is called false speech;

rather, it is the volition that originates it, together with the intimation and the sound, that constitutes false speech. "An object not grasped by way of the eye" means by that which is dependent on the eye.

An object not grasped by consciousness. Because the three faculties beginning with the nose grasp their objects when they are present, it is said: "having made them as if bound together by the three faculties.
This conventional expression, "seen by the eye," is well-known in the world—as in such phrases as "he pierces with a bow"—hence he says: "by way of the gross method alone."
11. "Without having reflected" means without having examined. "Without having considered" means without having determined. "Through dullness" means through ignorance.
"Having yoked the wooden cart and gone" intends to mean that he went after having yoked the wooden cart and sat upon it.
Because he spoke having made a definitive conclusion in that very manner, saying, "He will have gone," a false speech was committed. Some, however, [say] "in jest..."
As for the statement, "Because it is said 'one who acts thus,' one who speaks in this way incurs a wrong speech," that should not be accepted.
For it is stated that wrong speech occurs when one speaks out of a desire for sport using only the ten bases of abuse, such as birth and so forth. Indeed, this has been said:
"Whether superior or inferior [is addressed] by means of birth and so forth, whether the superior or the inferior..."
“Speak straightly, even under the pretext of a request; do not speak ill-spoken words out of negligence.
Because it was spoken by grasping at a greater quantity rather than a smaller one with the mind, false speech (*musāvāda*) arose even in such cases as “the village has one oil-lamp.
“They circulated” means they brought forward. [This refers to] the state of having deception as one’s primary aim, and whatever object [is targeted] with a deceptive mind...
The desire to speak and the effort to inform that person—these are the two factors here.

For one who speaks falsely for the purpose of proclaiming a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), it is a *pārājika* offense; for the purpose of slandering with a groundless *pārājika*, it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
for the purpose of slandering with a *saṅghādisesa*, it is a *pācittiya*; for a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), it is a *dukkaṭa*. "He who, in your monastery..."
When one speaks falsely with the intent of proclaiming superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) by means of such expressions as “I dwell [in this state],” etc.,

there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) for one who understands [the meaning], a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does not understand, and here, for one who merely speaks falsely [without such intent], a confession-offense (pācittiya) is stated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning false speech is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Backbiting (Omasavāda-sikkhāpada) 12.

Regarding the second [rule]: because they speak unpleasantly with harshness toward the ears, it is as if they were piercing the ears; thus it is said, "They backbite (*omasanti*) means they pierce (*ovijjhanti*).
They "overpower" (*padhaṃsenti*) means they overcome. 13. "At that time there was a Bodhisatta": at that time, the Bodhisatta was named Nandivisāla.

Meaning: The present tense is used in the sense of the past; or, while there is an application of the present tense due to a desire to express the time of an action, the understanding of its pastness may arise through the proximity of other words.
*Paccesi* means "he understood," [thinking] "this is unpleasant. *Heṭṭhārukkhe datvā* means "having provided supports.

*Pubbe patiṭṭhitārappadesaṃ puna are patteti* means: having again reached the place where the axle was previously established—[referring to] the axle which was previously established straight and facing downwards.
Having again rotated that very portion of the ground on that same spoke so as to reach the downward-facing position,
it is meant that after having been rotated while the portion of the rim was first established on the ground, it is once more established on the ground.
"Making loose" means the act of loosening.

15. "In the past" refers to the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*). "Carpentry work" (*tacchakakamma*) means the work of a builder (*vaḍḍhakī*). "Stone-cutting work" (*koṭṭakakamma*) means the work of cutting stone.

"Counting by hand-signs" (*hatthamuddāgaṇanā*) is counting by the mere contraction of the fingers. "Counting by means of objects" (*navantavasena gaṇanā*), such as with pebbles, seeds, or beans, is "counting without gaps" (*acchiddakagaṇanā*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes] counting by summation, multiplication, subtraction, division, and so on.
The counting of the leaves was undertaken while they were still growing. One who has mastered that [counting] knows, even upon seeing a tree, "there are this many leaves here.
Regarding the phrase *yabha methuna*: when the syllables *ya* and *bha* are joined together, it becomes a term for unwholesome conduct (*asaddhamma*). 16–26.

"He should be dealt with according to the offense" means he should be dealt with according to the *pācittiya* [offense], in the case of words such as *aticāṇḍāla*, which are distinguished merely by prefixes and the like.

Because they are included among those very [offenses] mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*). However, since phrases such as "you are a thief" are not found in the Canon by any means, a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated [for them]. "With the intention of joking" is an explanation of the meaning of the preceding phrase.

Even though it is not stated in the Canon, just as there is a *dukkaṭa* for one who reviles another in their absence using grounds for abuse such as birth and so forth—because those grounds are not different from [the actual offenses]—so too [is there a *dukkaṭa* here].
"Likewise, even for one who speaks in the absence [of the listener] out of a desire for sport, it is indeed a bad utterance (*dubbhāsita*)," so say the teachers.
Regarding the term "all beings" (*sabbasatta*), here even animals whose nature is to understand the meaning of words must be included. 35.
For one who speaks while standing with the intention of providing instruction, because of the mind’s state of rapid transformation (*lahuparivatti*), in the interval—
There is no offense even when anger has arisen. The four factors here are: the fact that the one being reviled is fully ordained;
the reviling by means of birth and so forth, without using another pretext; the awareness, "He is reviling me"; and the absence of having a purpose in view, and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Slanderous Speech (Pesuññasikkhāpada) 36.
Regarding the third [rule]: "Those among whom a quarrel has arisen" (*bhaṇḍanajātā*) means those for whom a dispute has occurred. "Secret consultation" (*sammantana*) means a private meeting.
"Those among whom a strife has arisen" (*kalahajātā*) means those for whom a conflict has reached its peak through such means as the laying on of hands. This leads to non-offensiveness (*anāpatti*).
One who has fallen into a dispute consisting of contradictory speech is "one who has fallen into dispute" (*vivādāpannā*).

Speech that leads to contention is "contentious speech" (*viggāhikakathā*). It "grinds down" (*pisatīti*), thus it is "malicious" (*pisuṇā*); the meaning is that it causes beings who are in harmony to be split into separate factions.

That which is malicious itself is "slander" (*pesuññaṃ*). One who possesses such speech is "malicious" (*pisuṇo*), and his action is "slander" (*pesuññaṃ*). [It is an obstacle] to the state of being dear...

By the phrase "the speech that makes empty," he explains the meaning according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) as: "it is malicious speech (*pisuṇā*) because it makes [relationships] empty of what is dear.

Here too, because of the statement, "One instigates malicious speech in ten ways," an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) applies to one who instigates malicious speech by means of the very ten bases of abuse.
However, regarding those not found in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), such as "thief" and so forth, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

It should be understood as follows: "However, for one who, out of a desire to be liked, utters speech that constitutes slander—speech which serves as a basis for abuse—even though no offense is seen under this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), they say that there must nevertheless be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) here.
Having heard [this] from a monk who was abusing [another] by means of birth and so forth, without using a pretext...
The three factors here are: the act of instigating, the intention to cause division through a desire for affection, and the other person's understanding of it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning malicious talebearing is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reciting Words Together.
45. In the fourth [case], "with one" means with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

"The latter expression is similar to the former expression" means that the word *anicca* in the phrase "feeling is impermanent" (*vedanā aniccā*) is similar to the word *anicca* in the phrase "form is impermanent" (*rūpaṃ aniccan*).
A "group of syllables" (*akkharasamūha*) is a group of syllables without case endings. A "phrase" (*pada*) is a group of syllables and consonants.

It states that a word (*pada*) ends in a case-suffix (*vibhatti*). Having taken only that which ends in a case-suffix as a word, it is said: "The first word is indeed a word; the second is a 'following-word' (*anupada*).
He speaks with reference to a verse-line (*gāthāpada*), meaning "one word. "By the counting of words" means by the counting of verse-lines. "Without reaching" means without having spoken together.

In the phrase "he stops (*runti*)" or "he causes to fall (*opātetī*)," the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) is stated by way of an augment (*āgama*), [as is the case] for what precedes a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).
It should be understood that [the vowel] has been shortened. Therefore he said, "only the letter *rū*.

And here, when being told, "Recite, 'form is impermanent,' novice," if one does not say *rū*, but instead says *ru*—making it short—that is called "reciting something else," and therefore there is no offense.
And having done so, even in the case of "feeling is impermanent," by means of the word "impermanent" alone...
It should be understood that an offense occurs. "This is the method" means that one stops after uttering only a single syllable.
For instance, when the verse "Mind precedes all phenomena" (*manopubbaṅgamā dhammā*) is being recited, one stops after uttering only the letter *ma*.

If, while reciting a sutta such as "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*), one stops after uttering the letter *e*, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for each syllable, provided the phrase remains incomplete.

When [the monk] has stood after speaking [thus], it is [an offense] by the secondary characteristic (*anubyañjana*). Regarding the sections: if one omits the first phrase, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the second phrase.
The *Anaṅgaṇa-sutta*, the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta*, and the *Mahāvedalla-sutta* were spoken by the General of the Dhamma;
the *Anumāna-sutta* was spoken by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna; the *Cūḷavedalla-sutta* was spoken by the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā. There are also those spoken by Paccekabuddhas.
Only that which was spoken by the Buddha is included [in the Canon].
By "based on the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathānissita*), he refers to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) recorded in the Māgadhī language during the previous compilation (*saṅgaha*).
Even now, they say that such commentary statements as "Just as the leopard, having hidden itself, seizes the deer," which were included in the compilation, should be accepted.

“Dependent on the Pāḷi” means it appears in the Pāḷi itself in such passages as, “The female monkey and the son of the Vajjis,” and so forth. “Dependent on turning away” (vivaṭṭūpanissita) means dependent on Nibbāna.
However, since “dependent on turning away” (vivaṭṭanissita) should be understood in its general sense, he said, “Even though,” and so forth.
“Of the Elder” refers to the Elder Nāgasena. The treatises include the *Maggakathā* and others. “He causes [the student] to recite by syllable; syllable by syllable...”

"An offense entailing expiation (pācittiya)" is what should be said; however, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "If he causes [the pupil] to recite by syllable, for each syllable there is an offense entailing expiation.

48. Regarding "there is no offense for one who takes up the recitation together with one who is not fully ordained": this states that there is no offense for one who sits together with one who is not fully ordained and takes up the recitation. "There is no offense for a young bhikkhu sitting... [etc. ...while speaking."
In this case, whether both [the teacher and the pupil] are standing or sitting, there is no offense for one who says, "I am speaking to one who is fully ordained.

"Having left the vicinity" means having left the twelve-cubit perimeter from the edge of the assembly. Even for one who says, "I am reciting to one who is sitting," there is no offense because he is sitting after having left the vicinity.
However, if he thinks, "I am reciting to one who is sitting at a distance," [there is an offense].
If one speaks after having observed [the other] individually, it is indeed an offense. Regarding "one foot does not come":
if it was previously mastered but later does not come because of failing to remember, there is no offense for one who speaks together [with the other], saying, "Speak thus.
"Opāpeti" means to converse with. The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are: the state of not being fully ordained, and the dharma possessing the stated characteristics.
Reciting word by word and reciting together—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the memorization of words is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning sharing a sleeping place.
49–50. "Groaning" (pañcame vikūjamānā) means sighing. "Choking" (kākacchamānā) means weeping.
Alternatively, this may be shown as an illustration of the case (*vatthu*). Since it was spoken by way of a question—“Was it indeed felled by him?”—there is no falsehood.
However, some say: “A statement made out of doubt is not called a lie; therefore, it was spoken thus. “Without going into his presence” means: “That which...”
Not having gone [to them] with the intention: "What is not allowable for these is not allowable for those either," [the text says]:

51. Regarding the phrase *dirattatirattaṃ* (two nights and three nights), it should be understood that the inclusion of the term *dirattaṃ* (two nights) is made merely for the sake of euphony in the expression.

For when a stay of three nights (*tirattaṃ*) is possible during a communal residence, there would be no need at all to mention two nights; thus, the mention of *dirattaṃ* is separate [from the three-night period].
He does not join [the two]. For this very reason, it was said: "The Blessed One granted the exemption of three nights for the sake of supporting the novices.
Alternatively, the mention of "two nights" was made in order to show that the three nights are continuous;
for if only "three nights" were stated, one might include a three-night period that is interrupted by staying elsewhere—[therefore it is specified as] distinguished by the two nights.
However, when "three nights" (*tiratta*) is mentioned, it indicates three nights immediately following that [period]. "Reclining" (*seyyā*) means a bed;

it is called "reclining" because one reclines upon it. Thus he said, "consisting of the stretching out of the body," and so forth. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because both [conditions] have been delimited.
"By five types of roofing" means by five types of roofing consisting of bricks, stone, plaster, grass, and leaves.
"By way of what has come to the tongue" means by way of being well-mastered. "One and a half cubits high" refers to the measurement taken by the carpenter’s hand-cubit.
"A single access" is said with reference to the unity of the entrance for use. The connection is: "Whether it be a hundred-roomed [building] or a four-sided hall, it constitutes a single access."
Regarding the phrase "of a dwelling whose walls are not connected with the upper floor": although it is stated that there is no offense when the walls are not connected with the upper floor—
even if one could lie within the beam, exit again through that same opening, and enter the lower floor through the space between the walls—
it is [here] specified that there is no offense even in the case of a dwelling where the walls are connected, provided it is impossible to enter in such a manner.

This was stated for the purpose of showing that there is simply nothing to be said [in this case], but it was not stated for the purpose of showing that there is no offense in the case of a wall with interconnecting partitions.

Furthermore, the statement "there is no offense for a bhikkhu lying in the lower story of a palace" was made to prevent the suspicion that an offense might arise for one lying on the lower floor in such a dwelling; it was not, however, intended for one lying on the upper floor.
The term "offense" is used for the purpose of showing [the scope]. Regarding "not within the vicinity":

this is said with reference to such places where people ascend to the upper floor by means of a ladder placed outside. Since there is no offense for one who lies down on the upper floor in an open courtyard, it is specified as "within the roof-covering."
“By way of a hall” means by way of the form of a hall. Regarding the phrase “in a half-walled dwelling”:
here, a “half-walled dwelling” is one where, having left one side open, walls are built on three sides;
or, where having erected a wall on one side, they erect walls on both sides only halfway.
“Such a lodging” is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. However, in the *gaṇṭhipada*, it is said:
“In ‘with half-walls’ means with walls that have not been completed by half”; this too is not incorrect. They say:
“A ‘tiger-roof’ (*vāḷasaṅghāṭa*) is called a roof constructed over pillars with tiger-figures. [The phrase] “outside the enclosure” refers to being beyond the boundary.
In this context, it should be understood that even in a place where there is no enclosure, there is no offense if one has gone beyond the area that would require such an enclosure.

Regarding the phrase "in an unenclosed inner courtyard": here, in cases such as a main hall or a large four-sided hall that has an open space in its center, it is impossible to enter all the inner rooms without descending into the open courtyard and passing through the main entrance.
Thus, when a wall is constructed by being drawn out on both sides of each individual room, it is called a "delimited precinct of a room" (*paricchinnagabbhūpacāra*);
however, since this [case] is not like that, it is said to be "in an undelimited precinct of a room" (*aparicchinnagabbhūpacāre*).
"They enter all the rooms" means that because the precinct of the rooms is undelimited, they do not descend into the courtyard but proceed directly through the entrance.
They enter various cells. Now, as for the statement that its enclosure alone constitutes the total enclosure because it is completely covered, he says:
"For its enclosure is indeed the enclosure of the cell. And this was said with reference to the walls surrounding the cell.
Even in a dwelling arranged according to the four-hall system, the front of the cell may be separate and not enclosed.
It is called "enclosed" by virtue of the walls of the surrounding chambers. [Objection:
But has it not been stated without qualification in the Andhaka-ṭīkā that "there is no offense when the entrance is unenclosed"?
Therefore, even in a dwelling situated as a four-hall complex, there would likewise be no offense when the entrance itself is individually unenclosed.
In order to release him from such an objection, this was said: "But as for what was stated... [etc.
...this was said with reference to rows of cells that are separate dwellings but have a single roof.
This is what is meant: "Regarding the statement 'there is no offense if the front is unenclosed,' that was not said with reference to rows of cells arranged in the manner of a four-hall structure."
"Furthermore, it is established separately with reference to a single enclosure wall (*gabbhapāḷi*).
For there is no offense when the entrance of such an enclosure wall is not enclosed, but this does not apply to that which is established by way of four walls (*catussāla*).
And having defined the precinct (*upacāra*) of each respective room by means of a single enclosure wall, even including small walls on both sides...
Even by the mere act of erecting [a wall], the front porch is said to be enclosed;
furthermore, when the chamber-walls are situated according to the four sides of a hall, the front porch is also said to be enclosed by means of those chamber-walls on both sides.
Therefore, there is an offense regarding that front porch which is enclosed by this characteristic, but not in other cases.
"There is no offense" is the definitive conclusion here.
Now, having stated, "There is no offense when it is in front of an unenclosed [space]," in order to clarify the intended meaning of that very statement, he said:
"This was spoken with reference to the space in front of the ground, excluding the railing. To demonstrate the inappropriateness of that [interpretation]:

The passage beginning with “yañca tattha” has been commenced. Regarding the statement, “It was said with reference to the front of a house on the ground without a foundation,” this is its intended meaning:

that which was stated as “there is no offense in an unenclosed area in front [of a house],” was said with reference to the front of a house built on the ground without a structural base. However, if it has a high foundation...
It is "prominent" (pamukha) because it does not count as an enclosure. For this very reason, he said:
"For even ten cubits in height, the earth does not count as an enclosure. It was also stated below, keeping this very point in mind:
"Even if it has a high base, one lying in front of it does not incur an offense for those lying inside the womb [of the enclosure]. Therein...
In the *Andhakavagga-aṭṭhakathā*. "Having stated the measurement of the terrace" means:
having stated the measurement by way of the height of the terrace, as in, "If one has descended from the terrace and is lying on the ground, one does not see what is lying above the terrace.

A palace constructed by being laid out straight and long in a single hall, etc., is called a "single-hall construction" (*ekasāla-sannivesa*). There are also those with "double-hall constructions" (*dvisāla-sannivesa*), and so forth.
It should be understood according to what has been stated. Furthermore, the distinction here from what was stated below lies solely in the illustration of the various types of *sāla* trees.

Regarding the phrase "building a wall in the middle," it should be understood that because the lower limit of the enclosure is one and a half cubits high, even if they build a wall in the middle to the height of one and a half cubits, it does not constitute a separate precinct (*anūpacāra*). Not...

Regarding the statement, "Indeed, if there is a hole, it is called 'having a single access' (*ekūpacāra*)," here, if there is a hole within one and a half cubits in height that is sufficient for people to pass through, that too is considered a door; thus, it has a single access.
When it is asked, "Is the enclosure excluded? he speaks with reference to the enclosure of the front porch (*pamukha*). In all cases, there are only five [factors].
Because it has come down in the tradition that there are five kinds of roofing, he says, "roofed with one of the five kinds of roofing.
By stating in the Pāḷi, "A bed (seyyā) is called one that is entirely roofed, entirely enclosed, mostly roofed,
or mostly enclosed," he indicates that a resting place (senāsana) which is mostly roofed and mostly enclosed is the limit for the offense of expiation (pācittiya).

By stating, "In a case where it is half-covered and half-enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," [the Blessed One] has shown that a lodging which is half-covered and half-enclosed constitutes the beginning of an offense of wrong-doing. Between these two cases, what must there be:
an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), or rather, an offense of wrong-doing? This applies to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning worldly transgressions (*lokavajja*) without exception.

Because it is established by way of making [the roof] manifest, and because this [category] is exempt from mere formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), a *pācittiya* offense is indeed unavoidable for one who has mostly covered and mostly enclosed, as well as for one who has half-covered and half-enclosed;
therefore, since one must stand firm in what is weighty within the Vinaya adjudication, even in the Aṭṭhakathā only a *pācittiya* is shown. Thus, "seven *pācittiyas*."
The offense of expiation (pācittiya) mentioned in the Pāḷi is stated by taking it as a single general category;

however, if they were taken separately, there would be eight offenses of expiation: "an offense of expiation for [a hut] entirely covered and entirely enclosed, and an offense of expiation for one mostly covered and mostly enclosed."

"It has the appearance of the Senambamaṇḍapa" means that, it is said, there is a gathering-hall (sannipātamaṇḍapa) of such a name on the island of Sīhaḷa which has high foundations and is entirely covered but not enclosed;

this was said with reference to that. If it were counted as being within the enclosure of the earth, then because of the hall's high foundations, its state of being "not enclosed" would be inconsistent; thus he said: "By this also..."
"It should be understood," and so forth. Furthermore, the "partially covered" (*cūḷakacchanna*) and other types should be understood in this way:
that which has one of its four parts covered and the remaining parts uncovered is "partially covered.
That which has two of its three parts covered and one part uncovered is "mostly covered. That which has one of its two parts covered and one part uncovered—
This is what is called a "half-covered" lodging. The "small-canopy-covered" and other such types should also be understood by this same method.

The rest is self-evident. The three factors here are: a lodging that constitutes the basis for an offense of expiation (pācittiya), lying down together with one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) in various places, and the setting of the sun on the fourth day.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sleeping together is finished.
6. Commentary on the second training rule regarding sleeping together: 55.
Regarding the sixth [rule], since it was stated in the first training rule that "with the exception of a bhikkhu, the rest is called 'one who is not fully ordained,'" [the meaning is as follows].

They say: "Since a woman is already included by the inclusion of 'one who is not fully ordained,' for one who lies down with a woman on the fourth day, there are two *pācittiya* offenses according to two training rules. However, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated:
"Because the woman is mentioned separately in this training rule, [the offense] in the first training rule [is for lying down with] a bhikkhu..."
It is said that "excluding [the ordained], the remainder is called 'unordained'";
thus, the inclusion of only the male is appropriate, and that alone is more logical.
Furthermore, regarding the reason given here—"on the first day as well"—by means of the word "also" (pi), it is implied "on the fourth day as well."

They say that even this is not a reason, because the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*) alone; for there is no fixed rule [that it must always mean "even"], and its sense as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is also possible.

Alternatively, the particle *pi* should be understood in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*). By this, it illuminates the following meaning: "If there is an offense even on the first day, what need is there to mention the second day and so forth?
Even when the particle *pi* is taken in the sense of inclusion, [the same applies].
By this very training rule, it is indicated that one may incur an offense on another day for an offense that was incurred [on the previous day];
however, it should be understood that there is no reason to think this applies to an offense incurred under the first training rule.

They say: "A dead woman, even though she is a basis for a *pārājika* offense, does not generate an offense for sleeping together because she stands on the side of what is not clung-to (*anupādinnapakkha*). "When the sun has set..."
Based on the statement, "When a woman is lying down, a bhikkhu lies down," it should be understood that for one who sleeps during the day, there is no offense of *sahaseyyā* (sharing a bed).
In this case, there are three factors: a lodging that constitutes the basis for a *pācittiya* offense, lying down there together with a woman, and the setting of the sun.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning sleeping in the same bed is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning teaching the Dhamma (60–64):
Regarding the seventh [rule], she who leads one to the house is a *gharaṇī*, that is, the mistress of the house. Therefore, he says “the lady of the house. She is a daughter-in-law (*suṇhā*).
“Daughter-in-law. In the phrases beginning with “not by a *yakkha*,” there is a connection with the word “except” (*aññatra*).
Even if she stands together with a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or an animal that has assumed a human form, it is not permitted for her to teach [the Dhamma].
Regarding the phrase “she teaches by means of syllables”: here, even if she intends, “I shall speak this word,” to go beyond five or six words, [it constitutes an offense] for even a single syllable.
They say: "If one remains after having spoken [it], it is indeed an offense.

66. Regarding the phrase "a single verse-line," they say this was stated specifically with reference to the composition of verses; however, in other instances, only a word ending in a case-suffix should be understood.
By the phrase "the Aṭṭhakathā, the Dhammapada, or the narrative material of the Jātaka and so forth," the ancient...

They say that the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other such works are indeed included in the *Saṅgīti*. Apart from the reading of the *Aṭṭhakathā* and so forth, it is permissible to speak according to one’s preference in other languages, such as Tamil.
By the phrase "the aforementioned classification regarding the recitation of words," he indicates that there is no offense in other instances.
"Having stood up and sat down again" refers to various postures by way of changing one's physical posture (*iriyāpatha*).
He explains that there is no offense. "Even if he recites the entire Dīghanikāya" means that he continues to recite it on the following day as well until it is finished.

The non-inclusion of a second wise man constitutes non-performance. The proximity of a woman and a wise man standing together should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on indeterminate offenses (*aniyata*).
The rest is self-evident. Regarding the characteristics already mentioned...
The teaching is above the six levels of speech; the female sex possesses the characteristics already stated; there is no turning back from the postures;
there is no presence of a wise man; and there is no answering of questions—these are the five factors herein.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the teaching of the Dhamma is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Misrepresentation of Spiritual Attainments (Bhūtārocanasikkhāpada) 77.
In the eighth [training rule], "at another time" means at a time other than the moment of final Nibbāna.
"Being pressed" means being importuned with the words, "Venerable sir, tell us, what have you attained? Even when not being pressed, if one is asked...
Or, even if not asked, it is indeed permissible to report [the matter] when such a reason exists. For this very reason, a certain elder, having been reproached by another young bhikkhu, said:
"Friend, do not exert yourself for the sake of the higher paths; you have been reproaching one who is an arahant.
And when the elder said to that young bhikkhu, "Friend, do you have a firm footing in this Dispensation? the young bhikkhu...

“Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer,” he said. Even though they know, “This one is a doer [of the practice],” the Noble Ones nevertheless reveal themselves for the purpose of inspiring and gladdening others by showing that the practice is not in vain.

“The qualities of learning, mastery, and virtue” refers to the quality of learning (*suta-guṇa*), the quality of mastery (*pariyatti-guṇa*), and the quality of virtue (*sīla-guṇa*). When stating the reason why a madman is not mentioned here...
It should be understood that the reason for not mentioning even the state of distracted consciousness (*khittacitta*) has already been stated.
Alternatively, by the word *iti* in the sense of "beginning with," it includes the state of distracted consciousness. For this very reason, he says:

"or because of the absence of mental distraction. "Of those endowed with right view" means those possessed of the view of the path and its fruit. For it is only among the noble ones (*ariya*) that there can be such states as insanity and so forth.
There is none. However, for one who has attained jhāna, if that [state] exists, they fall away from the jhānas;

therefore, for them, it should be said that there is no offense on account of announcing what is not true, but not on account of announcing what is true. For this very reason, he said: "It should not be said that there is no offense on account of announcing what is true.
"By those not previously stated" means by those not stated in the fourth pārājika. And this training rule is [given] by way of not knowing the formal promulgation (paṇṇatti).

It is an origination without consciousness. Furthermore, among these, noble ones (ariya) who understand the designation do not commit transgressions; however, worldlings (puthujjana), even though they know the designation, do commit transgressions.

It should be understood that because of the powerful unwholesome state of the volition to transgress the Teacher’s command, they fall away from jhāna—this being said with reference to the highest limit of noble persons.
It is with this intention that it was said: "With wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses, there are two types of consciousness.

However, for worldlings who have attained jhāna but do not understand the conventional designation (paññatti), it is not the case that they would not report [the attainment] even with an unwholesome consciousness due to greed regarding the object. Here, because of the absence of painful feeling, the term "two types of feeling" was used;
having made this appropriate, the phrase "two types of consciousness" was likewise stated. Or rather, it is in this way here:

The underlying intention must be understood. The rest is self-evident. Furthermore, the four factors here are: the actual occurrence of a superhuman state, the reporting to one who is not fully ordained, the understanding [of the report] at that very moment, and the location being other than the one [where the attainment occurred].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the reporting of what has actually occurred is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Proclaiming of What is Grave (Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada) 78. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of showing the meaning of the word *duṭṭhulla*":

this means for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the term *duṭṭhulla*. For when the meaning has been demonstrated, the word itself is also effectively demonstrated as being applicable to those meanings. "Whatever... [and so forth].
It is designated by the term "vulgar speech" (duṭṭhulla-sadda); the Pārājika rules were stated in order to demonstrate all of that—this is the intended meaning here.
Regarding this, "this investigation" (vicāraṇā) refers either to this investigation within the Canon (pāḷi) or to this investigation within the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) on the Canon.
"Therein it might occur" means that some person's doubt regarding that matter might be as follows. [Regarding] one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna)...
As in the case of reporting what is indecent, there must be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); thus he said, "one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Even one who reviles would incur an offense of wrong-doing; that is, one would incur an offense of wrong-doing through abusive speech.

To show that even by one who does not understand the underlying intention, one must abide by the words of the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā, it was stated: "The commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā alone are the authority here. Furthermore...
Establishing the words of the *aṭṭhakathā* as firm by means of logical reasoning, he said, "And by this also," and so forth.

(80) Because it was stated, "except by formal authorization of the Saṅgha (*bhikkhusammuti*)," it must be understood that such authorization exists; thus he said, "precisely because it is stated here," and so forth.

(82) "The first five training rules" refers to the five training rules beginning with the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*). "The remaining ones" refers to those beginning with eating at the improper time (*vikālabhojana*).
Some say, "Five," meaning that starting from the beginning there are five training rules, namely the emission of semen and so forth;
however, that should not be accepted. For only ten training rules, beginning with the destruction of life, have been prescribed for novices.
Indeed, this has been stated:
Then it occurred to the novices: "How many training rules do we have, and where must we train?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. "Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and novices must train in them:
abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given," and so forth.
An investigation into what constitutes a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*) and what does not should be conducted regarding those very training rules (*sikkhāpada*) that have been laid down for them;
it is not the case that seminal emission (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) and so forth were laid down separately for them. Then, [the author asks]:

"What indeed are seminal emission and so forth—reckoned as grave offenses for a monk—when it comes to one who is not fully ordained? To this he says: "Seminal emission... pe ...is called misconduct (*ajjhācāra*)," and so on.
By this also it is established that "for one who is not fully ordained, the emission of semen and so forth is not called *duṭṭhulla* (grave offense).

For by saying "it is called *ajjhācāra* (misconduct)," he indicates that for one who is not fully ordained, the emission of semen and so forth is merely *ajjhācāra*, but it is not *duṭṭhulla-ajjhācāra*.
And regarding the phrase "it is called *ajjhācāra*," in the *Aṭṭhakathā*...

Because it has been so stated and because they are of a nature not to be performed [by one who is fully ordained], matters such as the emission of semen by one who is not fully ordained fall on the side of disciplinary measures (*daṇḍakamma*);
and they say that a monk who reports these to another person who is not fully ordained out of a desire to disparage them incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, here, by the mention of "one who is not fully ordained," the male novices (*sāmaṇera*), female novices (*sāmaṇerī*), and trainees (*sikkhamānā*) are included.
The grasping [of the offense] is to be understood. The rest here is self-evident.

For a monk who has not committed the final offense, there are these three factors here: the offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa) together with its basis, the reporting to one who is not fully ordained, and the absence of authorization from the Saṅgha of monks.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the disclosure of a grave offense is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth (84–86).
Regarding the tenth [rule], "a single-facultied [being]": they say this thinking, "there is the body-faculty. "The measure of a fist" means...

It is the measure that can be grasped with a fist. Here, although the earth consisting mostly of sand and the earth consisting of little sand have been mentioned, the earth consisting of half-sand has not been stated;

nevertheless, since it is possible for there to be a rule with a remainder even among training rules concerning formal prescriptions (*paṇṇattivajja*), one should understand that there is indeed a *pācittiya* offense even for earth consisting of half-sand. Some, however, [hold that] regarding "all-covered" and so forth...
Some say: "Since it is stated that [the offense] for half [of the action] is a *dukkaṭa*, here too a *dukkaṭa* is appropriate.
That is not correct, because apart from the two kinds of earth—the basis for a *pācittiya* and the basis for no offense—there is no third kind of earth that has *dukkaṭa* as its basis.
For only two kinds of earth have been mentioned: "earth that is formed (*jātā*) and earth that is unformed (*ajātā*)."

Therefore, one of two things must be the case: either it is earth, or, since when a legal decision regarding the Vinaya has been reached one must stand by what is serious, it is impossible for there to be no offense here.
However, in the cases of "all-covered" and so forth, a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is appropriate, because in those instances such a basis for a *dukkaṭa* exists.
If one says, “Dig a pond,” it is permissible because it was spoken without specifying, “In this place.

Even when it is said, “Dig this creeper,” since the common expression is used with reference to digging the earth, there is an offense under this very training rule (sikkhāpada), not under the rule concerning the destruction of plant life (bhūtagāma-pātabyatā).
“With jars” means with pots. “Thin mud” means mud mixed with water.
And that is permissible because it follows the course of water. "Less than four months" (*omaka-cātumāsa*) means less than four months. "Covered by rain" (*ovaṭṭha*) means covered by the rain-god.
The phrase "in a place where no cliff has been made" is stated for the purpose of indicating a location that is not artificially leveled; for in such a place, there is the presence of an anthill.

"A mouse-dog" (*mūsika-ukkura*) is a mound of dust made outside by mice after they have dug. "In the same manner" means that only that which is less than four months and covered by rain is permissible. This is the meaning.
“Even for a single day it is not permitted”: even if the one-day limit has passed, it is not permitted to break [the boundary]. They say:

"Even if it is connected to the ground below, since it stands above having been cut from the earth at the base of the *gokaṇṭaka* (a type of grass), it is permitted to take it after cutting it off from its uppermost tip.
Even mud that has been trampled by feet and stirred up, having been moved from its original place, may be taken.
It is permissible to take it. "From there" means from that previous lodging.
"I am taking a brick," and so forth, was said with reference to a pure mind. "By water" means by water falling directly from the sky.
They say, "But if it has been moistened by water that fell after striking elsewhere, it is permissible. "Having lifted up" means having raised it.
"By that pretext" means by that excuse. 87–88.

"There is no offense because it is not within one's domain": here, even if it is possible to extinguish [the fire], because it was first given with a pure mind, there is no offense even if one remains after having observed, "Let it burn. "Covered and concealed" means first...

What was previously dug out is subsequently covered over. The rest is self-evident. "Earth that has been produced," "perceived as earth," and "either digging or causing to be dug"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the digging of earth is concluded.
The first chapter, on False Speech, is finished.
2. The Chapter on Living Plants.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Living Plants.
89. In the first [sutta] of the *Senāsanavagga*, "unable to restrain" means unable to hold back.
By this statement, it should be understood that the child’s having been brought there and his having been seen by him are already expressed.
Thus, when that bhikkhu began to cut down that tree, a certain young mother-devatā who had been reborn there—
Taking her son on her lap, she entreated him, saying, "My lord, do not cut down my tree; I shall not be able to wander about without a dwelling place, having to carry my little son.
He, thinking, "I will not find such a tree elsewhere," did not heed her words.
She thought, "Perhaps he will desist even after looking at this boy," and [placed] the son upon a branch of the tree.
He placed it [on the ground]. Unable to support the raised axe, that bhikkhu cut off the boy’s arm.
And because he was lying there, it is said, "as if lying in a celestial mansion atop a tree," considering that he was indeed lying in a celestial mansion atop a tree.
The phrase "in a celestial mansion atop a tree" refers specifically to a mansion situated on a branch. Above the tree...
For a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) that has arisen in connection with a tree is called a "tree-based mansion" (*rukkhaṭṭhaka-vimāna*).
A branch-based mansion (*sākhaṭṭhaka-vimāna*), however, remains supported by all the branches.
Among these, as long as a tree-based mansion remains even to the root of the tree, it does not perish; but a branch-based mansion [remains] upon the branches.
As those branches broke here and there, they broke off at their very roots; when all the branches were broken, everything was destroyed.
This celestial mansion (*vimāna*) was like a cluster of branches; therefore, when the tree was cut down, that mansion was utterly ruined.
Consequently, that deity dwelt in another mansion obtained from the Blessed One. He cut off the arm right at the base of the breast.

He cut off his arm together with the shoulder. By this it should be understood that while the limbs of tree-deities are subject to being severed, they are not indestructible like those of the Cātumahārājika devas and others.
"The nature of trees" (rukkhadhamma) means the natural state of a tree; the meaning is its inherent character.
For indeed, the "nature of trees" refers to their remaining unperturbed during cutting and other such treatments, just as is the case with actual trees.
"Arisen" means arisen. "Wandering" means running about. "Restrain" means one should subdue. This is what is meant:

just as a skilled charioteer restrains a chariot that is racing with excessive speed and directs it wherever he wishes, so too, the person who is able to restrain and subdue arisen anger—I call him a charioteer.
On the other hand, among kings, subordinate rulers, and others, there are those who are merely chariot-drivers and rein-holders, but they are not called supreme charioteers.

As for the meaning of the second verse: "He" (yo) refers to whoever has gone forth—whether from a kṣatriya family or from a brahmin family—and whether he is a novice, one of middle standing, or an elder. "Uppatitaṃ" means fallen upwards and upwards, having gone [to the heights].
The meaning is that they "proceed"; what is meant is that they have "arisen. Regarding "anger" (*kodha*):

there are eighteen bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), consisting of the nine stated in the Sutta according to the method beginning with, "Hostility arises [thinking], 'He acts for my harm,'" and another nine established as their opposites beginning with, "[Thinking], 'He does not act for my benefit.
Together with the nineteen bases such as stumps, thorns, and so forth, [there are twenty bases].
"Enmity arising from a particular ground for resentment. "Spreading" means expanded. "Snake venom" means the poison of a snake.
"Iva" is a word used as a simile; by eliding the letter *i*, it is simply stated as "iva. "With medicines" means with anti-poison drugs (*agada*). This is what is meant:
just as a physician who treats poison, having been bitten by a snake, [applies medicine] after the poison has pervaded his entire body.
Just as one might quickly neutralize the spread poison of a snake that has remained diffused throughout the root, trunk, bark, leaves, flowers, and so forth,
by employing various medicines or prepared elixirs, even so, one who— by means of the methods for subduing anger such as *tadaṅgavinaya* (subduing through its own factor)—
[removes] the anger that has arisen and pervaded the continuum of the mind due to the aforementioned grounds for resentment.
By some means he leads it away, does not tolerate it, abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end;

that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore. As that bhikkhu thus leads away anger—since anger is abandoned entirely by the third path—he leaves behind the five lower fetters known as "this shore" and "the far shore. For "the far shore" is used here without distinction.
It is called *tīra* (the shore); therefore, because they are both near and constitute the further shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra*, it is called "near-and-far-shore" (*orapāra*).

Alternatively, just as one might dispel spreading snake venom with medicines, he who dispels arisen anger—having completely dispelled anger through the third path and established himself in the fruit of non-returning—that bhikkhu abandons the "near-and-far-shore. In that context, "near" (*ora*)...

"This shore" is one's own individual existence (*sakattabhāva*); "the further shore" is another's individual existence (*parattabhāva*). Alternatively, "this shore" refers to the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatanāni*), and "the further shore" to the six external sense bases (*bāhirāyatanāni*).

Likewise, "this shore" is the human world, and "the further shore" is the divine world. "This shore" is the realm of sensual desire (*kāmadhātu*), and "the further shore" is the realm of form and the formless realm (*rūpārūpadhātu*).

"This shore" is existence in the realms of sensual desire and form (*kāmarūpabhava*), and "the further shore" is existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*). "This shore" is the self-body (*attabhāva*), and "the further shore" is the requisites for the happiness of that self-body.
Thus, by abandoning desire and lust for both this shore and the far shore through the fourth path, one is said to "leave behind both this shore and the far shore. And here,
although there is no desire or lust at all regarding this present existence and so forth because the non-returner has abandoned sensual lust,
nevertheless, for the purpose of illustrating his excellence, all these divisions of "this shore" and "the far shore" are included together.
In that context, it is said: "By abandoning desire and lust, he leaves behind both this shore and the far shore.
Now, to clarify the meaning of this, he provides a simile: "As a snake sheds its old and worn-out skin.

Therein, it is called a *uraga* because it moves by means of its belly (*ura*); this is a designation for a serpent. It is of two kinds: those capable of changing form at will (*kāmarūpī*) and those incapable of changing form at will (*akāmarūpī*).
Furthermore, the one capable of assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpī*) is twofold: water-born and land-born.

The water-born obtains the power to assume any form only in the water, not on land—as was the case with the Naga King Saṅkhapāla in the *Saṅkhapāla Jātaka*. The land-born [obtains it] only on land, not in the water.
He abandons the skin that has become worn out through decrepitude and ancient through the passage of long time; he abandons it in four ways.
"Standing in his own kind, loathing it, he relies on his strength. "Own kind" (*sajāti*) means being of the same species, namely the long-lived state of a serpent.

For snakes do not transcend their own kind in five instances: at birth, at death, when shedding their slough while asleep, when engaging in sexual intercourse with their own kind, and when casting off their old skin. Therefore, when they cast off the skin, at that time—
One abandons [the body] while remaining in its own kind. Even while remaining in its own kind, one abandons it with loathing.
"With loathing" means that when one is released from half the area and remains unreleased in the other half, hanging there, then one abandons it with dread;
thus, even while loathing it, one relies on a space between pillars, or a space between roots, or a space between rocks.
He abandons. Even when abandoning by relying [on something], he generates strength, exerts effort, and with vigor, having made his tail crooked and looking back, he abandons by spreading his hood.
Having abandoned in this way, he departs wherever he wishes.
In the very same way, this bhikkhu, desiring to abandon both this shore and the far shore, abandons them in four ways while remaining within his own class, feeling revulsion.
"Relying on one's own strength": by "own birth" (*sajāti*) is meant the virtue (*sīla*) of a bhikkhu, because of the statement, "born of noble birth.
For this very reason it was said: "A wise man, established in virtue...
Thus, standing firm in this own birth, the bhikkhu [overcomes] that suffering—which produces distress here and there—divided into his own personal existence and so forth, like a worn-out, old hide.
Disgusted by the perception of danger, and relying on spiritual friends, he generates strength characterized by supreme right effort; then,
according to the method stated as "purifying the mind from obstructive states while walking and sitting during the day," having divided the night and day into six parts,
striving and exerting himself, he [unfolds] the crooked tail like a snake, [namely] the cross-legged posture.
Hissing like a snake that has coiled itself up, he too exerts himself with unremitting energy; like a snake that has raised its hood, he too generates the expansion of knowledge;
and like a snake that sheds its skin, he too abandons this shore and the further shore.
Having abandoned them, like a snake that has cast off its skin, he departs wherever he wishes; he too, having laid down the burden, departs toward the realm of Nibbāna without residue.
90. By the word *bhavanti* (“they become”), he indicates young shrubs that have developed roots and are growing after attaining a state of greenness.
By the word *ahuvunti*, however, he indicates large trees, shrubs, and so forth, which have grown and remain established.
The explanation of *bhavanti* is “they are born and they grow,” while the explanation of *ahuvunti* is “they are born and they have grown. *Rāsī* means “heaps.”

A collection of eight pure phenomena (*suddhaṭṭhakadhammasamūho*). Regarding the phrase "of the elements" (*bhūtānaṃ*): it refers to those eight phenomena that have received such a conventional designation (*samaññā*).

Even when one says "a village of elements," since a composite whole cannot exist apart from its constituent parts, it is precisely those grasses, trees, creepers, and so forth, which possess the designation "elements," that are understood.
Having taken root in the earth and attained the state of greenery, trees, shrubs, and the like are protected by deities.
Therefore, they also say it is "a village of beings" because it is a dwelling place for beings. Regarding the phrase "of trees, etc.," by the word "etc.
(ādi), medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and so forth are to be understood.
But are not trees and the like not living beings because they lack consciousness? And their lack of consciousness is evident from the absence of movement even when they are cut.

It should be understood [that they are not living beings] because they grow from seeds, because they belong to a different species, and because they are not included within the four modes of birth (*yoni*).

Furthermore, since growth is found even in coral, stones, and salt, these are not grounds for their status as living beings. Their "perception of objects" is a mere mental construct, like the sleep of *ciñcā* trees and the like;
likewise with their "longings" (*dohala*) and so forth. In that regard, why is there an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for cutting or damaging a "grove of beings" (*bhūtagāma*)?
Why is it so stated? Because it is befitting for a recluse and because it protects the beings dwelling therein. For this very reason, he said:
"For people, O foolish men, perceive a living being in a tree," and so forth.
Regarding the phrases "growing from the root" and so on, the meaning is as will be stated by me later in the *Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā*.
Because it has been so stated, he said: “Even though this is so... they do not correspond. He said “vijātāni” because the word *vijāta* here is explained by eliding the syllable *vi*.
And since the word *vijāta*—as in expressions such as “a woman who has given birth” (*vijātā itthī*)—is a term for having brought forth, he said “pasūtāni.
Furthermore, what is meant here by “bringing forth” (*pasūti*) is the production of leaves and roots; thus he said “nibbattapaṇṇamūlāni.”
By this, he illustrates the following: "Seeds whose leaves and roots have already grown are indeed reckoned as 'living things' (bhūtagāma);
and while the term *bījajāta* primarily refers to those seeds, it is used by way of conventional metaphor (*ruḷhī*) for trees and the like as well.
However, in the previous interpretation of the meaning, the status of being a "living thing" was stated to apply only to the trees, creepers, and so forth that have arisen from seeds.
"Showing them" means showing those seeds. Regarding "root-seed" (*mūlabīja*) and so forth: a root that is itself the seed is a "root-seed.
The same principle applies to the others as well. "Node-seed" (*phaḷubīja*) is a joint-seed (*pabbabīja*).

The word "seed" (*bīja*) is conventionally used for a hard fruit capable of germinating because, when combined with other conditions, it serves as the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit. This is established through the accomplishment of that purpose.
Since [the term] occurs in some instances even for roots and so forth, it is stated as "seed-seed" (*bījabīja*)— distinguishing it by means of a single word "seed"—
in order to exclude it from being taken as a root and so on, just as in the cases of "matter-matter" (*rūparūpa*) and "suffering-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
This demonstrates that by the metaphorical designation of the effect (*kāriya-upacāra*), the cause is indicated by means of what has arisen from the seed.

92. Regarding the phrase "perceiving seed in what is seed," he says "In this regard, just as... and so forth, showing that here the effect is expressed by way of a metaphorical designation for the cause.
"Having released from the vegetable growth" means having freed it from the vegetable growth; the sense is "having separated it.
He speaks thus with reference to the meaning already stated: "those seeds which are called 'vegetable growth'"; therein, "whatever is seed... [and so on].
That seed from which leaves and roots have already emerged. "In that seed" means in that seed known as a *bhūtagāma*.

And here, it should be understood that the word "seed" (*bīja*) applies to trees and so forth by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), just as the term "born of seed" (*bījaja*) does. "According to the literal expression" (*yathāruta*) means according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
"At any place whatsoever" means at the base, the tip, or the middle.

"It is not permissible to intentionally uproot it" means that even if one emerges from the water while knowing it is clinging to the body, it is permissible because there is no intention (*saññā*) such as, "I shall pull this out.
"Torn away" means uprooted. "They fall under the category of seed-life" (*bījagāma*) because they have been liberated from the category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*).
It has been stated. By the mention of "endless" (*anantaka*), the mustard-seed-sized speck is included; for that is the name of that species of moss.
Because its roots and leaves are incomplete, it is called "an incomplete community of beings" (*asampunnabhūtagāma*).

Regarding the phrase "having the community of beings as its root": here, "root" means cause; thus, that which has the community of beings as its root or cause is "rooted in the community of beings" (*bhūtagāmamūla*). Alternatively, the "root" or cause of the community of beings is "the root of the community of beings" (*bhūtagāmamūla*).
For what is called a "seed-group" arises from a "being-group" (bhūtagāma) and is the cause for a being-group;

however, this [the mind] is not like that, which is why it is said, "because its root is a non-being-group. Because it exists therein [in the seed-group], it is said, "it is included within the seed-group.
And this [explanation] is stated because the meaning first mentioned in the phrase "because its root is a non-being-group" is applicable here.
For although the stump of a palmyra or coconut tree and the like is not the cause of a "community of beings" (bhūtagāma) because it does not grow further upward,

nevertheless, because it has arisen from leaves, roots, or seeds that have been produced and are reckoned as a community of beings, it is said to be "produced from a community of beings" and is thus included within the category of the "seed-planting" (bījagāma).
Having said, “When the sprout is green,” he explains that very point by saying, “when it has arisen with the color of a blue leaf”;
the meaning is that it has arisen with a color similar to the color of a blue leaf. Alternatively, the reading “nīlavaṇṇe jāte” (when it has arisen as blue-colored) should be accepted.

He says this referring specifically to the coconut tree, [implying] that it is included within the category of rootless living beings. “The moss on the outside of water-jars and so forth, in the water...”
They say that because it lacks a fixed nature and because it conforms to the category of seeds, it is a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even a *kaṇṇaka* mushroom is indeed not subject to the formal rule; even one that is blue in color is likewise not subject to it. *Seleyyaka* is a certain fragrant species produced from stone.
Because it is stated, "one violates the bark of a tree," any mushroom growing on a tree may be taken from the top without violating the tree's bark.
They say, "It is permissible to take it after cutting [the branch]. Regarding the phrase "it remains having detached from the tree," they say here:
"Even if it remains clinging slightly to the tree, provided that when being taken from the tree it does not damage the bark, it is permissible.
Regarding the phrase "it is not permissible from a fresh (wet) tree," here too, without damaging the tree's bark—
It should be understood that it is permissible to take [the water] after cutting it off from the top. "By means of hand-fidgeting" means by the lack of restraint of the hands;
it is said to mean by the restlessness of the hands. "Water should not be set aside" is said with reference to what has been set aside for one's own sake.
However, in the case of what has been set aside solely for the sake of one who is not fully ordained, if one later receives it from him...

"There is no such thing as 'it must not be stored. Some say that because it is stated, 'of those trees whose branches grow,' there is no need for the formal ritual of making things allowable (*kappiyakaraṇa*) in the case of those whose branches do not grow.
(93) "By the five monastic conventions" means by the five modes of expression used by monks. For even though seeds [are rendered allowable] merely by being touched by fire...
Merely scratching with fingernails and the like does not constitute the state of being non-growing;
nevertheless, because it is permitted when done in such a manner, the conventional designations "fire-purified" and so forth arose for ascetics. Therefore, the intended meaning is:
"I allow you to enjoy the fruit by means of those conventional designations used for ascetics. Thus, even seeds produced from seedless [plants] are allowable for ascetics.

Because they possess the state of being designated and proclaimed, they have come to be reckoned by the designation "ascetic. Alternatively, because the five things beginning with "won by fire" (aggiparijita) are indeed allowable, the intended meaning here should be understood as:
"I permit the enjoyment of the fruit [of the forest] for these five reasons known as the 'allowable things of an ascetic' (samaṇakappiya).
Regarding the terms "won by fire" (aggiparijita) and so forth, there is also the reading "accumulated" (paricita).

They recite [the following]: "Seedless" means young mango fruit and so forth. "Extracted seed" refers to mangoes, jackfruits, and the like—those seeds which, having been extracted and separated, can be consumed.

Since it is stated that "it must be made allowable (*kappiya*) before it may be done," this refers specifically to the manner in which the one who makes it allowable must act; therefore, it is permissible for a monk to do it even if he has not been told [to do so].

It should not be accepted. However, since it was stated at the very beginning that "it must be made allowable (*kappiya*)," it should be understood that when a monk says, "Make it allowable," the person who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) must say "It is allowable" and then perform the fire-sanctified (*aggi-parijita*) and other rites.
They further state that "the word 'allowable' may be spoken in any language whatsoever."

Because of the statement, "It must be done only after saying 'It is allowable' (kappiya)," it should be understood that one must first say "allowable" and afterwards perform the touching and so forth with fire and other means. Some say, "It is also permissible to place the fire down first,
or pierce [the object] with a fingernail or similar tool, and then say 'allowable' even without lifting it up."
Regarding "one seed" in the passage beginning with *vāti*, they say: "Even though there is the intention, 'I am doing only one,' because it is all connected as a single unit, everything becomes done.
Regarding "he pierces the wood," they say: "Whether he pierces it himself or causes it to be pierced after having known [the rule], it is indeed permissible.
Regarding "he pierces the rice-cake," the same principle applies here as well. "He pierces that; it is not permissible"—this refers to the following.
They say this is because ropes and such items fall under the category of vessels (*bhājanagatika*).

Regarding the phrase "mixed with black pepper, pakkā fruits, and so forth," here the state of being a single unit (*ekābaddhatā*) should be understood by way of its connection to the rice grains of the meal, not by way of a mutual connection between the fruits themselves.
"Having had it split, one should have it made allowable" is said because the husk, once freed from the seed, falls under the category of a vessel.
"To cause him to leave" means to cause that bhikkhu to leave. Regarding the phrase "if it is suitable for him," the intention might be this:

even though giving a counter-fire and so forth has been permitted for the purpose of protecting the dwelling, it is also permissible for one to do it oneself; thus, by this much alone, this too would be "suitable for him.
Giving a counter-fire and performing a protective chant (*paritta*) may be done for the purpose of protecting one's own or another's dwelling.

It is indeed permissible. Therefore, if this [action] were in accordance with that rule, how could one obtain this distinction—that "it is not permissible for oneself, but it is permissible for another"?
Thus he said: "It is not permissible for oneself... it is not possible to obtain.
The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are: a grove of living plants, the perception of it as such, and the destruction or causing of destruction.
These, however, are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning plants and forests is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning speaking otherwise.

94–98. "Another statement" (aññaṃ vacanaṃ) in the second [case] means that he evades with a different statement what was said by the accuser as a declaration exposing the fault of the one being accused.

Alternatively, "he evades one thing with another" (aññena aññaṃ paṭicarati) should be understood here to mean that he evades one reason with another reason—that is, the reason provided by the accuser for exposing the fault of the one being accused.
It is said; thus, it is meant that he conceals [the offense] by means of another reason which demonstrates its groundlessness when he is charged.
"Conceals" (*paṭicarati*) means he acts by way of concealment; the sense is that he proceeds [in such a manner].

Alternatively, the word *carati* has the meaning of "concealing," because verbal roots have multiple meanings. Therefore, he says: "he conceals. By the words "Who has committed [the offense]? and so forth...
In the Pāḷi, evading the charge without answering it by resorting to distraction is shown as "answering one thing with another.

Furthermore, there is another form of evading the charge by answering it and then diverting the conversation toward something external; this should be understood as "answering one thing with another" outside the Pāḷi.
For example, when asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense? one says, "Pāṭaliputta..."
Having said, "We have gone," and when it was further asked, "We do not ask you whether you went to Pāṭaliputta; we ask about your offense," he replied, "From there we went to Rājagaha.

When it was then said, "Whether you go to Rājagaha or to the brahmin’s house, you have committed an offense," he spoke such things as, "I obtained pork there," and so on—thus, even while diverting the conversation externally, he continued.
For this indeed receives the designation “he evades with one thing another.
That speech which proceeds by way of evading one thing with another is called “one who speaks otherwise,” because he says something else while setting aside the matter asked about;
thus it is said: “This is the name for evading with one thing another. This [is the name] for one who remains silent.
“Nāmantu” is a name for silence; or rather, this is the reading itself. “Let him be charged with speaking otherwise” means:

let the formal act of speaking otherwise be brought against him, or let the state of being one who speaks otherwise be charged by means of the formal act now being performed—this is the meaning. “Let him be charged with causing annoyance”:
here too, the meaning should be understood as “let the formal act of causing annoyance, or the state of being a causer of annoyance, be brought against him.”

The offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) mentioned for one who speaks otherwise when not having been formally charged is appropriate in the sense of evading the text by saying one thing while meaning another.

However, it should be understood that according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), when one has not been formally charged, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for lying by way of evading through something other than what is stated in the text; whereas when one has been formally charged, there is an offense of expiation by this very same means. Some, however, [say] "when charged..."
Some say that by speaking falsely to one who speaks otherwise, there are two *pācittiya* offenses; this should be investigated and then accepted.

As for the statement that there is no offense for a first-offender, it should be understood as being stated with reference to the practice of evading the matter by saying one thing when another is asked, or it may be intended to show that there is no offense under this specific training rule. The rest is self-evident.
The three factors here are: being charged with a formal legal act (*dhammakamma*); being interrogated regarding either an offense or its basis;
and either evading the matter by speaking one thing while meaning another, or remaining silent out of a desire to conceal it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who speak otherwise is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Rebuking (Ujjhāpanaka-sikkhāpada) 103.
Regarding the third [rule], since the verbal root *jhe* is listed in the *Dhātupāṭha* in the sense of "thinking," he says, "or causing to think of as inferior," and so forth.

Furthermore, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, it should be understood that this very root also carries the meaning of "looking at. In such expressions as "he causes to recite by means of syllables," etc., [the same applies].

He says "by desire" because the phrase "out of desire" (*chandāya*) was stated by way of a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). 105. "By which statement": by which statement such as, "Out of desire, so-and-so does this [act]"; and "by which they censure":
by which statement such as, "Out of desire, so-and-so," and so forth, within the hearing range of the monks in various places.
Standing there, they proclaim dispraise.
106. "He censures another who is not fully ordained" means he causes another who is not fully ordained to censure [him].
"Or he reviles him in the presence of that person" means he reviles that one who is fully ordained and authorized by the Saṅgha in the presence of that person who is not fully ordained.

“He reviles” means either he speaks dispraise or makes it known. Regarding the phrase “one not ordained who has been authorized by the Saṅgha,” here the term “authorized” (sammatā) is used in the sense of one who was previously authorized (sammatapubbā).
Therefore, he said “even though,” and so forth. Since both censuring and reviling proceed by way of false speech, there is no offense for a first-offender;
thus, in the case of a *pācittiya* rule and in the case of a *dukkaṭa* rule, it is by this very [principle].

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of showing there is no offense. And having established it thus, it follows that for one who reviles or censures, two offenses arise simultaneously. Alternatively, it should be understood that such a training rule was formulated prior to the prohibition against false speech.
The rest here is self-evident. [The validity of] being appointed by a formal act of the Saṅgha (dhammakamma).

The six factors here are: being fully ordained; not having gone on a wrong course; desiring to disparage him; the fact that he is fully ordained in relation to the person before whom one speaks; and either censuring or reviling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning censuring is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Lodgings (Senāsana-sikkhāpada), §§108–110.
Regarding the fourth [rule], "in the snowy season" (*himavasse*), only "snow" (*hima*) is mentioned. "Unknown" (*apaññāte*) means not well-known, or not established.
From the statement, "either in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree," it follows that it is also permissible to deposit [the bedding] in an open space.
This is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. "Intent upon their range" (*gocarappasutā*) means those who have entered their respective grazing grounds.

By the phrase "eight months," it is indicated that even if it does not rain for four months during the rainy season, [the robe] is indeed prohibited; thus he says: "Because of the statement 'eight months'...
it is not permitted to set it aside. In that context, "four months" refers to the four months of the rainy season.
