Regarding the phrase "within eight months": although this is permitted by the term "the fixed rendezvous" (*avassika-saṅketa*), it is said that "where it rains during the winter, there another four months are prohibited," based on the statement "by the words 'the fixed rendezvous,'" and so forth.
By this, he illustrates the following: "In whatever region it rains during the winter, having prohibited [staying] there for eight months..."
"Four months are permitted. However, where it rains during the rainy season itself, there eight months are permitted after setting aside four months.
By this same method, in the Middle Country, where the snowy rain falls in the winter, there too [eight months are permitted].

It should be understood that [staying for] months is prohibited. Therefore, during the rainy season, it is not permitted to spread out [a rug] in an open natural area, in a sheltered pavilion where rain falls, or at the foot of a tree;

however, during the winter season, it is permitted even in an open natural area or in a sheltered pavilion and so forth, provided that the lodging is not soaked by the falling snow. During the summer season as well, [it is permitted] in open natural areas and so forth.
It is indeed permissible, provided that there is no appearance of unseasonable clouds; however, it is never permissible at the foot of a tree where crows and other birds have their regular roosts.
This is how the analysis of this matter should be understood.
Furthermore, having taken this specific point into account, the Blessed One laid down the first training rule (sikkhāpada) right from the beginning. Thus [it is] separately [stated].
No supplementary rule (anupaññatti) was stated. For that very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:

"Thus, wherever and whenever it is not permitted to spread [a rug], all of that is included here under the category of 'open air' (ajjhokāsa). Alternatively, having prohibited spreading and causing to be spread without distinction in the open air, [the Buddha] said: "Place it at such a time and in such a place."
It should be understood that because it is sufficient by the mere act of permitting [the use], no separate supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) was recited for this training precept (*sikkhāpada*).
However, in the *Parivāra*, it is stated that there is "one supplementary rule" because it was formulated in accordance with this very training precept.
Regarding "newly woven," he said "or newly woven" because what is newly woven does not quickly perish. "Covered" means covered with leather.

"An open-air dweller of the highest grade" is merely a description of his reflection; however, there is no rule that a robe-shed is not permitted for one who is an open-air dweller of the highest grade.

"Because of following the body" is said with reference to the monk's state of being present right there. By this, it is stated that there is no offense at that very time [while remaining there], but having emerged from the robe-shed...
However, there is indeed an offense for one who goes elsewhere or enters for alms.
Since donors gave even a blanket worth a thousand coins at the very time of the gift, saying, "Use this as a foot-wiping cloth," it is permissible to use it exactly as given;
therefore, [one may use] this bedding such as beds and chairs even in the open air as one pleases.
"If it has been given by donors with the words, 'Enjoy this,' it is permissible to place it in the open air at all times," they say.
Regarding "one must go after sending [a messenger]": here, one should send [a messenger] by saying, "Give this to whichever bhikkhu comes to this place and stays."

By the phrase "having observed the state of the clouds not having arisen," it should be understood that this indicates that even during the summer, when clouds have arisen, it is not permissible to place any kind of lodging, such as beds or benches, in the open air. Regarding the expression "facing the place for placing the feet":
some say it means "facing the place where those sitting down would set their feet"; others say it means "facing the place for placing the feet of one who is sweeping."
Others say: "It is stated that the sand outside [the dwelling] must be swept toward the footprint-stand as a sign that no one has gone out.

Some explain that by saying, "The refuse must be taken up with the hands and thrown outside," it is indicated that the sand itself must not be discarded, lest one think, "I shall throw away the refuse by means of this sand."

"Having wound it inside and bound it" means: having made a braid with *eraka* grass leaves and the like, and having wrapped it many times around the wide sections on both sides of that braid, one then winds it by pulling it inward from there until reaching the middle section; having thus contracted it in the middle and bound it here and there crosswise, it is made. "Having obtained [the] kappa" means: [The remainder of the sentence follows: ...having obtained the formal act (*kamma*) of the *kappa*. This is said because, although the *kappa* was not actually performed at that time, it was performed by means of the *kamma* itself. It is like saying, "He has eaten the meal," when one has already eaten the food but says so because he has consumed the porridge, rice, and other items contained within that meal. Furthermore, it is like saying, "He has received the *pātimokkha*," when one has heard the recitation of the *pātimokkha* but says so because he has heard the *pātimokkha* itself. Or it is like saying, "He has obtained the *uposatha*," when one has observed the *uposatha* but says so because he has completed the observance of the *uposatha*. Therefore, even though the *kappa* was not actually performed at that time, it is said "having obtained the *kappa*" because it was performed by means of the *kamma*. This is the meaning. Alternatively, it may be understood as follows: the Blessed One, having seen that the monks were performing the *kappa* in various ways—some making it long, some short, some thick, some thin, some with uneven thickness, some with uneven width, some with uneven intervals between the folds, some with uneven binding, some with uneven contraction in the middle, some with uneven crosswise binding, some with uneven winding, and some with uneven binding—prohibited such practices and established the rule: "It should be made even in length, even in width, even in the intervals between the folds, even in the binding, even in the contraction in the middle, even in the crosswise binding, even in the winding, and even in the binding. Having obtained permission by means of the words "Go," there is no offense for one who goes by the command of the Elder.
"In the same manner as before" means in the very way previously stated, beginning with "sitting down and going oneself.
"He goes elsewhere" means he goes elsewhere after having passed beyond that path, because he stands outside the vicinity of the stone-throw.

“It must be made to be done with the lifting of the foot” means that for one going elsewhere, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) with the first lifting of the foot, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) with the second lifting of the foot.
“Without having restored it to its original state” means without having put it away.
“In an intermediate gathering” means in a gathering from time to time.
Regarding the phrase "it is an impediment for the residents alone":
here the intention is that even if newcomers arrive and sit there without saying anything, it is still an impediment for the residents alone.

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* commentary, the phrase "when others have arrived and are sitting" means whether they have said "these are ours" or not, they are sitting there. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says "an offense."

It is stated that this is indeed a *pācittiya*. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that when there is both spreading and causing to spread, a *dukkaṭa* should be understood [instead of a *pācittiya*] because it was prescribed as an offense even in the absence of an explicit instruction (*anāṇatti*).

On the other hand, because it was prescribed separately with the words, "This is for the auctioneer; this is for the Dhamma-preacher," the intention is that even in the case of what was prescribed without an explicit instruction, it must be a *pācittiya*—[this is the meaning regarding] "in that..."
It is said: "The obstruction belongs to him who has arrived and is sitting. However, some say:
"Even though it was prescribed without a formal injunction, since the preacher of the Dhamma must not be made to rise, there ought to be a *pācittiya* offense;
but as for the newcomer, since he must be made to rise by those who arrive later and are senior, a *dukkaṭa* is stated."
112. "It should be spread on the ground" means that if a rug (*cimilika*) is available, it should be spread upon it; if not, it should be spread on the bare ground.

By the statement, "The prohibition regarding the lion-skin and so forth should be understood as applying only to their wearing," he clarifies the intended meaning of the Khandhaka text which says: "Monks, great skins must not be worn—a lion-skin, a tiger-skin, or a leopard-skin;
whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is what is meant: "Even inside a bed..."

Since this training rule was laid down on account of the matter—"mats were prepared [inside] and mats were also prepared outside"—only the use [of the bedding] after spreading it upon the beds and chairs is prohibited;
however, use by way of spreading it on the floor is not prohibited. If that is so, why is it said that "the prohibition applies only to carrying [it away]"?

Is it said? Just as, from the statement, "Monks, I allow the use of all things for the enjoyment of palaces," even though it is permissible to use items such as golden water-jars that have been designated for the use of lodgings—even in private dwellings—it is not permissible to use them by making them one's own property; so too is this [the case] with regard to floor-coverings.

It is stated that "the prohibition should be understood as applying only to the carrying away" in order to show that it is not permissible to take various items belonging to one's own possession to another monastery and consume them there.
"A wooden seat" refers specifically to a seat made of planks. "A foot-rest" is a device for placing unwashed feet upon. In the open air...
"Having boiled the dye... [and so on] ... it should be put away": here, when there is no more dye left and the dyeing work is finished, it should be put away. 113.
Because it is stated that "a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or an ārāmika is conscientious," they say that it is not permissible to go without asking permission from one who is unconscientious.
Regarding the phrase "he goes while drying [the cloth]," although it is said, "one must go only as far as this distance..."
"There is no fixed limit; nevertheless, one should not go too far beyond the range of a clod-throw," they say.

The rest here is self-evident. However, the five factors here are: the beds and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha, spreading out or having them spread out on a place with the aforementioned characteristics, being unobstructed, the absence of an emergency, and going beyond the range of a clod-throw.
In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, regarding the phrase "or he may go without asking permission," it is explained as follows: "If a monk, a novice,
or a monastery attendant who is modest considers [the lodging] to be a personal impediment, yet departs without asking such a person for permission,
without having handed over that lodging to him, and goes away regardless, [he commits an offense] at the distance of a 'clod-throw' by a man of medium strength."

"If he should cross over, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for crossing with one foot beyond the distance of a stone's throw, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for crossing with the second foot.
Having said this, six factors were stated, including lack of concern regarding the [boundary] marks.
However, in the Canon and in the Commentary, this specific distinction—"he goes without concern"—is not seen; nor is the phrase "he goes while drying [the ground]" found in the context of drying.
Thus, it has been stated that there is no offense when one goes with a sense of expectation [regarding the lodging].

If there were to be no offense even when going with a sense of expectation for another purpose, then it would have been stated without qualification as "there is no offense when one goes with a sense of expectation. Therefore, having investigated this, one should adopt the more appropriate interpretation.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning lodgings is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Lodgings (Senāsana-sikkhāpada) 116.
It is stated in the Commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*) regarding the second training rule on lodgings that "only this much was spoken.

This was said for the purpose of showing that it is stated thus in the Commentaries; however, there is also another kind of spread for beds and chairs that is likewise considered a "bedspread" (*paccattharaṇa*).
This is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. However, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated with a restrictive definition:
“A ‘bedspread’ (*paccattharaṇa*) means only a woolen rug (*pāvāra*) or a horse-blanket (*kojava*). Therefore, what is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipadas* does not agree with this;
one should accept [the latter] after careful consideration. “From the lodging” means from the very last lodging. “Whoever” means anyone at all, whether a relative of his or a stranger.
117. *Pariveṇa* means the interior space enclosed by the boundary wall of each individual monastery.
In order to show this same meaning as explained in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* with further detail, the passage beginning with “Even though it has been said” is commenced.

The phrase “in an unenclosed pavilion” (*aparicchanne maṇḍape*) should be construed separately. For that very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* it says: “In an unenclosed pavilion, or even in one that is enclosed...”
"It is said to be the place where many gather. This same distinction applies even in the case of a dining hall (*bhojanasālā*).

"There is nothing to be said" means there is nothing specific to be stated [regarding the distinction]. "It perishes" (*palujjati*) means it is destroyed. "It might be lost" (*nasseyya*) means it might be stolen or destroyed by thieves and the like. 118.
That by which a bed or a chair is woven is the "weaving of beds and chairs" (*mañcapīṭhakavāna*). A "cave in a rock-formation" (*siluccayaleṇa*) refers to a cave within a mass of rock.

“Leṇaṃ” means a mountain cave. Because this rule was laid down on the occasion of the matter where “the lodging was gnawed by termites,” the Commentary states that there is no offense in the absence of suspicion of termites, according to the specific nature of that case.

Furthermore, because it was stated in the *Vattakkhandhaka* by one prescribing the duties for those departing, “the lodging must be asked permission for,” this [rule] is intended merely to show the manner in which such a duty should be performed.
It is stated that "asking for permission is a duty (*vatta*)," but this is not said to indicate that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to a breach of duty.
For that very reason, in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, regarding the passage "the lodging must be asked for permission," it says:
"In the case of a lodging constructed on a stone surface or upon stone pillars where termites do not infest, even for one who does not ask for permission..."

Since he will say, "there is no offense," one should not accept what is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "For one who goes to such a lodging without having asked for permission, there is no *pācittiya* offense;
however, for one who goes without asking by way of the duties of a traveler (*gamikavatta*), there is a breach of duty, and therefore one incurs a *dukkaṭa*."
"There is no release by means of the last person's awareness" is said because there is no other person following behind him.

"Or, having sent one [person], he should take leave": here, for one who goes without taking leave from the place where the intention to go has arisen, there is a *pācittiya* offense upon lifting the second foot.
Even though a bed or a bench may have been placed in the open air...
For one who departs from here, no separate offense has been stated;

nevertheless, it should be understood that for one who departs after having arranged beds and chairs in the open air at an improper time, there is a *pācittiya* offense under the preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*) once the distance of a stone’s throw (*leḍḍupāta*) is exceeded, and a *dukkaṭa* offense under this [present] rule once the boundary (*parikkhepa*) is exceeded.
By the phrase "in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree," the open air (*ajjhokāsa*) is indeed included.

In that case as well, it should be understood that the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is exactly what was stated here. However, for one who spreads out bedding in the open air and then departs, there is a *dukkaṭa* for both acts.

Some say: "Since a *pācittiya* is stated for one who departs after spreading out bedding belonging to the Saṅgha in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, there is a *dukkaṭa* for each of the two items when both belong to the Saṅgha."
The rest here is self-evident. The seven factors in this case are: a bed with the characteristics already described; its belonging to the Saṅgha;

spreading it out or having it spread out in a dwelling with the characteristics already described; that it is not obstructed; the absence of an emergency; departing for another region without looking back;
and crossing the boundary of the precincts.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Entering Uninvited (Anupakhajja-sikkhāpada) 119–121.
Regarding the sixth [rule], "having entered" means having approached. [This refers to] being of great assistance and possessing distinguished virtues.
"Observing" means observing the great helpfulness of the storekeeper and the excellence of the qualities of the Dhamma-preachers and others.
"A cubit and a half all around" is said with reference to the bed and chair arranged in the center.
"Having set aside the precinct" means having set aside the precinct defined by the aforementioned characteristics. "In a single dwelling" means in one lodging place.
“Within one enclosure” means inside the boundary of that monastery. Regarding the statements such as “a sick person enters,” the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries on all three [texts] state:

“Because the grounds for non-offense are present in cases such as ‘a sick person enters,’ there is no offense even for one who enters the precinct with the intention, ‘I will enter because I am sick,’ etc., despite the fact that he desires to crowd [the space].
And this being so, the state of not being sick, etc., is also a separate factor among the constituent elements.
It might be so stated; however, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, only this much is said:
"The four factors here are: [it being] a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, knowing that it is not to be cleared away, the desire to cause crowding, and sitting or lying down within the precincts.
Therefore, this should be investigated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting down intrusively is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Expelling (Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpada) 126.

Regarding the seventh [training rule], "outbuildings" (*koṭṭhakāni*) refers to gate-houses. They say: "Even if one hears the command 'go out,' if one goes out by one's own volition, there is no offense."

128. Regarding "expelling the shameless one" (*alajjiṃ nikkaḍḍhati*) and so forth: if one expels someone after first thinking, "I shall expel him because of his shamelessness," etc., there is no offense even if anger arises, due to the rapid transformation of the mind as it is being expelled. The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are:
a monastery belonging to the Sangha; the state of being free from quarreling and so forth for one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*); and expelling out of anger.
"Or causing to be driven out"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning driving out is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Upper Story (Vehāsakuṭi).
129–131. Regarding the eighth [offense], it is stated that it is “a roofed-over floor” because the floorboards have not been spread over the upper level.
“In the same manner as previously stated” means in the same manner as stated in the training rule on encroaching (*anupakhajja-sikkhāpada*).

The remainder is easily understood. A dwelling belonging to the Sangha; a loft cell where the head does not strike the ceiling; the lower part being used for other purposes; and a bed with detachable legs placed where there is no support.
"Or a sitting mat, or a bed"—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the upper-story hut is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule regarding large dwellings (*mahallaka-vihāra*).
135. Regarding the ninth [offense], since it is stated that "a 'large' (mahallaka) dwelling is one that has an owner," there is no offense for a hut built by means of a formal request (*saññācikā*).
He says, "That is well-stated" (*taṃ suvuttaṃ*), because the statement made as a maximum limit—"even two and a half cubits"—accords with the Canon (*pāḷi*).
[He adds: "In both the Canon and the Commentary, regarding the measurement of two and a half cubits as a maximum limit..."

Because the space has been shown [as the limit], they say that whether the door-panel be less than or more than two and a half cubits in width, the space is precisely the measure of two and a half cubits.
"In the middle of which" means in the middle of whichever monastery (*vihāra*). "It may also have an incomplete precinct" refers to it being opened.
The meaning is that whatever door strikes against a wall, that [wall] remains free from a zone (upacāra) equal in extent to the width of the door on all sides.

"Light-opening" (*ālokasandhi*) means it lets light through or covers it. Because the training rule was formulated due to the fault arising in this particular case—namely, that he had it plastered again and again and had it smeared again and again—and because of the permission granted for the application of plaster...
In the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated: "Because repeated plastering is permitted only within a space measuring two and a half cubits all around the door-frame,
if one repeatedly plasters or causes another to plaster elsewhere than that,
then once the work to be done with clay on the wall has been finished and a fourth layer of plaster is applied, there must be an offense of *pācittiya*."

However, regarding all three [cases], it is stated: "Since no *pācittiya* has been prescribed for anything other than the stated measure of repeatedly applying a coating, a *dukkaṭa* is the appropriate penalty. "To be determined" (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) means to be prepared or arranged.
Regarding the term "not on greenery" (*appa-haritē*), here the prefix *appa-* [is used] as in such expressions as "one of few desires" (*appiccho*).

He said "on what is not green" (*aharite*) because it has the sense of non-existence. "A place for falling" (*patanokāsa*) means that, due to being a place for falling, one intends that [something] might fall upon the bhikkhu standing there.
By the statement, "If he resolves while standing on what is green, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*), he illustrates this point:
if, within the aforementioned measurement of the boundary surrounding the monastery, there are no crops or the like...
Where there are [trees], a dwelling should be built there; however, for one who causes it to be built where there are none, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
In order to show that when one has erected each path straight and covered it with the path, it is called "covering by way of the path," it is said:
"for one covering by way of the path. By this method, when the entire dwelling has been covered once—
Taking that roofing as "one path," it was stated, "two paths," and so forth.
It is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that, "Even in the case of roofing by way of a method (*pariyāyena*), it should be applied according to this same principle.
This is [supported] by the canonical text, "He had it roofed again and again," and by the commentary statement, "And all this roofing should be understood as being above the roofing."

And since it is the same [in both cases], one should understand the meaning here as follows: having determined two roofs and having commanded regarding the third roof, "Cover it thus," one should depart; so too, having determined two paths and having commanded regarding the third path, "Proceed by this path," one should depart.
However, some say: "First, one should cover [the area] entirely once; then, having tied the roofing rafters again, it should be covered in the same way a second time;
when the third and fourth times arrive, one should determine two paths, give instructions, and then depart.
Others, however, say: "One may determine all three paths during the very first time."
"It is allowable; from the fourth [roof] onwards, there is an offense of *pācittiya*," so they say.
Neither of these two views accords with the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor with the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Regarding the phrase "the third roof" (*tatiyāya maggaṃ*):
here, *tatiyāya* is a dative-accusative form used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is "the third roof. "Of three roofs" refers to three coverings concealed by way of roofs. Of the three...

The phrase "by means" (*pariyāyānaṃ*) follows the same principle here as well. In the fourth [offense], whether it be "in the path" (*magge*) or "by means" (*pariyāye*), what is stated for those concealing [it] is specifically the fourth concealment.
The rest is self-evident. Furthermore, the three factors here are: being in a large dwelling, it being one's own residence, and the further formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning large dwellings is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings. 140.
Regarding this tenth training rule, the phrase "should sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled" refers to external usage.
Because it was formulated first, the training rule, “One should not consume water containing living beings,” should be understood as having been formulated for one’s own personal use,
such as bathing and drinking. Alternatively, even though that [previous] rule was formulated first, since it was formulated specifically for one’s own use,
this present training rule should be understood as being formulated for external use only.

Even for one who perceives water as containing living beings, if they know beforehand, "By using this, the living beings will die," then pouring it out or causing it to be poured—even without the intention to kill—is like lighting a lamp while knowing that insects such as moths will fall into it and die;
thus it is called a "formal offense" (*paṇṇattivajja*). The rest is of obvious meaning. [The nature of water] having living beings...

The four factors here are: knowing that the living beings will die from being sprinkled; the water being of such a nature [containing life]; and sprinkling grass and so forth with that very water for some purpose other than the intention to kill.
The commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings is finished.
The second chapter on lodgings is finished.
Its alternative name is also "The Chapter on Plant Life. 3.
The Chapter on Exhortation.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Exhortation (Ovādasikkhāpada) 144.
Regarding the first training rule of the Bhikkhunīvagga, "in accordance with the sequence of the discussion" means:

in accordance with the sequence of questions asked by those who inquire, "What was that elder’s character? What was his conduct? From which family did he go forth? and so forth. It is permissible to speak [in response].

They ought to speak with a mind that is indeed free from worldly motives (*nirāmisa*). Because the paths to heaven and liberation are not conducive to deliverance (*aniyyānika*), talk that is like that of animals is called "animal-talk" (*tiracchānakathā*);
thus he says, "even when proceeding on the path to heaven," and so forth. By the word "even" (*api*), he indicates that this is even more so when proceeding on the path to liberation.
"Animal-like" means that which acts as a barrier (*tirokaraṇa-bhūta*); it is said to be obstructive. Having acquired the habit (*laddhāsevanā*).
For worldly talk concerning animals is indeed an obstacle to heaven and liberation. *Samiddho* means fulfilled. *Sahitattho* means a meaningful or relevant sense.
It is *gambhīro* (profound) because it possesses profundity of meaning and so forth. It is *bahuraso* (multifaceted) because it possesses many flavors, such as the flavor of meaning.
It is *lakkhaṇapaṭivedhasaṃyutto* (connected with the penetration of characteristics) because it brings about the flavor of penetrating the characteristics of impermanence and so forth.
145–147. *Paratoti parattha*; the meaning is "higher" (*uttari*). *Karontova* means "while performing [the preliminary acts] outside.
*Pātimokkha* refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-sīla*), which is divided into what is to be practiced (*cāritta*) and what is to be avoided (*vāritta*).

For it protects (*pāti*) one who guards it, and it liberates (*mokkheti*) that person from the sufferings of the states of woe (*āpāyika*) and so forth; therefore, it is called "Pātimokkha. It is a restraint (*saṃvaraṇaṃ*).
Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the closing of the doors of body and speech. That by which these are restrained—that is, closed—is restraint;

this is a name for the non-transgression of bodily and verbal conduct. "Restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" means having the doors of body and speech closed by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*.
And because one who has become such is said to be "possessed" of it, it is stated: "endowed with."
“Proceeds” means he sets his personal existence in motion. “Dwells” indicates the dwelling in the postures of a bhikkhu established in the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
In order to clarify in detail the meaning stated in brief, the passage beginning with “For it has been said” is commenced.
Therein, "in the Vibhaṅga" means in the Jhāna-Vibhaṅga. "Virtue is established," and so forth, are synonyms for the Pātimokkha itself.

Therein, although "virtue" (sīla) is indeed a synonym for the Pātimokkha—which succeeds upon the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā)—nevertheless, in terms of its essential nature (dhammata), this is called virtue when one abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or when performing the duties of practice.
Or rather, the states such as volition (cetanā) and so forth should be understood as belonging to one who fulfills [the precepts].

However, because a bhikkhu is said to be "established" (paṭiṭṭhāti) in the Teaching by means of the morality of the Pātimokkha, it is therefore called a "foundation" (paṭṭhā). Alternatively, it is a foundation because the bhikkhu is established therein, or because wholesome states themselves are established therein;
this is the meaning of the verse: "A wise man, being established in virtue... (Sīle paṭiṭṭhāya naro sapañño).
And it should be understood by way of such suttas as: “Virtue, Great King, is the foundation for all wholesome states,” and “For one established in virtue, Great King, no wholesome states decline.
This [term] ‘foundation’ (ādi) is used in the sense of that which arises first. And this has also been said:
“Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the very beginning among wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is virtue that is perfectly pure and view that is straight.

For just as a city builder, wishing to construct a city, first clears the site for the city and subsequently builds the city by dividing it into sections such as streets, crossroads, and junctions, even so is the practitioner of yoga.
In the beginning, one purifies virtue; thereafter, one realizes concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
Or, just as a dyer first washes a cloth with three alkaline substances and then applies whatever dye he desires once the cloth is thoroughly cleansed;
or just as a skilled painter, wishing to paint a figure, first performs the preparatory work on the wall.

Just as a tree first produces roots and subsequently brings forth form, even so the practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara), having first purified his virtue (sīla), subsequently realizes states such as serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Therefore, virtue is called the "beginning" (ādi).
This virtue is called a "foot" (caraṇa) because of its similarity to a foot. For "feet" (caraṇā) are said to mean "feet" (pādā); for just as one whose feet are cut off—
Just as the volitional formation for a man’s journeying to a destination does not arise in one whose feet are incomplete, but arises only in one whose feet are whole,
even so, for one whose virtue is broken, flawed, and incomplete, the movement of knowledge toward the journey to Nibbāna does not succeed.
But for one whose virtue is unbroken, flawless, and complete, the movement of knowledge toward the journey to Nibbāna [does succeed].
It succeeds. Therefore, virtue is called "conduct" (*caraṇa*).
This very [virtue] is "restraint" (*saṃyama*) by way of restraining, and "restraint" (*saṃvara*) by way of shielding;
thus it is described both as the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃyama*) and the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*). As for the etymology here: it restrains (*saṃyameti*) the wavering of transgression.
It is *saṃyama* because it restrains the person or, by way of transgression, does not allow him to waver;
it is *saṃvara* because it restrains—that is, closes—the gateway through which transgression enters. "Liberation" (*mokkha*) means that which is supreme or the very mouth [of liberation].
For just as the fourfold nutriment of sentient beings, having entered through the mouth, pervades all the limbs and members, so too for the yogi...
Having entered by way of virtue, the wholesome states of the four planes bring about the accomplishment of the goal. Therefore it is said, "liberation" (*mokkha*).
That which is good in the presence [of others] is "emancipation" (*pamokkha*); the meaning is that it is the precursor, the foremost, and the best. Regarding "the attainment of wholesome states":
for the sake of acquiring the wholesome states of the four planes, it is the emancipation, the precursor, and the best.
It should be understood as "striving.
"Bodily non-transgression" refers to the threefold good conduct of body; "verbal" refers to the fourfold good conduct of speech;
"bodily and verbal" refers to both of these together. By this, he shows the inclusion of the eightfold virtue of livelihood (*ājīva-ṭṭhamaka-sīla*). "Restrained" means...
“Pihita” means one whose faculties are restrained; the sense is “one with restrained faculties.
Just as a house with its doors closed is called a “restrained house” or a “closed house,” so too here one whose faculties are restrained is called “restrained.
“By the restraint of the *pātimokkha*” means by the restraint known as the *pātimokkha*. All terms beginning with “endowed” (*upeta*) are synonyms for one another.
By the seven terms beginning with "he moves" (*iriyati*), the dwelling in the postures of a bhikkhu established in the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is described.
Therein, "he moves" means he moves by being possessed of one of the four postures.
Through those sets of four postures, he proceeds by the turning of the cart that is the body. One posture-suffering [is replaced] by another...
It protects by guarding the body through long-term stability after having interrupted [the flow of] the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
It sustains by proceeding through all postures without remaining fixed in any single one.
It maintains by keeping the body in such-and-such a state through each respective posture. It moves because it persists for a long duration. Having interrupted one posture with another posture...
He dwells by means of taking away life.
By "one who prohibits wrong livelihood":
"In this case, someone [engages] through the giving of bamboo, or the giving of bowls, or the giving of flowers, fruits, bathing powders, tooth-sticks, or through flattery..."
“Or if one makes a living by means of bean-soupery, or by mendicancy for hire, or by running errands on foot,

or by any other such wrong livelihood censured by the Buddha— this is called improper conduct. Thus, [it is defined] as the opposite of that wrong livelihood termed “improper conduct” which was just mentioned.
Not by conduct such as the giving of bamboo, etc., means: "In this case,
someone does not [attain it] by the giving of bamboo, nor by the giving of alms-bowls, nor flowers, nor fruits, nor bathing, nor tooth-sticks,
nor by flattery, nor by bean-soupery, nor by servility, nor by running errands on foot, nor by any other such thing."
"By means of a wrong livelihood censured by the Buddha, one makes a living; this is called 'conduct'.
It is not by such conduct as giving bamboo, etc., as stated there.
"Having abandoned the resort of prostitutes, etc."—this refers to [avoiding] improper spheres of activity.
“Here, someone has prostitutes as his resort, or widows, young girls, eunuchs, nuns, or taverns as his resort;
he dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and the disciples of sectarians, through improper association.
Furthermore, there are those families that are faithless, lacking confidence, ungenerous, and abusive and insulting.”
"Those families who desire what is harmful, what is disadvantageous, what is unpleasant, and what is not conducive to security from bondage for the bhikkhus,
bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— when one serves, frequents, and attends upon such families, this is called 'improper resort'.
Having thus abandoned improper resorts such as those involving prostitutes and the like.

Regarding the phrase "families endowed with faith and so forth," here the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the supporting condition (*upanissaya*), the field of activity (*gocara*), and others. For the field of activity is threefold:
the supporting condition field, the protective field, and the binding field. What is the supporting condition field?
It is a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) who possesses the qualities of the ten topics of discourse; relying upon him, one hears what has not been heard and purifies what has been heard.
He dispels doubt, straightens his view, and gladdens his mind.
Or else, by training under him, he increases in faith, in virtue, in learning, in generosity, and in wisdom—this is the resort of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-gocara*).
What is the resort of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*)? Here, a bhikkhu, having entered among the houses and set out upon the street, keeps his eyes cast down.
One who sees only the distance of a plow’s length goes restrained; he does not look at an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a foot soldier, nor a woman, nor a man;
he does not look upward, nor downward, nor does he go about glancing around in the various directions.
This is the range of protection (*ārakkhagocara*). What is the range of anchoring (*upanibandhagocara*)? It is the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*).
Wherever the mind is bound. For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s own range, his ancestral domain?
That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness. This is the range for binding.
Thus, it should be understood that these three kinds of ranges are included here by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
"In even minor faults" means in faults such as those consisting of unintentionally committing an offense against the training rules (*sekhiya*) or the arising of unwholesome states of mind.
"One whose nature is to see them as a danger" means one whose character is to regard even a minute fault as being like Mount Sineru, which is six hundred and eighty thousand *yojanas* high;
or one whose character is to regard even the lightest mere ill-spoken word as being like a defeat offense (*pārājika*).
"Having properly taken up" means having correctly, respectfully, or completely taken up.

It is "heard" (*suta*) because it is to be heard by those seeking escape from the suffering of *saṃsāra*; it refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). One who "bears that" is a "bearer of what is heard" (*sutadhara*), one who serves as the receptacle for what has been heard.
For in one from whom what was taken up here slips away elsewhere—like water from a cracked jar—he is not a bearer of what is heard.
One who does not retain it— who is unable to speak or recite even a single discourse or birth story in the midst of an assembly—
is called "one who does not possess the heard" (*na sutadhara*). However, one for whom the Buddha’s word that has been learned remains exactly as it was at the time of learning,
and is not lost even after ten or twenty years of not reciting it, is called "one who possesses the heard" (*sutadhara*).
For this very reason he said, "Whatever of it there may be," and so forth. It is called a "collection" (*sannicaya*) because even a single word or a single syllable is accumulated without being lost.
He said, "One in whom there is a collection of what has been heard is a 'repository of learning' (*sutasannicaya*)," explaining:
"In whom the heard is accumulated within the inner chamber of the heart, like an inscription on stone or [gold] in a golden vessel."

It remains well, like lion’s fat once it has been poured in; this is what is called the accumulation of what has been heard (*sutasannicaya*). Therefore he said: “By this... [etc. ...he shows its non-destruction.
*Dhātā* means well-mastered or committed to memory. For the Buddha-word learned by one person does not remain constant at all times; [one might think], “This particular sutta...”
When it is asked, "Recite a sutta or a Jātaka," he replies, "I shall know them after having mastered them by recitation, compared them with others, and penetrated their meaning through inquiry.

For one who has mastered [the texts], the flow occurs effortlessly and pleasantly—like the current of the Ganges and like the stream of the *bhavaṅga* consciousness—due to the absence of any interruption in the continuity. When it is said, "Recite such-and-such a sutta or Jātaka,"...
Having recited it, he extracts that very [passage] and speaks it. It is with reference to this that it is said, "the dhātā.

"Made proficient by speech" means: having been rehearsed orally according to the ten suttas, the ten chapters, and the ten fifties; the meaning is that they have been rehearsed orally after observing, "Ten suttas have been traversed," "Ten chapters have been traversed," and so forth. Of a portion of a sutta...
For here, familiarity with the mere words of the Sutta is not intended; rather, it is by way of the sections (*vagga*) and so forth.
"Examined with the mind" means examined repeatedly with the mind, scrutinized part by part, and reflected upon—this is the meaning.

"Of one who is reviewing" means of one who is reflecting with the mind on the Buddha’s word in order to recite it aloud. "Thoroughly penetrated" means [penetrated] so as to be free from the tangle (*nijjaṭa*).
Having made it free from confusion, they have thoroughly penetrated it according to its true nature.
"Two matrices" refers to the matrix for monks and the matrix for nuns. "Memorized by word of mouth" is a synonym for the former.

"Three expressions of appreciation" refers to the expression of appreciation connected with the benefits of giving at a meal for the Saṅgha, and [the expression of appreciation] at auspicious occasions such as the dedication of a monastery.
The three types of thanksgiving (anumodanā) are: thanksgiving for the *Maṅgalasutta* and so forth;

thanksgiving for funeral meals and other inauspicious occasions from outside the wall; and thanksgiving [for offerings] across the boundary. "The determination of what is action and what is not action" refers to the analysis stated in the Chapter on Action (*Kammavagga*) at the end of the *Parivāra*.
It is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "One who learns by way of insight (*vipassanā*) should learn it by means of the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*)."
Because it is unobstructed in the four directions, it "belongs to the four directions" (*catuddiso*); being thus "of the four directions," it is "four-directional" (*cātuddiso*).
Alternatively, it is "four-directional" because it deserves the four directions, or because it is excellent in the four directions.
In the *Abhivinaya*, that is, in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "To train" means to cause to learn. "The two Vibhaṅgas are mastered and committed to memory..."
They say that the phrase "it should be done" is stated with reference even to the method of learning by means of questioning.
Since what is forgotten by one person may be well-mastered by another, it is said: "It should be done in such a way as to be capable of being exchanged among three people.
Regarding the *Abhidhamma*: this refers to the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*. Or, "the three lower sections" refers to the *Sagāthakavagga* and the *Nidānavagga*, which are below the *Mahāvagga*.

The Khandhaka-vagga— these are the three sections. Since it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī that “it is permissible to learn the Dhammapada together with its *vatthu* stories,” even one who recites the Jātakas should, after learning the Jātaka together with its commentary (*saṭṭhakatha*),
likewise learn the Dhammapada together with its *vatthu* stories.

One who possesses speech that is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*), beautiful (*sundara*), and well-rounded in both words and phonemes (*parimaṇḍalapadabyañjana*) is called "one of auspicious speech" (*kalyāṇavāca*). Therefore, he said: "Endowed with speech...

[omitting] ...free from looseness, harshness, and so forth. In this context, "well-rounded in words and phonemes" means: because of the perfection of the places of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the modes of formation (*karaṇa*), and because of the perfection of training (*sikkhā*), there is no deficiency whatsoever;
thus, her words (*pada*) and phonemes (*byañjana*)—that is, syllables (*akkhara*)—are well-rounded, and she is therefore "one whose words and phonemes are well-rounded."
Alternatively, the phrase itself is the "phrase-and-word" (*padabyañjana*) because it expresses the meaning through its words.
When that [phrase] is spoken with the completion of its syllables, without omitting the tenfold phonetic qualities such as softness and hardness, it is called "perfectly rounded" (*parimaṇḍala*).
For the perfect rounding of the phrase-and-word consists in the completion of its syllables. Therefore it is said: "by speaking the soft, hard, and so forth, according to the rule."

"Parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā" means that her words and phrases (*padabyañjana*) are complete and well-rounded. Alternatively, "pada" refers to a name and so forth, because by means of it one attains (*pajjati*) or understands (*ñāyati*) the meaning.
"Byañjana" refers to a sentence, because it manifests (*byañjeti*) the intended meaning.
She is "parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā" due to the perfection of those two.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, while teaching the Dhamma in an assembly, sets aside a discourse (*sutta*) or a birth story (*jātaka*) and brings forward another discourse intended as a challenge,
he tells a simile for it, applies it to that meaning, and thus,
having grasped this and casting it there, carrying it along on one side, he knows the right time and rises; such is the discourse set aside.
However, it is merely set aside; its discourse is called "incomplete" because the meaning is not fully perfected.

But one who, having set aside either a Sutta or a Jātaka, without going even a single word outside of it, brings in another Sutta by way of commenting on the meaning of the Sutta as it was set aside, [preserves] both the connection of the text and its sequence.
Looking ahead, standing upon the method provided by his teachers, and like one delimiting [objects] with a balance-scale, he demonstrated each respective meaning having made it well-established;
like one pouring water into a deep basin, he brought forth the profound meaning;
and like a noble Sindhu horse, he struck word after word with a rhythmic, graceful gait, expressing a single word through many [meanings].

He proceeds by repeatedly praising [the teaching] through various methods; thus his discourse is called "perfectly rounded" (*parimaṇḍala*) because it is complete in every respect—being consistent with the Dhamma, consistent with the meaning, coherent in its sequence, logical from beginning to end, and in accordance with the teacher’s tradition.
It is with reference to such discourse that it is said: "with words and phrases that are perfectly rounded."
"Porī" means that which exists (*bhavati*) because it is full of qualities (*guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena*) in the city (*pure*);

the meaning is that this [speech] should be spoken by that bhikkhu because it is full of the qualities of the meaning (*atthassa guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena*), existing when the meaning is complete (*puṇṇabhāve*).

Alternatively, it is "porī" because it is like a city-woman (*nāgarikitthiyā*)—that is, a woman who has grown up in the city (*pure*)—due to its delicacy; the meaning is that it is delicate like a woman raised in the city. Of the city...
This is also called *porī*; the meaning is that it is the speech of a city, the talk of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers are speakers of refined speech;
they say "father" when there is merely the measure of a father, and "brother" when there is merely the measure of a brother.
Such speech is indeed dear and pleasing to many people; thus, by means of that refined (*poriyā*) speech.
"Vissaṭṭhāya" means unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and so forth, and free from faults such as being too hurried or too slow.

Alternatively, the speech of one who preaches the Dhamma to the assembly in accordance with their inclinations—neither too fast nor too slow, but continuously and with a single flavor—is called "vissaṭṭhā.
For a bhikkhu preaching the Dhamma, whether it be a Sutta or a Jātaka...
Or, having begun [the recitation], from the very moment it was commenced, he proceeds as if hurriedly churning a fire-drill,
or as if eating hot food; taking what has been grasped as already grasped and what has not been grasped as not grasped according to the sequence of the text and its connections,
he strikes here and there like one trying to rouse a monitor lizard moving among old leaves.

Having recited [the text], he rises and departs. For just as a lizard moving among old leaves is sometimes seen and sometimes not seen, so too the commentary on the meaning of certain passages is found in some places and not in others.
Furthermore, when one who is preaching the Dhamma speaks at times quickly, at times slowly, at times softly, and at times with a loud voice...

At the proper time he makes a brief sound; just as the fire issuing from the mouth of a *nijjhāmataṇhika* peta sometimes burns and sometimes goes out, so too is one called a "preacher of the dhamma for petas," who begins again when the assembly wishes to rise.
Furthermore, he who, while speaking, falters here and there and falls into a lack of eloquence...
Someone speaking as if sneezing or as if crying due to some illness—
none of these forms of speech are called "clear" (*vissaṭṭhā*), because they do not proceed easily. However, one who cites the suttas,
stands by the method provided by the teachers, does not abandon the teachers' grasp, and explains each respective sutta exactly as the teachers did— by that [method alone...]
By praising according to the method described as "neither too fast nor too slow," he makes the continuity of the discourse uninterrupted and causes it to flow like the current of a river;
he causes the discourse to proceed without interval, like water falling from the celestial Gaṅgā.
His speech is thus called "unimpeded" (*vissaṭṭhā*). It is with reference to this that it is said: "of unimpeded [speech]."
"Free from *ela-gaḷā*" means devoid of *ela-gaḷā*. For when someone speaks, *ela* (phlegm) flows out, saliva drips, or droplets of spittle issue forth;
the speech of such a person is called *ela-gaḷā*. The meaning is that it is the opposite of this.
"Capable of making the meaning understood" means having the capacity to make known the meaning spoken by making the beginning, middle, and end clear.
For the purpose of making known the meaning, for the sake of accomplishment.
Speech itself is the instrument, thus it is "vākkaraṇaṃ" (the instrument of speech), which is the sound of utterance. One who possesses beautiful and sweet speech is "kalyāṇavākkaraṇo.
For this very reason, he says "sweet-voiced. He despises means he looks down upon. "A woman" is the connection [of the sentence]. It causes the mind to fall away.

It is "pleasing" because it causes increase; therefore he said, "one who increases the mind. "Having threatened with the fear of the round of existence" means having terrified the nuns by means of the pride of youth and so forth, using the fear of *saṃsāra*.

"In the time of being a householder" means during one's own period as a layperson. "By [committing] sexual intercourse with a nun, one is a defiler of a nun" refers specifically to physical contact with a nun.
Regarding trainee nuns (*sikkhamānā*) and novice nuns (*sāmaṇerī*): [the same applies].

However, one who violates a nun by sexual intercourse is not considered a "defiler of nuns" (bhikkhunīdūsaka); thus it is said: "sexual intercourse with female trainees (sikkhamānā) and female novices (sāmaṇerī).

Because of the expression "clad in saffron robes," it should be understood that one who has previously committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) against immoral nuns, female trainees, or female novices is indeed excluded. Even in the absence of that particular nun, whichever [nun]...
They heard these words and, each thinking it was exactly so, [the Buddha] said, "Women indeed," and so forth.
Now, in order to demonstrate the combination of the eight factors, the passage beginning with "And herein" is commenced.

However, one who appoints someone not endowed with these eight factors by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), yet the monk remains duly appointed.
148. *Garukehi* means "by those things that are to be treated with gravity. *Ekato-upasampannāya* is a locative expression used in the sense of the accusative.

Alternatively, when the meaning of the verb *ovadati* is simply "speaks," the dative case is also appropriate. Those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of monks are, for example, those who have changed their gender or the five hundred Sakyan women.
149. Regarding the phrase "having prepared a seat," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "If the ground is pleasant, it is permissible not to prepare a seat.
By the mention of "women," nuns are also included; thus he says, "for the purpose of [receiving] a teaching on the Dhamma and for the sake of release from offenses.
This is because on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*), all nuns must come into the presence of the appointed monk for the purpose of exhortation.
With the words, “Sisters, are you all assembled? he asks whether they have all arrived; thus he says, “Have you all come?

Even if those who are ill do not arrive, since their non-arrival is permitted for the sick, and because all those capable of coming have indeed come, it is appropriate to say, “Venerable ladies, we are assembled.
Regarding the phrases “within the village,” etc., [it refers to] where the five factors...

Once she has placed her feet on the ground, it is not possible for her to pay homage; therefore, while remaining standing there, she may simply incline her body forward, raise her joined palms, and say, "I pay homage, Venerable Lady," and then depart. Regarding the term *antaraghara*:

in some contexts, the interior of a village is meant, starting from the threshold (*indakhīla*) outside the city gate; in others, it refers to the interior of a house, starting from the threshold of the dwelling.

Furthermore, since "in the village" (*antogāme*) is mentioned separately here, it should be understood that "or in the interior of houses" (*antaraghare*) refers specifically to the interior of a house.
"Anywhere" (*yattha katthaci*) means anywhere within the village and so forth.
"It is permissible" (*vaṭṭati*) means that it is permissible for those who have faith in the words spoken—namely, "Dwell here, noble ladies; we shall bring the bhikkhus"—to stay there.
It is permissible. "Not desiring to go after having been invited" means that they do not wish to go after having been invited by people;
the intention is that they wish to enter the rains residence right there.
"From" means from the nuns' quarters. "Having requested" means having requested, [saying]: "We too shall dwell according to the exhortation brought by you. "There" means in that nuns' quarters.
"One should dwell [in a residence] by means of exhortation from those who have arrived" means that one should spend the later rains retreat.

"An offense for one dwelling in a residence without monks" refers to a general application of offenses by way of a formal charge (*codanāmukha*), but it does not refer to that specific offense itself.
"An offense for one who goes after having broken the rains retreat" refers to the offense rooted in not entering the rains retreat.
Because there exists a reason for non-offense regarding the other offense, it is said, "that [offense] must be guarded against.

The meaning is that the offense rooted in not entering the rains residence must be guarded against; the intention is that one should enter the rains residence even in a monastery devoid of monks when such emergencies arise.
Therefore he said: "For in emergencies... [etc.]... it is stated that there is no offense. However, regarding the other offense, there is no offense.
If there is no cause [to go], one should not enter the rains retreat even for the later period (*pacchimikā*). For if monks are present and one does not enter the retreat, there is an offense.
Regarding the instruction "having gone there, one should perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*)," this is because an offense arises for those who do not perform the invitation ceremony there.
If the place where the monks reside is even distant, and it is possible to go on the ninth day and perform the invitation ceremony, then having gone there...
The invitation (pavāraṇā) should be performed. However, if it is not possible to depart on the ninth day and reach [the assembly], there is no offense for those who do not go.

Regarding "inquiring about the Uposatha" (uposathapucchanā): it is the inquiry concerning the Uposatha; by applying the *ka*-suffix and shortening the vowel, it is called "one who inquires about the Uposatha" (uposathapucchaka).
Thus he says, "inquiring about the Uposatha. One should inquire about the Uposatha by asking, "Venerable sir, when is the Uposatha?"
She should be asked. The monk should also say, "Sister, the Uposatha is tomorrow.

Sometimes monks perform the Uposatha on the fifteenth day as the fourteenth-day Uposatha, or the Uposatha on the fourteenth day as the fifteenth-day Uposatha; on whichever day the monks have performed the Uposatha, on that very same day the nuns must also perform the Uposatha.
With this underlying intention, it was said: "Having gone on the thirteenth day of the fortnight," and so forth.
When the bhikkhu has been asked thus, if they perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day, he should say, "Sisters, it is the fourteenth-day [Uposatha].
But if they perform it on the fifteenth day, he should inform them, "Sisters, it is the fifteenth-day [Uposatha]. "For the purpose of exhortation" means for the purpose of requesting the exhortation.
From the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada) onwards, one should go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
on the first day, one should go for the purpose of receiving exhortation (ovāda), and from the second day onwards, one should go at intervals for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
For even the receiving of exhortation is spoken of without distinction as "hearing the Dhamma" itself. "They approached the monastery continuously" means that they did so for the most part.

This was said with reference to the act of approaching. By the passage beginning with "Vuttañhetam" (For this has been said), the Pāḷi is cited for the purpose of illustrating the approach of all bhikkhunīs who intend, "We shall practice according to the instruction.
"Goes for exhortation" means she goes to request exhortation. "Two or three" means by two or by three; here the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
"By means of what is pleasing" means by means of faultless bodily action and so forth that produces confidence. "Should accomplish" means he should accomplish the threefold training.
If, upon seeing only the reciter of the Pātimokkha, those bhikkhunīs were to request the exhortation (*ovāda*), what should be done by him?
When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has assembled at the Uposatha hall, as a preliminary duty: "Is there..."
When asked, "Is there any bhikkhunī requesting the exhortation?",
the one receiving the exhortation should have another bhikkhu speak the words that are to be spoken [by him], while he himself speaks the words that are to be spoken by the reciter of the Pātimokkha;
then, having gone back again, he should announce it to the bhikkhunīs himself, or else another bhikkhu on that same day.
The Pātimokkha should be recited. This is what was said: the plural form “by them” (tāhi) was used.
The phrase “one bhikkhunī” refers to the reception of the message by a single bhikkhunī from many bhikkhunī residences;
it does not, however, refer to the absence of a companion. “From many bhikkhunī residences” [refers to this].
"Or on the way, or in that very village, there are many nunneries.
By this, he shows the words to be spoken by a nun who has arrived after receiving a message from various nunneries, using the expression: "The community of nuns, noble lady, and the individual nuns.
And this is stated as a mere illustration of one particular manner; in that regard—
In that nunnery, however, one should speak according to the number of bhikkhunīs observed there, following the corresponding method.
The phrase "of the community of bhikkhus, of the noble ladies, of the noble sir" is stated by way of abbreviation.
The expression "by the reciter of the Pātimokkha as well" is shown specifically by way of the Saṅgha’s Uposatha ceremony. But where [there are] three or two...
Or, if there is no recitation of the Pātimokkha in the place where one is staying, even there the motion (ñatti) must be proposed by another monk or by oneself according to this same method.

Even if one is alone, on the Uposatha day, after having accepted the request for exhortation, one must say to the nuns who arrive on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), "There is no one [here]," and so forth. If one has been appointed oneself...
"Yes," it should be said. One who does not know this procedure is intended here as a "fool.

Regarding the rules such as: "If one instructs a factional Bhikkhunī Saṅgha that is factional while perceiving it as factional during an illegal act (adhammakamma), there is an offense of Pācittiya," although there are also offenses of Dukkaṭa based on the presence of the characteristics of being factional and so forth, [the primary offense] is rooted in the illegal act.

Since it is stated in the Pāḷi that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) in every instance, he said: "In the case of an illegal formal act, there are eighteen offenses of expiation based on two [sets of] novices.

The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors in this context are: the state of not being authorized, the state of the nun having full ordination (upasampadā), and the recitation of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma) by way of exhortation (ovāda).
The commentary on the training rule concerning exhortation is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning when the sun has set: 153.
In the second [training rule], "for the constant practice of wholesome states" is stated by way of the preliminary practice.
"Munāti" means he knows. "By that knowledge" means by that knowledge reckoned as the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship.
"In the paths" means in the paths of means. Because the training of an arahant is fully accomplished, it says: "And this... [etc.]... was said.
Alternatively, the words "of one who is diligent" and "of one who trains" should be understood as having the sense of a cause; therefore, because of diligence and because of training—
And "adhicetaso" means "of one who is superior in mind. "Sorrows" refers to mental torments. Here, by the phrase "adhicetaso," the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) is indicated;
by "appamajjato," the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā); and by "sikkhato munino monapathesu," the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is indicated.

Alternatively, by the word "munino" (of the sage), the training in higher wisdom is indicated, and by "sikkhato monapathesu" (training in the paths of sagehood), the supramundane nature of those trainings is shown.
It should be understood that the benefits of fulfilling the training are demonstrated by such passages as, "In the preliminary stage of practice, sorrows do not arise.
*Kokanuda* is a specific type of lotus, just as in the expression "*kokāsaya*"; it is said to have many petals, be endowed with beautiful color, and be exceedingly fragrant.
Some also say that "*kokanuda*" refers to the white lotus (*setapaduma*). *Pāto* means early in the morning.
This is the meaning here: just as the lotus known as the *kokanuda* is, at the time of sunrise in the morning, blossomed, fully opened, not devoid of fragrance, and radiant;
even so, [the Buddha] was fragrant with the scent of his body and the scent of his virtues, shining like the sun in the autumnal sky, blazing with his own splendor, and emitting light from his limbs.
"Behold the Perfectly Enlightened One, Aṅgīrasa.
"He is incapable"—the meaning is that this Dispensation has practice as its essence, and practice is rooted in the scriptures (pariyatti);
since you are unable to master the scriptures, you are therefore incapable. "A mere piece of rag" refers to [his] supernormal power (iddhi).
It was a well-washed, pure rag. At that time, the Blessed One, thinking, "One who is unable to perform recitation does not become incapable in my teaching;
do not grieve, monk," took him by the arm, entered the monastery, and having miraculously fashioned a piece of rags, said:
"Come now, monk, while rubbing this, [think]: 'This is a dust-remover...'"
Having said, "Recite the *Rajoharaṇa* repeatedly," he gave it to him because of the merit he had performed in the past.
It is said that formerly, when he was a king, as he was circumambulating the city, sweat broke out from his forehead;
he wiped his forehead with a clean cloth, and the cloth became soiled. He thought, "Depending on this body, such a thing [as this]..."
The clean cloth, having abandoned its natural state, has become soiled; "impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena"—thus he acquires the perception of impermanence.
For that reason, the dust-remover itself becomes his requisite. It is called a *rajoharaṇa* because it removes dust (*rajaṃ harati*).
"Having acquired a sense of spiritual urgency" means having acquired a sense of urgency by establishing the perception of foulness and the perception of impermanence.

For indeed, emerging with wise attention, thinking, "The cloth is pure; there is no fault here, but this is a fault of the personal existence (attabhāva)," one acquires the perception of foulness and the perception of impermanence.

Then, by means of the discernment of name-and-form and so forth, one applies knowledge to the five aggregates, increases insight through the sequence beginning with the contemplation of the aggregates (kalāpasammasana), and proceeds through the stages beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa).
He brought insight (vipassanā) close to the stages of conformity (anuloma) and the lineage-knowledge (gotrabhu). It was with reference to this that it was said, “He undertook insight.
Regarding the phrase “he spoke the verse of illumination”: a verse spoken preceded by the emission of light is a “verse of illumination”; the meaning is that he spoke that [verse].

And here, it is stated specifically, “‘Of higher mind’—he spoke this verse of illumination. However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, and in the commentary on the *Theragāthā*, it is said:
“Lust is not called dust, nor is it called a particle of grit; ‘dust’ is a designation for lust.
Having completely abandoned this dust, the wise—”
They dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
“Hatred... [and so on] ...in the teaching.
Delusion is dust, but it is not called ‘dust’ (reṇu);”
"Passion" is a designation for delusion;
having utterly abandoned this passion, the wise dwell in the teaching of the one who is free from passion.
It is said: "He spoke these three verses of illumination.

Furthermore, that this is the *udāna* verse of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka is found in this very same canonical text (*pāḷi*). However, in the *Theragāthā*, this verse does not appear among the *udāna* verses of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka;
rather, it is stated there: "This is the *udāna* verse of the Elder Ekudāniya. Even so, [the verse remains].

Since this has been handed down thus in this text and its commentary, it should be understood that even for the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, this verse of inspired utterance (*udāna*) was spoken by the Blessed One as a "verse of illumination" (*obhāsa-gāthā*).
"He attained Arahantship" means he attained Arahantship accompanied by the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).
From the statement beginning with "He is incapable," etc., [it follows that] out of compassion, [the Buddha] [sent him] from the Saṅgha’s monastery to his own co-resident (*saddhivihārika*), etc.
It appears as if there is no offense for one who is having [the person] expelled. For it is impossible that the Elder would have done so intentionally;
or rather, it should be understood that he did so before the training rule regarding expulsion had been promulgated. 156.
"For one who exhorts [a nun], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)" means: when the sun has set, whether by means of the Garudhammas or by some other Dhamma.
Even for one who has been formally authorized, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for advising [a nun]. The rest here is self-evident.
However, the three factors here are:
the setting of the sun, the completion of full ordination, and the act of advising. The commentary on the training rule concerning the setting of the sun is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Nuns’ Quarters (Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 162.

The third [training rule] has its meaning already explained. Herein, there are four constituent factors: entering the nuns’ quarters, being fully ordained, the absence of a [permissible] occasion, and instructing them regarding the heavy rules (garudhamma).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the nuns’ quarters is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Material Gain (Āmisa-sikkhāpada) 164.
In the fourth [training rule], the connection for these terms—“one who is fully ordained,” etc., and “an instructor of bhikkhunīs”—is with the phrase “desiring to cause embarrassment.
However, by way of the phrases “desiring to cause disrepute” and “desiring to cause ill-fame,” [the connection applies] to the terms “one who is fully ordained,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “of one who is fully ordained” (*upasampannassa*), a change of grammatical case must be made;

it is with reference to this meaning that it is said, “the meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated for the offense of censuring. For one who speaks such words as “he advises for the sake of a robe,” a *pācittiya* offense should be understood to occur upon the completion of each individual statement. This is because of the canonical text which states: “one who is fully ordained but not authorized by the Saṅgha.”
And because of the commentarial statement, "Either by one authorized by the Saṅgha, or having been established as a burden," it refers to one who possesses the eight factors;
or, by one who wishes to live apart from an authorized person, having requested, "Let this be your burden until I return," it has been established;
or, in the absence of such a person, it has been established by the Saṅgha itself as a burden in that same manner, [concerning] the eight Garudhammas.
It should be understood that one may also exhort [them] by means of another teaching. Therefore, it should be taken that the rule, "Whosoever, monk,
should exhort nuns without being appointed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," was stated with reference to what was established after having first made it a burden.
168. There is no offense if [it is] by nature for the sake of a robe...pe... regarding the statement "he speaks while exhorting":
here, if one speaks thus with the perception that he is exhorting for the sake of material gain when he is actually exhorting for the sake of material gain, there is no offense;

however, if one perceives that he is not exhorting for the sake of material gain, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). But if one speaks with the perception that he is exhorting for the sake of material gain when he is actually exhorting for the sake of material gain... [the same applies].
There is no offense even for one who speaks [in this way], because the training rule concerns the state of having a conscious intention (*sacittakatā*). The rest here is self-evident.

However, the four factors in this case are: being fully ordained (*upasampannatā*), having received formal authorization in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammena laddhasammutitā*), the absence of any worldly motive (*anāmisantaratā*), and speaking thus out of a desire for disrepute (*avaṇṇakāmatāya*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning worldly motives (*āmisa*) is concluded.
169. The fifth [offense] has its meaning already explained.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Having a Robe Sewn.
175. Regarding the sixth: if that nun should put on that robe from the very beginning, and other nuns, seeing her...
They would have complained; therefore, thinking that the general public would not be allowed to see it, he said, "having carried it away as it was gathered and having set it down," and so forth.
176. *Nīharati* means he carries it out once. The connection is: "those who were dependent on them" (*ye pi tesaṃ nissitakā*). *Kathinavattaṃ* (the duty regarding the Kathina).
“Needlework may be done for one’s fellow celibates”—thus, making a needle is [permitted] by way of what ought to be done.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for teachers and preceptors because of undertaking what is unallowable. “Having deceived” means:
having said only this much, “for a certain bhikkhunī,” instead of saying, “for your relative. Having heard, “for a certain bhikkhunī,” they perceive her as not being a relative.

He said, "Because of being directed toward what is improper. Even if one does not say, "This is your mother's robe," and so forth, there is no offense even for having someone sew it with a pure mind, saying, "Sew this robe.
Regarding the phrase "a sandal-bag, etc.," by the word "etc.," it refers to whatever robe cannot be worn as an undergarment (*nivāsana*) or as an upper garment (*pārupana*).

That too is included. The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are: [the robe] belonging to an unrelated bhikkhunī, having reached the state of being an undergarment or an upper garment, and sewing it oneself or having it sewn by another in the manner already described.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sewing of robes is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Carrying [Burdens] Together (Saṃvidahana-sikkhāpada) 181.

Regarding the seventh rule, concerning the statement “while they were walking behind, thieves plundered them,” he says “the bowl and robe” because the word “bowl and robe” is to be supplied to the text.
“Those bhikkhunīs” refers to the bhikkhunīs who were walking behind.
The connection here should be understood by changing the case ending in the phrase “pacchā gacchantīnaṃ.
In the Canon, the arrangement beginning with the monks is stated as “Let us go, sister; let us go, lady,” while that beginning with the nuns is stated as “Let us go, master;
let us go, sister. “Ekaddhānamaggaṃ” means a single road designated as a journey.
A road, or a highway on one side. "Yesterday" means the day before. "The day after" means on the third day. 182–183.
"Of two kinds as described" means the classification stated as being of two types: by way of traveling on foot or by way of traveling by vehicle.
A "crossroads" (*catukka*) is a place where four roads meet; a "junction" (*siṅghāṭaka*) is a place where three roads meet.

Regarding the phrase “from village to village,” here “village interval” (*gāmantara*) refers to one village [relative to another]; thus it was said: “There is no offense upon departing... [etc. ... for the bhikkhu there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Because the word “having made an appointment” (*saṃvidhāya*) is stated in the Canon without qualification, it was said: “It does not agree with the Canon.

Because it was stated that “even when an appointment has been made within this interval, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the bhikkhu,” it was said: “It does not [agree] with the rest of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).”
It is said, “he meets. Regarding “for one who passes beyond half a yojana”: this refers to one who, in the absence of a village, passes beyond half a yojana.
For that place within half a yojana where there is no other village is what is intended here by “wilderness devoid of a village”;
however, if there is a village within half a yojana, the offense occurs simply by counting the transition from one village to another.
