185. "In the destruction of the kingdom" means during the plundering of the kingdom. "Mounted on wheels" means mounted on either a wheel of postures or a cart-wheel.

The rest is self-evident. Herein, these factors apply: both having made an agreement, setting out on the road, there being no signal, there being no time of restriction, there being no emergency, or entering another village, or traveling beyond half a *yojana*. These are the conditions here.

There are five factors. However, for one who travels together with those who have received ordination from only one side [of the Sangha] and so forth, there is an offense under the training rule concerning women.
The commentary on the training rule on making an appointment is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Boarding a Boat.
188. In the eighth [offense], the distinction lies in the phrase "having made arrangements out of a desire for sport, on account of intimacy with friends and worldly pleasures.
This is established by the passage "thus these... playing in a boat together with the bhikkhunīs," as well as by the passage "whether going upstream or downstream."
189. To the question, "How can there be 'between villages' across a river? he says, "Of whichever river," and so forth. Some say:
"Because it was stated with reference to traveling along only one bank—that is, 'along the bank-side of that river which has a village...

up to the calculation of half a yojana'—there is an offense for one traveling through the middle of such a river according to the calculation of 'between villages' and the calculation of 'half a yojana'."
By the phrase "In all the commentaries" (*sabba-aṭṭhakathāsu*), he supports the very point he has stated himself.

They say: "Since it is stated that there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) only for one who boards a boat on a river after making an appointment with a nun out of a desire for sport, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—not an offense of expiation—for one who does so in a reservoir, the ocean, or similar places out of a desire for sport. [This is said] by way of worldly pleasure and intimacy with friends.

Because of the statement, "Having made an arrangement with the intention of playing," some say that this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*) and a worldly offense (*lokavajja*).

That should not be accepted. For even if one has mounted [a vehicle] with the intention of playing, upon entering another village or traveling beyond half a *yojana*, one incurs an offense even while possessing a wholesome or indeterminate (*abyākata*) state of mind. If indeed...
Having attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he would either realize *arahantship*, fall asleep, or proceed while attending to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*);
how then could he possess an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*)—by virtue of which this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is called "unwholesome by way of worldly transgression" (*lokavajja*)?
Therefore, it is established that the three [types of] minds [involved here] are "offenses by way of formal rule" (*paṇṇattivajja*). The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the training rule regarding boarding boats is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding What is Prepared (Paripācita-sikkhāpada) 194.

Regarding the ninth [rule], "prepared" means prepared for the sake of the monks. As for the phrase "they are either relatives or have invited him": even if they might be non-relatives to the monk and not have invited him, it is permissible provided they are relatives to the nun and have invited her.
197. This was laid down for the purpose of cutting off the faction of wicked bhikkhus; therefore, an offense is stated only in regard to the five kinds of soft food (*bhojana*).

However, the statement that “there is no offense in all cases except for the five kinds of soft food” is spoken for the purpose of showing that there is no offense under this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
For one who consumes what has been obtained through solicitation (*viññatti*), according to the method stated elsewhere—
An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The rest is self-evident.

However, the five factors here are: the fact that it was prepared by a nun, the knowledge [of this], the absence of a layperson’s undertaking [to prepare it], the state of being one of the items such as boiled rice, and the swallowing of that [food].
The commentary on the training rule concerning what has been prepared is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting in Secret (Rahonisajja-sikkhāpada) 198.
Regarding the tenth [offense], the phrase "by means of the fourth training rule for Upananda" is said with reference to the training rule on sitting in secret with a woman in an unenclosed place.
Although that is the fifth training rule in the section on the naked ascetics (Acelaka-vagga), it concerns the Venerable Upananda.
However, among those rules prescribed with reference [to specific individuals], it is stated as "by the fourth training rule for Upananda" because of its position as the fourth.
Since the subject matter (vatthu) of this training rule arose before the subject matter of the fourth training rule, this training rule was prescribed first.
And by means of this training rule, it applies solely to a bhikkhunī.

It should be understood that while an offense was already prescribed for sitting in private with a woman, the offense for sitting in private with a woman in a secluded place above [the waist] is prescribed separately.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting in private is concluded.
The third chapter on the Bhikkhunīs is finished. 4.
The Chapter on Food.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Alms-food from a Resting Place.

206. Regarding the first training rule of the *Bhojanavagga*: "If one is able to go half a *yojana* or a *yojana*"—here, even for one who is able to go that far, if he has not obtained almsfood after going that distance, it is permissible for him to eat from here.
"Of these very ones" means of these very sectarians (*pāsaṇḍa*). "So many" means so many in this particular sect.
"One day it should be eaten" means that on one day it should be eaten only once.
From the statement "on one day it should be eaten," it should not be understood that it is permissible to eat repeatedly on that same day.
By the phrase "it is not permissible to eat again starting from the beginning," it is meant that one should not eat again at even a single place among those places where one has already eaten before.
This shows that it is not permissible to eat [the food].
Regarding the phrase "whether going or coming," they say this should be understood in terms of half a *yojana*.
The expression "at a place reached on the way" is said with reference to the property belonging to a single person. "The same principle applies even when coming" [is also said].
Explaining the meaning already stated in brief, he said, "Having gone and returning," and so forth.
Since it should be stated that there is no offense for one who eats again at the very place where the offense occurred, he did not mention eating for the first time during the going or the returning;
rather, he demonstrated eating repeatedly—once on the way and once at the place reached on a subsequent day.
However, on the day of departure and on the day of arrival, it is indeed permissible to eat while thinking, "I shall go" or "I shall return.
Even for one who eats repeatedly with a pure mind, there is no offense in eating again and again.
Since it is not permissible for a monk to accept food that has been prepared by designating it for someone else, he said, "only for the sake of the monks."
The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors in this case are: being alms-food from a public guest-house, not being ill, and eating after having stayed overnight.
The commentary on the training rule regarding alms-food from a guest-house is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating in a Group.

209. Regarding the second [offense], "having approached" means having gone near the two archers who were commissioned for the purpose of killing the Blessed One. "Concealed and hidden" means not manifest.

"He pierced" means he discharged [the arrow]. Since it is stated, "Did he not cause even the king to be killed?", it is established that this training rule was promulgated during the time of Ajātasattu; and this being so, in the subsequent supplementary rule (anupaññatti):
Now at that time, a kinsman of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha had gone forth among the Ājīvakas. Then that Ājīvaka approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha;
having approached, he said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha: “… [omitted] … being anxious, they do not accept it.”
Why was this said? It is said that the Ājīvaka gave that gift starting from the time of Bimbisāra;
later, during the time of Ajātasattu, after the precepts had been laid down, the monks, being scrupulous, did not accept that gift.
Therefore, it should be understood that this matter is shown starting from the very beginning. "Then..."
"He sent a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus"— this refers to the occasion when, from that time forward,

that Ājīvaka would occasionally invite the bhikkhus and give them alms; it was with reference to his sending a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus during the time of Ajātasattu, when the training rules had been laid down.
215. Because they are distinguished from one another, their kingdoms are dissimilar (*visadisa*); that which comes from such [kingdoms] or is born therein, or exists there, is called *verajja*.
Those very ones are the *verajjakas*. Since they, moreover, are of various kinds according to the distinctions of lineage, conduct, and so forth, it is said:
"from various kingdoms" (*nānāverajjake*). In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated: "those who have come from various other kingdoms."
The diversity of types has been stated specifically by way of the kings themselves. 217–218.

Since this training rule was formulated on the basis of the case of eating after having made a formal request (*viññatti*), group-eating (*gaṇabhojana*) is evident through the very nature of the matter (*vatthu*);
therefore, without stating that, it is said: "Group-eating means where... [etc. ...having been invited."
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), "eating" is stated as referring to group-eating (*gaṇabhojana*) specifically by way of an invitation.

However, some might suspect that "perhaps some training rule might even correspond to its own subject matter," and thus, in order to preclude that [misconception] regarding the statement in the word-commentary that group-eating occurs only by way of an invitation, [the text says]: "But this group-eating is [permitted] in two ways..."
It is said, "she gives birth. Regarding the phrase "taking the names of the five kinds of food," they say that even if it is said, "Take food," it still constitutes a group meal (*gaṇabhojana*).

"In the previous cases concerning the journey on foot and the boarding of a boat, when it was said, 'Eat right here, venerable sir,' they did not accept [the invitation] because they were afraid of wrongdoing; therefore, [in this case], when it is said, 'Eat'..."
"Even when [this] is said, it is still not a group meal (gaṇabhojana)," so it is stated in all three sections of the Gaṇṭhipada.

However, because it is stated that "one invites after taking the names of the five kinds of food," it constitutes a group meal only when the name of the food is taken by saying, "Eat rice," or "Eat the meal," and not otherwise. [For example: "Venerable sir, please eat right here."
In this case as well, it should be understood that they invited them only after saying "rice" or "boiled rice.
Alternatively, because they were invited by a group, those bhikkhus, out of ingratitude and fearing wrongdoing, did not accept;
this is our own view, but one should investigate and adopt what is more appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "taking from one side": here it should be understood that they are said to "take from one side" when they stand holding each other's hands at a distance of twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*).

This is because of the statement, "They might request, 'Give almsfood to all four of us,'" and because of the preceding statement, "Having requested thus: 'You give almsfood to one bhikkhu, you [give] to two.'"
It should be understood that even for one who consents to a request made by others for their own sake, it indeed constitutes *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group).
Thus, regarding the phrase "it arises from a request," when there is a request and those receiving eat together as one, an offense occurs under this training rule;
however, if they eat separately, an offense should be understood to occur through the specific requests for fine foods, such as rice-soup and boiled rice.
"Vicāreti" means he arranges it by way of five sections and so forth. "Ghaṭṭeti" means having cut it along the grain, he presses it with his hand or with a stick.
"Suttaṃ karoti" means he rolls it into thread. "Valeti" means he twists it upon a stick or in his hand.
"The making of a brand-new robe is what is meant here by 'robe-making' (cīvarakamma); [this does not apply] to an old robe."

They say, "There is no such thing as 'needle-work' (sūcikamma). They say, "Because of the statement, 'If they do not finish eating when a fourth person has arrived,' if there is no one else coming and the four who are sitting there themselves are unable to finish eating, it is not allowable.
It is called "an improper invitation" because it constitutes an invitation that gives rise to the offense of eating in a group. "Having made them enter" means...
“Having made them sit. “The group is split” means that the group does not incur an offense; this is the intended meaning.
Because of the connection with the canonical text, “Where four bhikkhus... eat,” it is said: “But he [the fifth] is the one who completes the group for the others.
“Without distinction” means without specifying, such as “one who is ill or one making robes,” but by using a term common to all.
Therefore, because there is no distinction [between them]. Regarding the phrase "when they have eaten and departed":

here, it is permissible to take [the food] even when they have not yet departed, provided the act of eating has been completed. Furthermore, as for the statement "those were not taken together by them":

those foods with which there was no disagreement regarding the meal were not taken together by those monks, because one of them was taken later by a single person. The term "Mahāthera" refers to the monks.
It has been stated. Furthermore, it was said "without standing at the village gate" out of fear that the messenger might return along the path and say, "Take food.
"Going here and there" means going to the presence of those standing in various places such as the middle of the street.
This same rule applies even when [food] is given after being placed at the door of a house for the sake of the bhikkhus. "Return," they say.
It is permissible to turn back at the point where it was said [to turn back]; because the words were spoken in sequence as “Turn back” and subsequently “Take food,” it is permissible.
The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are: eating in a group, the absence of a [proper] occasion, and the act of swallowing.
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating in a group is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule regarding eating in succession: 221.
In the third [rule], because it is given continuously by following the sequence of families without interruption, it is called "the sequence of meals" (*bhattapaṭipāṭi*).
“It does not stand still,” as it is said in the Pāḷi; this means that it proceeds without interruption, not stopping in between.
“By way of proximity” (upacāravasena) means by way of conventional usage (vohāravasena). For he does not give only the actual jujube fruit itself, but speaks thus by way of proximity.
That which is prepared with jujube powder, sugar, and so forth, is called “jujube salad” (badarasāḷava).

226. Since that food becomes non-existent by the very act of assignment (*vikappanā*), the assignment was set aside by way of a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*), and only the training precept (*sikkhāpada*) as originally laid down was established.

However, in the *Parivāra*, it is stated that there are "four subsequent rules" (*catasso anupaññattiyo*), treating even the permission for assignment as being equivalent to a subsequent rule. This refers to the method explained in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other such texts.
By speaking later in accordance with the Canon, he established that it was indeed an *aparamukhā-vikappanā* (assignment not in the presence [of the recipient]). However, some maintain:
"At that time, because there was no one else besides the Blessed One whom he could have placed near himself, the Elder did not perform an *sammukhā-vikappanā*.
Furthermore, the Blessed One did not explicitly state that an *sammukhā-vikappanā* must be performed separately; nevertheless, an *sammukhā-vikappanā* is also [valid]."
"It is allowable," they say. For that very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, it is stated:

"If a bhikkhu, regarding one among five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, says either in their presence, 'I give my expected meal to you,' or 'I assign it to you,' or in their absence, 'I give it to so-and-so,' or 'I assign it to so-and-so'—this constitutes the first invitation."

It is stated: "If, without having made a formal assignment (*avikappetvā*), one swallows even a single grain of rice from alms-food obtained at a family to which one was invited later, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

(229) Regarding the phrase "eating in succession" (*paramparabhojana*): for one who has been invited with five kinds of food, to eat the food of this or that [family] in reverse order from whichever one he was first invited, without having made a formal assignment, is called "eating in succession. Thus it says: "If..."
"However, the root invitation is at the bottom, and each subsequent one is above it; for one who eats starting from the top, there is an offense.
Having inserted the hand inside and taking the very bottom one, even that which stands in the middle has entered the hand;
thus he said: "But having inserted the hand... [or] for one who eats in whatever manner..."
“There is no offense. Because the milk and the juice remain on top without being mixed with the solid food, it is said:
“There is no offense for one drinking the milk or the juice.
“The great lay follower” refers to the head of the household. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, by the statement “there is an offense,” whereas in the *Kuruṇḍī* it says “it is permissible.”
"It appears as if the statements are contradictory, yet the intention of both is clarified in the *Mahāpaccarī*," so it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*.
"They all invite" means they invite with an improper invitation (*akappiya-nimantanā*). "'Successive eating' (*paramparabhojana*) means:
having been invited with one of the five kinds of cooked food, setting that aside, [to eat] another of the five..."
Because it is said, “He eats any one of the various kinds of food;
this is called ‘successive eating’ (paramparabhojana),” it is stated that even though alms-round is what is first obtained, “if he eats food obtained by wandering for alms, there is an offense.
It is described as “verbal action” (vacīkamma) by way of non-intimation (avikappa). The rest here is self-evident. [The section on] successive eating.
The absence of an agreement and the act of swallowing—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating in succession is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Kāṇamātā.
230–231. Regarding the fourth [case], "the mother of Kāṇā": this refers to the mother of the girl who had received the name Kāṇā.
As to why she was born with the name Kāṇā, he said, "It is said that of her... and so forth. When this girl was young, her parents, out of affection, addressed her as "Dear Kāṇā, dear Kāṇā";
from that time on, she became known by the name Kāṇā, and her mother was called "Kāṇamātā" (the Mother of Kāṇā).
"It became manifest"—thus they state the reason here. "The opposite direction" (*paṭiyālōka*) means the western direction;

"the reverse of the sun" (*paccādicca*) is what is meant. 233. "An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the count of cakes": this refers to an offense of expiation according to the number of cakes remaining above the lower rim of the mouth of the bowl.
For, from the statement "two or three bowlfuls may be accepted," it follows that [the limit] is the lower rim of the mouth of the bowl.
It is permissible to take two or three bowlfuls without exceeding [the limit].
As for the statement in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) that “...,” this was stated merely to indicate that such a passage occurs in the commentaries;
it was not stated for the purpose of establishing that particular position. For what is stated in the commentaries is not necessarily [identical to] the canonical text (pāḷi).
It does not agree with the Pāḷi. For it is stated, "from relatives" and "from those who have invited [one]," in order to show that there is no offense when receiving more than that [limit].

Otherwise, since the absence of an offense would already be established by the phrase, "there is no offense if one receives two or three bowlfuls," because that itself constitutes receiving a quantity that is within the proper measure, the words "from relatives" and "from those who have invited" would not need to be stated separately. If this is so, then [the statement] "it does not agree with the Pāḷi" [is incorrect].
Why was it not stated? It was not stated because it can be understood by the same method as that explained in the preceding training rule (sikkhāpada). For it was said there:

"In the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), however, it is stated that at a place where one is invited by relatives, even a large amount is permissible in its normal course, whereas for the purpose of preventing theft, only a measured amount is permissible;
this does not agree with the Canon (pāḷi). [And: "For the sake of those who have no provisions for a journey, etc."
Even for one who takes [food] with the perception that it has been "prepared," there is indeed an offense, because the training rule (sikkhāpada) is unintentional (*acittaka*).
It is called "verbal action" (*vacīkamma*) because an offense is incurred even by saying, "Give this into his hand," for the purpose of having it taken by oneself. The rest is self-evident.
[The factors are: the state of being cakes or dough as described, the state of not being left over, the state of not having ceased the journey, and the state of not being a relative and so forth.
"Accepting an excess" refers here to these five factors.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Invitation (Pavāraṇā).
236. *Bhuttāvī* means those who have eaten (*bhuttāvino*, *bhuttavanto*); it is said that they have completed their meal-duty (*katabhattakicca*). Regarding *pavāritā*:

among the four kinds of invitations (*pavāraṇā*), both the invitation to eat as much as desired (*yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*) and the invitation involving a refusal (*paṭikkhepa-pavāraṇā*) are applicable here; thus he says, "by the brahmin... [etc.

...invited by way of a refusal-invitation. For the invitation is fourfold: the invitation at the end of the rains-retreat (*vassaṃvuttha-pavāraṇā*), the invitation regarding requisites (*paccaya-pavāraṇā*), [the invitation to eat as much as desired, and the invitation involving a refusal].

There are the invitation by way of refusal and the invitation for as much as needed. In this context, "I allow, monks, that monks who have completed the rains residence invite one another on three grounds"—this is the invitation for those who have completed the rains residence.

It is called *pavāraṇā* because by means of it one causes [the Sangha] to invite [others] regarding what has been seen and so forth, distributes [the merit] among the Sangha and others, and makes it a shared meal; it is the relinquishing of oneself and the granting of space for the purification of offenses.
Since it is stated that this [invitation] is generally to be performed by those who have completed the rains-residence,

it is called the "Invitation of Those Who Have Completed the Rains-Residence" (*vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā*). Furthermore, regarding the phrases, "Venerable sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha for four months with medicine," and "except for the [regular] invitation and except for the permanent invitation," this is the "invitation based on requisites" (*paccayapavāraṇā*), which invites one to requisites.
It is called *pavāreti* because one causes [the other] to desire [food] by means of this; it is a designation for an invitation with robes and so forth.
“One is said to be *pavārita* when food is perceived, a meal is perceived, [the donor] stands within arm’s reach and offers [it], and a refusal is perceived—this is what is called *pavārita*.
This is the *pavāraṇā* consisting of a refusal (*paṭikkhepa-pavāraṇā*). It is accompanied by five factors, such as the fact that the meal has not yet been commenced.
In this context, *pavāraṇā* means a refusal that is appropriate for the manner [of the request], namely, the very refusal of food.

“He personally satisfied and served him with choice hard foods and soft foods” refers to the *yāvadattha-pavāraṇā* (invitation to eat as much as desired). An invitation to food until one’s need is satisfied is a *yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*.

237. The statement, “It is permissible to say [it] without using the word *ti*,” etc., is said for the purpose of showing the manner in which it should be spoken. However, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that “even when the word *ti* is used, it does not mean that [the invitation] has not been performed.

238–239. *Pavārito* means one who has been refused. For when someone, while eating, refuses food brought by a server because they do not wish for it, they are called *pavārito*, meaning they have been refused by him. As for the curry (*byañjana*), however—
In order to show merely the essential meaning without taking [the literal wording] into account, it is said:

"one who has performed the invitation and one who has performed the refusal. Since the meaning of the term "one who has eaten" (*bhuttāvī*) is already expressed by the word "food" (*āsana*) itself, no separate purpose for that [term] is found.
For if such a purpose were found, the invitation would result in being endowed with six factors.
Having taken this into account, he cites the canonical text beginning with “And it has been said” in order to demonstrate precisely the state of being endowed with the five factors.
However, some, treating “standing within arm’s reach and offering [the invitation]” as a single factor,
assert that “the invitation is endowed with four factors.”
"Such as sour milk-rice (*ambilapāyāsa*), etc."—by the word "etc.," milk-rice (*khīrapāyāsa*) and so forth are included.
Therein, by the mention of sour milk-rice, thick gruel mixed with sour substances such as buttermilk is meant; by the mention of milk-rice, gruel mixed with milk is included.
"It does not produce an invitation" means it does not effect the prohibition that is the basis for the offense of eating what is not left over (*anatirittabhojana*). Even if it has been [prepared]...
The rejection [of the rule] is not the cause for the offense of eating what is not left over; therefore, it remains in its very original place.

Thus it is said: "it does not produce an invitation (*pavāraṇa*). Regarding the word *yāgu*, since it is common to both the *yāgu* that produces an invitation and other types of *yāgu*, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"Even when it is said, 'Take the *yāgu*,' there is an invitation; thus, it certainly produces an invitation."
That which was stated does not agree with the reason given later in that very same passage, namely, “having brought rice gruel mixed with cooked food. For it is stated there:

“In the case of an invitation where no rice gruel is served, there is an *pavāraṇā* (invitation) because they say ‘take rice gruel’ while referring specifically to cooked food that has been kneaded together with water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth; [but] when it is mixed with cooked food...”
Regarding the phrase "having brought rice-gruel," since rice-gruel exists separately here, there is no *pavāraṇā*.

Therefore, the reason should be stated as follows: because it was said, "Take rice-gruel," referring specifically to the cooked rice (*bhatta*) mixed with milk and so forth according to the method explained therein, and because rice-gruel itself is not present there, there is a *pavāraṇā*. For it is thus...
If [the fish or meat] exists, it also accords with the reason stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Because of the presence of the person by whom one was requested”;
otherwise, a contradiction between earlier and later passages would arise within the *Gaṇṭhipada* itself, and it would not agree with the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
By the phrase “if... it is discerned,” the mere existence of a piece of fish or meat, or of sinew, of the size specified is indicated.
[The text] shows this. "By those" means by various [grains].
"Gruel made from rice, paddy, and barley" is stated according to the general rule; however, even that which is made from seven types of grain after they have been roasted is indeed just gruel.
For this very reason, it says: "Kangu, varaka... [and so on]... all fall under the category of gruel. "Gruel-cake" (sattumodaka).

“Uncooked sugar-cane juice” (*sattuguḷa*) is unrefined sugar-cane juice made by concentrating the sap. Because the state of being “unfinished food” (*vippakatabhojana*)—by virtue of being one of the five kinds of edible foods—has been interrupted, it is said:
“Not even a mustard-seed’s worth [of such food] remains in the mouth... [etc. ... nor does he invite [others to eat]. From the statement, “He rejects unallowable meat;
he does not invite,” it follows that if, whether knowing or not knowing, he realizes that a gain belonging to the Saṅgha will not reach him... [etc. ... [he may still eat].

Or he rejects [the invitation]; he does not perform the *pavāraṇā* because that which ought to be rejected has already been rejected. Even one who rejects what belongs to an unscrupulous person (*alajjin*) does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
"Because of the lack of a basis" means because the *pavāraṇā*—which establishes the offense for eating non-leftovers (*anatiritta*)—lacks a foundation.
By this, he illustrates the state of having already rejected that which ought to be rejected. For whatever is indeed to be rejected, [if it has been rejected, the *pavāraṇā* is not performed].
The refusal of that [offering] does not constitute a factor of an offense; therefore, it is said to be "not a basis for the invitation.

By the word "offers," he shows physical prostration. Even if one standing outside arm’s reach has the intention to give, for one who refuses, the invitation is absent precisely because of the distance;
thus, even in the case of the Elder, only the mere fact of distance is taken into account.
Showing the absence of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he said, "Because of the elder’s distance," but not because of the presence of an actual bringing (*abhihāra*) by the elder.
Even if one who has gone after taking [the food] stands within arm's reach, since he stands in the place of the support without saying anything, it is not called a "bringing";
thus it was said, "And because of the messenger’s non-bringing. "By him who has gone after taking [it], ‘Food...’"

In all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: "When it is said, 'Take [it],' this is called an *abhihāra* (offering). However, if a monk has come after taking [the food], ... [as it is said] ... there is an *pavāraṇā* (invitation). Some, however, say:
"It should be understood that it was said, 'Take this meal,' after having presented something toward the bowl. This appears to be reasonable.
Because the verbal offering is not intended here.
"In the dining hall" means in the refectory. "It has already been brought" means it has been brought by the server himself.
Regarding the statement, "There is an invitation for one who refuses someone wishing to give from that," here there is an invitation even for one who refuses someone who does not take [the food].
It indeed exists. Why? Because it has been brought forward out of a desire to give. For it is said: “Therefore, that [gift] is indeed one that has been brought forward.

For this very reason, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated: “When there is a bringing forward out of a desire to give, the mere act of taking [the gift] with the thought ‘I shall give’ does not constitute what is called ‘bringing forward’;
rather, whether one takes it or not while thinking ‘I shall give,’ it is precisely the bringing forward out of a desire to give that is called ‘bringing forward.’”
"Therefore, whether at the time of taking it or at the time of not taking it, for one who rejects it, there is an invitation (pavāraṇā). This was said.

Now, in order to show that even at the time of taking it, there is no invitation for one who rejects it if there has been no request from the one wishing to give it when it is absent, "But if... and so forth was said.
Because it was said, "Take the broth," while mentioning the name of the person who offered the invitation, it is stated that "there is no invitation for one who rejects it upon hearing that.
However, in the phrase "fish-broth" (*maccharasaṃ*) or "meat-broth" (*maṃsarasaṃ*), it is not understood merely as "the broth of fish" (*macchassa rasaṃ*);
rather, it means "the fish and the broth of the fish" (*maccho ca maccharasañca*).
Thus, because it is understood even by way of the common name that generates an invitation (*pavāraṇā*), for one who rejects it, there is indeed an invitation.
The same principle applies to the subsequent phrase, "fish curry.

Regarding the phrase, "even when told, 'Take this,'" although it is not stated in this specific way, if anything sufficient to constitute an invitation is brought forward, there is still an invitation for one who rejects it.
It should be seen. "Karambaka" is a designation for a mixture. For whatever they prepare by mixing various ingredients together is called "karambaka.

Even if it has been prepared mixed with meat, because it was stated by name as something fit for an invitation when saying, "Take the karambaka," there is no valid invitation for one who refuses it. "Meat-karambaka..."

When it is said, "Take [it]," however, it means "Take it mixed with meat"; therefore, it constitutes an invitation (*pavāraṇā*). Regarding the phrase "thinking it was prepared specifically for him," they say:

"Because the substance is allowable (*kappiya*), even if one rejects it due to a perception that it is unallowable (*akappiya*), there is still an invitation under this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) because of the absence of intentional wrongdoing.
This refers to the previous instance of being invited to a meal where no rice gruel (*yāgu*) was served.

They say that because it was said, "Take rice gruel," with reference specifically to rice that has been kneaded together with water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth, there is an *pavāraṇā* (invitation);
however, in the case of the statement, "Having brought rice gruel mixed with food," since the rice gruel exists separately [from the food], there is no *pavāraṇā*.
This is the intended meaning here; thus, the very matter stated by the passage beginning with "by whom [he] was asked" [is explained].
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). As for the reason here, it is difficult to see; regarding this, some first say:

"Because that which is called 'mixed with rice-gruel' (*yāgumissaka*) is not merely a meal (*bhatta*), but is indeed milk and so forth as well, therefore—as in the case of *karambaka*—there should be no invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
And this being so, if the rice-gruel is more abundant or equal [in quantity], one does not invite. [For instance,] 'the rice-gruel is thin...'"
"Regarding the statement, 'The meal is more abundant; he invites [him to eat],' the reason for this is difficult to see. Some, however, say:
"A meal mixed with rice-gruel is what is meant by 'meal'; therefore, for one who refuses it, there must necessarily be an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
And this being the case, the reason why it is said, 'In this instance there is an invitation, in that there is not,' is difficult to see."
And just as the reason here is difficult to see, so too it should be understood that the reason for the statement "take them mixed" in the subsequent passage is equally difficult to see.
For the smallness or largeness of those sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is not the cause for the presence or absence of the invitation;
rather, in this case, the mere mention of the name of the one who generates the invitation is the authority. Therefore, [the text says]: "And this with the *karambaka*..."
Even the reason stated in the passage beginning with "it should not be brought together," when compared with what was said previously,
does not accord. For if the term "mixed" were established as referring only to food mixed [with other substances],

then, just as when it is said, "Take the food-mixed [alms]," one would still perform the *pavāraṇā* (invitation to stop eating) regardless of whether the food is more, equal, or less [than the non-food portion].
Likewise, even when it is said, “Take mixed [food],” there must be an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) even if the food is less than that;
for “mixed” is a conventional term used specifically for food that is mixed. Thus, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
“Because ‘mixed’ is a conventional expression used specifically for food that is mixed, this, however, is stated as ‘only food that is mixed. Now, regarding “mixed”:
The term "mixed" (*missaka*) does not apply to rice mixed with other foods; rather, it was said, "Take the mixed," with reference specifically to mixed rice.

Thus, just as when one is invited to a meal that is not yet gruel, and the statement "Take the gruel" is made with reference only to rice that has been kneaded together with milk and so forth, the formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is valid; so too here, the statement "the mixed" refers only to mixed rice.
When it is said, "Take [it]," whether the food be little or much, there should indeed be an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
Therefore, whether the term "mixed" (*missaka*) refers to the conventional usage for mixed food, or was spoken with a specific intention, in either case the earlier and the later do not agree;
so what is the use of investigating the reason here? In such instances, one must proceed solely by the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*—this is our position.
"‘He gives after separating’ means he gives having taken out the sauce and so forth that is on top of the rice," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, some have said: "He presses firmly with his hand and strains it so that no rice grains fall.
Even so, no reason for this is seen; for [the rule applies] to whatever is mixed with the rice.
When one has brought rice gruel and, having said, "Take the rice gruel," refuses it even as the other offers food mixed with the gruel,
there is no *pavāraṇā*. Likewise here, when among foods containing much milk, curd, and so forth, one says, "Take the milk," etc.,
whether the other then gives the milk and such items alone, or food mixed with the milk and such, in either case there must be no *pavāraṇā*.
Therefore, the statement “he gives having set it aside” refers to giving in that specific manner;
it should not be understood as showing that the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) occurs for one who rejects what is being given mixed with food.

However, if the intention were that the invitation occurs when what is being given is mixed with food, then [the commentary] would have said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “having set it aside... [and so forth].
Thus it is said; therefore, in this matter, the commentary alone should be accepted as the authority, and no other reason should be sought.
If one sits in a squatting posture (*ukkuṭika*) without letting go of the feet and thus sits upon the ground, one is indeed disturbing the posture (*iriyāpatha*).
Therefore, so that one may sit comfortably without disturbing the squatting posture, [it says]: "But beneath that... [the] sitting-cloth."
It is stated: "It should be given. Regarding the phrase "without moving from one's seat": this means without releasing the flesh of the buttocks from the spot touched by the bench;

that is to say, "without rising. It is further stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "one must not consider the shifting of position as [a factor] like the offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*)."

Regarding the term *akappiyakataṃ* (made unallowable): because that which has been made unallowable itself lacks the status of being "leftover" (*anatiritta*), the roots, fruits, and so forth placed in that bowl before making them allowable are not considered leftover; however, the rest contained within the bowl is indeed leftover and may be consumed.
One who wishes to consume those roots, fruits, and so forth should take them out from there...
Having had it made allowable (*kappiya*) and having placed it in another vessel, one should eat it after having it declared as leftover (*atiritta*).

He is not permitted to do it again; because what is being done in that very same vessel becomes "done together" with what was first made allowable, he is not permitted to do it himself again, though another may. However, in another vessel, by him—
Or it is permissible for someone else to do it. Therefore he said: "That by which it was not done, by that it must be done; and that which was not done, that must be done.
In the phrase "by that also," the word *pi* (also) indicates not only the sense of "by another," but this further meaning as well.
"Done in this way" means done in another vessel. "Having sent" means having sent it into the hand of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). Of this...
Because it constitutes an act of discipline (*vinayakamma*), it is stated: "One must not cause [food] held in the hand of one who is not fully ordained to be made [into *atiritta*].

However, regarding the phrase "if they are mixed with food," it should be understood that if they are mixed even with food that has been taken into the mouth and is not yet leftover (*anatiritta*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Therefore, one who has already finished eating should have the food made into a leftover.
Even while eating, one should eat having made the mouth and hands clean so that it is not mixed with what has not been formally offered;

for although there is no offense even for one who has not been invited to eat things such as *yāmakālika* (medicines to be taken at the proper time) for the purpose of food before the meal, once invited, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) rooted in the invitation itself. Thus: "The *yāmakālika*... [and so on]... upon swallowing."
“There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” so it is stated in the Canon.
241. It is said to be “by body and speech” because one commits the offense by eating with the body or by commanding [another] with speech to make [the food] non-remaining (atiritta).
The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are: the state of having been invited to eat, the fact that the food is not non-remaining, and the swallowing at the proper time.
These, however, are the three factors here.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning invitation is finished.
6. Commentary on the second training rule concerning invitation.
243. Regarding the sixth [offense], "it is indeed common": it is common to the invitation (pavāraṇā) expressed by such phrases as, "Come, monk, eat," and so forth.
Because it is stated in the Mātikā that "when he has eaten, there is an offense of expiation" (pācittiya), the offense occurs at the conclusion of the meal, not with every single mouthful.
"If one invites him to bring food, there is an offense of expiation"—this too refers precisely to the conclusion of the meal.
It should be understood that this was spoken with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). The rest here is self-evident.

However, the five factors in this case are: the state of having been invited (*pavāritatā*), the perception of having been invited (*pavāritasaññitā*), the expectation of reproach (*āsādanāpekkhatā*), the invitation to bring food that is not left over (*anatirittena abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāraṇā*), and the conclusion of the meal (*bhojanapariyosāna*).
The commentary on the second training rule concerning invitations is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating at Improper Times 247.

Regarding the seventh [training rule], "the foremost performance" (*aggasamajja*) refers to the most excellent dance. It is said that this is performed by standing upon a mountain peak in honor of a particular deity.
"Dances and plays of actors" (*naṭanāṭakāni*) refers to dramas such as *Sītāharaṇa* (The Abduction of Sītā) and others. "When the training rule has not yet been laid down" (*apaññatte sikkhāpade*).
When the training rule regarding those under twenty years of age had not yet been laid down, they "gave" [the food] by saying, "Take it to the monastery and eat it.

248–249. The radish-root, the root of the radish, and so forth are to be understood from the commentary (*upadesa*) alone; for even if these were stated by means of synonyms, they could not be understood.
Indeed, even when stated with synonyms, there would be only confusion for those who do not know those respective names.
Since it may be so, we shall say nothing further on that point. "The purpose of solid food" (*khādanīyattha*) means the function to be performed by solid food.

"They do not suffice" means they do not produce [the necessary result]. Regarding the phrase "in various districts," some say: "If it accomplishes the function of food in one district, it is not allowable in other districts.
"Of trees, creepers, and so forth" has already been explained above.
This was stated by way of summary. "That which has gone into the inner earth" is said with reference to the trunk of the *sālakalyāṇī* tree.

"All allowable things" means that they are entirely allowable by way of their roots, trunks, bark, leaves, and so forth. The connection is that it is not possible to show the limit of even those [allowable things] by way of their names.
In order to show that the fruits of the *acchi* and other such trees are life-long (*yāvajīvika*) only when unripe:
“Unripe” is what was stated.
Regarding the phrase “the bones of harītakī and so forth,” the teachers maintain that the shells situated covering the marrow (miñja) are lifetime-medicines (yāvajīvika).
Some say that the marrow itself is also a lifetime-medicine. *Hiṅgu* is the resin exuding from the *hiṅgu* tree; *hiṅgujatu* and so forth are also [included].
These are simply varieties of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). In this context, "asafoetida extract" (*hiṅgujatu*) refers to a decoction made by boiling the stalks and leaves of the asafoetida tree;
"asafoetida powder" (*hiṅgusipāṭika*) refers to a powder made by drying and grinding the leaves of the asafoetida plant.

Some also say it is "made by mixing with other [substances]. "Clarified butter" (*taka*) is the solid residue that has emerged from the surface; "clarified butter from a vessel" (*takapatti*) is the solid residue that has emerged from the bottom of a vessel.
*Takapaṇṇi* refers to a paste made by roasting *palāsa* leaves. Some also say it is a paste extracted from a stalk.

The rest here is self-evident. However, these three factors are present here: being at the wrong time (*vikālatā*), being suitable for the proper time (*yāvakālikatā*), and swallowing (*ajjhoharaṇa*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating at the wrong time is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing (Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada) 252–3.

Regarding the eighth [rule], "such-like" refers to that which lacks soup or condiment. In the phrase "whatever is either for-the-time-being (yāvakālika) or for-the-watch (yāmakālika)," by the term "for-the-watch," it is shown that the offense of expiation (pācittiya) due to storing applies not only to things for-the-time-being, but also to those for-the-watch.

This, then, shows that it applies even to what is for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*). But is it not the case that what is for the watch of the night is included neither among things to be chewed (*khādanīya*) nor among things to be eaten (*bhojanīya*)?
For this very reason, in the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*), it says: "What is called 'things to be chewed' refers to the five kinds of cooked food;
excluding what is for the watch of the night, what is for seven days, and what is for life, the remainder is called 'things to be chewed. What is called 'things to be eaten' refers to the five..."
It is stated, "foods," and it is also stated, "Whatever monk should eat or consume solid food or soft food that has been stored, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Therefore, how is it understood that there must be an offense of expiation regarding what is for the duration of a watch of the night (yāmakālika)? It is said:
in order to show the meaning of the word "solid food" (khādanīya) in the word-commentary (padabhājana), [it says] "what is for the duration of a watch of the night..."
The phrase "excepting" was stated not for the purpose of showing that there is no offense due to the condition of storage (*sannidhi*).

For what is intended by "whatever may be eaten" is solid food (*khādanīya*); and among the medicines for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*), there is nothing to be eaten because they are meant to be drunk.
Therefore, although the medicine for the watch of the night is not included within solid or soft foods, nevertheless, by one who intends to show that there is no offense—

From the statement, “There is no offense if one eats after storing it for a watch of the night,” it is understood that once the watch has passed, there must be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) due to the condition of storage.

This same point is also established by the following: “Monks, what is allowable for a watch of the night—whether it be [food] allowable for seven days or [food] allowable for as long as life—is permissible during that watch if received on that very day; once the watch has passed, it is not permissible.”

For this very reason, the Aṭṭhakathācariyas, who understood the Blessed One’s intention, stated that there is an offense of *pācittiya* for what is to be consumed during the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
This was said with reference specifically to the act of receiving; for once it has been received, there is no further need for the act of receiving.
It is for this reason that it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "In the case of one who receives with the desire to swallow it, [the offense occurs] at the moment of receiving."
However, it is stated [in the Vinaya]: "In the case of one who takes [food] with the intention, 'I shall swallow it,' there is an offense in the receiving.

"Yaṃ" means that bowl. "Sandissati" means it appears on top of the rice gruel. Even though there is no oily substance in a bowl that has the color of oil, when one rubs it with a finger, a streak is discerned by way of its color;
therefore, to show that there is no offense in that case, it is said: "That is not subject to censure (abbohārikā)."
It has been stated: "Having accepted it oneself, it is not permissible on the second day as long as it has not been relinquished.
Here, by means of giving away without regard for the acceptance, or by giving to one who is not ordained without regard for it, the acceptance is abandoned;
thus, by the term "not relinquished," both ways of not having abandoned the acceptance are expressed. Therefore...

It should be understood that even if one has relinquished something to another, if it is not yet relinquished with respect to its acceptance—meaning the act of relinquishing was done without regard for its being accepted—that too is permissible on the second day.
If this is so, why is an offense stated in such cases as "the bowl is not properly washed"? [The answer is: because the acceptance has not been relinquished.

In all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: "If one has made [the bowl] empty by oneself or by another, but has not washed it properly and then finished using it, even if food adheres to it, it is still considered 'not relinquished' (*avijahita-paṭiggahaṇa*);

therefore, there is an offense in that case. "It is permissible; that which has not been relinquished is not permissible"—thus they say that even when the acceptance [of the gift] has been relinquished through the state of being without attachment, it is not permissible for one who is not fully ordained if it has not been relinquished. This does not appear to be reasonable.
For at the very moment that the acceptance is relinquished, at that same moment one does not create storage (sannidhi) of what has had its acceptance relinquished.

Because it is similar to what has not been formally accepted (*appaṭiggahita*). Furthermore, an offense due to storage (*sannidhi-paccaya*) is stated only in the case of what has been accepted and then stored.
For it is said: "This is a designation for that which has been accepted and spent for one night. In the Pali, it is stated:
"If one accepts seven-day medicine or lifetime medicine for the purpose of food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so forth.

Since it has been stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for swallowing [food] before the meal when seven-day or lifelong medicines are available, there must likewise be a separate offense of wrong-doing for swallowing [it] as food during the watch of the night; thus he said:

"For one who swallows it for the purpose of food, there is a *pācittiya* together with the *dukkaṭa*. Regarding "ordinary meat" (*pakati-āmiṣa*), this refers to allowable meats such as boiled rice and so forth.

Regarding "two [offenses] for one who, when there is a requisite, swallows with a mouth containing food": if one consumes yesterday’s *yāmaka*-time [food] received today before the meal with a mouth containing food, there is one *pācittiya* due to the requisite of stored *yāmaka*-time [food], and one [other *pācittiya*] due to the requisite of food mixed with what was stored;
thus, there are two *pācittiya*s. "In both cases" means with a mouth containing food.

"Without worldly motives" refers to the two methods previously described. "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) increases" means that an offense of wrong-doing increases on account of swallowing for the purpose of food.

"Both a grave offense (thullaccaya) and an offense of wrong-doing increase" means that a grave offense increases in the case of human flesh, while an offense of wrong-doing increases in the case of other unallowable meats.
255. Regarding "there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the condition of receiving": here, because it is stored, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing even for taking before the meal.

However, if there is a valid reason, there is no offense at all for one who takes and consumes even what has been stored, provided it is for seven days or for as long as life lasts, for the purpose of medicine.
The rest here is self-evident. [This concerns] the state of being for the duration of the day and the duration of the watch.
The state of being stored up and its consumption—these are the three factors here.

257–259. In the ninth [section], "refined foods" refers to foods mixed with refined [ingredients].

These are what are called [meats]; for the purpose of showing their classification, the passage beginning with “that is to say: ghee, fresh butter,” etc., was spoken in the Pāḷi.

For it is not the case that ghee and other such items [are forbidden] because they belong to beings whose meat is unallowable.

Regarding the term *sappibhatta* (ghee-rice): although it can be understood as "rice mixed with ghee" (*sappisaṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ*), and also as "ghee and rice" (*sappi ca bhattañca*), in the commentaries it is explained as being like "*sālibhatta*" (rice-gruel).
Having stated the reason, "There is no such thing as rice with ghee," and having made the *dukkaṭa* offense even more firm because it was so stated, it is not possible to say anything else.
For the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*) alone are the authority in such instances.
"Root" is said with reference to allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*). "No offense" means that due to the absence of a prior agreement (*visaṅketa*), there is no offense at all.
There is no offense. However, some say, "The absence of offense is stated only with regard to the *pācittiya*;
there is nevertheless an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for requesting soup and rice. That should not be accepted.

Furthermore, the terms "permissible ghee" and "impermissible ghee" are stated by way of permissible and impermissible meat; therefore, they mean "ghee from permissible meat" and "ghee from impermissible meat."
In this context, the meaning should be understood in this way. "Having various bases" is said with reference to ghee, fresh butter, and so forth.
261. Regarding the rule that one must be dealt with according to the Mahānāma-sikkhāpada:

"A monk who is not ill may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation; if he should accept beyond that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)."

This is the Mahānāma training rule (sikkhāpada). By means of this training rule, in a place where an invitation regarding the requisite for the sick has been extended by the Saṅgha, if a limit has been set there—either by saying "only so many nights" or "only so many medicines may be requested"—then [one must not request more] than that limit of nights or that limit of medicines.
If, however, beyond that limit of nights or that limit of medicines...

Furthermore, it has been stated that there is an offense of expiation for one who requests medicine for a purpose other than the need for medicine, or requests one medicine for a purpose other than the need for that medicine.

Therefore, when one who is not ill perceives himself as being ill and requests the five kinds of medicine, he is not one who "requests medicine for the purpose of needing medicine" [in the sense prohibited] by the Mahānāma training rule. Thus...
“It should be made to be done,” it is said. These “bases for confession” (pāṭidesanīyavatthu) are stated with reference to the ghee and so forth mentioned in the Canon.
However, it should be understood that those things not mentioned in the Canon, such as unallowable ghee and so forth, are bases for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even for bhikkhunīs.
Regarding the phrase “in the soliciting of curry and boiled rice”: these are bases for a pācittiya offense for bhikkhus, but they are bases for a pāṭidesanīya offense for bhikkhunīs.
This was stated with reference to the remaining modes of requesting, setting aside [the specific case]. The rest here is self-evident.

However, the four factors in this case are: the food being of a superior kind, the person not being ill, the obtaining [of it] through a request that was not made [by oneself], and the swallowing [of it].
The commentary on the training rule concerning superior food is finished.

264. "The mouth-door" means the throat-pipe. "Food" refers to anything that is to be swallowed, such as the *yāvakālika* (food to be consumed at the proper time) and so forth.

"Not being ill" refers to one who, being sick and unable to consume food with their own hands, receives it with the mouth. "Merely for the purpose of uttering" means...

Everything that is bound by both ends is indeed already accepted. However, as for the juice dripping from sugarcane being pressed for the sake of a monk standing within arm's reach...

It is permissible to take [the juice]; it is also permissible to take sugarcane juice that is flowing of its own accord from a trough, even if one has repeatedly blocked the middle and then released it.

In certain commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the term *asaṃhārima* means "that which cannot be carried by a man of medium strength. This is because of the statement: "on leaves such as those of the *tintiṇika* tree."
It should be understood that receiving [food] on the branches is permissible. Regarding the phrase "having wiped and received," some say:

"Or even without [the bowl] being released. Regarding "of those who cause to waver," it means "of those who cause to move"; this is indeed the reading. Because [the food] has been brought and placed on the ground, there is no "bringing forward" (abhihāra);

Therefore, regarding what is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "In the phrase 'that which is being given falls,' here, just as group-meals (*gaṇabhojana*) and so forth are permitted for those who are ill or otherwise apprehensive, [so too is this]."
"In this case as well, it was already accepted by the Blessed One and then permitted for the purpose of dispelling anxiety"—this should not be accepted.
Because it is stated without distinction that "when it is being given, it falls," this principle should be understood to apply to all four time-periods (kālika).

"With a knife" means with a knife that has been accepted. But why, in this context, [is there mention of] the condition of what has been stored (uggahita-paccaya) and the condition of what has been kept in reserve (sannidhi-paccaya)?
He said, "There would be no fault," explaining: "For they do not carry it for the purpose of personal consumption.

This being the case, if one were to take what was given by a non-ordained person for the purpose of external use and then keep it, one would have to say that there is an offense due to the condition of hoarding (*sannidhi*); furthermore, one could not say, "For they do not keep it for the purpose of use.

If this is so, should the qualification "for the purpose of use" be stated regarding the five factors of acceptance?
It need not be stated. For acceptance is indeed for the purpose of use; thus, without stating "for the purpose of use" separately, it is said simply:
"If a bhikkhu accepts it with his body or with what is connected to his body. Others [say]:...

However, they say: "Even though there is receiving, because it is stated here that 'there is no offense when one carries [it] for the purpose of not using it,' provided one does not carry it for the purpose of using it.

Regarding "or his bowl may be accepted," here too, the acceptance of the bowl should be understood as being for the purpose of internal consumption; it is intended to show that there is no fault when one gives by touching what is inside the bowl, provided the food remains on the hand.

here, for one who receives repeatedly, because he forms the definite conviction that what has been placed in his own bowl is "his own property," the act of receiving does not relinquish its presence in the hand;

However, once it has been placed [in the bowl], it is said to be "set aside" by one who is not fully ordained; thus, the formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is relinquished because of the state of having been abandoned.
Therefore it is said: "Because the novice... [etc. ...has abandoned it.

So it has been said by that very same teacher, the Elder Buddhadatta:
"Whether one brings oil and such for the sake of one's mother and father,

“Therefore, one must consider the cause of that distinction;

The commentary on the training rule concerning eating with [a person of the opposite sex] is finished.
284–289. There is nothing further to be said regarding the fourth and fifth [offenses].
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Conduct (Cāritta-sikkhāpada). 298.
Regarding the phrase "in ordinary speech" (*pakativacanena*) in the sixth [rule]: here, it refers to that which can be heard by one standing within a distance of twelve *hattha*.

If such a thing were to occur, that would be called a statement of natural fact. "He should ask for permission" means he should ask with words such as, "I am going to the house of so-and-so," or "I am going on a visit. The rest here is self-evident.
Accepting an invitation to any of the five kinds of cooked food while not asking permission from a monk who is present [constitutes an offense].
Entering another house from the house of a supporter, failing to pass the midday mealtime, and the absence of either a proper occasion or an emergency—
these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning wandering for alms is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 303.
Regarding the seventh [rule]: "Mahānāma by name" refers to the brother of the Elder Anuruddha and the son of the Blessed One’s younger paternal uncle.
For these five individuals—Suddhodana, Sakkaudana, Sukkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana—were brothers. The queen was named Amitā.
Their sister was [the mother of] the Elder Tissa; the Elder Tissa was her son. The Tathāgata and the Elder Nanda were sons of Suddhodana;
Mahānāma and the Elder Anuruddha were sons of Sukkodana; and the Elder Ānanda was the son of Amitodana. He was the younger brother of the Blessed One.
Mahānāma was older than him and was a noble disciple who had attained the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmi). Therefore it was said: "Mahānāma..."
“...is called ... a noble disciple. 305–306.
Regarding the word *ajjaṇho* in the text: the meaning is “today, on one day,” or the meaning “a person of today” (*ajjana*) should be understood; it does not mean “of us.
“You will bring [it] at the time” means you will bring it tomorrow. “If he should consent to more than that” means if, in that regard...

If a limit has been set by nights or by medicines, such as "only this many nights" or "only this many medicines may be requested," then if one should consent to requesting more than that limit of nights or that limit of medicines, [it is an offense]. [Thinking:
"We have been invited by you with these medicines; and for us, it is with these very medicines..."
Having explained, "This is the purpose," even one who is ill is permitted to request [medicine]. 310.
Since this procedure applies specifically to the Saṅgha Pavāraṇā, it is therefore stated: "those who have already performed their individual (puggalika) Pavāraṇā.
The rest is self-evident. [The factors are: the state of being a Saṅgha Pavāraṇā, the requesting of medicine, and not being ill.
"Transgressing the limit": these, moreover, are the four factors herein.
The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Troops on March.

311. The eighth [offense] has its meaning already explained. An army on campaign, going for the purpose of seeing it, seeing it other than at an authorized place, and the absence of such a condition or of an emergency—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding an army on campaign is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Staying with an Army.

317. The ninth training rule (sikkhāpada) is also straightforward. However, the three factors here are: exceeding three nights, the setting of the sun while with an army, and the absence of illness and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dwelling with an army is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Military Parades (uyyodhika).
322. Regarding the question "How many lakhs did you obtain?": the meaning is, how many people, who were the targets of your arrow-strikes, were obtained by you;
that is to say, how many were pierced by you. The rest here is self-evident. [The offenses include] going for the purpose of watching a battle and so forth;
seeing [such things] other than at an authorized place; and [the offense arising from] such a condition.
Or "the absence of danger"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning military displays is finished.
The fifth section, the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics, is completed.
6. Surāpānavagga 1.
Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā 326–328.
Regarding the first training rule of the Surāpānavagga: "fence" (vatiyā) refers to the fence surrounding a village. In the Pāḷi text...
Regarding flour-liquor (*piṭṭhasurā*) and the like: flour is placed in a vessel, water appropriate for it is added, and it is kneaded; this is what is called flour-liquor.

Similarly, when cakes (*pūva*) or boiled rice (*odana*) are placed in a vessel, water appropriate for them is added, and they are kneaded, these are called cake-liquor (*pūvasurā*) and rice-liquor (*odanasurā*).
Furthermore, the term "seed" (*kiṇṇa*) refers to the fermenting agent of that liquor. Those which are also called "liquor-morsels" (*surāmodaka*)...

Those that are made by adding [other ingredients] are called "mixed" (*kiṇṇapakkhittā*). Those combined with various ingredients such as *harītakī*, *sāsapa*, and so forth, are "composed of ingredients" (*sambhārasaṃyuttā*).

Flower-liquor (*pupphāsava*) is the juice of flowers such as *madhuka*, *tāla*, and coconut, which has been aged for a long time. Fruit-liquor (*phalāsava*) is the juice of fruits such as the *panasa*.

Honey-liquor (*madhvāsava*) is the juice of grapes. Molasses-liquor (*guḷāsava*) is the juice of sugarcane. [These are made from] various ingredients such as *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *kaṭukabhaṇḍa*, and so forth.
"Juice that has been stored for a long time and combined with various ingredients.

"Starting from the seed" means starting from the time the ingredients have been prepared and placed in the jar, and also starting from the very moment the fresh juice of the *tāla*, coconut, and other fruits has been extracted.
(329) "Salted sour gruel" (*loṇasovīraka*) is a specific type of fermented liquor (*āsava*) not containing alcohol, which is compounded with numerous medicinal herbs.
"For the purpose of causing the assumption of fragrance" means for the purpose of causing the assumption of a state of being fragrant.

Regarding the statement "it is unintentional and a worldly offense," whatever needs to be said here should be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the first *pārājika*. The rest here is self-evident.
Furthermore, the two factors here are: the state of being intoxicating liquor and the drinking thereof.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of fermented liquor is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule regarding poking with the finger. 330.
Regarding the phrase "even a nun standing in the position of one not fully ordained": here, even a monk [is included] in the position of one not fully ordained for a nun.

It should be understood as "standing. The rest here is self-evident. However, the two factors in this case are: the intention for amusement, and the physical contact with the body of one who is fully ordained by means of one's own body.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the poking with a finger is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Joking (Hasadhamma-sikkhāpada) 335.
The third [rule] is of plain meaning. However, the two constituent factors here are: being above the ankles, and playing with the intention to joke.
The commentary on the training rule concerning joking is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Disrespect (Anādariyasikkhāpada) 344.
Regarding the fourth [rule], "One should not take up a censurable teacher's instruction":

since sugarcane juice is to be used for seven days, while its dregs are to be used for life, and the stalk of sugarcane is the combination of both, therefore one may [take] a sugarcane stalk at the wrong time.
The disparaging statement of certain teachers, such as "it is permissible to eat sugar-coated myrobalan," should not be accepted.

Regarding the offense against worldly conventions (*lokavajja*), the acceptance of a teacher's word is not permissible; that is, whatever teacher’s opinion exists regarding a point of offense in the training rules concerning worldly conventions, that should not be accepted.
For one who, having transgressed what is forbidden by worldly convention, says, "This is our teacher’s acceptance," such acceptance is invalid.
The intention is that it is not permissible. "In accordance with the Suttas" refers to the Aṭṭhakathā (Commentary).

Regarding the statement, "It conforms to the convergence of what has come down through the lineage; therefore, only the teacher’s instruction handed down through the lineage should be accepted," the intention is that it is included within the very arguments of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā.
The rest here is self-evident. [Regarding the offense of] speaking to one who is fully ordained using what has been prescribed, it constitutes an act of disrespect.
However, there are these two factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning frightening [others].

345. The fifth [offense] has its meaning already explained. Here, however, there are two factors: the state of being fully ordained, and making an effort with the desire to cause fear within the range of his sight or hearing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing fear is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fire.

350. The sixth [chapter] concerns the Bhaggas, who were the princes of a certain district; because they resided there, that single district is called “Bhaggā” by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*).
Therefore it is said: “Bhaggā is the name of a district. At Susumāragira means in the city of that name.
It is said that on the day the site was selected for the purpose of building that city by a teacher of architecture (*vatthuvijjācariya*), [the following occurred].
Not far away, a crocodile let out a cry and uttered a sound.
Then, when the city was being built immediately thereafter, they took that very cry of the crocodile as an auspicious omen and gave it the name Susumāragira. However, some say:
"Because it is shaped like a crocodile, there is a mountain named Susumāra; since it is near that city, therefore..."
They say, "Because it has Susumāragiri, it is called 'Susumāragiri'. Whether that be so or otherwise, this is the name of that city;
thus he said, "Susumāragira is the name of the city. *Bhesakaḷā* is a specific kind of shrub named *ghampaṇḍa*;
some also call it a "white tree" (*setarukkha*). Because of their abundance, however—
That forest became known simply as Bhesakaḷāvana. There is also a reading, “Bhesagaḷāvane. Some say: “A certain yakkha named Bhesa acted improperly;
because that [forest] was the place where he oozed out (gaḷita), that forest came to be called Bhesagaḷāvana. 352. “Making light” means making fire.
The rest here is self-evident. However, the four factors here are: being not ill, the absence of having performed what is permitted, the desire to warm oneself, and the kindling of the fire.
The commentary on the Joti-sikkhāpada is finished.
7. Commentary on the Nahāna-sikkhāpada:
357. In the Pāḷi of the seventh training rule, "asambhinne" means "unbesmeared," that is to say, "unclean."
"Should bathe once every half-month": this means that starting from the day of bathing, one should bathe before the half-month is complete.

The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are: the Middle Country, bathing less than once every half-month, and the absence of the [permitted] occasions, crossing a river, or an emergency.
The commentary on the training rule concerning bathing is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Making [Cloth] Discolored (Dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpada). 368.
Regarding the eighth [rule], it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipadas* that "what is called 'leather-blue' is natural blue. In the *gaṇṭhipada*:
However, it is said: "Leather-workers throw tin dross and iron excrement into the water and blacken the hide;
that is called 'leather-blue'. The rest here is self-evident. Regarding the robe of the aforementioned type, there are three factors here:
its being unmade, its not being a robe [received] as alms, and whether it is worn as an undergarment or as an upper garment.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making [a robe] discolored is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule Concerning Reassignment (Vikappana). 374.
Regarding the ninth, "not having relinquished" (*apaccuddhāraṇa*) means: "Use what belongs to me, or dispose of it," and so forth.

"Without having performed the relinquishment" (*akata-paccuddhāraṃ*). "With whom the disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*) was performed" means with whom the disciplinary act was carried out. "In the commentary on the thirty [rules]" means in the commentary on the *Nissaggiya* rules.
Bodily action consists in using [the robe], while verbal action consists in not relinquishing it. The rest here is self-evident. These [three factors] are:
the personal assignment (*sāmaṃ vikappita*), the non-relinquishment, and the state of the robe being fit for assignment (*vikappanūpaga-cīvaratā*), as well as its use.
Herein, there are three factors.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the distribution [of robes] is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning the non-storing of robes.

377. The tenth [offense] has its meaning already explained. Herein, the two factors are: the hiding of bowls or other requisites belonging to one who is fully ordained, either with the intention to cause vexation or with the purpose of laughter.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the hiding of robes is finished.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Liquor, is completed.
7. The Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇakavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Intentional Killing (Sañciccasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 382.
Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Living Beings: one who shoots arrows or missiles is an archer (*issāsa*), meaning one skilled in the art of archery.
He said, "A master archer. They are called *dhanuggahas* because they take up a bow (*dhanu*) for the purpose of destroying enemies;

their teacher is a *dhanuggahācariya*. "The duty must be performed with diligence" means that the duty regarding the lodging should be performed by one whose mindfulness is well-established, so that those living beings do not die. The rest here is self-evident. The constituent parts (*aṅgas*) also—
They are to be understood according to the method explained under the training rule concerning human beings (*manussaviggaha*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning intentional action is finished.
