2. Commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings (*sappāṇaka*).
387. Regarding the second [offense], "in a place where water remains": this refers to a portion of ground where water, once poured out, remains still and does not quickly disappear.
The rest here is self-evident. The factors [of the offense] are exactly as described in the training rule on sprinkling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada) 392.
In the third [rule], it is stated for the purpose of showing the manner of their conduct: "They do not allow [the matter] to stand as it was originally established.
However, whatever legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) has been settled according to the Dhamma, that is indeed well-settled. If, however, the procedure (*kamma*) has been performed improperly...
If he protests, it must be done only after having persuaded him. Otherwise, the legal act (kamma) is invalid and the performers incur an offense.
The rest here is self-evident. Being struck down according to the Dhamma, knowing [the matter], and reopening [a settled case)—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning reopening is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Grave Offenses (Duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada) 399.
Regarding the fourth [rule], "of that very person": it refers to the one who has committed the offense.

"He informs" means he says, "Do not inform anyone," solely for the purpose of concealment. "The person regarding the matter" (vatthupuggala) is the person who has committed the offense. "By whom it was informed to him" refers to the second person.

It has been reported to the third monk. "The limit is cut off" means that because the second monk reported it to the third after having incurred an offense due to concealment, there is no further offense for him to incur on that account;
therefore, the limit of the offense is said to be cut off.

400. “The emission of semen and physical contact with one who is not fully ordained—this is what is called ‘grave misconduct’”—this does not accord with the commentary on the training rule regarding the reporting of grave matters (*duṭṭhullārocana*).
For it is stated there: “Regarding ‘grave or non-grave misconduct toward one who is not fully ordained,’ here the first five training rules constitute grave [misconduct]...”

“Misconduct (*ajjhācāra*) refers to the name [of the offense], while the rest are grave matters (*duṭṭhulla*); however, for one who has emitted semen, physical contact, or a grave matter involving lust, these are called misconduct.

Regarding the statement, “In the case of reporting, what is intended as a grave matter for one not fully ordained is different from what is intended in the case of concealing,” no distinguishing reason is seen here either;
therefore, the preceding and following parts of the commentary do not agree with each other.
However, one who desires non-contradiction should investigate the reason for this matter here. The rest is self-evident.

Furthermore, the two factors here are: the recognition of a grave offense by one who has been fully ordained, and the abandonment of responsibility with the thought, "I will not report it because I wish to conceal it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning grave offenses is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule for Those Under Twenty Years of Age 402.
Regarding the fifth [training rule], the *rūpasutta* is the discourse of the coin-exchangers (*heraññika*). "Ill-spoken" (*duruttānaṃ*) means spoken ill by way of abuse;
precisely because they are ill-spoken, they are "unwelcome" (*durāgatānaṃ*). "Paths of speech" (*vacanapathānaṃ*): here, speech itself is the path for those desiring to know its meaning.
The "path for those wishing to make known" is the path of speech (*vacanapatha*). "Those who must endure with difficulty" means those who are to be endured through suffering.
404. One who has twenty years including the time spent lying in the womb is "twenty by conception" (*gabbhavīso*).

It should be understood that "increasing and decreasing" refers to adding [the months] when there are more than the [standard] conception-months, and subtracting them when there are fewer. "Nineteen years" [is the minimum].
Having dwelt in the mother’s womb for twelve months, from the time of his birth until the Great Pavāraṇā, he was nineteen years old.
"On the first day of the month" means on the day of entering the rains retreat during the later period (*pacchimikā*).
Because of the statement, "A month consists of thirty nights and days," it is said that "four months are subtracted. "They postpone the rains" means they draw the rains retreat upward.
The meaning is that in the third year, by relinquishing one month due to an intercalary month, they draw the rainy season forward; therefore, the third year consists of thirteen months.
However, because a year consists of twelve months, it is stated that "six months increase" by taking the intercalary months separately over the course of eighteen years. From this...
"By the month": having become free from doubt means having become certain because of being twenty years old plus the extra months.

As for what was stated in the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Because eighteen years alone are counted by including the extra months, there are indeed extra days for the remaining two years as well;
it is with reference to those extra days that [the text says]..."
As for the statement, “having become free from doubt,” that should not be accepted. For there are no such things as "extra days" found separately within two years;
rather, it is only when an extra month is set aside by means of the postponement of the rains in the third year that an excess of one month occurs.
Therefore, so-called "extra days" do not exist separately within two years.
But why was it said, “Having taken those two months, twenty years become complete”? [The answer is: He said, “But here... [etc.
...it is said,” because when another year is added to the nineteen-year period, the twenty years become complete.
Furthermore, because particles have multiple meanings, the word *pana* has the sense of the word *hi*; thus, it is as if he had said “here, for (*hi*)... [or “but here, for..."].
This is stated by way of supporting the very point already mentioned. And by this, he illustrates the following:

"Regarding what was said—that 'they ordain a novice who is nineteen years old on the first day of the month, having passed the full-moon day of the departure-month'—therein, even without counting the months spent in the womb, it refers to one who is less than twenty years old by two months, and thus is called 'nineteen years old.'"
It has been said; therefore, when two extra months are included, the twenty years are said to be complete.
"Therefore" means because even the months of the womb are included in the calculation, therefore.
"He becomes twenty-one years old" means that while he is twenty years old from the day of birth, together with the months of the womb, he becomes twenty-one years old.

406. "Ordains another" means that one ordains while acting as a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or a teacher of the formal act (*kammavācācariya*). The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors in this case are: being under twenty years of age, the perception that one is under twenty, and the act of ordaining.
The commentary on the training rule regarding those under twenty years of age is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding a Thieving Caravan.

407. The sixth training rule is of plain meaning. However, the four factors here are: being a traveling caravan of thieves, knowing [it to be so], making an arrangement, and traveling without a prior agreement.
The commentary on the training rule concerning a caravan of thieves is finished. 412.
Regarding the seventh, there is nothing further to be said.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Ariṭṭha 417.

In the eighth [rule], “they afflicted” means they killed. That which comes (eti) into the midst (antara), that is, into the interval within the continuity of beings, by way of being an obstruction to various attainments, is an *antarāya*—that is, an evil such as misfortune pertaining to the present life and so forth. In the sense of not being transcended...
They are called *antarāyika* because they are engaged in an obstacle, or because they deserve an obstacle as their fruit, or because they have the habit of creating an obstacle.

Therefore it was said: "They create an obstacle, thus they are *antarāyika*. Regarding the phrase *ānantariyadhammā*: these are volitional states (*cetanā-dhammā*) whose intrinsic nature is that of an immediate result (*ānantarika-sabhāva*).
Herein, this is the etymological explanation: a result that follows immediately after death is called *anantara*; in that immediate [result]...
Those who are engaged in it, whose nature is to perform [the act] immediately following that [thought], or whose application is immediate, are called *ānantarikā*;
they are thus referred to as *ānantariya*. Those actions which are themselves obstacles are "obstructive actions" (*kammantarāyika*).

It is stated that this creates an obstacle specifically to liberation (*mokkha*) and not to heaven (*sagga*), because of the absence of the defining characteristic of sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*). For the state of being protected by the Dhamma does not belong to a bhikkhunī.
It exists. This has been stated with reference to an ordinary bhikkhunī. However, for a noble one (ariyā), that which occurs leads only to the states of misery;
the young brahmin Nanda is the illustration in this regard. Alternatively, there is no obstruction to heaven for both [the noble one and the ordinary one] because their aspiration is the same;
however, there is an obstruction to liberation because it defiles the practice undertaken for the sake of liberation. But in the case of proceeding after having overcome [it]...
Even the state of being an obstacle to heaven cannot be prevented.

Only the views of non-causality (ahetukaditthi), the view of non-action (akiriyaditthi), and the view of nihilism (natthikaditthi) have reached a state of certainty; these are the phenomena of fixed wrong view (niyatamicchāditthidhamma).
"Phenomena of rebirth-linking" refers to the arising of the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking. And the mention of eunuchs and so forth here is merely illustrative.

Because all rebirth-linking that is without root-cause (ahetuka-paṭisandhi) constitutes an obstacle to the fruition [of the path]. Those volitions by which one reviles a noble one constitute "reviling a noble one.
"Thereafter" means after having asked for forgiveness. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated in the discussion on the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).
"Offenses committed intentionally" refers to the seven classes of offenses (āpatti-kkhandha) transgressed intentionally. Intentionally...
For even a transgression as slight as a *dukkaṭa* or a *dubbhāsita* creates an obstacle to the path to heaven and the fruits of the spiritual life.

As long as one who has committed a *pārājika* offense continues to claim the status of a monk, he does not emerge from it; and as long as one who has committed a heavy offense other than *pārājika* does not emerge from it, nor confesses a light offense, [the obstacle remains].

“This bhikkhu” refers to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha. “Having blended the flavor with the flavor” means having brought together the flavor of enjoying blameless requisites with the flavor of enjoying the objects of sensual pleasure which are blameworthy.
“Free from desire and lust” means that through wise reflection, there is no desire or lust for this [enjoyment of requisites];
it is the enjoyment of requisites. “As if placing it near” means as if placing a bond near. “Striving”...
"Viya" is also a reading. "As if bringing together" means as if bringing together a similarity, because of casting [the state of] faultlessness upon that which is exclusively blameworthy.
"Evil" (pāpaka) means evil in the sense of being base and in the sense of leading to an unhappy destination.
"As if binding the great ocean" means as if binding the vast sea by means of constructing a bridge. By means of omniscient knowledge...
"Contradicting together" means contradicting that [omniscience] by apprehending as "blameless" what has been seen by the knowledge of omniscience as "blameworthy.

"In the wheel of the command" refers to the wheel of the command consisting of the first *pārājika* training rule and the teaching consisting of the instruction beginning with "having abandoned unchaste conduct."
"Skeleton" (aṭṭhikaṅkala) refers to the breastbone, the spinal column, or the skull. Because it is devoid of flesh, it is called "skeleton" (kaṅkala).
Indeed, the word *kaṅkala* is conventionally established for a single bone within a chain of bones from which the flesh has departed.
"In the sense of burning along with" means in the sense of burning along with [the practitioner] through wrong practice, both presently and in the future. "In the sense of great tormenting."
Because its intrinsic nature is unstable; because it must be dealt with for only a moment in the sense of presenting itself briefly;
because it is overcome by others in the sense of being temporary; because it serves as the basis for breaking and so forth in the sense of crushing all limbs and members;
because it is like a wound in the sense of being a sore; and because it enters within after producing a wound where there was none before.
In the sense of piercing through, and in the sense of being accompanied by danger and fear due to being the cause of harm in this present life and in future lives.
In the Pāli passage beginning with “with persistence and misapprehension,” the meaning should be understood as follows:

“With persistence” means with the persistence of views; the meaning is, by way of that view having become firmly established. “Misapprehension” means by way of the misapprehension of views, that is, by way of the misapprehension consisting of views.
The meaning is as follows: *diṭṭhi* (view) itself, having transcended the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), is *parāmāsa* (misapprehension) because it grasps at something else.
*Abhinivissa* means having adhered [to a view] through an adherence of views preceded by an adherence of craving, thinking, "This alone is the truth here.
*Voharati* means he speaks. *Yato ca kho te bhikkhū* means when those bhikkhus [speak thus]. "I am one who speaks thus, venerable sir."
"By the Blessed One"—this [the opponent] accepts through the power of the Blessed One, even though he wishes to say "it does not exist" out of a desire to conceal his own tenet.
Indeed, it is said that there is no one capable of engaging in two simultaneous discourses in the presence of the Buddhas.
"Of whom, O foolish man, are you [a disciple]?"—O foolish man, of which kshatriya...
"Whether it be a brahmin, a vaiśya, a śūdra, a householder, one who has gone forth, a deva, or a human—know that the Dhamma has been taught by me in this way.

The rest here is self-evident. Furthermore, these three factors constitute the offense here: the performance of a formal act (dhammakamma), the admonition (samanubhāsana), and the failure to relinquish [the wrong view] (appaṭinissajjana).
The commentary on the Ariṭṭha training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning association with one who has been suspended (Ukkhittasambhoga). 424.
"In the ninth [case], by the counting of the act" means by the counting of the acts of giving and receiving. Regarding co-residence, it is by way of the conclusion of the formal act (kamma).
The delimitation of the offense should be understood by way of the act of one person lying down while another is already lying down on a shared bed.
And here, because the word-commentary states "under one roof" (*ekacchanne*) without qualification, there is an offense for one who lies down under one roof even if they are in different locations.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Or they may lie down together—even if in different locations..."

"One should lie down under a single cover. It is stated as "three types of consciousness" because even an Arahant who is unaware of the formal rule (paṇṇatti) may incur the offense when his mind is a functional-ineffective (kiriya-abyākata) state.

As for what was said by someone else—"In this context, 'three types of consciousness' should be understood to mean that one might arrange a bed together with a resultant-ineffective (vipāka-abyākata) consciousness;
otherwise, because the training rule (sikkhāpada) pertains to a state of mind, [the offense would not apply]"—[this is incorrect].

The statement, “It is not appropriate [to say that] with reference to the functional-inefficient (kiriyābyākata),” should not be accepted. For it is not the case that the transgression of a training rule involving a conscious mind (sacittaka) is impossible for an Arahant.
For this very reason, in the case of the training rules involving a conscious mind—such as digging the earth and so forth—it is stated that there are only three types of consciousness (ticitta).
The rest here is self-evident. These are: non-compliance with the Dhamma, knowing [the offense], and engaging in communal sharing and so forth.
In this context, there are three factors.
The commentary on the training rule concerning social intercourse with one who has been suspended is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Thorns.

428. *Pire* is a particle (*nipātapada*). Since they say it has the same meaning as the word *para* when used in the sense of addressing someone, he says, "O *pire*, you who are not ours" (*amāmakā*), meaning those who have not become internal to us.
Alternatively, *pire* is a particle with the same meaning as *parato* (from afar/beyond); therefore, "Go away, *pire*; do not stay here"—thus it is used here.
The meaning is to be understood. The rest here follows the same method as stated in the two preceding training rules.
The commentary on the Kaṇṭaka training rule is finished.
The seventh chapter, the Sappāṇaka-vagga, is completed.
8. The Chapter on Fellow-Practitioners (Sahadhammika-vagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Fellow-Practitioners (Sahadhammika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) 434.
Regarding the first training rule of the Chapter on Fellow-Practitioners, "an offense for every word," this was stated out of fear of disrespect.

There is an offense for one who speaks thus with contempt. The rest here is self-evident. Speaking to one who is fully ordained using what has been prescribed [for others], and speaking thus out of a desire not to train—these are the two factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those in accordance with the Dhamma is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Scrutinizing (Vilekhana-sikkhāpada) 438.
Regarding the second [training rule], it is said that "the mastery of the Vinaya" means *vinayapariyatti*; thus he says, "for those mastering the Vinaya," and so forth.
"Well-guarded" (*sugutta*) means that, like a heap of jewels placed in a casket, it is not lost and does not incur failure.
"Thus well-guarded" means it is well-protected; "well-guarded" (*surakkhita*) is a synonym for that same state.
For just as one cannot be plundered by the thieves of the defilements (*kilesa*), so too is it always well-protected through the constant presence of mindfulness (*sūpaṭṭhita-sati*).

"Of those overcome by remorse" (*kukkuccapakatānaṃ*) means of those overwhelmed by remorse arising on account of what is allowable and what is unallowable (*kappiya-akappiya*). "Timidity" (*sārajjanaṃ*) is timidity, which is the fear of delusion. It is "gone away" (*vigata*).
"Confident" (*visārado*) means one who has confidence (*sārado*) in this. "With the true Dhamma" (*sahadhammena*) means with speech accompanied by reason.

"He refutes well" (*suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhāti*) means he refutes so thoroughly that they do not raise their heads again, but rather become speechless and embarrassed; thus he refutes them properly. Regarding "through shamelessness" (*alajjitā*):

this is a grammatical expression formed by the elision of the letter *ya*; it means "through shamelessness" (*alajjitāya*). The same method applies to "through ignorance" (*aññāṇatā*) and the following terms. "Dull and bewildered" (*mando momūho*): he is dull (*mando*) due to the state of ignorance, and bewildered (*momūho*) because of being without a sense object; the meaning is "one who is greatly deluded."
"Attapaccatthikā" means one's own enemies. The Vajjiputtakas are those who point out the ten points.
Regarding the phrase "those who hold views such as bringing [alms] from others, ignorance, doubt, and being led by others":

here, when the Mārakāyika deities see the emission of semen from those who claim to have attained Arahantship—whether they are overweening ones who perceive themselves to have attained what they have not, or deceivers who falsely claim Arahantship—they think, "The impurity of an Arahant..."
...they apply [these terms]," so they think—just as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas do; these are proponents of "inducing [wrong views] in others.

However, for those who hold that an Arahant has ignorance (*aññāṇa*) because of the absence of the occurrence of knowledge regarding the names, clans, and so forth of women, men, and others, and that there is doubt (*kaṅkhā*) in an Arahant because of the absence of certainty regarding those very things, since those objects [are not known by him]...
"Others cause [one] to cross over, they explain, and they declare; therefore, there is for an Arahant 'causing to cross over by others' (paravitāraṇā).
These three tenets are just like those of the Pubbaseliyas nowadays; they are proponents of the doctrines of ignorance, doubt, and causing to cross over by others.
Their refutation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Kathāvatthu*.
The phrase "the four paths and the fruits" is stated by way of an inclusive (ukkhaṭṭha) description;
likewise, the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), the three true knowledges (vijjā), and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) are also simply the true Dhamma of attainment.

Alternatively, the particle *ca* should be understood as having the sense of including those not explicitly mentioned. "Some elders" refers to the Dhamma-preachers; "they said" means that the Paṃsukūlika elders spoke thus.
When, then, did this discourse arise? Herein, this is the sequential account:
It is said that during the great terror caused by the Caṇḍāla-Tissa on this island, Sakka, the king of the gods, fashioned a great raft and announced to the bhikkhus: "A great danger will arise;
the rain-god will not send rain properly. The bhikkhus, being distressed for their requisites, will not be able to maintain the scriptures."
“Having reached the opposite shore, it is fitting that the masters preserve their lives.
Venerable sirs, board this great raft and go; those for whom there is no room to sit or stand may go placing pieces of wood against their chests.
There will be no fear for anyone. Then, having reached the shore of the ocean, sixty bhikkhus made an agreement.

Having resolved, "We have no need to go there; remaining right here, we shall protect the Tipiṭaka," they turned back from there and went to the southern Malaya country. There they lived, sustaining themselves on roots, tubers, and leaves;
when their bodies were strong, they would sit and recite, and when they were weak, they would clear away the sand and sit surrounded by it.

Placing their heads together in one place, they contemplated the scriptures (*pariyatti*). In this manner, for twelve years, they preserved the complete Tipiṭaka along with its commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*) in its entirety.
When the danger had subsided, seven hundred bhikkhus [recited] even a single syllable of the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries from the place where they had been.
Without losing even a single consonant, they arrived at this very island and entered the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery in the district of Kallagāma.
Hearing news of the arrival of the elders, sixty monks who had remained on this island went forth, thinking,
"We shall see the elders," and while purifying the Tipiṭaka together with the elders, [they found that] not even a single syllable or a single consonant was missing.
They did not see anyone named Asamanta. At that place, this discussion arose among the elders:

"Is the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) the root of the Dispensation, or is it practice (*paṭipatti*)? The Paṃsukūlika elders said, "Practice is the root," while the Dhamma-preachers said, "The scriptures.
Then the elders [addressed] them both: "By the mere words of you two..."
“It is not possible to know; bring a discourse spoken by the Conqueror,” they said. Thinking, “It is no burden to bring a discourse,” he said:
“Subhadda, if these monks were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants.
“Great King, the Teacher’s instruction is rooted in practice; Great King, the Teacher’s instruction has practice as its essence; while practice endures, the teaching endures.”
They cited a sutta.
Having heard this sutta, the Dhamma-preachers, for the sake of establishing their own position, cited it as follows:
“As long as the Suttantas endure, and as long as the Vinaya shines forth...”
“Just as they would see light when the sun has risen, so long will they see light.
But when the Suttantas have disappeared and the Vinaya has been forgotten,
there will be darkness in the world, like when the sun has set.”
“When the Suttantas are protected and preserved, the practice is protected;
the wise one established in the practice does not fall away from the security from bondage.
When this sutta was recited, the Paṃsukūlika Theras remained silent. It was only the words of the Dhammakathika Theras [that were spoken].
It appeared before him. For just as, in the midst of a hundred or a thousand cattle, if there is no cow that maintains the lineage, that breed and that tradition cannot be sustained;

even so, although there may be hundreds or thousands of monks who have begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*), if the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) is absent, there can be no penetration of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). And just as...

Just as a treasure jar does not become "lost" so long as the inscribed characters upon the stone surface remain legible for the purpose of knowing its location, even though the jar itself has vanished;
in the same way, as long as the *pariyatti* (the scriptures) endure, the Dispensation (*sāsana*) cannot be said to have disappeared.
"Dependent on that" (*tassādheyyo*) means dependent upon it.

439. *So pana* means "that same" Pātimokkha. The rest here is self-evident. However, the two factors here are: the desire to censure, and the disparaging of the training rules in the presence of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
The commentary on the rule concerning frivolous talk is finished.
3. Commentary on the Rule Concerning Confusion (*Mohana-sikkhāpada*).

443. The third [offense] is self-evident. However, the four factors here are: causing delusion, the desire to cause delusion, the state of having heard [the rule] in the manner already described, and the act of deluding.
The commentary on the training rule regarding deluding is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Striking.
452. In the fourth [offense], "with a mind colored by passion" means having a mind colored by passion for physical contact.
However, if one strikes while impassioned by the desire for sexual intercourse, it is merely a *dukkaṭa*. The rest here is self-evident.
Furthermore, the three factors in this case are: being provoked to anger, lacking the intention to release [the victim], and striking one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning striking is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning clods of earth. 457.

Regarding the statement, "In the fifth [rule], it is an offense of wrong-doing because it was given without the intention to strike": here, [the offense applies] when one has struck with the intention to strike.
By the previous training rule, it is a *pācittiya*; by this [present] one, it is a *pācittiya* when the mere act of spitting is done with the intention of making [the other] spit.
But since, having missed him with this [act], a blow was given, there is therefore a *dukkaṭa*.
Is this *dukkaṭa* on account of the blow, or rather on account of the spitting? Regarding this, some first say: "It is indeed on account of the blow."
"A *dukkaṭa* for the act of vomiting and a *pācittiya* for the subsequent striking; thus, a *pācittiya* together with a *dukkaṭa* is appropriate.
For the initial vomiting occurred first, and the striking occurred later; and the initial vomiting cannot be rendered free from the basis of an offense by depending on the subsequent striking.
However, we here reason as follows: "Because the vomiting itself is not established by its own intrinsic nature, [the offense] due to that..."

There should not be an offense of expiation (pācittiya); however, because the action was performed with an impure mind, it is impossible for there to be non-offense here, and thus a dukkaṭa is stated.

By the phrase "because it was given without the desire to strike," the reason is stated for why an offense of expiation does not arise under the previous training rule due to the condition of striking;
it does not, however, refer to the possibility of a dukkaṭa arising from the condition of striking.
"For it is not fitting that when a blow is struck with the intention of stealing, there should be an offense of *pācittiya* or *dukkaṭa* on account of the blow under the preceding training rule.
They say: "Even for one who, having become angry upon seeing animals and the like defecating and so forth, emits [semen] with the sole intention of release (*mokkha*).
The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are] being provoked by anger, and not the intention of release.
For one who is fully ordained, [the offenses of] throwing a clod of earth or spitting—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning throwing a clod of earth is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Groundless [Accusations].

459. The sixth [offense] has its meaning already explained. Herein, there are these four factors: being fully ordained, the groundlessness of the *saṅghādisesa* offense, the accusation, and knowing it at that very moment.
The commentary on the training rule concerning groundlessness is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Intentionality (*sañcicca-sikkhāpada*).
464. The seventh [offense] also has its meaning already explained. Herein, however, there are three factors: being fully ordained, a desire for discomfort, and the arising of remorse.
The commentary on the training rule concerning intentional [speech] is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eavesdropping.
471. "In the vicinity of hearing" (sutisamīpaṃ) means in the vicinity of sound. For "hearing" (suti) is that which is heard; it is a designation for sound.
The vicinity of that [sound] is "eavesdropping" (upassuti); thus, "in the vicinity of sound" is what is meant.
And in the *Gaṇṭhipadas*, it is stated that "hearing" (sutī) is simply sound itself. Standing where one is able to hear the sound, one stands in the vicinity of sound.
Regarding the phrase "he is called one who stands," it says, "standing where," and so forth. However, some say: "Suti means 'that wherein one hears.
This is the name for that place where one stands and hears. Upassuti is the vicinity of that.
But if this were accepted, it would follow that while one stands in a certain place and hears, one is standing in another location near it.
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in order to show the meaning of the word *upassuti* itself, it is said:
"standing where it is possible to hear their speech," and not [the meaning] of the word *suti*. Therefore, the former method alone is more commendable here.
Alternatively, *upassuti* is a place (*ṭhāna*) where one hears after having approached; that place which can be reached by one who has approached so as to be able to hear those speaking.

"In order to hear the sound"—thus the meaning of "therein" (*tattha*) should be understood. Regarding "while they were deliberating" (*mantente*), he says "while they were deliberating" (*mantayamāne*) because the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.
(473) "Of a single determination" (*ekaparicchedāni*): by this method—namely, "it may be an action, it may be a non-action"—they are of a single determination.
For these three training rules sometimes originate from an act (*kiriya*) and sometimes from a non-act (*akiriya*); they do not originate from both act and non-act at the same moment.
The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are: being fully ordained (*upasampannatā*), the intention to accuse (*codanādhippāya*), and hearing (*savana*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule Concerning Obstructing a Formal Act: 474. The ninth [rule] has its meaning already explained.

However, the three factors here are: it being a formal act in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammakamma*), the perception that it is a formal act in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammakamma-saññā*), and criticizing [the monks] after having given one's consent (*chanda*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the warding off of an action is finished.
10. Commentary on the tenth training rule concerning departing without having given one's consent.
479. The discussion regarding the application [of the rule], the nature of a formal act (*dhammakamma*), and the perception that it is a formal act.
Standing within the same boundary, being of the same communion, and withdrawing from hand-reach out of a desire to cause offense—
these are the six factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding departing without giving one's consent is finished.
11. Explanation of the Eleventh Training Rule (Dubbala-sikkhāpada) 484.

The eleventh rule also has its meaning already explained. However, the four factors here are: being fully ordained (upasampannatā), having received formal authorization in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammena laddha-sammutitā), giving a robe that has been designated for transfer to the Saṅgha (saṅghena saddhiṃ vikappanūpaga-cīvara-dānaṃ), and criticizing [the Saṅgha] out of a desire to disparage it afterwards (pacchā khiyyanā). These are the four factors in this case.
The commentary on the weak training rules is finished. 489.
In the twelfth [chapter], there is nothing further to be said.
The eighth section, the Sahadhammika-vagga, is concluded.
9. Rājavagga 1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Inner Apartment (Antepurasikkhāpada) 497–499.
Regarding the first training rule of the Rājavagga, everything in the commentary is already clear in meaning. In the canonical text (Pāḷi):
However, this is the meaning of the words that have not [yet] been explained: "Have done or will do" means they have committed or will commit sexual misconduct.
The word *imesaṃ* (of these) should be applied to both cases by changing its case-ending: "by these [they] have done" and "by these [they] will do.
*Ratanaṃ* (jewel) refers to any one among the jewels such as the maṇi-jewel and so forth. *Ubhato* (from both sides) means from two factions.
When only the phrase “well-born on both sides” (*ubhato sujāto*) is stated, it might be understood as being well-born by virtue of any two parts whatsoever;

furthermore, since the word *sujāta*—as in expressions such as “well-born and handsome” (*sujāto cārudassano*)—is used as a synonym for excellence of physical proportions, the words “on the mother’s side and on the father’s side” (*mātito ca pitito ca*) are stated specifically to clarify that the state of being well-born is by way of birth alone.
Even in the world, the conventional designations “mother” and “father” are seen to be applied even to those who are not biological sons.
Furthermore, in order to show that here [the mother] is intended specifically by way of being a legitimate son (*orasaputta*), it is said:
"one with a pure womb" (*saṃsuddhagahaṇika*). She conceives and carries a fetus, thus she is the "womb" (*gahaṇī*); this refers to the region of the mother's belly known as the seat of the fetus.
One whose womb is pure is "one with a pure womb"; what is meant is that her mother’s belly is pure. "Of one who digests evenly..."

Regarding the term "gahaṇī": here, it is called the "gaṇḍī" (digestive organ) because the kamma-born heat element takes up (*gaṇhana*) and does not discard the food as it is being digested after it has been eaten.

Regarding the phrase "as far as the seventh generation of ancestors": here, the father’s father is the "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*); the "generation" (*yuga*) of that grandfather is the "seventh generation of ancestors" (*pitāmahayuga*).
“Yuga” means the measure of a lifespan. This is merely a verbal expression; in actual meaning, however, the grandfather himself is the “grandfather-yuga.
Both father and mother are the “parents”; the parents of those parents are the “grandparents”; the pair of those is the “grandfather-yuga.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: “up to the seventh grandfather-yuga,” that is, up to the pair of great-grandfathers. For it is thus...

By the mention of the *pitāmaha* (grandfather), the *mātāmaha* (maternal grandfather) is also included. Furthermore, the word *yuga* (generation) here should be understood through the grammatical principle of *ekasesa* (elliptical remainder):
"the generation and the generation [are] the generation. For in this way, a *dvanda* compound is effectively captured in each instance;
therefore, all ancestors beyond that are included by the very mention of the "grandfather-generation" (*pitāmahayuga*). Thus, it extends as far as the seventh grandfather-generation.
Thus he is one whose lineage is completely pure.
"Not reviled" means not being reviled or insulted with such words as, "Take this man away! What is the use of him? "Not censured" means not being censured;
he has never before been subjected to abuse or blame. To the question "For what reason?", it is said: "On account of his birth."
And here, by the phrase “from both sides... through ten generations of ancestors,” the absence of defects in his lineage is shown by way of praising his pure descent;
by the term “uncensured,” the absence of any fault in his actions is indicated, for it is through faults in action that beings incur censure.
By the term “unreviled,” the absence of improper association is shown, for it is in dependence upon improper association that beings incur abuse.

They obtain [the offense]. The rest here is self-evident. However, the five factors here are: being a khattiya, being anointed [as king], neither having departed from their own bedchamber, not having been informed [of the departure], and crossing the threshold of the gatepost (indakhīla).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the inner palace is finished.
2. Commentary on the Jewel Training Rule (Ratanasikkhāpada) 502.

Regarding the second [rule], "a great ornament" (*mahālaṭaṃ*): it is said that for her as she was going to her husband’s family, her father had a jewelry set called the "Great Ornament" (*mahālaṭāpiḷandhana*) made.
In that ornament, there were four *nāḷi*s of diamond (*vajira*) to be set in their respective places.
They reached completion by way of application: eleven *nāḷis* of pearls, twenty-two *nāḷis* of coral, and thirty-three *nāḷis* of gems.
Thus, it was brought to its conclusion with these and other seven-colored jewels, such as beryl, ruby, and cat’s-eye.
That [crown], when fastened upon the head, extended down as far as the back of the feet.
It is said that even a woman possessing the strength of five elephants is able to support him; this was said with reference to her.
Furthermore, regarding the lodging (*āvasatha*), it should be construed as follows: its precincts (*upacāra*) are either the range of the pestle’s fall or the range of the mortar’s fall.

And here, "lodging" refers to one's own place of residence, whether it be within the monastery grounds or elsewhere. "Both through desire and through fear": [this refers to the motivation for the act].
[One might act] out of desire toward carpenters and the like, or out of fear toward those favored by the king.
"They suspect that very bhikkhu" means that at the time of departure, they suspect him because there is no one else behind him. What is appropriate?

It is either taking refuse-rags (pamsukūla) from what is considered a treasure, or departing without concern for a treasure. For if that which is considered a treasure is raw meat, [one thinks]: "There is none for him..."
He will take the refuse-rag [thinking], "It has an owner. If it is ownerless, he will go away without concern, his attachment to the refuse-rag being severed, [thinking], "This has no owner.
"Having induced another" means having induced someone else; the meaning is that he asks for it in the manner described: "The Noble Ones stand with reference to [others];
this is the way of begging of the Noble Ones. The rest here is self-evident. This is the performance of what is not permitted.
The four factors here are: that it belongs to another, the absence of the perception that it is a rag-patch robe obtained through trust, and either taking it up oneself or causing it to be taken up.
The commentary on the Jewel Training Rule (Ratana-sikkhāpada) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Entering a Village at an Improper Time (Vikālagāmappavisaṇasikkhāpada) 508.
Regarding the third [training rule], the phrase "of the noble path" (*ariyamagga*) should here include the path to heaven (*saggamagga*) as well.

Because the paths to heaven and liberation are not conducive to final deliverance (*aniyyānika*), talk that is like a beast is called "animal talk" (*tiracchānakathā*). The term "beast-like" (*tiracchānabhūta*) means that which acts as a barrier or an obstruction (*tirokaraṇabhūta*, *vibandhanabhūta*).
What is discourse connected with kings? It is discourse concerning a king, proceeding by way of such statements as, "Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, Dhammāsoka—so great was their majesty," and so forth.
And herein, talk based on the household life, such as "Such-and-such a king was handsome and beautiful to behold," is indeed frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).
However, that which proceeds thus, "Even he, who possessed such great majesty, has come to destruction," [is not frivolous talk].
It remains as a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) when connected with impermanence.

Even regarding heroes, talk such as "Mūladeva was so powerful" or "Meghamāla was so powerful," which depends on their deeds and exclaims "Oh, what brave men!", is merely worldly talk and thus frivolous chatter (tiracchānakathā).

Even regarding battles, such as the Bharata War and others, talk such as "So-and-so was killed by such-and-such in this way" or "was pierced in that way" is likewise based solely on the gratification of sensual desire (kāmassāda).
“Talk” refers to animal talk. However, when it occurs in the form, “Even they have indeed passed away,” it is in every case simply a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, regarding food and so forth, it is not permissible to speak with a sense of sensual gratification (*kāmasāda*), thinking, “We ate, we chewed, we drank, we enjoyed such food as this, which was so beautiful in color, fragrant in smell, delicious in taste, and perfect in texture”; rather, it should be spoken purposefully (*sātthakaṃ*).
However, after having performed [such deeds], it is appropriate to say, "In the past, we gave food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands,
and perfumes endowed with such qualities as beauty to those possessed of virtue, and we made offerings at the cetiyas. Even in conversations regarding relatives and the like,
one may speak out of a sense of gratification, thinking, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we traveled about in such various vehicles."

It is not permissible to speak [of these things] for their own sake; however, it may be spoken with a purposeful intent, such as saying, "Those relatives of ours have also met their end," or "In the past, we gave such sandals to the Saṅgha.

Even talk about villages—whether concerning their being well-situated or poorly situated, having plenty of food or scarcity of food, and so forth—or saying, "The inhabitants of that village are brave and capable," is not permissible if done out of a sense of gratification; however, it is permissible if done with a purposeful intent.
Having done so, it is permissible to say, "He was faithful and confident," or "He has reached destruction and vanishing. The same principle applies to talk concerning towns, cities, and provinces.

Regarding talk about women, it is not permissible to speak with a sense of gratification based on their complexion, shape, and so forth; however, it is permissible to say, "She was faithful and confident," or "She has reached destruction.
The same applies to talk about heroes, such as saying, "The warrior named Nandamitta was a hero."
It is not permissible to speak by way of gratification; rather, it is only permissible to say, "He was faithful, [his faith] has reached its end.
Regarding talk about streets as well, it is not permissible to say by way of gratification alone, "Such-and-such a street is well-built, poorly built, brave, or capable";
it is only permissible to say, "They were faithful and confident, [their faith] has reached its end."
The "Discourse on the Waterpot" (*kumbhaṭṭhānakathā*) refers to a discourse on a water-pot stand or a discourse on a bathing ford; or it refers to a discourse on a slave-girl who carries a water-pot.

Even that is not permissible by way of gratification if she is described as "charming, skilled in dancing and singing"; it is only permissible in the manner of [describing her] as "faithful, confident," and so forth.

The "Discourse on Deceased Relatives" (*pubbapetakathā*) is a discourse concerning relatives of the past. In this regard, the determination (*vinicchaya*) is exactly the same as for a discourse concerning relatives currently living.

“Discourse on diversity” refers to all other pointless talk of various kinds that is free from both prior and subsequent discourse. “Discourse on world-theories” refers to the talk of worldly sophistry and contentious debate such as:
“By whom was this world created? It was created by such-and-such a Pajāpati, Brahmā, or Īśvara;
a crow is white because its bones are white; cranes are red because their blood is red,” and so forth.
It is called *lokakkhāyikā* because it explains the world (*loka*) by way of its arising, persistence, and dissolution. As for what is called *samuddakkhāyikā*:
why is the ocean (*samudda*) called the sea (*sāgara*)? It is the sea because it was dug (*khatattā*) by the sons of King Sāgara;
or it is the ocean because it was announced (*niveditattā*) by a hand-gesture that "it has been dug by us"—such pointless talk as this is *samuddakkhāyikā*.
"Thus it is existence," "thus it is non-existence"—discourse that proceeds by stating such or other meaningless reasons is called "discourse on existence and non-existence" (*itibhavābhava-kathā*).

In this context, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to eternalism (*sassata*), and "non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to annihilationism (*uccheda*). "Existence" refers to growth, and "non-existence" refers to decline.
"Existence" refers to sensual pleasure, and "non-existence" refers to self-mortification. Thus, together with these sixfold types of discourse on existence and non-existence...

There are thirty-two kinds of "animal-talk" (*tiracchānakathā*). Alternatively, although not explicitly mentioned in the text, talk concerning forests, mountains, rivers, and islands is included by the word "and so forth" (*iti-śabdena*), and thus these are called the thirty-six kinds of animal-talk.

Here, in the phrase "or thus" (*iti vā*), the word *iti* signifies a manner or kind, while the word *vā* signifies an alternative. What is meant is this: "of such a kind as this, or another similar to it."

“...talking useless talk. Alternatively, the word *iti* has the sense of “namely,” as in such passages as, “He abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and watching shows, namely, from such things as these.
The meaning is: “They talk other similar kinds of talk as well, beginning with this. 512.

“The precincts of an unenclosed village should be understood in the same manner as described under the taking of what is not given (adinnādāna); by this [statement], the second throw of the clod is indicated.

Here, "neighboring area" is what is indicated. The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are: not asking a monk who is present, the absence of a permitted reason, and entering a village at an improper time.
The commentary on the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time is finished.
4. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Needle Case (Sūcighara-sikkhāpada) 517.

Regarding the fourth [offense]: because one must first break it and subsequently confess it with the words "that exists for me" (*taṃ assa atthīti*), it is called *bhedanaka*—meaning that the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) exists for that breaking.
Thus, it is a *pācittiya*. In this context, the suffix *-a* should be understood as having the sense of existence (*assatthiatthe*).
"Vāsijaṭā" means a needle-case. The rest here is self-evident.
However, the three factors here are: being a needle-case, being made of bone or other such materials, and its acquisition through having it made for one's own sake or having it made by others.
The commentary on the training rule concerning needle-cases is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Beds and Stools (Mañcapīṭhasikkhāpada) 522.
Regarding the fifth [offense], it is said that "the method of cutting" (*chedanaka*) is exactly as previously stated. "Cutting" itself is "cutting-ness" (*chedanaka*);

because one possesses that, it is called "cutting-ness"—this is how the meaning is understood. The rest here is self-evident. [The offense consists in] having a bed or stool that exceeds the prescribed measure.
"Whether making it oneself or having it made, the acquisition"—these are the two factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning beds and chairs is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Coverings of Cotton.
526. Regarding "having inserted cotton" (*tūla*) in the sixth [offense]: the meaning is that after spreading a mattress (*cimilika*) underneath, one inserts cotton on top of it.
"Cotton of *poṭaka* grass" refers to the cotton of any species of grass, such as *eraka* grass and so forth. The rest here is self-evident.
These [offenses] consist of either making for oneself or having someone else make a bed or chair covered with cotton, or obtaining one that has been so made.
In this context, there are two factors. For regarding what has been caused to be done by oneself, the offense of *pācittiya* occurs merely through the acquisition [of the object].
Therefore, it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "By means of the acquisition, having torn it out, one must confess the *pācittiya*.

However, as for the statement by someone that "regarding 'by means of the acquisition, having torn it out, one must confess the *pācittiya*', although it appears as if the *pācittiya* occurs merely through the acquisition..."
It is said: "It is seen that the offense should be regarded as occurring only upon consumption; the statement, 'Having obtained what was made by another, he consumes it:
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' is the proof for this," but that is merely his own opinion.
For the statement, "Having obtained what was made by another, he consumes it: there is an offense of wrong-doing," does not refer to what one has caused to be made by oneself.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*); by this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is stated on account of the act of having [a bed or chair] made, not on account of its use.
For it is stated in the *Khandhaka*: "Monks, a bed or chair upholstered with cotton down must not be used;
whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Thus, whether it has been made by oneself...
Or if it is by another means, for one who uses it, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense due to the act of using it, not a *pācittiya*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stuffed with cotton is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting Mats.

531. What needs to be said regarding the seventh [offense] has already been stated in the training rule concerning sitting mats (*nisīdana-santhata-sikkhāpada*). The two factors here are: the exceeding of the prescribed measurement for a sitting mat, and its acquisition either by having it made for one’s own sake or by having it made for one.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats is finished. 537–542.
Regarding the eighth, ninth, and tenth [offenses], there is nothing further to be said; their factors should also be understood according to the method already explained for the seventh.
The ninth chapter, the Rājavagga, is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Khuddaka section in the Sāratthadīpanī, the sub-commentary to the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā.
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) is finished.
6. The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa): Commentary on the Training Rules Concerning Offenses Entailing Confession.

552. Regarding the first *pāṭidesanīya*, because of the statement, "‘It is blameworthy, friend,’ etc., shows the manner in which the offense is to be confessed," the offense must be confessed according to the method found in the Canon itself.
"Unsuitable" (*asappāya*) means detrimental to heaven and liberation, or not conducive to them.
The rest here is self-evident. [The conditions are: being fully ordained, the person being unrelated by blood, and [the food] being from the hand of one standing within a house.
Receiving with one's own hand, being of a temporary nature, and swallowing—these are the five factors here.
Regarding the second, third, and fourth [offenses], there is nothing further to be said; however, among the factors, in the second offense, the factors are:

the state of being fully ordained, the state of being one of the five kinds of food, giving up [the meal] in a manner other than the permitted way while standing within a house, and not being restrained.
"Swallowing" refers to these five factors.

In the third [offense], there are these five factors: being designated as one who is still in training (*sekkha*), not having been previously invited, not being ill, stepping across the threshold of a house, and eating after taking other food—excluding regular meals and the like.

In the fourth [offense], there are these seven factors: the aforementioned state of being a forest dwelling, the fact that it is not produced for the purpose of a meal-time food (*yāvakālika*), not being ill, not being the remainder of what was not for the ill, not having made it known [that one is ill], receiving it within the monastery precincts, and swallowing it.
The commentary on the training rules for offenses entailing confession is finished. The section on offenses entailing confession is finished.
7. The Section on Training Rules (Sekhiyakaṇḍa).
1. Commentary on the Chapter on the Circular (Parimaṇḍalavagga):

"By one who has trained in the training regarding the Sekhiya rules" means by one who stands having trained in the three trainings via the four paths; it is said that he is "one whose duty is entirely completed. "Tādin" means "such-like," in the sense of being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions.
576. "The training is to be practiced" means the training in every respect—both in the monastery and within the village—with the thought, "I shall dress in this manner."
[The training rules] are to be observed. And here, since even the observances (vatta) stated in the Vattakkhandhaka are indeed *sekhiya* because they are to be trained in,
no specific limit [of offenses] is made— as is the case with the *pārājika* rules and so forth— and rather, for the purpose of showing the method of conduct, it says,
"A training is to be observed," instead of stating it by way of an offense name such as, "Whatever monk should wear [his robe] hanging down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."
Thus the text has been established for all training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

However, since it is stated in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) that "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," one should understand that in every case, a *dukkaṭa* occurs when there is a lack of respect. This is what was stated in the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*).
Because, when one sits having lowered [the robe] by only eight finger-breadths, it remains at only four finger-breadths [above the ground], therefore—
Both of these commentarial positions constitute a single section. "All those" refers to the faults regarding the lower robe (*nivāsana*).

As for "that," it refers to that lack of respect. Although the author of the *Kurundi* commentary, by stating later on that "there is no offense for one who does not know how to wear the lower robe evenly," establishes this point, nevertheless, the proper procedure for wearing the lower robe must certainly be thoroughly mastered.
For one who intentionally fails to observe [the rules], there may be disrespect (*anādariya*). Therefore, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "‘Not knowing’ means:
for one who does not know how to put on the lower robe properly, there is no offense; nevertheless, the procedure for wearing the lower robe (*nivāsana-vatta*) should be learned.

"With a conscious mind" (*sacittaka*) means: with a mind that knows the objective basis (*vatthu*) and with a mind that knows the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), it is "with a conscious mind"—[namely,] disrespect.

Because it is stated [in the texts] as "dependent upon. The Elder Phussadeva said: "Since the fault of wearing [the robe] improperly is not censured by the world in the same way as killing living beings and so forth, it is a 'prescribed offense' (paṇṇattivajja).
However, the Elder Upatissa said: "Because it is to be committed solely through a lack of respect, it is exclusively unwholesome;
furthermore, that is a natural offense (pakativajja), and its intentional transgression occurs only for one who is afflicted by dejection."
"Therefore, unwholesome consciousness involving what is forbidden by the world has painful feeling," he said.
Furthermore, there are three factors here: disrespect, the absence of a cause for non-offense, and wearing the lower robe improperly. And just as it is here, so it is everywhere:
there are only three factors—the first two and the performance of the opposite of what was stated in each respective case.

577. Regarding the second and subsequent cases, "the various kinds of lay dress" refers to the many varieties of lay attire, such as the white-cloth dress, the ascetic dress, the single-robe dress, and so forth.
Its meaning will be clarified in the Khandhaka itself. The phrase "even in the monastery" is said with reference to times such as when attending upon the Buddha.

578. Since it was stated, "well-covered," for one who might think, "He is 'well-covered' because he is covered up to his head in every way," [the text] says, "not by one covered up to the head," and so forth.

582. Regarding the phrase "standing in one place," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Even while walking, one may indeed look for the absence of dangers; likewise, one may do so in a village for the sake of receiving honor.
The commentary on the *Parimaṇḍala-vagga* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Ujjagghika-vagga*.
586. Regarding the phrase "in the second section, concerning the matter of laughing": it refers to a cause that gives rise to laughter.
The commentary on the Ujjagghika-vagga is finished.
3. Commentary on the Khambhakata-vagga.
603. In the third section, *saññā* means "perception regarding the bowl" (*pattasaññā*). One who possesses that is "one with the perception regarding the bowl" (*pattasaññī*);
the meaning is: having formed a fixed perception directed toward one's own vessel. However, in order to show the mere meaning without taking the literal expression into account, it is said:
"having made a perception regarding the bowl."
604. *Oloṇī* is a certain preparation of sauce (*byañjanavikati*). Some say it is "any pure liquid substance having the taste of sour gruel, curd, and so forth.

By the inclusion of the term "vegetable curry" (*sākasūpeyya*), any preparation of sauce made from vegetables is meant. Regarding the phrase "meat broth, etc.," it should be understood that by the word "etc.," all remaining preparations of sauce are included.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Excluding..."
"But the soup, and all the remaining soups and preparations of curry, are called 'the essence of flavor' (rasarasa).
605. "Evenly filled" (*samapuṇṇa*) means prepared without exceeding the rim-line of the mouth of a bowl that has been properly determined for its capacity.
"Equally heaped up" (*samabharita*) is a synonym for that same term. Regarding the phrase "fruits and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes boiled rice and other such items as well.
"It descends below" means that, because there is space all around, it falls down when shaken.
It is called a "cake-earring" (*pūvavaṭaṃsaka*) because the cake placed on top is like an earring; the same principle applies to flower-earrings and so forth.
Since the statement, "almsfood should be accepted level to the brim," means that the almsfood should be accepted when it is full, [the bowl should not be filled to overflowing].
It illuminates [the rule]; therefore, it shows that even if almsfood is being given into a bowl held in one’s own hand, it is permissible even if it is heaped up like a stupa.

For the statement, “He receives almsfood that has been heaped up like a stupa: there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” indicates that there is an offense for one who receives the almsfood after it has first been heaped up like a stupa. And [it applies] to one who receives it into a bowl...

It has been said by someone that "it becomes *thūpīkata* (heaped up); it is permissible because it was received when not yet heaped up, though there is no further preparation except in the eastern regions"—this should not be accepted as authoritative.

For the statement, "He does not accept alms-food that is heaped up," indicates that one first receives [the food] while it is still heaped up, and only afterwards does it become so. Indeed, it is not...
Even when receiving what is being given in a bowl that has already been placed in the hand,
one is not said to be "receiving almsfood heaped up," nor can it be understood that the almsfood has been received "level with the brim" by that act. Furthermore,
if "heaped up" (*thūpīkata*) is taken as a neuter noun in the locative case, this meaning becomes even more clearly evident.
The commentary on the Khambhakatavagga is finished.
4. Commentary on the Sakkaccavagga: 608.
Regarding the term *sapadāna* in the fourth chapter, here *dāna* refers to "breaking" (*avakhaṇḍana*). That which is devoid of breaking is *apadāna*.
“Without interruption” means without breaking. “With *apadāna*” means together with *apadāna*; it is said to be free from interruption, that is, in continuous succession.
Therefore he said: “without making a boundary here and there, in continuous succession. 611.
At whatever time kings cause the drum to be beaten, proclaiming, “No living being is to be killed,” this is the season of *māghāta*.
[This is] the name. Here, there is no offense for one who is ill and has not come; therefore, there is an offense even for the one who is ill. Regarding the training rule on requesting soup and rice:

here, "unintentionally" and "through forgetfulness" refers to one who, having put [the food] into the mouth, later feels remorse and discards it—this is called "unintentionally" when it enters against one's will. Whether it was requested or unrequested, it is established in this context.
"Taking [the food] suddenly and eating it is called 'eating without mindfulness'"; this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. 614–615.
"Perception of censure" (*ujjhāna-saññā*) means perception of censure; one who possesses that is "one with perception of censure.
Because of the statement, "A peacock's egg is too large," a mouthful the size of a peacock's egg is not permitted. However, some say, "It is not permitted if it is larger than a peacock's egg."
What they say should not be accepted; for since "not too large" specifically excludes what is excessively large, no offense is seen in the case of something small.
However, it should be understood that by the statement, "A peacock's egg is too large, a hen's egg is too small;
the measure is between those two," the limit is not shown because even the small is excluded on account of its unsuitability.
The commentary on the Sakkacca-vagga is finished.
5. Commentary on the Kabaḷa-vagga: 618.
Regarding the phrase "the whole hand" in the fifth vagga, the word *hattha* (hand) should be understood here as referring to the fingers, which are parts thereof.
Just as in the case of terms such as "hand-gesture" (*hatthamuddā*), where a conventional expression applied to a whole is also used for its parts,
it is not permitted to place even a single finger in the mouth.
The commentary on the section on mouthfuls (*kabaḷavagga*) is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Surusuru-vagga* 627.

In the sixth chapter, *sītīkato* means "one who seeks coolness," that is to say, one oppressed by heat. *Silakabuddho* is a term used in jest; for when people see someone with a certain appearance, they jokingly address them as "this is a Buddha.
634. *Vilīvacchattaṃ* is an umbrella made from bamboo shoots (*vilīva*). *Tatthajātakadaṇḍakena kataṃ* refers to a palm-leaf [fan] made from a stalk grown there.
Having cut it together with the handle, they make that very [piece] into a handle for the umbrella, just as cowherds and others do;
it is with reference to this that it was said. Regarding the phrase "it stands upon an umbrella-stand" (*chattapādukā*), here "umbrella-stand" (*chattapādukā*) refers to an umbrella-support.
An umbrella that is placed upon such an umbrella-stand so that it does not fall is called "an umbrella."
It should be brought near. Some also read, “The umbrella is standing on the umbrella-stand,” and there too the meaning is the same.
637. *Cāpa* is a type of bow that is curved in the middle, resembling a cane staff. *Kodaṇḍa* is a type of bow with a rounded staff. *Paṭimukka* means inserted or fixed.
The commentary on the *Surusuruvagga* is concluded.
7. Explanation of the Chapter on Sandals (Pāduka-vagga) 647.

Regarding the phrase "having hidden himself" in the seventh chapter: it is said that he went to the park during the night, climbed a mango tree, and wandered from branch to branch looking down at the mango grove. While he was doing exactly that, the night turned into dawn. He...
He thought, "If I go down now and proceed, they will see me and seize me as a thief; I shall go during the night.
Then, having climbed a branch and remained hidden there, he waited. It was with reference to this that it was said.
As he was descending from the tree, he took hold of a hanging branch and positioned himself between those two. It was with reference to this that it was said.
“It fell from the tree between those two. They do not understand the meaning of the text means they do not understand the meaning of what they have grasped.
However, this verse in the *Jātaka-pāḷi* is as follows:
“All this has been done in vain; both of you fail to see the Dhamma.”
"Both those who have passed away from their natural state, he who causes the mantra to be recited, and he who studies the mantra"—thus it is handed down. This is its meaning:
"All this has been done as the final act" refers to that which was performed by us three people.
"All this business is base, lawless, and contrary to the Dhamma.
Having thus censured his own thievery and their lack of respect for the mantras, he spoke the verse beginning with "Both do not see the Dhamma," censuring the other two as well.
Therein, "both" refers to these two people who do not see the ancient Dhamma worthy of veneration; therefore, from that very departure from the Dhamma...
Cutā. For *dhamma* is called "nature" (*pakati*) by virtue of its first arising. And this has been said:
"In the beginning, indeed, *dhamma* appeared;
afterwards, *adhamma* arose in the world."
"And who this" refers to both the one who, sitting on a low seat, causes [the pupil] to recite the mantras, and the one who, sitting on a high seat, studies them.
Regarding the phrase "of rice," there is also this verse:
"I eat the boiled rice of paddy, pure, with meat as a sauce;”
"Therefore, I do not practice this; I practice the Dhamma practiced by the seers"—thus it is recorded in the Jātaka.
In that context, *sucim* means white and pure. *Maṃsūpasecanam* means sprinkled with various kinds of meat preparations; the sense is "I eat," or "I am eating. The rest is self-evident.
*Dhiratthu* means "let there be shame" (*dhi atthu*); the sense is "let there be reproach"; the meaning is "we censure that. *Laddhalābho* means...

He speaks with reference to the acquisition of wealth and the acquisition of fame. "By way of being a cause for falling into ruin" means by way of its being a cause for falling into the states of misery (vinipāta).

"It is called a livelihood" means that both kinds of gain mentioned above are called a livelihood because they proceed—due to their leading to the states of misery—in the future as causes for falling into ruin, and because they proceed in the present through the practice of unrighteousness (adhammacaraṇa). Such [a livelihood]...
"Yā vutti" means such a way of life characterized by the acquisition of wealth and the acquisition of safety. "Adhammacaraṇena vā": the word "vā" has the sense of inclusion. "Tvam":
this is the nominative case used in the sense of the accusative; alternatively, the reading is simply "tam. "Asmā": this is a designation for a stone.
The commentary on the Pādukavagga is finished.
The rest is self-evident.
The Section on the Training Rules (Sekhiyakaṇḍa) is finished.
Regarding what is to be said concerning the methods for settling legal issues (adhikaraṇasamatha), we shall present it at the very places where it appears in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga in the Sāratthadīpanī, the sub-commentary to the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā.
The Mahāvibhaṅga is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Analysis for Bhikkhunīs 1.
The Section on Defeat (Bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)
1. Commentary on the First Pārājika Training Rule 656.
Regarding the phrase "in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga": *yo* means that which is the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) for the bhikkhunīs.

As for the term *Migāra-nattā*, he says, "she was the granddaughter of Migāra’s mother," explaining this by means of the elision of the middle term (*majjhapadalopa*). *Migāra-mātā* is a designation for Visākhā.

“Supervisor of new construction” means one who arranges new construction. Since the aspect to be penetrated regarding the phonemes is not very deep, what must be done there is simply the retention of what has been heard;
thus, the activity of mindfulness (*sati*) is predominant, while wisdom (*paññā*) is subordinate there.
Hence it is said, “by wisdom preceded by mindfulness. This means that mindfulness is its precursor.
"Preceded by mindfulness. Here, "preceding" means the state of being primary, as in such expressions as "mind is the forerunner" (*manopubbaṅgamā*).
However, because the object to be penetrated is extremely profound, the activity of wisdom (*paññā*) is predominant in the grasping of that meaning; thus he says, "by mindfulness preceded by wisdom.
"Free from sloth" means devoid of indolence. Just as others who are lazy remain seated wherever they have sat, [this mindfulness does not do so].
They remain exactly where they are situated; thus, without having previously existed [in that state], one accomplishes all tasks through the expansion of the mind.
All bhikkhunīs are of two kinds: those who have received full ordination from the Teacher and those who have received full ordination from the Saṅgha.

For it was through the undertaking of the heavy rules (garudhamma) that Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī received her full ordination directly from the presence of the Teacher; therefore, she is one whose full ordination was obtained from the Teacher.
[This is] the name. All the others have received full admission from the Saṅgha. They too are of two kinds: those fully admitted on one side and those fully admitted on both sides.

In that regard, those five hundred Sakyan women who went forth together with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī were fully admitted on one side, because they received full admission from the Bhikkhu-saṅgha alone; the others were fully admitted on both sides.

Because they were ordained by both Saṅghas. However, there are no bhikkhunīs who were ordained by the "Come, Bhikkhunī" formula, because such an ordination does not exist for them. If this is so, why is it said here, "Come, bhikkhunī"?

It is because [the term] falls within the scope of the teaching. For this state of falling within the scope of the teaching exists even when something is not included among those things that are actually obtainable in certain instances.

There is a case where a jhāna factor, although found in the *Manodhātu-niddesa* of the Abhidhamma, is not extracted [as such] because it is impossible for it to occur in any teaching applicable to the stream of the fivefold sensory consciousness;
this is like the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) in the *Vatthu-niddesa* of that same work.
There is also a case where it is included by way of its inclusion even though it is not found in some places, as in the *Yathāṭhita-kappa-niddesa*. As it is said:
“And what kind of person is one who stays for an eon (*ṭhitakappī*)?

Suppose there were a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and it were the time for the eon to be consumed by fire; yet the eon would not be consumed until that person has realized the fruit of stream-entry.”

In this case as well, it should be understood by way of the non-attainment of the taking [of the precepts]. For this is a hypothetical statement: "If the Blessed One were to say to some woman fit for the state of a bhikkhunī, 'Come, bhikkhunī,' then in that way the state of a bhikkhunī might come to be.
But why did the Blessed One not speak thus? Because there was an absence of those who had performed such service [in previous lives].

As for those who state the reason as being "due to the state of not being near or present," they say: "For it is the bhikkhus alone who are the Teacher’s attendants and are always present; therefore..."
They say that only those [monks] are worthy of being addressed as "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu), and not the nuns;

however, that is merely their own opinion, because the status of being near to or far from the Teacher is established by one's capacity or incapacity [for realization]. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, even if a monk were to follow close behind me, holding onto the corner of my outer robe..."

Even if he were to place foot after foot down, yet if he is covetous for sense pleasures, with intense passion, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt intentions, muddled mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties—then indeed he is far from me, and I am far from him.
Why is that? Because, monks, that bhikkhu does not see the Dhamma.
One who does not see the Dhamma does not see me. Even if a bhikkhu were to dwell a hundred yojanas away, bhikkhus,
yet if he is free from covetousness for sensual pleasures, without intense passion, with a mind free from ill will, with intentions that are not corrupt,
established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and with sense faculties restrained— then he is indeed close to me.
“[He is] mine, and I am his. For what reason? Because, monks, that monk sees the Dhamma;
seeing the Dhamma, he sees me.

Therefore, proximity or distance from the Teacher in terms of location is not the cause [of spiritual attainment]. However, it should be understood that because they had not performed the necessary service, the bhikkhunīs were unfit for the *ehibhikkhunī* (come, bhikkhunī) ordination.
If this is so, then as for that which was said by Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā in the Therīgāthā:
“Having pressed my knee to the ground and paid homage, I placed my joined palms before her;
‘Come, Bhaddā,’ she said to me—that was my full ordination.”
Likewise, in her own account (Apadāna), she says:
“Then the Leader said to me when requested, ‘Come, blessed one!
At that moment I was fully ordained, and I saw a small amount of water.”
How is that so? This was not said with reference to the full admission (*upasampadā*) by way of the "Come, Bhikkhunī" formula;
rather, it was said because [the Teacher’s command] was the cause for her full admission: "That which was the Teacher’s instruction—that has been my full admission.
For it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Come, lady! Go to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters, receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), and receive the full admission in the presence of the bhikkhunīs."
"He commanded me; that command of the Teacher became my full ordination (*upasampadā*) because it was the cause for my full ordination.
The meaning of the verse in the *Apadāna* should also be understood in this very way. Therefore, one must conclude that there is no "Come, Bhikkhunī" full ordination for bhikkhunīs.
And just as this [expression] "Come, bhikkhunī" occurs by way of falling within the range of hearing—

It has been stated that "one who is ordained by means of the three goings for refuge is a bhikkhunī"; this too should be understood as having been stated by way of inclusion within the scope of the discourse, because going for refuge as the mode of ordination is impossible for bhikkhunīs.
This is because in the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga, it is not said "she should consent to bodily contact," but rather "she should enter into [it]."
It is said: “A bhikkhu is not to be dealt with for an offense.
