By the method of “abundance thereof” (tabbahulanaya) means because of the predominance of that which originates from action (kiriyāsamuṭṭhāna). For such a designation is seen by way of abundance thereof, as in the expression “a brahmin village.
Even in a brahmin village, there are at least five other castes, such as washermen and so forth. And this [term] refers to the state of originating from action.
662. “In the same way” means that he is indeed one who is corrupted by the lust for physical contact. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the first *pārājika* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *pārājika* training rule.

666. In the second [section], because of the statement, "But why, noble lady, do you knowingly commit an offense involving defeat (pārājika)," and because of the statement, "Noble ladies, the eight offenses involving defeat have been recited," etc., upon reaching the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, the training rules common [to both orders] are applied to the very same cases that arose for the bhikkhus: "Whichever bhikkhunī, out of desire... [and so forth].
“Should one engage in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, one is defeated and no longer in communion”—

having established the matrix (mātikā) in this manner, both specifically and generally, [the Buddha] then elaborated upon it by sequentially explaining the word-commentary (padabhājana), the classification of offenses (āpattibheda), the analysis of the triads (tikaccheda),
and the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra) in their entirety. However, the compilers of the Council (saṅgītikāraka) [retained] only those rules that were uniquely prescribed (asādhāraṇapaññatti).
It should be understood that [the rule] was laid down in detail here.
Now, since the two subsequent rules have not yet been promulgated, the statement "one of the eight *pārājikas*" would not be appropriate;
therefore, he said: "And this *pārājika* was promulgated later," and so forth. If this is so, why was it [promulgated] at this point?
It is said, “It is established,” with the words, “But because of its being a pair together with the preceding one,” and so forth;

the intention is that it is mentioned here because of its state of having a single connection with what precedes it. Furthermore, from the statement, “One or another of the eight *pārājikas*,” it should be understood that whoever conceals a concealment of an offense (*vajjapaṭicchādikā*) is herself indeed a concealer of an offense. Even though the concealing of an offense...
Although it occurs by way of pleasure, nevertheless, because the mind that transgresses the training rule is indeed afflicted with dejection, it is called "painful feeling.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the second Pārājika training rule is finished.
668. The third [section] has its meaning already explained.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika Training Rule: 675.

Regarding the phrase "by way of intimacy with friends consisting of worldly pleasure," this means by way of intimacy with friends characterized as worldly pleasure. To clarify that very same point through a different expression, it is stated: "by passion for physical contact."
"Regarding the three women, he does not engage in sexual intercourse": among those three women who have been mentioned, he does not engage in that which is called sexual intercourse.
"Regarding the three men": having approached even these three men, he does not engage in sexual intercourse.
"And regarding the three ignoble paṇḍakas": these are the three ignoble ones reckoned as hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjana*), and the three *paṇḍakas*—these too [he avoids].
One does not engage in sexual intercourse after approaching six types of persons. Nor does one practice sexual intercourse with a "sign" (*byañjana*);

that is, even according to the *anuloma-pārājika*, one does not practice sexual intercourse with one's own [genital] organ. The question, "Could there be an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) on account of the practice of sexual intercourse?

Could there be a *pārājika* on account of the practice of sexual intercourse?"—this was stated with reference to the eight bases (*aṭṭhavatthuka*) alone. For, regarding that practice of sexual intercourse...
For one who strives to engage in physical contact as a preliminary stage, there is a *chejja* (cutting off) offense on account of sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*). *Chejja* is simply "cutting.

By the phrase "being a preliminary stage to sexual intercourse," it is demonstrated that only the physical contact which constitutes the preliminary stage to sexual intercourse is expressed here by the term *methunadhamma*, and not the actual mutual penetration of both organs. Regarding the term *vaṇṇāvaṇṇo*:
Two types of emission of semen have been mentioned. "Setting in motion a journey" refers to acting as a go-between.
"In all instances" refers to cases such as "if she should consent to the grasping of the corner of the outer robe," and so forth. The rest here is self-evident.
However, the three factors here are: lust for physical contact, the presence of intent, and the fulfillment of the eighth constituent of the offense.
The commentary on the fourth *pārājika* training rule is finished.
The commentary on the section on *pārājika* offenses in the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga* is finished.
The *Pārājika-khaṇḍa* is finished.
2. Saṅghādisesa Section (Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga) 1.
Commentary on the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 679.
Regarding the first training rule of the Saṅghādisesa Section: "In the case of two persons" means in the case of two persons who act as mediators in a lawsuit.
"Whoever" means anyone among those two, or someone else authorized by them. Regarding "he informs the second," it should be understood that the meaning here is:

"whichever of the two persons is the second, he informs him"—thus he says, "In the case of 'he informs the second,' this same method applies. "Gatigata" means that which has been in existence for a long time.

*Āpatti* means "the act of falling into [an offense]. *Saha vatthujjhācārā* means "together with the transgression of the basis. When there is the possibility of using the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*), this is used as an ablative case.
*Yaṃ* refers to whichever rule (*dhamma*). *Nissāreti* means she causes her to be expelled from the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs who has fallen into [an offense].
This is a metaphorical designation of the agent for the cause; for the rule that serves as the cause for the expulsion is called "expulsion" (*nissāraṇīya*). It is just like a debt (*gīvā*).
It constitutes an offense, yet it is not a *pārājika* because it was taken without formal authorization (*anāṇatti*).

Just as it is not permissible to accept slaves, slave-girls, ponds, and so forth, likewise it is not permissible to carry out transactions for their sake; thus he said, "This is called an improper transaction (*akappiya-aḍḍa*); it is not permissible.
And here, if one goes to the place of the legal dispute and says, "This is our slave, our slave-girl, our pond, our field, our monastery..."
To speak in such terms as, "The monastery site," "the cows," "the goats," or "the chickens," is improper (*akappiya*). [One may say instead: "This is our monastery attendant;
this pond was given by so-and-so for the purpose of washing the Sangha’s requisites;
from this field, from this monastery, let the four requisites arise; from these cows, from these buffaloes, from these goats, let dairy products arise; by so-and-so..."
They say: "Whether asked or unasked, it is permissible to say, 'It has been given to the Saṅgha. The rest here is self-evident.
However, these two factors are present here: the conducting of a lawsuit that was not brought forward, and the conclusion of the lawsuit.
The commentary on the first Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 683.
Regarding the second [rule], in the phrase "the group of wrestlers, the group of hired sons," and so forth:

the "group of wrestlers" (*mallagaṇa*) refers to a group devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa who performs meritorious deeds such as establishing water-stations and digging ponds here and there; the "group of hired sons" (*bhaṭiputtagaṇa*) refers to...

The *kumārabhattika-gaṇa* (the group of those who provide food for children). The *dhamma-gaṇa* (the group of the Dhamma) refers to the group that provides sustenance for the Dispensation (*sāsana-bhattika-gaṇa*) and the group that performs various kinds of meritorious deeds.
The *gandhika-seṇī* (perfumer’s guild) is a group that manufactures various kinds of fragrant preparations. The *dussika-seṇī* (cloth-dealer’s guild) is a group of weavers.
*Kappagatikaṃ* means having attained the state of being allowable (*kappiya*).

"Causing to emerge" means "conferring full ordination. It is said that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who, according to the stated method, ordains a female thief (*corī*) without having asked permission.

It should be understood that the phrase "three types of consciousness" (*ticitta*) is stated either because even Noble Ones (*ariya*) who are ignorant of the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*) cause her to emerge, or because at the moment of the completion of the ritual formula (*kammavācā*), she possesses a state of moral indeterminacy (*vipākābyākata*). The rest here is self-evident.
A thief, the perception of her as a thief, and giving her the full admission except for an authorized reason—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the second Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule.
692. Regarding "crossing the boundary in the third [case]": this refers to one who crosses the boundary of another village from her own village.

For according to the statement, "She should go to another village," an offense occurs only for one who crosses the boundary of another village, not for one who crosses the boundary of her own village.
Indeed, "another village" (gāmantara) means a different village. Regarding the vicinity of an unenclosed village:
Here, by the word "vicinity" (*upacāra*), the place suitable for enclosure—defined as the range of the first stone-throw from the vicinity of the house—is intended;
it does not mean the vicinity defined as the range of the second stone-throw. Therefore, he says "the place suitable for enclosure.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Canon: "for one who crosses the vicinity. Otherwise, as in the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time, [the meaning would be different].
It was said: "for one crossing the boundary of an enclosed village, or entering the precincts of an unenclosed village";
likewise here too, one should say: "for one crossing the boundary of an enclosed village, or entering the precincts of an unenclosed village. This is the meaning stated in brief.
Explaining by way of analysis, he said, "Furthermore, in this case... and so forth.
By the phrase "because the monastery is common to four villages," he states the reason for the statement, "It is permissible to go from the monastery to one village.
Indeed, precisely because the monastery is common to four villages, it is permissible to go to whichever one among those four villages is chosen.
"In which river" means in whichever river. Because of the statement, "For one lifting the first foot, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*;
for one lifting the second foot, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*," it is said that the offense applies only to one who has descended into the river and is crossing on foot;
thus he says, "If she goes by a bridge, there is no offense," and so forth. There is no offense for one who steps only onto the opposite bank.
There is no offense for one who, without descending into the river, travels by means of any vehicle or boat and steps onto the opposite bank itself.

Regarding the statement, "It is permissible if she wanders on both banks," it should be understood that this was said merely to show the result of the formal analysis (*vinicchaya*) that will be explained further below, even though there is no crossing to the other side of the river. If she returns to this very bank...
"An offense" is said because of having entered [the water] with the desire to go to the further shore. "That very shore" refers to that very near shore.
"No offense" means there is no offense due to the absence of the desire to go to the further shore.
"In such a forest" refers to a forest defined by the characteristic stated thus: "All this beyond the boundary-stake is forest. Now...
To explain how it is understood that such a forest has been entered, he says, "By that very [reason]," and so forth.

For by this statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is understood that an offense occurs even in such a case—namely, when one has left the range of sight near a village, even though the range of hearing still remains.
He says, "As if by the sound of those who have lost their way," meaning they are making a loud noise because they are lost on the road.
"Saddāyantiyā" means making a sound. "Purimāyo" means those who go ahead. "She takes another path" is because she is lost, not because she intends to abandon [the group];
therefore, there is no offense for either of the two. The rest here is self-evident. However, the three factors here are:
being in the same company without an obstacle, arriving at one of the conditions such as going between villages, and the absence of an emergency.
The commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the fourth Saṅghādisesa training rule: 694.
"Of the group of those who perform" means of the group of those who perform the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma). It consists of forty-three divisions.

The procedure (*vatta*) will be made clear in the *Khandhaka*. Regarding "the procedure for deliverance" (*netthāravatta*), it refers to the procedure that is the cause for deliverance. The rest is self-evident.
Here, however, there are these two factors: being suspended by a legitimate legal act (*dhamma-kamma*), and reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) except for a permitted reason.
The commentary on the fourth *saṅghādisesa* training rule is finished.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 701.
Regarding the fifth [rule], it is said: "This was not stated"—that is, this restriction, namely, "the lustful state of the bhikkhunī must be observed," was not stated.
"That" refers to that non-statement of such a restriction. It accords with the Pāḷi because [the text] says, "if one is lustful," without making a distinction.
This accords with the stated canonical text: "Knowing [the man] to be lustful, she accepts.

For if the lustfulness of the person were not a criterion, why would there be this statement, "Knowing [him] to be lustless," when it would have been sufficient simply to say, "There is no offense if both are lustless; if she is lustless, she accepts"?
It may be so. The meaning of this section on non-offense, which states, “Both are lustful, and she accepts it knowing them to be lustful,” is as follows:
If both are lustless, there is no offense in any respect whatsoever.
Furthermore, if a nun, being herself lustless, accepts from the hand of one who is lustful while perceiving him to be “lustless,” there is likewise no offense.
Now, even if she herself is not lustful, if she knows another who is either lustful or not lustful as being "lustful," it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For this has been stated in the immediately preceding training rule: "Why, noble lady, do you not accept [the gift]? "Because the noble lady is lustful. "But are you, noble lady, lustful?
"I am not, noble lady, lustful. The rest here is self-evident. From the water for rinsing the mouth.
Other edible food, being poured from both [hands], taking it with one's own hand, and swallowing—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the fifth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the sixth Saṅghādisesa training rule.

705. This is the meaning of the sixth verse in the section on attendants (*parivāra-gāthā*). "Neither gives nor receives" means that the instigator does not give, nor does the one instigated receive from her hand.

"There is no receiving by that means" means that for that very reason, there is no receiving by the one instigated from the hand of the instigator. "One incurs a grave offense" means even though this is the case...
If she encourages the taking of alms from the hand of one who is lustful, she incurs an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
And that [offense] is on account of consumption; moreover, while incurring that offense, she does so because of the consumption by the one she encouraged.
For at the conclusion of her meal, the one who encouraged it incurs the *saṅghādisesa*. The rest here is self-evident. [The factors are: being a human male...
"Having taken hard food or soft food, one eats except for a permitted reason"—this is the incitement.
By that statement, "having taken [it], until the end of her meal"—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the sixth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 709. Regarding the seventh rule, “*kin nu māva samaṇiyo*”:
“Are these indeed *samaṇīs*? means “Are these truly *samaṇīs*? “*Tāsāhaṃ*” means “I [am one] among them. The remainder is self-evident.
The commentary on the seventh Saṅghādisesa training rule is concluded.
715. The eighth [offense] has its meaning already explained.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule: 721.

Regarding the ninth, “one who conceals a fault” means one who conceals even a minor or very minor fault. Furthermore, at the time of the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*), two or three persons may be admonished together.
The commentary on the ninth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
727. The tenth [rule] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the Saṅghādisesa rules in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is finished.
The Section on Saṅghādisesa is finished.
3. The Section on Nissaggiya (Exposition of the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga). 733.
Among the Nissaggiya rules, the first is self-evident.
740. Regarding the second [case], "received by saying 'I give to the noble lady,'" this refers to what is received as a relinquishment (*nissaṭṭha-paṭiladdha*).
For that very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even after receiving what has been relinquished, it should be treated exactly as it was given.

"It should be treated exactly as it was given" means it should be handled in the same manner as it was given by the donor; that is to say, it should be placed within the category of out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*).

[The offense] exists. And herein, it is only the robe obtained by having it distributed that becomes subject to forfeiture; even after the formal act of the Vinaya has been performed, one does not receive it oneself.
The rest here is self-evident. These, however, are the four factors herein: (1) it being out-of-season robe-cloth; (2) the perception that it is so;
(3) the distribution by means of a pretext, having determined that it is "in-season robe-cloth"; and (4) the acquisition [of it].
743. Regarding the third [offense], "This is mine": because it was taken with the perception that it was one's own, a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa* are stated.

Otherwise, one should be dealt with according to the value of the article. The three factors here are: the state of being fully ordained (*upasampanna*), the fact that the robe has been exchanged and has not yet reached the stage of formal assignment (*vikappa*), and the act of taking back or causing it to be taken back while perceiving it as one's own.
748–752. "Having given the ghee brought in the fourth [instance]" means having given it to oneself.

"It should be cooked as a mixture" means that the ghee and the oil should be combined and cooked together. Furthermore, the three factors here are: the desire to take it by stealth, the requesting of another, and the acquisition.
753. In the fifth [offense], Sāti Thullanandā is the one involved. "She" refers to this *sikkhamānā*.
"Having caused to be exchanged" (*cetāpetvā*) means "having made known," according to what is stated here; however, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:

"'Having caused another to be exchanged' means having had another trade for it by saying, 'Bring such-and-such with your own allowable goods. Therefore, "having caused to be exchanged" (*cetāpetvā*) also means "having caused to be traded."

The purpose should be understood. "Should exchange for something else" means: thinking, "By giving this to me, he will bring me something else," she should exchange it for another thing, saying, "I have no need for this;

bring me such-and-such. 758. In the sixth [case], "duty of the Dhamma" refers to meritorious action. "Of the cloth merchant" means of the seller of fabrics. "By which it was exchanged" [refers to the means].

There is indeed the forfeiture and the recovery of what was forfeited; therefore, having recovered what was forfeited by that bhikkhunī, it should be handed over according to the original mode of giving, and must not be kept by herself.
"For the sake of another" means for the sake of one of the requisites, such as robes and so forth.
"Designated for another" is a further clarification of the same meaning. "As an article" means as an allowable object.
764. Regarding the seventh [case], "by what has been requested by oneself" (*sayaṃ yācitakena*): the meaning is "even by what has been requested by oneself.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "and having himself also requested that requisite" (*tena ca parikkhārena sayampi yācitvā*). Precisely for that reason, the meaning is stated in the *Mātikāṭṭhakathā*:
"'By what was agreed upon' (*saññācikenā*) means even by what has been requested by oneself."
768–773. The eighth, ninth, and tenth [rules] have their meaning already explained. 784.

Regarding the eleventh: since in a place where one has been invited (*pavārita*) no formal request (*viññatti*) ought to be prohibited, therefore, in a place where one has been invited by way of an invitation to the Dhamma (*dhammanimantanā*), when it is said, "Speak what you need," [the rule concerns] "not more than four *kaṃsa* [weights]."
It should be understood that the phrase "it must be requested" indicates the limit [of what may be asked for]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:

"Regarding 'it must be caused to be bought': setting aside those who are in accordance with the Dhamma (*sahadhammika*) and those who are relatives or invited guests, one should say to anyone else who is satisfied with some particular quality, 'I have need of such-and-such';
thus it is said, 'it must be requested.'"
788. The twelfth [section] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the rules for Nissaggiya-Pācittiya offenses in the Bhikkhunī-Vibhaṅga is finished.
The Section on Nissaggiya Offenses is completed.
4. The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (*Pācittiyakaṇḍa*) (Commentary on the Analysis of the Bhikkhunīs) 1. Commentary on the Chapter on Garlic (*Lasuṇavagga*) 793–797.

Regarding the first [offense] in the Chapter on Garlic among the *pācittiyas*: "One who remembers his birth" (*jātissara*) is so called because he remembers his birth. "By his very nature" (*sabhāvena eva*).
[This refers to] even without broth, condiments, and so forth. "Jujube-curry" (*badarasāḷava*) means a preparation of solid food to be made by drying and pulverizing jujube fruits.
The rest here is self-evident. As for "raw garlic" and "swallowing"—these two are the constituent factors (*aṅga*) here.
798–802. The second, third, and fourth [offenses] have meanings that are self-evident.
812. Regarding the phrase "above two joints on the fifth [finger]": here, when two fingers are inserted together, one joint is counted for each finger, and thus it means "above two joints.
It should be understood that if only one finger is inserted, it is not permissible to be above two joints.
This same method is also shown in the *Mahāpaccarī*. By way of the condition of purification by water...
However, even if there is an enjoyment of contact, there is no offense within the aforementioned limits.
815–817. In the sixth [case], "having shaken" means having caused to fall. "Curd-scum" (*dadhimatthu*) refers to the whey, the clear liquid from curd.
It is the standing within arm’s reach of a monk who is eating, or the taking up of drinking water or a fan.
However, there are these two factors here.
Regarding the seventh [offense], it says, “If she accepts it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)”; this is merely an illustration of the wrong-doing of the preliminary action.
Therefore, he said, “It does not occur only upon acceptance,” and so forth. “Measure” refers to the measure for an offense of expiation (pācittiya). By these very [factors]...
The meaning is that there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for two [specific cases], and not for others such as roasting and so forth.
To demonstrate this very point in detail, he said, "Therefore," and so on. He stated, "That is contradictory to what precedes and follows," referring to the claim that it was already mentioned;

for even if something is obtained through another formal request (*viññatti*), it belongs to the category of what is obtained through this specific non-request (*aviññatti*) because it lacks an explicit instruction (*anāṇatti*).

It follows; therefore, since there is no distinction stated below regarding the performance or causing of an act when there is no *viññatti* (intimation), the specific statement made here is contradictory to what precedes and follows.
If, in this case, there is a *pācittiya* offense for performing the act, then there must likewise be a *pācittiya* offense for causing it to be performed.

Alternatively, if there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for causing it to be performed, then there must likewise be a *dukkaṭa* offense for performing it oneself. For it is not the case that [the offenses differ] between performing and causing to be performed.

Or there is no distinction; therefore, for one who has obtained [food] through another means of communication and then eats it—whether she has prepared it herself by roasting it and so forth, or had it prepared—the offense is indeed *dukkaṭa*.
This is the definitive conclusion here. "Stated without distinction" means stated in general terms regarding both doing and having done.
The rest here is self-evident. It is the requesting of any one of the seven types of grain.
Or causing it to be made known, or obtaining it, or having performed or caused to be performed such acts as roasting and so forth, or swallowing it—these, moreover, are the three factors here.
In the eighth [offense], "procured" means established. "Keṇī" is a designation for the revenue to be paid to the king.
"Adjacent location" (*ṭhānantara*) means an adjacent location such as a village, a district, and so forth. The rest here is self-evident.

However, the five factors here are: the state of being [a place for] excrement and so forth, not looking [around], a place for use, being beyond a wall or fence, and either discarding or causing to be discarded.
In the ninth [offense], "of all" refers to both monks and nuns. In this context, the field-watchers and those who guard the monastery and so forth are indeed the owners.
836. "With a single act of attention" means with a single act of looking in one direction. "Of those very [people]" refers to those whose dancing one watches.

Although the offense of *pācittiya* for oneself [watching] dancing and so forth is not explicitly stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*), he said, "It is stated in all the Commentaries," in order to show that it must nevertheless be accepted on the authority of the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Standing in the monastery" means not only...

"Having stood, or even having gone from here and there, she incurs [the offense] through all modes of activity (*iriyāpatha*). However, the phrase 'standing in a monastery' (*ārāme ṭhitā*) was stated for the purpose of showing that she must be included within the precincts of the monastery.
Otherwise, even if she were sitting, she would not incur it. This is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* (commentaries on difficult points). The rest here is self-evident.
[The offense consists in] being any one of the [four types of] dancing and so forth, or going elsewhere except for an authorized reason, or seeing or hearing [such performances].
These, however, are the three factors here.
The commentary on the Garlic Chapter is finished.
2. Commentary on the Darkness Chapter.
In the first [sutta] of the Andhakāravagga, “on account of a gift or on account of an offering” means either for the sake of a gift or for the sake of an offering.

“He consults” means he speaks. Herein, there are four factors: the state of being in thick darkness; the man’s standing within arm’s reach or conversing with him; the absence of companions; and the expectation of privacy.
842–846. The second, third, and fourth [offenses] have their meanings already explained.
856–857. Regarding the fifth: “She who passes beyond the shelter from rain” refers to one who departs after sitting inside a covered place.
They say that “the precinct extends twelve cubits. “In a place not suitable for a cross-legged seat” means in a place where one cannot sit with the thighs bound together (ūrubaddhāsana).
When there is no space available: (1) being before the meal; (2) sitting in an inhabited area; (3) making a seat with a cushioned square;
(4) not asking permission except for a permitted reason; and (5) exceeding the stated limit—these are the five factors here.
859–864. The sixth, seventh, and subsequent [rules] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Andhakāravagga* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Naggavagga*, verses 883–887.
The first and second [suttas] of the *Naggavagga* have their meanings already explained.
893. "Having unsewn in the third case" means having unsewn and unraveled that which was poorly sewn for the purpose of sewing it again.
"Except on four or five days" means after the lapse of five days from the day it was unsewn.

[The offense occurs when there is] the status of being a robe suitable for an inner garment (*nivāsana*) or an upper garment (*pāvuraṇa*), the property belonging to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and the act of unsewing or causing to be unsewn for the purpose of sewing, except for the permitted reasons.
The five factors here are: (1) the passing of five days, (2) the laying down of the burden, and so forth.
898. Regarding the fourth [offense], "of the five robes": this refers to these five robes—the three robes, the rain-bath cloth, and the inner shirt.
[The factors are: being one of these five robes, the passing of five days, the absence of an authorized reason, and not exchanging it.
Here, however, there are these four factors.
The fifth has its meaning already explained. Regarding the sixth:

"the acquisition of a robe" refers to a robe that is to be obtained. The three factors here are: its being of a nature that may be assigned [to another], its having been formally dedicated to the Saṅgha, and its being made an obstacle without seeing any benefit [in doing so].
911. The seventh [verse] has its meaning already explained.
916. Regarding the eighth: *kumbhathūṇa* is a term consisting of the word *kumbha*; those who move about or play with it, or for whom that is their craft, are *kumbhathūṇikā*.
Therefore he said, "those who play with a small jar. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, [it is stated]: "*Kumbhathūṇaṃ*..."
It is said, “the square-drum (caturassa-ambaṇaka-tāḷa).
A square-drum is a musical instrument made by fashioning a square frame from the heartwood of trees, ivory, or other materials, covering the four sides with leather, and then playing it.
*Bimbisaka* is also a synonym for that very same thing; they are called *kumbhathūṇikā* because they play that [instrument] or because that craft belongs to them.

Therefore he said: “The Bimbisakavādakas also say so. Being a monastic robe, giving it to others—excluding those who share the same Dhamma and one’s own parents—and not being for a limited time: these are the three factors here.
The ninth [offense] has its meaning already explained.
927. Regarding the tenth [case], the "Dhamma-robe kathina-extension":

when a lay follower, desiring to give non-seasonal robe-cloth to all the bhikkhunīs, gives either more than or equal to the benefit derived from the spreading of the kathina, and the kathina is then removed by a unanimous community of bhikkhunīs through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma) while it is still in use; this is the kathina-extension for the sake of the Dhamma.

Its suspension is called "legitimate" (*dhammika*); the meaning is that such is the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. The rest is of plain meaning. The commentary on the section on the naked ones (*naggavagga*) is finished.
932. In the section on the one who rolls over (*tuvaṭṭavagga*), everything is of plain meaning.
5. Commentary on the Chapter on Picture Galleries (Cittāgāravagga) 978.
Regarding the first [offense] in the Chapter on Picture Galleries: "a pleasure grove for recreation" refers to one situated within the city;
"a park for recreation" refers to one situated outside the city. "Each a separate offense" means according to the number of times the neck is turned as part of the preparatory effort.

These are offenses, not by way of counting [the number of times] one opens [one's eyes]. Because of the statement, "If they build royal palaces and so forth within the monastery, there is no offense for her who sees them," it is also established that she may go here and there within the monastery to watch dancing and other such performances.
The second and subsequent [sections] have their meanings already explained.

1015. In the ninth [section], the word *sippa* (craft) should be applied individually to the elephant and the others; likewise, the word *manta* (incantation) is applied to the *āthabbaṇa* and the rest.
Therein, an *āthabbaṇa-manta* is an incantation prescribed by the *Āthabbaṇa-veda* that causes injury to others;

a *khīlana-manta* is a lethal incantation performed by consecrating a pillar of heartwood and driving it into the earth; and *agadappayoga* is the application of antidotes or the administration of poisons.
The *nāgamaṇḍala* is a protective circle-bound charm intended to prevent snakes from entering.
1018. The tenth [chapter] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the *Cittāgāravagga* is finished.
1021. In the Ārāmavagga, everything is already clear in meaning.
1067. In the Gabbhinīvagga as well, everything is easily understood.
8. Commentary on the Kumāribhūtavagga.

1119. Regarding the first [case] in the *Kumāribhūta-vagga*: "The two who are the very first among those undergoing training" refers to the two trainees (*sikkhamānā*) mentioned at the very beginning of the *Gabbhini-vagga*. They should be addressed simply as "trainee" (*sikkhamānā*) during formal acts of authorization (*sammuti-kamma*) and so forth.
If they say that they should not be addressed as either "married" (*gihigatā*) or "unmarried" (*kumāribhūtā*), then the formal act [is invalid].
The intention is that "it wavers. From here onwards, the conclusion of the ninth [section] is of plain meaning.

1163. Regarding the tenth, the heading "originations not previously mentioned" is stated with reference to the originations not permitted among the thirteen originations, beginning with the originations of the first *pārājika*. For such a heading concerning originations had not occurred prior to this.
Because it has not occurred before, it is called "the head of a previously unarisen offense.
1166. The eleven [offenses] beginning with that have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the section on unmarried girls is finished.
9. Commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear (Chattupāhanavagga) 1214.

Regarding the phrase "with reference to the precinct" in the eleventh [case] of the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear: this refers to the precinct extending twelve cubits all around. The remainder is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear is concluded.
Because it is stated that such things as the Giragga festival and similar gatherings are "unintentional" (*acittaka*) and "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*),

they are "unintentional" in the sense that an offense occurs for one who merely sees or bathes there without knowing whether dancing or singing is taking place— due to a mind that does not recognize the object;
they are "worldly offenses" in the sense that an offense is incurred through unwholesome states alone for one who sees or bathes there after knowing that dancing or singing is taking place.

These [offenses] are to be understood as follows: acts such as ordaining a female thief (*corīvuṭṭhāpana*) are *sacittaka* (requiring a conscious state of mind), because an offense occurs only when one performs them after having recognized the object (*vatthu*) by means of the term "female thief" and so forth.
On the other hand, acts such as conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) are *paṇṇattivajja* (offenses of formal rule), because they must never be performed with an exclusively unwholesome mind.

Here, the distinction between *sacittaka* and *acittaka* is not taken based on whether one knows or does not know the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), but rather based on whether one knows or does not know the object (*vatthu*).
"It should be accepted"—this is stated in all three sections of the *gaṇṭhipada*. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the minor rules (*khuddakavaṇṇanā*) in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* is finished.
The section on the *Pācittiya* offenses is finished.
5. The Section on Confessions (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa) (Exegesis of the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga):
Exegesis of the Training Rules on Confessions (Pāṭidesanīya-sikkhāpada). 1228.

“The ‘Confessions’ (pāṭidesanīyā) are those eight rules which have been included in the summary”—this is the connection [of the text]. “Regarding those not occurring in the Canon” (pāḷivinimuttakesu) refers to ghee and so forth that are not mentioned in the canonical text.
The commentary on the training rules for confession (pāṭidesanīya-sikkhāpada) is finished.
The section on confession (pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa) is finished.
As for the seventy-five training rules (sekhiya-dhamma) that have been recited, and those seven called "legal issues" (adhikaraṇa) that follow immediately after them—
The connection is "the teachings have been recited. Therein, "of them" means of those training rules (sekhiya).

"Called the seven methods for settling disputes" refers to those known as the seven principles for the settlement of legal issues (adhikaraṇasamatha). The meaning is: because the wise declare that the determination of their meaning is exactly like that [of the previous sections].
The connection is "how they were concluded. "The path that destroys all taints" means the path of Arhatship which eliminates all taints (āsava).
"Having attained" means having produced [the path] within their own mental continuum. "May they see Nibbāna" means may they realize Nibbāna through the eye of path-knowledge;
or alternatively, the reading is "may they reach it. In that context, "Nibbāna" should be understood as the parinibbāna of the aggregates.
Thus ends the *Sāratthadīpanī* commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is finished.
The commentary on the Ubhatovibhaṅga is finished.
The commentary on the Pācittiya is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Mahāvagga: 1.
The Great Chapter (Mahākhandhaka)
Commentary on the Discourse on Awakening (Bodhikathāvaṇṇanā):

Now, immediately after the two Vibhaṅgas, wishing to begin the commentary on the meaning of the Khandhaka—which has been included in the compilation and is comprised within the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga—the author says, "Of both Pātimokkhas," and so forth. Therein, "of both..."
"Of the two Pātimokkhas" refers to both the Vibhaṅgas of the Pātimokkha. Here, by the mention of "Pātimokkha," their Vibhaṅgas are included without distinction.
The connection is: "that Khandhaka which they recited. A collection of khandhas (sections) is a Khandhaka;

or, it is called a Khandhaka because it elucidates or illuminates the khandhas. And here, "khandhas" refers to those things designated as formal acts of the Vinaya, such as ordination (*pabbajjā*), full admission (*upasampadā*), and so forth.

And what is intended here are the formulations (paññatti) known as the training rules (sikkhāpada) consisting of conduct and avoidance. For indeed, because they were formulated by the Blessed One, the going-forth (pabbajjā) and so forth are called "formulations.
Furthermore, the word *khandha* is seen in the sense of a "formulation" in such instances as "a log of wood" (*dārukkhandha*) or "a mass of fire" (*aggikkhandha*).
Moreover, the sense of being a "portion" (*bhāga*) is also appropriate here for those formulations.
"Because of being divided into portions and because of being analyzed. "Skilled in the aggregates" means skilled in the meaning of the aggregates by way of their designation, portions, and divisions.
In the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*), one should connect it thus: "those words whose meanings have been elucidated by which methods of commentary.
"If we were to speak of those again" means if we were to speak of those methods of commentary once more. Alternatively, [it refers to] the word-analysis (*padabhājanīye*).
One should connect the sentence thus: "If we were to state again those meanings of those words which have been explained above.
For in this interpretation, the particle *hi* should be understood as a word-filler (*padapūraṇa*). "The conclusion" (*pariyosāna*) means the conclusion of the commentary.
"Those meanings which are clear" (*uttānā ceva ye atthā*) refers to those meanings which, although not previously explained, are clear—that is, not profound.

1. "There is no specific reason" means that, as in the case of the reason stated [in the Vinaya]—"At the time when a reflection arose in the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, which became the cause for his request for the laying down of a training rule"—there is no such specific reason here.
"This expression" refers to the expression "at that time. But what is the purpose of using this word? If...
The intention is: "There is no specific cause; what is the purpose of this statement? It should be construed that "the purpose is the showing of the origin" (*nidānadassana*).
To clarify that very point, it was said: "For that which by the Blessed One...
and so forth. "Mahāvelā" means like a great shore; the meaning is that it is like a vast beach (*velātaṭa*) due to its abundance of sand. Therefore he said:
“‘A great heap of sand’ is the meaning. The words *uru*, *maru*, *sikatā*, *vālukā*, *vaṇṇu*, and *vālikā* are synonymous;
there is only a difference in their phonetic forms (*byañjana*). Therefore he said, “*Uru* is called sand.
And from this point onward—
Since the meaning of the Sutta-pāḷi texts has been described in brief, we shall therefore provide an exposition of their meaning.
*Najjā* means "in the river," from the root *najjati*, which signifies "it flows" or "it runs"; thus, the meaning is "in that river," or "in the flowing stream. *Nerañjarāya*.
Where it should have been said “nelañjalāya,” the letter *l* was changed to *r*, and thus it is called “nerañjarāya”;
the meaning is: “of the river whose waters are free from defects such as mud, water-weeds, and moss. Some say that where it should have been said “nīlañjalāya,” it is called “nerañjarāya”;
however, it should be understood that this is simply the name of that river. To show the bank of that river where the Blessed One stayed:
It is said, “at the foot of the Bodhi tree. In the passage, “Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths,” it is the knowledge of the path that is called Bodhi;
in the passage, “the one of excellent and vast wisdom attains Bodhi,” it is omniscient knowledge.
Since the Blessed One attained both of these forms of Bodhi there, the tree also received the name “Bodhi tree. Alternatively, [it is so called because] seven...
The Blessed One is "Bodhi" because he awakens to the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). Because that tree is supported by him who awakens, it received the name "Bodhi-tree.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated—"Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths"—and so forth, in order to show the meaning only partially.
"At the root" means in its vicinity. "The first Fully Enlightened One" (*paṭhamābhisambuddho*) is [formed] here by the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).
He says, "the first awakening," which is the explanation (*niddesa*). The word "first" (*paṭhama*) is used here in the neuter abstract sense;
therefore, the connection in this context should be understood as: having become fully awakened, he dwelt at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the very first time.
Then, regarding the phrase "Then the Blessed One": here, *atha* should be taken to mean "at that time," since it possesses multiple meanings.
Regarding the particle *atha*: the meaning is "at the time when, having attained full enlightenment, he was dwelling at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Udāna-pāḷi: "Now at that time, the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation. Alternatively, in the sense of "afterwards," [it means] "in this matter."
*Nipāto* means "therefore"; thus, the meaning should be understood as "after that full enlightenment. *Kho* is a particle used for filling out the verse.

*Satta ahāni* means "seven days" (*sattāhaṃ*). This is the accusative case used to express continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*). Because the Blessed One dwelt during those seven days continuously and exclusively in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), it is called "seven days" by way of expressing such continuous duration.

The words of application have been stated. "With one cross-legged posture" means that from the moment he sat upon the Vajrāsana in the Aparājita-paryaṅka posture on the full moon day of Visākha while the sun had not yet set, he did not rise even once, but remained with that very same single cross-legged posture as it was folded. "Experiencing the bliss of liberation":

herein, among the liberations consisting of substitution by analysis (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi*), and final escape (*nissaraṇa*), [he experienced the last].
Since the Blessed One’s liberation of fruition—consisting of tranquility and release—is intended here among the five [types of liberation], it is said:
"experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the attainment of fruition.

As for "liberation" (*vimutti*), it should be understood as the state of the mind being liberated by way of the subsiding of defilements, or simply the mind itself thus liberated. [The bliss] is born from that liberation.

Or, the happiness associated with it is the happiness of liberation. Because of the statement, “Venerable sir, this equanimity has been called ‘peaceful happiness’ by the Blessed One,” equanimity here too should be understood as happiness itself. For it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*:
“But equanimity, because of its peacefulness, is spoken of as happiness. Indeed, the Blessed One [described] the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship belonging to the fourth jhāna...

It enters into that [state], not the other. Alternatively, just as in such passages as “The subsiding of those [formations] is blissful,” the subsiding of the suffering of formations is called “blissful,” so too here,

because it is the state of the subsiding of all the suffering of defilements, it is the liberation by subsiding (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti) obtained in the fruit of arhatship that should be understood as “bliss.”
Now, *atha* is a particle used in the sense of introduction (*adhikāra*), while *kho* is for the purpose of completing the metrical line.

Among these, by the word *atha* in the sense of introduction, it indicates an introduction other than the experience of the bliss of liberation. But what is this? It is the attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
*Rattiyā* is a genitive case used to express a part-whole relationship; *paṭhamaṃ* is an accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasamyoga*).
For the Blessed One was engaged throughout that entire first watch of the night with that very same mental attention.

"Conditionality" (*paccayākāra*) means the phenomena that serve as conditions, such as ignorance and so forth. "Dependent upon" (*paṭicca*) means having gone towards [the effect], that is to say, without rejecting the completeness of the causal complex. And this "going towards" occurs by way of the condition's being a constituent factor within that causal complex.
It is simply the arising of the fruit. "Without having rejected" means that, without becoming a constituent factor through that completeness of causes, it does not arise by itself;
by this, the multiplicity of causes is shown. For by way of each individual cause, such as ignorance and so forth, the entire collection of causes is indicated.
"Conjoined" means gathered together, that is to say, inseparable. For the conditioning factors beginning with ignorance—
It produces only those phenomena that are conjoined and exist in an inseparable state from one another. By this, the multiplicity of the phenomena arising through conditions is shown.
By both [of these points], the principle expressed in the passage beginning "one is not from one" is illustrated.
For here, there is no single fruit from a single cause, nor is there a multiple fruit; nor is there a single fruit from multiple causes. Rather, by multiple causes...

It is indeed manifold. For it is observed that from manifold causes—namely, those consisting of temperature, earth, seed, and water—there arises a manifold fruit, namely the sprout characterized by form, odor, taste, and so forth.

As for this demonstration of single causes and fruits, such as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises," there is no purpose for it in that context.

For the Blessed One, depending on whether a cause or a fruit is predominant in a given instance, whether it is well-known, whether it is unique, and in accordance with the elegance of the teaching and the dispositions of those to be trained, he illuminates either a single cause or a single fruit.

Thus, in the statement "With contact as condition, feeling arises," he mentions only a single cause and its fruit. For contact is the predominant cause of feeling, since feeling is established according to the specific nature of the contact.
Feeling is the primary fruit of contact, because contact is determined according to how one feels.
He mentions a single cause—“diseases arising from phlegm”—because it is evident; for in this case, the phlegm is manifest, whereas karma and so forth are not.
He mentions a single [cause]—“Whatever unwholesome states there are, bhikkhus, they all have their root in improper attention”—because it is unique.

He states the reason: for improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) is the specific cause (*asādhāraṇa*) of unwholesome states, whereas the physical bases, objects, and so forth are common causes (*sādhāraṇa*).

Therefore, although other bases, objects, co-nascent factors, and so on exist here as causes of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), ignorance (*avijjā*) alone is [the primary cause], because of the statements:
"For one who contemplates gratification, craving increases" and "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints (*āsava*)."

It should be understood that ignorance is explained as the cause of volitional formations because it is the primary cause among other causes such as craving, because it is evident from the statement, “Bhikkhus, the ignorant person, possessed by ignorance, performs even a meritorious volitional formation,” and because it is the unique (asādhāraṇa) cause of volitional formations.
In this way, in all instances where a single cause and its single fruit are illustrated, the method should be applied according to what is possible. Thus said the ancients:
“One is not one here, nor is the many not many;
there is no fruit, yet there is a purpose in illustrating the fruit of a single cause.
That which is worthy of being understood is "dependent" (*paṭicca*). For whoever understands and realizes this [truth], for them there is the absolute cessation of suffering.
It leads [to that]. It arises together correctly, thus it is "co-arising" (*samuppāda*).

For a conditioning state, when producing its own fruit, produces it only in its completeness, not in a deficient manner; and those states which it produces, it produces all of them simultaneously, not one by one.
Thus, because it is dependent (*paṭicca*) and it is co-arising (*samuppāda*), the meaning here should be understood as "dependent co-arising" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

"Exposition" (*vitthāro*) refers to the detailed commentary on the terms of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). We too shall not present it here for fear of excessive prolixity, nor the exposition that will be stated further below in the same way.

"In direct and reverse order" (*anulomapaṭilomaṃ*) is a neuter noun in the locative case, as in such expressions as "the moon and sun revolve unevenly. "That very same" (*so eva*) refers to that very mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) according to the method previously stated.
"Or stated" means the mode of conditionality stated by way of the formula beginning with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.

"In the course of occurrence" means in the occurrence of saṃsāra. "He brought to mind" means that he brought to mind, without error and without omission, every single condition—whether it be a causal condition or another—that serves as a condition for whatever conditioned phenomenon, and in whatever manner, such as by way of a root-condition (hetu-paccaya) and so on.
The meaning is that he applied it to the mind by way of reviewing them without exception.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*): ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it finds (*vindati*) what should not be found (*avindiya*), such as bodily misconduct; it is ignorance because it does not find what should be found (*vindiya*), such as bodily good conduct;
it is ignorance because it renders the non-perverted nature of phenomena unknown (*avidita*). [In the case of] that which is devoid of an end...

It is called *avijjā* (ignorance) because it causes sentient beings to run (*javāpeti*) through existence and the rest within *saṃsāra*. It is called *avijjā* because it runs toward things that do not exist (*avijjamānesu*) and does not run toward things that do exist (*vijjamānesu*).
Alternatively, *avijjā* is the opposite of *vijjā* (knowledge). It should be understood as fourfold, beginning with "ignorance regarding suffering" (*dukkhe aññāṇaṃ*).
It is a *paccaya* (condition) because, depending upon it and not without it, the fruit comes—that is, it both arises and proceeds. Its meaning is that of assistance (*upakāraṭṭha*).

Or it is a condition. Ignorance (*avijjā*) which is also a condition is "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccaya*); therefore, "with ignorance as condition. They form (*saṅkharonti*) thus they are "formations" (*saṅkhārā*);
these are mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*). They should be understood as threefold by way of meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable formations.
It cognizes (*vijānāti*) thus it is "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*); that is thirty-two-fold by way of mundane resultant consciousness. It inclines (*namati*) thus...

Name consists of the three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā). That which is affected is "form" (rūpa); this includes both primary form (bhūtarūpa) and derived form (upādārūpa), such as the eye and so forth.

It is called a "base" (āyatana) because it extends, or because it leads to the extension of the suffering of saṃsāra. Contact (phassa) is so called because it touches. Feeling (vedanā) is so called because it feels.
This pair [of name and form] is sixfold by way of its doors, and thirty-two-fold when taken by way of kamma-result.
It flows and it flows around, thus it is craving (*taṇhā*); in brief, it is threefold by way of craving for sense-pleasures and so forth, and in detail, it is of one hundred and eight kinds.
It grasps, thus it is clinging (*upādāna*); that is fourfold by way of clinging to sense-pleasures and so forth.

It comes to be and it causes to come to be, thus it is becoming (*bhava*); that is twofold by way of the distinction between kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. Birth is being born (*jāti*). Aging is...
*Jarā* means aging. *Maraṇaṃ* is so called because they die by means of it. *Soka* is sorrowing; *parideva* is lamentation. *Dukkhaṃ* is that which causes suffering.
Alternatively, it is *dukkha* because it digs away in two ways, by way of arising and by way of persistence. *Domanassaṃ* is the state of one who is dejected.
*Upāyāsa* is intense distress. "They arise" means they are produced. And not only by the terms beginning with sorrow (*soka*), but indeed by all the terms [in the formula].
The construction of the word "sambhanti" (arising) should be made. For in this way, the determination of the condition and the conditioned is shown by the statement:
"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. Therefore he said:

"In this manner, the meaning is to be understood for all the phrases, namely: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. Thus, regarding the passage "In this way... there is an origination": [The text continues with the application of this principle to each link of dependent origination.]

This, however, is the meaning: "Thus" (*evaṃ*) is a demonstration of the method already indicated. By this, he shows that it is through causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, and not through the creation of a Lord (*issaranimmāna*) and the like.
"Of this" (*etassa*) refers to what has been stated above. "Entirely" (*kevalassa*) means unmixed, or alternatively, whole.

"Of the mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandhassa*) means of the aggregate of suffering, and not of a sentient being, nor of beauty, pleasure, and so on. "Arises" (*samudayo hoti*) means its origination or coming into existence.
It is called *virāga* (dispassion) because by means of it one becomes utterly detached from the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). Thus he says, "by the path known as dispassion.
"Cessation without remainder" (*asesanirodha*) means cessation that leaves nothing behind;

it is the eradication, the cutting off, through the destruction of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) by means of the supreme path, which is the absolute uprooting of ignorance (*avijjā*). Even though [ignorance] may have been [partially] removed by the lower paths...
Ignorance (*avijjā*), when being abandoned, is abandoned precisely by way of its absolute eradication; nevertheless, it is not abandoned without remainder.
For the ignorance that leads to rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*) is abandoned by the first path;

likewise, the ignorance that serves as the condition for rebirth in this world, in all other worlds, and in the planes of the ignoble (*anariya-bhūmi*), is abandoned respectively by the second and third paths.
"It is abandoned, but not otherwise" means that by the path of Arahantship alone, it is abandoned without remainder.
"There is cessation through non-arising" means there is the complete cessation without remainder of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
For by the three lower paths, some conditioned phenomena cease while others do not, because ignorance has not been ceased without remainder; however, by the supreme path [it is so].
"With the remainderless cessation of that [craving], no formations whatsoever cease. Thus, "of those ceased" means of those ceased by way of non-arising cessation (*anuppādanirodha*).
The word *kevala* denotes "without remainder," as in "the whole of Aṅga and Magadha," and so forth;
it also denotes "unmixed," as in "pure rice," and so forth. Therefore, it expresses the meaning in both ways: "of the entire..."
"Or of the pure. In this context, "of the whole" means of everything without exception, including all states of existence and so forth.
"Devoid of a being" means devoid of a soul (*jīva*) as imagined by others.

Furthermore, although it is said here: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness," [the same applies].
To this extent, the cessation of the entire mass of suffering has been stated without remainder;

nevertheless, in order to demonstrate the meaning that, in the forward order (*anuloma*), through the existence of each respective condition-dharma, each respective conditionally-arisen dharma does not cease but rather proceeds—[the text says]:
"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise... [and so on]... [this is] the origin."

Thus it is said. In this way, for the purpose of showing that in the absence of each respective condition—by virtue of its being the opposite of that [condition]—each respective conditionally arisen phenomenon ceases and does not proceed, it is stated here:
"With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness;
with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form... [and so on] ...there is the cessation of the mass of suffering."
It was stated [in this way], but not for the purpose of showing the cessation of the mass of suffering (dukkhakkhandha) as included within the three times—as is the case with the *anuloma* [insight].

For indeed, it should be understood that this is another distinction: it is intended that the cessation of the mass of suffering—which is liable to arise only if the cultivation of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is absent—occurs through the cultivation of the Noble Path, specifically regarding that which is yet to come.
Regarding the word *hava*: here, *hava* is a particle used in the sense of "expert" (*byatta*). However, some explain its meaning as "in *āhava*, that is, in battle";
their intention is that it refers to the occasion of contending with the defilement-Māra, based on the statement, "Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the characteristic of closely contemplating the object": this means by way of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of closely contemplating the object.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the characteristic of contemplation of characteristics," the same method applies here as well.
In this context, "contemplation of the object" refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), because they contemplate the kasiṇa objects.

"Contemplation of characteristics" refers to insight (*vipassanā*), the path, and the fruit. For insight is called "contemplation of characteristics" because it contemplates the three characteristics; the path [is so called] because of its relation to insight...

“Contemplation of characteristics” (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) means that it accomplishes the task already arrived at; or, it is “contemplation of characteristics” because it contemplates the fruit, which is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) characterized as suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*).
“An improper question” (*no kalla pañho*) means an unfit question; the meaning is that this is a bad question (*duppañho*).
By the word “etcetera,” [the following is included]: “I do not say ‘he touches. If I were to say ‘he touches,’ then a proper question would be: ‘Who indeed... [and so forth].
“Does it touch, venerable sir? “I do not speak thus. If one were to ask me, ‘Venerable sir, what is the condition for contact?
that would be a fitting question. And the fitting answer therein would be:
‘Contact has the six sense bases as its condition; feeling has contact as its condition. Who, venerable sir, experiences feeling?”
"It is not a fitting question," the Blessed One said, "when one says 'it feels,' I do not say that it feels.
If I were to say that it feels, then it would be a fitting question to ask: 'Venerable sir, who is it that feels? But I do not say that.
And if someone were to ask me, while I am not saying this: 'Venerable sir, what is the condition for feeling?'—that is a fitting question."
In this context, the phrase "it is fitting to explain that 'with contact as condition there is feeling;
with feeling as condition there is craving'" includes the remainder of the canonical text.

Furthermore, regarding the expression "and by way of the method beginning with," the word "beginning" (ādi) here refers to such passages as: "Venerable sir, what now is birth? And for whom does it exist? etc.
The phrase "‘Birth’—the Blessed One said, ‘This is not a fitting question’" and so forth includes such passages. [Objection:
But surely here, "What, venerable sir, is aging-and-death? is a well-posed question? [Response:
Although it is indeed well-posed, it is like a fine meal served in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand coins, yet having only a single *āmalaka* fruit placed on top of it.
When a lump of excrement is placed [among food], all that food becomes unfit for consumption and must be discarded; in the same way,

by this statement asserting the existence of a sentient being— "To whom, then, does this aging-and-death belong?"— this entire series of difficult questions has become as unfit for consumption as that food was when defiled by the lump of excrement.
The sixteen doubts: "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist? What was I? How was I?
Having been what, did I become what in the past? Shall I exist in the future? Shall I not exist? What shall I be? How shall I be?"
"Shall I indeed exist? Having been what, shall I become what? Shall I indeed exist in the future? Am I indeed? Am I not indeed? What am I indeed? How am I indeed? From where has this being come?
Where will it go?"—such are the sixteenfold doubts that have arisen regarding the objects of the past, future, and present.
In this context, based on the mode of eternalism (*sassatākāra*) and the mode of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppattiākāra*), one doubts whether the self existed in the past or did not exist;

it should not be asked "for what reason," for the foolish worldling (*bālaputhujjana*) proceeds in whatever way, like a madman. Moreover, it is precisely improper mental attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) that is the cause here.

This is the reason. But what is the reason for improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*)? It is that very state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*), or the failure to see the Noble Ones (*ariya*) and so forth.
[Objection: Does not even a worldling attend properly (*yoniso manasikaroti*)? Who says that he does not attend?
However, in that case, the state of being a worldling is not the cause; rather, it is the lack of hearing the true Dharma, the absence of virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitta*), and so forth.
In this regard, there are several causes. For fish, meat, and so forth are not fragrant by their own nature;
rather, they become fragrant through the condition of artificial preparation (*abhisaṅkhāra-paccaya*).

Relying on birth, gender, and status, one wonders, "What was I like? and hesitates, thinking: "Was I a kshatriya? Or was I one among brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, or humans?"
"How indeed?"—relying on the mode of shape, one doubts: "Was I long, or short, fair, dark, large, small, or otherwise?
Some, however, say that one doubts from the perspective of cause, thinking: "By what cause indeed did I come to be? relying on such things as the creation of a Supreme Lord (issaranimmāna).
Thinking, "Having been what, have I become what? one entertains doubts regarding one's own succession based on birth and so forth, such as: "Having been a khattiya, have I become a brahmin...

[and so on] ...having been a deva, have I become a human? In all these cases, however, *addhāna* is a designation for time (*kāla*), and it should be understood as being in the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.

"Shall I exist, or shall I not?"—relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism, one doubts whether one's own self will exist or not exist in the future. The rest here is exactly as previously explained.
"Do I exist?"—one doubts the state of one's own existence. But is this reasonable? Whether it is reasonable or unreasonable—what need is there for such deliberation here?
Furthermore, they cite this example: it is said that the son of Cūḷamātā was bald.
The son of the chief queen was not shaven. They shaved him. Rising up, he thought, "Am I indeed the son of the junior queen?
Thus there arises the doubt, "Am I indeed [this]? He doubts his own non-existence, thinking, "Am I not [this]?
In this regard, there is this story: it is said that once, a certain man... [caught] fish.
While seizing [the boy], he struck his own thigh—which had become cold from staying long in the water—thinking, "It is a fish.
Another, guarding a field on the edge of a charnel ground, lay there cowering in fear.
Upon waking, he struck his own shins, thinking, "They are two *yakkhas*," and thus he doubted, wondering, "Am I not indeed [a ghost]?"
"How is it that one who is actually a khattiya doubts his own status as a khattiya, perceiving himself as a son of a charioteer like Kaṇha?
This same principle applies to the others. But there is no such thing as a deity who, while being a deity, does not know his own divine nature.
Even he doubts in this manner: 'Am I possessed of form, or am I formless? Why do the khattiyas and the others not know [their own status]?"
Why is this? Because their rebirth in various families occurs without prior announcement. Furthermore, householders such as Pātalika and others perceive themselves as renunciants;
renunciants likewise perceive themselves as householders, thinking, "Is my action perhaps subject to failure? and so forth.
And some humans, like certain kings, perceive themselves as gods.
"How indeed am I? is exactly as stated in the previous method.

However, here one should understand that having grasped the notion that there exists within what is called a "living soul" (jīva), and then doubting regarding its shape and form—wondering whether it is "long, or short, or square, or four-cornered, or six-sided, or eight-sided, or sixteen-sided," and so on—one doubts with the thought, "How indeed am I? This refers to the shape of the body.
However, there is no one who does not know the present.
He doubts the place from which this personal existence has come and where it will go, thinking, "From where has it come? Where will it go? "Vapayanti" means they disperse (*vi-apayanti*);

this is a designation formed by the elision of the letter *i*. What is meant is "they disperse" (*byapayanti*). Therefore he said, "They disperse, they depart. And as for this departing, it is by way of non-arrival and cessation; thus he said, "They cease."
3. But when do the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) or the factors of the Four Noble Truths become manifest, arise, and appear?

When the knowledge of the path of insight (vipassanā-magga-ñāṇa) is occurring. In that regard, first, within the knowledge of insight, mindfulness and the other factors associated with the knowledge of insight, as well as the knowledge of insight itself, each respectively within their own respective objects, by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna).
When abandoning the perception of beauty and so forth, these [factors] arise individually by way of the contemplation of the body and so on.

However, at the moment of the Path, having taken Nibbāna as their object and abandoning the opposites through complete eradication, they arise all at once by way of accomplishing the penetration of non-delusion regarding all four Noble Truths.
Thus, first, regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment here...
Manifestation should be understood in the sense of arising. As for the Noble Truths: in the case of mundane truths at the moment of insight, it is by way of their being made the object of insight;

in the case of supramundane truths, it is by way of the mind’s inclination toward them; and at the moment of the Path, it is by way of the clear realization of the Truth of Cessation as an object, and by way of the clear realization of the function of all [the truths].
Thus, they are to be understood in the sense of manifestation because of their state of being evident.
The manifestation [of this] is to be understood. Thus,
although all phenomena were manifest to his own knowledge in every aspect, the Blessed One—
because he had applied himself to insight by way of dependent origination and because the mode of conditions is subtle, profound, and very difficult to see— reflected upon that.

With a powerful joy having arisen through the destruction and elimination of opposing factors, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) here, which indeed illustrates the power of his own realization of that truth:

"Desires are your first army; the second is said to be discontent... In this manner, he spoke of the army of Māra as described in the passage beginning with "Desires are your first army. *“Kāmā te paṭhamā senā, dutiyā arati vuccati;”*
The third is hunger and thirst for you; the fourth is called craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor for you; the sixth is called fear.
The seventh is doubt for you; the eighth is flattery and obstinacy.
“Gain, fame, and honor, and whatever ill-gotten reputation one acquires;
whoever exalts himself and looks down upon others—
this, O Namuci, is your army, the assault of Kaṇha.”
“No hero is defeated by him; having conquered, he attains happiness.
By this method, [he describes] the army of Māra mentioned in that manner.
In this regard, since from the very beginning, the defilements of sensual desire delude beings who have become householders regarding the objects of sensual pleasure, having overcome them—
In those who have gone forth into the homeless state, a distaste for secluded lodgings or for various other superior wholesome states arises.
And this has been said: "Friend, it is difficult for one who has gone forth to find delight.
Consequently, because their livelihood depends on others, hunger and thirst afflict them; and being thus afflicted, the craving for seeking [food] arises.
The mind becomes weary; then, for those whose minds are weary, sloth and torpor descend.
Consequently, for those who fail to attain distinction while dwelling in forest and jungle retreats that are difficult to inhabit, a fearful sense of dread arises.
As they dwell thus, filled with suspicion and apprehension, though they have long been relishing the flavor of seclusion.
“Could this not be the path?”—thus doubt arises regarding the practice;
having dispelled that, as they dwell [onward], pride, disparagement, and rigidity arise due to the attainment of some slight distinction;
having dispelled those as well, as they dwell [onward], gain, honor, and fame arise based on a further superior attainment; and being infatuated with gain and the rest...
Displaying counterfeit dharmas and having attained false fame, they remain therein, exalting themselves through birth and other such factors while disparaging others;
therefore, desire and the rest should be understood as being like the first army and so forth.
Having thus pointed out this tenfold army, because it is endowed with dark qualities (kaṇhadhamma), it belongs to Kaṇha Namuci.
It leads to one’s benefit; therefore, by pointing it out as "your army," it was said: "This is Namuci’s army, the assailant of Kaṇha.
In this context, "assailant" (abhippahārinī) means a slayer and a crusher of recluses and brahmins; the meaning is that it creates obstacles.
"A coward does not conquer it, and having conquered it, one gains happiness"—thus, [the Buddha spoke] regarding your army in the body to one who is a coward.
The meaning is that a person who is attached to life does not conquer, whereas a hero conquers; and having conquered, he attains the happiness of the path and the happiness of the fruit.
"That brahmin too" refers to that brahmin whose taints are destroyed.
Now, at that time, the Blessed One remained seated cross-legged for seven days, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Then, at the end of those seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and, during the first watch of the night, carefully attended to dependent origination in forward order.
During the middle watch of the night, he carefully attended to dependent origination in reverse order.
During the last watch of the night, [he carefully attended to] dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.

In order to show that there is no contradiction between this Udāna passage—where it was said, “He attended closely with his mind”—and this Khandhaka passage, the section beginning with “But in the Udāna” is commenced.

Here, “by way of that” means by way of that comprehension of the mode of conditions and the attainment of the destruction of conditions. “Each single portion” refers to each single portion within the forward and reverse orders.

[He reflected on] the constituent parts. On the night of the first day of the fortnight, he thus applied his mind; that is, throughout all three watches of the night, he applied his mind in both forward and reverse order.

It is said that, with the exception of the seven days spent in the Jewel House, during the remaining six weeks the Blessed One dwelt for the most part experiencing the bliss of liberation, occasionally reviewing the Dhamma. During those seven days in the Jewel House...
However, he dwelt by means of the analytical investigation of the Abhidhamma alone. Therefore,

the intention [of the text] is that this was stated in this Khandhaka-pāḷi with reference to the attention produced on the night of the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada), among the instances of attention produced through the occasional reflection upon the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Discourse on Awakening is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Cowherd: 4.
"At the end of those seven days" means with the passing of the seven days spent in the cross-legged posture. "Having emerged from that concentration" means...
