Then, having emerged from the meditative attainment of the fruit of arahantship at the appropriate time, there are other qualities that bring about Buddhahood—qualities which, beginning from the full moon of Visākha, have been the cause of his state of constant concentration day and night—and other factors that establish his status as a Buddha, which reveal to others:
"This one is a Buddha. These are the qualities [that constitute] the state of being a Buddha.

The construction is: "What indeed exists? Regarding the phrase "of certain deities," this refers to those deities other than those who have attained the path and realized cessation, and who know the qualities of the Buddha even from a single point; setting them aside, it refers to other deities.

"With unblinking eyes" means with eyes devoid of blinking due to the immobility of their eyelashes, which is caused by the manifestation of serene confidence through the expansion of joy in the Dhamma. "On the jewel-walk" means on a walkway made of jewels constructed by the deities.

They also say that because it was there that the seven treatises consisting of the Jewel, as well as the unsurpassed Jewel of the Dhamma, were mastered, that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya (the Jewel House Shrine). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
"The so-called 'Jewel House' is not a house made of jewels; rather, the place where the seven treatises were mastered is the Jewel House."
"It should be understood" is what was said.
But why did it come to be called the "Goatherd’s Banyan Tree"? To this he says: "It is said that... and so forth. However, some [commentators] say:
"Because elderly brahmins, being unable to recite the Vedas there, [built] dwellings surrounded by walls..."
Having done so, they all came under his control; therefore, it is said that the name ‘Ajapāla-nigrodha’ (The Banyan Tree of the Unchanted) arose for it.
Herein, this is the etymological explanation: they do not chant (*na japanti*) thus they are *ajapā*; the meaning is those who do not study the mantras.
They take (*lanti*) their dwelling (*āvāsa*) here, thus it is *ajapāla*. Others, however, say: because at the time of midday, when [the herdsmen] had entered within...
"Today he protects and guards his own shadow; therefore, the name ‘Ajapāla’ (Guardian-of-the-Shadow) arose for him.
In every respect, this is the name of that tree.
"Experiencing the bliss of liberation" means that while investigating the Dhamma, from time to time he experiences the bliss of liberation.
"Experiencing," or rather, the reading "discerning the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation" should be understood here.
For this same reading is found even in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*. And in discerning the Dhamma here, he thus contemplated the path of method in the Abhidhamma:
first the treatise called the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, and after that the *Vibhaṅga* treatise.
The *Dhātukathā-pakaraṇa*, the *Puggalapaññatti-pakaraṇa*, the work called *Kathāvatthu*, the work called *Yamaka*, and then the great work called *Paṭṭhāna*.
Therein, when his mind had entered into the subtle and refined state, joy arose;
with the arising of joy, the blood became clear; with the clarity of the blood, the skin became clear; with the clarity of the skin—
From the front part of the body of the one who was thus inspired, rays of light the size of gabled houses and so forth arose and leaped into the sky;
like a herd of six-tusked nāgas, they surged into the infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) of the eastern direction.
From the back part of the body they arose and [surged] into the western direction; from the right shoulder-peak they arose and [surged] into the southern direction; from the left shoulder-peak...
Having arisen, they leapt into the infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) of the northern direction. From the soles of his feet, rays of light the color of coral sprouts issued forth;
piercing through the great earth, splitting the waters in two, and rending the mass of wind, they leapt into the cloudless sky.
From his head, a column of blue-colored rays issued forth like a jeweled garland being whirled around.
Having risen up, having pierced through the six celestial worlds, and having transcended the nine Brahma-worlds, they entered the cloudless sky.
On that day, in immeasurable world-systems, all immeasurable beings became entirely golden-colored.
And from the Blessed One’s body on that day, those rays of light issued forth which, it is said, even to this day pervade infinite world-systems.

They indeed departed. It should be understood that rays of light issued from his body not only while he was contemplating the Dhamma during these seven days, but likewise while he was comprehending the Paṭṭhāna during the seven days at the Jewel House.
For this is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
“During these twenty-one days, not even on a single day did rays issue from the Teacher’s body;
however, on the fourth week, he sat in the Jewel House in the northwestern direction. There [he recited] the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*...”

Even as he was reviewing [the Abhidhamma], rays did not issue from his body. Even as he was reviewing the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*, the *Dhātukathā*, the *Puggalapaññatti*, the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*, and the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa*, rays did not issue.
But when, having descended into the *Mahāpakaraṇa*, he performed the review: “Root condition, object condition... pe ...non-disappearance condition,” [rays issued].
Then, as he was comprehending the twenty-four *Samantapadṭhānas*, the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) found its exclusive place within the Great Treatise (*Mahāpakaraṇa*).
For just as the great fish Timirapiṅgala finds its place only in the great ocean, which is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep,
even so the knowledge of omniscience found its exclusive place only in the Great Treatise.
As the Teacher, having thus obtained the opportunity, was freely reviewing the subtle and delicate Dhamma with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),
six-colored rays— blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and radiant— issued forth from his body.
From the hair of his head and beard, and from the blue parts of his eyes, blue rays issued forth, by means of which the vault of the sky...

It was as if strewn with powdered collyrium, as if covered with umā-flowers and blue lotus petals, as if with jeweled fans being waved about, and like a dark-blue cloth spread out. From the skin and from the yellow parts of the eyes, yellow rays issued forth;
by means of which the quarters of the sky appeared as if being sprinkled with liquid gold or as if covered with a golden cloth.
They shone as if strewn with specks of saffron powder or *kaṇikāra* flowers.

From their flesh and blood, and from the red parts of their eyes, rays of light issued forth; by means of these rays, the quarters of the sky appeared as if colored with *cīnapiṭṭha* powder, as if being sprinkled with the juice of well-ripened lac, as if draped in red woolen cloth, and as if strewn with *jayasumana*, *pāribaddhaka*, and *bandhujīvaka* flowers.
And they shone brilliantly. From his bones, teeth, and the white parts of his eyes, white rays issued forth;

by means of which the quarters of the sky appeared as if strewn with streams of milk being poured from silver jars, as if covered by spread canopies of silver cloth, as if fanned by silver palm-leaf fans fluttering about, and as if overspread with flowers such as the *kunda*, *kumuda*, *sindhuvāra*, *sumana*, and *mallikā*.
And they shone forth. Furthermore, rays of deep crimson brilliance issued from various parts of his body.
Thus, those six-colored rays, having issued forth, took hold of the solid great earth.
"The great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness, was like a mass of refined gold."

They broke through the earth and seized the water below. The water that supports the earth, four hundred thousand yojanas thick and augmented by eight nahutas, was like molten gold being poured from golden jars.
Having pierced through the water, they seized the wind. The wind, nine hundred and ninety-six thousand yojanas thick, was like a mass of uplifted gold.
It was as if they had burst through the wind and plunged down into the cloudless space below. Having ascended by the upper path, they reached the realm of the Four Great Kings;

passing through that, they reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, then the Yāma heaven, then the Tusita heaven, then the Nimmānarati heaven, then the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven, then the nine Brahma-worlds, then the Vehapphala heaven, and from there—
Having pierced through the five Pure Abodes, they seized the four formless realms. Having pierced through the four formless realms, they entered the cloudless sky.
"In the horizontal directions, they entered infinite world-systems; in this much space, the radiance of the moon [is present]."
There was no light: in the sun there was no radiance of the sun; in the stars there was no radiance of the stars;
and in the deities’ parks, celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, bodies, and ornaments—there was no light anywhere.

Even the Great Brahmā, who is capable of pervading the light throughout the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, became like a glowworm at the rising of the sun; [so it was] regarding the moon, the sun, the stars, the deities, the parks, the celestial mansions, and the wish-fulfilling trees.
Only a mere limited portion became visible; this much space alone was completely pervaded by the Buddha’s rays.
And this was neither the Buddha’s power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) nor the power born of meditation (*bhāvanāmayiddhi*).
Rather, as the Lord of the World contemplated the subtle and delicate phenomena, his blood became clear, his physical basis (*vatthurūpa*) became clear, and the color of his skin became clear.
“The color-element originating from consciousness remained motionless in an area extending eighty cubits all around.
Thus, when he was seated means: having emerged from that meditative absorption, while sitting. “A certain brahmin” means:
a certain brahmin who was unknown and unrecognizable by name or clan. “Wandering about making the sound ‘hum hum’” means: [uttering this sound] regarding everything of an impure nature.
Having seen it, he wandered about feeling disgusted and uttering "hum hum. "He said this" means he spoke these words now to be spoken, beginning with "To what extent, indeed...
In that context, *kittāvatā* means "by what measure"; *nu* is a particle used in the sense of doubt;
*kho* is for the purpose of completing the meter; and *bho* is a form of address derived from the brahmin caste.
For thus it has been said: "He is called a 'Sir-sayer' (bhovādi) if he possesses anything.
He addresses the Blessed One by his clan as "Gotama. But how does this brahmin, having just now arrived, know the Blessed One's clan?
It is not that he has just now arrived; rather, [he learned it] from the group of five monks who attended upon him during the six years he was practicing austerities.
While traveling together, at a later time, having abandoned that ascetic practice, even when he was wandering alone and without a companion for alms in Senānigama at Uruvelā,
he was seen and conversed with by that brahmin; therefore,
recollecting the clan-name of the Blessed One as it had been used by the group of five monks, he addressed the Blessed One as "Master Gotama."

He addresses him by his clan name. From the time the Blessed One went forth on the Great Renunciation and was ordained on the banks of the Anomā River, he has been as well-known and renowned as the moon or the sun as "the ascetic Gotama";
nor is it necessary to seek a reason for knowing his clan name. "Brāhmaṇakaraṇā" means those which make one a brahmin.
“Brāhmaṇakaraṇā” means that which produces the state of a brahmin. Here, by the word “to what extent” (kittāvatā), he asks about the measure of those qualities by which one becomes a brahmin.
By the word “which ones” (katame), however, he asks about their specific nature.
“He uttered an inspired utterance” (udānaṃ udānesi) means he uttered the inspired utterance beginning with “He who is a brahmin,” and not [an utterance addressed] to that particular brahmin.
He did not teach the Dhamma. Why? Because [the Brahmin] was not a fit vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma.

For indeed, upon hearing this verse, that Brahmin did not attain the realization of the Truth (saccābhisamaya). And just as it was with him, so it was with Upaka the Ājīvaka, who likewise failed to realize the Truth upon hearing the proclamation of the Buddha’s qualities.
This was because [Upaka] had heard what was spoken by the Blessed One prior to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.

Even for Tapussa and Bhallika, who were merely listening to others, this [teaching] became conducive to spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*), but not yet conducive to the state of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*) or conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). For such is the nature of things (*dhammatā*).

Regarding the phrase "or the end through knowledge," here "end" (*anta*) refers to Nibbāna, the ultimate limit of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "These excesses do not exist" means that because they have been entirely abandoned, they no longer exist.
The commentary on the Ajapāla story is finished.
Commentary on the Mucalinda story: 5.
Regarding the phrase "at the foot of the Mucalinda tree," here *mucalinda* refers to the *nīpa* tree, which is also called *nicula*. At its...
The meaning is "in the vicinity. Some, however, say: "‘Mucala’ is the name of that tree;
but because it was the chief of the forest, it is called ‘Mucalinda. It arose: a great cloud arose, filling the entire interior of the world-system (cakkavāḷa).
Such a cloud, they say, rains only at two times: when a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) has appeared, or when a Buddha has appeared.
Or rather, it appeared here at the time of a Buddha’s arising. "Born in a lotus pond" means that there was a nāga-abode beneath the lotus pond, and he was born there.

"From his own abode" means from his own nāga-abode. "Having thus surrounded [the Blessed One] with his coils" means having encircled the Blessed One’s body seven times with the coils of his own body. On the top of his head, a great...
“He spreads his hood” means that he extends his own great hood over the region of the Blessed One’s head.
There is also a reading, “having made a hood,” which has the same meaning.
It is said that this Nāga king thought: “The Blessed One is sitting at the foot of a tree near my abode.”
“Since this period of seven-day rains is occurring, it is fitting that he obtain a dwelling.
Although he was capable of constructing a palace made of the seven precious gems, thinking, “If this were done, the essence of the body would not be grasped;
I shall perform service for the body of the One Possessing the Ten Powers,” he assumed a massive physical form and [massaged] the Teacher seven times with his hands.
Having encircled it, he spread his hood over it. It is stated here that "the space within the enclosure was the size of the storehouse chamber in the Lohapāsāda.
However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:
"The space inside the enclosure was the size of the Lohapāsāda below; [one could move] in whatever posture one desired..."
"It was the Nāga king’s intention that 'the Teacher shall dwell here,' and therefore he enclosed such a vast space.
In the center, a jeweled couch was prepared; above it was a canopy made of gold stars, variegated with hanging garlands of perfumes, flowers, and cloth.
At the four corners, lamps were lit with scented oil, and in the four directions, opened sandalwood caskets were placed."

It has been said. The thought that he would dwell in whatever posture he desired was merely the aspiration of the Naga king; however, the Blessed One spent the seven days exactly as he had sat down. Although...
[the text continues] ...it is appropriate to reflect on this, some here say: "The mention of 'heat' is a statement of the cause for making the circumference of his coils vast.
For if it were small, the Blessed One’s body—produced from the Naga king’s own substance—"
“Heat might afflict it; however, by making it vast in extent, may such heat not afflict it.
He said, “It is ‘protruding’ (ubbiddha) because it has pierced through,” for the meaning of the word with its prefix is understood even without the prefix.
And since that state of being protruding appears due to the removal of defilements and its distance [from them], he said, “become distant through the disappearance of clouds. (Indanīlamaṇi)
It shines and glows as if divine, thus it is *deva*; [here] it refers to space. "Having known" means having understood: "Now the sky is free from clouds;
there is no affliction of cold or other such things for the Blessed One. "Having removed" means having taken away. "His own form" means his own nāga-form.
"Having withdrawn" means having made it disappear. "The appearance of a young brahmin" means the physical form of a youth.
"Having understood this matter" means having known in every way this matter: that "for one who experiences the bliss of seclusion, there is only happiness wherever he may be.
"This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) which illuminates the power of the bliss of seclusion. "Of the Dhamma heard" means of the well-known Dhamma;
hence he said, "of the proclaimed Dhamma. "State of being unshakable" means the nature of being unshakable.
The commentary on the Mucalinda story is concluded.
Commentary on the Rājāyatana story: 6.
"He offered medicinal myrobalan" means that he offered not only the medicinal myrobalan, but also a tooth-stick.
Regarding the term *paccaggha*, some do not accept the first interpretation of its meaning; for that very reason, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated:
“*Paccaggha* means ‘new. Some say it is *paccaggha* because of being individually of great value (*mahagghatāya*), but that is not correct.
For the Blessed Buddhas neither accept nor consume anything of great value.”
The commentary on the Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Brahmā’s Entreaty: 7.
*Āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo*: the meaning is that it was both practiced by [the Buddha] himself and properly practiced by those who practice [after him]. By this—
"This reflection arises at the first full awakening of all Buddhas"—this shows that such is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in this matter.
Even though the Dhamma is profound, it may become perfectly clear through the destruction of opposing factors;
yet the destruction of opposing factors depends upon right practice, which in turn depends upon hearing the true Dhamma, and that depends upon confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma.

Thus, showing that [the teaching] was caused by the request of Brahmā— since it was the cause for the aspiration of beings toward the practice of the Dharma through a lineage of those who are especially worthy of esteem and reverence in the world— he said:
"Because of the desire to teach when requested by Brahmā," and so forth.

“Attained” (*adhigata*) means penetrated; the meaning is that it has been understood as it truly is through self-awakened knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) by way of the formula, “This is suffering,” and so forth.
“Dhamma” refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, because there is no other dhamma to be penetrated apart from those.

“Profound” (*gambhīra*) means that, like the great ocean, it cannot be sounded with the tip of a gnat’s beak or a needle, except by those who possess the accumulated and matured equipment of knowledge.
It is a state that cannot be reached by the knowledge of others. Because of its profundity, it is difficult to see and can only be seen with difficulty;

it is not possible to see it easily. For that which is a state unattainable by others cannot be seen easily—either in its essential nature or in its specific details—due to the impossibility of plunging into it;
rather, it must be seen by someone at some time only with great effort.
Because it is difficult to see, it is difficult to realize; it must be understood with difficulty, and it is not possible to understand it easily.
For when something cannot even be seen, there is no question at all of plunging into it and realizing it, because realization is so exceedingly difficult.
In this context: "What do you think, monks? Which is more difficult..."
The scriptural passage should be stated as: “...or more difficult to realize.
It is “peaceful” (santo) because it is peaceful through the subsiding of all fevers, owing to the absence of defilements and formations whose nature is unrest;
or it is peaceful because its object is peaceful. And here, the truth of cessation is the peaceful object.
It has a peaceful object; and since the truth of the path is both peaceful and has a peaceful object, it is "peaceful as its object" (*santārammaṇa*).

It is "sublime" (*paṇīta*) because it has been brought to a state of excellence. Alternatively, "sublime" means that, in the sense of being non-satiating, it is insatiable like a meal of delicious flavor.

Here, by the very fact of its being both peaceful and sublime, its insatiability should be understood through its quality of being non-satiating. For these two qualities belong exclusively to the supramundane.

This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). "Beyond the sphere of reasoning" (*atakkāvacara*) means that, because it is the object of supreme knowledge, it cannot be traversed or fathomed by reasoning;

it can only be traversed by knowledge itself. For that very reason, because it is the domain of subtle knowledge and because its intrinsic nature is delicate and refined, it is "subtle" (*nipuṇa*) and "delicate" (*saṇha*).
"To be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīya*) means that, because it is not the domain of fools, it is [to be experienced] by those who have entered upon the right practice.
This must be understood by the wise alone.
They are called *ālayā* because beings adhere to them and resort to them in the sense of taking delight; thus it is said:

"Beings adhere to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), therefore they are called *ālayā*. In that context, "they adhere to the five strands of sensual pleasure" means [they cling] to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The meaning is "they serve. "Those" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "They delight" means they find pleasure, play, and frolic.

They are called "attachments" (*ālaya*) because they serve them with a sense of fondness; these are the eight hundred modes of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*). Since they delight by means of those attachments, they are "delighting in attachment" (*ālayarāma*);
this is how the meaning should be understood here. For these beings, just as with the strands of sensual pleasure, so too with passion (*rāga*).

They indeed relish them and take delight in them. For just as a king who has entered a park endowed with well-arranged trees laden with flowers and fruit delights in each of those excellences— being enraptured, gladdened, and filled with joy, not feeling weary,
and having no desire to depart even after staying there for a long time— in the same way, sentient beings [relish] these abodes of sensual desire and abodes of craving.

They take delight; they dwell rejoicing and without weariness within the cycle of saṃsāra. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “delighting in attachment” (ālayarāmā), showing them both kinds of attachment as if they were a pleasure garden. “Ratā” means devoted.
“Sumuditā” means exceedingly joyful because of their lack of weariness.
"With reference to the word *ṭhāna*" means with reference to the term *ṭhāna*. In terms of meaning, however, by *ṭhāna* (basis) is intended precisely dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

It is called a *ṭhāna* because the fruit stands therein, owing to its dependence upon that; thus, it refers to ignorance and the other factors that serve as conditions for volitional formations and so forth.
"Conditioned by this" (*idappaccayā*) means the conditions for these volitional formations and so forth; they are indeed ignorance and the rest. [End of] "conditioned by this."
Thus, *idappaccayatā* (conditionality) is like "devo" being the same as "devatā.

Alternatively, *idappaccayatā* is the state of being a condition, or the capacity for producing, of the specific conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, in dependence upon their own fruit.

By this, dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is shown to have the characteristic of a capable condition. It is called *paṭiccasamuppāda* because the fruit arises (*samuppajjati*) in dependence (*paṭicca*) upon it.

By both phrases, the meaning of conditionality (*paccayaṭṭha*) regarding phenomena is elucidated. For "this conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*) and "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) are designations for ignorance and the other conditions such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
As for the passage beginning with "the stilling of all formations," all of it refers in meaning to Nibbāna alone;
for it is by coming to and depending upon that [Nibbāna] as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) of the Noble Path that [all formations are stilled].
All the stirrings of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are stilled and completely pacified; therefore, it is called "the stilling of all conditioned phenomena.
For when Nibbāna is dissociated from all that is conditioned, the designation "the pacification of formations" is indeed arrived at through logical reasoning.
Furthermore, this is its etymological derivation: it is called "the stilling of all conditioned phenomena" because all conditioned phenomena are stilled within it.
And because, by depending upon it, all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished through their total eradication and abandoned;
because all craving (taṇhā), in its hundred-and-eightfold variety, is exhausted; because all defilements and passions (rāga) fade away;

and because all the suffering of the round of existence, consisting of aging, death, and so forth, ceases—therefore, it is called "the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion."

"Cessation" is what is said; however, that craving which stretches out (*vinati*) and binds (*saṃsibbati*) from one existence to another existence by way of the state of longing for existence—or which, considering it as such, stretches out and binds karma together with its fruit—is called "vanana.
That which has emerged from that is "nibbāna" (*ni-vāna*). "Fatigue" (*kilamatha*) refers to bodily fatigue. "Affliction" (*vihesā*) also refers specifically to bodily affliction.
But in the minds of the Buddhas, both of these are absent, because they were utterly eradicated even at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Here, physical fatigue and bodily vexation are to be understood by way of backache and dryness of the palate and throat resulting from long sitting and speaking;
and this occurs specifically in relation to those who do not understand the meaning of the teaching and do not practice it. However, for those who do understand...
And for those practicing according to his teaching, even physical exhaustion does not exhaust the Teacher; therefore the Blessed One said, "The matter of the Dhamma does not trouble me.
For this very reason it was said: "That which is called teaching those who do not know would be weariness for me."
*Apissu* is a particle used in the sense of conjunction (*sampiṇḍana*). It indicates that not only did this thought occur, but these verses also flashed into his mind.

Regarding *Bhagavantam*, because it is joined with a reciprocal term (*paṭisadda*), it is the accusative case in the sense of a possessor (*sāmī-attha*); thus he says "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*).

Or, they are "wonderful" (*acchariyā*) because they have reached excellence (*vuddhi*), or they are "not wonderful" (*anacchariyā*). For the vowel *a-* also has the sense of excellence, as in the term "those beyond training" (*asekkhā*).

“Dhammā. Having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons solely for the purpose of sharing the Dhamma with the world including its devas, he has now attained the sovereignty of the Dhamma;

thus, the non-surprising nature of the meaning of the verse and its attainment of excellence should be understood, as it demonstrates his state of non-exertion therein. For by way of the meaning, the verses—

“Not being extraordinary” means that they became objects of experience; and since an object of experience is something to be reflected upon, he said, “they reached the state of being fit for thorough reflection.
“With difficulty” does not mean by way of a painful practice, for even all four paths of the Buddhas are indeed practices that are easy.
But at the time of fulfilling the perfections (pāramī), while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, he gave to arriving supplicants his head—adorned and prepared—having cut it off;
having drawn out the blood from his neck; having plucked out his well-anointed eyes;
and his son, the lamp of his family lineage, and his beloved wife, and so forth, as well as in other bodily existences similar to those of Khantivādi.
This was said with reference to the path leading back [to the world] for one who undergoes cutting, breaking, and so forth.
Or, *ha* is a particle used in the sense of "clever" (*byatta*). Some say it has the sense of "certainly" (*ekaṃsa*).
The construction is: "It is certainly (*ha*) clever (*byatta*), or indeed (*alaṃ*)—that is, useless—to teach such a Dhamma attained with difficulty. Or, *halam* has the same meaning as *alam*.
The word *pada* is used here as in such expressions as "I say that [a word] ends in a consonant" (*halanta*). Some also read it as *pakāsita*, which means "taught.
Thus, for this Dhamma attained with such difficulty, enough has been taught; it is sufficient. The sense is: "What is the use of teaching more?
By those "overcome by lust and hatred" (*rāgadosaparetehi*), meaning those touched by lust and hatred—just as by a snake touched by its venom—by lust...

"By those touched by hatred" means by those who are overcome by it; or alternatively, "by those overcome by lust and hatred" means by those followed by lust and hatred, that is, by those pursued by lust and hatred.
"Going against the stream" means going against the stream of the grasping for permanence and so forth—that is, proceeding toward impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.
The meaning is: "the Dhamma of the four truths as they occur. "Stained by lust" means stained by sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views.
"They will not see" means they will not perceive [things] according to their true nature—that they are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.
Since they do not see this, who will be able to make them know the Dhamma as it truly is through its true nature, such as impermanence and so forth?

This is the intended meaning. Their state of being overcome by lust and hatred is likewise due solely to their state of confusion; thus he says, "shrouded by a mass of darkness," meaning they are overwhelmed by the heap of ignorance.

As for the phrase "his mind inclines toward indolence": why does his mind incline in this way? Is it not the case that he [the Buddha] has said, "I am liberated, I shall liberate others; I have crossed over, I shall help others cross"?
"What is the use of my remaining in disguise?

Having realized the Dhamma here, and having attained omniscience, I shall deliver the world together with its devas"—having thus made this aspiration and fulfilled the perfections, he attained omniscience. This is indeed true; it was precisely through the power of that very reflection.

His mind inclined in this way. For when he had attained omniscience and was reflecting upon the density of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma, the density of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma became manifest to him in every aspect. Then [he thought]:
"These beings are like gourds filled with sour gruel, like basins filled with buttermilk, like rags soaked in fat and oil..."
As he reflected, "They are filled with defilements, exceedingly corrupt, dyed by lust, fouled by hatred, and bewildered by delusion—like one whose hand is smeared with collyrium;
what indeed will they penetrate? his mind inclined thus through the power of reflecting on the thicket of defilements:
"This Dhamma is profound, like the mass of water that supports the earth; it is as if hidden by a mountain..."
It was as difficult to see as a mustard seed placed [on a needle], or as minute as the tip of a hair split a hundredfold.
For while I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift that I had not given, no virtue that I had not guarded, and no perfections that I had not fulfilled;
yet even as I was dispersing the host of Māra, it seemed as if he were devoid of energy.
The earth did not shake when I was recollecting my past lives during the first watch of the night;

it did not shake even while I was purifying the divine eye during the middle watch; but only while I was penetrating dependent origination during the last watch did the ten-thousandfold world system shake.
Thus, even for one like me with such sharp wisdom, this Dhamma was attained only with great difficulty.

It should be understood that his mind was thus inclined by the power of reflection upon the profundity of the Dhamma, thinking, "Since I have penetrated this, how will the common people of the world penetrate it?
Furthermore, his mind was inclined in this way because he desired to teach when requested by Brahmā; for the Blessed One knew: "My..."
“While his mind is inclined toward indifference, Mahābrahmā will request a teaching of the Dhamma; and these beings hold Brahmā in high esteem.

Thinking, ‘It seems the Teacher was not willing to teach the Dhamma, but now that Mahābrahmā has requested him, he causes him to teach—how peaceful and sublime indeed is this Dhamma!’, they will listen with eager attention. This too is a reason for it.
It should be understood that his mind inclined toward non-exertion rather than the teaching of the Dhamma.

8. Regarding Sahampati: it is said that during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was an elder named Sahaka who, having attained the first jhāna, was reborn as a Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon in the plane of the first jhāna; there he was known as Sahampati.
They perceive it as "Brahmā. It is with reference to this that he says, "of Brahmā Sahampati.
"Alas, he perishes!"—it is said that he utters this sound in such a way that all the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system, upon hearing it, assemble together.
"Of little dust in their eyes" means that in the eye consisting of wisdom (*paññāmaya-akkhi*), there is but little, or minimal, dust of greed, hatred, and delusion (*rāga-dosa-moha-raja*).
"Of such a nature" means they are "of a nature with little dust. Those whose nature has little dust—such as the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth—are "of a nature with little dust";

this is how the meaning should be understood here. "By hearing" is a nominative form used in the sense of the instrumental, as in the phrase "having personally realized through direct knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā*);
thus, the meaning is "by means of hearing. "They will become" refers to those who have performed the requisite service by means of the ten meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.

Just as lotuses that have reached full maturity long for the touch of the sun’s rays, he shows that at the conclusion of even a four-line stanza there will not be just one or two, but many hundreds of thousands who are capable of entering the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*) and become knowers of the Dhamma.
"Appeared" (*pāturahosi*) means he became manifest. "Contemplated by the defiled" refers to the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others, who were possessed of defilements.
He thought: "For they had arisen earlier and, like one scattering thorns or pouring poison throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, taught the defiled doctrine of wrong view.

It is said that, having become curious upon hearing the rumors of the Buddha’s appearance, they deceived the world and, standing in hypocrisy while claiming omniscience, taught nothing but what was contrary to the Dhamma."
They declared it to be the Dhamma. "Open this" means: reveal this. "The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path, which serves as the gateway to the Deathless Nibbāna.

This is what is meant: with the hand of the teaching of the True Dhamma, open this great gate to the city of Nibbāna—the Noble Path—which has been closed since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation.
“Open the opening! [The meaning is: “May these beings hear the Dhamma realized by the Stainless One.

He thus requests the Blessed One: “First let them hear the Dhamma of the Four Truths realized by the Stainless Perfectly Enlightened One, who is stainless due to the absence of the stains of passion and so forth.
He says, “As on a rock,” because the Selapabbata (Rock Mountain) is high and firm, unlike a mountain of earth or a mixed mountain.
"Standing on the summit of a mountain. Its meaning is: "Remaining exactly as he is on the solid, rocky peak of a mountain.
For one standing there, there is no need for actions such as lifting the neck or stretching out the arms in order to see.
"Like that" (*tathūpama*) means similar to that, comparable to the rocky mountain. "The palace made of Dhamma" refers to the supramundane Dhamma; for it is...
It is entirely conducive to serene confidence, and because it has risen above all phenomena (*dhamma*), it is like a palace (*pāsāda*) in its sense of having ascended.
Alternatively, the word *dhamma* here refers to wisdom (*paññā*). For in the Abhidhamma, wisdom is defined as a "palace" in the sense of having ascended. Thus it is said:
"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, one who is free from sorrow looks down upon the sorrowing people."
“Just as one standing on a mountain peak gazes upon those on the ground, so does the wise man look down upon the foolish.

This is the summary of the meaning here: Just as a sighted person standing upon the summit of a rocky mountain would see the people all around him, even so, O Sumedha of beautiful wisdom, you are the All-Seeing One through your omniscient knowledge.

"The Blessed One, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and made of wisdom, himself free from sorrow, should look upon and take note of, and examine the people who are immersed in sorrow and overcome by birth and aging.
This, moreover, is the intended meaning here:
just as if, at the foot of a mountain, they were to clear a great field on all sides, build huts there among the field boundaries, and kindle a fire at night.

Suppose there were darkness endowed with four factors; then, for a man with sight standing on the summit of that mountain and looking down at the ground, neither the fields, nor the boundaries of the fields, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping therein would be discernible because of their lack of radiance;
however, in the huts, only the mere glow of a fire would be discernible because of its radiance.

Thus, as the Tathāgata, having ascended the Palace of Dhamma, surveys the multitude of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of the Buddha-eye even when sitting in a secluded dwelling on the right side of the knee;
because they are not ignited by the fire of knowledge and because they lack nobility, they are like arrows shot in the night. But those who...

Those individuals who are to be trained are of excellent character; even though they may stand far away, they come within his range because of the blazing state of the fire of his matured knowledge and because of the loftiness of his mental continuum—he being like that fire and like the Himavat mountain. And this has been said:
“The virtuous shine forth from afar, Like the Himavat mountain.”
"Those who are not present here are not seen, like arrows shot in the night.
"Arise!"—thus he speaks, requesting the Blessed One to undertake a journey for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
Or, "Arise! means: arise from the state of exhaustion resulting from the contraction known as being indifferent to teaching the Dhamma. Regarding the words "O Hero," and so forth...
The Blessed One is a *vīra* (hero) because of his possession of the preeminent energy of the fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*);
he is one who has "conquered the battle" (*vijitasaṅgāma*) because of his victory over the sons of gods, death, defilements, and volitional formations;

he is a "caravan leader" (*satthavāha*) because of his capacity to transport the beings to be trained across the wilderness of birth and so forth, and his capacity to bring them to the secure region known as Nibbāna; and he is "debtless" (*aṇaṇo*) because of the absence of the deer of sensual desire.

It is to be understood as follows: for one who, having borrowed a debt from others, squanders it, is unable to strike back at all—whether he is being urged by them, "Give the debt! or is being addressed harshly, reviled, or even beaten;
rather, he endures it all. For that debt is the very cause of his endurance. In exactly the same way, one who [is overcome] by sensual desire...
He is attached; by means of that grasping through craving, he clings to that object.
Consequently, even when he is spoken to harshly, reviled, or beaten, he is unable to strike back at all, but endures everything.

For this lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmacchanda*) is the cause of his endurance, just as in the case of women being harassed by their household masters. Why? Because lust for sensual pleasure is like a debt.
9. "Entreaty" (*ajjhesanā*) means a longing directed toward a more important purpose after having attended upon one who stands in the position of a teacher;

in its essential meaning, it is simply a request. "With the Buddha-eye" refers to both the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of underlying tendencies and dispositions (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*).
Indeed, these two knowledges are given the name "Buddha-eye," whereas the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*)— [...is called the "Buddha-knowledge" (*buddha-ñāṇa*).*]
"Samantacakkhu" (all-seeing eye) refers to the knowledge of the three lower paths. Regarding "those with little dust in their eyes" and so forth:
those who, according to the method already stated, have little dust such as passion in their eye of wisdom are "those with little dust in their eyes.
Those for whom that dust is great are "those with much dust in their eyes. Those whose faculties, such as faith, are sharp are "those with sharp faculties."
Those whose [faculties] are soft are "those of soft faculties" (*mudindriya*). Those whose very same qualities of faith and so forth are beautiful in form are "those of good form" (*svākāra*).
Those who perceive the reasons that have been stated and can be easily informed are "those easy to instruct" (*suviññāpaya*).
Those who view both the next world and moral fault as fearsome are called "those who see the fear in the next world and in moral fault" (*paralokavajjabhayadassāvī*).
"Uppalinī" means "that which has lotuses," referring either to a grove or a body of water; however, here a body of water is intended.
Therefore, the meaning of "uppaliniyaṃ" should be understood as "in a lotus grove. The same principle applies to the subsequent terms as well.
"Antonimuggaposīni" refers to those [lotuses] which, having remained submerged within the water, nourish and grow; these are the "antonimuggaposīni."
"Standing having emerged above the water" means they stand having transcended the water.
Among them, those that stand having emerged above [the water], awaiting contact with the rays of the sun, are those that flower today.
Those that stand level with the water are those that flower tomorrow. Those that have not risen from the water but remain submerged within it are those that flower on the third day.
Regarding "blossoming": there are indeed other types of lotuses and the like that have not yet emerged from the water and are diseased, which will neither bloom nor become food for fish and turtles;
these have not been included in the Canon (pāḷi), but they are explained in the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā) as having been brought forward for illustration.
For just as those four kinds of flowers, [so too are the four kinds of persons].

In the same way, there are four types of persons: those who understand through a brief statement (ugghaṭitaññū), those who understand through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū), those who are led to understanding (neyyo), and those for whom the words are the limit (padaparamo).

Among these, the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs at the very moment it is uttered—having directed their knowledge according to the teaching by means of a brief outline (mātikā) established in such a manner as "the four foundations of mindfulness"—attains Arahantship.
A person capable of grasping [the teaching] immediately upon hearing it is called one who understands through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

That person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail is called one who understands through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*).
That person for whom [realization occurs] through recitation, through inquiry, through wise attention, and through serving and associating with spiritual friends...
For one who attends upon [the teaching], there comes about the realization of the Dhamma by stages; such a person is called "one to be guided" (neyya).

As for that person who, despite hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma in this very life—neither the path nor the fruit, and at least not even jhāna or insight—within that same existence.
or cannot bring [it] to fruition—this person is called one who is "one for whom the word is the limit" (*padaparama*).

In this regard, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world system which is like a lotus grove and so forth, sees those who are *ugghaṭitaññū* as flowers blooming on this very day, those who are *vipañcitaññū* as flowers blooming on the morrow, and those who are *neyya* as flowers blooming on the third day; [he also sees] flowers that are food for fish and turtles.
He saw them as well as the words alone; and while seeing them, he saw them in every aspect, thinking: "So many have little dust in their eyes, so many have much dust in their eyes;
and among those, so many are those who understand through a condensed statement.
In this regard, for three types of persons, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma accomplishes its purpose within this very same physical existence.

For those for whom the word is the limit, there is a latent predisposition (vāsanā) for the sake of the future. Then the Blessed One, having understood that the teaching of the Dhamma would bring benefit to these four types of persons, and having conceived the desire to teach it, further divided all beings within the three realms of existence into two classes according to their capacity and incapacity.
With reference to them, it was said: "Those beings who, by way of the obstruction of karma..."

“Those who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma-result, possessed of the obstruction of defilements, lacking faith, lacking desire, and lacking wisdom—these beings are incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states; these are the beings who are incapable.
Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma… [and so on]… these are the beings who are capable.”
Therein, having abandoned all individuals incapable [of attaining the goal] and having discerned with wisdom only those individuals capable of it, he divided them into six classes, thinking:
"So many are of a lustful temperament (rāga-carita), so many of a hateful, deluded, discursive, faithful, or intellectual temperament (buddhi-carita).

Having done this, he thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma. And here, as he was reflecting by way of the categories such as "those with little dust in their eyes" and "those capable," etc., [the following occurred].
It should be understood that those beings appear to the Blessed One as masses upon masses, not individually.
"Paccabhāsi" means he replied. "Apārutā" means opened. "The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path.
For that is the door to Nibbāna, which is designated as the Deathless; it has been opened and set forth by me through self-born knowledge, supported by great compassion.
This shows that [the Dhamma] has been realized. Some read: “The door to the Deathless has been opened for them.
“Let them release their faith” means: let everyone release, relinquish, and proclaim their own faith; let them arouse within themselves the mode of believing in me and in the Dhamma taught by me.
Regarding the last two lines, this is the meaning: for I—
"Though this sublime and supreme Dhamma was familiar to me and well-mastered, I thought, 'I shall not speak it,' perceiving it as a weariness of body and speech;
I thought, 'I will not speak it. But now, let all people bring vessels of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations.
"He vanished" means that after honoring the Teacher with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he disappeared.

The meaning is that he has gone back to his own place. For when gods and Brahmās have approached the presence of the Teacher, their disappearance before him is simply their returning to their own places.
The commentary on the "Brahmā’s Request" is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Group of Five:
10. *Etadahosi* means "this occurred. The meaning is that this thought associated with the teaching of the Dhamma arose: "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
*Āḷāra* is his name; he was long and tawny-eyed (*dīghapiṅgala*).
This is his name. For he was tall because of his lofty body, and tawny because of his tawny eyes;
thus his name became "Āḷāra. "Kālāma" is his clan name. "Paṇḍita" means endowed with wisdom;
the meaning is that he was endowed with the state of being wise, which consists of proficiency in realization through the attainment of meditative absorptions. "Byatta" means by way of cleverness.
"Endowed" means endowed with proficiency, which is reckoned as the wisdom that prevents decline and serves as the condition for attaining meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Wise" (*medhāvī*) means endowed with the wisdom that arises from the situation (*ṭhānuppattiyā paññā*).

Alternatively, "wise" means endowed with *medhā*, which is reckoned as the wisdom of the three-root rebirth-linking (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi*) and the wisdom regarding the various duties to be performed in each respective circumstance.

The meaning here should be understood in this way. "One of little dust in his eyes" means one who is by nature free from defilements due to the suppression [of them] by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), a purified being. "He will understand" means he will observe and penetrate.
"Knowledge arose even for the Blessed One" means that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) arose for the Blessed One. It is said that the Blessed One...

Not reaching a conclusion even though it had been told by a deity, the Blessed One himself, surveying with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), saw that [the monk] would pass away on the seventh day from now and be reborn in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). With reference to him, he said: "The knowledge of the Blessed One also arose.
He is called "one who has lost much" (*mahājāniyo*) because he has fallen away from the path and fruit that were to be attained within seven days.

"Mahājāniyo" means one who has lost great wealth. He shows that he has become so impoverished because there is no foot to travel here to this place of Dhamma teaching where he was reborn at an inopportune time;
and even if I were to go there, he would have no clarity of hearing to listen to the Dhamma being taught once I had arrived.
But why did the Blessed One [not use] his own Buddha-power [to help him]?
Is it not possible to make the Dhamma known? Yes, it is not possible; for the realization of the Dhamma by disciples cannot occur without the sound of another’s voice.
Otherwise, there would have to be realization of the Dhamma even for one devoid of all other conditions, yet that does not exist.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, these two conditions lead to the arising of right view: from another..."
“And there was a sound, and internal wise attention.
“Udaka” is his name; because he was the son of Rāma, he is called “Rāmaputta. “Died at the end of the night” means he died at midnight.
“Knowledge arose for the Blessed One as well” means that here too, it is said, the Blessed One [knew] by means of the words spoken by the deity.
Without making a formal determination, he surveyed with his knowledge of omniscience and saw:
"Yesterday at midnight, having passed away, Udaka Rāmaputta was reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Therefore, it was said thus. The rest is exactly as before.
"Bahūpakārā" means those who were of great assistance. "Upaṭṭhahimsu padhānapahitattan" means they attended upon him whose self had been dispatched for the sake of striving.
They attended upon him by sweeping the courtyard at the place where he stayed, by following him with his bowl and robes, and by providing water for washing the face and tooth-sticks, and so forth.
But who were these known as the group-of-five?
They were those—Rāma, Dhaja, and Lakkhaṇa, as well as the counselor;...
Koṇḍañña, Bhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta—
these were the eight brahmins at that time who,
possessing the six factors, interpreted the mantra.
At the time of the Bodhisatta’s birth, there were eight brahmins who received his horoscope and interpreted his marks.
Among them, three gave a twofold prediction: “One endowed with these marks, if he dwells at home, will become a universal monarch (cakkavatti) king;
if he goes forth into homelessness, he will become a Buddha. Five brahmins, however, made a categorical prediction: “With these [marks]...”
“Endowed with these marks, one does not remain in the household life; one becomes a Buddha. Among them, the first three followed the words of the mantra exactly.

For they were unable to determine, according to the stated rule, that there are only two destinies for those who have practiced in accordance with the Vedic words known as the *lakṣaṇa-mantras* and nothing else; thus, they proceeded precisely as instructed, and not according to the Great Man.

They aspired to the attainment of Buddhahood. However, these five, beginning with Koṇḍañña, because they had reached a firm conviction that "the Buddha will certainly become one," transcended the words of the mantras.
Having distributed the gifts of satisfaction they had received among their kinsmen, they became free from doubt, thinking:
"This Great Being will not dwell in the household life; he will certainly become a Buddha."
They say that these were the sons of those who had gone forth as ascetics for the sake of the Bodhisatta; however, this is rejected in the Aṭṭhakathā.
It is said that even in their youth they mastered many mantras, and therefore the brahmins established them in the position of teachers.
They thought, "Later on, it will not be possible for us to go forth after having our children and wives cut off their matted hair."
Having gone forth at a very young age, they wandered about enjoying delightful dwellings.
From time to time, however, they would ask, "Sir, has the Great Being gone forth on the Great Renunciation? People would reply, "Where will you see the Great Being?
He is like a god, enjoying prosperity amidst various theatrical performances in his three palaces."
"They experience [it]," they said. Having heard this, they thought, "The knowledge of the Great Man has not yet reached maturity," and so they remained there with little concern.
But why did the Blessed One say here, "The group-of-five monks have been very helpful to me"? Was it only because they were benefactors?
"Does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not assist him? "He does not fail to teach.
For it was out of long-standing familiarity that he looked toward Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta.
However, within this Buddha-field, there is no one else capable of realizing the Dhamma first except Aññā Koṇḍañña. Why? Because of such a decisive supporting condition (upanissaya).
It is said that formerly, in a time when they were performing meritorious deeds, there were two brothers. They cultivated their crops together.
Regarding this, the elder brother thought, "I must give the gift of the finest crop nine times during the course of one harvest.
At the time of sowing, he gave what is called the "seed-portion," and at the time of the earing, he consulted with his younger brother: "At the time of the earing, having split open the ear..."
“I will give it. The younger brother said, “Do you wish to destroy the young crop? The elder brother, realizing that his younger brother would not comply with his wishes, divided the field;
from his own portion, he split open the ear of grain, extracted the milk, mixed it with ghee and molasses, and gave it [to him].

When it was time for the *puthuka* (threshed grain), he had the *puthuka* prepared and gave it; at the time of reaping, he gave the first sheaves of the harvest; at the time of binding them into bundles—
He gave the first-fruits of the crop nine times in this manner: the first-fruits of the bamboo when he had bound the bundles together for carrying by men;

the first-fruits of the sheaves when making them into bundles; the first-fruits of the threshing floor on the day the bundles were placed there; the first-fruits of the threshing-floor grain on the day the rice was trodden out and made into a heap;
and the first-fruits of the granary on the day the grain was put into the storehouse. Thus he gave the gift of the first-fruits nine times for a single harvest.
The younger brother, however, having harvested grain from the threshing floor, gave it on the day of collection.

Of these two, the elder became the Venerable Aññā-Koṇḍañña, and the younger became the wanderer Subhadda. Thus, because the nine foremost gifts were given regarding a single crop, there was no one else besides the Elder capable of realizing the Dhamma first. “Of the nine...”

"Because of having given the foremost gifts"—this was said because [the merit] was performed while he was practicing the perfections of a disciple, in accordance with the aspiration made for the sake of attaining the preeminence among those long-standing [disciples].

For indeed, when any of the three types of Bodhisattvas reach the pinnacle of their respective perfections, the merit or demerit they have performed results in a very heavy ripening; and as for the Dhamma...
How is the status of being foremost among those long-standing in the faith established without first-hand realization?
As for the statement, "The group-of-five monks were indeed very helpful to me," this was said merely by way of recollecting their assistance.
Regarding the phrase "at Isipatana in the Deer Park," it is said that in that region, before the appearance of a Buddha, Pacceka-Buddhas [dwelt] on Mount Gandhamādana.
Having spent seven days in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they emerge from that cessation, chew a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* vine,
wash their faces in Lake Anotatta, and taking their bowls and robes, they arrive by way of the air and alight there.
Having put on their robes there and walked for alms in the city, and having finished their meal, they likewise spring up from that very spot at the time of departure.
They go there. Thus, because seers (*isi*) alight and take flight at this place, it has come to be known as "Isipatana" (The Seers' Descent).
However, because it was given to the deer for their safety, it is called "Migadāya" (Deer Park). Therefore it is said: "At Isipatana, in the Migadāya.
Other Buddhas, when going for the purpose of their first teaching of the Dhamma, travel through the air and [arrive] right there.
[The others] were descending [the mountain], but our Blessed One, seeing that Upaka the Ājīvaka possessed the necessary conditions for support (*upanissaya*), knew:
"Upaka has set out on this journey; having seen me and conversed with me, he will depart, and then, becoming weary once more, he will return and realize *arahantship*.
Knowing this, he traveled the eighteen-yojana road on foot alone. For that reason...
It is said: "He set out on a wandering tour toward Bārāṇasī. 11.
"Between Gayā and the Bodhi" means at a place three *gāvutas* apart from the gap between Gayā and the Bodhi tree.
For Gayā is three *gāvutas* from the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and Bārāṇasī is eighteen *yojanas*. Upaka [was] of the seat of enlightenment...
And between Gayā and [the other place], he saw the Blessed One. Because it is joined with the word *antarā*, the accusative case is employed.
In such instances, grammarians employ the word *antarā* only once, as in the expression "he goes between the village and the river";
yet it must be construed with the second member as well, for if it were not so construed, the accusative case would [be unaccountable].
It does not attain the status of the agentive case because, in this context, the instrumental case is intended due to its connection with the word *antarā*.
However, here it is stated having been joined [to the noun]. "A journey on a road" (*addhānamagga*) means a road characterized as a journey; that is, a long road.
This is because, in the *Vibhaṅga* on the occasion of traveling a journey, there is the statement: "One may eat [before setting out] thinking, 'I shall go half a *yojana*,'" and so forth.
The road was even half a *yojana* in length. From the Seat of Enlightenment (*Bodhimaṇḍa*) to Gayā, however, it was three *gāvutas*.
"Completely serene" means very clear. "Faculties" refers to the faculties with the mind as the sixth.
"Purified" means faultless. "Brightly cleansed" is a synonym for that same state; for it is called "brightly cleansed" precisely because of its freedom from defilements, not because of its whiteness.
Having seen the purity of this [teaching], he understood the clarity of the faculties; for this was the wisdom of that Ājīvaka, which grasps the underlying method.
"All-conqueror" (*sabbābhibhū*) means he stands having overcome all phenomena of the three planes.

"All-knower" (*sabbavidū*) means he has known and understood all phenomena of the four planes because of his total abandonment of the veil of the knowable. "Unstained among all phenomena" means among all...
He is unsmeared by the defilement-stain of lust, hatred, delusion, and so forth, regarding the phenomena of the three planes.

He is "one who has abandoned all" because he stands having abandoned all phenomena of the three planes. For even that which is not to be abandoned—namely, the wholesome and the indeterminate—is indeed considered abandoned because it has been relinquished through the abandoning of the defilements bound to it.
He is "liberated in the destruction of craving" by way of making the destruction of craving, i.e., Nibbāna, his object.
"Liberated. "Having known by myself" means having understood all phenomena of the four planes by oneself alone. "Whom should I point to?
means whom else should I point to, thinking, "This one is my teacher"?

"I have no teacher" means that regarding supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*), I have no one who can be called my teacher. For even with respect to mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhamma*), [there is no such person].
The realization of the Lord of the World is such that there is no realization equal to it through instruction by another, nor is there even a trace of supramundane dhamma in anyone else.
"There is no one equal to me" means there is no person who could serve as my counterpart in virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth.
"Perfectly Enlightened One" (*Sammāsambuddha*) means he has awakened to the Four Truths for himself by way of cause and method.
"Cooled" means cooled by the extinguishing of the fire of all defilements; "extinguished" (nibbuto) because of the very cessation of the defilements.
"The city of Kāsī" refers to the city in the kingdom of Kāsī. "I shall beat" means I will strike.

"The drum of the Deathless" refers to the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, which is called the "drum of the Deathless" because it makes a proclamation for the sake of the realization of the Deathless by those to be trained, and for the attainment of the Wheel of Dhamma.
The meaning is: "I go thinking, 'I shall strike that drum of the Deathless.
"You are worthy to be an Anantajina" means you are fit to become an Anantajina. An Anantajina is one who possesses infinite knowledge and has conquered the defilements.
"Hupeyyapāvuso" means, "Friend, it might even be so; such indeed would be this jewel of form."
The intention is that he ought to possess such knowledge; for this became the condition for his going forth.
Indeed, he had already performed his duties; thus, for the sake of meeting him, the Blessed One set out on that road on foot.
"He departed" means he went to the country named Vaṅkahāra.
There he took up residence near a village of deer-hunters, and the chief hunter attended upon him.
In that district, there were fierce flies; therefore, they had him live in a single jar.
When the deer-hunter went far away on a hunt, he gave instructions to his daughter, named Cāpā, saying, "Do not neglect our Arahant."
He arrived together with his sons and brothers. His daughter was beautiful to behold and possessed of perfect limbs.
On the second day, when Upaka returned home, he saw that girl having performed all the customary services and approaching to serve him;
overcome by passion and unable even to eat, he took the food from the bowl, went to his dwelling place, and [ate] the food.
Having set it aside to one side, she lay down without food, thinking, "If I obtain the bow, I shall live;
if not, I shall die. On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka's condition.
She said, "He came only once, and since then he has never returned again."

The hunter, thinking, "I will approach him as soon as he arrives and ask," went at that very moment and, while touching his foot, asked, "What is it, venerable sir, that is causing you discomfort? Upaka merely lay there turning over and groaning.
The hunter said, "Speak, venerable sir; whatever I am able to do, I shall do it all. Upaka [said], "If you have a bow..."
“I gain [my livelihood], I live; if not, death would be better for me,” he said.
“Venerable sir, do you know any craft? “I do not know. “Venerable sir, it is not possible for one who knows no craft to maintain a household life.
He replied, “I do not know any craft; however, I shall become your meat-provider, and as for the meat—”

“I will sell it. The hunter said, “This is exactly what we also desire,” and having given an upper garment, he brought her home and gave her his daughter. Following their union, a son was born, and they named him Subhadda.
When he was crying, Cāpā would say, “Son of a meat-seller! Son of a deer-trapper! Do not cry, do not cry! and so forth.
While speaking, she mocked Upaka with a song praising her son, saying, "Bhaddā, you think I am without a protector;
I have a companion named Anantajina, and I shall go into his presence.
Knowing that he was thus distressed, Cāpā spoke to him again and again. One day, however, without informing her, he set out toward the Middle Country.
At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
Then the Blessed One gave instructions to the monks in advance: “Monks, if anyone comes asking for ‘Anantajina,’ you must show me him.
Meanwhile, Upaka, asking “Where does Anantajina dwell? gradually arrived at Sāvatthī and [stood] in the middle of the monastery.
Having stopped, he asked, "Where is the Jina Ananta? The monks led him into the presence of the Blessed One.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, he said, "Does the Blessed One recognize me? "Yes, Upaka, I recognize you. But where have you been living?
"In the country of Vaṅkahāra, Bhante. "Upaka, you have grown old; it is time for you to go forth."
"Will you be able? "I shall go forth, venerable sir. The Blessed One, having granted him the going-forth, gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
While practicing that meditation subject, he established himself in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and passing away, was reborn in the Aviha heaven.
At the very moment of his rebirth, he attained Arahantship. For seven beings who were merely reborn in Aviha attained Arahantship.
They attained [this state], and he was one among them. For it has been said:
"Seven bhikkhus reborn in the Aviha realm have attained liberation;
with lust and hatred utterly destroyed, they have crossed over the world's attachment."
“Upaka and Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti—those three;
Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi, and Saṅgiya:
having abandoned their human bodies, they have attained union with the divine.”
12. *Saṇṭhapenti*: they made an agreement, saying, "He is not even to be saluted," and so forth. *Bāhulliko*:

one who practices for the sake of an abundance of robes and other such things. *Padhānavibbhanto*: fallen away from striving—that is, having strayed, departed, and declined from the difficult practice undertaken prior to his striving.
*Āvatto bāhullāya*: turned back toward abundance—for the sake of a multiplicity of robes and so forth. Furthermore, [he took] a seat...
"It should be set aside" means, moreover, they said that even for one born into a high-born family, a mere seat should be set aside.
"Unable to stand firm" means, being overwhelmed by the power and majesty of the Buddha, they were unable to remain within their own agreement.
"They address him by name and with the term 'friend'" means they speak to him saying "Gotama" and "friend," [saying] "Friend..."

The meaning is that they spoke such words as: "Gotama, during our time of striving at Uruvelā, we carried your bowl and robes about, we gave you water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks, and we swept the dwelling-cell after you had stayed there;
who has performed these duties of service for you since then? We hope that you did not worry when we had departed."

"Before long" means very soon. "Sons of good family" (*kulaputta*) refers to two kinds of sons of good family: those by birth and those by conduct; these, however, are both indeed sons of good family.
"From the home" means from the house. That which is beneficial for the home is "domesticity" (*agāriya*);

it refers to the work of maintaining a household, such as agriculture and cattle-rearing. "Homelessness" (*anagāriya*) means that there is no domesticity here. This is a term for going forth (*pabbajjā*).
This is a designation. "They go forth" means they approach or draw near. "That unsurpassed" means that which is supreme.
"The consummation of the holy life" refers to the end of the holy life of the path; what is meant is the fruit of arahantship.
For it is for the sake of that that sons of good family go forth. "In this very life" means in that very personal existence.
"Having realized by one's own direct knowledge" means having made it manifest through one's own wisdom; the meaning is that one has made it independent of another.
"Having attained and dwelling" means having reached and having accomplished, you shall dwell. "By conduct" means by difficult conduct.
"By practice" means by difficult practice. "By the performance of what is difficult" refers to such things as consuming food measured out morsel by morsel, such as a soup of mung beans, and so forth.

“By means of the practice of austerities. “Superhuman states” (*uttari manussadhammā*) means above human nature. “Worthy of being made noble” (*alamariyaṃ*) means one who is capable of the state of a noble one (*ariyabhāva*);
this is what is meant. “Distinction in knowledge and vision” (*ñāṇadassanavisesa*) is simply knowledge and vision itself.

“And that distinction in knowledge and vision which is worthy of being made noble” is thus “the distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of being made noble” (*alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa*). “Knowledge and vision” (*ñāṇadassana*)—

And the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), the fruit (*phala*), the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), and even omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) are all called "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*).
For in the passage, "Being diligent, he attains knowledge and vision," it is the divine eye that is called "knowledge and vision.
In the passage, "He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision," it is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*). [In the passage], "They are incapable... [it is the path].
In the passage, “...for the sake of knowledge and vision, for unsurpassed full enlightenment,” this refers to the path.
In the passage, “This other distinguished state of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a superior human state, has been attained, a dwelling in comfort,” this refers to the fruit.
And in the passage, “Knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My liberation of mind is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no further existence. this refers to the fruit.
In this context, it is the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). In the passage, “And the knowledge and vision arose in me:

‘Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago,’” it is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). However, here what is intended is either the Noble Path which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause, or the knowledge of omniscience itself.
"Do you recall from me? means "Do you indeed recall from me? Regarding the phrase "such as this was cultivated," the meaning here is "a variety of such statements. [The Buddha said:

"Did I, while striving at Uruvelā for the sake of supporting you and so that you would not be weary, come to you by night or by day and say: 'Friends, do not think: "We shall go wherever we please."'?"
The intention is that he did not utter any such variation of speech as, "A radiance or the sign of my meditation subject appears to me.

Having regained mindfulness with a single word, they felt reverence and, having gained faith, saying, "Surely this one has become a Buddha," they replied, "Certainly not so, Bhante. The Blessed One was indeed able [to convince] the group-of-five monks.
"To convince" means that the Blessed One was able to make the five bhikkhus of the group know, "I am the Buddha.
"They established their minds on higher knowledge" means they directed and applied their minds toward the attainment of *aññā*, which is *arahatta* (Arahatship).
Commentary on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.
13. "Bhikkhus, these two extremes": this means, bhikkhus, these two portions, two parts.
Here, the word *anta* (extreme) has the sense of "portion," as in such expressions as "knowledge of the past limit" (*pubbante ñāṇaṃ*) and "knowledge of the future limit" (*aparante ñāṇaṃ*).
At the very moment this phrase was uttered, by the power of the Buddha, the sound that arose spread below to the Avīci hell and above to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
Having pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system, he remained there.
At that very moment, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, whose roots of merit were fully ripened and who had performed the necessary service for the full awakening to the Truths, assembled.
While the sun was setting in the western quarter, the full moon, joined with the Āsāḷha constellation, was rising in the eastern quarter. At that time, the Blessed One...
Beginning with the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*, he said: "Bhikkhus, these two extremes," and so forth.
Therein, "by one who has gone forth" means by one who has gone forth after cutting the bonds of the household life. "Should not be pursued" means should not be indulged in, should not be devoted to.

"And this devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires among sensual pleasures" refers to that which consists of the pleasure of defilement (*kilesa-kāma*) regarding objective sensual pleasures (*vatthu-kāma*).
*Anuyoga*: the meaning is that it follows after pleasure associated with the defilements of sensual desire. *Hīna*: base or inferior. *Gamma*:
belonging to village-dwellers, because it is to be practiced by them. *Pothujjanika*: practiced by the common person (*puthujjana*), that is, by the blind and foolish folk.
*Anariya*: not noble; not purified; not supreme; or not belonging to the Noble Ones (*ariya*). *Anatthasaṃhita*: not connected with what is beneficial.
"Independent" means a cause that brings about welfare and happiness. "Devotion to self-mortification" means devotion to one's own exhaustion;
the meaning is the infliction of suffering and the production of suffering. "Suffering" refers to that which brings about suffering through bodily afflictions such as lying on a bed of thorns.
"The middle way" is said with reference to the Noble Path, for the Path avoids both devotion to sensual pleasure and devotion to self-mortification.
One extreme is devotion to self-mortification; one extreme is devotion to self-indulgence. He does not approach, he does not resort to these two extremes;
being liberated from these extremes, it is therefore called the "Middle Way.

It is called "middle" because it exists between these two, and it is called a "way" because it is to be practiced by those seeking escape from the suffering of saṃsāra. Likewise, greed is one extreme...
"One extreme is [the view of] fault; one extreme is eternalism, and one extreme is annihilationism"—this should be elaborated upon in the same manner as previously stated.
With the words "it makes the eye," etc., he praises that very path. It "makes the eye of wisdom" (*paññācakkhu*);
for it leads to the seeing of the four truths, specifically to the seeing distinguished by full comprehension, clear realization, and so forth.

It is called "the maker of vision" in the sense of its occurrence. Although there is no difference between the path and this [vision], it should be understood that this statement is made by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because a meaning established through its constituent parts is ascribed to the whole.

The second term is a synonym for that very same thing. "For the sake of tranquility" means for the purpose of the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*). "For direct knowledge" refers to the four truths.
For the sake of full knowledge. "For enlightenment" means for the sake of awakening to those very things. "For Nibbāna" means for the realization of Nibbāna.
Alternatively, "for Nibbāna" refers to Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). By the phrase "for peace," Nibbāna with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbāna*) is included.
