Now, wishing to show that Middle Way in its true nature, he asks, "And what is it? and then states, "This very [path]," and so forth.
He answered by way of method. In this context, the restrictive phrase "this very" is for the purpose of negating the existence of any other path leading to Nibbāna.
For here, the negation is the exclusion of sentient beings (*satta*), because no other path is found.
It is called "noble" (*ariya*) in the etymological sense (*niruttinaya*) because it is remote from the defilements (*kilesa*); it is also so called because it leads to the abandoning of enemies.

It is called *ariya* because by means of it noble ones (*ariya*)—those of evil nature (*pāpadhamma*)—go away (*yanti*), that is, depart. It is also *ariya* because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is noble (*ariya*).
Furthermore, it is *ariya* because it leads to the attainment of the state of a noble one (*ariyabhāva*).

In this context, however, the word *ariya* should be understood as being formed by dropping the latter member of the compound *ariyakara* (noble-making), thus becoming *ariya*. [It is endowed] with eight factors.

It is "eightfold" because it is possessed [of these factors]. For the designation "path" applies to the collection of path-factors, and a collection is said to be "possessed" by its constituent members.
Here, however, is the etymological meaning: it is called "eightfold" (*aṭṭhaṅgika*) because it has eight factors as its own constituent parts.
But in the ultimate sense, the factors themselves are the path—just as in the case of a "five-limbed orchestra" and so forth—and it is not [the path] that possesses them.
It is like the Veda with its six limbs, being free from [deficient] members. It is called the "path" (*magga*) according to the method of etymology because it goes while slaying the defilements;
or else, it is the path because it seeks (*maggati*) or searches for Nibbāna, for the Noble Path acts as if searching while making Nibbāna its object.

Or again, it is the path because it is sought by those who desire Nibbāna, starting from the performance of merit that serves as the necessary condition for the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

It is called the path (*magga*) because it is practiced for that purpose, or because one proceeds by means of it. Here, however, the etymological derivation should be understood through an inversion of the beginning and the end.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "if it is asked, 'Which is that? or "What are those eight factors? (*katamāni tāni aṭṭhaṅgāni*).
For this particle is common to all genders, cases, and numbers. Each individual factor is indeed the path itself.
As it is said: “Right view is both the path and the cause. The Ancients also say: “Right view is the path of seeing;
right intention is the path of directing onto; ... [and so on] ... right concentration is the path of non-distraction. But are not these factors...
Is it that when combined they constitute the path, because of the absence of the Noble Eightfold Path if even one of its seven factors were missing?

This is true in regard to the penetration of the truths; however, by virtue of being conditions for the path and by performing their respective functions, each of them individually is indeed the path.
Otherwise, even when combined, the function of the path would not be possible for them. [This applies] to right view and the rest.
One sees rightly, thus it is right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*); one intends rightly, directing associated mental states toward the object known as Nibbāna, thus it is right intention (*sammā-saṅkappo*);
one speaks rightly by means of this, thus it is right speech (*sammā-vācā*);

one acts rightly by means of this, thus it is right action (*sammā-kamma*), which is itself right action-interval (*sammā-kammanto*); one lives rightly by means of this, thus it is right livelihood (*sammā-ājīvo*); one exerts oneself rightly...
"It exerts itself" means right effort (*sammāvāyāma*); "it remembers and recollects correctly" means right mindfulness (*sammāsati*);

"the mind is rightly concentrated by means of this" means right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*)—thus the derivation should be understood. Now, with the words "This, monks, is that," he concludes that very same practice.
Its meaning is as follows: that which consists of the four supramundane paths taken together...
Having done so, the Eightfold Path was taught: "This, monks, is that [path]... which leads to Nibbāna.
(14) Having thus shown the Middle Way in its essential nature, he now spoke the passage beginning with "But this, monks," in order to show the Four Noble Truths.
Therein, regarding the word *dukkha*: here, the sound *du-* is used in the sense of something contemptible (*kucchite*).
It is seen as such. For they call a contemptible son "one with a bad son" (*duputta*); moreover, the word *kha* refers to what is empty (*tuccha*).

Indeed, empty space is called "the void" (*kha*). And this first Truth is contemptible because it is the locus of manifold calamities, and it is empty because it is devoid of the permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood imagined by foolish people; therefore, due to its contemptibility and its emptiness—
And it is called "suffering. Furthermore, because the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others, have penetrated this, it is called an "Ariyasacca" (Noble Truth).
For a truth that is to be penetrated by the Noble Ones is called an "Ariyasacca" by eliding the latter member of the compound in the first phrase.
Alternatively, it is an "Ariyasacca" because it is the truth of the Noble One, the Tathāgata; for it has been realized by the Tathāgata himself.
It is called "Noble Truth" (*ariyasacca*) because it has been proclaimed by him, and because it is to be realized by others; thus, it belongs to him.

Alternatively, it is called "Noble Truth" because, through his full awakening (*abhisambuddha*), the state of being noble (*ariyabhāva*) is established, and it is that which accomplishes the noble; thus, it is a "Truth of the Noble" (*ariyasacca*), with the middle term elided as before.

Or else, it is called "Noble Truth" because it is to be sought after (*araṇīya*) and attained due to its state of being non-false (*avitatha*); thus, it is a "Noble Truth. This is the meaning of "Truth" (*sacca*).
However, we shall later demonstrate all four truths together as a whole.
Now, in order to show that noble truth of suffering (dukkha-ariyasacca) according to its specific nature, he said, "Birth, too, is suffering," and so forth.
In this context, the word *jāti* has multiple meanings; for instance, in the passage "one birth, two births," it occurs in the sense of existence (*bhava*).
“In the Nikāyas, it is said: ‘Visākhā, there is a class of recluses called Nigaṇṭhas. In the context of the characteristics of the conditioned, it is said: ‘Birth is included within two aggregates.
In the context of rebirth-linking, it is said: ‘That first consciousness which arises and first manifests in the mother’s womb—taking that as its basis, this is his birth. [And: ‘Just born,’” etc.
In the phrase "O Ānanda, the Bodhisatta," [the term refers] to the birth. In the phrase "uncensured and unblamed regarding his birth-status," it refers to the family.

Here, however, for those born from a womb, it should be understood as referring to the aggregates (khandhas) that occur from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) until the emergence from the mother's womb;
for others, it refers only to the moment of rebirth-linking itself. And this too is merely a figurative explanation (pariyāyakathā).
In the ultimate sense (*nippariyāya*), however, birth is the first manifestation of those aggregates that appear for beings as they are reborn here and there.
Why, then, is this suffering? Because it serves as the basis for many kinds of suffering; for indeed, there are many sufferings.
That is to say: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, figurative suffering, and non-figurative suffering.
Therein, bodily and mental painful feelings are called "the suffering of suffering" because they are suffering both by their intrinsic nature and by name. Pleasant feeling...

Suffering due to change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*) is so called because it is the cause for the arising of suffering through transformation. The feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*) and the remaining formations (*saṅkhāra*) belonging to the three planes are suffering due to formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) because they are oppressed by arising and passing away.

Physical and mental afflictions such as earaches, toothaches, the fever born of lust, and the fever born of hatred are "concealed suffering" (*paṭicchannadukkha*), because they are to be known through inquiry and because the means [of their removal] are not manifest. [Suffering] originating from the thirty-two tortures of judicial punishment, etc.,...
Affliction (*ābādha*) is "unconcealed suffering" because it must be known even without being asked about, and because its manifestation is evident.

With the exception of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), all other suffering mentioned in the *Saccavibhaṅga*—such as birth and so forth—is "suffering by way of metaphor" (*pariyāyadukkha*), because each serves as the basis for its respective form of suffering. However, the suffering of suffering is "suffering in the primary sense" (*nippariyāyadukkha*).

It is said: "In this context, birth is 'suffering' because it serves as the basis for that suffering which was shown by the Blessed One in the *Bālapaṇḍita-sutta* and other discourses by way of simile—the suffering pertaining to the states of deprivation—and for that suffering which arises even in the happy destinies within the human world, beginning with the descent into the womb. Thus spoke the ancients:
“If a being were not to be born in the hells,
where there is the unbearable agony of fire and other such torments,
and if one were to experience suffering with no place of refuge anywhere— ”
Thus the Sage here has said that birth is suffering:
"In the animal realm, suffering is manifold,
consisting of being struck by whips, goads, sticks, and the like."
Whatever kind of birth there might be therein,
even without that birth, it is suffering.
Furthermore, among the departed (petas), there is the suffering of hunger and thirst.
Since the various [sufferings] arising from wind, heat,
and so forth do not exist for one who is unborn,
for that reason too the Sage declared birth to be suffering.
“In the blinding darkness and the unbearable cold,
and whatever suffering exists among the Asuras in the intermediate worlds—
that would not exist there for him, nor would there be birth.”
This birth is suffering even more than that:
"And just as a being dwells for a long time within the mother's womb like a pit of excrement, so too is it when emerging from there."
One encounters suffering that is most terrible;
yet even this does not exist without birth—for indeed, this birth itself is suffering.
What is the use of much speaking? Is it not true that wherever one goes...
"Is there here any suffering whatsoever at any time?
No, because of the absence of birth, O Great Seer.
Therefore, he spoke of 'birth' first of all as suffering."
Regarding the statement "aging, too, is suffering": here, aging is twofold—the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), which is recognized as decrepitude and so forth;
and the state of antiquity of the aggregates included within a single existence throughout the continuum (*santati*). It is this latter kind that is intended here.

Furthermore, this aging is suffering both because it is of the nature of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and because it is a basis for suffering. For it has many conditions, such as the loosening of limbs and members, the disfigurement resulting from the transformation of the sense faculties, the destruction of youth, the loss of vigor, the fading of mindfulness and intelligence, and being treated with contempt by others.
Bodily and mental suffering arises; aging is its basis. Thus the ancients said:
“Due to the loosening of the limbs, the transformation of the faculties, the destruction of youth, and the impairment of strength.”
“Because of being separated from one’s own children and wife,
and because it inspires little confidence, as well as for the sake of falling further into foolishness—
the bodily and mental suffering that a mortal undergoes— ”
"All this has aging as its cause; therefore, aging is suffering.
As for the phrase "sickness is also suffering," this passage does not appear in the *Vibhaṅga* within the text of the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca-niddesa*).
For that very reason, it was not cited even in the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering in the *Visuddhimagga*. It appears only in the text of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*.
However, since it is indeed found [in the texts], one must investigate the reason why this statement occurs here and not elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "death is suffering" (*maraṇam pi dukkham*), there too death is twofold:

the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) and that which is intended when it is said, "Old age and death are comprised within two aggregates. [The latter] is the severance of the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) included within a single existence.
And that which was said, referring to this: "There is constant fear of death," is what is intended here.
Its synonyms are death conditioned by birth, death by violence, death by one's own nature, death through the exhaustion of the life-span, and death through the exhaustion of merit.
This should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for suffering. Thus the ancients have said:
For one who contemplates the signs of evil, such as wicked deeds,
for one whose prosperity cannot withstand the loss of beloved objects,
and for one who is dying— the mental suffering that arises is, without distinction, the same.
“And whatever suffering born of the body there is for all those whose vital points (*marmans*) are being pierced—
such as the severing of joints and ligaments— that is unbearable and incurable; since this is the nature of such suffering, [one should reflect upon it].”
“Death is the basis for this; therefore it is called suffering.

And in this context, it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*, in the exposition of the Truth of Suffering: “Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are also suffering”; however, that [expression] is not found here, so the reason for this must be sought there as well.

Regarding “association with the unpleasant is suffering,” here “association with the unpleasant” means being brought together with disagreeable beings and formations. That too is suffering by way of being a basis for suffering. Thus said the ancients:
“Having seen the unpleasant, suffering first arises in the mind;
thereafter, it arises in the body through the application [of that mental state] here [in this world].
Therefore, regarding both types of suffering, their basis was taught by the Great Sage.”
“It should be understood that ‘meeting with those who are unpleasant’ is said to be suffering.

Regarding the statement “separation from those who are pleasant is suffering,” here “separation from the pleasant” means being parted from agreeable beings and formations. That too is suffering by way of being the basis for the suffering of sorrow. Thus said the ancients:
“From separation from relatives, wealth, and so forth;”
“Afflicted by the essence of grief,
fools are tormented from every side;
therefore, separation from the beloved is considered suffering.”

Regarding the phrase "not obtaining what one desires": here, in instances such as "O, that we were not subject to birth!", it is the very desire for unobtainable objects that is called "not obtaining what one desires" (*yampicchaṃ na labhati*). That too is suffering because it is a basis for suffering.
Thus the ancients said: "Because of the non-attainment of this or that, For those who long for this or that..."
“The suffering consisting of affliction that arises here for sentient beings—
The cause of that is the longing for things that cannot be obtained;
Therefore, the Victor declared that suffering is the non-attainment of what is desired.”
Regarding the statement, "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering": herein, because birth and the other [afflictions] oppress the pentad of the aggregates of clinging in various ways—
just as fire oppresses fuel, weapons a target, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like a herd of cattle, reapers a field, and village-robbers a village—
they do so upon the earth, just as grasses, creepers, and the like [oppress] the ground.
Just as flowers, fruits, and shoots arise upon trees, so too do they arise within the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) alone.
Furthermore, among these aggregates of clinging, birth is suffering at the beginning, aging is suffering in the middle, and death is suffering at the end;

and for those who encounter the frustration of their desires, there is the suffering of the failure of wishes, which is the non-attainment of what is desired. Thus, when examined in these various ways, it is only the aggregates of clinging that [constitute suffering].
Regarding "suffering": even if one were to describe each individual instance, it would be impossible to state them exhaustively even in many eons;

therefore, in order to show that all such suffering is condensed within any of the five aggregates of clinging—just as the taste of the water of the entire ocean is contained in a single drop of water—it is said: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging..."
“It is suffering,” the Blessed One said. Regarding this, the ancients have said:
“The suffering beginning with birth that was spoken of here by the Neutral One (Tādi), and that which was not spoken of—all that does not exist without these [two].”
“Therefore, for this reason, these aggregates of clinging have been briefly called ‘suffering’ by the Great Seer, the teacher of the end of suffering.
Having thus shown the truth of suffering according to its specific nature, he now shows the truth of the origin: “And furthermore, this—”

“Monks, this is the origin of suffering,” and so forth, he said. In that context, the word *saṃ* in *saṃyoga* (conjunction) indicates conjunction, as seen in such terms as *samāgama* (meeting) and *sameta* (united).
The syllable *u* in *uppatti* (arising) indicates arising, as seen in such terms as *uppanna* (arisen) and *udita* (risen). The word *aya*, however, indicates a cause.
And this second truth is the cause for the arising of suffering when there is the conjunction of the remaining conditions.
Because it is the cause for the arising of the conjunction with suffering, it is called "the origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*).
"That which is this craving" (*yāyaṃ taṇhā*) means that which is this craving. "Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobbhavikā*): "renewed existence" (*punabbhava*) is the making of renewed existence;

by the elision of the final member of the compound, it means "that whose nature is renewed existence. "Accompanied by the lust of delight" (*nandīrāgasahagatā*): accompanied by the lust of delight. This is what is meant.
It is called "accompanied by delight and lust" because it functions in all its states without abandoning the state of delight and lust, due to the nature of delighting and being attached.
"Delighting here and there" means that wherever a personal existence (*attabhāva*) is produced, there one delights.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; if one asks what its meaning is, it is this: "it is as follows. It is sixfold, divided into craving for form (*rūpa-taṇhā*) and so forth.
Craving is said to be threefold—namely, craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) and so forth—according to the different modes of its occurrence.

Indeed, when craving for form itself occurs by way of relishing a visible object that has come into the range of the eye through the gratification of sense-pleasures, it is then called "craving for sense-pleasures.
When that same object is regarded as permanent and eternal by means of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) occurring [in that manner], [it is called craving for existence].
When it occurs together with that [view], it is called craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). For lust accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is termed "craving for existence.

But when it occurs together with the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*)—which functions [thinking] that very same object is cut off or destroyed—it is then called craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
For lust accompanied by the annihilationist view is termed "craving for non-existence."
This is what is said. This same method applies to craving for sounds and so forth as well.
But why, in this context, is craving alone stated to be the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*)? Because it is the specific cause.

For ignorance, by concealing the danger in states of existence (*bhava*), causes craving—which is intent upon grasping at views and the like—to increase further and further in each respective instance.

Faults (*doṣa*) and so forth are also causes of karma; however, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), by desiring the diversity of various existences, modes of birth, destinies, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, classes of beings, families, enjoyments, sovereignty, and so on, becomes the decisive support for the diversity of karma and acts as its companion, thereby determining the diversity of existence and the rest.
Therefore, because it is a specific cause of suffering, [craving is the primary factor] even among others such as ignorance (*avidyā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and karma.

It should be understood that although other defilements, unwholesome roots, and so forth—which are causes of suffering—are mentioned in the Sutta and Abhidhamma, it is craving alone that is designated as the "truth of the origin.
Now, in order to show the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, he said: "But this, monks, is the cessation of suffering," and so forth.

In this context, since the word *ni-* signifies absence and the word *rodha* indicates confinement, it is called "the cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodha*) because there is an absence here of the confinement of suffering—known as saṃsāra—due to the emptiness of all states of existence;

or else, because when that [cessation] is attained, there is an absence of the confinement of suffering known as saṃsāra, owing to its being the direct opposite of that [suffering]. Thus it is "the cessation of suffering."
It is called "the cessation of suffering" because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering.
Now, one might ask: since the cessation of suffering is being shown here, why has the cessation of the origin—by way of the method beginning with "that very craving"—also been stated?
It is because the cessation of suffering occurs through the cessation of its origin, just as the subsiding of a disease occurs through the subsiding of its cause.
For indeed, with the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of the fruit; therefore, suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin, and not otherwise. Thus it was said:
"Just as a tree, though cut down, grows up once more If its root remains unharmed and firm;..."
"Even so, as long as the underlying tendency to craving has not been uprooted, this suffering arises again and again. Thus,
because suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin, the Blessed One, in order to demonstrate the cessation of suffering—

He taught by means of the cessation of the origin [of suffering]. For Tathāgatas conduct themselves like lions. When they bring suffering to an end and teach the cessation of suffering, they apply themselves to the cause, not to the fruit.

Just as a lion displays its own strength against the very arrow shot at itself, and not against the arrow itself, so too is the application of the Buddhas toward the cause, not toward the fruit. As for the sectarians...
But those who live like dogs— though they suppress suffering and teach the cessation of suffering—
they apply themselves toward the fruit through teachings such as the practice of self-mortification, rather than toward the cause. For just as dogs, when struck by someone with a clod of earth,
bark and eat the clod but do not rise up against the one who threw it, so too the followers of other sects, though desiring to suppress suffering, [apply themselves in this way].

They devote themselves to bodily exhaustion rather than to the cessation of the defilements; in this way, first, the purpose of the teaching should be understood by way of the origin and the cessation of suffering.
This, however, is the meaning here: "of that very craving" refers to that which was described as "leading to renewed existence," [namely] by way of sensual craving and so forth.

[It is] the analysis of craving. Dispassion (*virāga*) is called the Path. For it is said: "Through dispassion one is liberated. Cessation by means of dispassion is "cessation through dispassion" (*virāganirodha*);
because of the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), it is cessation without remainder, which is "cessation through dispassion without remainder" (*asesavirāganirodha*).
Alternatively, "dispassion" is said to mean abandoning; therefore, it is "abandoning without remainder" and "cessation without remainder" due to the uprooting of the underlying tendencies.
The application [of the terms] here should be understood in this way; however, in terms of meaning, all of these are synonyms for Nibbāna.
For in the ultimate sense, Nibbāna is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
Since craving both fades away and ceases by resorting to it, it is therefore called "fading away" (*virāga*) and "cessation" (*nirodha*). Since...

And it is precisely by resorting to that [renunciation] that one possesses such qualities as generosity; furthermore, among the bases of attachment such as the strands of sensual pleasure, not even a single base of attachment exists here.
Therefore, generosity is called relinquishment, liberation, and non-attachment.
Now, in order to show the Noble Truth of the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, [the Buddha said]: "But this, monks—"

"...the way leading to the cessation of suffering," and so forth. However, because this noble truth goes toward the cessation of suffering by virtue of its object—since it is directed toward that [cessation]—and because it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering, it is therefore called "the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
The rest here is exactly as previously explained. But what is this?

Is it the true nature (*saccaṭṭha*) of suffering and the other [truths]? That which, when examined with the eye of wisdom, is not like an illusion—deceptive—or like a mirage—misleading—and is not, as the self of the non-Buddhist sectarians (*tīrthika*) [is said to be], of an unfindable nature;

rather, by way of its being a reality that is authentic, non-erroneous, and factual, in the manner of affliction, origination, and the path of departure, it is indeed the objective domain of noble knowledge (*ariyañāṇa*). This is just like the characteristic of fire, which is the very nature of the world.
And the state of being unerring, non-perverted, and real, like that [fire], should be understood as the "true meaning" (*saccaṭṭha*). Herein, the characteristic of fire is heat.
For that is never, at any time, deceptive, perverted, or unreal with respect to the various kinds of fuel such as wood;
rather, it is the worldly nature of birth and so forth, as stated thus: "Subject to birth, subject to aging, and likewise subject to death."

They should be understood as follows: "The horizontal length of certain animals, the vertical height of humans and so forth, and the cessation of further growth once the state of full development has been reached"—such things are called the "natural laws of the world" (lokapakati).
Furthermore—
Since suffering is not oppressive by itself, and nothing other than suffering is oppressive,
it is considered a truth by virtue of its inherent quality of being oppressive.
Without that [truth], there is no suffering from any other source, nor does that [suffering] arise from anything else.
By the principle of the cause of suffering, thus is craving the truth.
There is no peace other than Nibbāna, and since that which is peaceful is not non-existent,
therefore, by the principle of the state of peace, this is considered the truth.
There is no other path that leads to liberation, nor is this one itself non-liberating;
because it possesses the state of being a true path, it is thus recognized as the Truth.
Thus, in all four [truths], there is the state of being real and free from perversion.
"The wise have declared the meaning of the truths without distinction regarding suffering and the rest.

(15) "In regard to things unheard of before" means: prior to this, in regard to the Dhamma of the Four Truths which had not been heard before—that is, which had not been heard in such terms as "This is suffering," and so forth.
"The eye," and so forth, are merely synonyms for knowledge (*ñāṇa*). For here, it is knowledge itself that is meant in the sense of seeing through direct perception.
It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing; "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing; "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the sense of discerning in its various modes;
"true knowledge" (*vijjā*) in the sense of penetration; and it is called "light" (*āloka*) in the sense of illumination because it dispels the darkness of delusion that conceals the truths.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this is described as being both mundane and supramundane with respect to the four truths.

16. *Yāvakīvañca* means for as long as. *Tiparivaṭṭaṃ* means "having three turnings" by way of the three turnings consisting of the knowledge of the truths (*sacca-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the tasks (*kicca-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of what has been done (*kata-ñāṇa*).

Indeed, this insight-knowledge (*ñāṇadassana*) is called "having three turnings" because it possesses these three turnings by way of the knowledge of the truths and so forth. And herein: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the origin of suffering..."
Thus, knowledge of the four truths as they truly are is called "knowledge of the truths" (sacca-ñāṇa).

Within those same truths, the knowledge that discerns the tasks to be performed—namely, "it must be fully understood, it must be abandoned, it must be realized, and it must be developed"—is called "knowledge of what is to be done" (kicca-ñāṇa).

The knowledge that discerns the state of having completed those tasks—namely, "it has been fully understood, it has been abandoned, it has been realized, and it has been developed"—is called "knowledge of what has been done" (kata-ñāṇa). This constitutes the twelve modes.

In each of those very truths, by way of three aspects each, there are twelve aspects. "Knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*) refers to the vision consisting of knowledge that has arisen by way of these twelve aspects of the three turnings.
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ*) refers to the perfect, self-awakening that is supreme, the best of all, and free from anything higher. Then...
Or the praised and beautiful Bodhi. Here, "Bodhi" is intended to mean the path of Arahatship of the Blessed One.
Is the path of Arahatship of the disciples the "unsurpassed Bodhi," or is it not? It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities.
For among them, the path of Arahatship for some bestows only the fruit of Arahatship; for some, the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā); for some...

[The Buddha] bestows the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), in some cases the four analytical knowledges (*catasso paṭisambhidā*), and in some cases the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).

He bestows upon the Paccekabuddhas only the knowledge of Pacceka-enlightenment (*paccekabodhiñāṇa*), but for the Buddhas, he bestows the attainment of all qualities (*sabbaguṇasampatti*), just as an anointing ceremony (*abhiseka*) confers upon a king the state of sovereignty over the entire world.
Therefore, no one else whatsoever possesses unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhi*). Thus, [he is called] "the Fully Enlightened One" (*Abhisambuddho*).
"I have directly known" means: "I have awakened; having attained and penetrated [the truth], I stand firm"—thus did I declare.
"And knowledge and vision arose in me" means: the reviewing-knowledge capable of seeing the qualities already attained as they truly are has arisen in me.
"My liberation is unshakable" means: this liberation of mine, which is the fruit of Arhatship, is unshakable by opposing factors.
"It is not to be shaken"—thus knowledge arose. In this regard, its unshakability should be understood in two ways:
by way of the cause, which is the Path, and by way of the object. For it is unshakable by way of the cause because the defilements, having been eradicated by the four paths, do not return;
and it is unshakable by way of the object because it proceeds having made Nibbāna—the unshakable state—its object. Thus, for those whose objects are unshakable...
Because of the absence of that [craving] in mundane attainments (*lokiya-samāpatti*). "Last" means final. "There is now no further becoming" means that now there is no further existence whatsoever.
And "in this exposition" means in this Sutta without verses (*niggāthaka-sutta*); for a Sutta without verses is one accompanied by questions and answers.
It is called "explanation" (*veyyākaraṇa*). "While being spoken" (*bhaññamāne*) means while being recited; the sense is "while being taught.

"Dustless" (*virajaṃ*) means dustless through the disappearance of the dust of passion and so forth that leads to rebirth in the states of misery. "Stainless" (*vītamalaṃ*) means stainless through the removal of the stains of all views and doubt;
or alternatively, it is dustless because of the absence of the dust of defilements to be abandoned by the first path, and stainless because of the removal of the fivefold stain of immoral conduct.
"Free from stain. Regarding the "Dhamma-eye": in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*, the three lower paths are mentioned;
in the *Cūḷa-Rāhulovāda*, it is the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*); but here, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is intended.

It is called the "Dhamma-eye" because it is an eye in the sense of seeing those phenomena (*dhamma*) comprised within the Four Noble Truths; or alternatively, among the three lower path-phenomena, it is one, namely that which is designated as the path of stream-entry.

“Eye” (*cakkhu*) means the eye of Dhamma (*dhammacakkhu*). It is called the eye of Dhamma because it is produced by the Dhamma of serenity and insight, or because it consists of the Dhamma of the threefold aggregate of virtue and so forth.

To show the manner of its arising, he said: “Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation. But is it not the case that path-knowledge has the unconditioned Dhamma as its object?

"Is it not an object consisting of conditioned phenomena? This is true; however, because it arises by taking cessation as its object and, through its functional mode, penetrates all conditioned things by way of non-delusive penetration, it is described in that way. 17.
Regarding "the Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*): both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching are called the "Wheel of Dhamma" in the sense of being a wheel of setting in motion.

Indeed, both the penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) consisting of twelve aspects that arose regarding the Four Truths while [the Buddha] was seated at the Bodhi throne, and the teaching-knowledge (*desanā-ñāṇa*) that set forth the teaching on the Truths with its twelve aspects while he was seated at Isipatana, are called the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
For both of these are simply the knowledge proceeding from the breast of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (*dasabala*). Both of them are contained within this teaching.

By the Blessed One proclaiming it, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been set in motion. However, that Wheel of Dhamma is said to be "set in motion" by the Blessed One only as long as the elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, is not yet established in the fruit of stream-entry;
this is because the function of setting it in motion remains uncompleted. Once [they] are established, it is considered "set in motion."
This refers to the period from the disappearance of the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa until the arising of a Buddha;

it is because [the Dhamma] was set in motion for the first time during this interval that it is said: "And when the Wheel of the Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One, the earth-dwelling deities raised a cry," and so forth.
In this context, *bhummā* means the deities dwelling on the earth. *Saddamanussāvesuṃ* means they proclaimed the sound.
Giving their approval all at once, they made the proclamation, saying, "This has been done by the Blessed One," and so forth.
"Radiance" (*obhāsa*) refers to the light produced by the power of the knowledge of omniscience, arising from the mind-conditioned temperature (*cittapaccayautu*).
For at that time, it shone forth, surpassing even the splendor of the gods. Regarding the exclamation, "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!"—this too [is an utterance of joy].
The sound of the proclamation spread throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system and remained there.
For just as at the commencement of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, so too at its completion, an exceedingly sublime joy and gladness arose in the Blessed One. 18.
"Diṭṭhadhammo" means that by him the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen; this same method applies to the remaining terms as well. And here—
Since there is another kind of "seeing" (dassana) apart from the seeing of knowledge (ñāṇadassana), the term "one who has attained the Dhamma" (pattadhammo) is stated in order to exclude that.

Since there is also another kind of "attainment" (patti) apart from the attainment of knowledge, the term "one who has understood the Dhamma" (viditadhammo) is stated for the purpose of distinguishing it from that.

However, since this state of having understood the Dhamma can occur even partially, the term "one who has fathomed the Dhamma" (pariyogāḷhadhammo) is used to show that the state of understanding is complete and without exception.

Thus it was said. This indicates his very realization of the truths. For path-knowledge, by accomplishing the tasks of full understanding and so forth through a single penetration (*ekābhisamaya*), is said to have "plunged all around" into the phenomena of the Four Truths without exception.

He is one who has "crossed over doubt" (*tiṇṇavicikiccho*) because he has crossed over the doubts based on the sixteen grounds and the eight grounds, which are like a perilous wilderness. Regarding the occurrence [of defilements] and so forth...
"Is it thus? Is it not thus?"—one for whom such occurring doubt has departed and been cut off is "one who has transcended doubt.

"Attained to self-confidence" means that because the evil states that cause timidity have been abandoned, and because one is well-established in the qualities of virtue and so forth which are their opposites, one has attained and reached a state of fearlessness and proficiency. This very state of being well-established through the attainment of self-confidence...
"Where? he asked; [the Buddha] replied, "In the Teacher’s Dispensation. Because he has attained it through his own direct experience, he does not rely on another;
he does not proceed here by means of another's faith, nor is there anyone else for him to rely upon—thus he is "one who relies on none other" (*aparappaccaya*).
"May I obtain" (*labheyyāhan*) means "may I obtain"; this is a word of supplication. "Come" (*ehi*) refers to those who have been supplicated for the going-forth and full ordination.
It is a statement that reveals the existence of what is consented to; therefore, the meaning is: "Come, accept the specific [stages] of going-forth and full ordination as requested.
The word *iti* indicates the conclusion of the statement regarding the cause for obtaining the *ehibhikkhu* (come, monk) ordination.
For his status as a monk is established by the end of that [statement]. Thus he said: "By the Blessed One’s words, ‘Come, monk,’ it was brought about..."
“This was that venerable one’s full ordination by the ‘Come, monk’ formula. “Practice the holy life” means: attain the holy life (brahmacariya) comprised of the three higher paths.
For what purpose? For the complete ending of suffering. Here too, the word “said” (avoca) should be connected [to the verb].
Regarding the phrase “nine thousand million,” etc., this refers to the many thousands of types of restraints and disciplines mentioned.
*Upasampadā* (full ordination) is the attainment of being superior and pre-eminent through the practice of having formally undertaken [the precepts]. 19.
*Nīhārabhatta*: "one whose meal is brought out"; the meaning is that the meal was brought out from the village as alms-food and given by the monks.
For the Blessed One, treating those monks like young children, [provided for them] starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*).
Without even entering the village for the sake of alms-food, he remained right within the monastery.
The commentary on the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Anattalakkhaṇa-sutta*.

20. "He addressed" means that on the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī, when the group of five beginning with Aññā-Koṇḍañña had gradually established themselves in the fruit of stream-entry since the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, he addressed them on the fifth day of the fortnight, thinking, "Now I shall teach the Dhamma for the destruction of their taints.
"Not-self" (anattā) means in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery and in the sense of having no owner.
It is non-self by way of emptiness and by way of the negation of a self; thus it is non-self for four reasons. Therein, there is no mastery on the part of anyone over the thought:
"Let arisen form not reach stability; let what has reached stability not decay; let what has reached decay not break up; let it not be wearied by rise and fall.
This is its meaning of being subject to lack of mastery (*avasavattanattha*). For one who has become a master...

The meaning of "absence" (*abhāva*) is the state of being ownerless. The meaning of "emptiness" (*suññata*) is emptiness from that [self] due to the absence of a dweller, a doer, an experiencer, and a controller.

The meaning of the "negation of self" (*attapaṭikkhepa*) is precisely the absence of the intrinsic nature of a self imagined by others. Now, in order to clarify non-selfhood (*anattatā*) itself, he said:
"And this form, monks... and so forth. Therein, "there would be a self" means: a doer, an experiencer, one who is his own master.
The intention is: "May the self become thus. For if this were so, the fact that form leads to affliction would be untenable.

Although here it appears as if the suffering nature of form due to its being non-self is being elucidated by the statement, "And because, monks, form is non-self, therefore form leads to affliction," nevertheless, [the text continues]: "Because form leads to affliction..."
“...it leads [to suffering], therefore it is non-self. By this, the absence of a core of self in form is made clear through its manifest liability to affliction.

And for that very reason, the lack of mastery over form and the manner in which one has no control over it are shown by the statement: “And one does not obtain regarding form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
21. "What do you think about that, monks?"—why was this begun?

It should be understood that up to this point only the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) has been explained, not the characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*) and suffering (*dukkha*). Now, having shown those [two] and bringing them together, this [question] was begun in order to show all three characteristics.
"It is impermanent, venerable sir" (*aniccaṃ bhante*): venerable sir, because having come to be, it does not remain.

Therefore, it is impermanent (*anicca*). Because it was previously non-existent, comes into being through the convergence of conditions, and then ceases to exist through its own dissolution, it is not permanent;
thus it is "impermanent" (*anicca*), meaning it is unstable—this is the intended sense. Alternatively, it is impermanent for these reasons as well:
because it possesses arising and passing away, because it is merely temporary, and because it is the very limit of transformation, which is the negation of permanence. Herein...

The state of having arising and passing away (uppādavayavantatā) results from its occurrence by way of arising and ceasing at every moment. Its temporariness (*tāvakālikatā*) follows from that momentariness.

Its limit of change (*vipariṇāmakoṭi*) follows from its state of being subject to transformation; for matter, undergoing transformation through the attainment of changes such as arising and so forth, reaches destruction.
The negation of permanence (*niccapaṭikkhepo*) is simply the absence of a permanent intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); for [all things] are indeed impermanent.
By their very nature of impermanence, these phenomena (dhammā) effectively reject permanence in terms of their actual meaning.

"Suffering, venerable sir" (dukkhaṃ bhante): it is suffering, venerable sir, by way of its mode of oppression. For matter (rūpa) constantly afflicts [the mind] through its arising, aging, and dissolution;
this is its state of suffering by way of its mode of oppression. Alternatively, it is suffering in the sense of burning (santāpa) and in the sense of being painful (dukkha).
Suffering (dukkha) is so called for four reasons: by way of being the basis for suffering, and by way of being the opposite of pleasure.

In this context, "torment" (santāpa) means the tormenting and burning [of beings] by way of the suffering of suffering (dukkhadukkhatā) and the other two types of suffering. Precisely because of that, it is characterized as suffering due to its difficult-to-bear nature.
It is the basis for suffering (dukkhavatthukatā) because it serves as the foundation for the three types of suffering and for the suffering of saṃsāra.
The absence of the intrinsic nature of pleasure is itself the negation of pleasure. "Subject to change" means having the nature of transformation through aging and death.
"Is it proper? means "is it fitting? "That" refers to form which is thus impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.

"This is mine" is the grasping of craving, because of its state as the "mine-making" (mamankāra). "I am this" is the grasping of conceit, because of its state as the "I-making" (ahaṅkāra). "This is my self" [is the grasping of views].
The "grasping at views" arises from the grasping at the perversion of selfhood (*attabhāva-vipallāsa*).
Furthermore, here the "grasping by craving" is to be understood by way of the one hundred and eight modes of craving’s movement; the "grasping by conceit," by way of the ninefold conceit;

and the "grasping by views," by way of the sixty-two views. What is meant by the question "Is that appropriate? is: "Is it appropriate [to hold such a view] by way of these three graspings—craving, conceit, and views?"
Thus the Blessed One demonstrated the characteristic of non-self precisely by way of impermanence and suffering.
For the Blessed One demonstrates selflessness in some instances by way of impermanence, in some by way of suffering, and in some by way of both. Thus, for example:
"If one were to say, 'The eye is the self,' that is not tenable; for the arising and the passing away of the eye are discerned. Of that which..."
Furthermore, both arising and passing away are perceived;
thus, the thought occurs to him, "My self arises and passes away," and therefore that [position] is untenable.
And in this *Chachakka Sutta*, he demonstrated non-selfhood by way of impermanence: "Bhikkhus, if this form were the self... [etc.]..."
In this very *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*, he demonstrated selflessness by way of suffering, saying:
"Monks, form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self;
what is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'"
In this *Arahattasutta*, [the Blessed One] demonstrated selflessness (*anattā*) by way of both [impermanence and suffering]. Why?
Because impermanence and suffering are manifest, whereas selflessness is not manifest. For when things such as utensils used for enjoyment are broken, people say, "Oh, how impermanent!
but there is no one who says, "Oh, how selfless! However, when boils or pustules arise on the body...
When pricked by a thorn, people say, "Oh, what suffering! but there is no one who says, "Oh, what non-self! Why is that?
For this characteristic of non-self is obscure, difficult to see, and hard to establish. Indeed, even teachers such as Sarabhaṅga and others did not perceive it;
how then could they have established it? Therefore, the Blessed One [taught it] by way of impermanence or by way of suffering.
Or he showed it by way of both. This has been shown here in this triple cycle specifically by way of impermanence and suffering.
The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
"Therefore, then" (*tasmātihā*) is simply said as "therefore" (*tasmā*). The syllables *ti* and *ha* are particles; because these five aggregates—
"Impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—this is the meaning of "therefore. "Whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is an expression that exhaustively includes everything without exception.

For "whatever" (*yaṃ*) indicates non-specification by way of generality, while "whatever" (*kiñci*) indicates non-specification by touching upon the various distinctions of its modes. By both terms together, [it refers to] whatever is past...
or near, whether little or much, or of such a kind or that kind, provided it is suitable for designation in the neuter gender.
It encompasses and includes everything; therefore, the expression "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is used to denote the inclusion of all things without exception.

This being the case, seeing that the same grammatical rule applies to other neuter nouns as well, and observing that [the term] occurs there by chance without intending this specific meaning, the word "matter" (*rūpa*) is stated in order to restrict the over-extension of the application. Thus, by these two words, [the definition of] matter—
The inclusion of everything without exception has been accomplished. Then he begins its classification into the past and so forth, starting with the words "past, future, and present," and so on.
For some [of these] are past, while others are distinguished as future and so on.

This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. In that regard, first, matter is called "past" in four ways: by way of extent (*addhā*), continuity (*santati*), period (*samaya*), and moment (*khaṇa*); likewise for the future and the present.
In this context, first, by way of duration (*addhā*): for a single being in a single existence, that which is prior to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is past;
that which is subsequent to death (*cuti*) is future; and that which lies between the two is present. By way of continuity (*santati*):

even while occurring in a sequence of prior and subsequent moments, that which is produced by a homogeneous temperature (*utu*) or produced by a homogeneous nutriment (*āhāra*) is present; that which is produced by heterogeneous temperature or nutriment prior to that is past.

The past is prior, and the future is subsequent. That which is mind-born—arising from a single cognitive series (*vīthi*), a single impulsion (*javana*), or a single attainment (*samāpatti*)—is present;
what precedes it is past, and what follows it is future. For that which is kamma-born, there is no distinction of past and so forth by way of a separate continuity (*santati*).
Rather, its status as past and so forth is determined by way of its support for those very [material phenomena] born of temperature, nutriment, and mind.

It should be understood as follows. By way of time (*samaya*), matter that exists within its respective time—such as one moment, forenoon, afternoon, night, or day—and which proceeds by way of continuity, is called "present. Prior to that is "past," and subsequent to it is "future.
By way of moment (*khaṇa*), that which is included within the three moments of arising and so forth is "present"; prior to that is "past," and [subsequent to that is] future.
"Later" refers to the future; this alone here is the literal sense, while the rest is figurative discourse.
"Either internally or externally": the fivefold form, beginning with the eye, is "internal" because it occurs in dependence upon the personal organism (*attabhāva*);
the remainder is "external" because it is outside of that. Furthermore, here "internal" also includes one's own internal [sense bases].
And it should be understood that even what belongs to another person is "external. As for "whether gross or subtle":
the twelve kinds of material form—namely, the nine beginning with the eye and the three elements excluding the water element—are "gross" because they are to be apprehended by way of impingement;
the remainder is "subtle" because it is the opposite of that. Regarding "whether inferior or superior," here the state of being inferior or superior is figurative.
And [this is so] from the non-figurative standpoint (*nippariyāyato*). In this regard, the form of the Sudassī devas is inferior to the form of the Akaniṭṭha devas;

that same [form] is superior to the form of the Sudassa devas. Thus, up to the forms of beings in the hells, the state of being inferior or superior should be understood from the figurative standpoint.
However, from the non-figurative standpoint, whatever object one takes as a basis for the arising of unwholesome resultant consciousness (*akusalavipākaviññāṇa*) is inferior.
Because of its undesirable nature. However, that object which, being taken as an objective support, gives rise to wholesome resultant consciousness, is excellent because of its desirable nature.

For just as unwholesome resultant [consciousness] is itself undesirable and arises only with respect to what is undesirable, not what is desirable, so too wholesome resultant [consciousness], being itself desirable, arises only with respect to what is desirable, not what is undesirable. Whether it be far or near...
That which is subtle is "far" because its nature is difficult to penetrate; the other is "near" because its nature is easy to penetrate.
Furthermore, in this context, distance and proximity should also be understood as relative to their respective locations.
"All that" refers to all material form (rūpa) previously specified by the terms "past" and so forth. "Should be seen with right wisdom" means together with insight (vipassanā).
It is to be seen by means of the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*).

Furthermore, in such passages as "whatever feeling," etc., the past, future, and present states of feeling are to be understood both in terms of continuity (*santati*) and in terms of moments (*khaṇa*).

Therein, in terms of continuity, [feelings] comprised within a single cognitive process (*vīthi*), a single impulsion (*javana*), or a single attainment (*samāpatti*), arise through conjunction with a single type of object.
And for one who sees the form of the Buddha and hears the Dhamma even during the day, the feelings accompanied by active faith and so forth are present;
those prior to that are past, and those subsequent are future. By way of moment, those included within the three moments are present;
those prior to that are past, and those subsequent are future. The distinction between internal and external is according to what is "one's own" (*niyakajjhatta*).

It should be understood according to the classification of the gross and the subtle. This is to be understood by way of genus, intrinsic nature, person, mundane, and supramundane, as stated in the *Vibhaṅga* in such passages as: "Unwholesome feeling is gross; wholesome and indeterminate feeling is subtle.
First, by way of genus: unwholesome feeling has an unpeaceful mode of existence because it is the cause of reprehensible activity and because its intrinsic nature is the torment of the defilements.

Wholesome feeling is gross compared to unwholesome feeling because it involves active engagement, exertion, and result, and because its nature is the burning of the defilements and it is accompanied by blame.
It is gross compared to resultant-indeterminate feeling because it involves result and its nature is the burning of the defilements, and because it is accompanied by malice and is blameworthy.
Furthermore, wholesome and indeterminate feelings are gross compared to unwholesome feeling by way of the reverse of what has been stated.

Subtle. Both types of feeling—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are gross, as the case may be, compared to the two kinds of indeterminate (abyākata) feeling, because they involve active engagement, exertion, and result.
Conversely, both kinds of indeterminate feeling are subtle in comparison to those.
Thus, first of all, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of their intrinsic nature (jāti).

By way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), however, painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*) is grosser than the other two because of its lack of relish, its expansive impact, its capacity to cause agitation, and its overwhelming force;
the other two, moreover, are subtle compared to the painful feeling, respectively, because they are pleasant, peaceful, sublime, agreeable, and neutral.
Both pleasure and pain, however, are coarse due to their expansive impact and their capacity to cause disturbance.

In terms of manifestation, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is gross; by the reverse of what was stated, that same feeling is subtle compared to both [painful and pleasant feelings]. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of intrinsic nature.

By way of person, however, the feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross because it is distracted by various objects, whereas the feeling of one who has attained absorption is subtle; the opposite applies to the other.
Thus, the grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of the individual. However, by way of the mundane and the supramundane, feeling associated with the taints (*āsava*) is mundane.

Because it is a cause for the arising of taints, and because it is subject to the floods (*ogha*), the yokes (*yoga*), the ties (*gantha*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the clingings (*upādāna*), and the defilements (*saṃkilesika*), as well as being common to worldlings (*puthujjana*), it is gross compared to that which is free from taints; the latter is [subtle] by way of the opposite.
[The latter] are subtle when associated with the taints (*āsava*). Thus, the grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of the mundane and supramundane.
In this context, confusion regarding their classification (*jāti*) and so forth must be avoided.

For feeling associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, although it is subtle because it is indeterminate (*abyākata*) by way of its genus (*jāti*), it is nevertheless gross by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and other such factors. For this has been said:
“Indeterminate feeling is subtle; painful feeling is gross. Feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross; feeling that is subject to taints is gross.
Just as with painful feeling, so too pleasant feeling and the others are gross by way of their birth, but subtle by way of their intrinsic nature and so forth.
Therefore, the grossness and subtlety of feelings are established in such a way that there is no confusion regarding their classification by birth and the other criteria.
They are to be understood as follows: by way of birth, the indeterminate states are subtler than the wholesome and unwholesome.

Therein, one should not investigate distinctions such as their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) by asking: "Which are the indeterminate? Which are painful? Which are pleasant? Which belong to one who has attained meditative absorption? Which belong to one who has not attained it?
Which are with taints (sāsava)? Which are without taints (anāsava)? This same method applies everywhere.

Furthermore, according to the statement, “In each case, feeling should be regarded as gross or subtle relative to [other] feelings,” even among unwholesome states and the like, feeling accompanied by greed is gross because it burns its own support like fire, whereas that accompanied by greed is subtle.

Feeling accompanied by hatred is also gross when it is of fixed result (*niyata*), and subtle when it is of unfixed result (*aniyata*). Even when of fixed result, [it is gross or subtle depending on the degree of intensity].
Those lasting for an eon (*kappaṭṭhitika*) are gross; the others are subtle. Even among those lasting for an eon, the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) are gross, while the others are subtle.
Furthermore, those accompanied by greed and associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) are gross, while the others are subtle.
Among those, the fixed (*niyata*), eon-lasting, and unprompted are gross, while the others are subtle. Generally speaking, unwholesome states that have abundant fruition are gross.
Those with little result are subtle. However, wholesome states with little result are coarse, while those with much result are subtle.
Furthermore, sense-sphere wholesome states are coarse, fine-sphere states are subtle, those of the formless sphere are subtler than those, and supramundane states are subtler still.

Within the sense sphere, states consisting of giving are coarse, those consisting of virtue are subtle, and those consisting of meditation are subtler than those. As for those consisting of meditation...
Those with two roots are gross; those with three roots are subtle. Among those with three roots, those that are prompted are gross, while those that are unprompted are subtle.
In the fine-material sphere, those associated with the first jhāna are gross … [and so on] … those associated with the fifth jhāna are subtle.
In the immaterial sphere, those associated with the base of infinite space are gross … [and so on] … those associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are subtle.
Furthermore, supramundane feelings associated with the path of stream-entry are gross... [and so on] ...up to those associated with the path of Arahantship, which are subtle.

This same method applies to resultant and functional feelings of each respective plane, and to the feelings described by way of being painful and so forth, non-attained and so forth, and with taints and so forth.
By way of location as well: in hell, painful feeling is gross; in the animal realm, it is subtle... [and so on] ...up to the Paranimmitavasavatti [devas].
Subtle. And just as with the painful, so too should the pleasant be applied everywhere as appropriate.
Furthermore, by way of basis, any feeling based on an inferior basis is gross, while that based on a superior basis is subtle.
Among the division of inferior and superior, that which is gross should be understood as inferior, and that which is subtle as superior. As for the word "distant," it refers to the unwholesome.
Feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings; unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling—thus it is analyzed by way of such passages as "the state of proximity.
Therefore, unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings by virtue of being dissimilar, unassociated, and unlike;
likewise, wholesome and indeterminate feelings are distant from the unwholesome. This same method applies to all sections. Unwholesome...

Furthermore, feeling is proximate to the unwholesome by way of its commonality, its association, and its similarity. It should be understood that this is likewise the case for perception and the other mental factors associated with each respective feeling.
23. "Learned" (sutavā) means one who possesses great learning, which consists of both scriptural knowledge and realization. "Becomes disenchanted" (nibbindati) means...
He becomes weary. And here, "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) is intended as insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*). "Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate":

here, the four paths are spoken of by way of dispassion (*virāga*). "Through dispassion, he is liberated": by means of the path characterized by dispassion acting as the cause, he is liberated by way of liberation through subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*).
By this, the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are spoken of. When there is liberation...
By the phrase "the knowledge that it is liberated," the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) is explained.
By the words "birth is destroyed" and so forth, its ground is indicated; for by means of that knowledge, the noble disciple, while reviewing, understands:
"Birth is destroyed," and so on. But what birth of his is destroyed, and how does he understand it? First of all, his past birth was already destroyed long ago.
Because they have been exhausted; they are not future because there is no effort toward the future, nor are they present.

However, that birth—which, due to the non-cultivation of the Path, would arise in one, four, or five-aggregate existences as a distinction of one, four, or five aggregates—is exhausted by the fact that it has reached the state of non-arising through the cultivation of the Path.
Thus, he [the practitioner], by means of the cultivation of the Path, regarding the defilements abandoned...
Having reflected, one understands that even though karma exists when defilements are absent, it will not lead to rebirth in the future.
"Lived" (*vusita*) means lived, fully lived; the meaning is that it has been performed, practiced, and brought to completion. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Path.
For the seven types of trainees, together with the virtuous worldling, are said to be "living" the holy life of the Path, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed—
Having completed the residence [in the training], the noble disciple, reviewing his own life of purity (*brahmacariya*), understands: "The life of purity has been lived.

"What was to be done has been done" means that the sixteenfold task—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing, with respect to the four truths and the four paths—has been brought to completion.
For even those such as the virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) [have not yet finished] that task.
...they perform [it], having exhausted the taints and done what was to be done. Therefore, when a noble disciple reviews his own task, he understands:

"What was to be done has been done. He understands: "There is nothing further for this state"—that is, for this present condition characterized by these sixteen duties, or for the exhaustion of the defilements;
there is no further task for him regarding the cultivation of the path. Alternatively, "for this state" (*itthattāya*) means for this very condition.
He understands: "From this present continuity of aggregates of such a kind, there is no further continuity of aggregates for me;
these five aggregates, however, remain with their roots cut, like trees that have been fully understood.
With the cessation of final consciousness, they will go out like a fire without fuel."
24. With delighted minds, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Those bhikkhus, being well-disposed and satisfied in mind, or with minds fully filled with rapture and joy, [listened] to the speech of the Blessed One as he spoke with a Brahma-voice—sweet as the song of the karavīka bird, pleasant to the ear, like a consecration of nectar to the hearts of the wise—which was well-spoken and well-delivered.
“Even so it is, Blessed One; even so it is, Sugata. This means that by receiving [the words] with their heads, they both expressed approval and accepted them.
For this word *abhinanda* occurs in the sense of craving in such passages as “he delights in, he speaks out for”;
and it also occurs in the sense of approaching in such passages as “Both gods and humans delight in food alone.”
In such passages as, “Relatives, friends, and dear ones rejoice at the arrival of a man who has lived abroad for a long time and has returned safely from afar,” it refers to welcoming.
In such passages as, “Having rejoiced and having expressed appreciation,” it refers to appreciation. And here, it refers to both appreciation and welcoming.
This is appropriate. Therefore it was said: “They both rejoiced and accepted.

“Their minds were liberated from the taints through non-clinging” means that as the taints were ceasing by way of non-arising and cessation, their minds were liberated without clinging—that is, without grasping at any phenomenon as “I” or “mine.
“Six Arahants”: together with the Blessed One, there were six.

"Persons" refers to *arahants*. However, since it is possible for others—even gods and *brahmās*—to attain *arahantship*, he said, "six persons are *arahants*," intending this specifically to refer to human *arahants*.
The commentary on the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* is concluded.
The Discourse on the Group-of-Five is finished.

Now, in order to show the going-forth of Yasa, the passage beginning with “At that time” is commenced. Herein, this [is the commentary]: 25. Commentary on the Discourse on the Going-forth of Yasa: Now, at that time... (and so forth). Therein, this [is the explanation].
An Explanation of the Non-Obscure Terms: Regarding "hemantika" and so forth, that which is pleasant to dwell in during the winter season is "hemantika.
The same method applies to the others as well. Herein, this is the etymological meaning: dwelling in winter is "hemanta";

by dropping the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*), it becomes "hemantika," meaning "that which deserves the winter. The same method applies to the others as well. Among those, "vassika" [is explained as follows]:...

The palace is neither too high nor too low; its doors and windows are neither too numerous nor too narrow. Here, a mixture of floor coverings, rugs, and various kinds of food—both solid and soft—is permitted.
During the winter, the pillars and walls are low, while the doors and windows are narrow with fine lattices;
wall-protrusions are used for the purpose of admitting warmth, and there are floor coverings, rugs, undergarments, and upper robes.
In this [autumn] season, warm items such as woolen blankets are appropriate, as are foods that are oily and seasoned with pungent spices.
In the summer, the pillars and walls are high, while the doors and windows are numerous and spacious;
cool-spreading floor coverings made of fine linen (dukūla) are suitable, and the foods and drinks should be sweet-tasting and cooling.
And here, having placed new troughs near the wind-towers, they fill them with water and cover them with blue lotuses and other flowers;
in various places they create water-channels from which streams of water gush forth as if when the devas are raining.
"Nippurisehi" means devoid of men. And here, it is not only the musical instruments that are devoid of men, but all the locations as well.
There were only women. Even the gatekeepers were women, and even those who performed services such as bathing were women. It is said that the father appointed only women to all duties, thinking:
"If a man is seen enjoying such a state of sovereignty, power, and prosperity, suspicion will arise;
may that not happen to my son. [He provided him] with the five strands of sensual pleasure.

By means of the five divisions of sensual pleasure, namely visible forms, sounds, and so forth. "Of one who is endowed" (*samappitassa*) means of one who is properly provided with them; "of one who has approached" (*upetassa*) is the meaning.
"Of one who has become possessed of" (*samaṅgībhūtassa*) is a synonym for that same term. "Of one who is enjoying" (*paricārayamānassa*) means of one who is moving about completely;
the meaning is of one who is directing the sense faculties toward each respective quality of sensual pleasure. "Āḷambaram" refers to a small drum (*paṇava*). "Vikesikam" [refers to...]
"Muttakesaṃ" means with disheveled hair; "vikkheḷikaṃ" means with saliva trickling down. "Vippalapantiyo" means either speaking incoherently or weeping.
"Susānaṃ maññe" (I thought it was a cemetery) is connected as: he saw his own retinue as if they were in a raw-flesh cemetery.
"Udānaṃ udānesi" means he uttered an inspired utterance out of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); that which proceeds from a sense of spiritual urgency.
The meaning is: "He utters speech. 26.
"This indeed, Yasa," the Blessed One said, referring to Nibbāna; for that is neither afflicted nor oppressed by the defilements such as craving.
"Graduated discourse" means: after giving comes virtue, after virtue comes heaven, and after heaven—
They investigate in this manner according to the sequential order. Therein, "discourse on giving" means:
"This so-called giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, the foundation of wealth; for one who has fallen into adversity, it is a refuge, a shelter, a resort, and a supreme goal.
In both this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, object, refuge, shelter, resort, or supreme goal equal to giving. For this..."

In the sense of providing shelter, it is like a lion-throne made of jewels; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth; in the sense of being an object, it is like a supporting rope.
For this [Dhamma] is like a ship in the sense of crossing over suffering; it is like a hero in battle in the sense of providing consolation;
it is like a well-constructed city in the sense of protection from fear; and it is like a lotus in the sense of being unstained by the impurity of stinginess and the like.
In the sense of consuming them, they are like fire; in the sense of being difficult to approach, they are like a venomous snake;

in the sense of not causing terror, they are like a lion; in the sense of possessing strength, they are like an elephant; in the sense of being esteemed as highly auspicious, they are like a white bull;

and in the sense of leading to the attainment of the land of safety, they are like Valāhaka, the king of horses. This gift is indeed the path traveled by me; this is my own lineage, [practiced] by me while fulfilling the ten perfections.

Many great sacrifices were performed—the Velāma Great Sacrifice, the Mahāgovinda Great Sacrifice, the Mahāsudassana Great Sacrifice, and the Vessantara Great Sacrifice. By offering himself into a blazing mass of fire when he had become a deer, he captured the hearts of the supplicants who had arrived.
For in this world, giving bestows the attainment of Sakka, the attainment of Māra, the attainment of Brahmā, and the attainment of a Wheel-turning Monarch.

“...it bestows the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection, the knowledge of individual enlightenment, and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment”—such was the discourse connected with the virtues of giving.
However, because one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*), he spoke on the discourse of moral discipline immediately thereafter.
For what is called “giving” consists of [bestowing] one’s own possessions upon those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*) with an intention for their welfare or an intention for their honor.
Relinquishment; therefore, a person who gives is one whose aspiration is solely for the welfare of beings, and it is impossible that such a person would take what belongs to others.
Thus, because one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*), moral discipline is taught immediately after generosity.
Furthermore, the discourse on generosity is easy to practice and is common to all people, as it occurs even among the masses.
And because it serves as the means for establishing oneself in virtue (*sīla*), it is taught first.
For a person whose nature is generosity (*pariccāga-sīla*) easily undertakes the precepts due to their lack of attachment toward possessions and becomes well-established therein.

Having spoken of benefiting others through virtue by way of the purification of both giver and recipient, [the text] speaks of the duty of action (*kiriyadhamma*) by way of desisting from harming others.

Having spoken thus, and having explained the cause for the attainment of wealth and fame by means of discourse on non-action, as well as the cause for the attainment of existence by means of discourse on action, the discourse on virtue was taught immediately after the discourse on giving. As for the discourse on virtue, it is said:
"Virtue indeed is a support, a foundation, an object of focus, a refuge, a shelter, a destination, and a final resort."

This virtue is indeed my lineage. During the time of the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, during the time of the Naga King Bhūridatta, during the time of the Naga King Campeyya, during the time of the Naga King Sīlavā, during the time of the Elephant King Mātuposaka, and during the time of the Elephant King Chaddanta—in these and countless other existences—I fulfilled virtue.
For in this world and the world beyond, there is no refuge like virtue, and no foundation like virtue.
“There is no refuge, no shelter, no resort, no final goal; there is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue.

Indeed, even the world with its devas never tires of beholding one who is adorned with the ornament of virtue, bedecked with the blossoms of virtue, and anointed with the perfume of virtue. Such is the discourse associated with the qualities of virtue.
However, he spoke on the topic of heaven immediately after that of virtue in order to show that this heaven is obtained by relying upon this virtue.
As for the "discourse on heaven," it means: "This so-called heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; here there is constant play and constant attainment of prosperity.
The gods of the Four Great Kings enjoy divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years."
“They attain [it] for thirty-three koṭis and six hundred thousand years”—such is discourse connected with the qualities of heaven.
Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas never tire of speaking of the excellence of heaven. And this has been said:
“In many ways, monks, I could speak on the topic of heaven,” and so forth.
