Having thus enticed him with talk of heaven, he then decorated an elephant and, as if cutting off its trunk, spoke in the manner beginning with, "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair;
the danger therein is greater," in order to show that even this heaven is impermanent and unstable, and that no desire or passion should be placed in it.
Thus he described the danger of sensual pleasures.

He spoke of defilement (*saṃkilesa*). In this context, "disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) means fault; the meaning is the state of being corrupted by impermanence and so forth, and by the lack of gratification and so forth.
Alternatively, it is called *ādīnava* because it flows toward (*vāti*) what is base (*ādi*); that is, extreme wretchedness.
And thus, for those who contemplate sensual pleasures as they really are, these [disadvantages] present themselves. "Base" (*oka*) refers to the state of being inferior or lowly.
The fact that they are to be pursued by the ignoble and not pursued by the noble. "Corruption" (saṃkileso) means the defiling of beings by them;
the sense is that they are to be harassed and tormented.
Having thus threatened [beings] with the danger of sensual pleasures, he revealed the benefit in renunciation. And however many dangers there are in sensual pleasures—

The benefits of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) are exactly as many as its opposites. Furthermore, he proclaimed the benefits of renunciation in such a manner as: "This renunciation is unconfined and undefiled;

it has gone forth from sensual desires, gone forth from the perception of sensual desire, gone forth from thoughts of sensual desire, gone forth from the fever of sensual desire, and gone forth from ill-will," and so on.
[He likewise proclaimed them] regarding the benefits of going forth (*pabbajjā*), the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), and so forth.

And he analyzed and extolled its virtues. Here, after describing heaven, the Path must be described immediately following heaven in order to show that while this heaven is defiled by lust and other such factors, the Noble Path is entirely undefiled.
And when describing the Path, one must describe the means for its attainment, starting first with those things included within heaven, let alone others.
The danger of sensual pleasures (*kāma*) is that all sensual pleasures indeed have many disadvantages, are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change;
their degradation and lowliness is that they are base, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
the defilement therein is that all states of existence (*bhava*) serve as the basis for the defilements; and Nibbāna is that which is completely free from all defilements.
"The benefit of renunciation should be told" means that the danger, degradation, and corruption found in sensual pleasures, as well as the benefit of renunciation, should be made manifest;
this is how it should be understood.
"A ready mind" refers to a pliant mind, [freed] from the mental defects such as lack of faith and so forth that occurred during the preceding teaching.
The meaning is that it is a "workable mind" (*kammakkhamacitta*) because, through the removal [of defilements], it has become a fit vessel for the higher teaching.

Alternatively, since lack of faith and so forth are like diseases of the mind, and these have then departed from it, the meaning is that it is a "ready mind" (*kallacitta*), a "healthy mind" (*arogacitta*).

Through the disappearance of defilements such as wrong view and conceit, it is a "pliable mind" (*muducitta*); through the disappearance of sensual desire and so forth, it is an "unobstructed mind" (*vinīvaraṇacitta*); and through right practice—
With a mind uplifted through the application of sublime rapture and gladness. In this context, the connection is: "when the Blessed One knew that his mind was serene" due to the perfection of faith.
Alternatively, "with a pliant mind" means a healthy mind through the departure of sensual desire;

"with a malleable mind" means a non-rigid mind through the departure of ill-will by way of loving-kindness; "with a mind free from hindrances" means [free] through the departure of restlessness and remorse.
"Because of the absence of distraction, his mind is not obstructed by that. "Exalted mind" means a mind that is not dejected due to the departure of sloth and torpor, by way of being uplifted.
"Serene mind" means a mind intent upon right practice due to the departure of doubt;
this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Self-exalting" (*sāmukkaṃsikā*) means self-lifting up (*sāmaṃ ukkaṃsikā*), having raised oneself up by one's own effort.
"Seized" means seen by self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) as not shared with others; this is the meaning. And what is that? It is the teaching of the Noble Truths. For this very reason he said:
"Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
With the words "Just as if," etc., he demonstrates through a simile both his abandonment of the defilements and the arising of the Noble Path. "With the black parts removed" means...
"Free from blackness. "Properly indeed" (*sammadeva*) means "thoroughly. "Dye" (*rajanam*) refers to the various colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
"One would take up" (*paṭiggaṇheyya*) means one would grasp it; it would become radiant. "In that very seat" (*tasmiṃyeva āsane*) means in that very sitting posture.

By this, his state of being a swift practitioner of insight (*lahuvipassaka*), his possession of sharp wisdom (*tikkhapaññatā*), and his state of easy practice and quick direct knowledge (*sukhapatipada-khippābhiññatā*) are demonstrated. "Stainless," etc. (*virajam-ādī*).
It is exactly as described above. Herein, this is the correlation with the simile: the cloth is like the mind;

the state of the cloth being soiled by adventitious stains is like the state of the mind being defiled by the stains of lust and so forth; the washing stone is like the progressive discourse (anupubbikathā);
and the water is like faith. By repeatedly moistening [the cloth] with water and then treating the dark spots with alkaline substances such as ash, cow-dung, chaff, and lye...

Just as the process of washing a cloth involves moistening it repeatedly with the moisture of faith (*saddhā-sineha*), so too, having softened the defects through mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, one exerts energy (*vīriyārambha*) in purifying the mind by means of the methods of virtue, learning, and so forth.

By that application, the suppression of defilements (*kilesa-vikkhambhana*) through the exertion of energy is like the removal of black stains from the cloth; the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is like the dye itself.
Just as a clean cloth possesses a radiant quality, so too the mind, from which the defilements have been suppressed, is purified by the Path.
27. *Assadūte*: messengers mounted on horses. *Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ*: an exercise of psychic power (*iddhi*).
*Abhisaṅkharesi*: he performed; the meaning is that he did it. If one asks for what purpose: for the sake of preventing any obstacle to the specific excellence to be obtained by both of them.
For if he had seen his son, there would have been neither the attainment of Arahantship by the son nor the acquisition of the Dhamma-eye by the merchant.
Indeed, how could one who has not yet seen the Truths, while pleading, "Give back my mother's life," avoid distraction and,
following the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, direct his knowledge and acquire the Dhamma-eye?
And how, when entreated in this way by Yasa, could he have dispelled that distraction and established himself in Arahatship?

He spoke these words—“Excellent, Bhante,” and so forth—in order to express his deep appreciation for the Blessed One’s teaching. Here, the word *abhikkanta* signifies rejoicing; therefore, it means “Well said, well said, Bhante! [As the verse says:
“In fear, in anger, in praise, in haste, in curiosity, or in joy;”
"A wise person should utter a reduplication (*āmeḍita*) in cases of laughter, sorrow, and confidence.
By this very characteristic, it should be understood that here [the word] is stated twice, by way of confidence and by way of praise.
With the words "Just as if," etc., he praises the Blessed One’s teaching by means of four similes. Therein, "overturned" (*nikkujjitaṃ*)...
"Placed face down" means turned with the face toward the ground. "Should turn it over" means one should make it face upward.
"Covered" means concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth. "Should uncover" means one should remove [the covering]. "Of one who is lost" means of one who has lost his sense of direction.
"Should point out the way" means taking him by the hand, one should say, "This is the way. "In the darkness" means at midnight on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
[The darkness] was like a dense forest thicket or a mass of clouds.
Having thus praised the teaching, and while manifesting his faith in the Triple Gem through this teaching with a mind full of confidence, he said, “Esāhaṃ,” and so forth.
Therein, “Esāhaṃ” means “this I am. “Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretū” means “May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka).”
“Let him be remembered as ‘this is a lay follower’”—the meaning is that he should know [this]. Regarding the term *ajjatagge*: here the word *agga* (top/first) has the sense of “beginning”;
therefore, *ajjatagge* should be understood to mean “starting from today. *Ajjataṃ* means the state of being today. Alternatively, there is the reading *ajjadagge*;
the letter *da* is for the purpose of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*), and the meaning is “making today the beginning. *Pāṇupetaṃ*...
Endowed with life. As long as my life continues, for that long I am endowed [with it].

May the Blessed One accept and recognize me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, who has no other teacher, and who acts as a provider of what is permissible (*kappiyakāraka*).
For even if someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, "He is not the Buddha," nor of the Dhamma, "It is not the Dhamma."
Or, one might say of the Saṅgha, "It is not the Saṅgha. It was in this way, by surrendering himself, that he went for refuge.

Thus, the meaning of the words beginning with "Excellent" (*abhikkanta*) should be understood as not yet fully explained; however, the detailed exposition has already been given in the commentary on the Verañjā Chapter below, and therefore it is not shown here.
28. “While reviewing the ground” means while reviewing the matter he himself had seen.
“He quelled the exercise of psychic power” means he made a resolution such that the householder Seṭṭhi would see the young man Yasa even while sitting right there.
“May he consent” means may he accept. “For today” means [that which is] from you... for me today.
"To one who offers hospitality today there will be merit as well as joy and gladness; it is for that purpose. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent:
this means that without moving either his body or his speech, the Blessed One consented through silence, manifesting acceptance within himself;
it is said that he accepted with his mind alone for the sake of favoring the merchant.

“Come, monk,” the Blessed One said; for it is said that, observing the supporting conditions for his supernaturally produced bowl and robes, and seeing in many previous births his giving of the eight requisites beginning with robes, he said, “Come, monk.
At that very moment, he became shaven-headed, clad in saffron robes, with the eight requisites of a monk already fastened upon his body, appearing like an elder of sixty years standing.

He sat down as if paying homage to the Blessed One. For whoever, having given the eight requisites such as robes—or even just the bowl and robe—to a noble one who has attained the stream-entry and so forth, or even to an ordinary person endowed with virtue, makes this aspiration:
"May this gift of requisites be a condition for the state of being an 'Ehi-bhikkhu' (Come, monk! in the future," then, provided that his merit is perfected, that aspiration will bear fruit.
It should be understood that this leads to the acquisition of supernormal requisites in the presence of the Buddhas. 29.

"With excellent" means with the highest. "With one's own hand" means with one's own hand. "Having satisfied" means having thoroughly satisfied, having made them full, well-fed, and as much as they required.
"Having invited to eat" means having properly invited, [saying] "Enough, enough," by means of a hand gesture.

Having had [him] cause [it] to be refused. "One who has finished eating" (*bhuttāvī*) means one who has eaten. "One who has removed his hand from the bowl" (*onītapattapāṇi*) means one whose hand has been removed from the bowl;
it is said to mean "one whose hand has been taken away. There is also the reading "onittapattapāṇi"; its meaning is: *onitta* means become separate, become apart;
if the bowl is separated from the hand, he is "one whose hand is separated from the bowl" (*onittapattapāṇi*). That is "one whose hand is separated from the bowl," and [regarding] the hand...
The meaning is that they washed their bowls, set them aside to one side, and sat down.
"They sat down to one side" means that, having recognized the Blessed One in such a state, they sat down in a certain place. Regarding the phrase "with a discourse on the Dhamma," and so forth:
having demonstrated the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life with a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate to that moment, [he established them] in what is wholesome.
Having exhorted him to the Dhamma, having incited him toward it and filled him with enthusiasm,
and having gladdened him by that enthusiasm as well as by his other existing virtues, he rained down the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma and, rising from his seat, departed.
The commentary on the account of Yasa’s going forth is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Going-forth of the Four Companions (Catugihisahāyapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā) 30.
Now, showing the going-forth of his companions, he said, "They heard," and so forth. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained:
*seṭṭhino ca anuseṭṭhino ca* means those families which belong to the heads of guilds and the sub-heads of guilds; these are the "families of heads and sub-heads. Of those heads and sub-heads...
"Of families" means of those families endowed with both *seṭṭhis* and *anuseṭṭhis* who have come down by way of lineage.
"Vimala," and so forth, are the names of their sons. "Having shaved off hair and beard" means having removed both the hair of the head and the facial hair.
"Yellow robes" means robes dyed yellow with astringent juice, which are suitable for those leading the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Garments. "Oraka" means inferior, deficient, or wretched. The rest here is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Going-forth with Four Householder Friends is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Going-forth with Fifty Householder Friends.
31. That which ought to be said regarding the going forth of the approximately fifty lay companions has already been stated.

However, since the prior application (*pubbayoga*) of all these individuals must be told, he said, "This is the prior application of the noble sons Yasa and the others," and so forth, in order to show that.
In that context, "by forming a group" means by forming a community; it is equivalent to saying they were united. "The bodies of the helpless" means...
"Helpless" refers to the corpses of the dead. "Tending to them" means carrying them outside and cremating them.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the renunciation of the fifty householders and their companions is finished.
The commentary on the discourse concerning Māra.
32. Now, in order to show the formal admission through going for refuge (*saraṇagamana-upasampadā*), the passage beginning with “Then the Blessed One” is commenced.
Herein, this is the word-by-word commentary in sequence: “I am liberated” (*muttāhaṃ*) means “I am freed. “Wandering” (*cārikaṃ*) refers to a wandering consisting of successive travel;
the meaning is a wandering characterized by proceeding in due order through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. “Travel” (*caratha*) means going no further than a *yojana* during the day.
"Caratha. "Do not go two by one": when two people have set out on the same path and one is teaching the Dhamma while the other remains silent, it is necessary for one to stand [in silence];
therefore he spoke thus. "Beautiful in the beginning" means beautiful, excellent, and auspicious at the beginning;
likewise in the middle and at the end. And this triad of beginning, middle, and end applies both to the Dispensation (sāsana) and...
And it is twofold by way of the teaching. In that regard, virtue is the beginning of the Dispensation;
serenity, insight, and the path are the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end. Alternatively, virtue and concentration are the beginning;

insight and the path are the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end. Or again, virtue, concentration, and insight are the beginning; the path is the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end.
Regarding the teaching, first, in the case of a four-line stanza, the first line is the beginning, the second and third are the middle, and the fourth is the conclusion.
In stanzas of five or six lines, the first line is the beginning, the final line is the conclusion, and the remaining lines are the middle.
In a sutta with a single thematic connection, the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning, the words "Thus he spoke" (*idamavoca*) are the conclusion, and the rest is the middle.

In a discourse with many connections, even though there are many intermediate connections, they are still considered "in the middle"; the introduction is the beginning, and "this he said" is the conclusion.
"With meaning" means: teach having made it meaningful. "With phrasing" means:
teach having made it complete both with respect to its expressions and its words. "Entirely perfect" means: completely whole. "Pure" means: free from defilement.
"Brahmacariya" refers to the holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings. "Proclaim" means make manifest.
"Of a nature with little dust in their eyes" means those whose nature possesses little defilement-dust within the eye of wisdom;
the meaning is that there are beings capable of attaining Arahantship at the conclusion of even a four-line stanza, like [a cloth] covered by fine linen or hemp. "They fall away" means...

Through the loss of what they have not gained, they fall away from the Dhamma. For this very reason it was said: "Not attaining what has not yet been attained, they fall away from the attainment of distinction.
*Senānigama* means a market town (*nigama*) belonging to an army (*senā*). It is said that in that place there was a military encampment (*senānivesa*) for the people of the first cosmic age;
therefore, that region is called "Senānigama. There is also a reading, *Senānigāma*; [the word] *senāni* means...

"Sujātā’s father" means his village. "I shall go there" means: "I will not stay here after sending you away to have monasteries and the like built, while being attended by such people as my personal attendants;
rather, having displayed three thousand four hundred and fifty miracles to the three matted-hair ascetics, I shall go there specifically to teach the Dhamma."
33. *Māra* the Evil One (*pāpimā*): he is called *māra* because he kills (*māreti*) those beings who have set out to transcend his own domain;
he is called *pāpimā* because he enjoins others to evil or is himself engaged in evil.
He has many other names as well, such as Kaṇha, Adhipati, Vasavattī, Antaka, Namuci, Pamattabandhu, and so forth; however, only two names are taken here.
"He approached" means he approached after thinking: "This ascetic Gotama, as if deliberating on a great battle, dismisses sixty people, saying, 'Do not go two by two;
teach the Dhamma. Yet, when even one person teaches the Dhamma, there is no satisfaction for my mind;
how then could there be any when many are teaching? I shall prevent him. Thus he approached.

"From all snares" means from all snares of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Those which are divine and those which are human" means that you are bound by all those things called snares of the defilements, namely those consisting of divine sensual qualities and those consisting of human sensual qualities; thus he says.
"Bound by a great bond" means bound by the great bond of the defilements, or bound within a great bondage—of the bondage of the defilements.
The meaning is: "He is bound in the prison of existence, which is his proper place. "O ascetic, you shall not escape from me" means: "O ascetic, you will not be released from my domain.
And this statement, "O ascetic, you shall not escape from me," was spoken by Māra because he did not believe the Blessed One’s words, "Monks, I am released from all snares";
or even if he did believe them, [he spoke thus] thinking, "In this way, for other beings..."
“...one would not exert effort for liberation,” he says thus while standing in deceit (*kohañña*), threatening [the opponent].
“Defeated” (*nihata*) means you have been struck down by me; the sense is that you have been rendered devoid of guile and vanquished.

He is called a “sky-walker” (*antalikkhacara*) because he binds even those who move through the sky, possessing the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*); for the snare of passion (*rāga-pāsa*) accomplishes its task even among those who move through the sky.
“He is called a ‘wonder-worker’ (antalikkhacaro), and for that very reason Māra also imagines him to be a wonder-worker.
“Born of the mind” means *mānaso*; the meaning is that he is associated with the mind. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the discourse concerning Māra is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Going-forth and Full Ordination (Pabbajjūpasampadākathāvaṇṇanā) 34.

Regarding the section of the Canon beginning with “I allow you, monks,” which sets forth the determination concerning going-forth and full ordination, the following was said in order to show it in detail: “When one is giving the going-forth to a clansman seeking it,” and so forth. Therein:
The connection is: "those persons who are prohibited. "He himself should ordain" means he should ordain while performing the cutting of hair and so forth himself.
For one who performs these three—the cutting of hair, the donning of the saffron robes, and the giving of the refuge—is said to "ordain.
Even one who performs only one or two of these is designated in that very way; therefore, [the instruction] is: "Ordain him."
This was said with reference to the cutting of the hair and the donning of the saffron robes.

The same principle applies here as well regarding the phrase "he causes [the candidate] to go forth with reference to the preceptor. "Having led him to the boundary" is stated for the purpose of avoiding the disclosure of the shaving of the head.
Therefore, it is not permissible to say to anyone else in a monastery where monks reside, "Shave this person's hair. "Having caused him to go forth" refers to the cutting of the hair.

He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). It is said with reference to the granting of the refuges (*saraṇadāna*) that no one other than a monk is permitted to grant the going-forth (*pabbājeti*).
For this very reason, he says, "But as for a novice," and so forth. "Capable" (*bhabbarūpa*) means having a capable nature. He clarifies that same point by another way of expression:
"endowed with causes" (*sahetuka*). "Renowned" (*ñāta*) means well-known. "Famous" (*yasassī*) means possessed of an excellence of retinue.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "by making manifest the state of being impure, loathsome, and repulsive by way of color, shape, smell, location, and place.
In this context, these head-hairs (*kesā*) are repulsive by way of color; they are also repulsive by way of shape, smell, location, and place.
For even if one sees something the color of head-hair in a bowl of agreeable rice gruel or a bowl of cooked rice, [one finds it repulsive].
“Take this away, it is mixed with hair!”—thus they feel disgust; in this way, hair is repulsive by way of its color.
Even those who eat at night, upon touching a tuft of hair—whether from a grain husk or a piece of coarse cloth—feel the same disgust;
in this way, hair is repulsive by way of its shape. And as for hair that is devoid of any refinement such as anointing with oil, flowers, incense, and so forth...
The smell is extremely repulsive, and even more repulsive than that is the smell of [hair] when it has been cast into a fire.

For while hair might not be disgusting in terms of its color or shape, it is indeed repulsive by its smell. Just as the excrement of a young child is yellow in color like turmeric and in shape like a lump of turmeric, yet when discarded in a place of refuse, it is repulsive.
The body of a black dog that is bloated is, in terms of color, the color of a ripe palm fruit; in terms of shape, it has the shape of a discarded, round *mudiṅga* drum;
its fangs are like jasmine buds. Both of these might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, but they are indeed repulsive by their odor.
In the same way, even hair might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, but it is indeed repulsive by its odor.

Just as vegetables grown in a place of filth through the seepage of village runoff are disgusting to city-dwellers and unfit for consumption, so too these hairs are supremely disgusting because they are produced by the seepage of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so forth;
thus they are repulsive by way of their source. Furthermore, these so-called hairs are like weeds springing up in a heap of dung.

They are like those born from a heap of thirty-one parts; because they are produced in an impure place—like vegetables grown in a cemetery or a rubbish heap, or like lotuses and water lilies growing in a ditch—they are supremely loathsome.

Thus, the meaning is that [the meditator] demonstrates the repulsiveness of the fivefold skin in terms of its color and other qualities, by way of the method beginning with "repulsive according to location."
"Or, by making manifest the state of being devoid of a living soul or a sentient being": these things called "head-hairs" have grown on the skin that envelops the skull.

In this regard, just as when *kuntha* grass grows on the top of an anthill, the top of the anthill does not know, "The *kuntha* grass has grown upon me," nor do the *kuntha* grasses know, "We have grown on the top of an anthill."
In the same way, the skin enveloping the skull does not know, "Hair has grown on me," nor do the hairs know, "We have grown on the skin enveloping the skull.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, what is called "hair" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, and devoid of a living being.
By means of the method beginning with "The earth element is rigid," etc., he demonstrates the state of being devoid of a living soul and devoid of a sentient being.

"In the past" means in the presence of previous Buddhas. "One who has crushed the formations" means one whose formations have been thoroughly rubbed away by knowledge through the discernment of name-and-form and the investigation of conditions.
"One who has developed meditation" means through the complete development of wholesome states by means of the comprehension of groups and so forth.
"Pūraṇa, whose cultivation was perfected":

here they say that the going-forth does not take root for one who thinks, "What is not given is not permissible. "Ordination permitted" means ordination permitted by a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*).
"Perfection of place and effort": herein, the chest and so forth are the places (*ṭhāna*), while the lips and so forth are the efforts (*karaṇa*).
These [terms] are to be understood. To show that they should be given with a nasalized ending (*anunāsika-anta*), without making an interruption in the middle at the time of giving, it is said:
"connected as one" (*ekasambandhāni*). "Having interrupted" means having made an interruption at the time of giving by ending with the letter *m*.

"Everything, whether allowable or unallowable for him, should be explained" refers to that which is distinct from the ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*), such as the various types of misappropriation (*parāmāsa*) and non-misappropriation.

What is allowable and what is unallowable must be explained. By the phrase "he is to be trained in the matters of proper conduct" (*ābhisamācārika*), it is indicated that he must fulfill the training rules (*sekhiya*), the duties toward the preceptor (*upajjhāyavatta*), and other such matters of proper conduct;
furthermore, it shows that in those matters, he becomes subject to disciplinary action for failing to do what ought to be done or for doing what ought not to be done.
The commentary on the discussion of going forth and full ordination is concluded.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra (Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā) 35.
Now, regarding the text beginning with “Then the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat,” this is the commentary on the previously unexplained words.

“Appropriate attention” (*yonisomanasikāra*) means by way of skillful attention; the meaning is: by attending to things such as impermanence as impermanent, and so forth. “Appropriate right exertion” (*yoniso sammappadhāna*)...

The meaning is: by means of energy as skillful means (*upāyavīriya*), that is, by means of active energy (*pavattavīriya*) through the method of not allowing unarisen unwholesome states to arise and so forth.

"Liberation" (*vimutti*) is stated here as the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*) by way of an exalted description. "He addressed [him]" (*ajjhabhāsī*): [the Blessed One thought], "Even though he has attained Arhatship by exerting energy himself, he is not yet satisfied; now he encourages others as well, saying, 'May you attain it! I shall restrain him."
Thinking thus, he spoke. "By the snare of Māra" means by the snare of the defilements (*kilesa*). The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the second discourse concerning Māra is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning the group of Bhaddas.
36. Regarding the account of the group of thirty noble ones (*tiṃsabhaddavaggiya*): "having dwelt as long as he desired" means having dwelt according to his inclination.

For when Buddhas dwell in a single place, there is no such thing as dissatisfaction arising from a deficiency in shade or water, or from an uncomfortable lodging, or from people being faithless and so forth; rather, it is due to their excellence.
Thinking, “Let us dwell here in comfort,” they take their pleasure, yet there is no long-term residence.

However, wherever the Tathāgata dwells, beings either establish themselves in the three refuges, undertake the precepts, go forth into homelessness, or become a sufficient support for others to attain the path of stream-entry and so forth;
it is with the intention of establishing beings in those attainments that Buddhas [reside] there.
They dwell [there], and in their absence they depart. Therefore it is said: "having dwelt according to their inclination.
"Having plunged in" means having entered. "About thirty" means numbering thirty. The rest here is exactly as explained by the method already stated.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Bhaddavaggiyas is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Miracle at Uruvelā (37–38).
Regarding the account of Uruvelakassapa: *jaṭila* means one who wears matted hair; for he is called *jaṭila* because he possesses (*atthi*) matted hair (*jaṭā*).
*Nāyaka* means a leader; one who leads by himself and teaches his own doctrine is a *vināyaka*. "If it is not a burden to you, Kassapa... [etc.]
“Kassapa, if you have no heavy burden or any discomfort... ‘In the fire-chamber’ means in the fire-hall.
‘When both were aflame’ means when both were burning with flames. ‘For indeed where’ means ‘in which case. 39. ‘This very day’ means on this one day.
‘In the fire-hall’ means in the fire-chamber. ‘With a mind like a *sumana* flower’ means with a mind characterized as beautiful.”
"Skilled in the fire-elements" means skilled in the attainments of the fire-kasiṇa. "They looked up" (*udicchare*) means they gazed upward, or alternatively, it means they surrounded him.
"Having placed it in the bowl" means having put it into the bowl. "With constant alms-food" means with his regular meal.
Regarding the phrase "when the night had passed": here the word *abhikkanta* refers to exhaustion; thus, it means "when the night was completely spent."
The meaning is as follows: For these four Great Kings arrived immediately after the middle watch of the night.
It is indeed the fixed rule for deities that when they come to attend upon Buddhas or Buddha-disciples, they arrive immediately after the middle watch.
"Of surpassing beauty" means of beautiful skin-color; it is said to mean of desirable color, of pleasing color.
...there is. For when deities come to the world of humans, they abandon their natural form and natural psychic power;

instead, they assume a gross physical body and, by means of emitting radiance through an exceeding beauty of complexion, garments, ornaments, and the like, as well as manifesting divine psychic power and majesty, they do so with a contrived [form], just like people going to theatrical performances and the like.
They come by means of the body. Among them, those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) are able to come even without being intentionally manifested because their form is gross;
for they subsist on physical food. However, those belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) are not able to come with an unmanifested body because their form is subtler;
for their personal existence (attabhāva) is exceedingly subtle, and it is not capable of assuming the postures of movement.
Therefore, even in the Brahma-world, Brahmas for the most part proceed by means of created forms alone.
For their fundamental rebirth-form is an exceedingly subtle great materiality; it remains merely as a support and basis for the arising of consciousness, existing only as something possessing shape.
Regarding the term *kevalakappa*: here, the word *kevala* has the sense of "without remainder," and the word *kappa* has the sense of "all-around.
Therefore, *kevalakappaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ* means "the entire forest grove without exception on all sides.
For even if a radiance is capable of pervading without remainder, it might—due to some cause—pervade only a single part; this [is not the case here].
However, the word *kappa* is taken here in the sense of "all around" (*samanta*) in order to show that it pervades everywhere. Alternatively, *kevalakappaṃ* means "entirely incapable.
For deities illuminate with their own radiance only those areas not yet illumined by the radiance of the Blessed One.
Indeed, the radiance of the Blessed One is never overcome by the radiance of anything else; rather, it overcomes even the radiance of the sun and other celestial bodies.
"He stands" means: "having illumined" refers to having pervaded [the area] with the radiance issuing from his robes, ornaments, and body;
the meaning is that he made it a single expanse of light and a single blaze, like the moon or the sun.

For the bodily radiance of deities remains pervading a space of ten or twelve yojanas, and even more than that, as does the luster issuing from their robes, ornaments, and so forth. "In the four quarters" means:
In the four directions. "Yatra hi nāma" means "indeed that which. 43.
"Aṅga-Magadha" refers to the inhabitants of both the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha. "Iddhipāṭihāriya" means a miracle consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*);

the meaning is that it is not a miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā*) or instruction (*anusāsanī*). For there are three kinds of miracles: the miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and [the miracle of instruction].

The miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*). In this context, the miracle of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*) refers precisely to the various modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha*) that proceed according to such methods as: "Here, a bhikkhu, having been one, becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears. Furthermore:
"Here, a bhikkhu declares the minds of other beings, of other persons, and he declares their mental concomitants (*cetasika*)."

The miracle of declaration (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) is the speaking after having known the mind of another, proceeding in such a manner as: "He declares what has been thought, he declares what has been reflected upon:
'Such is your mind, and so too is your mind,' and so forth. "In this case, a monk instructs thus:
'Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend to the mind in this way; do not attend to the mind in that way.'"

"Abandon this; having entered upon this, dwell in it"—instruction such as this, which proceeds in this manner and is the teaching of the Dhamma to be taught at all times to both disciples and Buddhas, is the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
In that regard, the etymological meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya* is "a miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes adversaries, that is, because it takes away the defilements such as lust.
They say this. However, for the Blessed One, there are no opposing factors such as lust (*rāga*) that need to be removed;
even for ordinary persons, when the mind is free from defilements, endowed with the eight qualities, and has destroyed its opposites, the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) function.
Therefore, because of the conventional usage prevalent in that context, it cannot be called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) here. But if [one considers] the Greatly Compassionate One...
The defilements residing in those to be converted are the adversaries of the Blessed One; it is called a "manifestation" (*pāṭihāriya*) because of the removal of them.
This being so, this [etymology] is appropriate. Alternatively, the heretics are the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Teaching;
it is a manifestation because of the removal of them. For they are incapable of proclaiming their own views due to the removal of their views.
They are called *paṭihāriya* because they are carried away or removed by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*), direct instruction (*ādesanā*), and teaching (*anusāsanī*).
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "afterwards," as in such phrases as "When he had entered [the water], another brahmin arrived.
Therefore, it is *paṭihāriya* because it is to be carried out or performed afterwards—once the mind has been concentrated, free from defilements, and its task accomplished.
When one's own defilements have been removed by means of the fourth jhāna and the paths [of the four supramundane stages], the subsequent removal is a "manifestation" (*paṭihāriya*).

Furthermore, the supernormal powers (*iddhi*), the mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and the instruction (*anusāsani*) should be exercised again for the benefit of beings once one is free from defilements and has completed one's task.
Moreover, because they effect the removal of the defilements of other beings when one's own defilements have already been removed, they are called "manifestations."

They are "miracles" (*pāṭihāriya*) because they are marvelous (*paṭihāriya*). Alternatively, each individual member within the aggregate of psychic power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*)—which constitute the marvel—is called a "miracle.
Or else, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "marvelous" (*paṭihāriya*) because they remove opposing factors;

that which is born therein, or has that [fourth jhāna] as its sign, or has come from that, is thus called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*). "For tomorrow" (*svātanāya*) means for the purpose of what is to be given on the morrow.
44. "A rag from a dust heap has arisen" means it has arisen by way of being obtained while one is searching for it.
That search was indeed for the purpose of displaying a manifold miracle. Because that lotus pond was created as soon as it was touched by his hand, it is said:
"having dug a lotus pond with his hand."
46–49. *Jaṭila* means ascetics (*tāpasa*). For they are called "jaṭila" here because they wear matted hair (*jaṭā*).

During the eight nights between [the full moons], that is, during the time when snow falls—specifically, during the four nights at the end of the month of Māgha, which is within the winter season, and the four nights at the beginning of the month of Phagguṇa—thus during those eight nights between the two [full moons] at the time of snowfall. They were emerging from the Nerañjarā River.
Some, having first submerged their entire bodies in that water which is regarded as a sacred ford, then emerge, rise up, and float about.
"Submerging" means they sink into the water up to their heads.
"Performing submerging and emerging" means they perform acts of submerging and emerging again and again. For therein, some [think]: "Purification from evil occurs by a single emergence alone."
Those who hold such a view emerge and then depart; yet since there is no emergence without immersion, they necessarily undergo immersion as well due to their inseparable connection.

Likewise, those who hold the view that "purification from evil occurs through a single immersion" also immerse themselves only once, and by the same principle mentioned above, they necessarily emerge as well.
Having done so, they depart. Others hold the view that "by repeatedly rising up and diving down while bathing, there is purification from evil";
these people rise up and dive down from time to time. It is with reference to all of them that it is said:
"they emerge, they submerge, and they perform both emerging and submerging. And here, although...

Emerging is preceded by submerging; however, since only a few actually perform the submerging, while many perform both emerging and submerging, "emerging" was mentioned first in order to show their predominance.
50–51. *Udakavāha* means a flood of water. *Reṇuhatāya* means covered with dust; it is said to mean strewn with dust.
"Nor indeed, Kassapa, are you an Arahant"—by this he rejects Kassapa’s state of being one beyond training (*asekha*);
"nor have you entered the path to Arahantship"—by this he rejects his state of being one in training (*sekha*). By both [statements], he demonstrates that he is simply a non-noble person (*anariya*).
"That practice of yours does not exist, by which you might either be an Arahant or have entered the path to Arahantship."
By this, however, he also rejects his status as a "good worldling" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*).

In that context, "practice" (*paṭipadā*) refers to the six purifications beginning with purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*). It is called "practice" because by means of it one proceeds upon the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

"Assasi" means "you would be. "From long ago" (*cirapaṭikā*) means from a long time past; the meaning is "from the time of Nāgadama. "Mixed with a load of salt" (*khārikājamissa*): here, "a load" (*khārī*)...

The requisites of an ascetic (*tāpasaparikkhāra*) include the fire-drill (*araṇī*), water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), needle (*sūci*), and so forth; the task of carrying these is the "burden of the pack-animal" (*khārikāja*). "Mixed with the fire-oblation" (*aggihutamissa*) refers to the implements for fire-worship, such as the sacrificial ladle (*dabbi*) and others. 52–53.
"Calamity" (*upasagga*) means misfortune. Now, in order to show the three thousand five hundred miracles (*pāṭihāriya*) by counting them together as one:
“By the Blessed One’s resolution, five hundred pieces of wood did not split,” and so forth, begins [the section].

However, the sixteen miracles such as the taming of the nāga and others are not counted here; it should be understood that together with those, there are more than sixteen and less than two thousand miracles.
*Commentary on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta*

54. Now, in order to show that those one thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship through the teaching on the discourse concerning the burning, the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One" is commenced. Therein, "He was dwelling at Gayā on Gayāsīsa":
because it exists not far from the river named Gayā, the village is called Gayā; he was dwelling in that Gayā. And this [locative case] is used in the sense of proximity.

This is the locative case. For not far from the village of Gayā, there is a lotus pond called Gayā, as well as a river, and a boulder on the back of a hill named Gayāsīsa that resembles an elephant’s frontal globe;
it is large enough to accommodate a thousand bhikkhus. It was for this reason that the Blessed One dwelt there.
Thus it is said, “at Gayāsīsa,” meaning on the boulder named Gayāsīsa near the village of Gayā.
"It is said that he dwelt [there]. "He addressed the bhikkhus" means that, having discerned a teaching on the Dhamma suitable for them, he addressed them with the thought, "I shall teach that.
For the Blessed One, taking that thousand of ascetics who were wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power, went to Gayāsīsa;
and sitting there surrounded by them, he reflected: "Which discourse on the Dhamma would be suitable for these?"
Reflecting, "These people tend the sacrificial fire morning and evening;
I shall show them the twelve sense-bases as if they were burning and blazing, so that they will be able to attain Arhatship," he made this resolution.
Then, in order to teach them accordingly, he spoke this Discourse on Burning, beginning with the words, "Monks, everything is burning."
In this context, "all" is fourfold: all-in-all, all as sense bases, all as personal existence, and partial all. Regarding these:
"There is nothing here that he has not seen, Nor anything unknown or yet to be known."
“He has directly known everything that is to be known;
therefore the Tathāgata is the one with universal vision”—this is called the "all-in-all.
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the all; listen to it”—this is the "all" as sense bases (*āyatana*).
“Monks, I will teach you the exposition on the root of all phenomena”—this is called the "all-encompassing" (sabbadhamma) in the sense of the entire mass of personal existence (sakkāya).

“In regard to all phenomena, first there arises attention, mind, intellect, mentation, and the corresponding element of mind-consciousness”—this is called the "partially all-encompassing" (padesasabba).

Thus, the mere five objects of experience constitute the partially all-encompassing, while the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence constitute the all-encompassing in the sense of the entire mass of personal existence.
The "all" of the four planes consists of all bases (*āyatana-sabba*), which is the "all of all" (*sabbasabba*)—whatever is knowable.

The "all" of a particular portion (*padesa-sabba*) does not encompass the "all" of personality (*sakkāya-sabba*), because it does not include even a single part of the phenomena belonging to the three planes.
The "all" of personality does not encompass the "all" of bases, because it does not include supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*). The "all" of bases does not encompass the "all of all."
Why? Because by the term "all bases" (*āyatana-sabba*), only phenomena belonging to the four planes are included, not the characteristic marks (*lakkhaṇa*) or designations (*paññatti*).
However, in this sutta, "all bases" is intended in its specific sense; even there, only those phenomena that have entered into insight (*vipassanā*) are to be taken.
"The eye" (*cakkhu*) refers to two kinds of eyes: the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) and the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*). Therein, the eye of knowledge is fivefold.
The Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the universal eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom-eye.

Among these, the "Buddha-eye" refers to both the knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the degrees of maturity of the faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*), which is mentioned in the passage: "Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye.
The "Dhamma-eye" refers to the three lower paths and the three fruits, which is mentioned in the passage: "The dustless..."
The stainless Dhamma-eye arose. Thus it is said. The "all-seeing eye" (samantacakkhu) is omniscient knowledge, which is mentioned in the passage:
“Having ascended the palace, the all-seeing one. The "divine eye" (dibbacakkhu) is the knowledge that arises through the increase of light, which is mentioned in the passage:
“With the purified divine eye. The "wisdom-eye" (paññācakkhu) is the knowledge that discerns the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding that which is stated as "the eye arose": the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) is twofold, namely, the eye with its constituent parts (*sasambhāracakkhu*) and the sensitive eye (*pasādacakkhu*).
Of these, that which is a mass of flesh enclosed by the eye-sockets and the eyelids—wherein, in brief, there are thirteen factors:
the four elements, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, birth, life-force, existence, the sensitivity of the eye, and the sensitivity of the body—is the eye with its constituent parts.
In brief, there are [eight] constituents; however, in detail, there are nine: the four elements, and color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence, which arise from the fourfold origination.

Together with life, existence, the sensitivity of the eye, and the sensitivity of the body—these four arising from kamma—there are forty constituents. This is called the "eye together with its constituents."
Now, that mere sensitivity capable of seeing forms, which is situated within the visual circle (diṭṭhimaṇḍala) surrounded by a black circle and demarcated by a white circle—
this is called the "sensitivity eye" (pasādacakkhu). An extensive discussion of this and the subsequent [sensitivities] such as the ear and so forth has already been given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
In this context, having taken that which is the physical eye (*pasādacakkhu*), the Blessed One said, "The eye is on fire," and so forth.
Therein, "on fire" (*āditta*) means blazing, fully aflame; the meaning is that it has become a single mass of flame due to eleven fires.
Consciousness dependent upon the eye is "eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*); or, consciousness whose cause is the eye is "eye-consciousness. Granted...
Visible forms, light, attention, and so forth are also causes of that consciousness; however, those are common causes, whereas the eye is the uncommon cause.
This designation is made by way of the uncommon cause, just as one says, "a barley sprout.
The same method applies to ear-consciousness and the others. Eye-contact is contact dependent on the eye; this is a term for the contact associated with eye-consciousness.
This is a designation. The same method applies to ear-contact and the others as well. Regarding the statement, "Feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact":

this refers to the feelings that have arisen having made eye-contact their primary condition—namely, the feelings of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*), investigating (*santīraṇa*), determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), impulsion (*javana*), and registration (*tadārammaṇa*).
However, regarding the status of eye-contact as a condition for the feeling associated with eye-consciousness, it goes without saying.

There is none. For eye-contact is a condition for feeling that arises simultaneously with it by way of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*), etc., and for feeling that does not arise simultaneously with it by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), etc.
Therefore it is said: "Dependent on eye-contact, there arises a felt experience—either pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
This same method applies to the feelings of the ear-door and so forth. Herein, however, "mind" (is...)
The life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) is intended here as the mind-door (*manodvāra*). "Phenomena" (*dhammā*) refers to the mental object.

"Mind-consciousness" (*mano-viññāṇa*) refers to the impulsion (*javana*) accompanied by the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). "Mind-contact" (*manosamphassa*) is the contact co-nascent with the life-continuum.

"Feeling" (*vedayita*) refers to the feeling of the impulsion together with the feeling of the adverting consciousness; however, there is no need to mention the feeling associated with the life-continuum itself.
Alternatively, "mind" (mano) refers to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) when it has not yet been displaced from its state as the adverting consciousness (āvajjana).

"Phenomena" (dhammā) refers specifically to the object of phenomena. "Mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa) refers to the impulsion consciousness (javana-viññāṇa). "Mind-contact" (manosamphassa) is the contact co-nascent with the life-continuum and the adverting consciousness.
"Feeling" (vedayita) is the feeling co-nascent with the impulsion; however, that which is co-nascent with the life-continuum and the adverting consciousness is also permissible.

In the passage beginning with "the fire of lust" (*rāgaggi*), lust itself is called "fire" in the sense of burning; thus it is the "fire of lust. For lust, arising in its sharp intensity, burns and consumes sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "fire. The same method applies to the other two as well. Here are some examples:
A certain young bhikkhunī, having gone to the Uposatha hall at the Cittala-pabbata monastery, [beheld] the form of the gatekeeper...
She stood gazing [at him]. Then, passion arose within her with even greater intensity;

consequently, the fire element originating from that passion, together with its co-nascent mental states, consumed the region of her heart with extreme sharpness, just as the external fire element consumes its own support.
Having been thus consumed, that bhikkhunī passed away. The bhikkhunīs...
As they were walking along, they said, "This young woman is standing there; call her! One of them went and seized her by the hand, asking, "Why are you standing there?
As soon as she was seized, she turned around and fell down. This, first of all, is the story regarding the failure of passion to burn away.

Regarding the failure of hatred to burn away, however, the Manopadosika deities (Angry-Minded Devas) are to be understood. It is said that among them, a certain son of the gods [was watching] a festival...
Thinking, "I shall play," he sets out upon the street in his chariot with his retinue. Then another person, coming out and seeing him going ahead, becomes angry, thinking:
"O, this wretch! Having seen one never seen before, he goes along as if bloated with joy and as if bursting.
The one going ahead also turns back toward that angry man.
Seeing that those who are angry are easy to recognize, one perceives the other's state of anger and retaliates, thinking: "What can you do to me while you are angry?
This prosperity was obtained by me through the power of generosity, virtue, and so forth, not by your power.
For when one person is angry, the other who is not angry protects himself; for as long as the other does not become angry, that anger of the first person remains ineffective against him.
One who is without clinging (*anupādāna*) cannot be made to fall away even by arising once without repeated practice; like a fire that meets water, he is extinguished.
Therefore, one who is not angry protects him from falling away.
But when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other’s, and the anger of that one also becomes a condition for the other’s; thus, they both continue merely weeping.

And they pass away from their confinement. For when anger arises—whose function is to burn up its support through the process of mutual intensification as both parties become increasingly enraged—it burns away the heart-base and destroys the extremely delicate physical body;
consequently, the entire personal existence vanishes. This is the basis for the statement that anger does not burn itself away.
Furthermore, because they do not burn away delusion (*moha*), the gods corrupted by play (*khiḍḍāpadosika*) are to be observed.
Indeed, through the influence of delusion, their mindfulness (*sati*) becomes confused; therefore, by means of their play, they pass the time for taking food and die.

It is said that while sporting in a festival with the great majesty and splendor of themselves attained through specific merits, due to the greatness of that prosperity, they [fail to attend to] "food..."

They do not even know whether they have eaten or not. Then, from the moment they have passed the single meal, though they continue eating and drinking without interruption, they still pass away and do not remain. Why? Because of the strength of the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*).
For humans, the fire born of karma is weak and the body born of kamma (*karaja-kāya*) is strong. Due to the weakness of that fire, the body born of kamma—
Even after passing seven days, a strong person can support the physical body with warm water, clear gruel, and so forth.
However, the bodily heat of devas is powerful because it is produced by sublime merit and because they consume and digest a food of sublime, heavy, smooth, and pure ambrosia (*sudhā*);
whereas the material body is weak due to its soft and delicate nature. For this very reason, the Blessed One [stood] upon the natural ground in the Indasāla Cave.
When Sakka, the king of the gods, was unable to remain stable, [the Buddha] said to him, "Resolve upon a gross body.
Therefore, they were unable to remain steady after even one mealtime had passed.
It is just as when a lotus or a blue water-lily placed on a heated stone in the midday heat of summer cannot be revived even if it is sprinkled with a hundred jars of water in the evening.
It is not natural; it simply perishes. In the same way, even though they eat and drink continuously afterwards, they still pass away and do not remain.
What, then, is their food, and what is the time for eating? For all the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), ambrosia (sudhā) is the food;
among them, that of each higher level is more refined than that of each lower level. According to their respective days:
They eat every day. Some, however, say: "They eat a meal of fine white rice (*sudhāhāra*) the size of a cat's paw.
As soon as it is placed on the tongue, it suffuses the body from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails;
it is sufficient to sustain them for seven days according to their own reckoning."
But who are these so-called "deities corrupted by play" (*khiḍḍāpadosika*)? There is no specific investigation regarding their identity in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

However, because it is stated without distinction that "the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*) is powerful, while the fire born of the physical body (*karaja*) is weak," it should be understood that whoever among those subsisting on solid food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) acts in such a way, they pass away in this manner.
Some, however, say: "The *Nimmānarati* and *Paranimmitavasavatti* [deities]..."
“Those gods are called ‘corrupted by play’ (khiḍḍāpadosika) simply because they corrupted themselves through play.

However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself that the “corrupted by mind” (manopadosika) gods belong to the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika). Some, however, say that the “corrupted by play” gods also belong to the Realm of the Four Great Kings.
Thus, first of all, the three beginning with lust should be understood as “fires” in the sense of being secondary combustibles. The triad beginning with birth—
Furthermore, it is called "fire" because it burns away by being the basis for various kinds of suffering. That it burns away sorrow and so forth is indeed evident.
The rest here follows the same method already stated. Thus, in this sutta, the characteristic of suffering is explained;
for the state of suffering is explained through the fact that the eye and the other faculties are painful due to their being ablaze with eleven fires.
The commentary on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the discourse regarding the miracle at Uruvelā is finished.
The commentary on the discourse regarding the meeting with Bimbisāra.

55. Now, in order to show the commentary on those words not previously explained in the passage beginning, “Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Gayāsīsa for as long as he pleased,” the section beginning with “At Laṭṭhivana, that is, in the Palm Grove (Tāluyyāna)” is commenced.

Therein, “in the Palm Grove” means in the park that received this name because of the great number of palm trees (*tāla-rukkha*). Regarding the passage beginning, “some, having extended their joined palms toward where the Blessed One was,” etc.:
"Having paid homage with joined palms": this was said with reference to those who belonged to both sides. They thought thus:

"If those of wrong view should reproach us, saying, 'Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?', we shall say to them, 'Is it not considered homage even by the mere act of joining one's palms? But if those of right view should reproach us..."
"If you ask, 'Why did he not pay homage to the Blessed One? I shall say: 'Is it only by striking the ground with one's head that homage is rendered?
Is not the performance of the añjali-gesture also indeed homage?
"Having announced his name and clan" means that those who say, "O Gotama, I am the son of so-and-so, named Datta or named Mitta, and have come here," are indeed announcing their names.
“O Gotama, I am Vāseṭṭha by name, Kaccāna by name, who has come here”—thus they are said to proclaim their lineage (*gotta*).
It is said that these impoverished sons of noble families did this so that they would become well-known by way of name and lineage in the midst of the assembly.
But those who sat down in silence were both fickle-minded and blind fools. In this regard:
The stingy ones think, "If one engages in one or two conversations, one becomes a trusted friend; and when there is such trust, it is not right not to give even one or two alms.
Thus, seeking to protect themselves from blame, they sit in silence.
The blind fools, like lumps of clay cast away simply because of their ignorance, sit in silence wherever they are.

Regarding "the exhorter of the emaciated" (*kisakovadāno*): first, to show this analysis of the meaning—that he is the exhorter of those who are emaciated (*kisaka*)—it is said, "because his body was emaciated due to the practice of an ascetic. "Fire-sacrifice" (*aggihutta*) means the tending of the sacrificial fire.

Since it is forms and so forth that are here called "desires" (*kāma*) in the sense of being objects of longing, he says, "these forms and so forth are the desires. "They approve of sacrifices" (*yaññā abhivadanti*).
They say that sacrifices succeed because of this cause. Regarding the phrase "in the acquisitions" (*upadhīsu*), there are four acquisitions here:

the acquisition of sensual pleasures (*kāmupadhi*), the acquisition of the aggregates (*khandhupadhi*), the acquisition of defilements (*kilesupadhi*), and the acquisition of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārupadhi*). For sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) also constitute the basis for the pleasure described thus: "Whatever happiness and joy arise dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification in sensual pleasures. This is because they serve as the foundation for such pleasure.

They are called "upadhīs" (acquisitions) in the sense of the word "that wherein happiness is acquired. The aggregates are called "upadhīs" because they serve as the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates;
the defilements are called "upadhīs" because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the woeful states;
and volitional formations are called "upadhīs" because they serve as the basis for the suffering of existence. Among these, it is the aggregate-acquisition (*khandhupadhi*) that is intended here.

He said: “Having known that [the sacrifice] is a stain among the aggregates (khandha) and acquisitions (upadhi). They say that the sacrifice is indeed a stain; thus they say that for the sake of sacrifice, only a stain succeeds.
“In the great sacrifice” means in the *yiṭṭha*; “in the fire-oblation” (*huta*) means in the daily service of the sacrificial fire.
“Unattached to the realm of sense-desire” (*kāma-bhava*) means not clinging to the realm of sense-desire; it is said to be liberated from that.
57–58. *Āsīsana* means aspiration. Because of the supreme excellence of *siṅgīsuvaṇṇa* (red gold) even among divine golds, it is described as "having the color of molten *siṅgī* gold.
For just as among gold used by humans, that which is fashioned by craftsmanship is inferior, while that refined by chemical processing (*rasaviddha*) is superior;
and superior to that refined gold is gold produced from a mine (*ākara*); and superior to that is any kind of divine gold—so too, among divine golds, [it is superior] to *cāmīkara*.
Sātakumbha gold is superior to ordinary gold; Jambunada gold is superior to Sātakumbha; and Siṅgīsuvaṇṇa is superior to Jambunada; therefore, it is the most excellent of all.
A "Siṅgī-nikkha" is a gold plate made from Siṅgīsuvaṇṇa weighing exactly one nikkha.
For a plate made with less than a nikkha is not capable of enduring rubbing and polishing, whereas one made with more than a nikkha can withstand rubbing and polishing.
However, it is not beautiful; it appears to be of coarse substance. Polishing and rubbing with a *nikkha* both endure and it becomes beautiful.
Some say that a *nikkha* is twenty pieces of gold (*suvaṇṇa*); others say twenty-five.
In the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "A *nikkha* is five pieces of gold. Gold (*suvaṇṇa*).
They call this the "Four Supports.
Regarding "one who has completed the residence in the ten noble abodes":
"Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, possesses one guard, and has four resources for retreat..."

One who has dispelled individual speculative truths, who has utterly abandoned seeking, whose intentions are undisturbed, whose bodily formations are tranquil, and who is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
"And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has abandoned five factors?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, he has abandoned ill will, he has abandoned sloth and torpor, he has abandoned restlessness and remorse..."
Doubt is abandoned. In this way, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors.
“And how, monks, is a monk possessed of six factors?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.”
Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad;
he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. In this way, monks, a monk is possessed of the six factors.
“And how, monks, is a monk one who has a single guard? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has a single guard.
“And how, monks, is a monk one who has four supports? Here, monks, a monk, having reflected, partakes of something;
having reflected, he endures something; having reflected, he avoids something; having reflected, he dispels something.”
“In this way, monks, a monk has four supports.
And how, monks, does a monk have individual truths dispelled?
Here, monks, whatever various individual truths there are among the many ordinary recluses and brahmins—all those are dispelled by him.”
They have been dispelled, abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and cast off.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk has dispelled his individual truths.
“And how, monks, does a monk completely abandon his quests? Here, monks, for a monk...”
The search for sensual pleasures has been abandoned, the search for existence has been abandoned, and the search for a holy life has been stilled.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk has completely relinquished his searches.
“And how, monks, does a monk have untroubled intentions? Here, monks, a monk’s intention regarding sensual pleasures [is absent]...”
Ill will has been abandoned, harmful intent has been abandoned.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose intentions are undisturbed.
"And how, monks, is a monk one whose bodily formations are tranquil? Here, monks, a monk..."
With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. In this way, monks,
a bhikkhu has tranquilized the bodily formations.
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu well-liberated in mind? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, and his mind is liberated from delusion.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is well-liberated in mind.”
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one whose wisdom is well-liberated? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands:
‘Lust has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. He understands:
‘Hatred has been abandoned by me… Delusion has been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.’”
"He understands: 'It is of a nature not to arise again. In this way, monks, a monk is one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
Thus ends the dwelling in the ten abodes of the noble ones as they have come down to us.

In that context, "abodes" (vāsā) means those wherein they dwell; "abodes of the noble ones" (ariyavāsā) means the dwellings of the noble ones alone, as opposed to the dwellings of the ignoble or those similar to them.
Because it is impossible [otherwise]. Here, by way of an inclusive designation, "noble ones" (ariya) refers to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).

"One with a single guard" (ekārakkha): he has a single guard, which is mindfulness (sati); thus, he is one with a single guard. For in the case of one whose taints are destroyed, mindfulness performs the function of guarding at all times across the three doors.
Therefore, whether walking or standing, sleeping or waking, his mindfulness is constant and continuous.
"It is said that knowledge and vision are present.

Regarding "one who has the four supports" (*caturāpasseno*): one for whom there are four supports or props is "one who has the four supports. "By means of reflection" (*saṅkhāya*) means by means of knowledge.
"He practices" (*paṭisevati*) means that having known by means of knowledge, he practices only that which is fit to be practiced. Its detailed explanation begins with "reflection... (*paṭisaṅkhā*)...
It should be understood according to the method beginning with, “He uses his robe wisely.
As for “having reflected, he endures one thing,” having known through wisdom, he endures only that which is fit to be endured.

The detailed explanation here should be understood according to the method beginning with, “Having reflected wisely, he is patient toward cold,” and so forth. As for “he avoids,” having known through wisdom, he avoids only that which is fit to be avoided.
He avoids it. Its detailed explanation should be understood according to the method beginning with, "Having reflected thoroughly, he avoids a fierce elephant.
He dispels means that having known through wisdom, he dispels—drives away and removes—that which must be dispelled, not allowing it to remain within.
Its detailed explanation should be understood according to the method beginning with, "He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought."

"One who has dispelled individual truths" (*panuṇṇapaccekasacca*) means one by whom the individual truths of speculative views—so called because they were grasped individually in the form "only this view is truth, only this is truth"—have been dispelled, removed, and abandoned; thus he is "one who has dispelled individual truths.
"Of many recluses and brahmins" (*puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ*) means of numerous recluses and brahmins. And here, "recluses" (*samaṇā*) refers to those who have entered the homeless life.
"Brahmins" refers to those who address others as "bho. "Many individual truths" means many separate truths;
the meaning is that many truths have been grasped individually, each thinking, "This very view is the truth, this alone is the truth. "Expelled" means removed.
"Completely expelled" means thoroughly removed. "Abandoned" means let go. "Vomited" means cast out. "Released" means...
"Severed bonds" means they have been cut. "Abandoned" means they have been relinquished. "Renounced" means they have been given up in such a way that they do not recur in the mind again.
All of these are synonyms for the state of having discarded the grip of views previously held prior to the attainment of the Noble Path.

Regarding the term *samavayasaṭṭhesanā*: here, *avaya* means "not deficient" (*anūna*). *Saṭṭha* means "abandoned" (*nissaṭṭha*). Thus, one whose search (*esanā*) is completely (*sammā*) abandoned (*avaya*) and relinquished (*saṭṭha*) is called *samavayasaṭṭhesana*; the meaning is "one who has completely cast off all searches.

The accomplishment of the function of the Path is stated by such passages as "the mind is liberated from lust," because these demonstrate the state of having abandoned lust and the other defilements. "Lust... [and so forth].
The noble fruit (*ariyaphala*) is described by way of reflection through such phrases as "it has been abandoned by me.

For when the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) is attained, one understands the state of the absolute non-arising of lust and the other defilements; and that understanding is the knowledge of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).

In this context, the abandoning of the five factors, the individual realization of the truths, the dispelling of search, and the attainment of composure are expressed as: "Having reflected, he resorts to one [thing]... (*saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati*).
Regarding the reasons stated—“he endures, he avoids, and he dispels”—dispelling (*vinodanā*) is indeed a function of the Path, while the others are accomplished by the Path alone.
“The One of Ten Powers” (*dasabala*): he is called the One of Ten Powers because he possesses ten powers, namely, those consisting of bodily power and those consisting of knowledge-power.
For the power of a Tathāgata is twofold: physical power and the power of knowledge. Of these, the physical power is to be understood by way of the lineage of elephants.
For this has been said by the ancients:
“The black-and-white, the Ganges-born, the white, and the tawny-brown;”
“Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—these are the ten [kinds of] elephant breeds.
These indeed are the ten elephant breeds. Therein, “Kāḷāvaka” should be understood as the ordinary elephant breed.
The bodily strength of ten men is equal to that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The [strength] of ten Kāḷāvakas...
The strength of one Gaṅgeyya elephant is equal to that of ten Gaṅgeyyas;
the strength of ten Paṇḍaras is equal to that of one Paṇḍara; the strength of ten Tambas is equal to that of one Tamba;
the strength of ten Piṅgalas is equal to that of one Gandhahatthin; the strength of ten Gandhahatthis—
That which is the strength of ten Maṅgala elephants is the strength of one Hemavata elephant.
That which is the strength of ten Hemavata elephants is the strength of one Uposatha elephant. That which is the strength of ten Uposatha elephants is the strength of one Chaddanta elephant.
That which is the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is the bodily strength of a Tathāgata. It is also called the strength of the Nārāyaṇa-composition.
This is what is called [the Vajirasaṅghāta-bala]. In this context, "nārā" refers to rays; because many various kinds of these arise from it, it is "nārāyaṇa," which is the thunderbolt (vajira).
Therefore, the meaning is "the strength of the assembly of thunderbolts.
By the standard calculation for ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand million elephants; by the calculation for men, it is the strength of ten thousand million men.
This, first of all, is the bodily power of the Tathāgata.
As for his power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), it is indeed included in the Canon.
Here is the passage from the Canon: "Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which..."
The Tathāgata claims the place of the bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are these ten? Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
And that, Sāriputta, which the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, as the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible...

He understands it. This, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
(1) “Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma—past, future, and present—in terms of its basis and its cause. … [as before] … (2)”
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading everywhere...
(3) “Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the world with its many and diverse elements...
(4) “Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among beings... (5)”
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals...

(6) “Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence from the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments...
(7) “Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes. That is to say:”

(8) "Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details, such as one birth, two births... [and so on]... thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details."...

(8) "Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate..."
He understands beings according to their kamma... [as before] ...
