(9) "Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom... [as before] ... This too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power."

The Tathāgata possesses the power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel. These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata. (10)
Therein, "the possible as possible" means the cause as cause. One who understands:
"Whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states—that is the possible (ṭhāna).
Whatever states are not the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states—that is the impossible (aṭṭhāna)"—understands the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
He understands it as it really is. "By which" (*yampīti*) means by means of which knowledge.

"Of undertakings of action" (*kamma-samādānānaṃ*) refers to wholesome and unwholesome actions performed after having undertaken them; or, "undertaking of action" (*kamma-samādānaṃ*) is simply action itself.

"According to the footing and the cause" (*ṭhānaso hetuso*) means according to both the condition and the cause. In that regard, destiny, the basis, time, and effort [are the conditions] for the ripening.
The basis is the cause, which is the action.
"Leading everywhere" means leading to all destinations, both those that are good destinations and those that are bad destinations. "Practice" means the path.
"He understands it as it really is" means that even when many people are killing a single living being, although the volition belongs to all of them, it belongs to that one person alone.
They have the life-faculty as their object, yet that karma of theirs is of various kinds. For among them, one performs it having generated zeal with reverence;
another performs it being pressured by others, who say, "Come, you too do it";
and another wanders about as if possessing the same zeal, not being restrained. Therefore, among them, one is reborn in hell by that very same karma.

One [being] is in the animal realm, and one is in the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya). At the very moment of their karmic accumulation, the Tathāgata knows: "Because of being accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in hell; this one in the animal realm; this one in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Even as they are being reborn in hell, he knows: "This one will be reborn in the great hell (mahāniraya); this one in the auxiliary hells (ussadaniraya)."
Even when being reborn in the animal realm, he knows: "This one will be footless; this one will be two-footed; this one will be four-footed; this one will be many-footed.
Even when being reborn in the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), he knows: "This one will be of parching thirst; this one will be of hunger and thirst;
this one will be dependent on the gifts of others. And regarding those karmas, [he knows]: "This karma [will bring about] rebirth-linking..."
"He will draw [the result] toward himself; this will be the ripening of the substrate for a rebirth-linking given by another"—thus he knows.

Likewise, when all the inhabitants of a village give alms-food together, although the volition of all of them has indeed the alms-food as its object, that karma is nevertheless of different kinds for each of them.
For among them, one performs it with reverence, and so on—all the rest being similar to what was stated previously.
Therefore, among them, some are reborn in the world of the devas and some in the human world. The Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of their accumulation [of kamma]:
"Because of the way this has been accumulated, this one will be reborn in the human world; this one in the world of the devas;
and even there, this one in a khattiya family, this one in a brahmin family, this one in a vessa family, this one in a sudda family, and this one among the Paranimmitavasavatti devas."
"Here [is one] among the Nimmānarati devas, here among the Tusita devas, here among the Yāma devas, here among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, here among the Cātumahārājika devas,

here among the Bhummadeva devas"— in such ways, at the very moment of accumulation, he knows each respective distinction, categorized as inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly, having few attendants or many attendants, and so forth.
Likewise, while they are still establishing insight, [the teacher thinks]: "In this manner, he will not be able to discern anything; he will define only the primary elements (mahābhūta);

he will remain at the stage of grasping material form (rūpa) alone; he will remain at the stage of grasping the immaterial (arūpa) alone; he will remain at the stage of grasping name-and-form (nāmarūpa) alone;
he will remain at the stage of grasping conditions (paccaya) alone; he will remain at the stage of insight having the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) as its object alone."
He knows: "This one will attain the first fruit itself; this one the second fruit itself; this one the third fruit itself; this one will reach Arahantship.
Even among those performing the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, he knows: "For this one there will be only the preliminary work;
this one will produce the sign; this one will reach absorption itself; this one, having made jhāna the basis and established insight..."
He knows: “He will attain arahantship.
“Many elements” means many elements by way of the eye-element and so forth, or by way of the sense-sphere element and so forth.
“Diverse elements” means elements of various kinds because those very same elements possess distinct characteristics. “The world” means the world of aggregates, bases, and elements.
"He understands as it really is" means he penetrates the specific nature of those elements without error.
"Diverse inclinations" refers to the state of having diverse inclinations through low and other such dispositions. "Of other beings" refers to preeminent beings;
"of other persons" refers to those other than them who are inferior beings. Alternatively, these two terms have the same meaning, depending on the capacity of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

However, it is stated in two ways. "Knowledge of the higher and lower faculties" (indriyaparopariyatta) means the higher state and the lower state, as well as the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith and the rest.

"Of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments" refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first, and [the form-sphere attainments] such as "possessing form, one sees forms," and so forth.

Of the eight liberations, the three concentrations beginning with that accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and the nine successive attainments beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.
"Corruption" refers to states conducive to decline. "Purification" refers to states conducive to distinction.
"Emergence" means both purification itself as emergence, and also emergence from each respective concentration.
Thus it is said: both the familiar jhāna and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) are [the emergence].
For each successively lower familiar jhāna serves as the proximate cause (padatthāna) for each successively higher one; therefore, "purification" is also called "emergence.
Emergence from all jhānas occurs by means of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), while emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs by means of the attainment of fruition.
There is emergence. It is with reference to this that it is said: "Emergence from each respective concentration is also emergence.
Furthermore, the detailed analysis and exposition of all types of knowledge is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.
However, the discussion concerning the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints has already been explained in detail in the *Verañjakaṇḍa*.
“Sāriputta, these indeed are those”—this refers back to what was previously stated: “Now, Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata.
He thus brings them to completion. In this regard, there is a statement by opponents: “There is no such thing as the knowledge of the ten powers distinct [from others];
it is merely a classification of omniscient knowledge itself. That should not be viewed in that way; for it is indeed something else.
Indeed, the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabalañāṇa*) is distinct from the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions, whereas the knowledge of omniscience understands those as well as everything remaining beyond them. For among the knowledges of the ten powers, the first knows only what is possible and impossible;
the second, only the various results of kamma; the third, only the limits of kamma; and the fourth...
The first [basis] is the very cause for the diversity of elements; the second is the very inclinations and dispositions of beings; the third is the very sharpness or dullness of the faculties;

the fourth is the very defilement and so forth of those [faculties] along with the jhānas and other states; the fifth is the very underlying tendencies of beings; the sixth is the very continuity of the aggregates in previous existences;

the seventh is the very death and rebirth-linking of beings; the eighth is the very delimitation of the truths; the ninth is the very knowledge of all modes; and the tenth is omniscient knowledge itself.
However, by means of these [powers], one knows what is to be known and understands what is beyond that; yet one does not perform all the functions of these [powers].
For, having become meditative absorption (jhāna), it is unable to enter [it]; having become supernormal power (iddhi), it is unable to perform transformations;
and having become the path (magga), it is unable to exhaust the defilements (kilesa). Thus, because it is endowed with both the aforementioned power of the body and the power of knowledge...
The Blessed One is called "the One Possessing the Ten Powers.

He is endowed with the ten factors of one beyond training (*asekha*): right view of one beyond training, right intention of one beyond training, right speech of one beyond training, right action of one beyond training, right livelihood of one beyond training, right effort of one beyond training, right mindfulness of one beyond training, right concentration of one beyond training, right knowledge of one beyond training, and right liberation of one beyond training.

He is endowed with the ten qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha-dhamma*) mentioned as follows: right mindfulness, right concentration of one beyond training, right knowledge of one beyond training, and right liberation of one beyond training.
Furthermore, all the factors associated with the fruit (the *phala*), beginning with right view, are indeed qualities of one beyond training.
And here, right view and right knowledge are both stated to be wisdom (*paññā*) in two places, in the sense of "right seeing."
"Right view is right knowledge in the sense of right understanding. For there is indeed a distinction in the mode of occurrence regarding the objects of seeing and knowing.
By the phrase "right liberation," however, it should be understood that the remaining states associated with the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) are included.
For even those states associated with the noble fruits (*ariyaphala*) possess a complete liberation from their opposites.
They receive the designation "liberated by means of [something].
59. By the word "speech," it means that even for travelers passing through the vicinity of the monastery, there is little sound of speech.
By the phrase "the noise of the city," it means, in its unelaborated sense, by the clamor of people in the city.
"Sound" (*nigghoso*) refers to the noise produced when people come together and speak in unison. "Of the people wandering about" means of the people moving within [the monastery].
"A place suitable for the secret activities of men" means appropriate and fitting for the performance of secrets by men.
"Conducive to seclusion" means suitable for solitude. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Meeting with Bimbisāra is finished.

Now follows the commentary on the Discourse on the Going-forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna (60), concerning the explanation of previously unexplained terms in the passage beginning, "At that time, the wanderer Sañcaya... and so forth.
Showing this, he said, “Sāriputta and Moggallāna,” and so forth. In that context, Sāriputta is the son of the brahmin woman Sārī;

Moggallāna is the son of the brahmin woman Moggallī. It is said that even before our Blessed One was born, Sāriputta took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin woman named Sārī in the village of Upatissa, not far from the city of Rājagaha. On that very same day, his...
His companion also took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin woman Moggallī in the village of Kolita, not far from Rājagaha itself.
It is said that these two families had been close-knit companions for seven successive generations.
On the very same day, they provided nourishment for the pregnancies of both women. When ten months had passed, those two were born.

Sixty nurses were appointed for them. On the day of the naming ceremony, because the son of Sārī the brahmin woman was born as the eldest son of a prominent family in Upatissa village, they gave him the name "Upatissa";
because the other was born as the eldest son of a prominent family in Kolita village, they gave him the name "Kolita.
Therefore it is said: "In their time as householders, they were known by the names Upatissa and Kolita."
Regarding the phrase "accompanied by two hundred and fifty young men," some say it means "accompanied by five hundred young men. For this is stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary*:
"When the young man Upatissa was going to the river or to the park for recreation, he had five hundred golden palanquins as his retinue;
the young man Kolita had five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses. Both men were accompanied by retinues of five hundred young men each."
In Rājagaha, there was an annual festival called the Giraggasamajja. For both of them, they prepared a single couch in one place.
Sitting together on that same seat, they watched the festival;
they laughed at things that were laughable, were moved by things that inspired spiritual urgency, and gave gifts at places where it was appropriate to give. In this very manner, for them—

One day, as they were watching the festival, because their knowledge had reached full maturity, there was no laughter where they would have laughed on previous days, nor any agitation where they would have been agitated, nor any giving of gifts where it would have been appropriate to give gifts.
However, both men thought thus: "What is there here to look at? All these people, before even a hundred years have passed..."
“They will go to the state of being unmanifested; however, it is fitting for us to seek the Dhamma of liberation.
Having taken this as their objective, they sat down. Then Kolita said to Upatissa: “Friend Upatissa, you are not as joyful as on other days;
you are dejected in your elements. What has been observed by you? “Friend Kolita, [I have observed this].”
“I am sitting here thinking: ‘There is no essence in looking at these things; this is useless. It is fitting to seek the Dhamma of liberation for oneself.
But why are you dissatisfied? He too spoke in the same manner.
Then, knowing that his disposition was identical to his own, Upatisso said: “The thought we both have conceived is well-conceived.”
"However, for those seeking the Dhamma of liberation, it is necessary to obtain the going forth under someone; under whom shall we go forth?
At that time, the wanderer Sañcaya was residing at Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers.
They thought, "We shall go forth under him," and [approached] Sañcaya along with five hundred young brahmins.
They went forth into homelessness in his presence. From the time they were ordained, Sañcaya attained an abundance of extra gains and the highest excellence.
Within just a few days, they had mastered the entirety of Sañcaya’s system and asked him, "Teacher, is this all that you know, or is there more beyond? Sañcaya replied, "This is all."
"Have you yourselves known it? he asked. Having heard his words, they thought: "If this is so, living the holy life (brahmacariya) in his presence is useless;
we have gone forth seeking the Dhamma of liberation, yet it cannot be realized in his presence.
Moreover, Jambudīpa is vast; by wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, we shall surely find one who teaches the Dhamma of liberation."
“We shall find a teacher. From that time forth, wherever they heard that there were wise recluses and brahmins, they went to those places and engaged them in debate on questions;
there was no one capable of answering the questions put by those [two], yet they [the two] answered the questions of those [others]. Thus, having searched throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, they—
Having returned to their own respective places, they made an agreement, saying: "Friend Kolita, whoever first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other.
Showing this very story in brief, he said: "There, seeing the great multitude... [they] made an agreement."
In that context, "of the wandering ascetic Channa" refers to the wandering ascetic who wears white robes;

by this, he shows that this is not a naked wandering ascetic. Regarding the phrases "with inspiring approach," and so forth: "inspiring" (*pāsādika*) means bringing about confidence, being appropriate, and befitting a recluse.
"Approach" (*abhikkanta*) refers to the manner of going forward. "Withdrawal" (*paṭikkanta*) refers to the manner of turning back. "Looking ahead" (*ālokita*) refers to looking toward the front.
"Looking" means looking here and there. "Contracting" means the contraction of the limbs. "Stretching" means the extension of those very same limbs.
In all these instances, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*);

therefore, because they have been thoroughly conditioned by mindfulness and clear comprehension, he becomes one who is graceful in his advancing and retreating, and in his looking forward and looking aside, and in his contracting and stretching.

This has been said. "With downcast eyes" means with eyes cast downward. "Endowed with deportment" means endowed with deportment through that [deportment] which is pleasing and characterized by such qualities as being dignified in walking and so forth.

"Propounded by those seeking it": Nibbāna is called "that which exists" because it is apprehended as existing by inferential knowledge (*anumāṇa-ñāṇa*) in the manner of, "If death exists, there must also be the Deathless. Seeking—that is, searching for—that [Nibbāna], [he thought]: "What if I..."
The connection is: "They should follow closely behind this bhikkhu.
Regarding the manner described in the *Sudinnakaṇḍa*: "In the houses of donors there are halls, and seats are prepared there;
water and gruel are set out, where those who have gone forth, having wandered for alms, sit down and eat. If they so desire, [the donors also...]"
“They take what belongs to others; therefore, this too should be understood as the base of a wall in such a hall belonging to a certain family”—this is the manner in which it was spoken.
“Speak little or much,” [said the Blessed One]; the wanderer replied, “I am named Upatissa; you, according to your ability, [speak] little...”
Having thought, "Whether it be little or much that is spoken, it is my burden to penetrate this by means of a hundred methods and a thousand methods," he spoke thus.

He said "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) and so forth, showing that both cessation (*nirodha*) and the means to cessation are expressed as "cessation" by way of the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (the retention of one member of a class when the members are similar).
"Concluding" (*paṭipādento*) means bringing [the discourse] to its close. Having heard this Dhamma-discourse...
Regarding the statement, "The dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose," it should be understood that the wanderer,

upon hearing only the first two phrases, was established in the fruit of stream-entry endowed with the thousandfold method; the other two phrases were completed at the time he became a stream-enterer.
Regarding the phrase "through many hundreds of thousands of *nahutas*": here, ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand;

a hundred thousands make a hundred-thousand (*satasahassa*); a hundred hundred-thousands make a *koṭi*; a hundred hundred-thousand *koṭis* make a *pakoṭi*; a hundred hundred-thousand *pakoṭis* make a *koṭipakoṭi*;
and a hundred hundred-thousand *koṭipakoṭis* should be understood as one *nahuta*.
61. Then the wanderer Sāriputta approached the wanderer Moggallāna.
Having become a stream-enterer, and perceiving that further distinctions were not arising, he reflected, "There must be a reason for this," and said to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, do not extend your teaching of the Dhamma further; let it remain at this much. Where is our Teacher?"
“...is dwelling. [Thus it was said: “The wanderers in the Bamboo Grove. “Venerable sir, you go on ahead;
I have a companion, and we made a pact with one another: ‘Whoever first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other.
Having fulfilled that promise, I shall take my companion and follow the very path you have taken to the presence of the Teacher.”
"I shall come," he said; then, prostrating himself at the elder's feet with the fivefold salutation, circumambulating him three times, and taking his leave, he set out toward the wanderers' park.
There he spoke thus to the wanderer Sāriputta: "Today the complexion of my friend's face is not as it was on other days."
"Surely he must have attained the Deathless," thinking thus, he asked about the attainment of the Deathless and spoke these words.
The other replied to him, "Yes, friend, the Deathless has been attained," and having acknowledged this, he related the entire occurrence and recited that very verse.
At the conclusion of the verse, the wanderer Moggallāna was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Therefore it was said: “Then, to the wanderer Moggallāna... the Dhammacakkhu arose.
[Thinking] “Friends, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One,” he asked, “Friend, where does our teacher dwell?
and when it was replied, “Friend, it is said he is at Veḷuvana; thus was it told to us by our teacher, the Elder Assaji,” he spoke as follows.
Now, this Elder Sāriputta was always devoted to honoring his teacher; therefore, he said to his companion, the wanderer Moggallāna:
"We shall tell our teacher Sañjaya the wanderer of the Deathless we have attained.
If he understands, he will penetrate it; if he does not penetrate it, he will believe us and go into the presence of the Teacher."
“Having heard the teaching of the Buddhas, he will realize the penetration of the paths and fruits.
Thereupon, both men went into the presence of Sañjaya. Thus it is said: “Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached the wanderer Sañjaya.
And having approached him, they said: “Teacher, what are you doing? A Buddha has arisen in the world!”
“The Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced it rightly; come, let us go and see the One of Ten Powers!
But he said, “What are you saying, dear ones? and having stopped them as well, he pointed out to them only the preeminence of their gains and the excellence of their status.
They replied, “May such a residence for our pupils be ours forever; as for your going or not going, you may decide that yourselves.”
Sañcaya, realizing that "these people, knowing only this much, will not do my bidding," said:
"Go, dear ones; in my old age, I am no longer able to live in the manner of a teacher with pupils.
Unable to persuade him by means of hundreds of various reasons, they took with them those people who were following his advice and went to Veḷuvana.
They arrived. Of the five hundred disciples, two hundred and fifty turned back, while two hundred and fifty went along with them.
Therefore it is said: "Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna, taking those two hundred and fifty wanderers, approached Veḷuvana."

The connection is as follows: having declared that Sāriputta and Moggallāna were "liberated"—meaning they were intent upon the liberation of fruition which has as its object Nibbāna characterized as previously described—the Teacher, while teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, expanded his discourse on the Dhamma according to the conduct of that assembly;
that is, with the exception of the two chief disciples, all the two hundred and fifty wanderers.
They attained arahantship. The Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks," and the hair and beards of them all vanished;
divine robes and bowls appeared, fastened to their bodies. Divine robes and bowls also appeared for the two Chief Disciples, yet the task of the three higher paths was not yet completed for them.
Why? Because of the greatness of the knowledge of the disciples' perfections (sāvakapāramīñāṇa).

Then, on the seventh day after his ordination, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was practicing the duties of a recluse near the village of Kallavāḷa in the kingdom of Magadha, he fell into sloth and torpor. Being stirred by the Teacher, he dispelled that sloth and torpor;
and while listening to the meditation subject on the elements bestowed by the Tathāgata, he brought the work of the three higher paths to completion.

He reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). The Elder Sāriputta, too, having passed half a month from the day of his going forth, was dwelling together with the Teacher near that same Rājagaha in the Sūkarakhatā Cave;
and while the Discourse on the Comprehension of Feelings (Vedanāpariggaha-sutta) was being taught to his own nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha—
Having directed his knowledge according to the Suttas, he reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), like one eating food prepared by another.
For this very reason it was said: "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna was established in Arahantship in seven days;
the Elder Sāriputta, in half a month."
Although the Elder Mahāmoggallāna attained Arahantship before long,
and the Dhammasenāpati (Sāriputta) did so much later, nevertheless, the Elder Sāriputta alone possessed greater wisdom (*mahāpañña*).

For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, while striving for seven days, comprehended only a single portion of the analytical range of the disciples as if pressing it with the tip of a staff, and thereby attained Arahantship.

[The Elder] attained [it]. The Elder Sāriputta, setting aside the range of contemplation belonging to Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, contemplated the range of contemplation of disciples in its entirety; contemplating thus, he strove for half a month.
Because the range of contemplation of disciples was being practiced in its entirety at the highest level, and likewise because of the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection...

Because they must be brought to maturity. For example, suppose a man, thinking "I shall take a bamboo pole," sees a bamboo with many knots and, thinking "there will be much delay for one who cuts through the knots," thrusts his hand inside and, having cut the pole right where it is reached—both at the base and the tip—takes it and departs;
although he goes earlier than the other, [he still takes the time required].
But suppose he does not find a pole that is either strong or straight. Another man, seeing a bamboo of exactly that kind, thinks:
"If I take a pole of such perfection, I shall not obtain one that is strong or straight.
He binds his loincloth, cuts the bamboo thicket with a large knife, selects and takes away poles that are both strong and straight, and departs. Although this [second man]...
He goes last, yet he obtains poles that are both strong and straight;
in the same way, such is the nature of the striving of these two elders.
Here, the "course of comprehension" (sammasanacāra) should be understood as the plane of insight (vipassanābhūmi), for it is called the "course of comprehension" because one comprehends there.

Having done so. In that regard, they say that the range of the Buddhas’ contemplation consists of the formations contained within the mental continuums of beings throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system, as well as those not bound by the sense-faculties.
Others say it extends through a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

For indeed, having entered into the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) by way of what belongs to oneself, the great diamond-like knowledge (*mahāvajirañāṇa*) of the Buddhas operates through thirty-six hundred thousand times ten million modes.

[They are] occurring. They say that for Paccekabuddhas, the "course of comprehension" consists of the formations belonging to the mental continuums of beings dwelling in the Middle Country, together with those belonging to their own mental continuum, as well as those not bound by the sense faculties. Some say they belong to the mental continuums of inhabitants of Jambudīpa.

Regarding all phenomena belonging to one's own continuum and those belonging to the continua of others, without making a distinction between the continua, [one contemplates them] by way of their commonality as being external.

This is the method of comprehension for disciples. However, the Elder Moggallāna also comprehended external phenomena by selecting various ones according to their respective continuity, yet he did so merely by touching them with knowledge.
Therefore it is said: "Comprehending only a single portion, as if pressing down with the tip of a stick. In that context, by means of knowledge—
Because he did not proceed as far as the object required for the full turning [of insight], it is said, "as if pressing with the tip of a stick";
because he lacked the insight into phenomena according to their specific sequence (*anupadadhammavipassanā*), it is said, "comprehending only a single portion.

Even for the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), the range of comprehension was merely the stage of insight belonging to the aforementioned disciples. However, in that regard, the Elder (Mahāmoggallāna) was preeminent.
He saw it correctly, without remainder and in accordance with the sequence. Therefore it is said: "He comprehended the range of comprehension for disciples without omission.

And herein, among the six types of persons—the dry-insight practitioner, the worldling who has attained mundane direct knowledge, the ordinary disciple, the great disciple, the chief disciple, and the paccekabuddha—because the dry-insight practitioners have not attained the wisdom and proficiency that come through the jhānas and direct knowledges, [they are distinguished from the others].
At the time of insight (vipassanā), there is no cultivation of whichever dhammas one desires, as if walking toward a desired destination while blind;
rather, they develop insight only upon those dhammas already delimited.
However, ordinary disciples who have attained mundane direct knowledge (lokīyābhiññā) expand their insight even beyond the specific gateway through which they initially began it.

Because of their vast knowledge, they are able to expand insight (*vipassanā*). Because the Great Disciples (*mahāsāvaka*) were endowed with the excellence of their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), they were able to expand insight even more extensively than that.
Among the Chief Disciples (*aggasāvaka*), the second [disciple] expands insight even more than that because his concentration (*samādhi*) was superior due to the perfection of his initial resolve.
However, the first [disciple] expands it even further than that because of his great wisdom (*mahāpaññā*).

Having made it non-common to his disciples, he causes insight (vipassanā) to spread widely. Paccekabuddhas, because of their great resolve (mahābhinīhāra), cause insight to spread even more widely than that, in accordance with their own resolve.
For Buddhas, [insight] is developed through the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) fully fulfilled;
it is suitable for the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), just as, for example, [skill in archery] is due to practice in hitting a target with a reed-shaft.
Just as an arrow shot by a marksman like Sarabhaṅga falls upon the target itself without being obstructed by trees, creepers, or other things along the way—
neither sticking nor missing its mark— so too, insight (vipassanā), without being obstructed or missing its mark in between,
proceeds toward the phenomena to be comprehended through various methods according to their true nature; this is what is called "the great diamond-like knowledge" (mahāvajirañāṇa).

Among these, the practice of insight (vipassanā-cāra) for those practicing dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka) is like the light of a firefly; for ordinary disciples who have attained direct knowledge (abhiññā), it is like the light of a lamp;
for the great disciples (mahāsāvaka), it is like the light of a torch; for the chief disciples (aggasāvaka), it is like the light of the medicinal star (osadhitāraka);
for the paccekabuddhas, it is like the light of the moon; and for the perfectly enlightened Buddhas (sammāsambuddha), it is like the orb of the autumn sun adorned with a thousand rays.
Having offered it, it stands near. Thus, the practice of insight for those who practice dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka) is like the walking of blind people with the tip of a staff;

for ordinary disciples who have attained mundane supernormal powers (lokīyābhiññā), it is like walking on a bridge made of sticks; for the great disciples (mahāsāvaka), it is like walking on a bridge made of logs;
for the chief disciples (aggasāvaka), it is like walking on a bridge made of carts; and for the Paccekabuddhas, it is like traveling on a great highway.
It is like the great caravan road traveled by the Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas).

Likewise, the insight of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas should be understood as having become self-origined knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) because it is developed through knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayañāṇa*); whereas that of others is born from the instruction of others because it is developed through knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayañāṇa*).
Now, in order to show the past conduct (*pubbayoga*) of both elders, he said, "In the past, it is said... and so forth. All of that is of plain meaning.
63. *Giribbaja-nagara*: It is called *Giribbaja* because it stands surrounded on all sides by mountains like a fence (*vaja*);
thus is named the city of Rājagaha. Regarding the phrase "or in the sense of the accusative," this is stated with reference to its status as the object of the act of envy.
The commentary on the account of the going-forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is finished.
Commentary on the Account of the Duties toward a Preceptor (Upajjhāyavatta): 64.
One who contemplates what is blameworthy and what is blameless is a preceptor (*upajjhāya*); those who have no such preceptor are "without a preceptor" (*anupajjhāyaka*).

Therefore he said: "devoid of a teacher who scrutinizes what is blameworthy and what is blameless. In this context, "blameworthy and blameless" (*vajjāvajja*) refers to both minor and major faults (*vajja*).
This prefix *a-* has the sense of increase (*vuddhi*), as in the word "various fruits" (*phalāphala*) and so forth. Regarding the term "leftover bowl" (*uttiṭṭhapatta*):
here, the word *uttiṭṭha* has the same meaning as the word *ucchiṭṭha*. For this very reason it was said: "In that regard, people perceive it as leftover (*ucchiṭṭha*)."

"Therefore, it is said: 'Arise, O bowl! By the phrase "the bowl for wandering for alms," however, the reason for its designation as *ucchiṭṭhaka* (leftover) is clarified by way of showing the bowl's actual nature. "In that" means in that bowl used for wandering for alms.
65. Regarding the words "respectful and deferential": here, *gārava* is the state of being weighty; it is the quality of being held in high esteem, like a stone parasol.
"With respect" means possessing respect (*sagāravā*). "Obedience" (*patissa*) is the act of listening with a sense of reverence when something is said by one who is venerable;

the meaning is that "respect" (*gārava*) refers to anything that constitutes such obedience or is of a similar nature. "With obedience" means possessing obedience (*sappatissā*), which signifies receiving instruction.
Alternatively, "obedience" (*patissa*) is that which is to be obeyed—that is, what is to be revered. "With that obedience" means together with that reverence.

"Respectful. In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, without analyzing the phrasing, it is said "having established both the state of being venerable and the state of being senior," merely to show the sense.

"Sāhu" means "well done. "Lahu" means "not heavy"; the meaning is: "In my being your preceptor, there is nothing burdensome. "Opāyika" means connected with skillful means; [it refers to] your taking of a preceptor.
By this means, it is said: "From now on, you have become a burden to me. "Patirūpaṃ" means a suitable choice of preceptor for you.
"Pāsādikena" means by means of a pleasing application of body and speech. "Sampādehi" means accomplish the threefold training.
"Kāyena vā" means either by showing hand gestures and so forth with the body.
“Makes known. When it says, “… you have accepted… he makes known,” this means that by saying even one of these words such as “Very well” (sāhu), he is said to make this matter known.
For this very reason, it says, “For this indeed,” and so forth.
“With regard to the acceptance ‘Very well’” means with regard to the accepting word “Very well” spoken by the student when the preceptor has said “Very well.”
Why is it not considered a formal measure? He says: "Merely by means of a request and a gift," and so forth.

The meaning is: merely by the act of requesting on the part of the *saddhivihārika* (resident pupil), saying, "Venerable sir, please be my preceptor (*upajjhāya*)," and merely by the act of giving a verbal response on the part of the preceptor, saying, "Very well," and so forth.
In this case, formal acceptance is not a constituent factor; for here, the statement of acceptance belongs to the *saddhivihārika*.
In the taking of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), [the student] is not a constituent factor.
66. "Proper conduct" (*sammāvattanā*) means right behavior. "Of him" (*assā*) refers to the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*).

"The same kind of water for rinsing the mouth should be given" means that it should be given of the same kind when the season and the physical condition are identical. "Two robes" (*dve cīvarāni*) refers to the upper and lower garments.
He speaks with reference to the *saṅghāṭi* (outer robe). If this is so, why is it said "the *saṅghāṭīs*"? He says:

"For all robes are called *saṅghāṭī* because they are sewn together (*saṅghaṭita*). Regarding the phrase "by the strides of the feet" (*padavītihārehi*): here, that wherein one places the foot is a "foot-stride" (*padavītihāra*), meaning the place where the foot is placed;
[this refers to] walking at a moderate pace, without making the gait too hurried or too slow, for the two [monks].
"A space of one *muṭṭhi-ratana* between the feet. Or, "the stepping of the feet" means placing them down after having moved them forward;
this is how the meaning should be understood here. "From this point on" means starting from the word "not" (*na*) as stated in the passage:
"Not [while] the preceptor is speaking. In all such cases, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is to be understood; even for one who is ill... [in such instances].
This was stated for the purpose of showing that one is not released [from the offense].

For indeed, in all cases where one who is not ill fails to perform the aforementioned duties toward the preceptor out of disrespect, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) offense for the breach of duty. Therefore, he will say:
"Even a *saddhivihārika* who is sixty years old must perform all the duties toward the preceptor when not ill; for one who performs them disrespectfully..."
"In the case of a breach of the formal procedure (vatta), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

However, regarding those instances associated with the word 'not' (na-kāra), even for one who is ill, performing an action that is prohibited constitutes an offense of wrong-doing. The phrase "speech proximate to an offense" refers specifically to speech that generates an offense.
For whatever speech by which one incurs an offense, that speech is said to be "proximate" to that offense.
"Having wrapped the bowl with a robe": regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "having wrapped it with one corner of the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
"In a village" means in some such place included within a village. "In a house" means inside a dwelling.
"At the place of returning" means in the assembly hall (*āsanasālā*). The connection is: "He should be asked three times for water"—namely, at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
The meaning is that he should be asked three times. "Upakaṭṭho" means near. "Dhotavālikāya" means with sand that is free from dust and perfectly pure.
"Sace pahoti" clarifies the same point already stated: "he is not overcome by any illness.
"Pariveṇaṃ gantvā" means having gone to the preceptor’s courtyard.
The commentary on the section concerning the duties toward the preceptor is finished.
67. The section concerning the duties toward the co-resident student is of obvious meaning.
Commentary on the section concerning improper conduct, etc.
68. Regarding the discussion on "love based on the household" (*gehassita-pema*) in the *Nasammāvattanādikathā*: "Love arisen thus, 'This is my father'" refers to the love that has arisen.
For here, "love based on the household" means precisely the manifestation of the mind toward one's father as a father.
This is not stated with reference to the unwholesome side of love based on the household, because such love is impossible for those who have penetrated the Truths and have abandoned all attachment.

The Blessed One does not enjoin the bhikkhus toward defilement; rather, it should be understood that here the moisture of loving-kindness (*mettāsineha*) is spoken of by way of affection, because it resembles the affection rooted in the household life. From the statement, "If among them one bhikkhu is perfect in his duties...
[omission] ...for them there is no offense," it follows that if one bhikkhu who is perfect in his duties says, "Venerable sirs, you remain free from anxiety; I shall [attend to you]," etc.
If he says, "I will attend to my co-resident or pupil when they are ill; I will instruct them;

and I will exert myself in their duties," or if those co-residents and others say to him, "Venerable sir, you should remain entirely free from such concerns," or if they do not consent to the proper conduct (*vatta*), then from that point on...
They say there is no offense for teachers and preceptors. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the discussion concerning improper conduct is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the story of the Brahmin Rādha.
69. In the story of the Brahmin Rādha, "he became emaciated" means that being unable to eat or consume food, he became thin, with little flesh and blood.
"Becoming pale and wan" means having become pale and wan, resembling a withered leaf.
"With veins covering his limbs" means that because his flesh and blood were completely exhausted, his body was covered by a network of veins. "The task" (adhikāraṃ) [refers to...]
"Service" means honor; this is what is meant. "Grateful" (*kataññuno*) means those who know what has been done for them; "thankful" (*katavedino*) means those who know it by making it manifest.

But does the Elder not know that the Blessed One, at Bārāṇasī, permitted both the going forth and the full ordination through the threefold taking of refuge? No, he does not not know it. If that is so, [why did he say], "Venerable sir, how shall I..."?
With reference to the inquiry, "Why did he say, 'I ordain this brahmin; I confer full admission upon him'?", [the Buddha] said, "Even though the Venerable Sāriputta," and so forth.

"Parimaṇḍalehi" means "with those that are complete. Or rather, it could be stated as follows: "He says one thing when another should be said"—that is, where "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*) should be said, he says "Bound One" (*bandhe*).
71–73. *Samanantara* means immediately following. "He commits a transgression of the rules" (*paṇṇattivītikkama*) means he commits a transgression of the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*).

They are called "supports" (*nissaya*) because they are relied upon for the sake of maintaining one's person; they are the four requisites, beginning with the food of alms-gathered morsels (*piṇḍiyālopabhojana*).
Among these, "the food of alms-gathered morsels" refers to the food obtained merely in mouthfuls by wandering on the strength of one's calves.

"Extra gain" (*atirekalābha*) refers to gains in excess of the food obtained from alms-gathering—as described by the phrase "subsisting on morsels of alms-food"—such as meals provided by the Saṅgha (*saṅghabhatta*), and so forth.
Among these, a meal to be given to the entire Saṅgha is a *saṅghabhatta*.
A meal to be given specifically for a designated number of bhikkhus is an *uddesabhatta*. A meal to be given after having invited [the recipients] is a *nimantana*.
“Ticket-food” (salākabhatta) is food to be given after having tickets distributed. “Fortnightly food” (pakkhika) is food to be given on one day during a fortnight.
“Uposatha food” (uposathika) is food to be given on the Uposatha day. “First-day-of-the-month food” (pāṭipadika) is food to be given on the first day of the lunar month.
An extensive explanation of these will appear in the commentary on the Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka).
“Vihāra” refers to the entire dwelling enclosed by a wall.
“Aḍḍhayoga” is a long palace; some also say it is a palace shaped like a garuḷa. “Pāsāda” is a square palace.
“Hammiya” is a palace with a flat roof. Others, however, say: “Vihāra” is a long-faced palace, while an “aḍḍhayoga” is...
A "one-sided-roofed" lodging is so called because, it is said, the wall on one side is higher while the other side is lower;
thus, it has a roof on only one side. A "pāsāda" is a long or square palace; a "hammiya" is a flat-roofed structure provided with a courtyard.
A "guhā" is a mountain cave. "Pūtimutta" refers to any kind of urine. Just as even one who is gold-colored...
The body is called a "putrid body," and likewise, even fresh urine is simply putrid urine. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the story of the Brahmin Rādha is finished.
The commentary on the discourse on the teacher’s duties.
75. In the *Upasena-vatthu*, "accustomed" (*āciṇṇa*) refers to conduct, duty, and accordance with the Dhamma. "Is it endurable for you, monk? means:
Is this body of yours—with its four wheels and nine gates—endurable for you? Is it possible for you to endure, to bear, and to maintain it?
Does it not produce any suffering? "Is it sustainable? means: In all your affairs...
"It can be maintained; it shows no obstacle whatsoever. Even though the Tathāgatas know [the answer], the passage beginning with "Thus, etc.
was spoken for the purpose of providing an answer to what another asked later, starting with, "Bhikkhu, how many years have you been ordained?
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: although the Tathāgatas know, they nevertheless ask if there is such a reason for asking.

But if there is no such reason for questioning, they do not ask even though they know [the answer]. However, because there is no such thing as ignorance on the part of the Buddhas, it was not said that "they do not ask because they do not know.
"Knowing the right time, they ask" means: if that is the proper time for that question, then knowing that time, they ask; if it is not the proper time, then likewise—

Having understood the proper time, they do not ask. Even when they do ask, the Tathāgatas ask only that which is beneficial, that which is grounded in purpose and grounded in reason; they do not ask what is unbeneficial. Why?
Because for the Tathāgatas, there is a destruction of the bridge regarding what is unbeneficial. "Bridge" is a term for the path; it is by means of the path that such speech [is avoided].
"Striking" means "complete eradication.

Now, regarding the phrase "connected with the goal" (*atthasaṃhita*), the Blessed One speaks of "in two ways" and so forth, demonstrating that speech which is based on a specific purpose (*atthanissita*) and which the Tathāgatas inquire about.
In this context, "ways" (*ākārehi*) means "reasons" (*kāraṇehi*). "I shall teach the Dhamma" refers to [teaching] that which is connected to the origin of the matter (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
We shall either recite a sutta connected with past deeds, or a Jātaka;

or we shall lay down a training rule for the disciples—meaning that, having made manifest through that question of the disciples a transgression, we shall lay down a training rule that is either heavy or light, and establish an injunction. "Too quickly" means too hastily.

76. Regarding the case of one who was formerly a member of another sect (*aññatitthiyavatthu*): "one who was formerly a member of another sect" (*aññatitthiyapubbo*) means one who previously became a member of another sect.

Herein, the "ford" (*tittha*) is to be understood, the "founder of the ford" (*titthakara*) is to be understood, the "members of other sects" (*titthiya*) are to be understood, and the "disciples of those members of other sects" (*titthiyasāvaka*) are to be understood.
In this context, the "ford" refers to the sixty-two views; for it is here that beings cross over and float.
They perform the act of diving in and out; therefore, they are called "ford-makers" (*titthakara*). One who causes those views to arise is called a "ford-maker," such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others.
Those who have gone forth having adopted his doctrine are called "sectarians" (*titthiya*). For they are called sectarians because they were born at a ford (*titthe jātā*);
or alternatively, they are called "ford-possessors" (*titthika*) because these [views] possess a "ford" consisting of the aforementioned range of views.
"Titthiyā" means those belonging to other sects (titthikā). Those who provide requisites for them should be understood as "titthiya-sāvakā" (disciples of other sects).

"Being spoken to by one who belongs to the same Dhamma" (*sahadhammikena vuccamāno*) means being addressed by one who shares the same Dhamma; here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent.
It is called "sahadhammika" because it is to be trained in by the five [factors] belonging to the same Dhamma, or because it belongs to them, and it is designated by the Buddha.
The meaning is: "being addressed by a training rule. *Pasūra* is his name. A *paribbājaka* is one who has gone forth, having abandoned the bonds of a householder.

Regarding the phrase "that very sectarian foundation" (*titthāyatana*): here, the sixty-two views themselves are the "sect" (*tittha*), and that [sect] itself is the "foundation" (*āyatana*); thus it is a "sectarian foundation."
They are called *titthin* because they have a "ford" (*tittha*) [of views]; thus they are the *titthiyas*. The "source" (*āyatana*) of those [titthiyas] is also called the *titthāyatana*.
Regarding the term "source" (*āyatana*), in such passages as "Kamboja is the source of horses; the Southern Route is the source of cattle," it means a place of birth.
[As in: "In delightful sources, birds frequent them."
“Those seeking shade go to the shade; those who eat fruit go for the sake of fruit.
Here [the term] refers to a place of assembly (*samosaraṇaṭṭhāna*). In the passage, “Bhikkhus, there are these five bases of liberation,” it refers to a cause (*kāraṇa*);
all of that is applicable here as well. For all those who hold views (*diṭṭhigatika*), when they are being born, [do so] within these very sixty-two [views].
They are born amidst views; even when gathering together, they gather and assemble within these very [views].
And it is these sixty-two views that are the cause for their state of being followers of false views (diṭṭhigatika).

Therefore, because it is the aforementioned *tittha* (ford) in the sense of being the place of birth and so forth, it is a "source of fords" (*titthāyatana*); and in that same sense, it is also the "source of those who follow fords" (*titthīnaṃ āyatanaṃ*), thus it is called *titthāyatana*.
Regarding the phrase "I will live depending on the Venerable One" (*āyasmato nissāya vacchāmi*): here, "of the Venerable One" (*āyasmato*) is the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative;
the meaning is "I will live depending on the Venerable One. "Qualified" (*byatto*)...

[as far as] "...is precisely the characteristic already stated"—this is said with reference to one who is well-versed in the scriptures and capable of attending to the assembly. Regarding the passage beginning "With five factors, Upāli," whatever is to be said therein will be made clear further on.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Duties toward the Teacher is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Sending Away and the Asking for Forgiveness: 80.
The connection is with the phrase "the characteristic which was stated previously"; by that very characteristic, [it applies] to the resident pupil (*nissaya-antevāsika*).
The reading found in the manuscripts is, “the offense is to be understood [as such]”;
however, the reading to be understood here is, “the offense of the resident pupil (nissayantevāsika) is not to be understood by that same characteristic.

Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood as follows: the offense of the resident pupil is not to be understood by the characteristic stated for the student (saddhivihārika). Otherwise...
Otherwise, this would contradict the statement: “Indeed, as long as a resident dependent lives in dependence upon his teacher, he must perform all the duties toward the teacher.
For this statement indicates that an offense occurs for a resident dependent who, while not yet released from dependence, fails to perform the duties.
Therefore, [the rule applies] to a student living with his teacher who fails to perform the aforementioned duties while not yet released from dependence.

It should be understood that there is an offense even for one who has not relinquished [the connection], but for one who is under formal dependence (*nissaya*), the offense applies only to one who has not relinquished that dependence.
For this very reason, in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the discussion on the impediment of relatives (*ñātipalibodha*), it says:

"Relatives means: those who are one’s teacher (*ācariya*) or preceptor (*upajjhāya*) in the monastery, as well as one’s co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), one’s own dependent pupil (*antevāsika*), one who shares the same preceptor (*samānupajjhāyaka*), and one who shares the same teacher (*samānācariyaka*)."
At home, there are mother, father, sisters, brothers, and so forth. When they are ill, they become obstacles for him;
therefore, that obstacle must be severed by attending to them and restoring them to health.
In this regard, if first the preceptor falls ill and does not recover quickly, he must be looked after for as long as he lives. The same applies to the teacher of the going-forth.
“The preceptor for full ordination, the student living with him, those who have been ordained and given the going-forth by him,
and those who share the same preceptor— these must be looked after. Furthermore, the teacher of dependence, the teacher of recitation, the dependent student, the student of recitation,
and those who share the same teacher must be looked after as long as the dependence and the recitation are not yet terminated.”

It was stated by way of distinction. Furthermore, this distinction would not be tenable if the reading were, "By that same characteristic, the offense of the resident pupil (nissayantevāsika) is to be understood.

For this reading [implies] that just as for the co-resident (saddhivihārika), so too for the resident pupil who fails to perform the aforementioned duties—whether he has been released from dependence or not—there is an offense; such is the meaning.
It illuminates [the meaning]; therefore, the reading should be accepted here exactly according to the method already stated.

Regarding the duties toward those who have gone forth, those who are ordained, and Dhamma-students: “… until such time as these duties must be performed”—thus the duties as previously described must be performed for the teacher of going forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of ordination (*upasampadācariya*), and the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*).
Among them, he by whom the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were given is the teacher of going forth.

He by whom the formal act of ordination (*upasampadakammavācā*) is recited is the preceptor for ordination (*upasampadācariya*). He who provides the recitation (*uddesa*) or the interrogation (*paripucchā*) is to be understood as the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*). The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the dismissal and the asking for forgiveness is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Dependence (Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā) 83.
In the discussion on the cessation of dependence, "gone to a region" means that he has gone to some region for the purpose of staying, whether intending to return again or not intending to return.
"Having observed the bhikkhu’s companionship" means having examined his state of being virtuous. "Having looked upon" means having scrutinized.

"Venerable sir... [and so on] ... "one must go there": if, due to some business, one is unable to go that very day but has the intention to go, thinking, "I will go after a few days," they say that one maintains [the dependence]. "Do not return here" means do not enter here.
"One must dwell right there" means one must dwell having received dependence (*nissaya*) right there. That very...

Regarding the statement, "It is permissible to dwell in a monastery...," because [the student] has been relinquished by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), there is no exemption from the requirement of being in the presence of the preceptor;
therefore, even if one is in the company of the preceptor, the formal dependence (*nissaya*) received from the teacher (*ācariya*) is not suspended.
Regarding the suspensions of dependence from a teacher, in the case where it is said, "The teacher has departed," here "departed" means [having gone to] a direction...
The method of decision regarding the departure of a preceptor, which was stated in the passage beginning with "gone," can be understood here as well by the very same method explained there;
therefore, without repeating that, another method is commenced beginning with "some teacher departs after having asked for leave.
And this method should certainly be understood to apply to the departure of a preceptor as well. For in such instances...

The characteristic stated in one place should be understood to apply elsewhere as well. If he returns after having passed two *leḍḍupāta*s (the distance of a stone’s throw), it is said that "he has become pacified";
in this context, he is considered to have gone away from his district, and thus the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended even for a pupil who has not relinquished his duties.
If the teacher or preceptor goes to another monastery beyond two *leḍḍupāta*s...

“They dwell” means that they dwell in another lodging outside the outer boundary (bahi-upacāra-sīmā), having passed beyond two throws of a clod from the dwelling place of the resident pupils and co-residents;
however, even if they dwell inside the inner boundary (anta-upacāra-sīmā) after passing beyond two throws of a clod, the dependence (nissaya) is not suspended.
“Even if the teacher, wishing to release [the pupil], [proceeds] with the dismissal from dependence...”
The entire passage beginning with “paṇāmeti” should be understood as applying even when the preceptor gives an instruction. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the cessation of dependence is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion regarding the five things that must be conferred for full ordination.

84. Regarding the passage beginning with "Endowed with five factors, monks... and so forth, the phrase "a novice should not be attended" means that one should not accept a novice [as a pupil] while acting as his preceptor (*upajjhāya*). This meaning has indeed been stated in the *Aṅguttara-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā*:
"First, one should establish oneself in what is appropriate;
then one may instruct others; thus the wise man shall not come to grief."

In accordance with this [subject], first, in order to direct him toward the perfection of self (*attasampatti*), it was said, "Not by the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training" (*na asekkhena sīlakkhandhena*), and so forth;
it was not said by way of the factors of an offense (*āpattiaṅga*). Therein, "by the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training" means:

the aggregate of virtue belonging to one beyond training is called the "aggregate of virtue of one beyond training. For that which belongs to one beyond training (*asekkha*) is "of one beyond training"; such is the aggregate of virtue. This applies everywhere in the same manner.
And by doing so, the state of being beyond training (asekkhatā) is established even for the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), which is termed "knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, by the term "virtue of one beyond training" (asekkhasīla), not only the Path and Fruition are intended;

rather, it refers to whatever virtue occurs within the continuum of one beyond training, because here virtue—whether mundane or supramundane—is what is intended. This applies likewise to the aggregate of concentration and the other aggregates.

This same method applies to the conclusions of the sections on the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*). Therefore, just as the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom are intended here in their mixed form, so too is the aggregate of liberation;
thus, it should be understood to include liberation by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and the others, and not merely liberation by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhivimutti*).
However, the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is purely mundane. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*:
“By the first four terms, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are explained;
the knowledge and vision of liberation is reflective knowledge, which is purely mundane.

Regarding the three bases beginning with “one who lacks faith”: one who lacks faith (*assaddho*) is so called because he has no faith in these [bases]. On the side of the bright, one who has faith (*saddahati*)...

One who has faith, or one in whom faith exists, is "faithful" (*saddho*). One who lacks moral shame (*hirī*) is "shameless" (*ahiriko*); this is a designation for one who feels no disgust toward the attainment of unwholesome states.
One who possesses moral shame is "possessed of shame" (*hirimā*). One who does not feel dread is "without dread" (*anottappī*);
this means he does not fear the attainment of unwholesome states. The opposite of that is "one who has dread" (*ottappī*). One who sinks into what is contemptible is... [the term *sīlavā*].

“Laziness” (*kusīta*) is a designation for one who possesses inferior energy. “One whose energy is aroused” (*āraddhavīriya*) means one whose energy has been initiated; it is a designation for one who is engaged in the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).

“One whose mindfulness is muddled” (*muṭṭhassati*) means one whose mindfulness is lost; what is meant is that his mindfulness has perished. “One whose mindfulness is established” (*upaṭṭhitassati*) means one whose mindfulness is firmly set;
it is a designation for one whose mindfulness constantly proceeds directed toward the object of focus.
One who has failed in virtue regarding higher morality (*adhisīla*) and has failed in conduct regarding higher conduct (*ajjhācāra*), having committed an offense and not having emerged from it;
or, that which grasps or causes others to grasp an "extreme" defined as eternalism or annihilationism is "extremist view" (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*). The first two phrases refer to:
"He is not capable of attending to, or causing another to attend to, a sick pupil (*antevāsī*) or co-resident (*saddhivihārī*)."
“...to cause one who is dissatisfied to depart, or to have him caused to depart”—these are the two phrases.
Excellent and supreme conduct is *abhisamācāra*; because it is to be trained in, it is a training (*sikkhā*), thus it is the training of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārikā sikkhā*);
or, the training prescribed with reference to higher conduct is the training of higher conduct. Of the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*)...

“Fundamental” (ādibhūta) means fundamental to the holy life (ādibrahmacariyaka); this is a designation for the training included within the two Vibhaṅgas. For that very reason, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:
“That which is included in the two Vibhaṅgas is fundamental to the holy life; that which is included in the Khandhakas and the Vattas is pertaining to proper conduct (ābhisamācārika).
Therefore, regarding the phrase “in the presentation of the trainee” (sekkhapaṇṇattiyaṃ), all [training] included in the two Vibhaṅgas is so called because it is to be trained in.
It should be understood as "a designation" (*paṇṇatti*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*:

"'In the designation of training for those in training' means in the designation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) that must be practiced, beginning with the *pārājika*. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the discussion of the five things to be ordained is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Former Life as a Member of Another Sect (Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā): 86.
Regarding the section on "a member of another sect," there are two kinds of naked wanderers (*naggaparibbājaka*): the Ājīvaka and the Acelaka. Thus it was said:
"Of either a naked wanderer or an Ājīvaka," and so forth. In that context, an Ājīvaka wears a single garment by tucking it into his armpits.
"Down below" means naked. "A naked ascetic" (acelaka) means one who is entirely naked in every respect.
87. "The offering of some small material thing" refers to the giving away of even a very trifling object worthy of being given.
"Those who live by their beauty" means those who subsist solely by relying on their own physical form. "The resort of courtesans" is a place to be approached by way of intimate friendship.
"Assa" means one who frequents prostitutes. This same method applies everywhere.

By both terms—“those who have reached youth” and “those past youth”—he refers specifically to old women who are not yet widowed or unmarried girls. "Bhikkhunīs" refers to those whose holy life (*brahmacariya*) is flourishing;
the same applies to monks as well. Because they constitute a mutual basis for what is unbecoming (*visabhāga*), if one approaches them out of intimacy, in just a few days...
"It may become an obstacle to the holy life," he said, "for with them there is quickly intimacy, and from that the virtue is broken.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the account concerning those who were formerly members of other sects is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Bases for Illness (Pañcābādhavatthukathāvaṇṇanā):

88. Regarding the phrase "the size of a fingernail's surface" in the section on the five bases for illness, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "the surface of the fingernail of the little finger is intended.
"And if even that size of a fingernail's surface is situated on the side of growth..."
By the statement, “He exists; he should not be ordained,” the general characteristic is shown.
Therefore, it is established that if [a mark] anywhere on the parts of the body is of the size of a fingernail’s back and stands on the side of being increased, it is not permitted.
And this being so, if even a mark the size of a fingernail’s back stands on the side of not being increased, it is permitted everywhere.
Since that which has been transgressed is not intended here in its general sense, he says “If, however,” etc., showing it by restricting it to a specific portion.

For if, without distinction, even the size of a fingernail were permitted when situated in a place not subject to growth, he would not have made the restriction of the location as “in a place naturally covered by the undergarment and upper robe. Therefore, [regarding] the undergarment and upper robe—
It is established that, other than in a naturally concealed place, it is not permitted even if it remains on the non-expanding side, provided it is the size of a fingernail’s back;
however, if it is smaller than the size of a fingernail’s back, it is permitted whether it remains on the non-expanding side or the expanding side.
On the expanding side, [it is permitted] for something smaller than the size of a fingernail’s back, on both the expanding and non-expanding sides.
Or rather, because [the use of a cloth] for the mouth and so forth has already been prohibited.
By this same method, the decision regarding the boil (*gaṇḍa*) should also be understood.

However, since even a boil smaller than a jujube seed (*kolaṭṭhi*) is not permitted on the mouth and other such parts, it was not mentioned separately. "On the mouth and other uncovered places... [and so on].
For there, it is stated only thus: "Even one who stands on the side of the non-proliferating [growth] is not permitted.

Nevertheless, according to the method explained regarding skin diseases (*kuṭṭha*), it is understood that even a boil smaller than the size of a jujube stone (*kolaṭṭhi*) on the face or other parts is not permitted;

therefore, in the phrase "even one who stands on the side of the non-proliferating," the word *pi* (even/also) has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned. By this, from the size of a jujube stone...
The meaning that "even something smaller than that is not permitted" has indeed already been shown; this is our own position.
"Born in its natural color" is said with reference to the absence of any disfigured color caused by disease. "The size of a jujube stone" means the measure of a *badara* fruit pit.
"Having had the skin removed" means having had the skin stripped away. There is also a reading, "having had the skin made whole" (*sañchaviṃ kāretvā*), which refers to the skin that is still present.
"Having caused [it] to be made"—this is the meaning. "The color of the petals of the red and white lotuses" refers to the color of lotus petals by way of the red lotus and the white lotus.
"The disease of emaciation" is a wasting disease.
The commentary on the discussion of the five bases for affliction is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Cases of the King’s Servant and Others (90–96).
Regarding the cases of the king’s servant and others, the phrase "people said" (*āhaṃsu*) means that people spoke.

Therefore... [omission] ...he spoke thus: because he himself is the Lord of Dhamma, he ordained the thief Aṅgulimāla—who had not been ordained by the monks—for the sake of his future abstention from such deeds.
While laying down the training rule for the bhikkhus, he said: "Bhikkhus, a bandit with a raised banner should not be ordained;
whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "They desist" means they cease, they turn back. "Having broken" means having broken the bond of fetters.
"Having cut" means having cut the bond of shackles. "Having released" means [having released] the bond of ropes.
"Having released. "Having opened" means having opened the village gates and so forth among the village bonds and the like.
"Or he flees while they do not see him" means he flees while the men guarding him do not see him. "Little by little" (upaḍḍhupaḍḍhaṃ) means bit by bit. 97.
At coronations and other such occasions, they clean the prisons and so forth; with reference to that, he says: "or by way of what is common to all."
If they themselves draft the document, it is not permitted. Thus, those free-born women, thinking "we too shall become slaves," have themselves write a slave-document;
this is not permitted. They are like those who have poured buttermilk over their heads;
just as those making a mirror wash their head with buttermilk and thereby make it a non-mirror, so too [the document] is rendered invalid because it was given by the word of a monastery attendant.
The intended meaning is "he is not a slave. However, they say that pouring oil [on the head] was the custom in the island of Sri Lanka.

It is said that "he must not be ordained" because, even if he were given by means of a formal declaration of validity (*kappiya-vacana*), he would still be a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*) belonging to the Saṅgha; it is for this reason that it was stated thus.
One called a "slave without an owner" is one whose owners—including wife and children—have died, and no one remains to claim him as their own; such a person may also be ordained.

It is not permissible; however, it is permissible for him to make himself a free man (*bhujissa*). Or, it is also permissible for him to have [the status] arranged by those who are the masters in that kingdom.
It is stated in the *Tīsu Gaṇṭhipadesu* (The Three Knots): “It is permissible to ordain the son of Devadāsi.
They say that there is no offense for a slave who, having gone forth, flees upon seeing his own master.
The rest is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the account concerning the king’s soldiers and so forth is finished.
The commentary on the account concerning the release from dependence.
103. Regarding the fivefold and sixfold duties for one who is released from dependence (*nissayamuccanaka*), it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that:
"Furthermore, this entire classification is understood once the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* has been understood," specifically in the passage beginning with "Both... [and] the secondary characteristics.
And regarding the phrases "knows the offense" (*āpattiṃ jānāti*) and so forth, even if the text itself is not recited, [it means] "having done such-and-such, one incurs such-and-such an offense."
"If he knows [this], it is permissible"—this was stated right there [in the text].

Furthermore, some say that this should be understood as applying only when the previous recitation has been mastered, and that the same principle applies to teachers and preceptors as well. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the discussion concerning release from dependence (*nissaya-muccanaka*) is finished.
Commentary on the Story of Rāhula (Rāhulavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 105.
Regarding the phrase "they dwelt right there" in the story of Rāhula: from the moment they all attained Arahatship, being noble ones (ariya), they remained indeed equanimous;
thus, without reporting the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha), they remained right there.
They lived there. One day, a minister named Kāḷudāyi was born; it is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.

While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who inspire confidence in families. Having performed a meritorious deed, he [aspired to] that very station.

He made this aspiration. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, on the very day the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of our mother, he himself took rebirth in Kapilavatthu in the house of a minister.
Because he was born on that same day as the Bodhisatta, on that very day [they placed him] in a swaddling cloth...

Having laid him down, they led him away for the purpose of attending upon the Bodhisatta. For together with the Bodhisatta, these seven were known as "co-born" (sahajāta), because they were born on the same day:
the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four jars of treasure, the state elephant Ārohaṇa, Kaṇḍaka, Channa, and Kāḷudāyī.
Then, on the day of his naming ceremony, throughout the entire city...
Because he was born on a day when the mind was uplifted, they gave him the name Udāyin; however, because his complexion was somewhat dark, he became known as Kāḷudāyin.
Growing up together with the Bodhisatta, playing as children, he attained maturity.
[He spoke] in about sixty verses:
“Now the trees have become like glowing coals, O Blessed One;
having cast off their foliage,
they shine forth as if possessed of flames.”
“O Great Hero, it is the proper time for the Bhāgīrathī rivers.
It is neither too cold nor too hot, nor is there excessive famine or drought;
the earth is lush and green—this is the season, O Great Sage.”
It consists of approximately sixty initial verses. Regarding the phrase "pokkharavassa," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that it means "water having the appearance of a lotus leaf.
They also say that it rains in drops the size of a lotus leaf, rising up in the center and gradually becoming a hundred-fold or a thousand-fold sheet as it falls.
It is said that when this rain falls, only those who wish to get wet get wet; it does not [wet others].

As for the others: not even a single king—or [as before]—among his kinsmen who had departed after hearing the Dhamma teaching remained to invite him, saying, "Come and receive alms from us tomorrow. Nor was there even a single king or royal minister who had gone [to invite him].
His father, the Great King Suddhodana, thought: "Where will my son go without coming to my own home?"
Having merely invited him, he departed; but having gone home, he had rice-gruel and other offerings prepared for twenty thousand bhikkhus and had seats arranged.
"In the city of the family" means in the city of his own kinsmen. "Starting from the *uṇhīsa*" means starting from the head.
For *uṇhīsa* is a designation for the Blessed One’s full forehead and full head, because it resembles a turban (*uṇhīsa*).
Indeed, from the right ear-apex of the Blessed One, a layer of flesh rises up, covering and filling the entire forehead, and proceeding on to rest upon the left ear-apex;
by virtue of its extreme softness, golden hue, radiance, and fullness, it shines like the bound turban-ribbon of a king. Of the Blessed One...
