It is said that having seen this mark, kings fashioned turbans for themselves. Other people, however, have incomplete heads:

some have shaven heads (*kappa-sīsa*), some have fruit-like heads (*phala-sīsa*), some have bony heads (*aṭṭhi-sīsa*), some have gourd-like heads (*tumba-sīsa*), some have jar-like heads (*kumbha-sīsa*), and some have sloping heads (*pabbhāra-sīsa*).
But the Blessed One’s head is perfectly complete, as if turned on a lathe, and resembles a water bubble.
Because his head resembles one wrapped in a turban, and because his head is perfectly round in every respect like a turban,
the Blessed One is called "Uṇhīsasīsa" (Turban-headed).
By means of the eight verses known as the *Narasīhagāthā*—
“With glossy, dark, soft, and curly hair;
with a forehead like the stainless surface of the sun;
and with a nose that is well-proportioned, prominent, and delicate.”
“The Lion among Men, spread with a network of rays”—with these eight verses beginning thus. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it says:
“His beautiful feet are marked with the excellent wheel;”
Adorned with the marks, with long heels;
his feet graced by the fly-whisk and the parasol—
this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
“The excellent Sakyan prince, delicate and refined,
his body adorned with the marks of a great man,
that hero among men has gone for the welfare of the world.”
For this is your father, a lion among men.
The color of his face resembles the full moon;
beloved even by gods and men, he is a bull among men.
Moving with the graceful gait of a lordly elephant in rut—
this indeed is your father, a lion among men.
Born of the Kṣatriya lineage, of the foremost noble family;
With feet honored by gods and humans,
with a mind established in virtue and concentration—
this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
His nose is well-proportioned and beautifully shaped;
his eyelashes are like those of a cow and his eyes are deep blue;
his lips are deep blue like the bow of Indra.
For this is your father, a lion among men:
with a neck rounded, well-turned, and beautifully shaped;
with jaws like a lion’s; and with the body of the king of beasts.
With a complexion like excellent, pure gold—
this indeed is your father, a lion among men.
With a voice that is affectionate, deep, and sweet;
With a beautiful tongue as red as vermilion or the bandhuka flower, and twenty even, white teeth—
this indeed is your father, a lion among men.
With hair as beautiful and deep blue-black as the color of collyrium,
with a forehead as pure as a strip of gold,
and with a face as bright and clear as the white medicinal herb (osadhi);
For this father of yours is a lion among men.
He goes like the moon on its path through the sky,
his form encircled by a host of stars.
“The Lord of Ascetics has entered among his disciples;
for he is your father, O lion among men.
These nine verses are also shown here, but they do not agree with the statement “by means of eight verses.”
Even the sequence described as "from the uṣṇīṣa down to the soles of the feet" is not seen there. "Bhikkhācāra" means one who goes for alms. Regarding "uttiṭṭhe":
having risen and stood at the door of another's house, one should receive the alms-food to be taken. "Nappamajjeyya" (one should not be negligent):
by neglecting the duty of wandering for alms and seeking out choice foods, one is said to be negligent when rising; [one should instead proceed] in regular succession.
But one who wanders for alms is said to be "not negligent"; acting thus, he should "arise and not be negligent. Regarding "the Dhamma":

having abandoned improper means of livelihood, wandering from house to house in regular succession, he should practice that very same well-practiced way of life consisting of the conduct of begging for alms.
"He sleeps in comfort"—this is merely a figurative expression; for one who thus practices this duty of wandering for alms is a practitioner of the Dhamma (*dhammacārī*).
The meaning is that he dwells happily in both this world and the next, and in all four modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).

Regarding the second verse: "He does not practice misconduct"—even while wandering in improper resorts (*agocara*) such as among prostitutes and the like, he does not truly practice that way of life for alms-seeking as misconduct;
rather, by not acting in such a manner, he should practice that dharma as good conduct, not as misconduct.
The meaning here is exactly as previously stated. It should be understood, however, that this second verse was spoken after he had gone to his father’s residence.
For this very reason, it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla in his *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"On the second day, having entered for alms, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry with the verse beginning, ‘Arise, do not be negligent.’"

"Having gone to the residence, by means of the verse, 'One should live according to the Dhamma, practicing good conduct,' he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and the King in the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala). It is also stated in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*:
"On the following day, having entered for alms, by means of the verse, 'Arise, do not be negligent,' he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry."
“By means of the verse ‘One should live according to the Dhamma,’ he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the King in the fruit of once-returning.
Having heard the Dhammapāla Jātaka, [the King] was established in the fruit of non-returning.
On another day, having partaken of his morning meal at the royal palace, the King sat to one side and said, “Venerable sir, when you were practicing austerities, a certain deity approached me and—”
When it was said, “‘Your son has died,’ he replied, ‘I do not believe her words; my son does not die until he has attained enlightenment. Now, how will you believe this?
Even previously, when they showed him bones and said, ‘Your son is dead,’ you did not believe it. On account of this occasion, [the Buddha related] the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka.
He preached [the Dhamma]. Having heard it, the king was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
"The shaving of the hair" refers to the cutting of the hair according to family custom. "The binding of the turban" refers to the binding of the crown prince’s turban.

"The festival of entering a new house" is the auspicious ceremony of the house; "the festival of performing a marriage" is the auspicious ceremony of the wedding. "The auspicious ceremony of the parasol" means...
The Auspiciousness of the Crown Prince’s Umbrella. "Janapadakalyāṇī" means she is beautiful and supreme in the land; she is free from the six bodily defects and endowed with the five excellences.
For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair;
thus, having transcended human beauty yet not reached divine beauty, she is free from the six bodily defects.

Because she is endowed with these five excellences—excellence of skin, excellence of flesh, excellence of sinews, excellence of bones, and excellence of youth—she is called "endowed with the five excellences. For she has no need for the function of adventitious light;
by the radiance of her own body alone, she creates light within a space of twelve cubits, and she is the color of yellow *piyaṅgu*.

Her skin is like refined gold; this is her excellence of complexion. Furthermore, her four hands and feet, as well as the area around her face, are like red coral or red woolen cloth, as if treated with lac-dye; this is her excellence of flesh.
Her twenty nails, where they are not detached from the flesh, appear as if filled with lac-dye, while where they are detached...
They are like streams of milk; this is her excellence of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth appear perfectly smooth, like a row of well-polished diamonds;
this is her excellence of bones. Even though she is a hundred and twenty years old, she appears as if she were sixteen years of age, free from wrinkles and grey hair;
this is her excellence of vitality. Thus, because she is endowed with these five excellences...
She is called the "Beauty of the Land.
*Tuvaṭaṃ* means quickly. He too, being unable to say to the Blessed One, "Please take the bowl," went back to the monastery itself.
It is said that out of reverence for the Tathāgata, he was unable to say, "Venerable Sir, please take the bowl."
He thought, "The Teacher will take the bowl at the head of the stairs. But the Teacher did not take it there either.
He thought, "He will take it at the foot of the stairs. The Teacher did not take it there either. He thought, "He will take it in the royal courtyard.
The Teacher did not take it there either. The prince, wishing to turn back, went along with reluctance.
Out of reverence for the Teacher, he was unable even to say, "Take the bowl," and so he walked along thinking, "He will take it here;
he will take it there. And the words spoken by Janapadakalyāṇī remained in his heart as if they were engraved across it.
Indeed, the consecration ceremony of Prince Nanda did not afflict him as much as the words of Janapadakalyāṇī did.
Because those words had been spoken, his mental anguish became intense. Then, even as he was thinking, "He will turn back at this spot;
he will turn back at that spot," the Teacher led him to the monastery and said, "Nanda, will you go forth?
Out of reverence for the Buddha, he did not say, "I will not go forth," but replied, "Yes, I will go forth. The Teacher—
Having said, "In that case, let Nanda go forth," he caused him to go forth. Thus it was said: "Even though he was unwilling, the Blessed One caused him to go forth.
In the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "The Teacher, having gone to Kapilavatthu, caused Nanda to go forth on the third day.
However, in the *Aṅguttara-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā*—
The Mahāsatta, having attained omniscience and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, was bringing benefit to the world;
he went from Rājagaha to Kapilavatthu and, at his very first sight, established his father in the fruit of stream-entry.
On the following day, having gone to his father’s residence and given exhortation to Rāhula’s mother, he preached the Dhamma to the rest of the people as well. On the next day...
"While the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s consecration, entry into his new home, and marriage were taking place,
[the Blessed One] went to his residence, had the prince take up his bowl, and set out toward the monastery to ordain him.
However, it is stated here that "the Blessed One, having arrived at Kapilavatthu, ordained Nanda on the second day."
All of this has been stated in various ways because it was handed down by the Teacher through successive oral tradition from those respective reciters;
thus, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the Teacher’s words. "Brahma-like form" means a form similar to the form of Brahmā.
"Tyassa" means "of him. "Included in the round" means comprised within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"With affliction" means with affliction because it is accompanied by suffering; that is, "with pain. The sevenfold noble wealth is as follows:
"The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame and dread of blame, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and wisdom is indeed the seventh wealth."
Thus the sevenfold noble wealth has been described. "By means of wandering for alms" means by means of the practice of begging. Regarding the statement:

"Venerable sir, affection for a son... [omitted] ...arising, it shakes the entire body and remains striking against the marrow," he said this because affection for a son, due to its powerful nature, [shakes] the force of the co-nascent joy.
Due to its expansive nature, by way of pervading through the material phenomena originated by it, it agitates the entire body and remains in contact with the marrow.
"Yatra hi nāma" means "he who indeed. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the story of Rāhula is finished.
**Commentary on the Discussion of the Basis for Punishment by Means of the Training Rules (Sikkhāpada-daṇḍakamma-vatthu-kathā-vaṇṇanā)** 106.
Regarding the passage beginning with, “I allow, monks, ten training rules (sikkhāpada) for novices,” the term *sikkhāpada* refers to those words (*pada*) that are to be trained in (*sikkhitabba*).

The meaning is "sections of training" (*sikkhā-koṭṭhāsa*). Alternatively, *sikkhāpada* means the words of the training (*sikkhāya pada*), namely, the training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.

The meaning is "the means for attainment. In terms of its actual referent (*atthato*), however, it refers to the abstentions (*virati*) associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-kusala-citta*);

the factors associated with those [abstentions] are also to be understood here by the inclusion of that term itself. "Over-throwing" (*atipāta*) is the act of causing to fall prematurely—that is, falling before its own natural momentum has exhausted itself;
the meaning is "causing to fall quickly, not allowing it to fall slowly. Or, it is "overcoming," meaning to surpass or to overcome by means of weapons and so forth.

"Overthrowing" (*pātana*) means "overstepping" (*atipāta*); "overstepping with regard to a living being" (*pāṇassa atipāto*) is "killing a living being" (*pāṇātipāto*). What is meant is: the slaying of a living being (*pāṇavadha*), the killing of a living being (*pāṇaghāta*).

In this context, from the conventional standpoint (*vohārato*), a "living being" (*pāṇa*) is a sentient being (*satta*); from the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

Now, when one perceives a living being as a living being, the volition (*cetanā*) of a killer—which arises through either the door of body or the door of speech and originates from an effort that cuts off the life-faculty—is "killing a living being. Killing a living being is [the act] proceeding from that volition.

*Veramaṇī*: It "drives away" (*maṇati*) the unwholesome states such as the taking of life—which are designated as "enmity" (*vera*) because they are the cause of enmity—by saying, as it were, "How can you come to me while I am standing here? Thus it is *veramaṇī*.

Alternatively, although it should be called *viramaṇī* in the sense that "one abstains by means of this," it is stated as *veramaṇī* according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*). In terms of meaning, however, *veramaṇī* is [the state] associated with wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere.

Abstinences. This [abstinence] is described in the *Vibhaṅga* by way of such passages as: "For one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, that which at that time is the non-delight, abstinence, refraining, avoidance, non-doing, non-performance, non-transgression, not overstepping the limit, and the destruction of the bridge [of transgression] regarding the killing of living beings.
Granted, this so-called "avoidance" (veramaṇī) exists even as supramundane; however, here it is that which proceeds by way of formal undertaking (*samādāna*).

"Abstinence is intended" means that because it is impossible for abstinence to occur through the undertaking of supramundane abstinence, the abstentions associated with sense-sphere wholesome consciousness (*kāmāvacara-kusala-citta*) are to be understood.

Regarding "abstaining from taking what is not given" (*adinnādānā veramaṇī*) and so forth: "taking what is not given" (*adinnādāna*) refers to the taking of what has not been given, the seizing of another's property, theft, or robbery—this is what is meant.
In this context, "what is not given" (*adinna*) is that which is possessed by another. Where another has the right to act as they wish [over an object], [that object is said to be possessed].
One who commits [an act] while being unaware that it belongs to another is neither subject to punishment nor blameless;

however, when there is the perception that something belongs to another and one takes it, the volition of theft—which originates from the effort of taking—that constitutes *adinnādāna* (taking what is not given).
Unchastity (*abrahmacariya*) means ignoble conduct; it is the attainment of the union of two by two. For it has been said: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering..."

Because it is disparaged by such statements as, “There are many troubles; the danger here is even greater,” it is called *aseṭṭhacariyā*—meaning either conduct that is ignoble and unpraised, or the conduct of ignoble and base men and women—and because it is such ignoble conduct, it is also called *abrahmacariya*.
In terms of its actual meaning, however, it is the activity proceeding from the door of the body with the intention of engaging in unrighteous practices (*asaddhamma*).
Volition that originates the practice of a path that is not a true path is unchaste conduct (*abrahmacariya*).
"False" (*musā*) refers to an object that is unreal and untrue; "speech" (*vāda*) is the making known of that [object] as real and true.
By way of its characteristic, however, it is the volition that originates such an informative intimation (*viññatti*) by one who desires to make another understand an untrue object as being true.
*Musāvāda*: It is called *musāvāda* because one speaks what is false (*musā*) by means of it.

*Surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāna*: Here, "liquor" (*surā*) refers to five kinds of liquor: flour-liquor, dough-liquor, rice-liquor, that into which grain has been put, and that prepared from various ingredients.
"Intoxicant" (*meraya*) refers to flower-wine, fruit-wine, honey-wine, and molasses-wine.

"Connected with fermenting ingredients" refers to the five *āsava*s (fermented liquors). Among these, *pūvasurā* (cake-liquor) is that which is made by putting cakes into a vessel, adding the appropriate water, and kneading them together.
The same applies to the other types of liquor. "Kiṇṇa," however, is said to be the seed of that liquor;

those which are called *surāmodaka* (liquor-extracts) are put into it, and thus it is "kiṇṇa-pakkhittā" (added with seeds). [It is also made] from various fermenting ingredients such as *harītakī*, *sāsapa*, and so forth.
"Blended" means mixed with various ingredients. Flower-liquor (*puṣpāsava*) is the juice of flowers such as *madhuka*, palm, and coconut, which has been aged for a long time.
Fruit-liquor (*phalāsava*) is the juice of fruits such as jackfruit. Honey-liquor (*madhvāsava*) is the juice of grapes. Molasses-liquor (*guḷāsava*) is the juice of sugarcane.

Ingredient-liquor (*sambhārāsava*) is the juice of various ingredients such as *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *kaṭukabhaṇḍa*, and so forth, which has been aged for a long time and mixed with those ingredients. All of these are "intoxicants" (*majja*) by virtue of their capacity to cause intoxication; one who drinks them...
Because it intoxicates. "A basis for negligence" means a cause of negligence. This is a designation for that volition by which they drink that fermented liquor;
thus, "fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that are a basis for negligence" is *surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhāna*. Therefore, [the phrase is] *surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhānā*.

"Unseasonable eating" (*vikālabhojana*) refers to the period from sunrise until midday. This is called the "proper time for eating," which has been practiced and traditionally observed by the Buddhas and other Noble Ones;
any time other than that is the "unseasonable time" (*vikāla*). It is called "food" (*bhojana*) in the sense of being something to be eaten;

this includes everything such as rice gruel and solid food that is suitable for consumption during the permitted time. And just as in the expression "one who refrains from eating at night" (*rattūparato*), [the term refers to] eating during the night.
"Night" (*rattī*) is spoken of here by means of eliding the latter member of the compound; likewise, in this context, "eating" (*bhojana*) refers to the swallowing of food.

"Eating at the wrong time" (*vikālabhojana*) means eating at a time other than the proper time; thus, it means the swallowing of things that are permitted only during the proper time (*yāvakālika*) at an improper time.
Alternatively, the word *bhojana* here is not used in the sense of an object of action (*kamma-sādhana*) denoting "that which is to be eaten," but rather—

The term should be understood as having an instrumental sense (*bhāvasādhana*) expressing the act of swallowing; therefore, "unseasonable eating" (*vikālabhojana*) means the swallowing of food at an improper time. But of what is there the swallowing?

Since items such as those permitted for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) have been allowed, it is understood from the word "unseasonable eating" that this refers to the swallowing of what is permitted for the duration of the day (*yāvakālika*);
however, in terms of its actual meaning, it is the [swallowing] proceeding through the door of the body.
The volition of consuming what is not permitted at the improper time (*vikāla*) should be understood as "eating at the improper time" (*vikālabhojana*).
Regarding "dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing spectacles": here, because it is contrary to the Teaching (*sāsana*), it is a spectacle that acts as an obstacle;
thus, it is called "witnessing spectacles. For the viewing of dancing and so forth proceeds from desire and lust; in brief, [it is thus defined].
The teaching of the Blessed One, which proceeds in the manner beginning with “the non-doing of all evil,” does not conform [to such views].
Dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of performances constitute “dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of performances.

Herein, dancing performed by oneself and dancing caused to be performed by others are both included by the single term “dancing” (*nacca*) in the Canon, due to their commonality as the state of dancing.
Likewise, singing, causing others to sing, playing instruments, and causing others to play instruments are included by means of the sounds of song and instrumental music.

Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: it is the abstention from dancing, singing, and instrumental music—whether performed by oneself through dancing or causing others to dance, and so forth, or even those occurring as mere spectacles such as the dancing of peacocks—and from watching them, whether one intends to employ these dances oneself or [has them performed] by others.
It is not permissible for either monks or nuns to cause [a robe] to be made or to see those who have been commissioned [to do so].
Here, hearing is also included within seeing by way of the grammatical principle of "the remainder of the dissimilar" (*virūpekasesanaya*).

Just as, because the five types of consciousness have the intrinsic nature of perceiving their own respective objects, even the act of hearing can be subsumed under the category of "seeing," such that they are referred to simply as "seeing."
Thus it was said. For this very reason it was stated: “One does not cognize any phenomenon with the five types of sensory consciousness, except for the mere impact.
In this context, an offense occurs only for one who approaches out of a desire to see and actually looks;
however, if one sees what has come into range while walking—whether it occurred while standing, sitting, or lying down—there may be defilement, but no offense.
Regarding the phrase "wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, and using ornaments and finery": here, "garland" (*mālā*) refers to any kind of flower.
Although in common worldly usage the word *mālā* denotes a strung garland, in the Teaching it is used by convention for flowers as well;
therefore, any flower whatsoever—whether strung or unstrung—all that should be understood as "a garland. "Perfume" (*gandha*)... [text continues]
"Perfumes" refers to any kind of fragrant substance other than incense powder, smoke, and so forth, [used] for the purpose of anointing.

"Anointing" (vilepana) means anything prepared by grinding for the purpose of anointing that serves to color the skin. "Adorning" (piḷandhana) is wearing [ornaments]; "beautifying" (maṇḍana) is filling out deficient parts;
and "decorating" (vibhūsana) is the delighting in [these things] by way of fragrance and by way of coloring the skin. For this very reason, it is said in the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*:
In the *Madhuranikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "When one wears [it] as an ornament, it is called ‘bearing’ (*dhāreti*); when one fills a deficient place, it is called ‘adorned’ (*maṇḍeti*);
and when one accepts it by way of fragrance and by way of coloring the skin, it is called ‘decorated’ (*vibhūseti*).

However, in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya, only this much is said: "The acts of bearing and so forth regarding garlands and the rest should be applied according to their respective order."

It has been said. "Place" (*ṭhāna*) means a cause; therefore, that unwholesome volition (*dussīlya-cetanā*) by which the great multitude performs such acts as wearing garlands and so forth is the "place" for wearing, adorning, and beautifying.
Regarding the term "high and large beds and seats" (*uccāsayana-mahāsayanā*): here, *uccā* is another word having the same meaning as the word *ucca*. One lies down (*seti*).

"Herein" refers to the bed (*sayana*). "High beds and large beds" (*uccāsayanamahāsayana*) means high beds and large beds. A "high bed" is said to be a couch or similar furniture that exceeds the prescribed dimensions.
A "large bed" is a chair or similar furniture spread with unallowable coverings. It should be understood that here, the seat (*āsana*) is included within the category of the bed itself;
for when the physical basis (*ādhāra*) is prohibited, the action based upon it is likewise prohibited.

It is already excluded; therefore, it is stated simply as “high and large beds and seats. However, in terms of meaning, it should be understood that the abstention from sitting and lying down on things used for such enjoyment is what is shown.

Alternatively, this designation is made by the method of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*) regarding the sense “high and large beds and seats,” just as in the expression “the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form” (*nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ*), because the action of lying down is preceded by the action of sitting.
It should be understood that by the mention of "lying down" (sayaṇa), "sitting" (āsana) is also included.
Regarding the phrase "accepting gold and silver" (jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇa): here, "gold" (jātarūpa) means refined gold.

"Silver" (rajata) refers to those things that enter into commerce, such as the kahāpaṇa coin, the copper māsaka, the wax māsaka, and the wooden māsaka. Acceptance of both of these constitutes "accepting gold and silver."
And herein, acceptance is threefold: by body, by speech, and by mind. Therein, acceptance by body is taking up;
acceptance by speech is causing to take up; acceptance by mind is consenting.

Having taken all three kinds of acceptance together—either by a general designation or by the method of retaining one out of a group—they are called "acceptances. Therefore, it is not [permissible] to take up...
It is not permissible to have [such things] fetched, nor to accept what has been set aside for one. However, these ten training rules (sikkhāpada) are common to householders as well.

For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "The five training rules by way of the perpetual virtue (niccasīla) for male and female lay followers, or ten when there is the effort [to observe more], and eight by way of the factors of the Uposatha—this is the virtue of the householder."
For here, "ten" refers to the precepts that must be observed by novices, as in the case of Ghaṭikāra and others.

However, in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya, it is stated: "The first two and the fourth and fifth [precepts] are common to both lay followers and novices by way of the constant precepts (*niccasīla*);
but by way of the Uposatha precepts, the seventh and eighth constitute a single factor for lay followers."
It is said that "all except the very last are common to all novices (sāmaṇera), but the last one is a specific distinction for novices alone";
however, this does not accord with the statement, "or ten [days] if there is an effort.
"Grounds for loss" (nāsanavatthu) means the ground for the loss of the marks (liṅga); it is said to be the basis, the foundation, or the cause.
107. "By what means, indeed? [The question] "Kintī" means "by what means. Regarding the phrase "one's own cell," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that this refers to private property (*puggalika*).

This is the intention of the authors of the *Gaṇṭhipada* here: by the expression "the lodging obtained through the distribution of the rainy season," the communal lodging (*saṅghika-senāsana*) obtained by him through the distribution of the rainy season is meant;
and by the expression "one's own cell," [it refers to the same].
"It is said that this refers to one's own private lodging. However, our own view on this point is as follows:
by the phrase "wherever he dwells," whether it be a communal (saṅghika) or a private (puggalika) lodging, what is meant is the lodging where he habitually resides.
But by the phrase "or wherever he retreats," what is meant is the place where his teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya) dwells for the purpose of attending upon them and so forth.
It is said that he enters what has been assigned; this refers to the dwelling place of his teacher (ācariya) and preceptor (upajjhāya).
Therefore, in order to show both of these, it was said: "By both [means], his own cell (pariveṇa) and the lodging obtained by lot (vassa) are indicated.
Therein, by the phrase "his own cell," the dwelling place of the teacher and preceptor is shown; by the phrase "by lot... [the lodging obtained by lot is shown].
"An alms-bowl and a seat" refers, however, to his place of residence. Whether both of these belong to the Saṅgha or to an individual, they must certainly be screened off.
"Oral" means that which is to be consumed through the mouth-door. "Having performed an act of punishment" means having applied a disciplinary measure.
It is called *daṇḍa* because by it they punish (*daṇḍenti*) or discipline (*vinenti*); since that very thing is to be performed, it is called *kamma*.
The penalty of *daṇḍakamma*, the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the basis for the penalty of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of the basis for the obstruction [of ordination] due to not having asked permission, and so forth.
108. "Inflict disciplinary action upon him" means: apply disciplinary action to him; command it. Alternatively, *daṇḍakamma* is a punitive act;
therefore, what is meant is: "inflict punishment upon him. This same method applies in all such instances.
By the phrase "and the taking of lodgings is suspended," it is indicated that he has also broken his rains-residence (*vassa*).
"If he is indeed one whose faults are manifold and does not abide in restraint for the future, he should be expelled.
Regarding this, if he does not desist even when told up to three times, he should be destroyed after seeking permission from the Saṅgha.

They say that even if he requests ordination again, he should be ordained only after seeking permission. "He shall receive the later rains-residence" means that he shall [spend] the rains-residence again during the later period.
Because he has approached [the Saṅgha], he shall receive it. "Having obtained permission, the gain should be given" refers to one whose rains-residence (vassa) has been interrupted.

"The other five training rules" refers to the five beginning with eating at the improper time. "He should be made to confess his transgression" means he should be made to confess in the manner beginning with, "Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me."
The commentary on the section beginning with the account of the obstruction without having asked for permission is finished.
Commentary on the account of the paṇḍaka (eunuch):
Regarding the account of the paṇḍaka, it is said: "One who is female during the dark fortnight and male during the bright fortnight—this is a *pakkhapaṇḍaka*."

Some say: however, since the commentary states, "In the dark fortnight he is a paṇḍaka, but in the bright fortnight his fever subsides," it is understood that because the subsiding of the fever is mentioned specifically for the non-paṇḍaka period, the state of being a paṇḍaka consists in having intensified fever during the paṇḍaka period;
therefore, this alone should be accepted here as the essential point. [The state of] femininity and masculinity.

"Abhāvaka" means one for whom [the state of being a paṇḍaka] does not exist. Regarding the statement, "In that very same faction, the going forth is prohibited," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"Having been ordained in the faction of those who are not paṇḍakas, he is to be expelled upon reaching the faction of paṇḍakas.
However, some say, "One ordained in the faction of those who are not paṇḍakas need not be expelled if he attains the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*). That is merely their own opinion.

Because it is impossible for a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) to reach the destruction of defilements (*kilesakkhaya*), and because one whose defilements are destroyed cannot possibly exist in the state of a *paṇḍaka*.
Indeed, in the discussion on rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), it is stated without qualification that a *paṇḍaka* possesses rootless rebirth-linking.

Furthermore, they say that for the *āsitta*, *ussūya*, and *pakkha* types of *paṇḍaka*, the nature of being a *paṇḍaka* exists from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, and not merely during the course of existence (*pavatti*). For this very reason, in the description of rootless rebirth-linking:
The paṇḍaka is not specified by means of a term denoting birth (jāti), as is the case with those who are blind from birth, deaf, and so forth.

Here too, in the commentary on the fourth pārājika, it is stated without distinction: "When one points out persons incapable [of progress], there are three types of those deficient in the objective basis—the paṇḍaka, the animal, and the hermaphrodite—who possess rebirth-linking without roots; for them, heaven is not barred, but the Path is barred."
The commentary on the account of the eunuch is finished.
Commentary on the account of one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka):
Regarding the term "kinsmen" (kolañña) in this context, it refers to all those born in the maternal and paternal lineages, beginning with one's mother and father.
"One who lives in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) means one whose communion is by way of theft. And here, it is not intended merely as one who steals the [formal] communion;
rather, it refers to one who steals the [monastic] emblem, both of those, or all three. Thus he said, "There are three kinds of *theyyasaṃvāsakas*," and so forth.
"Does not consent to salutation according to seniority" means [he does not consent to] the salutation of monks or novices according to their seniority.

"He does not consent": he consents to the salutation according to seniority (*yathāvuḍḍha*) means that, having himself committed an act of false speech, he consents to the salutation according to seniority corresponding to the number of rains (*vassa*) he has displayed.
By the phrase "the counting of a bhikkhu’s years of seniority, etc.," it is shown that here "living together" (*saṃvāsa*) refers not only to communal legal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth.
Regarding "by fear of a king...": here the word *bhaya* (fear) should be applied to each [term], such as "by fear of a king, by fear of famine," and so forth.
"He does not consent to co-residence" means that as long as he is one whose mind is pure—because he has assumed the outward signs due to fear of a king and so on—he does not consent to co-residence.
For he who, without fear of a king or the like, merely deceives the bhikkhus...

If one takes up the outward marks out of a desire to live together with them, he becomes what is called a "one living in communion by theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) precisely because of that taking of the marks due to his impure state of mind.

However, this person—because he lacks the desire to deceive the monks with such an impure mind—is not yet called a "one living in communion by theft" for as long as he does not consent to living in communion. For this very reason, [the text says] "out of fear of kings, etc."...

"In the case of those who have assumed the outward signs [of the monkhood], even though there is a deceptive intention—thinking, 'May they know me as a recluse rather than a householder'—no fault arises because monks lack the desire to deceive," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. However, some say that "the state of having fear subsided" here means "purity of mind";
and if that were the case, then as long as that person whose fear has subsided does not consent to living in communion (*saṃvāsa*), [there would be no fault].
From this it is understood that one is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft) [only] at that time.
And if this were the meaning [of the rule], then it would follow that even if one consents to living in communion while the danger has not yet subsided, one would not be a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*;

however, the *Aṭṭhakathā* does not show that one is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* even when consenting to live in communion while the danger has not yet subsided. [The text says: "He eats the food of all heretics."

And by this, it is indicated that one must dwell even while not consenting to co-residence (saṃvāsa) due to its lack of peace. For that very reason, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"Because it is difficult for one who has come to a monastery and takes what belongs to the Saṅgha to avoid co-residence, therefore it is said:
'eating the food of all heretics. Therefore, [this applies] when there is fear of kings and so forth.
In this context, "purity of mind" should be understood as the very state of having assumed the outward marks (of a religious order).
"Food for all sectarians" refers to food that has been set aside and placed at crossroads and similar locations to be given in common to all members of various religious communities.
"To be carried by the body" means it must be borne on one's person. "They go forth toward" means they advance directly forward.
They go away. "By means of performing work" means by doing tasks such as plowing or tending cattle.

"Taking that very same bowl and robe, he goes to the monastery" means taking the robes for wearing as an undergarment and as an upper garment, and hanging the bowl over his shoulder, he goes to the monastery.
"Nor does he himself know" means: "He who goes forth in this manner is one who dwells in communion through theft."
He does not know whether [the offense] exists, or whether "one is not permitted to act in this way," or whether "one who has gone forth in this manner is not a recluse.
That one who goes forth in such a way is called a "thievish associate"—this, however, is merely an illustration.

By the phrase "at the very time of non-ordination," it is indicated that even if one hears [of the offense] at the time of full ordination and does not report it, one does not become a thievish associate.
Regarding the statement, "Without renouncing the training... he is not one who lives in communion by theft":

this is said because, since he has not relinquished the outward signs given by the bhikkhus, he is not a thief of signs; and because he has consented to a communal life corresponding to those signs, he is also not a thief of communion.
In the case of the passage, "A certain bhikkhu, still intent upon the saffron robes, put on white garments," the reason here is also this very same one.

This must be understood. Later, regarding the rules stated for a novice (*sāmaṇera*)—such as "a novice remaining in his own status" and so forth—the same method applies to those on the side of one who does not live in communion (*atheyya-saṃvāsaka*).
The same method applies to a nun (*bhikkhunī*) as well; this very point is clarified by the passage beginning with, "For she too, desiring the state of a householder," and so forth.
The phrase "anyone who has gone forth in old age" is said with reference to a novice. By the expression "in the great baskets (*mahāpeḷā*), etc.,"...
The taking of what belongs to a householder has been demonstrated. "Even one who is himself merely a novice...
is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft)"—here, although he is indeed not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*, he nevertheless incurs a *pārājika* offense. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the discussion of the subject of the *theyyasaṃvāsaka* is finished.

Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Has Gone Over to a Sectarian School: In the discussion concerning one who has gone over to a sectarian school, it is stated that "one becomes a sectarian convert as soon as their insignia are taken up.

This is said because, for one who has gone [to the sect] with the thought, "I shall become a sectarian," by the very act of assuming their insignia, their adherence to their tenets is also thereby understood.
However, some have stated: "One becomes a renegade to the faction of the heretics as soon as those signs are taken up, whether the doctrine has been adopted or not.
This should not be accepted. For there is no such thing as the adoption of a doctrine other than the assuming of the signs by one who has gone forth with the thought, "I shall become a heretic.
Indeed, by the very act of assuming the signs, he becomes one who has adopted that doctrine.
For that very reason it is said: "For the sake of testing, [he takes] grass-cloths and so forth... until he does not accept them, his adherence (laddhi) remains protected;
the moment he accepts them, he has gone over to the faction of the heretics (titthiyapakkantaka). He goes naked to the dwelling place of the Ājīvakas;
for every step taken, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on account of going with an impure mind, thinking, "I shall become an Ājīvaka."
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) has been stated. Even for the reason of going forth while naked, one is certainly not released from the dukkaṭa.
"Counting false rain" means that having counted false rain, one consents to living in community; this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the discussion regarding those who have gone over to the sect of the titthiyas is finished.
111. The account concerning animals (*tiracchānagatavatthu*) is indeed clear.

112. In the accounts concerning those who have killed their mother and so forth, "removal" (*apavāhana*) means going away; the meaning is "reparation. Just as [in the case] of one of the same class...
The kamma involved in violating [a relative] is weightier, whereas it is not so for one of a different species; thus he said, "having become a human female.

The designation "mother" and "father" is established through the connection of having a child; however, the usage of the term "child" is also seen in the world by way of being given away, being adopted, and so forth.

But since that is merely figurative, he said, "the mother who gives birth," in order to show that this is established in its primary, non-figurative sense. Just as [this applies] only to one remaining in a human existence...

Just as the attainment of sharpness, clarity, and proficiency regarding wholesome states occurs—as it did for the three Bodhisattas at the arising of the threefold enlightenment—so too does the attainment of sharpness, clarity, and proficiency regarding unwholesome states occur while remaining in a human existence; thus he said, "he himself, being of human birth.
That which follows immediately after death is called "immediate" (*anantara*); in that immediate [succession]...
It is so called because it is connected with, or has the nature of performing [the act] immediately after its production, or because it has immediate purpose;

thus, by that "immediate" (ānantariya) deed of matricide. Regarding patricide as well, when a human father who is one's progenitor is intentionally deprived of life by one who is himself of human birth, this is [an offense] by way of the immediate deed of patricide.
"One should understand everything by means of the passage beginning with 'the matricide' and so forth," thus he said:

"The same method applies even to the case of one who kills his father. Even for one who deprives his mother or father of life when their gender has been changed, there is still an immediate kamma (*ānantariya-kamma*).

For even though the gender has changed, that very same continuum of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and the continuum of the underlying consciousness (*bhavaṅga*) produced by that single action remains.
And [the phrase] "not another" [is used]. However, if one who is himself a human being deprives his mother or father—who have become animals—of life;

or if one who is himself an animal deprives a human being of life; or if one who is an animal deprives another animal of life—the kamma of such a person does not constitute an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense, yet it is still grave (*bhāriya*). It is simply not an immediate offense.
It persists. Here, the "fourfold case of the sheep," the "fourfold case of battle," and the "fourfold case of the thief" should be explained.

For even with the intention, "I am killing a sheep," if one kills a mother or a father who is actually a human being standing in the place of the sheep, one incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*);
this is because the object of the immediate retribution has been violated by the very intent for death. [This applies] despite the intention being directed toward a sheep.

However, one who kills a sheep without the intention (*abhisandhi*) directed toward one's mother or father does not incur an immediate offense (*ānantariya*), because the objective basis for such an offense is absent.
One who kills one's own mother or father with that specific intention certainly incurs it. This same principle applies to the other two tetrads as well.
And just as it is with respect to one's mother and father, these tetrads should be understood to apply to an *arahant* as well. For in all cases, the former...

The underlying intention (*abhisandhicitta*) is immeasurable; however, the murderous intent (*vadhakacitta*), its object, and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) are the criteria for determining whether an action is an immediate offense (*ānantariya*) or not.

Even if one who has committed an immediate offense were to fill the entire world-system (*cakravāḷa*) with golden stūpas the size of the Great Stūpa (*mahācetiya*) and sit there filling the whole world-system, thinking, "I shall ward off the ripening (*vipāka*) of that karma," [it would still bear fruit].

Even after giving a great alms-offering to the community of monks and wandering about without letting go of even the corner of the Blessed Buddha’s outer robe, one is reborn in hell upon the breakup of the body and does not obtain the going-forth. 115.
"If he so desires" means if he desires to wear white garments. For this very reason it is said: "As soon as he has accepted the state of a householder."
The detailed explanation regarding the schism in the Saṅgha will be made clear later on.

"Of the four formal acts" refers to the four formal acts beginning with the *apalokana* (announcement). By the phrase "with a corrupt mind," he clarifies the meaning already stated as "with a murderous mind.

For here, a mind defiled by the intention to kill is what is meant by a "corrupt mind. Regarding the expression "he sheds blood": because the Tathāgata possesses an indestructible body, [it cannot be pierced].
There is no such thing as blood flowing from a cut in the skin caused by another's assault;
rather, the blood collects within a single spot inside the body itself, becoming accumulated through the agitation of resentment.
Even the splinter that flew off when the stone hurled by Devadatta shattered struck the edge of the Tathāgata’s foot, as if it were a hatchet.

The foot became as if struck, with blood flowing from within. However, at the Tathāgata’s wish, Jīvaka cut the skin with a blade, drained the corrupted blood from that place, and restored it to health; thus, for him, it was solely a meritorious deed.
Therefore, he said, "Just like Jīvaka," and so forth.
Now, what happens to those who destroy a shrine (*cetiya*) after the Tathāgata has attained *parinibbāna*, cut down a Bodhi tree, or cause injury to the relics (*dhātu*)?
Such an act is a grave deed, similar to an immediate offense (*ānantariya*).
However, it is permissible to cut a branch of the Bodhi tree if it is obstructing a stupa or an image that contains relics. This applies even if birds are perched there.
If they drop excrement upon a cetiya, it is indeed permissible to cut [the branches]. For the bodily relic cetiya (sarīracetiya) is more venerable than a cetiya used for offerings (paribhogacetiya).
If someone is walking away after breaking the site of a cetiya, it is permissible to cut [the tree] even at the foot of the Bodhi tree and carry it away.
However, if a branch of the Bodhi tree obstructs the Bodhi hall, one does not have permission to cut it down for the sake of protecting the building.
For the house is for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house; the same principle applies to the shrine room (*āsana-ghara*).
However, it is permissible to cut a branch from the Bodhi tree for the purpose of protecting the shrine room in which a relic has been deposited.

It is likewise permissible to cut off a branch that withers vitality or a rotten spot for the purpose of tending to the Bodhi tree; merit is gained just as when one tends to the physical body of the Teacher.
The commentary on the account of the cases concerning matricides and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the Account of the Cases Concerning Hermaphrodites (Ubhatobyañjanaka): 116.

The term *ubhatobyañjanaka* means "one who has both sexual characteristics" (*ubhato byañjanam assa atthi*). By this [definition], it refers to a domain that is not in grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇa*).

This demonstrates that this is a *bahubbīhi* compound with the elision of the case-ending (*vibhattialopa*) in the first member. Here, "sex organ" (*byañjana*) refers to both the female sex organ and the male sex organ.
Now, does a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) have only one faculty (*indriya*), or two?
Only one. [Question: "Does the male faculty arise in one in whom the female faculty arises? [Answer: No. In one...

Or, when the male faculty (*purisindriya*) arises, does the female faculty (*itthindriya*) arise for that person? "No. This is because the arising of two faculties within a single continuum is prohibited;

and this refers to the female faculty in the case of a hermaphrodite with female characteristics (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*), and the male faculty in the case of a hermaphrodite with male characteristics (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*).

If this were so, it would follow that there is no such thing as a hermaphrodite with dual characteristics (*dutiyabyañjanaka*). For the faculty is the cause of the sexual characteristics (*byañjana*).
It has been stated that he does not possess that [organ]. To this it is replied:
His faculty is not the cause for the second sexual characteristic. Why? Because it is always absent.
For when a mind of lust arises in a hermaphrodite woman, at that time the male characteristic becomes manifest while the female characteristic remains concealed and hidden; likewise...
One [organ] for the other. And if their faculty were the cause for the second sexual organ, then both organs would always remain;
yet they do not remain. Therefore, this should be understood: "That [faculty] is not the cause of that organ;
rather, in this case, the mind of lust accompanied by karma is the cause."
Because he possesses only one faculty, the hermaphrodite female (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) both conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive.
The hermaphrodite male (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka) causes another to conceive, but does not conceive himself.
Whether there is a male characteristic at rebirth-linking or a female characteristic at rebirth-linking—regarding that rebirth-linking:

The existence of gender-signs (*liṅga*) is stated in the *Kuruṇḍī*, but that is incorrect. For it is only during the course of existence (*pavatti*) that feminine gender-signs and the like arise, not at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
At rebirth-linking, however, only the sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise, not the gender-signs and the like.

Nor can it be said that the sense-faculty itself is the gender-sign, because the sense-faculty and the gender-sign possess distinct intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*). For this has been stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:

“‘This state’ (*itthatta*) and ‘the female state’ (*itthibhāva*) have the same meaning; the sense is ‘the female nature. This [nature] is born of karma and originates from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
However, the female sex organ and so forth originate during the course of existence (*pavatta*) dependent upon the female faculty (*itthindriya*).
Just as when a seed exists, depending on that seed and with that seed as a condition, a tree grows, becomes endowed with branches and foliage, and stands filling the sky.”

In the same way, when the female faculty (itthindriya)—which is designated as the state of being female—is present, the female sex characteristics and so forth come to be. For the female faculty is like a seed;

just as a tree, having grown dependent on a seed and standing filling the sky, arises, so too do the female sex characteristics and so forth arise during the course of existence dependent upon the female faculty.
Among these, the female faculty is not cognizable by the eye-consciousness; it is cognizable only by the mind-consciousness.
“Feminine gender and so forth are cognizable by eye-consciousness as well as by mind-consciousness.

For this very reason, he said: “The sequence of investigation therein should be understood in detail from the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* (the Commentary on the Compendium of States) in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the matter of those with both sexual organs is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Cases Concerning Those Without a Preceptor, etc., 117.
“The training rule had not yet been laid down”: this refers specifically to the training rule laid down in this very context.
“Without having caused him to take a preceptor”: that is, without having caused him to take a preceptor by saying, “Venerable sir, please be my preceptor.”

Furthermore, it should be understood that the proclamation of the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) has indeed been performed within the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*). Otherwise, because the failure of the ritual mentioned in the rule "he does not designate the person" would occur, the ritual would be invalid;

for this very reason, instead of saying "without proclaiming the preceptor," it is said "without having him take the preceptorship. And just as at the time of ordination for one whose bowl and robes are incomplete...
Even if the formal act (*kammavācā*) is performed after reciting a non-existent basis, such as "the bowl and robes are complete," the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is valid;

likewise, if the formal act is performed by merely expressing a statement about what exists while reciting a non-existent person, such as "this Buddharakkhita is seeking full ordination from the Venerable Dhammarakkhita," the full ordination is [valid].
"It should be understood that it indeed takes root. For this very reason, he said: "But the action does not fail.
Since only this much was stated—"Monks, one who lacks a preceptor must not be ordained;

whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—and because it was not said, "And that person is unordained," and because the characteristic of a failure of the formal act (kamma) is impossible [in that case], [the rule] "that should not be accepted" [does not apply].
It has been said: "Monks, if a formal act (*kamma*) that requires a quorum of five should be performed with a paṇḍaka as the fifth member, it is not a valid act and is not to be carried out.

From such statements, it follows that for those beginning with the *paṇḍaka* and ending with the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), the formal act is invalidated only when they serve as a filler for the quorum, and not otherwise.
Therefore, he says: "The same principle applies even in the cases of the hermaphrodite and the one who lacks a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*)."
The commentary on the discussion of the cases concerning those without a preceptor is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Cases Concerning Those Who Have Not Attained [Alms], etc. (118):
“Or other monks may wish to give” is the connection. “Unselected alms-food” means that which has not been taken as the first portion (*agga*).

Regarding the alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*): as for the phrase "the portion of requisites equal to the novices' share," although there is no separate portion called the "novices' share" because it is given in an amount exactly equal to the novices' share of requisites, the food going downward might sometimes be meager;
therefore, one should not take from above, but rather take from the novices' row itself and give it to them.

This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, this portion [of the penalty] is assigned only to one who is certain to go forth. For that very reason, it is stated: "a bowl that is not yet baked," and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning those who have not received the bowl, etc., is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning those with severed hands, etc.
119. *Ajapadake* means in a place shaped like the foot of a goat (*ajapada*). *Brahmujugatto* means straight-limbed like Brahmā. *The remaining being* refers to a being devoid of this characteristic.
By this, he shows that, setting aside the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) and the Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravartin*), other beings are "hunchbacked-winged" (*khujjapakkhika*).
For, generally speaking, beings [are bent] at three places: the shoulders, the waist, and the knees.
They bend at three places. Bending at the waist, they lean backward; bending at the other two places, they lean forward.
Those with long bodies are crooked on one side. Some walk with their mouths upturned as if counting the constellations.
Some have little flesh and blood and are like spears. Some [lean] forward...
They become overhanging; they move while quivering. *Parivaṭuma* means round on all sides.
*Aṭṭhisirācammasarīra* means a body consisting of nothing but bones, sinews, and skin. *Kappasīsa* means a head split in two.
*Kekara* means looking askance. In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is stated: "The so-called 'water-star' (*udakatārakā*) is a water-bubble. *Akkhitārakā* refers to the pupil of the eye.
*Akkhibhaṇḍaka*: "One with eyes devoid of eyelashes" means one whose eyes are bereft of the hairs on the eyelids.

For the word *pakhuma* is conventionally established in common usage to refer to the eyelash hairs. "The *paṭaṅga* frog" refers to a large-mouthed frog. "One with a dripping mouth" (*eḷamukha*) means one whose mouth constantly drips with saliva.

"All this" is said with reference to [the passage beginning] "or having itchy limbs," and so forth. "One with testicular swelling" (*vātaṇḍika*) refers to one who has a disease characterized by the enlargement of the testicles.
He is endowed [with these]. "Vikaṭa" means one who moves sideways on his feet, and whose knees go outside when he walks.
"Paṇha" means one who moves with his feet turned backward, and whose knees enter inside when he walks.

He clarifies the reason for being "kudaṇḍapāda" (having club-like feet) by saying "because his feet are contracted in the middle. "Because his feet are contracted at the tips"—this refers to those whose feet are bent at the toes.
This is an illustration of the reason for being "Kuṇḍapāda. It clarifies that he has the natural gait of one who walks on tiptoes, as indicated by the phrase "walking on the tips of his heels.
*Mamma* is a word for stumbling; it is a designation for one who repeats a single syllable four or five times.
The commentary on the account of the cases concerning those with severed hands and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the Account of the Cases Concerning Reliance on Those Without Shame (Alajjī): 120.

Regarding the cases connected with reliance (*nissaya*): one who possesses a share in common with the monks in terms of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth is called "one who shares in the community of monks" (*bhikkhusabhāga*).

Its state is "likeness to the bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusabhāgatā*). Regarding the statement, "One who wishes to leave after staying for two or three days may stay without formal support (*anissita*)," the intended meaning here is that it is permissible to stay without support even without the mental application (*ābhoga*) of thinking, "I shall remain until I have learned the likeness to the bhikkhus.
However, once one knows the likeness to the bhikkhus, thinking, "I will go tomorrow; what need have I for formal support? [one should depart] at dawn...
One is not permitted to rise [from one's seat]. If one lies down with the intention, "I will rise before dawn and depart," it is permissible even if dawn breaks.
However, for one who forms the attachment, "I will stay for seven days," a formal dependence (nissaya) must be taken.
Thus, having set aside the burden of thinking, "I will stay for only seven days; what is the need for knowing whether I am in the company of monks?"—

The meaning is that one does not obtain permission to dwell; rather, after having examined the suitability for membership in the community of monks (*bhikkhusabhāgata*), formal support (*nissaya*) must be taken.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Bases for Support, such as for those Travelling:
"While resting on the road... [etc. ... there is no offense" means that there is no offense when there is no provider of support (*nissayadāyaka*). Regarding him—
“Depending on” is stated in accordance with the canonical text (*pāḷi*); the meaning is “relying upon that. However, regarding the passage beginning “If, in the month of Āsāḷhī...

[and] one should go there,” if he wishes to go when the commencement of the rains (*vassūpanāyikā*) is near and hears, “Such-and-such great elder (*mahāthera*) will come,” and he waits for him, it is permissible.
If the day of the commencement of the rains arrives while he is still waiting, [it is likewise permissible].
"Let it be; one should go to that place where one can obtain a preceptor. However, some say:
"If, while going there, he perceives a danger to life or a danger to the holy life, he should remain right there.
*Commentary on the Discussion on the Permission for Proclamation by Clan Name*
122. Because the proclamation for the announcement of names has come down as, “So-and-so [is the candidate] of the venerable so-and-so,” it was said, “I am not able to take the name of the elder.

The meaning is: “I am not able to take the name in this way: ‘[He is] desirous of full ordination from the venerable Pippali. Because of the statement, “Let him announce [the name] even by clan,” by whatever convention—
It is established that one may use whatever name is conventionally employed, as it is sufficient for that purpose. It is also established that when asked, "What is the name of your preceptor?

one should answer by taking the clan name (gotta) itself as the name. Therefore, they say that the proclamation (anussāvana) should be performed using whichever of the four types of names is appropriate.
In cases where a person has many names, one name may be used for the motion (ñatti) and another for the proclamation.
It is not permissible to do so; the proclamations (anussāvanā) must be identical both in meaning and in wording.

Although in the canonical text (pāḷi) the word "of the venerable one" (āyasmato) is stated later as "so-and-so [is the candidate] for the venerable so-and-so," yet in the ritual text (kammavācā-pāḷi) it is written first as "this Buddharakkhita [is the candidate] for the venerable Dhammarakkhita"; thus, that is in reverse order.

It should not be assumed that [the name] was stated [in the text]. For in the Pāḷi, only the general sense—“so-and-so [is the name] of such-and-such a venerable one”—is shown; therefore, although not explicitly stated in the Pāḷi, the usage “this Buddharakkhita [is the name] of the venerable Dhammarakkhita” is demonstrated in the Kammavācā text.
And as for the passage: “‘I have never seen him before,’ thus said the venerable Sāriputta.”
They say that this is shown by the first instance of the application [of the term], namely, “the Venerable Sāriputta is skilled in meaning.
In some places one says, “of the Elder Buddharakkhita,” while in others one announces simply, “Buddharakkhita”;
it is not said that the announcement is deficient because the name has not been omitted, so some say. If, in some places, “of the Venerable... [is used...]
Having said, "Of Buddharakkhita," if he proclaims it somewhere as "of the venerable Buddharakkhita," some say that because it conforms to the wording, it enters the field [of validity] itself;
however, they say that due to the contingency of a difference in the phrasing, this is not permitted for the proclamations.
But if he speaks in this very manner in every instance, it is permitted.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Bases for Those Seeking Ordination, etc., 123.

Regarding the phrase *ekānussāvane*: here, it should be understood as an external-object compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) with a non-co-referential scope (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), meaning "those for whom there is a single proclamation (*anussāvana*) together.
For this very reason, he says: "two [persons] who have a single proclamation together. In that context, "together" means at one and the same moment.
This is a designation [for *ekatoanusāvane*] by means of the elision of a case ending (*vibhattialopa*).

"To perform the simultaneous proclamation (*ekatoanusāvane*) according to the previous method" means that it should be performed by two or three teachers, or by one teacher, according to the method previously stated as "one [teacher] for one [candidate], another for the other," and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Procedure for Ordination (Upasampadāvidhikathāvaṇṇanā) 126.
It shows that there is also a word *upajjhā* which has the same meaning as the word *upajjhāya*, namely: "one who contemplates what is blameworthy and what is blameless.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Four Supports and so forth (Cattāronissayādikathāvaṇṇanā)
130. “In sharing” means in sharing the Dhamma and in sharing material goods. Regarding the phrase “there is no offense in sharing while living together,” this is the intended meaning:

because he has been subjected to the act of reinstatement (*osāraṇakamma*) and thus stands in the position of one who is regular (*pakatatta*), there is no *pācittiya* offense on account of sharing and so forth with one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*), nor is there an offense on account of using [things] with one who is shameless (*alajjī*).
It is an *dukkaṭa* because the characteristic of one who is shameless is not established here. For if someone,
having formed the perception that it is permissible to eat sugarcane at an improper time because sugarcane juice and molasses are allowed for seven days or for life,
eats it and does not see an offense on account of that— due to such a perception that "it is permissible"— or if, having admitted to having committed an offense...
“He adheres to the thought, ‘I will not make amends’—such a person is called one who is shameless, as it is said:
‘He intentionally commits an offense, he conceals his offense, and he goes upon a wrong path;
such a person is called one devoid of shame.’”
One who does not fall away from the characteristics already stated is not called "shameless.

Therefore, just as previously there was no offense for communal enjoyment or co-residence with him for as long as the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) had been carried out, so it is here as well;

thus it should be understood that an offense is stated only in cases where there is absolutely no basis for an offense. For the Blessed One did not [allow] the possibility of an offense arising on account of communal enjoyment with one who is shameless.
When [the rule] states, "There is no offense in sharing and living together," some have said regarding this:

"By the words 'there is no offense in sharing and living together,' it is stated that there is no offense for this *pācittiya*; however, one still incurs a *dukkaṭa* due to the fact of using [the items] while being shameless.
Having said this, they have elaborated at great length; yet that should not be accepted as the essential meaning. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahākhandhaka in the Sāratthadīpanī, a sub-commentary to the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya-ṭīkā. 2.
The Uposathakkhandhaka.
**Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Permission for Assemblies, etc.** 132.

In the *Uposathakkhandhaka*, a "ford" (*tittha*) is so called because fools cross over and swim there. "From here" (*ito*) means from having obtained [it] within this Dispensation (*sāsana*). "They discuss that" means they speak of it by saying, "On such-and-such a day or at such-and-such a moment, this should be done," and so forth. 134.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Let the venerable ones hear me," whatever needs to be said has already been explained in detail in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* (the Commentary on the Schedule); therefore, we shall not elaborate upon it here. Those who desire [further detail] should take it from that very source.
135. Regarding the phrase "or having fallen into it, emerged from it," it should be understood that even an offense that has been confessed is called "non-existent.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "But for one whose offense is thus either not yet committed, or who, having committed it, has emerged from it, or has confessed it, or has declared it—that offense is called 'non-existent. False speech (*musāvāda*).
He said, "It does not have the characteristic of false speech," because a name comes into being conditioned by a vocal expression.
But what occurs regarding intentional false speech through the word of the Blessed One? It is by this statement: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Thus, there is an offense originating from non-action at the door of speech, because for whichever monk, while sitting in silence after having given an undharmic promise...

There is no such thing as an offense at the mind-door; however, because he did not reveal what ought to have been revealed, there is for him an offense originating from non-action at the door of speech.
"Vācā" means by speech; this designation is formed by the elision of the letter *ya*. It should be construed as: "not speaking with speech by any person."
"Nor should one speak words to others" means that with regard to other persons, thinking "they will hear this," one should not even utter a sound.
"One would incur a verbal offense" means one would incur an offense arising from speech.
"It is an obstacle-maker" because, by being a basis for remorse, it prevents the arising of joy and so forth, thereby obstructing the first jhāna and the rest.
It is an obstacle to spiritual attainment. "That bhikkhu dwells at ease" means that, by way of joy and the other qualities rooted in freedom from remorse, that bhikkhu’s practice proceeds happily.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the permission for communal assemblies is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Recognition of the Boundary (Sīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 138. "The other one as well" refers to a mountain of pure earth, sand, and so forth.

A mountain the size of an elephant is, at its lowest limit, seven and a half ratanas in height. "Therefore" means because it is not permissible with only one [person]. The measure of a ball of molasses weighing thirty-two palas—
It should be taken by its thickness, not by weight or number. "Mixed with heartwood" means mixed with trees that have heartwood inside.
"The size of a needle-shaft" is said to be the size of a writing-stick in the island of Sri Lanka;
it should be understood as being the measure of the little finger. "This" refers to the emergence of new roots and branches. "It is proper to praise on the other side" means having gone outside.
It is appropriate to recite this in four places: "In each of the eight directions among those established [on the path], one [robe] for one direction and one for another.
This training rule (*sikkhākaraṇīya*) applies to any bhikkhunī crossing over water when her inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) becomes wet;
having covered the three circles (*timandaḷa*) according to the characteristic of the rule's arrival, she must not lift up her inner robe while crossing by a ford or a non-ford.
If even a space of one or two finger-breadths of a nun’s inner robe becomes wet, it is considered a "river" for her.

Here, the mention of the "nun" is made specifically because the definition of a river in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* was introduced by way of the nun; it is stated thus so that the same principle may be applied.
For those establishing a boundary, this river—characterized as described above—is the "mark" [for the boundary], leading to the ocean.
Or whether it enters a pond, from the point of its source onwards there is a sign.
"Having overflowed, the obstruction continues to exist" means that the obstruction flows over and continues to flow. "Not flowing" means the water is not moving.
For when the water reaches an obstruction in a river, however much space remains where the water does not flow but stands still, that is the river's boundary-mark (*nadī-nimitta*).

It is not permissible [to establish a boundary] there. It is permissible only at a place where water flows above; however, at a place where it does not flow, it is permissible to establish a water-mark (udakanimitta).
For it is only water that is stationary which is permissible for a water-mark, not water that is flowing. Therefore he said:
"It is permissible to establish a river-mark (nadīnimitta) at a place where water flows, and a water-mark at a place where it does not flow. "Having broken through the river" means...
Having broken through the riverbank by means of the gateway of the *mātikā*. "To be lifted up" means it must be taken up as if being hoisted out of a well.
"Shaped like a crossroads" means shaped like a three-way junction of streets. "Shaped like a *mudiṅga* drum" means it is broad in the middle and tapered at both ends, like a *mudiṅga* drum.
"Having set aside the precinct" means for those who later establish the boundary.
"Having set aside space for the boundary. Regarding the phrase "but by those who have gone inside the markers":

this is stated because, when there is a desire to make half of a single village part of the interior, there is no purpose for everyone to come; thus it is said. And the word "should come" is stated in the sense of proper conduct (*sāmīci*);
it is not a fixed rule that "one must certainly come. Therefore he says: "Both coming and not coming are permissible."

For when a boundary is unbounded, because various village fields have the nature of distinct boundaries, there is no *vagga-kamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly) even if they do not attend;

therefore, their non-attendance is permissible. But when a boundary is bounded, because it has the nature of a single boundary, they must certainly come if another formal act is to be performed within that boundary. Thus he said: "In the case of the 'non-separation boundary'... [they] must come."

At the time of announcing the boundary marks, there is no fault even if the boundary has not been formally purified, because the announcement and other formal acts required for the announcement of the marks are absent.

The mention of "going forth" (*pabbajjā*) refers to the inquiry regarding the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*). "For the sake of making it easy" means for the sake of making it easy for those who are fewer by avoiding the fatigue of assembling everyone.
"He takes twenty-one monks" is said because the minimum requirement for performing an act by a group of twenty is fulfilled.
He takes twenty-one monks together with one who is eligible for the formal act (*kamma*) of the Saṅgha.

This is stated with reference to those who are actually seated; for at the very least, it is permissible to bind the boundary (*sīmā*) over whatever area can accommodate twenty-one monks sitting down.
"They will not be able [to sit]" means that he has failed to take notice of the fact that the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) has already been established.
Those who strive with the thought, "We shall abolish only the boundary of common residence," will not succeed.

For as long as the boundary of non-separation has not been abolished, even if a formal act (*kammavācā*) is performed with the thought, "We shall abolish the boundary of common residence," that boundary remains unabandoned.
Indeed, one must first abolish the state of non-separation and only afterwards abolish the boundary. [The boundary] is the measure of a single *ratana*.
It is said, “it is permissible [to mark it] with the size of a single jewel,” because it is easier to recognize [the boundary] in that way.
Even a space of only one finger-breadth between the markers is permissible; for even by that much, the boundary remains unconfused.
“The remaining markers” refers to the markers on the outer side of the great boundary (mahāsīmā). The binding [of the boundary] begins from the partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā).
Because it has been customary, and because confusion does not arise through such established practice, he said:
"It should be marked starting from the broken boundary. "Kuṭigeha" means a hut-house; the meaning is a ground-hut. "Udukkhala" means a small pit.
"The sign should not be made" means that neither that line nor the pit should be made as a sign.
"It does not descend below" means that because signs have been established and marked on the wall and beyond it, it does not descend into the space of the air below.
"It also descends below" means that if there is space for twenty-one monks within the wall below, it descends there.
And when descending, it does not descend by the measure of the upper boundary, but rather by the measure of the wall all around.
