It descends. Whether there is a descent or a non-descent should be understood according to the method already stated: if there is space for twenty-one bhikkhus below, it descends;
if not, it does not descend—this is the intended meaning.
"The entire palace stands within the boundary" means that whether its walls are connected as one with the upper floor or not, the whole palace stands within the boundary.
"Tālamūlaka mountain" means a mountain resembling the base of a palmyra tree. It should be understood that it is large at the bottom and becomes gradually thinner.
"In the shape of a drum" means it is thin in the middle and broad at the base and the top.
"At the bottom or in the middle" refers to the bottom of one shaped like a *mudiṅga* drum and the middle of one shaped like a *paṇava* drum. "A mountainous expanse of space."

A mountain cave that is not enclosed by walls. "There is a cave within" means there is a cave inside the mountain. "In a boundary pavilion" means in a pavilion within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).

"Having cleared the great boundary, the formal act should be performed" means that the monks situated within the great boundary must either be brought into hand's reach (*hatthapāsa*) or moved outside the boundary;
this is the intended meaning. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it says: "By those situated within the great boundary..."
The statement, “The intention is that the monks should stand without touching that branch or sprout,” should not be accepted. Regarding the phrase “in the former manner as well”:
this refers even to a tree that has grown out from within a *khaṇḍasīmā* (a partial boundary) and leans over into a *mahāsīmā* (a great boundary).

It is not permissible to establish [the boundary] by having the tree uprooted; for because the tree stands within the *khaṇḍasīmā*, one standing there [within it] is still within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) of it.
“It should be brought” means that it is not permissible to do so by having it carried across [on one's back].
140. *Pārayati* means it covers over. *Pārā* is a feminine designation referring to the boundary (*sīmā*). *Assa* means “it would be.
Showing the measurement of the boat intended here, he said: “At the very least limit... [omission] ...three people.”
"Carries [across]. By this, it is shown that even though a small boat of the aforementioned size exists, it belongs here to the category of those not [included].
The connection is: "It must necessarily be a permanent boat. The phrase "made by cutting down a tree" is a supplement to the text.
"On the opposite bank, in the place facing it" means: in the place facing the sign of the furthest limit on this side of the bank.
"Having made the monks standing within all the landmarks reach handspan distance":
here, if it is a single village precinct, they should be appointed after making the monks standing within all the landmarks on both banks reach handspan distance.

If it is the precinct of separate villages, it is permissible for them not to come [together] at the time of binding the boundary for a common residence. Regarding the appointment of a non-separation boundary:

However, one must certainly come [to the island]. Since an island is not considered "included" merely by the description of signs on both its shores, for that reason the signs on the island itself must also be described separately; thus he said:
"The sign should be described at both the near shore and the far shore of the island. "The summit of the island" means the top of the island. "Shaped like a mountain" means...
It is stated because of the greater importance of the lamp.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the boundary is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the Uposatha hall and so forth.

142. "Stated by way of the occasion" means it was said because the hearing of the *pātimokkha* is mentioned in the context of the occasion: "We have heard the *pātimokkha* while sitting on ground where we were not authorized.
"In front of the *uposatha* hall" (*uposathappamukha*) means a place directly facing the *uposatha* hall.
In the Canon, after merely stating, "First, the signs must be proclaimed," regarding the authorization of the boundary (*sīmāsammuti*), [the following is said]:
Because no specific signs have been shown—such as "the mountain sign" or "the rock sign"—but rather by way of a comparison, it is said: "or small...
or whatever signs there may be. This connects with the phrase "it is proper to describe them.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).

144. "Of the community" means of the community of bhikkhunīs. "Both boundaries" refers to the two previously mentioned: the boundary for non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) and the boundary for common affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*).
"They do not make the formal act (*kammavācā*) incomplete" means they do not break the formal act; the intention is that they do not invalidate the legal procedure (*kamma*).

"In this case" refers to the phrase "excepting the village and the vicinity of the village. "It does not extend over the village and the vicinity of the village" means [the boundary] does not encompass them.
Because it is stated, “excluding the village and the vicinity of the village,” it is reckoned as a *sīmā* (boundary) itself; that is, it is reckoned as a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).
“Even if one family has entered” means that among newly built houses, there is even a single family that has entered first.
“Or [if] none have come” means that in an ancient village, when other houses have been abandoned and people have departed, there is not even a single family remaining.
The statement "the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā) should not be dismantled" refers to the great boundary (mahāsīmā).
The phrase "standing in places free from fear" is said because there is no room for a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) within the courtyard of a shrine (cetiyaṅgaṇa) and similar locations;
for when they establish a partial boundary, they do so by avoiding such places and establishing it in another secluded spot. [This is said] thinking, "Perhaps they will be able to dismantle it."
They will be able to abolish only the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), not the fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍa-sīmā*). However, they will certainly not be able to establish it;

because they do not recognize the fragmentary boundary, they will not be able to do so. "It should not be abolished" means that it should not be abolished by those who do not know the fragmentary boundary.
Because the *uposatha* has been treated separately, commonality of affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsatā*) should be understood in terms of the remaining formal acts (*kamma*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Village Boundaries, etc., 147.
“Unbounded” means not having a boundary established by way of a formal delimitation. “Not made by anyone digging” means not made even by digging as little as a mere animal-track.
One who stands outside the reach of his hand [from that spot] may perform the ritual act.
By the phrase "does not disturb," it is shown that regardless of where one stands— so long as one is within the external boundary—
one does not disturb the action. However, what was stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*— "Even if one stands outside the boundary after having left the hand's reach within the boundary,
or even if one stands without overstepping another boundary of exactly the same size beyond the original boundary, one disturbs the action"— [is explained as follows:]...

“This is the conclusion in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Regarding this, the statement, "Even if one stands without transgressing that very same boundary, one still invalidates the formal act (*kamma*)," is found neither in the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor in the commentaries.
Furthermore, since this was stated in the context of two Saṅghas performing formal acts such as the Uposatha separately, it refers to [an area] outside the splash of water.

It might have been stated with this intention: that the Saṅgha, standing within another water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepa*) without overstepping it for the purpose of performing the Uposatha and other rites, invalidates the formal act (*kamma*) because of the resulting confusion of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*).
This would be logical if that were the case. For this very reason, it is said in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Mātikā*:
"Another [boundary] of exactly that same extent—that is, a second water-sprinkling."

"Even one who has not transgressed [the boundary] causes a disturbance. Why? Because his own *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (water-throw boundary) covers over the *udakukkhepa-sīmā* of others, there is a merging of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*); therefore, he causes a disturbance.

This should be understood as having been stated with the intention that "this is the definitive conclusion in all the commentaries," because in all the commentaries a merging of boundaries is not accepted.

For it is said by that very [text]: "Another water-sprinkling boundary must be established between the limits of one's own water-sprinkling boundary and those of others for the sake of the boundary-line (*sīmantarikā*).
However, others here elaborate differently; that should not be accepted.
"The Saṅgha sits everywhere" means they sit without relinquishing hand-contact (*hatthapāsa*). This is the ritual for the water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepasīmākamma*).
Regarding the phrase "there is none": because the entire river area has been encompassed by the monks, there is no need for the throwing of water since the river is absent on all sides.
The boundary (sīmā) defined by the extent of the throwing of water is much easier to discern, and it ensures that no suspicion of the overlapping of boundaries arises;
thus, another throwing of water is prescribed for the purpose of clearly indicating the limit. "Another throwing of water is for the sake of the boundary-mark."
It is said, "it must be set aside. However, it is indeed permissible to set aside as much as is necessary so that there is no overlapping of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*).
For this very reason, the ancients said: "It is permissible to set aside even that amount by which no confusion of boundaries occurs.

But it is not permissible to set aside too little; for this [latter case] also gives rise to the suspicion of boundary overlap, since the water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) expands according to the surrounding area.
The word "siyā" (might) is stated specifically for the purpose of excluding that [case].

However, regarding the statement "it is not permitted to do so on a moving boat," it should be understood here that it is permitted to do so on a boat that is turning without exceeding the limit of the water's splash.
Regarding the phrase "or having cleared the boundary," "clearing the boundary" refers to [the clearing of] village boundaries and so forth.
"Bringing [water] within arm's reach of those who are standing" refers to such acts.

The phrase "the embankment was built below" clarifies the meaning previously stated as "having destroyed the river, they made a pond"; the sense is that the embankment was built after blocking the river from below.
"Discarded water" means water discarded to one side for the purpose of protecting the pond. "When it does not rain" refers to even during the rainy season in times of drought.

"When it rains from the sky": "Having risen up" means having ascended. "It flows after having inundated the boundaries of villages and market towns" means that during the aforementioned rainy season, it flows continuously for four months.
"The monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*)" refers to a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*).
"A place where there is no path for going" refers to a location such that one cannot go there and return on the same day; such a place is designated as a forest boundary (*araññasīma*).
"He goes" is said with reference to the boundary of seven *satta*-intervals. "Of them" refers to the fishermen.

"On this side of the limit of the journey" is stated with reference to the island and the mountain on the near side (*orimattha*) of the limit of the journey, not to a location within the ocean itself. 148.
By the phrase "interconnected branches," he illustrates their mutual proximity. "It is bound" [refers to] the western direction.
This was said with reference to the boundary (*sīma*). "Its location" means a place where monks are able to perform formal acts (*kamma*);

however, if they establish a boundary by including within it a location where it is impossible for those standing there to perform formal acts, they are said to be "conflicting one boundary with another. This serves as the marker for two boundaries.
It is stated that because the sign (*nimitta*) is outside the boundary (*sīmā*), there is no "confusion of boundaries" (*sīmāsambheda*).

The phrase "he creates a confusion of boundaries" is said because, when [the sign] has been extended and entered the area of the boundary, the location where the two boundaries meet is difficult to discern;
it is not, however, intended to show that performing formal acts (*kamma*) there is not permitted. For the boundary does not cease to be a boundary merely by that much.
However, because two boundaries have been subsequently overstepped by a growing tree, they become a single continuous unit;
therefore, those performing an act while standing in one place must perform it after having cleared the other.
The commentary on the discussion of village boundaries and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Breach of the Uposatha, etc.
(149) "An illegal, incomplete Uposatha transaction": here, where four [monks] reside, the recitation of the Pātimokkha is permitted;
where two or three reside, it is the Uposatha of purification (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*). But here, in that manner...
It is called "by what is not Dhamma" because the Uposatha of purity was performed in three of the four dwelling places,
while the Pātimokkha was recited in only three of the dwelling places. It is called "in a faction" (vagga) because not all [monks] assembled,
and because the formal consent (*chandapārisuddhi*) comes only into the midst of the Saṅgha, not into the midst of a group.
Commentary on the Recitation of the Pātimokkha 150.
Regarding the phrase “I shall bear this in mind thus,” after saying “I shall bear this in mind thus” at the point where it says, “But, venerable sirs, you have heard [the introduction],” one says:
“Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited; but, venerable sirs, you have heard the four pārājikas.”
The word "dhammā" should be spoken. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "In that regard, I ask the venerable ones:
'Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask... [and so on]... Therefore, being silent, I consider it thus:
'Venerable ones, the introduction has been recited,' and so forth; when the remainder has been announced by means of hearing, it is said to have been 'recited' (*uddiṭṭha*)."
“By what has been heard” means by the portion already heard. “Fear of forest-dwellers” means fear of those who roam the woods; thus he said, “fear of non-humans in the wilderness.

Because of the statement, “the remainder should be announced by what has been heard,” one might think that since the recitation of the introduction (nidāna) is not yet finished, there is nothing to be announced by what has been heard;
therefore he said, “in the second and subsequent recitations. For the mention of “the remainder” is made with reference to the portions already recited; therefore—

When the Nidāna has been recited, if an obstacle arises while any portion of the Pārājika section or other parts is being recited, the remainder should be announced by means of oral transmission together with that [obstructed portion].
"By all three methods" refers to recitation, exposition, and formal debate. And here, it is because of the desire to state the meaning of the Sutta...
*Osāraṇā* means *osāraṇa*. The explanation and exposition of its meaning is called *kathana*.
Reciting the sutta or its meaning with a melodic chant is called *sarabhañña*. "Having resolved upon recitation" means having generated the thought, "I am performing recitation.
"But while explaining after having recited" means first chanting it out and subsequently explaining the meaning.
Regarding the statement, "It is permissible for people to say, 'Speak,'" it means that even while sitting on a higher seat, one may say "Speak" only after specifically addressing "people";
however, it is not permissible to say so without such specification.
"By one who is reciting" means by one who is reciting while seated anywhere. "An elder" refers to anyone who is senior to oneself.
"Having asked permission from one" means having asked permission from one who is senior. "Another arrives" means another who is even more senior than that person arrives.
The commentary on the section concerning the reciter of the Pātimokkha is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section concerning the request for the reciter of the Pātimokkha, etc.
155. *Codanāvatthu* is the name of a certain city. It is ninefold, distinguished by the Uposatha of the Saṅgha and so forth:

namely, three according to the agent—Uposatha of the Saṅgha, Uposatha of a group (*gaṇa*), and Uposatha of an individual (*puggala*); three according to the manner of performance—recitation of the Suttas, Uposatha of purity (*pārisuddhi*), and Uposatha of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*);
and [the remaining] three—the fourteenth-day, the fifteenth-day, and the Uposatha of concord (*sāmaggī*).
Thus, by way of the day, it is ninefold. Regarding the fourfold Uposatha transaction: there is the Uposatha transaction that is illegal and with an incomplete assembly;
the Uposatha transaction that is illegal but with a complete assembly; the Uposatha transaction that is legal but with an incomplete assembly;
and the Uposatha transaction that is legal and with a complete assembly—thus the Uposatha transaction is fourfold. The Pātimokkha is twofold.
The Pātimokkha is twofold: the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha. There are nine ways of reciting the Pātimokkha:
for Bhikkhus there are five recitations, and for Bhikkhunīs, excluding the recitation of the *Aniyata* rules, there are the remaining four; thus, there are nine ways of reciting the Pātimokkha.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning the permission to learn the counting of the fortnights and so forth.

158–161. *Samannāharatha* means “you should observe. *Pariyesitabbāni* means “they are to be sought” by means of wandering for alms. 163. Commentary on the account of the grounds concerning those traveling to other regions:
*Utuvasse yeva* means “only during the proper season,” that is, during the winter and summer.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Granting of Complete Purity (Pārisuddhidānakathāvaṇṇanā) 164.
“He makes himself understood by any limb or member whatsoever” means that having thought it in his mind, he makes himself understood by any means such as the movement of the hands and so forth.
“The Saṅgha is not sufficient” means [that they must remain] without relinquishing hand-contact between every two persons.
It is not possible for it to remain in a fixed sequence.
Regarding the other, called "the purity like a cat’s chain" (biḷālasaṅkhalikā-pārisuddhi), some say: "A cat’s chain remains bound because it is employed only within the house;
the intention is that just as it does not go anywhere else, so too this [purity] does not go [elsewhere]. Otherwise, the qualification would be meaningless."

[It] "comes to be. But others say: "Just as when many people have their own individual shackles bound around the necks of a single cat, those shackles move when that cat moves because they are bound to it, yet they do not move when another cat moves because they are not bound to it;
even so, for this bhikkhu, there is the purification of zeal (chandapārisuddhi) which is like many shackles..."
They say: "It was given; it follows that monk as he walks because it is bound to him like a chain, but not another because it is not bound to him.
All of this should not be accepted as the essential truth. However, the essential point here is this:
just as the first link of a chain reaches the second link and not the third, so too does it follow him.
Thus, this too is called a "cat's chain" (*biḷālasaṅkhalikā*) because it is like a chain: once given by the giver of purification to someone, it does not go elsewhere.
Furthermore, the mention of the "cat's chain" here should be understood as merely an illustration for any kind of chain whatsoever.
Commentary on the Story of the Impulsive Gift (Chandadānakathāvaṇṇanā) 165.

When it should have been said, "There are duties to be performed for the Saṅgha," it is stated as "a duty to be performed" (*karaṇīya*) due to a transposition of words. It has no function regarding the granting of formal consent (*sammutidāna*). "He must indeed be brought within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*)"—this is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Saṅgha’s Observance Day (*Saṅghuposatha*), etc.
168. It is said that the *pubbakaraṇa* (preliminary duty) is to be performed first from among the duties of the assembly;
however, although it is to be performed after the *pubbakaraṇa*, it is called the *pubbakicca* (prior task) because it must be performed before the Uposatha ceremony itself.
Since both of these are to be performed prior to the Uposatha ceremony, they are sometimes designated simply as the *pubbakicca*. [The text asks: "What for the Saṅgha..."
[It is used] as in the phrases "prior duties" (*pubbakicca*) and so forth. "Uposatha" refers to any one of the three Uposatha days.

For when that day exists, this formal act of Uposatha for the Saṅgha is said to be "timely" (*pattakalla*), but not when it does not exist. As it is said: "And, monks, Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day."
"As many bhikkhus as are entitled to perform the formal act" means as many bhikkhus as are eligible,
suitable, and appropriate for that Uposatha formal act— at the very minimum, four bhikkhus who are regular members—
and who stand within the same boundary (*sīmā*) without having left hand's reach of one another. "And there are no common offenses" means that here, the entire Saṅgha...
One incurs a light offense through a similar basis, such as eating at an improper time; such cases are called "similar bases" (*vatthusabhāgā*).
For when these [similar bases] are absent—even if dissimilar ones (*visabhāgā*) are present—it is indeed the proper occasion (*pattakalla*).
Furthermore, because there are no persons to be avoided (*vajjanīyā puggalā*) in that assembly, it is said: "Monks, [this should not be done] in an assembly including householders."
A householder; and those mentioned by way of the following method: "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly where a bhikkhunī is sitting," namely:

a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), one who has renounced the training, one who has committed an extreme offense, one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not making amends for an offense, and one who does not relinquish a pernicious view.

The twenty persons— namely, one who has been suspended (*ukkhitto*), a eunuch (*paṇḍako*), one living in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsako*), one who has gone over to another sect (*titthiyapakkantako*),

an animal (*tiracchānagato*), a matricide (*mātughātako*), a patricide (*pitughātako*), a murderer of an arahant (*arahantaghātako*), one who has violated a nun (*bhikkhunīdūsako*), a schismatic (*saṅghabhedako*), one who has caused the blood of a Buddha to flow (*lohituppādako*), and one who possesses both sexual organs (*ubhatobyañjanako*)—
these twenty together with [the one already mentioned] make twenty-one persons who are called "those to be avoided" (*vajjanīyā*); they are to be excluded from the reach of one's hand (*hatthapāsa*).
They are to be avoided. For when these three types of suspended persons (ukkhitaka) are present, the Saṅgha incurs a *pācittiya* offense if it performs the Uposatha;
in the remaining cases, there is a *dukkaṭa*. And here, "an animal" (*tiracchānagata*) refers specifically to one for whom full admission (*upasampadā*) has been prohibited;
those belonging to other sects (*titthiya*) are included under the category of householders. These too must be avoided. Thus [is] the proper time.
It should be understood that [the Uposatha] is comprised of these four factors.
By the word *pi* (also) in the phrase "Today is my Uposatha, the fifteenth," it is indicated—according to the method found in the Pāḷi—that it is also permissible to say, "Today is my Uposatha.
However, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Today is my Uposatha, the fourteenth... or...
It is said: "Having stated 'fifteen,' one should say 'I resolve'. The commentary on the discussion concerning the Uposatha of the Saṅgha and so forth is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion concerning the procedure for the remediation of offenses.

169. But surely, since it is stated, “Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed by one who has an offense; whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing,” an offense specifically prescribed for performing the Uposatha while having an offense is not seen;
therefore, why was it said by the Blessed One, “The Uposatha should not be performed by one who has an offense”? To this he says: “Yassa siyā... (For whomsoever there may be... [and so forth].

“It should be understood that an offense... has been laid down. Although no specific offense is seen to have been laid down separately, the intention is that it is indeed laid down by implication through such statements as, “Whoever has an offense should disclose it,” and so forth.
And by this very act of laying down the giving of purity, it is also demonstrated that “one who is guilty of an offense must not give purity.”
This is so because one who is actually guilty of an offense is not fit to say, "I give my purity; take my purity;
announce my purity. Therefore, by one giving purity, any existing offense must first be confessed:
"Friend, I am in doubt regarding such-and-such an offense; when I become free from doubt, then..."
Having said, "I will make amends for the offense," the Uposatha should be performed.

Because of the statement, "The Pātimokkha should be heard," as long as one has not become free from doubt, one is not permitted to accept a similar offense; furthermore, one is considered pure for other formal acts (kamma).
It is neither stated in the Canon nor [in the commentaries] that, "Once one has again become free from doubt, one need not confess."
"It exists in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but there is no fault in its being taught.

"The same principle applies here [in the case] of thinking, 'Having emerged from this, I will make amends,'" as stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. Just as the entire Saṅgha, having fallen into a shared offense, is permitted to perform the Uposatha after proposing a motion (*ñatti*) thus: "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me... [omission] ...I shall make amends," so too...
If three [monks] establish a formal motion for the group, saying: "Venerable sirs, listen to me; these monks have fallen into a shared offense.

When they see another monk who is pure and free from offense, they will then confess that offense in his presence," it is permissible for them to perform the Uposatha after two have announced this to one another. Even with one [monk], [saying] "I am pure..."
They also say that it is permissible to make an effort with the thought, "Having obtained [the opportunity], I shall perform the atonement.

The commentary on the discussion regarding the procedure for the atonement of offenses is finished. Now begins the commentary on the discussion regarding the demonstration of gender and other characteristics.
179. *Ācārasaṇṭhānaṃ* means the stability of conduct (*ācārasaṇṭhiti*). It is called an *ākāra* because by it something is performed or made manifest.

It is called a *liṅga* because it causes one to go toward what is sluggish or brings about awakening. It is called a *nimitta* because by it things are marked off and known through delimitation. It is called an *uddesa* because by it things are pointed out or referred to.
"Unknown" (*aññātaka*) means that which is not recognized or not understood as "this is ours. And in terms of its actual meaning, that is simply the property of another.
He said, "It belongs to others.

(180) "The state of being of a different communion" means the state of having a different tenet-based communion. Its "overpowering" is defined as causing them to relinquish that tenet; thus he said, "the meaning is that they do not cause him to relinquish that view.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning where one may or may not go.

181. It is stated that one should not go even to a boundary or a river for the purpose of formally resolving on the *uposatha*, because the recitation of the *pātimokkha* is heavy and must be relinquished, whereas the light [recitation] is not to be performed.

"By a forest-dwelling monk" means by a forest-dwelling monk who wanders alone, or by one living in such a forest where there are no monks sufficient to constitute a *saṅgha*. Therein, the *uposatha*...
"Having done so, one must go" is said because the Saṅgha’s Uposatha is not performed at his place of residence. "An obstacle to the Uposatha" refers to an obstacle to one's own Uposatha.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the pointing out of persons who should be avoided.

183. "The reaching of hand's reach alone is the measure": the intention is that whether the bhikkhunīs and others are standing or sitting, the reaching of hand's reach (*hatthapāsa*) is the sole measure for an offense.
Therefore, even within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*), it is permissible to perform the Uposatha after having relinquished the hand's reach. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Uposatha Khandhaka is finished.
3. The Khandhaka on Entering the Rains Retreat.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Permission to Enter the Rains Retreat.

184. Regarding the phrase "the word *idha* [in the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*]," it is stated that it is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*), because it is impossible for it to indicate a location and because no other meaning is understood.

By the expression "of one who has gone on the following day" (*aparajjugatāya assa*), he shows that this is an external compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) whose scope is not one of grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*).
"The following day" (*aparajju*) means the day subsequent to the full moon of Āsāḷhī; that is, the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*).
The meaning is as follows: "Assā" means on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion concerning the prohibition of wandering during the rains, [it is said]:
"The offense should be understood as occurring either by departing without regard [for the rainy season] or by causing dawn to rise elsewhere. Herein—

An offense is to be understood as occurring when one passes beyond the vicinity by traveling without concern; an offense is to be understood as occurring when one causes the dawn to rise elsewhere by traveling with concern.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization for seven-day business (sattāhakaraṇīya), §§ 187–189.
"The three things abandoned" refers to those things that have been relinquished because toilets and such items are prohibited for bhikkhunīs.
"Vāreyya" refers to the auspicious ceremony of marriage. "Suttanta" refers to one's own suttantas that are well-mastered.
"Does not perish" means it does not go to ruin or disappear.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the permission granted specifically when sent.
199. "Belonging to the class of bhikkhus" means one who depends on bhikkhus. Since he lives together with the bhikkhus, it is said:
"a man living together with the bhikkhus. Regarding "breaking the night by causing dawn to rise outside after having gone for a seven-day purpose":
it is not permitted to go there uninvited; here, because one has not been invited, one must first resolve upon the seven-day business.
It should be understood that for one who departs, there is both a suspension of the rains-residence (*vassa*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

For it is said that even for one who goes with the thought, "I will stay in another monastery and then return," provided there is no cause for interrupting the night as previously described, there is a suspension of the rains-residence.

"It is permissible to go" means it is permissible to go on account of a seven-day business. And by one going in this manner, while still standing within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), [the following applies].

One should go after making the mental resolve: “I will return within seven days. They say that if one crosses the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) without having made such a resolve, one’s rains-residence is considered broken.
Regarding “belongings,” this is said with reference to the robe. “They send” means they send it by means of tasks such as washing the robe.
“It is permissible if he is unable to reach it” refers to the following: “on this very day...”

"I will return. If, while going to a neighboring monastery and returning again, dawn breaks on the way, they say there is no interruption of the rains residence, nor is there an offense of wrong-doing for interrupting the night.
However, one is permitted to go with the thought, "I will see my teacher," even if not ill;
thus, for a seven-day purpose such as, "I will see my teacher or preceptor," [one may go].

He is permitted to go. However, if the teacher says to him, "Do not go today," it is allowable. Thus, for one who has gone on a seven-day business and returns again within those seven days, if the teacher or the preceptor says, "Do not go today," it is allowable;
the intention is that even if the seven days have elapsed, there is no offense. Nevertheless, there is indeed a breach of the rains residence (*vassa*).
It must be seen that [the period] has been spent outside for more than seven days.
201. Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the non-offense concerning the interruption of the rains-retreat due to obstacles:

if one has gone far away, the dawn must be caused to rise within the seven-day limit; by this, it is indicated that when there is a reason for interrupting the rains-retreat, it is permissible to go on a seven-day mission.
Commentary on the Discussion of Entering the Rains Retreat in Caravans, etc., [203]:

“I enter the rains retreat here”—this must be stated three times. Because there is no monastery (*vihāra*) in a caravan, one should not say “in this monastery,” but rather only “I enter the rains retreat here. However, it is not permissible to enter the rains retreat in a caravan.
"It is allowable" means that in the absence of a hut or similar dwelling, it is not allowable to enter [the rains residence] by making a verbal declaration such as "I enter the rains residence here";
the intention is that it is allowable merely by making one's abode there. "It becomes scattered" means it goes separately.
Regarding the three cases, "there is no offense in breaking the rains residence" means that for one who goes along with them, there is no offense.
However, if one departs after being separated from them, it is indeed an offense, and one is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
Commentary on the Discussion of Places Where One Should Not Enter the Rains Retreat (Vassa): 204.
Regarding the phrase "just as if they were little *pisācas*": here, *pisācas* themselves are called *pisācillikas*; some also say they are "little *pisāca* children."
"Having fitted the entrance door" means having fitted it with a door-panel attached.
"Of the five kinds of roofing" refers to the five kinds of roofing known as grass, leaves, bricks, stone, and plaster.

This should be understood as being stated by way of generality, since it is also stated that one may enter the rains residence in a hut roofed with planks made from trees and so forth. "Monks, one should not enter the rains residence without a dwelling place."
They say that the prohibition refers specifically to entering the rains-retreat after having made a verbal declaration, and not to entering by way of merely establishing a dwelling-place (*ālaya*).

However, because it is stated without distinction in the Canon, and because it is said in the commentary on the second *pārājika*—“For one who enters the rains-retreat, even if he has undertaken the practice of Nālaka, [he must do so] with one of the five types of coverings... —[the rule applies generally].
"One should enter the rains residence only in a lodging that has six doors secured. Therefore, if one obtains a lodging during the rainy season, that is good.
If one does not obtain one, one should do so even by seeking manual labor [to build it].
If manual labor is not available, one must do it oneself; however, one should never enter the rains residence without a lodging," he said firmly.
Because it is stated thus, it is our view that for one who does not possess a lodging, staying elsewhere apart from a boat or similar vessel is not permitted.
For it has been specifically authorized—whether or not a lodging exists—that "Bhikkhus, I allow you to enter upon the rains residence on a boat," and so forth;
yet it is said, "Bhikkhus, [it is not allowed] by one who does not possess a lodging... [and so on].

"The rains residence must be entered"—this prohibition does not apply there; thus, even in the absence of a formal dwelling, it is stated that one may enter boats and the like by way of taking them as a place of abode.
A "stilted bed" (ṭaṅkitamañca) is a bed made by boring holes in the middle of long bed-legs and inserting cross-pieces (aṭani).
For such a bed, there is no distinction of "this is above" and "this is below," as it can also be used when turned upside down.
It becomes just like that; they place it in a charnel ground or a shrine for deities. A house built by placing a stone on top of four stones is also called a "stake-bed" (*ṭaṅkitamañca*).
The commentary on the discussion regarding places where one should not enter the rains residence is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Unlawful Agreements (Adhammikakatikakathāvaṇṇanā) 205. Its characteristic has been stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga;

thus, the characteristic of the practice of an unlawful agreement is shown here in the commentary on the fourth Pārājika: “Whosoever shall depart first from this residence, we shall know him to be an Arahant.”
He speaks with intentional meaning; furthermore, an unrighteous formal agreement (*katikavatta*) will also be revealed in the commentary on the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Offense of Wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for Contradicting [the Agreement]: 207.
Because when one is spending the rains retreat in two residences within different boundaries, and the thought "I am staying" arises in the second [residence],...
The taking of the first lodging is suspended; when the thought "I shall dwell" arises again at the very first [lodging], the second [claim] is suspended.
Therefore it is said: "For that bhikkhu, O bhikkhus, the earlier period is not recognized.
Even though there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the breach of a promise, that offense occurs only when the promise has indeed been made.
He said: “For each respective promise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For this very reason he said: “…but that is due to subsequent deception.
“Not having business” means not having business on account of a seven-day matter. “Having business” means having business on account of a seven-day matter itself.
If this is so, why was it not stated as “not having business or having business on account of a seven-day matter”? [The answer is: “Not having business”...

Even though it was stated [previously], it was not mentioned here because the state of having business to attend to or not having business to attend to is understood through the phrase "on account of business to be done within seven days.
If this is so, why is it that in the subsequent passage—"he departs on account of business to be done within seven days"—it is stated only "he departs having business to attend to" on two occasions?
It is said in reply: in that case, instead of saying "on account of business to be done within seven days," it says "having business to attend to."
When it is said, "he departs," one cannot say that he spends those seven days outside; therefore, it is said, "he departs on account of a business to be done within seven days.
For when it is stated thus, because the seven-day period is exceeded [by the duration of the task], one can say that he spends those seven days outside.
And here, the first four cases are stated with reference to departing without looking back; even among those, the first two...
The first instance is stated with reference to one who has not entered the rains residence; the latter two instances, however, are with reference to one who has entered the rains residence.
The final two instances are stated with reference to departing while still having expectations [of returning].

Even there, the first instance is for the purpose of demonstrating that the rains residence is broken if one goes on a seven-day business even while having expectations, yet spends those seven days outside [the monastery].
The former [statement] was spoken to show that there is no interruption of the rains-residence for one who returns within seven days after having departed according to the method already described.

This section, however, beginning with "He departs on business when the invitation ceremony is yet seven days away," was spoken to show that there is likewise no interruption of the rains-residence even for one who,
having departed from the ninth day onwards, spends seven days outside the boundary.

And here, since the second section beginning with "He departs without having performed [the duty]" has not yet arrived, it should be understood that one may go starting from the ninth section only when there is a duty to be performed, and not otherwise.
These seven sections have been presented by way of one who has performed the uposatha outside;
another seven are by way of one who has gone inside the monastery and performed the uposatha. Thus, regarding the earlier period (purimikā):
By way of this [first] period, fourteen instances are stated; beyond that, by way of the final period, those same fourteen instances are stated.
Thus, their distinction should be understood.
However, in order to show the meaning stated throughout all these periods in a condensed form, it says: “‘On that very day he was not to do so,’ and so forth.”
"It has been undertaken. But what need is there to mention one who stays for two or three days and returns within seven days?

The intention is that there is no question at all regarding one who, having entered the rains residence and stayed for two or three days, goes on some business for seven days and returns within those seven days.
However, "if through forgetfulness one does not enter the rains residence" refers to [thinking], "In this monastery..."
Having made the verbal declaration, "I enter the rains residence for three months," he does not actually enter it.
On the *komudī* full moon of the fourth month (*cātumāsinī*)—that is, on the full moon of the month of Kattika:

for that [moon] is called *komudī* because of the presence of water lilies (*kumuda*), and it is called *cātumāsinī* because it marks the conclusion of the four months of the rainy season; for at that time, the water lilies...
They are in full bloom; therefore, it is a multitude of *kumuda* lilies, or the *kumudas* themselves are called *komudas*.
Because they exist there, it is called “*komudī*,” which means “possessing *kumudas*. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the offense of wrong-doing for making a formal agreement is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Entrance into the Rains Retreat is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Invitation:
Commentary on the Discussion of Living Uncomfortably.
209. In the *Pavāraṇakkhandhaka*, "talk" (*lāpa*) from the beginning is "conversing" (*ālāpa*); "discussion" (*sallāpa*) is talk that is reciprocal through the exchange of words and replies.
"He should return from alms-round" means he should return after having wandered for alms in the village.
"Having washed the scrap-bowl, he should set it out" means that, having removed the extra alms-food, he should wash one box-like bowl (*samuggapāti*) for the purpose of setting it aside.
He should set it down. "A box-bowl" (*samuggapāti*) means a bowl resembling a box or casket.
"In a place where there is no green growth" (*appaharite*) means in a place where there is no grass that would be liable to perish by being strewn over with almsfood; the meaning is: in such a place.
By this, both a place devoid of grass and a great thicket of tall grass are included, where even if almsfood were discarded by cartload, the grass would not perish.
And that place must be enclosed. This is stated for the purpose of not violating the training rule regarding plant life (*bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*).
"In one devoid of living beings" means in a mass of water free from creatures that would die from being overwhelmed by the alms-food;
for it is only in small amounts of water that tiny creatures die when agitated by the throwing in of food, but not in large reservoirs and the like.
For this was said for the purpose of protecting living beings. "Should submerge" means she should cause [it] to sink.
"A chamber-pot" (vaccaghaṭa) is a vessel for rinsing water. "Empty" means void; "hollow" is a synonym for that same thing.
"Unbearable" means too heavy to be lifted. "By a movement of the hand" means by a gesture of the hand. "Lifting with the hands" [is the meaning].
"Hand-overlapping. Therefore he said, "by one who raises the hand. Alternatively, it is called *vilaṅghaka* because by means of it one causes [the other] to reach another place;
thus, the hand itself is the overlapping, which is "hand-overlapping.
By that, "by the hand-overlapping," it is meant "with hands interlaced with one another. For two people, having interlaced hand with hand...
"Raising [the bowl] by holding it with both hands" means they raise it by leaping up with their hands.
"Adopted by the sectarians" means that which should be adopted by the sectarians.
The commentary on the discussion regarding dwelling in discomfort is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Breaking of the Invitation (Pavāraṇā): 212.
“Bhikkhus, there are these two invitations: that on the fourteenth day and that on the fifteenth day.

Herein, for those who have completed the preceding rains residence, the full moon of the month of Kattika is the [first] invitation; if they are troubled by quarrelsome persons, they may postpone their invitation.

Now, it should be understood that there are three days for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*): either the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika, or the full moon of the latter Kattika, or specifically the full moon of the latter Kattika for those who have completed the final rains retreat.
This is stated according to the normal course of conduct; however, when such circumstances exist, [the ceremony may also be held] on the two preceding fourteenth days of the two Kattika full moons.
It is permissible to perform the *pavāraṇā*. For that very reason, in the Mahāvihāra, the monks perform the *pavāraṇā* on the fourteenth day and grant formal unity (*kāyasāmaggi*) on the fifteenth;
they also go on the eighth day for the purpose of seeing the great sights of Cetiya Mountain, and this too is intended specifically for those who wish to perform the *pavāraṇā* on the fourteenth day.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Permission to Grant the Invitation (Pavāraṇā). 213.
"But if he is senior" means if the monk who grants the invitation is senior. "By that monk" means by the monk who grants the invitation.
Commentary on the Fifteenfold Discussion on Non-offenses.
222. “When the invitation has just been performed” means immediately after the invitation.
“While the assembly has not yet risen” means while they are conversing with one another after having invited.

“When some have risen” means when some have remained as they were seated while others have gone to their respective places. “The invitation must be performed again” means that everyone must gather once more and perform the invitation again.

"They arrive at exactly the same time; one should perform the *pavāraṇā* in their presence" means that when they have gone out, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* in the presence of those who remain seated, without having brought back those who went out.
"They arrive at exactly the same time when the entire assembly has risen;

one should perform the *pavāraṇā* in their presence" means that if everyone has risen and departed such that it is impossible to assemble them all, one may perform the *pavāraṇā* after having assembled some of them.

It is permissible; because there is no formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) to be performed after having established a motion (*ñatti*), it does not constitute a quorum-deficient assembly (*vagga*). The same principle applies to the Uposatha as well.
Commentary on the Discussion of Postponing the Invitation (*pavāraṇā*): 237.
Wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) consisting of ten bases, proceeding in the manner beginning with "There is nothing given," etc. [The ten bases are: "A Tathāgata exists... [and so forth].

It is called "clinging to extremes" because it grasps at the extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism, such as by saying, "The Tathāgata exists after death," or "The Tathāgata does not exist after death.
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Basis for Quarreling*

240. "When the fourth [day] has been made, they hear" means that when the fourteenth-day *uposatha* has been performed on the fourteenth day, they hear: "They will suspend our *pavāraṇā*. In this way, there are two [instances of] the fourteenth-day [observance]; together with the third, there are two instances of the fourteenth-day [observance].
Commentary on the Discussion of the Inclusion of the *Pavāraṇā*: 241.
This inclusion of the *pavāraṇā* is such that even if it is granted to one person, it is as if granted to all; thus he said: "By means of even one..."
"must be given. Because visiting monks do not obtain lodgings from them, even if sixty-year-old bhikkhus arrive, they do not obtain lodgings.
However, it is said that after the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, they may depart on tour even before the end of the rains retreat;
thus, when the *pavāraṇā* has been held, those who wish to depart in the interim should have the Saṅgha assembled.
They are permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*. The rest here is easily understood from the *Pāḷi* and the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
The commentary on the *Pavāraṇakkhandhaka* is finished.
5. The *Cammakkhandhaka* (The Chapter on Leather).
Commentary on the Story of Soṇakoḷivisa 242.

Regarding the phrase *uṇṇapāvāraṇaṃ* in the *Cammakkhandhaka*: it means a cloak (*pāvāraṇaṃ*) made of wool (*uṇṇāmayaṃ*). Regarding the phrase *vihārapacchāyāyaṃ*: it means in the shade at the edge of the monastery. Some also say it means "in the shade where the shadow of the monastery is expanding.
Commentary on the Story of Soṇa’s Going-forth.
243. As for the meaning of the sutta, it should be understood from the commentary on the sutta itself; herein follows that commentary on the sutta.

"In Sītavana" means in the forest of that name. It is said that five hundred walking-paths were laid out there in succession, and among them, the Elder would choose a walking-path suitable for himself and practice the duty of a recluse. Having thus applied energy, he—
As he walked back and forth, the soles of his feet were split; as he walked on his knees, his kneecaps and palms were also split, and they became perforated.
Although he dwelt thus with such exerted energy, he was unable to produce even a mere sign of light.
As his body grew weary from that effort, while he was seated on a stone slab at the end of the walking path, this thought arose:
In order to show how that [realization] arose, the passage beginning with “Then, to the Venerable... was spoken. Therein, “having aroused energy” means having fully exerted energy.
Regarding the thought, “My mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging,” he reflected:

“If I were one who understands through a condensed teaching, or one who understands through an elaborated teaching, or one who is led to understanding by another, my mind would not fail to be liberated; yet it is certain that I am merely one who relies on the literal word, which is why my mind is not liberated.”

Having reached this conclusion, he reflected on the passage beginning with, "But there exist... In this context, the word *bhogā* (enjoyments) is used in the accusative case to signify the object. Regarding the phrase *pāturahosi* (he appeared):
having known the Elder’s mental disposition, [the deity] thought, "This Soṇa is sitting today in the Sītavana meditation grove, reflecting upon this very thought.
I shall go and seize his thought along with its underlying motive, and provide him with a meditation subject comparable to a lute."
"I shall speak," he said, and appeared in the Cool Grove (Sītavana). Regarding the phrase "on prepared seats":

when the Blessed Buddha came to exhort the monks striving in meditation at their own dwelling places, those monks prepared seats according to what was available for the Buddha to sit upon while they practiced their exertion;
failing to find anything else, they gathered old leaves and spread their upper robes (saṅghāṭi) over them.
The Elder, too, having prepared a seat, applied himself to striving; it was with reference to this that it was said, "on the prepared seat.
"What do you think?"—the Teacher [said this] thinking: "This bhikkhu has no need for any other subject of meditation;
he is skilled in the art of music and has mastered its practice; when something is spoken within his own domain, he will quickly comprehend it."
In order to explain the simile of the lute, he said, “What do you think? and so forth. Skill in the strings and notes of the lute means skill in playing the lute;
and he was skilled in that. For his parents thought, “If our son learns another craft, he will weary his body;
however, this can be mastered while simply sitting in a chair,” and thus they taught him only the craft of music (gandhabba-sippa).
They had him learn this:
"Seven vowels, three groups, twenty-one modes of modulation,
forty-nine positions— these are the circles of vowels."
The art of the Gandhabba was entirely proficient from the very beginning. "Accāyatā" means excessively long; "kharamucchanā" means harsh in its execution.
"Saravatī" means endowed with resonance. "Kammaññā" means fit for work, suitable for performance. "Atisithilā" means too loose, or executed with slackness.
"Same guṇe patiṭṭhitā" means fixed upon the middle pitch, having been established in the median tone.
“Over-exerted” means excessively tight. “Leads to agitation” means it leads to a state of restlessness.
“Too slack” means excessively loose. “To idleness” means for the sake of a state of indolence. “Resolve upon energy and calm” means resolve upon calm associated with energy;
the meaning is: join energy with calm. And “resolve upon the evenness of the faculties.”

Resolve upon the evenness and the balanced state of the faculties beginning with faith. In this regard, by one who joins faith with wisdom and wisdom with faith, energy with concentration and concentration with energy, the evenness of the faculties is said to be resolved.
Mindfulness, however, is all-pervading; it must always be powerful. Furthermore, that [mindfulness] of theirs—
The method of application should be understood according to the system set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*. And therein, regarding the instruction "grasp the sign":

when that state of equilibrium exists, the Teacher says to him, "Grasp—that is, produce—the sign by which [the object] must arise, whether it be the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*), the sign of insight (*vipassanā-nimitta*), the sign of the path (*magga-nimitta*), or the sign of the fruit (*phala-nimitta*), just as the reflection of a face appears in a mirror. Thus spoke the Teacher.
Having assigned him to the state of an Arahant, he taught him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Therein, "he took up the sign" means he took up both the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*) and the sign of insight (*vipassanā-nimitta*).
"Alone" means without a companion. "Withdrawn" means withdrawn from sense-pleasures of the objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and sense-pleasures of the defilements (*kilesa-kāma*), both by body and by mind.
"Appamatta" means not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Ātāpī" means one who is ardent through the ardor of bodily and mental energy (*vīriya*);

it is called "ardor" (*ātāpa*) because one burns away the defilements (*kilesa*), thus it is energy. "Pahitatta" means one whose self is directed toward, or whose personal existence is relinquished, through lack of regard for body and life;
or, one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna. "Na cirasseva" means not long after the commencement of the meditation subject.

"Cireṇeva" means "in no long time. "Aññataro" means "one [of them]. "Arahaṃ" means that he was one of the great disciples (mahāsāvaka) among the Blessed One’s disciples who were arahants; this is the meaning.
"Vusitavā" means one who has completed the dwelling of the holy life (brahmacariya). "Katakaraṇīyo" means having performed what was to be done by means of the four paths.

He stands firm. "One who has laid down the burden" means he stands having set down the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*), the burden of the defilements (*kilesa*), and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"One who has attained his own goal": the "own goal" (*sadattha*) refers to Arahantship; the meaning is that he has reached it. "One whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed":
one whose bonds to existence have been exhausted. "Liberated through perfect knowledge": liberated by knowing correctly through the proper cause and reason. Six.
"Grounds" (*ṭhānāni*) means six reasons. "Is intent upon" (*adhimutto hoti*) means that having penetrated [the truth] and made it manifest, one stands firm.

The entire passage beginning with "intent upon renunciation" (*nekkhammādhimutto*) is stated with reference to Arahantship. For Arahantship is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) because it has emerged from all defilements; it is "seclusion" (*paviveka*) because it is secluded from those very same [defilements];
it is "non-affliction" (*abyāpajja*) due to the absence of affliction; and [it is the relinquishing] of clinging...

It is called the "destruction of clinging" because it arises at the point of the destruction of clinging; it is called the "destruction of craving" because it arises at the point of the destruction of craving;
and it is called "non-delusion" because of the absence of delusion.
"Mere faith" means that which is devoid of penetration—mere faith unmixed with the wisdom of penetration.

They "accumulate" by means of repeated performance, thereby increasing. "Being free from lust" means that because lust has been destroyed through the penetration of the Path, he stands having penetrated and realized the state of Arahantship known as renunciation;
he dwells in the meditative attainment of the Fruit (phalasamāpatti), and his mind is inclined toward that—this is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"Gains, honor, and renown" means the acquisition of the four requisites, as well as the state of having performed good deeds and the speaking of one's praises.
"Desiring" means wishing or longing for them. "Devoted to seclusion" means he declares his attainment of Arahatship thus: "I am devoted to seclusion. This is the meaning.

“Adherence to rules and observances” (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) means merely grasping what has been grasped by adhering to both precepts and vows. “Perceiving it as essential” (*sārato paccāgacchanto*) means knowing it as being of the nature of the essence.
“Devoted to non-affliction” (*abyāpajjādhimutto*) he declares non-affliction to be *arahantship*.
In this same manner, the meaning is to be understood in all sections. Furthermore, here, in the phrase “devoted to renunciation,” *arahantship* [is intended].
Some say that among the remaining five [terms], "nibbāna" is what is spoken of;
others say that "nibbāna" is spoken of specifically in the phrase "inclined toward non-delusion," while in the remaining cases it refers to "arahantship. However, the essential point here is this:
in all of these, both "arahantship" and "nibbāna" are indeed spoken of.
"Terrifying ones, powerful, resembling divine forms"—they are unable to seize and remain within the mind of this one whose taints are destroyed.
For it is when defilements arise that they are said to "seize" the mind.
"Unmixed" means unmixed. Defilements mix the mind with their object; because of their absence, it is unmixed.
"Established" means firmly grounded. "Attained to imperturbability" means attained to immovability.
"And he contemplates its passing away" means that he sees both the arising and the passing away of that mind. "A violent wind and rain" refers to a powerful mass of wind.
"It would not shake it" means it would not be able to move it even slightly. "It would not cause it to tremble" [refers to] a pillar.
It would not be able to shake it from every side as if it were something else. "It would not cause it to tremble" means that after shaking and trembling it, it would not be able to topple it over.
"For one intent on renunciation" means for one who stands having penetrated to Arahatship. In the remaining phrases as well, it refers only to Arahatship.

It has been explained. Regarding the phrase "of the destruction of clinging" (*upādānakkhayassa*): this is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. "And non-delusion of the mind" (*asammohaṃ ca cetaso*) means: for one whose mind is intent upon non-delusion.

"Having seen the arising of the sense-bases" (*disvā āyatanuppādaṃ*) means: having seen both the arising and the passing away of the sense-bases. "The mind is rightly liberated" (*sammā cittaṃ vimuccati*) means:
by means of the correct cause and method, through this practice of insight, by way of the attainment of the fruit.
The mind is liberated; it is resolved upon Nibbāna as its object. Alternatively, by this the preliminary practice of one whose taints are destroyed is described.

For, having seen the arising of the sense bases, his mind is rightly liberated from all defilements through the power of the Noble Path attained by means of this insight. Thus, for him who is rightly liberated... [etc.]
It does not exist. In this context, "one whose mind is peaceful" means one whose mind is extinguished (*nibbuta*). The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the account of Soṇa’s going forth is finished.
The commentary on the discourse refuting [robes] that are entirely blue and so forth.
246. *Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā* means having the color of a fresh *ariṭṭha* fruit. Some also say it has the color of a crow’s wing moistened with water.
Commentary on the Discussion Prohibiting Sandals within the Monastery (Ajjhārāme upāhanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā):
248. That by which one lives is called *abhijīvanika*. What is that? It is a craft (*sippa*). Therefore he said, "by whatever craft," and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of Wooden Sandals, etc. (251).
"Sandals made of wool" refers to sandals made from blankets consisting of woolly hair, or sandals made from the woolly hair itself.

In such passages as, "Monks, one must not take hold of cows by their horns," and so forth, [the prohibition applies] to taking hold of the horns and so on with the intention of escaping [from danger].
"It is permissible," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion concerning the prohibition of vehicles and so forth:
"I allow you, monks, a handcart drawn by men. Herein, "I allow you, monks... [and so on].
“Monks, I allow a handcart yoked with men”—thus he said, intending that the completion of each individual clause should be understood as follows:
“Whether it has a woman as a driver... or men, it is indeed permissible.
A *pīṭhaka-sivika* is a chair-carriage. *Pāṭaṅki* is a designation for a swing-cot.
Commentary on the Discourse Prohibiting High and Large Beds (Uccāsayanamahāsayanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā) 254.
"Beasts of prey" refers to artificial representations of beasts of prey. It is stated in the *Sārasamāsa*: "A couch or bedstead cluttered with improper forms is an *akappiya-rūpa*.
"A long-haired great woolen rug" means a black woolen rug whose pile exceeds four finger-breadths. [The text continues: "Exceeding four finger-breadths..."
Based on the statement, “It is said that his body hairs [do not grow] below four finger-breadths,” they say it is permissible [to use a rug] below that depth.
A variegated woolen spread (*uṇṇāmayattharaṇa*) is a woolen spread made colorful by means of wall-patches and so forth. A thick-floored woolen spread is a red woolen spread.
A natural cotton mattress (*pakatitūlikā*) is one filled with any one of the three types of cotton known as tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and silkworm-cotton.
*Tūlikā*. Regarding this, the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* states: “*Uddalomī* is a woolen spread with the fleece on both sides;
*ekantalomī* is a woolen spread with the fleece on one side. However, in the *Sārasamāsa*, it is stated: “*Uddalomī* is that which has the flowered patterns raised on one side;
*ekantalomī* is that which has the flowered patterns raised on both sides. [Regarding] “*koseyyakaṭṭissamayan*” [it means] “made of silk cloth (*kaṭṭissa*) and silk (*koseyya*)”.
This was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla. "Pure silk" (*suddhakoseyya*) means free from being sewn with jewels.

However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said here: "With the exception of the mattress (*tūlikā*), all [bedspreads] such as the *gonaka* and others are permissible provided they are sewn with jewels.
In that context, by the phrase "with the exception of the mattress," it is indicated that even a mattress free from being sewn with jewels is not permitted.

Regarding the statement, “Those that are sewn with jewels are allowable,” it should be understood that this indicates those things which are sewn with jewels may be used as floor coverings or placed upon beds and such furniture as appropriate.

Furthermore, since one must stand firm in what is weighty when reaching the Vinaya method, the legal decision here should be understood according to the very method stated in this context. In the teaching of the Sutta [method]...
However, because it was also stated with reference to householders, others say that the phrase "except for a mattress... it is permissible" was spoken in order to include them.
"With antelope skins" means with the skins of the *ajina* deer. It is said that those skins are very fine;

therefore, they are sewn together after being made into double or triple layers. For this reason, it is called "an antelope-skin mat. That which covers the upper part is the "upper covering" (*uttaracchada*).
Regarding the canopy, it is said that "a red canopy" is what is intended here by the phrase "by a red canopy fastened above.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated: "Among red canopies, saffron (kāṣāya) is permissible, but those dyed with safflower (*kusumbha*) and the like are not permissible.
A "large pillow" (*mahāupadhāna*) is a pillow that exceeds the prescribed measure. Furthermore, although in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*...
“It is indeed permissible to have two [mattresses] without red coloring; having obtained more than that, they should be given to others.
If one is unable to give them away, one may even lie down after spreading them crosswise on the bed and placing a coverlet over them”—thus it was stated without distinction.
However, in the commentary on the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, it says: “For one who is not ill, there is a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet.”
"Only two things are permitted; it is also permitted for one who is ill to lie down after spreading out pillows and placing a coverlet on top.
Because this has been said, it should be understood that only one who is ill is allowed to lie down by spreading [the bedding] crosswise upon a couch.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the prohibition of high and large beds is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Allowance for a Layperson’s Robe (Gihivikatānuññātādikathāvaṇṇanā) 256.
“To sit depending upon” means to sit relying upon [a house].
Commentary on the Story of Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa (Soṇakuṭikaṇṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā)
Regarding "At the mountain Pāpataka": here they also read "at the mountain Pavatta";
the meaning is "at the mountain named Pavatta. Regarding "the lay follower Soṇa" and so forth: by name he was Soṇa;

by means of the three goings for refuge and the declaration of his status as a lay follower (*upāsaka*), he was a lay follower; and although he ought to be called "Koṭikaṇṇa" because he wore an earring worth a million [pieces of gold], [he is referred to thus].
"Kuṭikaṇṇo" is his well-known name; the intended meaning is not "one with delicate calves.

For this man, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Venerable Mahākaccāna, became deeply devoted to the Teaching, established himself in the Refuges and the Precepts, and having built a monastery on Mount Papataka—a place endowed with shade and water—lodged the Elder there and served him with the four requisites.
He attended upon him. Therefore it is said: "He was the attendant of the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
From time to time he went to attend upon the Elder, and the Elder taught him the Dhamma;
through that, he dwelt full of spiritual urgency and possessed of zeal for the practice of the Dhamma. On one occasion, he set out with a caravan for the purpose of trade to Ujjenī.
While traveling, he fell asleep on one side after moving away from the caravan that had halted in the forest during the night, out of fear of the crowd of people.
When the caravan rose and departed at dawn, not a single person woke Soṇa; they all went on, forgetting him.
When the night had turned to morning, he woke up, arose, and seeing no one, [realized he was left behind].
Taking the path traveled by the caravan and proceeding very quickly, he approached a banyan tree.
There he saw a man of massive body, hideous in appearance, and loathsome, standing and eating his own flesh that had fallen away by itself.
Having seen him, he asked, "Who are you? "I am a peta, venerable sir," he replied. "Why do you act in this way?"
"By my own past karma. "But what was that karma? "In the past, while living in the city of Bhārukaccha, I was a fraudulent merchant;
I deceived others and consumed their property, and when ascetics came for alms, I reviled them, saying, 'Eat your own flesh!
By that karma, I am now experiencing this suffering. Having heard this, Soṇa—
He experienced an extreme sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Proceeding further, he saw two *peta* children with black blood trickling from their mouths;
he questioned them in the same manner, and they too told him of their own karma. It is said that in their youth, in the city of Bhārukaccha, they had been engaged in the trade of perfumes.
While making their living, they went to the house of their own mother—who had invited and was feeding an arahant monk—and reviled her, saying:
"Why do you give what belongs to us to these ascetics? May the black blood flow from the mouths of those ascetics who eat the food given by you!
Having been cooked in hell because of that deed, as a remainder of its karmic result, they were reborn in the womb of hungry ghosts.
Having been reborn, they then experience this suffering. Upon hearing that as well, Soṇa became exceedingly moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone to Ujjenī and completed that business, he returned to Kuraraghara; approaching the Elder and exchanging greetings, he reported the matter to him.
The Elder, for his part, explained to him the dangers and benefits regarding the course of worldly existence and its cessation.
He taught the Dhamma. Having paid homage to the Elder, he went home; after eating his evening meal, he went to his bed and, having slept only a little, woke up.
Sitting upon the bed, he began to reflect upon the Dhamma exactly as he had heard it.
As he reflected on that Dhamma and recollected those states of existence as a peta, the suffering of saṃsāra [dawned upon him].
It appeared to him as exceedingly terrifying, and his mind inclined toward the going forth.
When the night had turned to dawn, he attended to his bodily needs, approached the Elder, declared his own aspiration, and requested the going forth.
Thus it was said: “Then the lay follower Soṇa... ‘Venerable sir, may the noble Mahākaccāna grant me the going forth.’”
In this regard, the concise meaning of the phrases beginning with "in whatever way" is as follows:
in whatever manner the Venerable Mahākaccāna teaches, declares, describes, establishes, reveals, analyzes, clarifies, and makes manifest the Dhamma, as I examine it in that very way, it occurs to me:
"This holy life of the three trainings, even for a single day..."
It must be practiced as entirely fulfilled, because it must be brought to completion in the final moment of consciousness by making it unbroken;

it must be practiced as entirely purified, because it must be brought to completion in the final moment of consciousness by making it unstained even for a single day by the impurities of the defilements;

it must be practiced as "smooth as a polished shell," resembling a polished conch or like the luster of a cleansed conch—this is not easy for one living the household life while dwelling in the midst of a home.
“...to practice the practice that is entirely fulfilled by Vassa,” and so forth.
Having thus reported his own reflections to the Elder, the lay follower Soṇa, desiring to undertake that practice, said, “I wish, venerable sir,” and so on.
But the Elder, having considered that “his knowledge has not yet reached maturity,” [waited for] the maturity of knowledge.
Reflecting on this, he restrained his desire for the going-forth with the words, “It is indeed difficult,” and so forth. In that context, “solitary dwelling” means dwelling without a companion.

Here, by the term “dwelling,” it is the physical seclusion regarding the four postures—expressed in the manner of “standing alone, walking alone, sitting alone,” etc.—that is illustrated, not merely lying down alone. “A single meal” means...
“He eats but one meal a day, refrains from eating at night, and abstains from eating at improper times”—this is said with reference to the abstinence from eating at improper times as thus described.

“The holy life” (*brahmacariya*) refers either to the holy life consisting of abstinence from sexual intercourse, or to the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*), which is characterized by devotion to the three trainings. “Come, indeed!
(*iṅgha*) is an indeclinable used in the sense of an exhortation. “Right there” (*tattheva*) means right in the household itself. Of the Buddhas...

"One who devotes oneself to the teaching" means: one should devote oneself to the fivefold, eightfold, and tenfold moral discipline (sīla) consisting of the constant precepts, the Uposatha precepts, the restrictive vows, and so forth, as well as to the cultivation of concentration and wisdom appropriate thereto.
For this is what is called "devoting oneself to the Buddha's teaching" by a lay follower during the preliminary stage.
Therefore, he said: "At the proper time, sleeping alone, eating one meal a day, and living the holy life."
In this context, "timely" means joined with the time known as the fourteenth, fifteenth, eighth, or the day of a miracle;
or it means that for you who are devoted [to practice] at the aforementioned times, it is appropriate, fitting, and possible—meaning it is not the case that everything is possible at all times.
All of this is due to the fact that his knowledge is not yet mature and because of the difficulty of abandoning sensual desires.
He says this in order to have him made fit for the right practice, not to deter his desire for the going-forth.

"The volitional formation of going-forth" (*pabbajjābhisaṅkhāra*) means the undertaking, the effort, to go forth. "It subsided" (*paṭippassambhi*) means it was pacified because the faculties were not yet mature and because the sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) was not very intense.
Even though it subsided, he nevertheless followed the procedure prescribed by the Elder.
From time to time, approaching and attending upon the Elder, he listened to the Dhamma.
In the same manner as previously described, the thought of going forth arose in him for a second time, and he informed the Elder; yet for a second time, the Elder refused.
However, on the third occasion, perceiving that his knowledge had reached maturity, the Elder thought, "Now is the time to ordain him."
He granted him the going-forth; and after that one who had gone forth had passed three years, he sought out a group and conferred full ordination upon him.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "A second time, Soṇa... [and so on] ...conferred full ordination.
In this context, "one with few bhikkhus" means one having only a few bhikkhus. At that time, it seems, the bhikkhus were for the most part in the Middle Country alone.
They resided there; therefore, only a few were present. And they lived separately: one in a certain village and two in a certain town.
"With difficulty" means with suffering. "With hardship" means with exertion. "From here and there" means from those various villages and towns.
For when the Elder had brought a few monks and others were being brought, [he thought:]...
Those who had been brought previously departed for some business; after waiting for a certain time, when they were being brought back again, others departed.
In this way, through repeated arrivals and departures, the assembly was formed only after a long time. At that time, the Elder also lived alone.
Therefore it is said: "After three years... having caused them to assemble."
“Having spent the rains retreat” means having entered and completed the rains retreat. “Of such and such a kind” means of this or that sort.
