“The Blessed One was heard by me only as being endowed with such excellence of the form-body and endowed with such excellence of the Dhamma-body;
but he was not seen by me face-to-face”—herein, there is the faith of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

Thus the Venerable Soṇa was desirous of seeing the Blessed One. Later on, however, having stayed together with the Teacher in the same fragrant cell, he was requested by the Teacher at the time of dawn to recite the sixteen verses of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the presence of the Teacher.

Reciting them while giving full attention, applying his mind, and concentrating with his whole heart, he did so while experiencing the meaning and the Dhamma, through the gateway of joy associated with the Dhamma.
Being concentrated, at the conclusion of the *sārābhaya* recitation, he established insight (*vipassanā*) and, contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), gradually attained *arahantship*.
For it is said that it was for this very purpose that the Blessed One commanded him to dwell together with himself in the same fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*).
However, some say: "The statement 'I have not seen him face-to-face' was spoken specifically with reference to the sight of the physical body (*rūpakāya*)."
For the Venerable Soṇa, having gone forth and received a meditation subject from the Elder, was striving and exerting himself;
while still unordained, he became a stream-enterer. After being ordained, he thought, "If lay followers can become stream-enterers, and I too am a stream-enterer, what is there to be concerned about?
Thus, increasing his insight for the sake of the higher paths, he completed his residence within that very rainy season.
Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges, he performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for the sake of purification.
By the vision of the Noble Truths, the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One is said to have been seen. For it has been said: “Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, he sees me.
Therefore, his seeing of the Dhamma-body was already accomplished; however, after performing the invitation ceremony, he desired to see the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

The meaning of the words beginning with "pāsādika" (serene) is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself. Therein, "of the writhings and wrigglings" (*visūkāyika-vipphanditānaṃ*) means of the writhings of views and the mind, which are their opposites.

Alternatively, "serene" (*pāsādika*) refers to the person occupied with beholding the form-body (*rūpakāya*), due to the excellence of his own bodily radiance, which is serene on all sides and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide halo, and the jewel-garland.

It brings confidence in every respect. "Confidence-inspiring" (*pasādanīya*) means that it is worthy of inspiring confidence, or indeed inspiring confidence, in those who examine it, due to the perfection of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*), which is endowed with an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as the ten powers (*dasabala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*), and the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇikabuddhadhamma*).
"With peaceful faculties" (*santindriya*) means having the five faculties—beginning with the eye—calmed through the departure from their restlessness. "With a peaceful mind" (*santamānasa*)...
With a mind calmed by the attainment of the state of non-activity of the sixth faculty, the mind-faculty (*manindriya*).
Having reached and attained the supreme taming and tranquility— namely, the supreme taming and tranquility consisting of supramundane wisdom-liberation and mental liberation—
it stands as "tamed" because of the absence of misconduct regarding hands and feet due to the extreme purity of bodily conduct.

It is “tamed by body” because of the absence of shouting and so forth. It is “guarded” because of the utter purity of verbal conduct, due to the absence of useless speech and the absence of shouting and so forth.

It is “with restrained faculties” because of the utter purity of mental conduct, and because, through the application of noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*), there is an absence of agitation and lack of reflective equanimity by way of the mind-faculty. It is “without a goad” because of [the absence of] desire and so forth.
It is called a *nāga* for these reasons: because of its non-coming; because of the non-returning and non-reoccurrence of the abandoned defilements such as lust;
because of the absolute non-performance of any offense whatsoever; and because of the non-coming of renewed existence (*punabbhava*).
And herein, by the term "inspiring" (*pāsādika*), he demonstrates the Blessed One’s perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*); by the term "serene" (*pasādanīya*),...
"By means of the Dhamma-body. By the remaining phrases beginning with "with peaceful faculties," he illuminates his status as the standard (pramāṇa);
thus it should be understood that within the world-dwelling consisting of the four standards, the Blessed One’s status as the standard for all beings without exception has been made manifest.
"In a single dwelling" means in a single fragrant cell (gandhakuṭī). For here, "dwelling" (vihāra) is intended to mean a fragrant cell. "To dwell" (vatthuṃ) means to reside.
258. “Having spent the time in the open air” means having spent the time sitting in the open air.

Because the Blessed One, while providing hospitality for the Venerable Soṇa by entering all the meditative attainments shared with his disciples in both forward and reverse order, spent most of the night sitting in the open air, [he washed] his feet...

Some say: "Having washed his feet, he entered the monastery; therefore, the Venerable Soṇa, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, entered into all those meditative attainments accordingly, spent most of the night sitting in the open air, and then, having washed his feet, entered the monastery. And having entered, being permitted by the Blessed One—
Having made his robe a screen, he spent the time sitting at the side of the Blessed One’s feet.
“Ajjhesī” means he commanded. “Paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsituṃ” means: “O Bhikkhu, let the Dhamma manifest to you for the purpose of speaking;
let the gateway of knowledge arise within you; speak the Dhamma exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was mastered. This is the meaning.
"All the Aṭṭhakavagga discourses" refers to the sixteen discourses beginning with the *Kāmasutta* that constitute the Aṭṭhakavagga.
"He recited them aloud" means he recited them with the tone used for rehearsing the suttas; the meaning is that he spoke them by way of *sarabhañña* (oral recitation).
"At the conclusion of the *sarabhañña*" means at the end of the rehearsal. "Well-learned" means properly mastered. "Well-attended to" means thoroughly kept in mind.

A certain person, although having correctly grasped [the teaching] at the time of learning, later, at the time of mental attention through recitation and so forth, either misplaces the phrasing or commits errors in the sequence of the words; this is not the case here.
Rather, these have been attended to exactly as they were correctly grasped. Therefore it is said: "well-attended to" means "properly attended to."
"Thoroughly mastered" (*sūpadhāritāni*) means they have been well-pondered even in their meaning. For when the meaning is thoroughly pondered, it is possible to recite the text correctly.

"Endowed with lovely speech" means endowed with speech that is rounded in its words and syllables, elegant, and articulated according to the rules regarding the placement of soft and hard consonants and so forth. "Lucid" (*vissaṭṭhāya*) means liberated.
This shows his state of being one who speaks with liberation. *Anelagalāya*: "Ela" is said to mean fault (*dosa*); that which does not flow out (*paggharati*) is "anelagalā.

The meaning is: by means of that which is faultless. Alternatively, *anelagalāya* means both "anelā" and "agalā": by that which is faultless and by that which has no leaking words or syllables, meaning by that which has not lost its words or syllables.
For it was thus that the Blessed One declared of her: "This is the foremost..."
“Monks, among my disciples who are monks of beautiful speech, this Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa is the foremost”—thus he placed him in that rank.
“Capable of making the meaning known” means capable of making known the intended meaning.
“How many years [of seniority]?”—it is said that he was situated in the third division of middle age and was endowed with proper deportment, as well as for others...
He appeared as if he had been ordained for a very long time. Some say that the Blessed One questioned him with this in mind, but that is not the reason.

Rather, the Teacher asked him, "How many years have you been ordained? in order to inquire why he had fallen into negligence for such a long time when he was fit to experience the bliss of concentration thus attained. For this very reason, he said: "But why, monk..."
“Thus he stayed for so long. In this context, *kissa* means “for what reason. *Evaṃ ciraṃ akāsī* means “he delayed thus for such a long time”; the sense is:

for what reason did he dwell in the midst of the household life instead of going forth into homelessness for such a long period? *Ciraṃ diṭṭho me* means “I saw him after a long time,” that is, after a long interval.
*Kāmesu* refers to both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāmā*) and defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāmā*). *Ādīnavo* means danger.
Fault. Furthermore, even though the danger in sensual pleasures had been seen by him in some way, he was still unable to go forth from the household life.
Why? "Household life is confining; the state of a householder is crowded with various duties and obligations.
For this very reason, he said: "I have many tasks, many duties."

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood in every aspect this matter—that for one who sees the danger in sense pleasures as they truly are, the mind does not leap forward even after dwelling long in the household life, but rather turns back entirely like a drop of water on a lotus leaf;
and that he, knowing correctly both occurrence and cessation, [utters] this inspired utterance regarding occurrence...
And because he never finds delight even in that [conditioned world], he uttered this *udāna* which illuminates this very meaning.

Therein, "having seen the danger in the world" means having seen with the eye of wisdom the danger and fault in the entire world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*)—namely, that it is "impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
By this, the practice of insight (*vipassanā-cāra*) is described. "Having known the Dhamma that is without substrate (*nirupadhī*)"—
Having known, as it truly is, the state of Nibbāna which is without substrate because of the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*sabbūpadhipaṭinissagga*);

and having penetrated it through path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) as being by nature escape, seclusion, unconditioned, and deathless. Regarding the phrases "having seen" and "having known," they are used here just as in such examples as: "Strength comes from drinking ghee;
fear arises from seeing a lion; and for him, having seen with wisdom, the taints (*āsava*) are utterly destroyed."

The meaning of "cause" (hetu) is to be seen. An *ariya* does not delight in evil because he is far removed (*ārakattā*) from the defilements; the noble person (*sappurisa*) does not delight even in the slightest evil.

Why? Because he does not delight in evil, he is "pure" (*suci*). Due to his perfectly pure conduct of body and so forth, he is a pure person who, like a royal swan, does not delight in or take pleasure in evil, that is, in defiled states, as one would not in a place of excrement. "Evil..."

The reading “he does not delight even in what is pure” (suciṃ) is also found; its meaning is as follows: a wicked person does not delight in what is pure, blameless, and of a nature conducive to purification;
on the contrary, like village pigs and the like, he delights only in what is impure, a place of excrement, and of a defiled nature.
Thus, it turns the teaching by way of its opposite.
The commentary on the account of Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa is finished.
259. *Kāḷasīha* refers to a species of black-faced monkey. The rest here is easily understood from the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā.
The commentary on the Cammakkhandhaka is finished.
6. The Chapter on Medicines (Bhesajjakkhandhaka).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Medicines, etc., §261:
"They do not relish" means they do not produce a sense of liking [for it].
262. *Susukā* is a species of fish found in the ocean; some also call it a *kumbhīla*. *Saṃsaṭṭha* means strained. "By way of use as oil" is said with reference to use for seven days.
263. *Piṭṭhehi* means by means of flour. *Ubbhida* is made from saline soil. 264. *Chakaṇa* means cow dung.
"Ordinary powder" (*pākatika-cuṇṇa*) refers to uncooked alkaline powder. They say that, with the exception of fragrant powders, all other types are permitted.

265. “Gold-ochre” (*suvaṇṇageruka*) refers to gold, tin, and so forth. “Powder for ointment” (*añjanūpapisana*) refers to any kind of powdered substance that should be ground for the purpose of making an ointment. 268. Regarding the phrase “having taken it oneself”:
here it should be understood that even if it has been taken by another monk for the sake of one bitten by a snake, it is still reckoned as having been taken by oneself.
269. “A disease given by a householder” (*gharadinnakābādha*) refers to a disease arising from medicine administered by a housewife for the purpose of subjugation (*vasīkaraṇa*).
Therefore he said: "a disease arising from a love-potion. Here, the word *ghara* (house) is intended in its general sense as referring to the housewife (*gharaṇī*).
Regarding the terms *akaṭayūsa* and *kaṭākaṭa*, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "*Akaṭayūsa* means unprepared bean soup;
*kaṭākaṭa* means bean soup that has been strained without having been stirred after the beans were boiled."
Commentary on the Story of the Permission for Sugar (Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā): 272.
"Making sugar" (guḷakaraṇa) means a place where sugar is made; it is what is called a sugar-cane shed (ucchusālā).
274. "Lacking confidence" (avissatthā) means being apprehensive (sāsaṅkā).
276. "They invite [others] even when [the food] is only a small amount" means they invite even when only a small amount has been taken;
the intention is that, thinking "if much were taken, there would not be enough for others," they take only a small amount and then invite.
"They refuse even after reflecting" means they refuse even after observing that "it will be for the purpose of a daytime meal."
279. In a crowded place, the act of burning is permissible provided there is no prohibition. 280.
*Ubhatopasannā* means "confident on both sides. *Māghāta* refers to a day proclaimed for non-slaughter, such as one with the proclamation, "Do not kill living beings.
[This concludes] the commentary on the discussion concerning rice-gruel, honey-cakes, and so forth.
282. *Madhugoḷaka* refers to a cake prepared with sugar and other ingredients. "Gives life" means he gives a gift of longevity. "Beauty" refers to the beauty of the body.
"Happiness" refers to physical and mental happiness. "Strength" refers to bodily vigor. "Ingenuity" refers to ingenuity in appropriate and excellent expression.
"Accords with the wind" means he carries it along, conforming to the movement of the bodily winds. "Cleanses the bladder" means he makes the channels pure.
"He cooks what remains raw" means that if there is something remaining raw, he cooks it. "He offers" means he gives.
It should be connected with the phrase "and he dispels the wind. [Question:
But why was it said, "he should be made to undergo the offense of eating in succession"? For eating in succession applies to the five [types of persons].
When one who has been invited to any one of the [five] kinds of cooked food eats another of those five kinds of cooked food, setting that [invitation] aside,
it occurs [as an offense]. And since these monks consumed *bhojjayāgu* (rice-gruel fit for eating),

he said, "For there is an invitation regarding *bhojjayāgu*," meaning that it is an invitation regarding any one of the five kinds of cooked food for one who rejects [the invitation to eat] any one of the five kinds of cooked food.

The invitation (pavāraṇā) has already been stated; it applies even to one who rejects the rice-gruel (bhojjayāgu). Therefore, the intention is that the rice-gruel also falls under the same category as the boiled rice (odana).
284. "They threw in fine food": thinking, "The Blessed One will partake of it," they threw it in.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Site of Pāṭaligāma.
285. *Pāṭaligāma*: This was the name of a certain village in the kingdom of Magadha.
It is said that on the day that village was being founded, two or three *pāṭala* sprouts emerged from the earth at the site of the village square.
Because of this, they designated it as "Pāṭaligāma. *Tadavasarī*: He arrived at, that is, reached, that Pāṭaligāma. *Pāṭaligāmikā*: [The inhabitants] of Pāṭaligāma.
“Residents of Pāṭaligāma. Regarding “lay followers” (*upāsaka*): it is said that some among them, upon their first sight of the Blessed One, were established in the refuges and the precepts;
therefore, he says “lay followers. “They approached the place where the Blessed One was”:
it is said that in Pāṭaligāma, people belonging to Ajātasattu and the Licchavi kings would go from time to time to the houses of the householders.
Having been driven out, they would stay for a month or even half a month.

Because of this, the people living in Pāṭaligāma were constantly troubled, thinking, "There will be a place for them to stay when they arrive. Thus, on one side there was a place for the storage of the lords' goods;
on another side, a place for their own residence; on another side, for visiting travelers and wayfarers; and on another side, for the poor.

Thinking, "This will be a dwelling place for poor people and for those who are sick on one side," they had a great hall built in the middle of the city, large enough to accommodate everyone without crowding one another; its name was *āvasathāgāra*.
It is called *āvasatha* because travelers (*āgantuka*) come and dwell there; that very thing being a house (*āgāra*), it is thus called *āvasathāgāra*.

On that very day, they reached completion. Having gone there and observed from the gateway onwards that it was perfectly finished and well-adorned—resembling a celestial mansion by way of its brickwork, plastering, and painting—they thought, "This guest-house is exceedingly delightful and beautiful; by whom, indeed, has it been used first of us?"
They thought, "May it be for our long-term welfare and happiness," and at that very moment they heard, "The Blessed One has arrived at that village.
Consequently, with joy and gladness arisen within them, they thought, "The Blessed One might have had to be brought here by us after we went to fetch him;
yet he has reached our own dwelling place of his own accord. Today, having caused the Blessed One to dwell here..."
"First we shall cause it to be enjoyed; likewise, when the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus has arrived, the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas will have come to them.
We shall cause the Teacher to pronounce auspicious blessings and cause the Dhamma to be preached.
After these Three Jewels have been enjoyed, there will be enjoyment for ourselves and others; thus it will be for us for a long time."
Having made the resolution, "It will lead to their welfare and happiness," they approached the Blessed One for that very purpose.
Therefore, they said: "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to our rest-house. They approached him;
although on that very day it had been completed and was as well-adorned and well-maintained as a celestial mansion, [they approached nonetheless].
However, it was not laid down after having made it suitable for a Buddha. For Buddhas are indeed inclined toward the forest and delight in the forest;
whether they should dwell within a village or not, [the monks] thought, "We shall lay down the rule only after knowing the Blessed One's preference," and so they approached the Blessed One.
Now, desiring to lay down the rule accordingly after knowing the Blessed One's preference, they went to where the rest-house was.
They approached him. Regarding the phrase "having spread out the entire *āvasathāgāra* (rest-house)": here, *santharaṇaṃ* (the act of spreading) is *santhari*;
thus, it is *sabbasanthari* because the whole (*sabba*) or entire thing is spread out (*santhari*) therein. Alternatively, that which is spread out is *santhari*;
the whole is spread out, hence *sabbasanthari*; that is the *sabbasanthari*. This is a neuter abstract designation (*bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa*), just as in the case of "all" (*sabba*).

"It is spread" (*santhataṃ hoti*); the meaning is "having spread it in this manner. First of all, thinking "cow dung is suitable for all auspicious occasions," one should have even ground that has been prepared with plaster covered with fresh cow dung.

Once it is known to be completely dry, one should smear it with the four kinds of fragrant scents in such a way that the footprint is visible in the place where one steps, and then [on top of that]...

Having spread various colored rugs upon the floor, they had the entire area covered with various colored coverings—beginning with large leather mats and including elephant-ride blankets and so forth—as was appropriate to be spread. Therefore it is said:
"having spread the guest house with all kinds of carpets."
Regarding the seats: first, in the central area, having prepared a magnificent Buddha-seat supported by an auspicious pillar,
and having spread upon it whatever coverings were soft and beautiful, and having placed a pleasing pillow red on both sides,
he then fastened above it a canopy variegated with stars of gold and silver.
Having adorned it with garlands of perfumes, garlands of flowers, garlands of leaves, and so forth,
and having had a lattice-work of flowers made in a space twelve cubits on all sides, he had the area measuring about thirty cubits enclosed with a curtain.
Then, leaning against the western wall, he had seats prepared for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, such as cross-legged seats, backrested seats, and cushioned seats, covered above with white spreadings.
Having had it spread out, they had the eastern side of the hall prepared for his own seating; it is with reference to this that it is said, “having prepared seats.
“A water-jar” (udakamaṇika) refers to a large-mouthed water-vessel with a rim. Thus the Blessed One and the community of monks [prepared everything].

Thinking, "They will wash their hands and feet as they please, and they will rinse their mouths," they filled various places with water the color of jewels, added various flowers and scented powders for the purpose of perfuming, covered them with plantain leaves, and set them out.
Therefore it is said: "Having set out jars of water."
"Having raised oil-lamps" means having lit oil-lamps on staff-lanterns made of silver,
gold, and so forth, as well as in small bowls made of gold, silver, and so forth, held in the hands of figures such as *yonaka*s.
"They approached the Blessed One" refers here to those lay followers of Pāṭaligāma who did not go merely to the rest-house (*āvasathāgāra*), but...

Then, having had the streets throughout the entire village prepared and banners raised, and having had full water-jars and plantain trees set up at the doors of the houses, and having made the whole village appear like a sky strewn with stars by means of rows of lamps, [he gave this command]:
"Give milk to the infants who drink milk; feed the young children very quickly and put them to sleep; [avoid] loud noise..."
"Do not do so; today the Teacher will dwell within the village for one night. Buddhas, indeed, desire little noise.
Having had this proclamation made by the beating of a drum, they themselves took up torches and approached the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, went together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to the guest-house.
"He approached him" means that when they had thus announced the time, saying, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now consider it the right time," the Blessed One—
having arranged his double-layered robe, which was as deep red as the color of a *koviḷāra* flower soaked in lac juice and dyed a beautiful crimson,
like one cutting a lotus with a knife— and having covered the three circles [of his body] while wearing a golden waistband; he approached.
As if encircling a cluster of lotuses, having fastened a waistband with the splendor of lightning flashes,
as if wrapping an elephant’s frontal globe with red woolen cloth, as if casting a net of coral over a golden pinnacle a hundred cubits high,
as if donning a cloak of red woolen cloth upon a great golden cetiya— [he approached] the full moon as it moved along.
As if shrouding everything like a crimson cloud, as if sprinkling well-ripened lac juice upon the summit of the Golden Mountain,
and as if encircling the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa with a network of lightning-garlands, he shook the entire world-system— including Sineru, Yugandhara, and the great earth—
and donned a choice red rag-robe (paṃsukūla) the color of which was like a fresh *nigrodha* sprout, emerging from the dense forest.
Like a lion with a mane, like the full moon emerging from the peak of the mountain of sunrise, and like the morning sun, he emerged from the grove of trees where he was seated.

Then, rays of light issued forth from his body like flashes of lightning from the mouth of a cloud, making the trees on all sides appear as if their leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, and trunks were drenched in a stream of molten gold.
At that very moment, the great community of monks, each taking his own bowl and robe, [approached].
They surrounded the Blessed One. And those monks who stood surrounding him were such as these:

few in desire, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, speakers, patient with correction, reprovers, censurers of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Surrounded by them, the Blessed One shone like a mass of gold encircled by red woolen cloth,
like a golden ship situated in the midst of a cluster of red lotuses, or like a golden palace surrounded by a coral railing.
But the great elders, headed by Mahākassapa, having donned rag-robes the color of clouds, appeared like great elephants clad in armor of precious gems.
Those who were free from passion, whose defilements were shattered, whose tangles were disentangled, whose bonds were severed, and who clung neither to family nor to group, surrounded him.

Thus the Blessed One—himself free from passion, surrounded by those free from passion; himself free from hatred, surrounded by those free from hatred; himself free from delusion, surrounded by those free from delusion; himself without craving, surrounded by those without craving;
himself without defilement, surrounded by those without defilement; himself awakened, surrounded by those who have awakened after him—was surrounded by a retinue of bowls.
Like a pericarp surrounded by filaments, like a central whorl surrounded by filaments,
like the six-tusked king of elephants surrounded by eight thousand other elephants, like the swan-king Dhatarattha surrounded by ninety thousand swans,
like a universal monarch surrounded by his military divisions, like Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of Maruts, and like [Brahmā] surrounded by hosts of Brahmās...
Having subdued Great Brahmā, like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars,
he set out upon the road toward Pāṭaligāma with the peerless appearance of a Buddha and the immeasurable grace of a Buddha.
Then, from his front body, thick golden rays of light issued forth to a height of eighty cubits.
From the lower part of his body, from the right side, and from the left side,
dense rays of golden light arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits; from the hair at the crown of his head,
dense Buddha-rays, the color of a peacock’s neck, arose from every pore of his hair and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky.
From the soles of his feet, rays the color of coral rose up and reached eighty cubits into the solid earth;
from his tusks, from the white parts of his eyes, and from the fleshless parts of his nails, pure white Buddha-rays rose up and reached eighty cubits;
and from the places where the red and yellow colors were blended, [rays of those colors likewise issued forth].
Beams of light the color of madder rose up and reached a height of eighty cubits;

rays of radiance emerged everywhere, shining brightly. Thus, for a space of eighty cubits all around, the six-colored rays of the Buddha shone, quivered, and flashed forth, as if issuing from golden-staffed torches and leaping into the sky.
Like a great mass of flames from a great lamp, and like flashes of lightning issuing from a great cloud over the four continents,
they shot forth in every direction. By them, all the quarters of space were as if strewn with golden campaka flowers,
as if being drenched by streams of liquid gold pouring from golden jars, and as if encircled by outstretched bands of gold.
They shone as if strewn with the pollen of *kiṃsuka*, *kaṇikāra*, and *kikirāta* flowers tossed up by the *verambha* wind,
and as if colored by the powder of Chinese lacquer. The Blessed One’s body, too— resplendent with the halo of his eighty minor marks and the circle of fathom-wide radiance,
adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man— shone like the vault of heaven illuminated by brilliant stars, freed from the impurities of clouds, mist, and the like.
It shone as if it were a forest of lotuses in full bloom, or like a hundred-yojana *pāricchattaka* tree in all its splendor; it blazed forth,
as if overwhelming with its own glory the majesty of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two universal monarchs (*cakkavattī*),
thirty-two kings of the gods, and thirty-two great Brahmās, arranged one after another, as is fitting for those ten [directions].
Adorned with the thirty perfections— namely, the ten *pāramīs*, the ten *upapāramīs*, and the ten *paramattha-pāramīs*— all perfectly fulfilled;
and by the gift given, the virtue guarded, and the wholesome karma performed over four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons,
which, having converged into a single existence, found no opportunity to yield their fruition [otherwise].
It was like the time when the goods of a thousand ships, having been loaded onto a single ship by one who had fallen into distress;
like the time when the goods of a thousand carts were loaded onto a single cart;
and like the time when twenty-five Ganges rivers, having burst forth, became a single mass at their mouth.
While the Blessed One was being illuminated by this radiance of the Buddha, they raised up many thousands of torches before him, and likewise behind him, on his left side, and on his right side.

There were flowers such as *jātisumana*, campaka, jasmine, red lotuses, blue lotuses, *bakula*, and *sinduvāra*, as well as fragrant scented powders of blue, yellow, and other colors; and showers of water released from great clouds that extend over the four continents.

They scattered as if in competition. The sounds of the fivefold musical instruments and the voices of praise connected with the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha filled all directions, making them resound as if they were vocal.

The eyes of the devas, supaṇṇas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and humans felt as if they had obtained the drink of the Deathless (amata). Standing at this spot, [he spoke] in praise of the journey by means of thousands of verses.
It is appropriate to speak thus. Herein, this is merely the opening:
“Thus, endowed with all limbs, making the earth tremble, without harming living beings, the Guide of the World proceeds.”
“Raising his right foot first, the Bull among Men, endowed with glory, moves along;
the Supreme among Bipeds shines resplendent.
As the Best of Buddhas walks, the soles of his feet are soft.”
It touches the earth evenly and is not defiled by dust.
As the Leader of the World walks, the low ground rises up;
the high ground becomes level, even though the earth is insentient.
“Stones and gravel, potsherds and stumps and thorns—
all these obstacles are cleared away as the Leader of the World proceeds.
He does not lift [the foot] too far, nor does he set it down too close.”
He proceeds without clashing his knees or his ankles.
The Sage, whose conduct is perfected, does not set out too quickly, nor does he walk too slowly;
moving with a concentrated mind, he goes with composure.
“Neither looking upward, nor downward, nor across, nor toward the cardinal or intermediate directions does he walk; for he gazes only the distance of a yoke.
With the stride of an elephant, the Conqueror shines as he goes.”
The Chief of the World proceeded gracefully, bringing joy to the world including the devas.
Resplendent like the king of bulls, like a four-legged lion with a mane,
gladdening many beings, he approached the best of villages.

This, it is said, is the time for praise. In such occasions as these, whether regarding the physical beauty of the Blessed One’s body or the praise of his virtues, the only measure is the strength of the preacher.
He should say as much as he is able, whether in prose or in verse;
he should not be told, "It is poorly composed," or "He has leaped over the ford. For the Buddhas possess immeasurable praise.
O Blessed Ones, even the Buddhas themselves would be unable to describe their excellence in its entirety;

for even if they were to speak for an entire eon, they could not reach the end, let alone other beings. Having entered the village of Pāṭaligāma, which was adorned and prepared with such splendor and magnificence, the Blessed One [was honored] by the people with devout hearts with flowers, perfumes, incense, ointments, powders, and so forth.

Being honored, he entered the rest-house. Therefore it was said: “Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached the rest-house together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Regarding the phrase “having washed his feet”: although dust and dirt did not adhere to the Blessed One’s feet, for the sake of those lay followers...
Desiring the increase of wholesome qualities and wishing to set an example for others to follow, the Blessed One washed his feet.
Furthermore, since even a body subject to grasping can become cold, the Blessed One likewise performed the acts of bathing and washing his feet for that purpose as well.
"Placing the Blessed One at the head" means placing the Blessed One in front. In that regard, the Blessed One...
Seated in the midst of the bhikkhus and lay devotees, having been bathed with scented water,
dried with a *dukūla* cloth, and anointed with red vermilion, he shone most brilliantly like a solid image of red gold placed upon a seat draped with a red woolen blanket.
This, moreover, is the manner of praise used by the ancients in this context:
“Having gone to the circular pavilion, he who moves with the majestic stride of an elephant,
the foremost of the world, sat upon the excellent seat,
illuminating [all around]. Seated there, the charioteer of men to be tamed,”
The God beyond gods, endowed with the hundred marks of merit,
shines resplendent seated upon the Buddha-throne,
like a golden necklace upon a pale woolen cloth.
“Like a piece of gold from the Jambu River set upon a yellow blanket,
it shines, free from stain, like the radiant Vairocana gem.
Like a great sal tree in full bloom, it is adorned like King Meru.”
“Resembling a golden stupa, like a lotus within its sheath;
blazing like a lamp-tree, or like a fire upon a mountain peak;
like the Pāricchattaka tree of the devas, he shines forth in full bloom.”

“He addressed the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma”: because many people among those lay followers were established in virtue, he first pointed out the danger of failing in virtue, and then, in order to show the benefit of perfection in virtue, he addressed them for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma with the words, “Householders, there are these five,” and so forth. In this context, “one who is immoral” means one who lacks virtue.

Here, the word *du-* has the sense of "absence," as in "one of poor wisdom" (*duppañña*) and so forth. "One who has failed in virtue" (*sīlavipanna*) means one whose virtue has failed, whose restraint is broken.
And here, by the term "immoral" (*dussīla*), the absence of virtue in a person is stated. That absence of virtue in him is twofold:
either through non-undertaking, or through the breaking of what was undertaken. Of these two, the former is not as blameworthy as the latter.

It is more blameworthy. To show, by means of a teaching focused on the person, the absence of virtue as the sign of the disadvantage intended, it is said "one who has failed in virtue" (*sīlavipanna*); by this, it demonstrates the meaning of the term "immoral" (*dussīla*).
"On account of negligence" (*pamādādhikaraṇa*) means because of negligence. And this sutta is presented with reference to householders, yet it certainly applies to those who have gone forth as well.
For a householder, by whatever craft or means he maintains his livelihood— whether by agriculture, trade, or cattle-herding—
if he is negligent through such acts as the taking of life, he will be unable to accomplish those tasks at their proper time,
and thus his work will perish. Furthermore, if he commits the taking of life, theft, and so forth during the time of the Great Sacrifice (Māghāta), [his merit will be lost].

By means of punishment, one incurs a great loss of wealth. A monk who has gone forth but is immoral, due to negligence, incurs loss in terms of virtue, the word of the Buddha, meditative absorption (jhāna), and the seven treasures of the noble ones.
There is an evil reputation for the householder: "Such-and-such a person, born into such-and-such a family, is immoral, of evil nature, and has abandoned both this world and the next."
An evil report spreads through the midst of the four assemblies, saying: "He does not give even a mere ticket-meal. Regarding his having gone forth, an evil report likewise spreads, saying:
"Such-and-such a person, having gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation, was unable to guard his moral precepts, nor was he able to master the Buddha’s word;
he lives by means of medical practice and the like, and is possessed of the six kinds of disrespect. Thus an evil report spreads.

Regarding "lack of confidence": first, a householder approaches with fear, thinking, "Surely someone in this assembly will find out my business and then rebuke me," or "They will report it to the royal family.
Thus, he sits down dejected, with shoulders slumped and head bowed, unable to speak with confidence.
Even though he has gone forth, he approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks have assembled;
surely someone will find fault with my conduct, and then they will suspend my Uposatha and Pavāraṇa ceremonies, deprive me of my status as a recluse, and cast me out.
Thus, being lacking in confidence, he is unable to speak. On the other hand, some person, though being immoral, speaks as if he were full of self-assurance.
He too becomes dejected by his own disposition because of his state of remorse.
"He dies deluded" means that for an immoral person lying on his deathbed, the places where he undertook and practiced unwholesome deeds come into his field of vision.
Opening his eyes, he sees this world through the sight of his children, wife, and so forth.
He sees; by means of the appearance of the sign of his destination after closing his eyes, he sees the next world, and the four states of misery appear to him according to his karma.
It is as if he were being struck by a hundred spears or embraced by a mass of flames.
Crying out, "Save me! Save me!", he dies. Therefore it is said: "He passes away deluded."
"With the breakup of the body" means with the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been grasped. "After death" means immediately thereafter, at the seizing of the reborn aggregates.
Alternatively, "with the breakup of the body" means the cutting off of the life-faculty. "After death" means after the moment of death (*cuti*).
"The state of deprivation" (*apāya*) and so forth are all synonyms for hell (*niraya*). For hell is [the opposite of] merit, which consists of the causes for heaven and liberation.
It is an *apāya* because of the departure from happiness, or because of the absence of the arrival (*āya*) of happiness.
It is a *duggati* because it is the destination or refuge for suffering, or because it is a destination produced by defiled (*duṭṭha*) karma due to an abundance of hatred.
It is a *vinipāta* because those who have committed misdeeds fall into it helplessly (*vivasā*), or because they fall into it while their limbs and members are being shattered.
*Vinipāta* (falling away). There is no "going" (*aya*) here that is perceived as a gratification; thus it is *niraya* (hell).

Alternatively, by the mention of the "states of loss" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*). For the animal realm is a state of loss because it is departed from the "good destination" (*sugati*);

yet it is not a "bad destination" (*duggati*) because of the possibility of great beings such as the Nāga kings being born there. By the mention of the "bad destination," he indicates the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*).

It illuminates this. For that [state] is indeed a *apāya* (a state of loss) and a *duggati* (an unhappy destination), because it is removed from the *sugati* (happy destination) and because it is a place where suffering goes;

however, it is not a *vinipāta* (a fallen state), because the *asuras* do not fall [into it] in the same way. The celestial palaces (*vimānas*) of the *petas* possessing great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) are also produced there.
By the inclusion of the term *vinipāta*, he illuminates the host of *asuras*; for that, in the sense already stated, is both an *apāya* and a *duggati*.
And it is called a "state of ruin" (*vinipāta*) because one falls away from all heights of excellence.
By the mention of "hell," however, he indicates hell itself in its many forms, such as Avīci and so forth. "Is reborn" means to be produced.
The discourse on benefits should be understood by reversing what has been stated above. This, however, is the distinction: "one who is virtuous" is so by virtue of undertaking [the precepts].
"Virtuous. "Endowed with virtue" means one who is endowed with virtue by having accomplished virtue that is both pure and complete.

"A mass of wealth" means a heap of wealth. Regarding "a happy destination, a heavenly world": here, by the inclusion of "happy destination" (*sugati*), the human realm is also included; by the inclusion of "heavenly world" (*sagga*), only the divine realm is meant.
In this context, a "happy destination" (*sugati*) is a beautiful state of existence, [characterized] by sense objects such as forms and so forth.
"Very excellent" means heaven (*sagga*); that too is called "the world" (*loka*) in the sense of being subject to breaking up and disintegration.

For a long time during the night, [the Blessed One spoke] to the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma with a discourse on the Dhamma; that is, both with a discourse on the Dhamma not bound by the specific wording of the Canon and with a discourse expressing appreciation for the guest-house.
For at that time, since Ajātasattu was building the city of Pāṭaliputta there...
While measuring out [the city], he brought together those householders from other villages, market towns, and royal capitals who were endowed with virtue and good conduct;
having granted them wealth, grain, houses, sites for dwellings, fields, and exemptions, they were settled there.
Therefore, because the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma saw these benefits, they especially honored virtue, and because virtue is the foundation of all qualities.
Having first proclaimed the benefits of virtue to them, he thereafter— like one causing the celestial Ganges to descend,
like one drawing up the essence of the earth, like one grasping a great rose-apple tree by its crown and shaking it,

and like one pressing a great honeycomb measuring a league in size with a wheel and making them drink its most sweet nectar— brought about the welfare and happiness of the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma.
Even when delivering miscellaneous discourses, he would say: "Householders, this gift of a dwelling place is a source of great merit.
Your dwelling has been used by me, it has been used by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and when used by both me and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is as if it has been used by the Jewel of the Dhamma itself.
Thus, when used by these Three Jewels, its merit is indeed immeasurable."
Furthermore, when a dwelling is given, it is as if every kind of gift has been given;
the merit of constructing a ground-floor hut of leaves or a pavilion of branches dedicated to the Saṅgha cannot be measured.

Indeed, by the power of giving a dwelling, even for one being reborn in a future existence, there is no such thing as a cramped confinement in the womb; rather, they dwell in a chamber twelve cubits square.
“...the mother’s womb is indeed unconfined for the embryo. Having thus delivered many discourses on the Dhamma, variegated by various methods, he said:
“It wards off cold and heat, as well as wild beasts, And snakes, mosquitoes, the chill, and even the rains.”
“Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, one encounters them;
[the dwelling] is for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and for the purpose of meditating and practicing insight.
The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised as supreme by the Buddha.”
Therefore, a wise person, seeing his own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those who are learned to dwell therein;
and he should provide them with food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings.
“One should give with a serene mind to those who have become upright;
they will teach him the Dhamma that removes all suffering,
by knowing which Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.”

Thus, for much of the night—indeed, for more than one and a half watches—he explained the benefits of giving a dwelling, saying, "This too is a benefit of giving a dwelling; this too is a benefit of giving a dwelling.
Among these, only these verses were included in the compilation, whereas the miscellaneous discourses on the Dhamma were not included in the compilation.
The meanings of the words "having shown" (*sandassetvā*) and so forth have already been explained.
"Abhikkanta" means "passed beyond"; two watches of the night have gone by. "Yassadāni tumhe kālaṃ maññatha" means:
regarding whatever departure you consider to be the time, it is now the time for your going; the meaning is, "Go. But why did the Blessed One dismiss them? Out of compassion.
For those who had spent the three watches of the night sitting [in meditation], there was bodily affliction.
"If a large community of monks were to arise, it would be necessary to find space for their beds and seats;
thus, out of compassion for both, he urged them [to leave].
"An empty place" (*suññāgāra*) means a separate, distinct empty place; there was none of that there. It is said that those householders [belonged] to him alone.
Having had a curtain draped around one side of the assembly hall, they prepared a proper couch, spread it with suitable coverings,
and tied a canopy above it adorned with garlands of flowers and perfumes and decorated with stars of gold and silver;
then they set up oil lamps fed with fragrant oil, thinking, "Perhaps the Teacher, rising from his Dharma-seat..."
“Desiring to rest for a short while, one might lie down here; thus this lodging hall, having been used by the Blessed One in all four postures, will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time.
The Teacher, intending that very thing, spread out his outer robe there and assumed the lion’s posture. It was with reference to this that it was said: “An empty dwelling...”
"...entered. Therein, from the place for washing the feet up to the Dhamma-seat, he went; over this extent of space, the act of going was accomplished.
Having reached the Dhamma-seat, he stood for a short while; this was his standing there. He sat upon the Dhamma-seat for two watches of the night;
over this extent of time, the act of sitting was accomplished. After dismissing the lay followers from the Dhamma-seat...
Having ascended, he lay down in the lion’s posture at the place as previously described. This spot had been used by the Blessed One for all four modes of conduct.
The commentary on the account of the site of Pāṭaligāma is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse concerning Sunīdha and Vassakāra: 286.
"Sunīdha and Vassakāra" refers to two brahmins, Sunīdha and Vassakāra.
"Ministers of Magadha" means the chief ministers of the King of Magadha, or the high officials within the kingdom of Magadha; they were endowed with great authority and power.
"The high ministers of Magadha. "They are building a city in Pāṭaligāma" means they are building a city on the plot of ground designated as Pāṭaligāma;
the meaning is that they are now constructing a city at the place which was formerly known by the name "Pāṭaligāma.
"For the sake of warding off the Vajjis" means for the purpose of cutting off the source of income for the Licchavi kings. "Sites" means...

"House-sites" refers to locations for establishing houses. "Their minds incline toward designing dwellings" means that the minds of those who recite the science of site-selection (*vatthuvidyā*)—who design dwellings for kings and royal ministers—incline [toward their work].
It is said that by the power of their craft, they perceive within a space of thirty cubits beneath the surface of the earth: "In this place is the dwelling-territory of *nāgas*."
“Here is the dwelling-place and domain of spirits (yakkhas), here is that of elemental beings (bhūtas);

here there is a rock or a stump,” they know; then, having recited their craft-mantras, they avoid such sites involving harm and, as if consulting with those deities who have taken possession of the site, they construct various dwellings on ground free from harm.
Alternatively, deities, having become intent upon their bodies, incline their minds toward constructing dwellings here and there.
Having struck stakes at the four corners, they vanish as soon as the site has been taken up.
Faithful deities do this for families of the faithful, and faithless deities do so for families of the faithless.
And why? For those with faith think thus: “When people here are building a residence, they will first have the Saṅgha of monks sit down and have auspicious blessings recited;

then we shall be able to see the virtuous ones, hear a Dhamma talk, receive answers to questions, and hear the expression of thanksgiving, and by giving gifts to these men, we shall obtain our own merit.”
"...will show [it]. Even deities who lack faith act in such a way, thinking, "How can we obtain the opportunity to see and hear their practice according to our own desires?
Regarding "by the Tāvatiṃsa [gods]": for just as there might be one wise person in a single family, or one [wise person] in a single monastery...
Just as, depending on a learned bhikkhu, a reputation arises—“The people in such-and-such a family are wise;
the bhikkhus in such-and-such a monastery are learned”—even so, depending on Sakka, the king of the gods, and the divine son Vissakamma, the reputation arose:
“The Tāvatiṃsa gods are wise. Therefore he said, “by the Tāvatiṃsas. Regarding the phrase “just as if,” etc.:
This shows that Sunīdha and Vassakāra were building the city as if they had consulted with the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
"As far as the noble domain" means as far as there is a place for the noble persons to resort to.
"As far as the marketplace" means as far as there is a place for buying and selling where merchants have their goods brought and piled up in heaps.

There is a place for merchants to dwell. "This shall be the preeminent city" means that among those marketplaces—the seats of the noble ones—this city will be the foremost, the eldest, and the chief. "Puṭabhedana" is a place for opening packages of goods;
what is meant is a place for untying the bundles of merchandise. For even goods not obtainable anywhere else in the whole of Jambudīpa...
The meaning is: "He will obtain it right here; even if it goes for sale elsewhere, it will come back for sale here;

therefore, he will break open the bundle right here. As for "income": four [hundred thousand] at the four gates and one in the assembly hall—thus five hundred thousand will arise there day after day; these are his prospective incomes (*āyāni*).
[The text] shows this. In the phrases "by fire" and so forth, the word *vā* has the sense of *ca*;
thus the meaning is: "It will be destroyed by fire, by water, and by dissension. For one portion of it will be destroyed by fire, such that it cannot even be extinguished;
one portion the Ganges will carry away; and one [portion] will be unmentioned for the other.
"By this [city], which has been left unsaid by us who speak thus through malicious speech, it will perish through the mutual dissension of people already divided.
Having said this, the Blessed One went to the bank of the Ganges at dawn, washed his face, and sat down waiting for the time of the alms-round.
Sunidha and Vassakāra also thought, "Our king is a supporter of the ascetic Gotama."
When we have arrived, he will ask us: "It is said that the Teacher went to Pāṭaligāma; did you approach him, or did you not approach him?
When we say, "We approached him," he will ask, "Did you invite him, or did you not invite him? When we say, "We did not invite him," he will impute blame to us.
"He will restrain them, and furthermore, we shall establish a city in this place where nothing has been built before;
for wherever the ascetic Gotama goes, ill-omened beings retreat from that place; therefore, we shall have the auspicious rites for the city recited there.
Having thought thus, they approached the Teacher and invited him. Thus it was said: "Then Sunīdha and Vassakāra... and so forth.
"At the time of the morning" means during the morning period. "Having dressed" means having put on the lower robe in the manner used for entering a village, and having fastened the waistband.
"Taking bowl and robe" means having taken up the bowl and the robe and made them part of one's bodily equipment;
the meaning is that he put on the upper robe and held the bowl in his hand.
“Virtuous here” means virtuous ones in this place where one dwells. “Self-restrained” means restrained in body, speech, and mind.
“One should dedicate the offering to them” means that when the four requisites have been given to the Saṅgha, one should give the merit (patti) to those household deities.
“Being honored, they honor in turn” means: “These people are not even our kinsmen, yet they give us the merit.”
"Give [them offerings] and provide well-arranged protection," they say; thus, they provide excellent protection.

"Honored, they honor in return": being honored from time to time by the performance of offerings, [the deities] think, "These people are not even our kinsmen, yet they perform offerings for us every four or six months," and so they honor them in return, removing any dangers that have arisen.
"Then they lead him away" means they lead that person who is wise by nature away from there. "Orasa" means one raised having been placed upon the breast;
just as a mother feels compassion for her own breast-born son and strives solely for the sake of removing any danger that has arisen for him, so too does she feel compassion—this is the meaning.
"She sees auspicious things" means she sees beautiful things.
"Having rejoiced" means that, by way of rejoicing in the merit they had just performed, he gave them a discourse on the Dhamma.
Sunidha and Vassakāra, having heard the Blessed One’s words, "Whatever deities were there, dedicate the offering to them," gave the merit to those deities.
That became known as the Gotama Gate; it was through this gate of the city that the Blessed One—
He departed; that became known as the Gotama Gate. However, because he had not yet crossed over for the purpose of crossing the Ganges, it was not yet called the Gotama Ferry (*gotamatittha*).
"Full" (*pūrā*) means filled. "Level with the brim" (*samatittikā*) means the water was so full and overflowing that it reached the very edge of the bank.

"Drinkable by crows" (*kākapeyyā*) means the water was such that crows standing on the bank were able to drink from it. By all three terms, the state of being completely full, level with both banks, is expressed.

He speaks. A *uḷumpa* is that which is constructed by taking light wooden poles for the purpose of crossing to the other shore, fashioning pegs to join them together like door-panels, and thus forming what is designated as a boat.
A *kulla* is that which is made by gathering reeds, rushes, and so forth, binding them into bundles with creepers and the like.

"Having understood this matter": having understood in every way that the great multitude was incapable of crossing even the mere waters of the Ganges, while he himself and his community of monks had stood after crossing the ocean of saṃsāra—which is exceedingly deep and vast—he uttered this *udāna* (inspired utterance) to illuminate that meaning. As for the meaning of the *udāna* verse:

This is indeed shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Therein, "this is a designation for a place of water" means that this term *aṇṇava* is a designation for any place of water as previously described, and not exclusively for the ocean; such is the intended meaning.
"River" (*sara*) is intended here [as a river], based on the derivation "it flows" (*sarati*), meaning it runs. "Deep and wide" means deep in the sense of being bottomless.

It is "extensive" because it pervades the entire threefold world (*tiloka*). "He crosses over" means without clinging, without adhering, and without even reaching the marshes, since they cannot be crossed by such means.
"For people bind a raft" means that people undergo the exertion of binding a raft. "Without even a raft" means without such a raft as this.
"The wise have crossed over" refers to those who possess the knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*).
Because they are endowed with wisdom, the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha are wise; they have crossed over and are established on the further shore.
The commentary on the account of Sunidha and Vassakāra regarding the site [of Rājagaha] is finished.
The commentary on the discourse on truth at Koṭigāma.
287. *Koṭigāma*: This is the village built at the corner of King Mahāpanāda’s palace;
the meaning is that it was established at the site where the pinnacle of the fallen palace stood. *Ariyasaccānaṃ*: Of those truths which, when penetrated, produce the state of a noble one (*ariya*).
*Ananubodhā*: By way of non-awakening, that is, by not understanding. *Appaṭivedhā*: By way of non-penetration. *Anubodho*... [etc.]

And here, "prior knowledge" refers to the knowledge belonging to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāgiya-ñāṇa*), while "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization (*abhisamaya*) by means of path-knowledge.

In this context, since penetration is preceded by awakening (*anubodha*) and does not occur without awakening, and since some forms of awakening are connected with penetration, and the wandering in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-saṃsaraṇa*) is caused by the absence of both of these, it was said: "Through non-awakening... [etc. ...and for you. In that passage, "wandered about" (*sandhāvitaṃ*) means:
"It has run on" (*sandhāvitaṃ*) means it has wandered from one existence to another by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"It has transmigrated" (*saṃsaritaṃ*) means it has transmigrated through successive deaths and births. "Both mine and yours" (*mamañceva tumhākañca*) means both by me and by you.
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "The running on and the transmigrating—the wandering and the transmigration—belonged to both me and you."
"Saṃsitaṃ" means transmigrated. "The uprooting of the conduit to existence" (bhavanetti):

just as a man with a rope in his hand leads a bird bound by a long cord to another place, so too, volitional formation (abhisaṅkhāra) leads the continuum of beings bound by the cord of craving to another state of existence;
thus it is the "conduit to existence. That cord of craving, which is capable of leading one from one existence to another, [is severed] by the sword of the Noble Path.
"Completely struck down, cut off, and rendered non-existent" means that the conduit to existence (*bhavanetti*) has been uprooted.

**Commentary on the Story of Ambapālī (288):** "The ground for vehicles" refers to where it is possible to travel by mounting a vehicle; this is called the "ground for vehicles. "Having descended from the vehicle" means having stepped down from the vehicle at the outer gatehouse of the monastery.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Licchavis (Licchavīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 289.
“Blue” is a term that encompasses all [colors]. “Of blue color,” and so forth, is for the purpose of showing its specific divisions.
In this context, their natural color is not blue; rather, it is said so because they are smeared with blue ointment. “Clad in blue garments.”
Even their garments—linen, fine silk, and so forth—are exclusively blue. "Blue ornaments" means they are adorned with blue jewel-ornaments and blue flowers.
It is said that those ornaments, though variegated with gold, appear as if they were purely blue due to the radiance of sapphires;
likewise, their chariots are inlaid with sapphires, draped in blue cloth, and equipped with blue banners and blue fenders.
The meaning in all instances should be understood according to this method: [chariots] yoked with blue ornaments and blue horses, and even the goads and poles were blue.
"Paṭivaṭṭesi" means she struck. "Kissa je Ambapālī?"—the word "je" is a form of address; it means, "Lady Ambapālī, for what reason?
"Sāhāram" means that from this [chariot], these royal men bring forth strength.
"Food" refers to the country where that food is consumed; "with its food" means together with its country—that is the meaning.
"They snapped their fingers" means they moved their fingers. "Ambakāya" means by a woman; for this is a term of address used for women, namely:
*ambakā*, *mātugāma*, and *jananikā*. "Look! means see! "Gaze! means look intently, again and again.
"Behold" is the meaning. "Bring near" means: bring this assembly of Licchavis close to your own minds as being like the Tāvatiṃsa devas;

bring them near, cause them to be joined with them. The meaning is: behold them by making these Licchavi kings equal to the Tāvatiṃsa devas, thinking, "Just as the Tāvatiṃsa devas are handsome, pleasing, and of various colors such as blue and so forth, so too are these Licchavi kings."

But why did the Blessed One, having prohibited the grasping of signs regarding forms and so forth through the eye and other faculties in hundreds of discourses, here encourage the grasping of signs with such great effort?

It was out of a desire for their welfare, just as he desired the welfare of the Venerable Nanda by showing him the excellence of heavenly rebirths. For it is said that among those monks there were some...
To those whose energy was slackened, [the Buddha] spoke—enticing them with the prospect of prosperity—in order to generate enthusiasm for the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), saying:
"For those who practice the duty of a recluse with heedfulness (*appamāda*), such a perfection of sovereignty as this is easily obtained. Alternatively, this is not an instruction to grasp at signs;
rather, it is merely part of the gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*) intended to show that "the sovereign power of these kings is like a divine attainment."
It should be regarded as being like a description of prosperity. Furthermore, he spoke thus for the purpose of manifesting the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*).
For before long, all these will meet their destruction through Ajātasattu;

then, seeing the splendor and prosperity of their kingdom, those bhikkhus who remain will perceive the characteristic of impermanence, thinking: "Indeed, even such splendor and prosperity shall be seen to perish."
He spoke for the purpose of clarifying the characteristic of impermanence, [thinking]: "Having developed [this], they will attain Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Why did he say, "May he consent," even though he already knew that Ambapālī had invited him? It was because of their lack of faith and because of the formal requirements of etiquette.
For that woman was a profligate who might have said, "She invited me," even without having been invited; therefore, [he spoke thus] to them.
It came to pass. It is indeed the custom of men, after hearing the Dhamma, to extend an invitation at the time of departure before leaving.
The commentary on the account of the Licchavis is finished.
The commentary on the account of the General Sīha follows.
290. *Abhiññātā* means known, renowned, and well-known. *Santhāgāre* refers to a hall built for the purpose of providing rest for the great multitude.
It is said that this assembly hall was located in the center of the city;
it was visible from the four gates, and people arriving from the four directions would first rest there before proceeding to their own respective comfortable locations.
They go. They say that even the house built for the purpose of attending to royal affairs for the royal families is [a "palace"].
For it is there that the Licchavi kings sit down to attend to, perform, and deliberate upon their royal duties.
"Seated" means on costly rugs spread out specifically for them to sit upon, with white parasols raised above.
Seated upon their seats, they praised the Buddha in many ways.
This means that after attending to both the duties of the royal household and matters for the welfare of the world, they praised the Buddha for numerous reasons.
For those kings were wise, endowed with faith, and were noble disciples—some stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners—and all of them...
Having severed the worldly tangle, they speak the praise of the Three Jewels, beginning with the Buddha. In that regard, the praise of the Buddha is threefold:
the praise of his conduct (*cariyā-vaṇṇa*), the praise of his physical form (*sarīra-vaṇṇa*), and the praise of his qualities (*guṇa-vaṇṇa*). Herein, these kings began the praise of his conduct:
"Indeed, a difficult task was performed by the Perfectly Enlightened One throughout more than a hundred thousand eons..."
"By fulfilling thirty perfections— namely, four incalculable eons of the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten near-perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)—
and by bringing to their highest point the conduct for the benefit of oneself, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood,
while relinquishing the five great sacrifices," they spoke thus, extolling the virtues of the Buddha through one hundred and fifty Jātaka tales.
Having brought him to the Tusita heaven, they established him there. Praising the excellence of the Dhamma, however, they spoke of its qualities by way of its divisions, saying:

"The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One consists of five Nikāyas according to collection, three Piṭakas according to basket, nine Aṅgas according to limbs, and eighty-four thousand dhamma-kkhandhas according to aggregates."
Speaking in praise of the Saṅgha: "Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, sons of noble family who have acquired faith abandon their vast wealth and circle of kinsmen;

disregarding the white parasol, the position of viceroy, commander-in-chief, guild-leader, treasurer, and other such ranks, they go forth and enter the sublime dispensation of the Teacher. For those who have gone forth, having abandoned the white parasol..."
"At the time of the Buddha, there were eighty thousand who had gone forth, beginning with the great kings Bhaddiya, Mahākappina, and Pukkusāti;

yet there is no limit to those such as the noble sons Yasa, Soṇa the merchant’s son, Raṭṭhapāla the son of a treasurer, and others, who abandoned wealth amounting to many koṭis and went forth—noble sons of such and such kinds go forth in the Teacher’s dispensation. Thus it was said by way of a summary of the going-forth.
They spoke of the virtues of the Saṅgha.
"Sīho Senāpati" means a commander-in-chief of that name. For in Vesālī there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings;
all of them having assembled and taken counsel together, [decided] to govern the kingdom.

"Search for one who is capable," they said. While searching, they saw Prince Sīha and, concluding "This one will be able to do it," they gave him the general’s parasol covered with a woolen cloth the color of a red gem.
With reference to this, it is said: "Sīha the general. "A disciple of the Nigaṇṭha" means a disciple of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
He was a provider of requisites and an attendant. For in the land of Jambudīpa, there were three people who were the chief attendants of the Nigaṇṭhas:
the householder Upāli at Nālandā, Vappa the Sakyan at Kapilavatthu, and this General Sīha at Vesālī.
He was seated; for while seats had been prepared for the other kings within their respective retinues, for Sīha, however, a seat was prepared in the very center.
"Taking his place" means he was seated upon that costly royal throne which had been prepared for him. "Without doubt" means free from uncertainty;
"certainly" means with absolute conviction. They do not praise anyone of little standing in such a manner with hundreds of reasons.
"He approached the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta"—it is said that the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta [thought], "If this Sīha [is indeed] someone..."
Having heard the praise of the ascetic Gotama being spoken, he will approach to see the ascetic Gotama, and my own decline will come to pass.
Thinking thus, he spoke first to the general Sīha:
“General, many in this world say, ‘I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha. If you [should see] anyone...”

"I wish to go to see him; you should ask me about it, and I shall send you only to a suitable place and keep you away from an unsuitable one. Recalling those words, he thought, "If he sends me, I will go;
if not, I will not go," and so he approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Having heard his words, the Nigaṇṭha was overwhelmed by intense grief as if struck by a great mountain;
thinking, "I have become desirous of going to that very place where I did not wish her to go; I am ruined," he became displeased.
Then, resolving, "I shall devise a means to turn him back," he said, "But what [is it]? and so forth. Speaking thus, he [seized] the ox as it was walking by the muzzle.
As if striking out a burning lamp, as if extinguishing it, and as if overturning a bowl filled with food, he destroyed the rapture that had arisen in the lion.
"The volitional formation for departure" refers to the exertion engaged in by means of preparing elephant-vehicles and so forth, and taking perfumes, garlands, and other such items;
"that was stilled" means it was pacified.
"Once more" (*dutiyampi kho*) means for a second time. And in this section, while praising the Buddha, they described the beauty of the Blessed One’s body—
delimiting it from the Tusita heaven down to the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhipallaṅka*)— by way of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*dvattiṃsa-mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa*),
the eighty minor characteristics (*asīti-anubyañjana*), and the fathom-wide aura (*vyāma-pabhā*), from the soles of his feet below to the tips of his hair above.
While praising the Dhamma, they spoke of its qualities by way of its being well-expounded, saying: "There is not even a single word or a single syllable that is flawed.
While praising the Sangha, they said: "Having renounced such fame, glory, and wealth, those who have gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation are not of a lazy nature;
rather, they are practitioners who fulfill the thirteen ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa)."

Having performed the work of the seven contemplations (*anupassanā*) and employing the thirty-eight classifications of objects (*ārammaṇavibhatti*), they spoke of the qualities of the Saṅgha by way of the practice (*paṭipadā*).
On the third occasion, however, while speaking the praise of the Buddha, they did so according to the method of the Suttanta, beginning with: "Such indeed is that Blessed One."
They spoke of the Buddha’s qualities, beginning with, “The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One,” thus describing the qualities of the Dhamma according to the method of the Suttas;

and they spoke of the qualities of the Saṅgha, beginning with, “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way,” thus describing the qualities of the Saṅgha according to the method of the Suttas.
Then Sīha thought: “From the third day onward, these Licchavi royal families [have been speaking] of the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.”
As they spoke, their mouths could not suffice; "Surely that Blessed One is endowed with extraordinary qualities;
today, without abandoning this arisen rapture, I shall see the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then the thought occurred to him: "What indeed can the Nigaṇṭhas do to me? In this context, "What indeed can the Nigaṇṭhas do to me? means: what indeed can the Nigaṇṭhas possibly do for me?
"They will do so. "Whether asked or unasked" means whether they have been requested or not requested.
For it is not the case that they will show me their excellence of vehicles, mounts, wealth, sovereignty, and glory only if asked, nor will they kill me if not asked;
the intention is that their asking is fruitless.
"During the day of the day" means as soon as midday has passed. "He departed from Vesālī":
just as in the summer season, when it has rained, water flowing down enters a river and, having gone only a short distance, stops and does not continue on;
even so, on the first day, because of the joy that had arisen in Sīha’s mind thinking, "I shall see the One of Ten Powers," [the pain subsided].

The time when he was repelled by the Nigaṇṭha was like this: on the second day, when it rained and the flowing water entered a river, after going a short distance and striking a heap of sand, the flow ceased;

in the same way, on the second day, the time when Sīha’s joy—which had arisen thinking, "I shall see the One of Ten Powers"—was repelled by the Nigaṇṭha, was like that which occurred on the third day.
When it rains, the water flowing down enters a river;
as it sweeps along old leaves, dry stalks, reeds, rubbish, and so forth, it breaks through the mound of sand and flows only toward the ocean’s depth.

In the same way, on the third day, having heard the discourse on the virtues of the three [other] systems, Sīha experienced joy and gladness and thought: “The Nigaṇṭhas are fruitless, they are without result.”
"Nigaṇṭhas, what will these people do for me? I shall go into the presence of the Teacher.
Having thus resolved to depart, he left Vesālī. As he was departing, he thought, "It has been a long time since I have desired to go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers;
yet it is not fitting for me to go in an unknown guise. Thinking, "Whoever desires to go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers..."
Having caused the proclamation to be made, "Let everyone come forth," and having had five hundred chariots prepared, he mounted the finest chariot.
Surrounded by those five hundred chariots and a great assembly, and having had perfumes, flowers, powders, incense, and other offerings taken up, he set out.
As he approached the Blessed One, entering the monastery, even from afar he beheld the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura of radiance, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Seeing the six-colored, dense rays of the Buddha’s light, he thought, "I have not seen such a person living so near to me for all this time; I have indeed been deceived! What a loss to me!

Thinking thus, like a poor man who has discovered a great treasure, he was filled with rapture and joy and approached the Blessed One. [The verse says: "They explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma."
They explain this as a secondary reason for what was stated by the Blessed One Gotama.
Here, the word *dhamma* has the sense of "reason" (cause), as in such passages as "the analytical knowledge of phenomena is knowledge regarding the cause.

And here, "reason" is intended to mean the meaning of the word as it occurs, because that [meaning] is the cause for the occurrence of the word; for the employment of a word is invariably connected with its meaning.
"Anukāraṇaṃ" (imitation/reasoning) means that when he is thus addressed by others, his response is a legitimate discussion or counter-argument (*sahadhammiko vādānuvādo*).

Because it is supported by reasons corresponding to the reasons stated by others, neither his own argument nor the subsequent counter-argument reaches even the slightest point or reason that ought to be censured by the wise. This is what is meant: in no way whatsoever...
"In your doctrine, there is no ground for censure. "Not wishing to misrepresent" means not wishing to speak with what is untrue. 291–292.
The meaning of the passages beginning with "There is a method, Sīha," etc., should be understood according to the manner set forth in the Verañjakaṇḍa.
"With the supreme consolation" means with the highest consolation, which consists of the four paths and the four fruits. [He taught] the Dhamma for the sake of consolation.

"He teaches" means he teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of encouragement and for the purpose of providing support. Thus the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to Sīha the General by way of these eight factors.
"Having investigated" means: having understood, having reflected, and having weighed it, you should do what ought to be done; this is what is meant.
“Sādhu hoti” means he is beautiful. For when people like you see me and go for refuge to me, while seeing a Nigaṇṭha and going for refuge to a Nigaṇṭha, the censure arises:
“Why does this lion go for refuge only to whoever he has seen?
Therefore, he shows that careful investigation is good for people like you. “Paṭākaṃ parihareyyun” means...

It is said that having obtained such a disciple, they would raise a banner and wander through the city proclaiming, "A certain king, or royal minister, or merchant has gone for refuge to us and become our disciple. Why?
[They thought], "In this way, our greatness will be made manifest. But if he were to ask, "Why have I gone for refuge to these?"...
