“...gone,” and remorse might arise; yet, having dispelled that by thinking, “Many know my state of having gone for refuge to them, and it would now be difficult to turn back,” he will not retreat. Therefore he said, “They would carry aloft a banner.
“A well” means standing like a prepared reservoir. “Family” means your residence.
"You should think it ought to be given" means: "In the past, even when you saw ten, twenty, or sixty people arrive, you did not say 'there is nothing' but gave;
now, for the mere reason that I have gone to you for refuge, do not cut off these things to be given.
For indeed, what has been obtained must be given"—thus he exhorted him. "I heard that from you, venerable sir. From whom did you hear it? From the Nigaṇṭhas.
The Santikas. It seems they proclaim thus among the households: “We say that a gift should be given to whoever has attained [perfection];
however, the ascetic Gotama says, ‘A gift should be given to me alone… [and so on] … what is given to other disciples does not bear great fruit.
With reference to them, he said: “I have heard this,” and so forth.
294. "Meat that has come into being" (*pavattamaṃsa*) refers to meat that is naturally available and permissible; the intention is: "Go and seek it at the market after taking the price.
"Many Nigaṇṭhas" refers to about five hundred Nigaṇṭhas. "A fat animal" (*thūlaṃ pasuṃ*) refers to a large-bodied animal, such as a cow, a camel, a buffalo, or a pig.
"Specially prepared for him" (*uddissakataṃ*) means prepared by designating oneself [as the recipient]; "killed" (*māritaṃ*).

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the term *paṭiccasamuppāda* (dependent origination), here the word *kamma* functions as the object (*karmasādhana*) and refers to the past; thus it is said, "done depending upon itself.
This is a designation for the "efficient cause" (*nimittakamma*), as in such expressions as "one touches the dependent-origination-action" (*paṭicca kammaṃ phusati*).
"Of the efficient cause" means of that action which is to be obtained by way of being a sign or condition (*nimittabhāva*), not by way of performing or causing to perform.
"Meat with action" (*paṭiccakamma*) means that action is present therein; for example, "one who has the Buddha [as his object] is a Buddha.
Alternatively, a textual supplement should be understood as "it touches action dependent upon [the meat]";
the meaning is that this act of killing living beings touches that person in dependence upon this meat. For half of that unwholesome [kamma] belongs to the giver, and half...
"It belongs to the recipient"—this is their tenet. "Upakaṇṇake" means at the root of the ear. "Alaṃ" is a word of refusal;

the meaning is, "Let it be, what is the use of this? "And yet they do not grow old"—these venerable ones, though for a long time having been desirous of disrepute and speaking disrepute, do not grow old through their calumny; they do not reach the end of their slander.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, in the sense of "shame," this word *jiridanti* should be understood as "they are ashamed," not in the sense of "they do not feel shame.
The commentary on the story of the General Siha is finished.
The commentary on the discourse authorizing the use of a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a place where food may be prepared).
295. "Mere talk" (*abhilāpamatta*) means mere teaching. "For the purpose of eating food" (*āmisakhādanatthāya*) means for the purpose of eating food discarded here and there.
"Even before [the meal] has arrived" (*anuppageva*) means at the very time of dawn. "A loud noise" (*oravasadda*) means a great sound.

"But even without saying that" (*taṃ pana avatvāpi*) means even without saying it according to the method stated in the Andhaka-Ṭīkā. By the word "even" (*pi*), he also permits speaking in that manner.
"By the method stated in the commentaries" means by the method stated in the other commentaries.

"The common characteristic [is found] when it is said, 'We are building a kitchen' (*kappiyakuṭi*) or 'a kitchen' (*kappiyakuṭī*)," refers to the characteristic of building a hut with a formal proclamation (*ussāvanantikā-kuṭikaraṇa-lakkhaṇa*), as stated in all the commentaries.
"Piling up" (*caya*) means the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). "From which point onwards" means from whichever brick, stone, or lump of clay one begins.

"It is not permissible [to say] 'we are making a *kappiyakuṭi* (a building for allowable goods)' regarding bricks and so forth placed beneath the wall" means that bricks and other materials being established on the ground beneath the first layer of bricks of a wall are considered "belonging to the earth" (*bhūmigatika*); therefore, it is not permissible to establish them while saying, "we are making a *kappiyakuṭi*.
If this is so, why is it permissible to do so for pillars that are being established after being buried in the ground? [The answer follows:]...

"It is permissible to fix them" means he said, "but pillars... are permissible. "Only belonging to the Saṅgha" refers to a dwelling-place belonging to the Saṅgha that was made for the purpose of residence.
"Belonging to an individual monk" refers to a private dwelling-place of a monk made specifically for the purpose of residence.
By the term "storing near the mouth," only the offense of dukkaṭa incurred by keeping it inside is indicated.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the *kappiya-bhūmi* (the site for allowable goods) is finished. 300.

Commentary on the story concerning the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya: In the passage beginning with "He went to where the market was," etc., "market" (*āpaṇa*) is a designation for a certain town (*nigama*). In that [town]...
It is said that twenty thousand shop-fronts were laid out in that market town; thus, because of the abundance of its shops, it came to be known simply as "Āpaṇa.
Not far from that market town, on the bank of a river, there was a large forest grove with dense shade and a delightful terrain, where the Blessed One was staying.
His name was Keṇiya, and he was called a "jaṭila" because he wore matted hair acquired through ascetic practice.
The ascetic was, it seems, a wealthy brahmin who, for the sake of protecting his wealth, had taken up the ascetic life.
Having presented a gift to the king, he obtained a plot of land, built a hermitage there, and established a trade with five hundred carts.
He lived as a support for a thousand families, and in his hermitage there was a single palm tree.
They say that it releases a single golden fruit day after day.
During the day he wears saffron robes and binds his matted locks, but at night he enjoys the excellence of sensual pleasures.
"Proponents" (*pavattāro*) means those who cause [the teaching] to proceed; the meaning is those who speak by way of the sacred word (*pāvacana*). "Of whom" (*yesaṃ*) means belonging to whom.

*Mantapada*: Having excluded the word *manta* [from its common sense], it is called *mantapada* because these very *manta*s—meaning the words of the Vedas—are to be spoken in secret (*raho bhāsitabbaṭṭhena*), and they are the "footings" (*pada*) for the attainment of their respective goals.
*Gīta*: Recited by the ten ancient Brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka and others, through the perfection of their vocal qualities, such as the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) accents.
*Pavutta*: Spoken to others according to the tradition of the scriptures; the meaning is "recited. *Samihita*: Collected.
"Collected and heaped together" means that it has been placed there as a single mass by way of the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, and so forth;
and even within those, by way of the individual *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, and by way of recitation and vocalization.

"They sing after that" means that nowadays the brahmins sing after—that is, they recite in accordance with—that which was sung by them in the past. "They speak after that" means they speak in accordance with that.
This is a synonym for the preceding term. "Repeating what has been spoken" means they repeat what has been spoken and recited by them.
"Teaching what has been taught" means they teach others what has been taught by them. "Namely" (*seyyathidaṃ*) means "which ones are they?

*Aṭṭhaka* and so forth are their names. It is said that by means of the divine eye and the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), [they saw...]

Having observed, through the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), the fact that beings are the owners of their own karma and so forth, as well as the methods for the secrecy of mantras among the brahmins in past aeons,
they composed the mantras by not causing harm to others and by harmonizing them with the words of the Blessed One,

the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, which were concerned with the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭasannissita*). Furthermore, other brahmins who appeared during the time of King Okkāka and subsequent periods...
Having included [the prohibitions against] killing living beings and so forth, they split the three Vedas and made them contradictory to the word of the Buddha.
"Night-eating" is *ratti*; one who abstains from that is *rattūparatā*. Eating after midday until the setting of the sun is called "untimely eating" (*vikālabhojana*);
because of abstaining from that, one is "abstinent from untimely eating. "Having had prepared" means...

Having had a well-prepared drink prepared with ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, as well as black pepper—why did the Blessed One repeatedly refuse, thinking, "The community of monks, Keṇiya, is large"?
It was because of his conviction in the refusal of the sectarians (titthiyas). For the sectarians thought, "Oh, how modest he is, who does not accept even when being invited!"
Some say that they were pleased by his refusal when he was being invited; however, this is not the reason. There is no such hypocrisy on the part of the Buddhas for the sake of requisites.
Rather, seeing these one thousand two hundred and fifty monks, [the king] will prepare almsfood for exactly this many;
and tomorrow that brahmin Sela, together with three hundred men, will go forth.
"It is improper for me to send the junior monks elsewhere and go with these [senior ones], or to send these elsewhere and go with the junior monks.
Furthermore, if I take all of them along, there will not be enough almsfood.
Then, while the monks are wandering for alms, people will complain: 'After such a long time, Keṇiya has finally..."
“Having invited Gotama, he was unable to give even enough for his sustenance,” and he himself will feel regret.

But once the refusal has been made, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama repeatedly mentions the name of the brahmins, saying, ‘You have great faith in the brahmins,’” he will desire to invite the brahmins as well; therefore, [the brahmins...]
He will invite them individually; those monks, having been invited by him, will eat, and thus his faith will be preserved.
Thinking this, he refused again and again. With the words, “But even though, Master Gotama,” he intended to show this:
“Master Gotama, what has happened? If I have full confidence in the brahmins, may your reverence consent.”
“Gotama, I am able to give to the brahmins as well as to you.
Regarding the phrase “except for the juice of grain and fruit,” they say that even the water used for washing rice is indeed a grain-juice.
Regarding the phrase “I allow, monks, the juice of sugarcane,” it should be understood here that pure sugarcane juice is permitted for seven days.
“With these verses” means with these verses that were in accordance with Keṇiya’s mind.

Therein, because there is no sacrifice for brahmins without the tending of the fire, it is said: “Sacrifices have the fire-oblation as their head. The meaning is that they have the fire-oblation as the best, having the pouring of oblations into the fire as their primary feature.
For brahmins arrange a sacrifice preceded by the pouring of oblations into the fire, according to the Vedic injunction: “The gods have fire as their mouth. By those reciting the Vedas...
Because it is to be recited first, the Sāvittī is called the "mouth" [of the Veda], meaning that the Sāvittī is the precursor to the Veda, since the hearing of the Veda is preceded by it.
Because of his preeminence among humans, the king is called the "mouth.
And because he is the receptacle for rivers as they descend into him, and because he is the place of refuge to which one must go, the ocean is called the "mouth."
It is said: because it is recognized through its conjunction with the moon as "today is Kattikā," "today is Rohiṇī," and so forth;
because it outshines the constellations by producing light; and because its nature is exceptionally gentle compared to the constellations—it is said, "The moon is the mouth of the constellations.
Because they are the foremost among the blazing streaks of lightning, such as "the crest of a lamp-flame," "a mass of fire," or "a circle of thunderbolts," [it is called the chief].

The sun is called "the foremost of those that give heat. However, because they are the supreme among those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), it is said specifically at that time with reference to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha:
"For those desiring merit, the Saṅgha is indeed the foremost of those who sacrifice.
By this, he shows that the Saṅgha is the gateway for the influx of merit due to its status as the most preeminent recipient of offerings.
The commentary on the story of Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic is finished.
Commentary on the story of Roja the Mallian: 301.
Regarding the phrase "the monastery in the place of Roja," they said this with reference to the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi). "Without haste" means not being hurried; slowly.

The meaning is: while placing his foot down step by step, having performed the proper conduct (*vatta*), he does not disturb the sand—which has been well-swept and resembles a carpet of pearl-petals and *sinduvāra* flowers.
"Āḷinda" means the porch. "Having coughed" means having made the sound of a cough. "Aggaḷa" means the door-panel.
"Strike" means strike it slightly with the tip of your fingernail near the keyhole; this is what is said.
It happened thus: it is said that non-human beings knock on the door from too high up, while animals of various kinds knock from too low down;
instead of knocking there, humans knock near the opening in the middle. Those explaining this say, "This is the practice regarding the knocking on the door.
When it is said, "The Blessed One opened the door," it does not mean that the Blessed One rose and opened the door himself; rather, he extended his hand [thinking], "Let it be opened."
Then, [thinking], "For many millions of eons you have been giving gifts,
yet you have never personally performed the task of opening a door," the Blessed One opened the door himself. However, because it was opened by the Blessed One's mind,
it is said, "The Blessed One opened the door."
The commentary on the Story of Roja Mallaputta is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Elder Who Went Forth: 303.
Regarding the story of Ātumā, "a certain elder who had gone forth" refers to a certain bhikkhu named Subhadda who, at an advanced age, went forth.
Because he had gone forth [into the religious life] while old, he is called "one who went forth in old age. "Two boys" refers to two sons established on the level of novice monks (*sāmaṇera*).

"With a *nāḷi* measure and a bag" means with both a *nāḷi* and a pouch. "They collected" means that when people saw those two boys speaking so sweetly and being so eloquent, whether they wished to have them do it or not, they would indeed have them do it; and once it was done, they would ask, "What will you take?"
“Father! they asked. They replied, “We have no need for anything else;
our father, however, wishes to offer a gift of rice gruel when the Blessed One arrives. Hearing this, the people gave them everything they were able to carry without even calculating the amount.
Even what they could not carry themselves, they sent by means of other men. Therefore, those children had much.
They brought salt, oil, ghee, rice, and hard food.
"Dwelling at Ātumā" means dwelling in dependence on Ātumā. "In a straw hut" means in a small house made of straw.
It is said that there, having cleared the straw out from within a large heap of straw, [they built] a structure like a hall for those who have gone forth.
It was made like a place suitable for dwelling, and at that time the Blessed One resided there.
Then, when the Blessed One had returned from his alms-round and entered the hut of straw, Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening and addressed the people:
"Lay followers, I do not expect anything else from you; I require only the oil and other provisions brought by my children."
“They are sufficient for the Saṅgha; give me enough hand-labor. “What shall we do, venerable sir?
“Take this and that,” he said, and having had all the requisites brought, he had hearths built in the monastery.
Then, putting on a black *kāṣāya* robe and draping himself in one just like it, he wandered about throughout the entire night, saying, “Do this! Do that!”
Having spent a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he had prepared *bhojja-yāgu* and honey-balls (*madhu-goḷaka*).
"Bhojja-yāgu" is rice-gruel that is to be drunk after first eating;

therein everything that is called "hard food" (*khādanīya*)—such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, and the juices of flowers and fruits—is included. It is fragrant and suitable for anointing the heads of those wishing to play.
Then the Blessed One, having attended to his physical needs at an early hour, set out toward the town of Ātumā for alms, surrounded by the community of monks.
People informed him, "The Blessed One is entering the village for alms;
for whom has the rice-gruel been prepared? He, dressed in those very black robes he had on, with a single...

Taking the ladle and the spoon in his hand, and placing his right knee upon the ground like Brahmā, he paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice gruel. Thus it was said:
"Then, at the end of that night, that elder who had gone forth into homelessness had a great quantity of rice gruel prepared and offered it to the Blessed One."
“Even though the Tathāgatas know, they ask,” and so forth, is exactly as previously stated. “From where? means “from what source does this come? The rest here is self-evident. 304.
“Having given a tenth part” means having given a tenth portion. For this very reason he said: “Having divided it into ten parts, one part should be given to the owners of the land.
The commentary on the account of the Elder Who Went Forth is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities (Catumahāpadesakathāvaṇṇanā) 305. "Rubbing" means examining. *Pattuṇṇa* is cloth produced in the region of Pattuṇṇa;
for it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* that it is a specific kind of silk (*koseyya*). *Cīnapaṭa* and *somārapaṭa* are cloths produced in the regions of Cīna and Somāra respectively.
The three types beginning with *pattuṇṇa* (fine cotton) are similar to silk because they consist of thread produced by insects.

That which is "produced by psychic power" (*iddhimayika*) refers to robes manifested through the merit-based psychic power of "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) monks; since these are made from one of the materials such as *khoma*, they are similar to those very same materials.
A robe given by deities is "deity-given" (*devadattiya*). This was manifested on the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) for the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī.
It is similar to "given cloth" (*dinnavattha*). That too conforms only to *khoma* and the rest, because it is of the nature of one or another among them.

The two types of cloth are mentioned by way of illustration; this is intended merely to show their specific forms, not to exclude others, since even *pattuṇṇa* cloth is mentioned by way of illustration.
"Tumba" means containers. "Fruit-tumba" refers to gourds and the like. "Water-tumba" is a small vessel for carrying water.
"A palm-leaf umbrella" (*kilañjacchatta*) means an umbrella made by weaving bamboo and *vilīva* grass. "Mixed juice" (*sambhinnarasa*) means juice that has become blended.

"A drink has been received" (*pānakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ hoti*) means that a drink such as mango juice and so forth has been received; because its flavor is not mixed [with other substances], it is permissible even at an improper time (*vikāla*).
"Together with that which was received on that very day" (*tena tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhim*) means together with that seven-day medicine which was received on that same day.
Together with [the previous]. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Four Great Authorities is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Medicines is finished.
7. The Kathina Khandhaka: Explanation of the Discourse on the Authorization of the Kathina 306.

In the Kathina Khandhaka, the phrase "by way of the head" means by way of the primary factor. Regarding the term "Kathina": it is so called because of its capacity to include within itself five benefits (*pañca-anisamsa*).

"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: 'The meaning is "firmly established. Regarding the phrase 'It will belong to them,' it is appropriate [to say] 'it will be theirs' rather than saying 'it will be yours'; thus the expression 'it will be theirs' (*nesaṃ*) is appropriate.

As for the phrase 'those who have performed the *kathina* ceremony,' the meaning is that it will belong not only to you, but also to others who have performed the *kathina* ceremony. 'Wandering without having asked permission' refers to the training rule concerning wandering."
Wandering among families without having asked permission in the manner already described. "The robe of one who has died" means a robe belonging to a deceased person.
"Brought by means of what arises thereon" means brought by means of fields, grounds, and so forth, belonging to the monastery.
"Invited at the first invitation" is said for the purpose of showing that the rains residence was completed without breaking it.
It is stated [thus] because the spreading of the *kaṭhina* is possible even for those who have completed the rains-residence (*vutthavassa*) but were not invited [to the ceremony] due to an obstacle.

For that very reason, instead of saying "or those who were not invited," it was stated only this much: "or those whose rains-residence was interrupted, or those who arrived during the later period, do not receive [the cloth].

Even those who have completed the rains-residence in another monastery do not receive it; this refers to those who have completed the rains-residence in a different monastery within a different boundary (*nānāsīmā*).
The meaning is that they do not obtain the spreading of the *kathina* in this monastery.
"A garment smeared with bran" is said with reference to an unwashed cloth. "The formal act of giving" refers to the formal act of giving the *kathina* cloth.

"It is not permissible not to do it"—by this, he indicates that for one who fails to do so out of disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, only a single formal act is permitted.
At the time of giving the cloth for the Kathina ceremony, only one formal act (kammavācā) is required.
When another cloth is subsequently given to him, there is no need to perform the formal act again; the intention is that a mere announcement (apalokana) suffices.
308. "Mahābhūmika" means having a great scope; it is said to be "of great extension" because it possesses twenty-four modes.
It exists. "Fivefold" means five sections. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
"The first *cimilika*" refers to one's own original *cimilika* (lining) other than the cloth for the Kathina ceremony.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "'Merely having sewn after making a *kucchicimilika*' is a designation for sewing together old and worn-out *cimilikas*. In the *Mahāpaccarī*:
And in the *Kurundi*, they say: "The statement was made for the purpose of showing that the difference lies only in the phrasing (*byañjana*), and not in the meaning (*attha*).
"By the mere application of a longitudinal wind" means by the mere application of a wind along the length.
"By the mere application of a transverse wind" means by the mere application of a wind across the width. "It becomes appropriate" means...
It is suitable for a recluse. "By means of what has been relinquished at night" means by that which has passed the night.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the *kaṭhina* robe is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion beginning with the group of seven rules concerning taking [robes].
311. "The suspension of the *kaṭhina* occurs through the cutting off of hope.

It is not stated here [in the *mātikā*] because it is not mentioned in the *pāḷi*—specifically, in the commentary on the *mātikā* words, immediately after the section on "hearing"—but rather in the context of the suspension of the *kaṭhina* by crossing the boundary (*sīmātikkantika*).

Regarding this, some have said: "The 'crossing the boundary' refers to crossing the boundary of the robe-season (*cīvarakāla-sīmā*). [Others say: "Outside the boundary, at the time of the robe-season..."
“Because it has been exceeded, it is called ‘exceeding the boundary’”—this is our accepted position.

In the *Sahubbhāra*, the reading “he whose robe has been made” (*so katacīvaro*) is seen; and if that were the case, it would be understood that the impediment of the robe (*cīvarapalibodha*) is severed first.
However, here in the *Parivāra-pāḷi* and elsewhere, because of the statement “the two impediments are severed neither before nor after [each other],” that [reading] does not agree.
Therefore, the reason for this must be investigated.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points): "The section on 'taking up' (*samādāya*) is similar to the section on 'taking' (*ādāya*); the only difference here is the prefix.
However, some say: "One who departs without leaving behind any of one's own requisites is said to 'depart taking [them] up' (*samādāya pakkamati*)."
...so it is said. Furthermore, the connection is that those very same [cases] are shown even in the section on undertaking [the robe-making ceremony].
Because the suspension of the *kaṭhina* by departure is impossible when the robe has not been completed, it is stated “as far as possible.
For the suspension of the *kaṭhina* by departure is taught only with reference to one whose robe is finished: “A bhikkhu who has spread the *kaṭhina* and whose robe is made...”
Because it is stated, “having taken it, he departs,” therefore a robe that has been left unfinished is not possible; thus, only six cases of relinquishment (*ubbhāra*) are shown therein.
Herein, this is the analysis of the sections starting from the beginning: there are seven sections on “taking” (*ādāya*), and likewise two sets of seven sections on “undertaking” (*samādāya*).
Then, excluding the section on departing (*pakkamanantika*), by way of the sections on “taking” and “undertaking” for a robe that has been left unfinished...
There are two groups of six; beyond that, three groups of three are shown by way of *niṭṭhāna*, *sanniṭṭhāna*, and *nāsanantika*.
Therein, the first triad occurred outside the boundary (*bahisīmā*) without having applied the procedure of “I shall return” or “I shall not return” within the boundary;
therefore, it consists of the *pakkamanantika*, the *sīmātikkantikā*, and the *saubbhārā*.
In that regard, they are not applicable. The second triad concerns what was undertaken within the boundary with the thought, "I will not return.
The third triad is undertaken by qualifying it with the term "not determined" (*anadhiṭṭhita*); in meaning, it corresponds to the first triad.
And "by one who has not determined" means by one who has not determined, i.e., not fixed, [the thought] "I will return" or "I will not return. Immediately after the third triad...
The fourth triad is possible within the boundary (sīmā) through the specific expression “I shall return.

When applied in this way, it is not in conflict with the others, such as the “hearing-limit” (savanantika) and so forth; thus, rather than being a triad, it should be understood as having become a hexad.
In this manner, the first group of fifteen should be understood as consisting of three triads and one hexad.
316–320. Then, this very group of fifteen [rules] is made into a second "group of fifteen on undertaking" (*samādāya-paññārasaka*) by means of a specific prefix.
Furthermore, the third "group of fifteen" is shown by the phrase "having taken up an unfinished robe," and the fourth "group of fifteen" is shown by the phrase "having undertaken";
thus, four groups of fifteen are to be understood. Among these, in the first and second...
It should be understood that among the fifteen cases, "an unmade robe" is intended in all instances, while in the other two, it is "unfinished.

Beyond that, according to the method beginning with "he departs with hope for a robe," there is one section consisting of the completion, the determination, the non-staying, and the cutting off of hope;
thus, this constitutes one tetrad. Therefore, the triads mentioned previously, together with the three [sections] concerning the cutting off of hope, [make up the total].
And the phrase "and the three groups" should be understood as the "twelvefold set on non-hope.

Although the first twelvefold set is obtained in the immediately following "twelvefold set on hope," nevertheless, because that [first] twelvefold set is indistinguishable, it is taken as established by implication;
and in order to show the distinction starting from the beginning, it is stated: "I shall return within the boundary. This [occurs] in the second tetrad.

It should be understood that this is for the purpose of providing the occasion for the statements beginning with “he hears while outside the boundary,” as well as for the [rules] such as those ending with hearing (*savanantika*) in the third tetrad.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this twelvefold set—which can also be obtained by way of non-intention (*anāsāya*)—is not explicitly shown here, as it is established by implication through what has been stated.
Thus, two twelvefold sets should be extracted from this context. In the twelvefold set concerning duties (*karaṇīya*), too...

Two sets of twelve [factors] should be extracted: the set of twelve beginning with "non-hope" (*anāsā*) as it has been shown, and the set of twelve beginning with "hope" (*āsā*), which are established even without being explicitly stated. 321–322.

Since in the section on the nine [factors] concerning one who is departing for another region, the phrase "he departs" itself establishes—even without being stated—that "he will not return," therefore that was not mentioned. By this much, the absence of the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*) is demonstrated.
"Anticipating his share of the robe-cloth" indicates that he possesses the obstacle of robe-cloth (*cīvara-palibodha*).
In this context, "his share of the robe-cloth" refers to the portion of robe-material he is entitled to receive. "Anticipating" means desiring it.
When he obtains the robe-cloth, there is one triad based on the *niṭṭhāna*, *sanniṭṭhāna*, and *nāsanantika* [modes of determination] regarding the residence where he has spent the rains retreat.
By means of those very [factors], one should understand one set of nine based on three triads: one for the interval along the way and one for the place reached.

Following that, the pentad of comfortable dwellings (*phāsuvihāra*) is stated by way of completion, determination, destruction, the end, the crossing of the boundary, and the good burden. The rest here is easily understood from the Pāḷi and the Commentary.
The commentary on the discussion of the sevenfold group beginning with "taking up" is finished.
The commentary on the Kathina-khandhaka is finished.

337. *Itarītarena* means "by this or that. Since the word *itara* signifies "indefinite" and is stated twice, it has the same meaning as the expression "whatever.

The *caturaṅgula* flower and the *kojava* rug.

"Having placed it in the middle of the dye-pot" means having placed it inside the dye-pot; thus, upon a circular stand...

346. *Uddhaste aruṇe* means when the tip of the dawn has risen. *Nandimukhiyā* means with a joyful face.
