348. *Acchupeyyaṃ* means one should fix it in place. *Hatavatthakānaṃ* means of worn-out cloths. *Uddharitvā allīyāpanakhaṇḍaṃ* means a piece of cloth for patching after removing the weak spots.
Commentary on the Story of Visākhā (349–351).

Regarding the story of Visākhā: “With body refreshed” (*kallakāyā*) means with body untiring, her frame suffused with rapture and joy. “Destination” (*gatī*) refers to the destination of knowledge, that is, the attainment of knowledge. “Future state” (*abhisamparāya*) refers to the future state accompanied by knowledge, the condition after death associated with knowledge.
The Blessed One will declare this for him—that is, he will declare his destination of knowledge by saying, “That bhikkhu is a stream-enterer,” or “a once-returner,” and so forth.

Thereafter, he will reveal his future destiny through knowledge with such words as: "He is fixed, destined for full enlightenment; having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering.
"Leading to heaven" means conducive to heaven. "Dispelling grief" means it drives away or removes sorrow.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Allowance for Sitting Mats, etc. (353):
"He sleeps badly" means that seeing various kinds of dreams, he sleeps poorly. "He wakes up badly" means that even when waking, he wakes with terror and horripilation, thus waking poorly.
Commentary on the Discussion of Robes and so forth obtained through subsequent determination.
359–362. "To sew the mouth of the bowl with an eight-padded covering" means to sew it by showing recesses here and there at the mouth of the bowl in the shape of an eight-padded board.

"The protection of the bolt alone is the measure": the intention is that even when placing [the bowl] for these four reasons of depositing it, it is permissible to place it only in a monastery protected by a bolt.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Production of Robes for the Saṅgha (Saṅghikacīvaruppādakathāvaṇṇanā) 363.
“For five months” is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*).

“From a deposit placed after investing it at interest” means from a deposit placed by attendants for the purpose of the rainy-season robe (*vassāvāsika*) after they have invested it at interest. “From what is produced there” means...
Regarding the source of the material, such as from coconut groves and so forth: although it has been stated without distinction that "robes arising for the Saṅgha—
whether by way of the rainy-season residence gift, the robes for the deceased, the source of the material itself, or by any other means—
all such robes accrue for five months to one whose kaṭhina has been spread, and for one month to one whose kaṭhina has not been spread," it is further stated:
In order to show the specific distinction that arises by way of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gains, the passage beginning with “But this which... is commenced.
Therein, the word “here” (*idha*) is merely a conventional expression; the same principle applies even when it is said, “We give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains.
Because it arises by way of the *vassāvāsika* gains, it accrues for five months even for one who has not performed the *kathina* ceremony.

It reaches [the recipient] five months after the rains have been completed. However, as for the reason stated by some—that it is because [the gift] is restricted by the word "here" (*idha*)—that is not a valid reason.

For even without being restricted by the word "here," if one gives a robe during the winter with the intention of it being a *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gain for the Saṅgha that has completed the rains, saying, "We give this to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains," or "We give this as a *vassāvāsika* [gift]," then it belongs to the Saṅgha even if the *kathina* has not been spread.

It reaches five months for one who has completed the rains residence; therefore, later, in the explanation of the phrase "gives to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains" among the eight matrix rules, it says:

"From the month of the robe onwards until the last day of winter—if it is said, 'We give the *vassāvāsika*,' then regardless of whether the *kathina* has been spread or not, [the gift is valid] only for those who have completed the rains residence of the past year."
"...attains" is what was said. "After that" means after five months; the meaning is: starting from the first day of the summer season. "Why?
Because it arose during the 'back' period"—this should be seen as following immediately after the phrase "or rather, in the coming year.

For it is precisely because [the rain] arises starting from the first day of the summer season that it is said to have arisen during the "back" period; thus, [the question is]: "Was it in the past year?"
One should ask by saying, "Is this for the rains-residence? and so forth. For that very reason, he will say further on:
"Starting from the first day of the summer months, however, the schedule (mātikā) should be set forth: 'Five months of the past rains-residence have elapsed;
with the passing of four months, the future one will come; for which rains-residence is it intended? If [he says], 'It is for those who have already spent the past rains-residence...'"
If one says, "I give," it reaches [the recipient] only after they have completed the rains residence for that year.

However, in the manuscripts, immediately after the statement, "Even for one who has not performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, it reaches them for five months," they write: "Why? Because it arose during the 'back' season (*piṭṭhisamaya*).
This is not tenable; for it does not refer to what arose during the 'back' season when it is said, "Even for one who has not performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, [it lasts] five..."
It is said, "it reaches [the robe] within a month. However, that which arises at the time of the *piṭṭhi* (the subsequent period) does not reach only those who have completed the rains-residence;
it reaches all those who are present. For this very reason, he will say later: "One says, 'To the Saṅgha who has completed the rains-residence in such-and-such monastery.
There, it reaches only those who have completed the rains-residence, until the lifting of the *kaṭhina*. But if, from the first day of the hot season..."
From that point on, when one speaks in this way, it accrues to all those who are present there. Why?
Because it arose at the time [the robe was] behind them. However, regarding the statement "the *ṭhitikā* does not remain":
here, if the *ṭhitikā* has not remained fixed, then when another robe arises and a single monk arrives, it should be divided in half and taken by both. But if the *ṭhitikā* has remained fixed...
Furthermore, when another robe has arisen, if one who is junior arrives, the turn passes downward;
if one who is senior arrives, the turn ascends upward. If there is no other [junior or senior], it should be taken again after making it one's own.
Regarding the phrase "they are wrongly received," the intended meaning here is that they belong solely to the Saṅgha. It is already taken.
Regarding the phrase "nāmā" (by name): although it is not known that "this belongs to this person," the intention is that those portions are, in fact, theirs.
"Itova" means precisely because they are to be given to the elders.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the arising of robes belonging to the Saṅgha is finished.
Commentary on the Story of Upananda the Śākyaputta (364).
Regarding the phrase "he causes dawn to rise every seven days," this is merely a figurative expression, as there is no actual business to be done for seven days within a single monastery.

"This" refers to a gift given with a single intention. Regarding the phrase "in various gains" (*nānālābhehi*) and so forth: those in which the gain (*lābha*) is various—that is, separate or distinct—are called "various gains."
There are two monasteries, distinguished by their different acquisitions. They have separate and distinct precincts demarcated by walls and so forth; thus they are "of different precincts.
"By monasteries within a single boundary" means by two monasteries situated within a single precinct-boundary.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Sick Ward.
"Palipanna" means submerged; the meaning is "smeared. "Having lifted up" means having raised [the bowl].

Regarding the term "one who has the same teacher": here they say that even if one teacher has one resident pupil (antevāsika) and one co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika), these two are also considered "those who have the same teacher" in relation to each other.
366. "Unable to compound medicine" means that when a physician says, "Having taken this and that medicine, it should be given after compounding them with this," he is unable to do so accordingly.
"To take out" (nīhātuṃ) means to remove; the meaning is to discard. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Property of the Deceased.

367–369. Regarding the phrase “when a bhikkhu has passed away,” the word *kālakato* here is an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*); thus he says, “by the act of passing away. Regarding “in this or that community (*saṅgha*)”: it means in the community of each respective monastery. 376.
Regarding the discussion on the arising of robes when the Saṅgha is split:

“Where, however, the water of donation is the criterion” means that in whatever kingdom the monks become owners of the gift merely by receiving the water of donation; this is the intended meaning. “Beyond the ocean” refers to Jambudvīpa.

378. Regarding “he determines it as a robe for the deceased”: here, if while traveling on a road he hears of someone’s death and, knowing that there are no other monks within twelve *ratana*s of that non-monastery location, he determines it, saying, “This robe falls to me,” it is properly determined.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Eightfold Matrix of Robes (Aṭṭhacīvaramātikākathāvaṇṇanā) 379.

Regarding the phrase "stated by way of reference to the person" (*puggalādhiṭṭhānanayena*): although one should have said "giving within the boundary" (*sīmāyadāna*) and so forth, the expression "gives within the boundary" (*sīmāya deti*) and so forth is stated by way of reference to the person.
By the phrase "delimited by a place capable of being enclosed," [the meaning is] that which is not enclosed...
This indicates that the "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīmā*) is the area within the first stone’s throw from the place where the community regularly assembles in the monastery.
Now, in order to show that the area within the second stone’s throw is also indeed the proximate boundary, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) is commenced.

Even the place of regular assembly must be understood as being situated within the limits [of the monastery]. [This applies to] the nuns’ entry into the monastery, their inquiry regarding lodgings, and so forth.

The procedures for the announcement of probation (*parivāsa*), the announcement of penance (*mānatta*), the interruption of the rains-residence (*vassa-ccheda*), the taking of formal support (*nissaya*), the assignment of lodgings (*senāsana-aggāha*), and so forth—all this is to be understood as pertaining only to this very "boundary of functional proximity" (*upacāra-sīmā*). A boundary established for the purpose of receiving gains is a "gain-boundary" (*lābha-sīmā*). Regarding what is given within the boundaries of common affiliation (*samāna-saṃvāsa*) and non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), this is the distinction:
that which is given with the words, "I give it within the boundary of non-separation," does not reach the village site.

Why? Because it is stated: "Excluding the village and the vicinity of the village. However, what is given with the words, "I give within the boundary of a common residence," reaches even those staying in the village.
"Dwelt in by the Buddha" means dwelt in by the Blessed One, the Buddha. "In one" means in a single monastery. "The enclosure wall" means...
The cycle of giving (*dānavatta*). It "turns" means it proceeds. It is permissible for those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*) as well;
for it is said, "We give to the monks," or "We give to the elders," rather than saying, "We give to you," therefore it is permissible for those who wear rag-robes.
"Already processed" means already processed for the purpose of a sandal-bag and so forth.
"Half is to be given" means that of what has been given to both Saṅghas, half is to be given to the monks and half to the nuns.
Even if there is only one monk or only one nun, at least half must be given even to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
However, when it is said, "To the Saṅgha of monks, to the nuns, and to you," [the distribution is as follows].
The statement that "the person is not obtained separately" must be accepted solely on the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

For no specific reason for [such a distinction] is found here. Indeed, just as when it is said, "I give to both the Saṅgha and to you," the person is obtained separately because it is encompassed by both general and specific expressions, so too here in the case of "to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to you."
Because there exist both general and specific designations, it is understood that there must indeed be a separate individual classification;

therefore, the word of the *Aṭṭhakathā* alone is the authority here. "He receives only one from the place of attainment" means that he receives only one portion from the place reached according to his own seniority (*vassa*). Regarding this, he states the reason: "Why? Because of the mention of the *bhikkhu-saṅgha*..."
"Because it is included": the intention is that by the mention of the "Bhikkhu-saṅgha," the individual (puggala) is also included.

Although it says "he carries for the Bhikkhu-saṅgha," it is stated [that this is not a lay service] because such a task as carrying things is not considered a lay-vaiyāvṛtya (lay service). "Those who know the characteristics say":
this is a statement of definitive conclusion; however, because it has not been recorded in the Aṭṭhakathās (Commentaries), it is thus...
It is said: "Within the outer boundary of the precincts... it reaches all. The intention is that it reaches all those who have spent the rains retreat (vassa) anywhere at all.
For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, it says:

"But if one standing outside the precincts of the boundary says, 'To the Saṅgha who has spent the rains retreat,' [it applies] to all those who have spent the rains retreat anywhere at all who are present."
It is said, "it reaches [them]. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated:

"Because it was spoken while standing in a location unsuitable for the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsa*), it reaches everyone—both those who have completed the rains-residence and those who have not. This should not be accepted.

For if one says, "I give this to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence," it does not reach those who have not completed the rains-residence. Thus he speaks: "To the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence..."

He says, "I give. Regarding the phrase "he has come to receive the recitation," this refers to the time from when he arrives with the intention, "I will receive the recitation," even if he has not previously received it from him, until he enters into the status of a resident pupil (*antevāsika*). The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the exposition of the eightfold matrix of robes (*aṭṭhacīvaramātikākathā*) is finished.
The commentary on the Cīvarakkhandhaka is finished.
9. Commentary on the Campeyyakkhandhaka:
The narrative concerning the monk of the Kassapagotta clan.

380. In the Campeyya Khandhaka: "In the city named Campā. For in various places such as the parks and lotus ponds of that city, *campaka* trees alone were abundant; therefore, it came to be known by the designation "Campā.
On the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, not far from that city of Campā, [belonging to] the royal consort named Gaggarā—

There was a lotus pond known by the name “Gaggarā” because it had been dug out; on its banks, all around, was a vast grove of *campaka* trees adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue and others.
In that *campaka* grove, fragrant with the scent of blossoms, the Blessed One dwelt.
With reference to this, it is said: “on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond. Regarding the word “bound with cords” (*tantibaddho*): a “cord” (*tanti*) is so called.

“Activity”: the meaning is that he is bound to it, intent upon it, and has become zealous for it; he prepares lodgings not yet prepared in that residence, repairs those that are worn out, and becomes the master over what has been prepared—this is the intended sense. Therefore he said:
“Because of the duties to be performed in that residence, he is bound by the [monastic] rule”; the meaning is that he has undertaken enthusiasm for the work to be done.
Commentary on the Discussion of Formal Acts Deficient in Motion, etc. (385–387).
"While they are protesting" means while they are obstructing. "There is neither omission nor alteration":

because a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñatti*) is to be performed by that single motion alone, an omission from it is impossible; and because there is no proclamation (*anussāvanā*), [alteration] subsequently...
There is no acting otherwise than by means of the two types of *ñatti* (proposals) and the method of performing [the act] with two *ñattis*.
389. Commentary on the Discussion of the Fourfold Assembly and Other Matters:

One who has been subjected to an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) is one who is "separated from the community" (*nānāsaṃvāsa*) by way of the formal act; one who follows the suspended person is "separated from the community" by way of their doctrinal position (*laddhi*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Expulsion, etc., §395:
"Not having reached expulsion. Here, the formal act of expulsion (*nissāraṇakamma*) is permitted only for those who corrupt families;
yet this person, being described as "foolish and incompetent" and so forth, is not a corrupter of families. Therefore, it is said, "not having reached [the grounds for] it."
[It has been] stated. If this is so, how is it "well-performed"? Even for one who possesses the qualities of being foolish, incompetent, and so forth, it is stated in the Kammakkhandhaka:
"If the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform an act of banishment. For that very reason, he said: "And this... [omitted] ...therefore it is well-performed.
In that context, "this" refers to the act of banishment; "he" refers to the person specified by the description beginning with "foolish."
"By a unique characteristic" means by the characteristic of being a corrupter of families, which is the unique quality of the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*).
Having first shown the meaning with reference to the intended act of banishment in the phrase "If the Saṅgha expels him, he is rightly expelled," [the text now continues:
if there is an expulsion by way of the acts of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) and so forth, as in the phrase "If the Saṅgha expels him..."
When that [person] is intended, he has already reached the point of being expelled;

yet, in order to show the meaning by way of contrast—that he is "well-expelled" through such means as censure (*tajjanīya*)—the meaning is stated again by referring to him with the words, "If the Saṅgha expels him.
He is called *anapadāna* because there is no *apadāna* for him, which is to say, no breaking off or limit to his offenses. Expulsion occurs even by each individual factor.
"Authorized" means authorized in the Kammakkhandhaka. The rest here is easily understood from the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the two types of sending away is finished.
The commentary on the Campeyyakkhandhaka is finished.
10. The Kosaṃbaka Khandhaka: Commentary on the Discussion of the Dispute at Kosaṃbī. 451.

In the Kosaṃbaka Khandhaka, if [a monk] thinks, "If there is one, I shall confess it," because of his easy-to-speak-to nature and his desire for training, [he does not incur] an offense regarding the transgression.
“He saw. He said this with the intention that the side of non-offense (*anāpattipakkha*) is also possible here, thinking, “There is no offense.
However, it is indeed an offense. Therefore he said: “He held the view that there was no offense regarding that offense.
453–454. “In the sense of haste” means in the sense of urgency. “Without cause you have suspended that bhikkhu.”
"Should speak": because previously, by the words of the *vinayadhara*, he promised, "If there is an offense, I shall confess it," and now again, by his own words,
perceiving there to be no offense because it was done unintentionally and through forgetfulness, saying, "There is no offense here"— therefore,
if [the proponent] says to the monks who have suspended that monk, "That monk has been suspended by you without cause..."
The intended meaning is "he should speak. Or, he might say to those who follow one who has been suspended, "You have fallen into an offense.

Since this is a formal offense involving a conscious state (*sacittaka-āpatti*) by virtue of the mind that recognizes the basis of the offense, and since he perceives what remains of the water as remaining water, he says "you have fallen into an offense" with the intention:
"You are acting out of partiality," [addressing] one who is indeed possessed of an offense.
One may speak regarding those who follow one who has been suspended. 455–456.

"He invalidates the formal act" means: because of such statements as, "Monks, if one who belongs to a different community should perform a formal act as the fourth member, it is not a valid act and is not to be performed," if the Saṅgha were to perform a formal act by making that person the one who completes the quorum, this [invalidates the act].
The intention here is that even while sitting there, one commits that offense. Regarding the phrase "relinquishing the vicinity" (*upacāraṃ muñcitvā*):
here, "vicinity" (*upacāra*) refers to a place where [two people] can reach one another with their hands.

457. In the passage beginning with "engaged in quarreling" (*bhaṇḍanajātā*), "quarreling" (*bhaṇḍana*) refers to the preliminary stage of a fight; those in whom this has arisen are called "those engaged in quarreling."
“Engaged in quarreling” (*kalahajātā*) means those for whom a dispute has arisen that has reached its peak through such acts as seizing one another by the hands.

“Fallen into contention” (*vivādāpannā*) means they have entered into a discourse consisting of opposing arguments. “With the weapons of the mouth” (*mukhasattihi*) means with the weapons of speech. “Piercing” (*vitudantā*) means stabbing.
“He said this to the Blessed One” refers to the statement beginning with: “Venerable sir, here in Kosambī, the bhikkhus are engaged in quarreling.”
He spoke not out of a desire for affection, nor with the intention of causing division, but rather out of a desire for their welfare and benefit.
It is said that this monk was a peacemaker; therefore, he thought:
"Since these monks have begun a dispute, it is impossible for me, nor for any other monk, to bring them to harmony. Perhaps [I should appeal to] the Supreme Person in the world with its devas..."

“Either the Blessed One should go himself, or having summoned them to his presence, he should bring about their reconciliation by delivering a discourse on the principles of conciliation connected with patience and loving-kindness.
Out of a desire for their welfare and a desire for their benefit, he went and spoke thus.
Therefore, he spoke in this way out of a desire for their welfare; it was not that he disregarded the word of the Blessed One. Those...
However, at that time they did not accept the Teacher’s words; saying nothing, they stood silent and abashed.
Therefore, neither group showed a disrespectful attitude toward the Teacher.
The commentary on the account of the Kosambī dispute is finished.
In the commentary on the "Story of the City of Dīghāvu" (Dīghāvuvatthukathāvaṇṇanā),

regarding the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus," the phrase "in the past" (*bhūtapubbaṃ*) indicates that the Blessed One was revealing a former dwelling concealed by existence,
as if he were uncovering a treasure hidden in the earth and piling it up before him.
He said: "Aḍḍha" means a lord. Anyone who is wealthy by means of his own possessions and resources is simply "wealthy" (aḍḍha);
however, this one is not merely wealthy, but is "of great wealth" (mahaddhana), meaning he is endowed with great, immeasurable riches.
Because they are to be enjoyed and utilized, especially in relation to sensual pleasures, they are called "possessions" (bhoga); therefore, by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure—
One who has great and abundant wealth is *mahābhoga*. One who possesses a great army-force as well as a great strength of endurance is *mahabbala*.
One who has a great vehicle consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth is *mahāvāhana*. One who has a great conquered realm is *mahāvijita*.
Regarding "one whose treasury and storehouse are full": the *kosa* is called the inner chamber of the storehouse containing the essential goods.
A "storehouse" (*koṭṭha*) is said to be a place for storing grain; a house that serves as such a storehouse is a "granary" (*koṭṭhāgāra*).
The meaning is: one whose treasury (*kosa*) is filled with wealth stored away and kept, and whose granaries are filled with grains.
Alternatively, the treasury is fourfold: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. For just as there is a protector who maintains the sharpness of a sword, so too...
"Retinue" is called a "treasury" (*kośa*); likewise, because it protects the king’s state of sharpness [prowess], the fourfold army is called a "treasury.
There are three kinds of storehouses: the storehouse of wealth, the storehouse of grain, and the storehouse of clothing.
Since he possesses all of these in their entirety, he is one whose treasury and storehouses are full. The fourfold army consists of those known as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
An army endowed with four factors. "Having equipped" means having caused the armor to be put on by means of leather bindings and so forth.
"He marched out" (*abbhuyyāsī*) means he went forth, having set out facing [the enemy]. "Even a single blow" (*ekasaṅghātam-pi*) means even a single strike.
"Washing" (*dhovanaṃ*) means washing water. "Having carried away" (*parinetvā*) means having brought out. In the word "anatthado," which should have been *anatthado*, the letter *da* [is used].
Having inserted the letter *ta*, it is stated as “from what is harmful” (*anatthato*);

thus he says “or else,” and so forth. 464. Or, because of its quality of being manifold, the sound is diverse; hence it is called the “diverse sound” (*puthusaddo*). “The common folk” (*samajano*) refers to people whose intentions are focused on quarreling.
“Therein” (*tattha*) means in that mass of people. “I did not think ‘I am a fool’” means that even though he was established in the characteristics of a fool, he did not think, “I am...”

“He does not think, ‘I am a fool. And furthermore (bhiyyo ca): because he does not recognize his own foolishness, he did not think—that is, he was unaware—that he himself was becoming the cause for a schism in the Saṅgha, as if it were the further escalation of a quarrel.
Or, those whose range of activity consists solely of speech that proceeds by way of strife are called *vācāgocarā*. ‘In the mouth’ (*mukhāyāmaṃ*) means by way of disputing.”
"Stretching out their faces while speaking": "They do not know that" means they do not know that quarrel. Indeed, there is no one who, while making a quarrel, does not know it.
However, to show how they do not know it, he said: "Thus this is full of danger.
This so-called quarrel, because it destroys the welfare of oneself and others and gives rise to harm, [is dangerous] even in this very life...
"In this world and in the future life" means it is accompanied by danger and fault. "They do not know that" means they do not know that quarrel. How do they not know it?
He says: "In this way it is accompanied by danger"—meaning they do not know that quarrel in this way, thinking, "This quarrel is thus accompanied by danger."
In the passage beginning with *akkocchi maṃ* ("he abused me"), *akkocchi* means he abused; *avadhī* means he struck;
*ajinī* means he defeated, either by presenting false testimony, by counter-arguing in debate, or by gaining a legal victory;

*ahāsī* means he took away something belonging to me, such as a bowl or other belongings. And those who... refers to whoever they may be—whether gods or humans, whether householders or those gone forth.
They harbor resentment (*upanayhanti*), meaning they pursue it by way of enmity (*upanāhavasena*), repeatedly wrapping around that anger—
which has as its basis such thoughts as "He abused me"— just as one wraps a cart yoke with leather thongs or as one wraps putrid fish and the like with *kusa* grass;
for them, the enmity once arisen does not subside.

"And those who do not harbor it" means that through lack of mindfulness or lack of attention, or by way of reflecting on the action and so forth, they do not harbor that anger based on abuse and the like, thinking:
"In a previous existence, you too must have abused someone who was innocent, or struck them, or won a case by bringing in false witnesses; or you must have forcibly seized something from someone..."
"Since it will not be cut off, you shall therefore incur abuse and the like even though you are blameless"—thus they do not harbor resentment.
Even if enmity arises toward them through negligence, by this non-harboring of resentment it is extinguished like a fire without fuel.
For "enmities are not stilled by enmity. Just as a place smeared with impurities such as spittle and mucus is not cleansed by those very same impurities, so too...
Just as one who washes cannot make something pure and odorless, but rather that place becomes even more impure and foul-smelling,
even so, by reviling one who reviles and striking one who strikes,
one cannot pacify hatred with hatred; rather, one creates even more hatred.
Thus, what are called enmities are never appeased by enmity at any time; rather, they only increase.

But "by non-enmity they are appeased" means that just as those impurities such as spittle, when washed away with clear water, vanish and that place becomes clean and odorless, even so, by non-enmity—that is, by the water of patience and loving-kindness and by wise attention—[enmities are pacified].
Through reflection and through reviewing, enmities are stilled, they subside, and they come to non-existence.
"This is the ancient Dhamma": this is the ancient Dhamma consisting in the pacification of enmity by means of non-enmity;
it is the path traversed by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed.
“Do not know” means that they do not establish the perception of impermanence; this is the intended meaning. “Then their disputes are stilled”:
for that reason, from that cause, their quarrels (*medhaga*)—that is, their conflicts—are stilled and go to cessation. To the question, “How are they stilled?
he says, “For thus they know,” and so forth. Therein, “for thus they know” means those wise ones [know] that “we are going into the presence of Death.”
Knowing this, they arouse wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and proceed toward the pacification of disputes and quarrels;
then, by that practice, their disputes are settled—this is the intended meaning.
"There is also a coming together for them" refers to those who cut up the bones of their parents, seize living beings, and [take] cattle and so forth.
The intention is: "Even for those who plunder a kingdom by force, such a gathering occurs; how much more so, then, should it not happen for you?

These [verses] were spoken for the purpose of illustrating the contrast between praise and blame: "Because of their companionship with fools, these bhikkhus are prone to quarreling; [but what of those] whose companions are wise..."
However, this [verse] was spoken for the purpose of illustrating the praise and blame of one who has wise companions and one who has foolish companions.
"Nipaka" means endowed with discerning wisdom (*nepakkapaññā*). "Sādhuvihāri dhīraṃ" means a wise person who dwells in an auspicious manner.
"Having overcome both manifest dangers and concealed dangers" refers to manifest dangers such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
And having overcome all perils—such as the fear of passion, the fear of hatred, and other concealed dangers—they wandered alone.
Thinking, "This kingship is a great occasion for negligence;
what use have we for exercising kingship?", they abandoned the kingdom, entered the great forest, and having gone forth into the ascetic life, remained in the four postures.
The meaning is: "They wandered alone.
"The wandering of one is better" means that for one who has gone forth, from the time of going forth onward, the wandering of one who delights in solitude is better.

"There is no companion for a fool" refers to the Shorter Code of Discipline (Cūḷasīla), the Intermediate Code of Discipline (Majjhimasīla), the Greater Code of Discipline (Mahāsīla), and the Ten [Precepts].

The thirteen bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*), the ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), the four paths, the four fruits, the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*), the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and the deathless great Nibbāna—this is what is called "companionship. One cannot attain this by relying on a fool;

thus, there is no companionship with a fool. In the phrase *mātaṅgo araññe mātaṅgaraññe*, the compound is formed by the elision of the vowel *a* (*saralopa*) according to the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
There is also a reading “of King Mātaṅga,” meaning one who is like a wild forest elephant (*araññaka-mātaṅga*).
Since the state of being an elephant is already expressed by the word *mātaṅga* itself, he said,
“‘Nāga’ is a designation for greatness,” because the word *nāga* is a synonym for greatness in such passages as, “This is the nāga of the nāga, the tusker with tusks like plow-poles.”
The commentary on the Discourse on the Story of Dīghāvu is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Journey to Bālakaloṇakagāma:
465. “Bālakaloṇakāragāma” is the name of a wealthy village belonging to the householder Upāli. “He approached him” means...
Without informing either the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the General of the Dhamma, or the eighty great disciples, or even the Elder Ānanda,
the keeper of the Dhamma-treasury, he took his bowl and robe and approached all alone—
like an elephant that has left the herd, like a black lion that has left its lair, and like a cloud scattered by the wind.
Why did he approach? It is said that having seen the danger in living in a group, a desire arose in him to see a monk who dwells alone;
therefore, he approached like one oppressed by cold and the like who longs for heat and the like.

Alternatively, the Blessed One had long since fully understood that danger, and the Teacher was not weary of it; however, during that rainy season, there were some who were to be converted by the Buddha.
Because they did not exist [there], the Teacher went toward Pālileyyaka with the intention that going elsewhere would be a means for taming those monks;
while traveling there, he went specifically to encourage the Venerable Bhagu, who was dwelling alone.
When the Teacher had thus departed, five hundred monks said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Friend Ānanda, the Teacher has gone all alone; we..."

“We shall follow him. “Friend, when the Blessed One himself puts his lodgings in order, takes his bowl and robe, and goes out alone without informing his attendants, without taking leave of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is the Blessed One’s intention to travel alone.
A disciple, indeed, should act in accordance with the Teacher’s intention.”
"Therefore, the Blessed One should not be followed for these days," he said, and thus he prevented him; he himself also did not follow after him.
"With a talk on the Dhamma" means with a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the advantages of living in solitude.
The commentary on the account of the journey to Bālakaloṇaka is finished.
The Explanation of the Discourse on Going to the Eastern Bamboo Park (Pācīnavaṃsadāyagamanakathāvaṇṇanā) 466. As for "where the Eastern Bamboo Park was," why did he go there?
It was just as one who is hungry goes to food, one who is thirsty to drink, one touched by cold to warmth, one touched by heat to coolness, or one who is suffering to happiness.

Just as delight arises [in the mind], even so, while the Blessed One was reflecting upon the Kosambī monks who were living in discord after falling into mutual dispute—wishing to take hold of them as they lived together in harmony—these three sons of noble family came into his range of vision;
then, desiring to encourage them, he approached them, thinking: "In this very sequence of practice, for the monks of Kosambī..."
"...is a means of discipline. "They dwell" means they dwell experiencing the flavor of concord. "A park-keeper" is a forest-guardian.
He [guards] the forest so that people, having entered by whatever path they desire, do not carry away flowers, fruits, resin, or forest materials from there; thus, by means of a fence...
Sitting at the gate of an enclosed forest that has been set up, he guards the forest; therefore, he is called a "guardian of the grove" (*dāyapāla*).
They dwell desiring their own welfare means they dwell having made it their very nature to desire their own benefit.

For one who, even after going forth in this Dispensation, [engages] through the twenty-one modes of improper search—such as by means of medical practice, acting as a messenger, or going on errands—...
...makes his living; this person is not one who acts according to his own will.

But he who, having gone forth in this dispensation, abandons the twenty-one kinds of improper search, establishes himself in the fourfold purification of virtue, masters the word of the Buddha, resolves upon suitable ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), takes up a meditation subject from among the thirty-eight objects according to his own preference for the mind, and leaves the vicinity of a village for the forest—
Having entered and attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwells practicing the work of insight (*vipassanā*);
such a person is called "one who desires his own welfare. Those three sons of good family were also like this. Therefore it is said: "They dwell as those desiring their own welfare.
"Do not cause them discomfort" means "do not make them uneasy"; thus she restrained the Blessed One. For this was her thought:
He thought, "These sons of good family live in harmony, yet in the absence of some of them, quarrels, disputes, and arguments arise;
he wanders about like a fierce bull with sharp horns, goring [others]. Now, two cannot travel by the same path;
perhaps he too, acting in this way, might break the harmonious dwelling of these sons of good family."
Moreover, this man is handsome and golden-hued; I suspect he is greedy for flavors.
From the moment he departs, by praising his own supporters who provide him with choice food and so forth, he will disrupt the state of heedfulness of these sons of good family.
Furthermore, the dwelling places of these sons of good family are fixed and delimited—there are only three leaf-huts.
“There are three walking-paths, three places for daytime standing, and three beds and seats; yet this ascetic is large-bodied and, I suspect, older.
He will likely rouse these sons of good family from their lodgings at an improper time, and thus they will be uncomfortable in every way.
Not wishing that, [the householder] prevented the Blessed One, saying, “Do not cause them discomfort.”
But did he forbid him knowing [the answer], or not knowing? He did not know.

For when the Perfectly Enlightened One wanders about, surrounded by many thousands of monks, displaying the majesty of a Buddha with his fathom-wide radiance, his eighty minor marks, and the glory of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he is to be recognized even without asking, "Who is this? However, at that time, the Blessed One—
Thinking, "Let no one recognize my Buddha-power," he concealed that entire display of Buddha-power within his robe as if with a cloak, through such a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-abhisaṅkhāra*).
Like the full moon hidden by a mass of clouds, he took his bowl and robes and departed in an unfamiliar guise. Thus, the park keeper stopped him without even knowing who he was.
"Thus he spoke": it is said that the Elder, having heard the park keeper's words "Do not, O ascetics," thought to himself, "We three persons dwell here;
there is no other who is called a renunciant. Yet this park keeper speaks as if with a renunciant.
Who could this be? Rising from his daytime resting place, he stood at the gate and [looked] toward the path.
As he looked, he saw the Blessed One. At the very moment of seeing him, the Blessed One emitted a radiance from his body;
his fathom-wide aura, adorned with the eighty minor marks, shone like an outspread cloth of gold.
The elder thought, "This park keeper is like one who extends his hand to seize a hooded cobra by its neck—[yet here is] the Supreme Person in the world..."
Even while speaking together, he did not realize [who it was], as if he were speaking with some other bhikkhu;
thus, restraining him, he spoke these words beginning with, "Do not, friend, [enter] the park-keepers' area.
Why did he approach the Blessed One without having gone out to meet him? It is said that this thought occurred to him:
“We three live together in harmony; if I were to go out to meet him alone, our state of living in harmony would no longer exist.
Therefore, I shall go out to meet him taking my dear friends with me.
Just as the Blessed One is dear to me, so too are these companions dear to me. Desiring to go out to meet him together with them, he himself—
Without doing so, he approached. Some, however, say: "The path by which the Blessed One was coming led to the edge of the walking-path at the door of those elders' leaf-hut;
therefore, the Elder went along as if giving them notice. "Come hither" means: come from this direction.
"He washed his feet" [means] with webbed hands resembling blossoming lotuses, [he washed] the jewel-colored...
Taking water and pouring it over his golden-colored heels, he washed them by rubbing foot against foot.
One might ask: since dust and dirt do not adhere to the bodies of Buddhas, why did he wash them?
It was for the sake of allowing his body to take on the seasonal temperature and for the sake of gladdening their hearts. "With the water brought by us, may the Blessed One..."
"He washed [his feet] at their feet; he made use [of them]"—because the minds of those bhikkhus were gladdened by a powerful surge of joy, he washed [them].
"The Blessed One said this to the Venerable Anuruddha"—it is said that he was the eldest among them, and [the Buddha spoke thus] for the sake of winning him over.
Since the remainder [of the sentence] has been completed, this statement beginning with "Kacci vo, Anuruddhā" was spoken by the Elder alone.
Alternatively, it is stated using the method of *ekasesa* (single-remainder), because even the *virūpa-ekasesa* (single-remainder of dissimilar forms) is acceptable;
and by doing so, the use of the plural number is justified. *Kacci* is a particle used in the sense of inquiry. *Vo* is a genitive case ending.
This is what is meant: "I hope it is bearable for you, Anuruddhas; I hope your mode of conduct is comfortable; I hope you are getting by;
I hope life is sustained and maintained for you; I hope you do not suffer from lack of almsfood; I hope almsfood is easily obtained for you;
and I hope that when people see you arrive, they provide you with ladlefuls of gruel or spoonfuls of food."

"Or they think it should be given," he says, asking about the conduct for wandering for alms. Why? Because it is possible to practice the *śramaṇadharma* without being exhausted by [the lack of] requisites, or because this is simply the proper conduct (*vatta*) for those who have gone forth.
Then, when he has given his reply, [Anuruddha said]: "Anuruddhas, you are royal renunciants of great merit; people [should give] to you..."

"Thinking that they would give this to someone else rather than to those dwelling in the forest, [the Blessed One] asked about the flavor of concord, saying, 'But after you have eaten this, do you dwell rubbing against one another like young deer, or is there a state of harmony among you?
Thus he said, 'I hope, Anuruddhas, that you are in harmony,' and so forth. In this regard:

"Like milk and water mixed": just as milk and water blend with one another, do not remain separate, but come together as if into a single unity—does he ask this, "Do you dwell with such a state of mind that has attained unity through harmony?
"With loving eyes": because they look upon others having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), these are eyes that manifest affection.
“Having loving eyes” means: he asks, “Do you dwell looking at one another with such eyes?
*Taggha* is a particle used in the sense of certainty; it is equivalent to saying, “Certainly, Venerable Sir. Regarding the phrase *yathā kathaṃ pana*:
here *yathā* is a mere particle, while *kathaṃ* is an inquiry into the reason: “In what way, however, do you dwell thus?”
"For what reason do you dwell? Tell me that reason"—this is what is meant.

"Loving bodily action" (*mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ*) refers to bodily action proceeding by way of a mind of loving-kindness (*mettacitta*). "Both openly and in secret" means both in the presence of others and behind their backs.
The same method applies to the other [actions] as well. In this context, bodily and verbal actions in the presence of others occur during cohabitation.
The other [offenses] are incurred when one is away from one's belongings; mental action (manokamma) is incurred in all cases.

For instance, if while living together, a bed, a stool, a wooden utensil, or a ceramic vessel has been left outside by one person, and another sees it—without showing contempt by asking, "Who used this?"—but rather takes it as if it were his own and puts it away, [there is no offense].
Furthermore, when one cleans a place that requires cleaning while the person [to whom it belongs] is present, that is called bodily action of loving-kindness in their presence (*sammukha*).
When one puts back bedding and requisites that were poorly arranged by someone who has departed, or when one cleans a place that requires cleaning while the person is absent,
that is bodily action of loving-kindness in their absence (*parammukha*).

This is what is called [verbal loving-kindness]. Furthermore, when living together with elders, engaging in sweet, friendly conversation, greetings, polite discourse, talk on the Dhamma, recitation, discussion, asking questions, and answering questions—performing such acts as these is what is called verbal action of loving-kindness in their presence. But when the elders have departed, [thinking] "In my..."
When one speaks of the virtues of a dear friend, such as, "The Elder Nandiya and the Elder Kimila are thus endowed with virtue,
thus endowed with proper conduct," this is called verbal action of loving-kindness (*mettā-vācākamma*) performed in their absence.

However, for one who directs their attention thus, "May my dear friends, the Elder Nandiya and the Elder Kimila, be free from enmity, free from affliction, and happy," this constitutes loving-kindness both in their presence and in their absence.
It is indeed mental action.
"For our bodies, venerable sir, are indeed diverse," for this body cannot be kneaded together like flour or clay;
"but our mind, I think, is one," for our minds are as one with each other as they are with ourselves.
It shows that they were of one mind through their disposition toward welfare, their disposition toward non-conflict, their absence of division, and their state of harmony.
But how did these monks, having set aside their own opinions, act according to the opinion of the others?
For instance, in one man’s bowl dirt appeared; in another’s robe there was a stain; in another’s case, there was work to be done on the border. In that situation, for whichever...
Stain had arisen on his bowl. When he said, "Friend, stain has arisen on my bowl;
it ought to be fired," the others did not say, "My robe must be washed" or "My border-work must be done";
instead, they entered the forest, brought firewood, split it, and applied a coating of thick clay to the interior of the bowl.
Having prepared the bowl and cooked [the meal], they thereafter wash their robes or perform repairs.
Even if one has already announced earlier, saying, "Friends, my robe is soiled; it ought to be washed," or "My leaf-hut is messy;
it ought to be repaired," the same rule applies.
Now, asking about their characteristic of diligence, he said, "But how is it with you, Anuruddhas?
and so forth. In this context, *vo* is merely a particle, or it is the genitive plural; the meaning is "of you. *Amhākaṃ* means "among us three persons.
*Piṇḍāya paṭikkamati* means "he returns from wandering for alms in the village. *Avakkārapātiṃ*...
Having removed the extra alms-food, he washed one casket-bowl and set it aside for the purpose of storing it.

It is said that those elders did not enter the alms-round together; rather, being devoted to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), they would attend to their physical needs early in the morning, fulfill their duties, enter their dwellings, and having fixed a time limit, enter into the attainment of fruition.

Having sat down after lighting [the fires], among them, he who sat down first and rises first according to his own allotted time for the meal, having wandered for alms and returned, arrives at the place where the meal is to be taken and knows: "Two monks are behind me;
I have arrived first. Then, having covered the bowl and performed the arrangement of seats and other duties, he sits down.
If there is only enough for one bowlful, he sits down and eats;
if there is more than that, he puts it into the alms-bowl cover, closes the bowl, and eats.
Having finished his meal, he washes the bowl, rinses it, places it in its bag, takes his bowl and robes, and enters his own dwelling place.
The second one also arrives and realizes, "One has come first; the other came later. If there is just the right amount of food in the bowl, he eats it.
If it is insufficient, he takes more from the refuse-receptacle and eats.
If there is an excess, he puts it into the refuse-receptacle, eats only the right amount, and goes to his dwelling place just as the elder who arrived first did.
He enters. A third person also arrives and realizes, "The first two have already come;

I am the last. Like the second elder, he too eats, completes his meal duties, washes his bowl, dries it, places it in its bag, puts away the seats, and, having discarded any remaining water from the drinking jar or the rinsing jar, [departs].
Having set down the bowl in the water-jar, if there is any leftover food remaining in the alms-bowl, he discards it according to the prescribed method, washes the bowl, and puts it away.
He sweeps the dining hall; having thrown out the rubbish and put away the broom, he places it where it is free from ants.
Then, taking his bowl and robe, he enters his dwelling place.
This is the procedure for the dining hall in the forest monastery where the elders perform their meal duties.
It is with reference to this that the passage beginning with "He who comes later," and so forth, was spoken.

However, the passage beginning with "He who sees," and so forth, should be understood as the procedure for them within the monastery. In this context, *vaccaghaṭa* refers to the water-pot for rinsing.
"Empty" (*rittaka*) means void. "Hollow" (*tuccha*) is a synonym for that same thing. "Unbearable" (*avisayha*) means too heavy to be lifted.
"By a movement of the hand" (*hatthavikārena*) means by a gesture of the hand.
It is said that they would take whatever was empty among the water-jars and so forth, go to the lotus pond, wash it inside and out, strain the water, and set it down on the bank.
They address another monk by means of a hand gesture, rather than making a sound specifically or non-specifically.
Why do they not make it specifically? Because the sound might disturb that monk. Why do they not make it non-specifically?
If a sound were made non-specifically, both [monks] might come out, each thinking, "I am first, I am first. Then, regarding the task to be performed by the two...
There would be an interruption of the formal act for the third person. However, making a sound by clapping his hands, he goes near another monk’s daytime resting place;
having ascertained that he has been seen, he makes a hand signal. By that signal, the other comes;
then the two men, interlocking hand with hand and placing [the body] upon both hands, lift it up. That—
Having spoken with intentional meaning, he said: "Having addressed the second [monk] with a gesture of the hand, let us attend upon him by passing the hand [to him].
As for the phrase "every five days," this refers first of all to the regular hearing of the Dhamma on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days;
having kept that intact, on every fifth day, after the two elders had bathed not too late in the afternoon, [they would go to] the Elder Anuruddha.
They go to the place of residence. There, all three sit down and ask one another questions on one of the three Piṭakas, and they answer one another. While they are doing this, the dawn breaks.

It was with reference to this that it was said. Up to this point, by the Elder, having been asked about the characteristic of heedfulness by the Blessed One, [he spoke] regarding the very grounds for negligence.
The characteristic of heedfulness (*appamāda*) has been explained. For other monks, there is the time for entering on the alms-round,
the time for departing, the changing of undergarments, the donning of robes, wandering for alms within the village, preaching the Dhamma, giving thanks,
departing from the village, performing the meal duties, washing the bowl, and putting away the bowl.
“Attending to the bowl and robe” refers to these occasions for proliferation. Therefore, the Elder said:
“Having set aside this much ground, these are the points where we might neglect the meditation subject by engaging in idle talk;
yet even there, venerable sir, we do not practice in a way that is contrary to the meditation subject. Thus he spoke regarding those very grounds for negligence of others.
He released his own characteristic of heedfulness, which had reached its peak.

By this very act, he demonstrates that for us there is no such thing as a time of negligence, since we have abandoned these places and no longer resort to the meditative attainments (*vihāra-samāpatti*) elsewhere.
The commentary on the account of the journey to the Pācīnavaṃsa Grove is concluded.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Journey to Pālileyyaka:
"By a talk on the Dhamma" means by a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the benefits of living in harmony.
"Wandering on tour by stages" means wandering on tour in successive order through villages and market towns. "Where Pālileyyaka was."

He set out alone for the village of Pālileyyaka. The inhabitants of the village of Pālileyyaka went out to meet him, gave an offering to the Blessed One, and having built a leaf-hut for the Blessed One in a protected grove not far from the village of Pālileyyaka, they requested, "May the Blessed One dwell here," and so they provided him with lodging. It was called Bhaddasāla.
However, there was a certain beautiful *laṭṭhika* (cane) *sāla* tree there. The Blessed One, depending on that village, dwelt at the foot of that tree near a leaf-hut in a grove of woods.
Therefore it is said: "He was dwelling at Pālileyyaka, in the protected grove, at the foot of the auspicious *sāla* tree.
Then, the passage beginning with "Now, while the Blessed One was alone" and so forth, demonstrates the Blessed One’s reflection upon the bliss of seclusion. [The word] *ākiṇṇo*...
"I did not dwell in comfort; I dwelt crowded and beset. But does the Blessed One have any crowding or social entanglement? No.
For no one is able to approach the Blessed One against his will. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are difficult to approach and are entirely unsullied;
yet, out of compassion for beings and with a desire for their welfare, [they appear].

"Having been liberated myself, I shall liberate others"—in accordance with this promise, he accepts the approach of the eight assemblies to his presence from time to time for the purpose of crossing over the four floods; and being himself impelled by great compassion, he approaches them at the proper time, knowing the right occasion.
This is the established practice of all Buddhas. It is not intended here that he dwells in a state of crowdedness.
Furthermore, he lived in the same monastery together with those quarrelsome monks from Kosambī;
because there was no one to be trained at that time, he made his dwelling crowded, and thus it was said: "Formerly, being crowded, I did not dwell in comfort.
For this very reason, he said: "By those quarrelsome monks from Kosambī," and so forth.
“With young calves” means with young elephant calves, which are also called *bhiṅkās*. “By them” refers to the elephants and so forth.

“Muddy waters” means waters mixed with mud. “Plunging into” (*ogāha*); here the reading is also found as “plunging” (*ogāhanti*). “Of him” refers to the noble elephant. “Rubbing against” means striking against.
Even while being rubbed against, he does not become angry because of his own sublime nature.
Therefore, they were indeed trampling them. "Withdrawn" (*vūpakaṭṭho*) means withdrawn, having become distant.
"From the herd" (*yūthā*) means from the elephant herd. "He approached where the Blessed One was" (*yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī*):
it is said that this noble elephant, weary of living in the herd, entered that forest grove. Having seen the Blessed One there, his distress was extinguished by a thousand jars [of water].
Having become as if extinguished, he stood before the Blessed One with a serene mind; from that time forth, taking charge of the duties,
he cleared the area around Bhaddasāla’s leaf-hut of all weeds and swept it by breaking off branches,
provided the Blessed One with water for washing his face, brought water for bathing, gave him tooth-sticks, and [brought] sweet [fruits] from the forest.
Having gathered various fruits, he brought them to the Teacher, and the Teacher consumed them. Therefore it is said:
“With his trunk, he presented the Blessed One with drinking water and food,” and so forth.
It is said that he would bring firewood with his trunk, strike it against one another to produce fire, kindle the wood, and heat pieces of stone therein.
Having wound those [rope-coils] around his trunk, he threw them into his proboscis; and having perceived the heat of the water, he approached the presence of the Blessed One and stood there.
The Blessed One, thinking, "The noble elephant desires my bath," went there and performed the act of bathing.
The same procedure applies to the drinking water as well. However, when it has become cool, he approaches it. It is with reference to this that it was said:
"He presented the Blessed One with drinking water and food for consumption from his own trunk.
And "having known his own seclusion" means having known the physical seclusion obtained by being unencumbered by anyone.
However, the other types of seclusion are always present in the Blessed One. He uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) regarding himself...
He uttered this *udāna* to illustrate the state of having a similar disposition regarding delight in seclusion with the elephant-nāga.
Furthermore, the construction of the meaning of the verse should be understood as follows:
"The mind of this elephant-nāga—whose tusks are like the pole of a chariot—is in harmony and coincides with the mind of the Buddha-nāga. In what way does it coincide?

Why is this? Because just as the Buddha-nāga—having felt revulsion for his former crowded dwelling, thinking, "In the past, I lived surrounded," and thus cultivating solitude—now delights and finds joy being alone and without a second companion in the forest and the wilderness;
even so, this elephant-nāga [formerly] lived surrounded by other elephants and the like.
Having become disgusted [with the world], he now delights in and rejoices in dwelling alone in the forest without a companion;
therefore, his mind is "equal to that of the elephant. This means that because it is equal to his [the elephant's] mind, it becomes identical with him through the joy of solitude.
The commentary on the account of the journey to Pālileyyaka is concluded.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighteen Bases (Aṭṭhārasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā): 473.
Regarding the rule, "Whoever should prevent [another] incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)": here, the offense falls upon whoever prevents a dwelling from one who is entitled to it.

However, in this case, there is no offense for those such as quarrelsome persons if they act according to a formal agreement made by the Saṅgha, such as "there is no space [for you here]," and so forth.
There is no offense for one who, having announced [the time], does not designate [a seat] for someone who— claiming "I am old"— seizes it by force,

The meaning that "it must be done on account of a *saṅghādisesa* offense" is thus established. If it is argued that this contradicts the statement in the bright side [of the commentary], namely, "it has been done for an offense that comes to confession," [the answer is:

Regarding the story of Sudhamma at Macchikāsaṇḍa, that is, in the city of that name.
It is said that there, the householder Citta saw Mahānāma Thera, who was among the group of five, walking for alms; [and he observed] his deportment...
Having gained confidence, he took the bowl, led him into his house, and fed him.
At the conclusion of the meal, while listening to the discourse on the Dhamma, he attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

With unshakable faith, desiring to establish a monastery for the Saṅgha in his own pleasure grove called Ambāṭakavana, he poured water into the Elder’s hand and offered it. At that moment, [it was proclaimed]: "The Buddha's Dispensation is firmly established!"
The great earth trembled as far as the limits of the ocean, and the Great Merchant had a great monastery built in the park.
There, this monk Sudhamma was a resident. It is with reference to him that it was said:
“The Venerable Sudhamma was a resident at Macchikāsaṇḍa for the householder Citta,” and so forth. In that context, *dhuvabhattika* means one who takes regular meals.

On another occasion, having heard a discourse on the virtues of Citta, the two Chief Disciples, desiring to show him favor, went to Macchikāsaṇḍa together with a thousand bhikkhus. With reference to this, it is said:
"Now at that time, a number of elder monks... and so forth. Having heard of their arrival, the householder Citta [went out] for about half a yojana.
Having gone out to meet them and taken them with him, he led them into his own monastery.

After performing the duties for guests, he requested the Dhamma-Generals (the Elders) thus: "Venerable sirs, I wish to hear a brief discourse on the Dhamma. Then the Elder said to him, "Lay follower, we are indeed weary from the journey;
nevertheless, listen briefly," and he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to him. Thus it was said: "To one side..."
When the householder Citta was seated, the Venerable Sāriputta instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma;
at the end of which, while listening to the elder’s Dhamma talk, he attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
[The Venerable Ānanda] was unable to ask the householder Citta for forgiveness, so he went there and said, "Householder, it was my own fault..."
Although he said, "That was wrong; forgive me," he was refused by the other who replied, "I will not forgive you.
Dejected, he was unable to obtain his forgiveness. He returned once more to the presence of the Teacher.

The Teacher, though knowing that the lay follower would not forgive him, devised a means for him to obtain forgiveness, thinking: "This man is stiff with pride; let him return only after traveling thirty yojanas."

He dismissed him without even speaking to him. Later, when he returned with his pride humbled, the King gave him an accompanying messenger and said, "Go, go together with this man and ask the lay follower for forgiveness.

He added, "For one who calls himself a recluse, it is not fitting to harbor pride or envy, thinking, 'This is my monastery; this is my dwelling place; this is my lay follower; this is my lay follower-woman.'"
"For one who acts in this way, the defilements such as desire and pride increase," he said, advising him:
"One might wish for the cultivation of what is non-existent,
Preeminence among the monks, Authority over monasteries, And honor in other families."
“Let both householders and those gone forth think: ‘It was done by me alone;
may they be entirely under my control in every matter, whether what ought to be done or what ought not to be done.
Such is the thought of the fool, and thus his desire and pride increase.”
The Buddha spoke these verses in the Dhammapada.
Having heard this exhortation, the Elder Sudhamma paid homage to the Teacher, rose from his seat, and having performed a circumambulation to the right, departed together with that attendant monk.
Once he had come within the sight of the lay follower, the Elder confessed his offense.
He asked the lay follower for forgiveness. The lay follower replied, "I forgive you, venerable sir; if there is any fault on my part, forgive me.
Having been thus forgiven, he followed the instruction given by the Teacher and, within just a few days, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

For when disrespect is shown toward even a single bhikkhu, it is already shown toward the Saṅgha. However, one who does not fulfill the three trainings is called "one who does not practice the fulfillment of the training.
[The phrase] "for the harm and suffering of gods and humans" refers to a dispute that has arisen between two bhikkhus in a single monastery.
How does it lead to the harm and suffering of gods and humans?
For instance, as in the Kosambakakkhandhaka, when two monks have fallen into dispute, their pupils in that monastery dispute;
the community of nuns who receive their instruction disputes; then their lay supporters dispute; and thereafter, among the people...

The guardian deities fall into two groups. Among them, the guardian deities of those who speak according to the Dhamma are speakers of the Dhamma, while those of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma are speakers contrary to the Dhamma.
Consequently, the terrestrial deities who were friends with the guardian deities become divided.
Thus, by way of succession up to the Brahma-world, all gods and humans—with the exception of the noble disciples—fall into two groups.
[They] are [thus]. However, those who speak what is not the Dhamma (adhammavādī) are more numerous than those who speak the Dhamma.
Consequently, thinking, "That which is accepted by the majority is the truth," they abandon the Dhamma and adopt what is not the Dhamma.
Dwelling with what is not the Dhamma placed before them, they are reborn in the states of misery (apāya). Thus, a dispute arises between two bhikkhus in a single monastery.
It leads to the harm and suffering of many. "Internally" means within oneself or within one's own assembly.
"Externally" means in another person or in another's assembly. "For the sake of non-outflow in the future" means for the sake of its non-arising in the future.
"Spiteful" means endowed with spite characterized by the disparagement of others' virtues. "Envious" means [endowed] with the characteristic of grasping at opposition.

"Endowed with malice": possessed of malice characterized by envy toward the honors and other benefits received by others. "Envious": possessed of envy characterized by the act of envying the honors and so forth of others.

"Miserly": possessed of the five types of miserliness, such as the miserliness regarding one's dwelling. "Crooked": a deceiver. "Guileful": one who conceals the evil they have committed. "Of evil desires":
an immoral person who desires to be esteemed despite not being worthy of esteem. "Of wrong view": one who holds nihilistic views or the doctrine that there are no causes for phenomena.
One who propounds non-action (*akiriyavādī*). "One who clings to what is seen" (*sanditthiparāmāsī*) means that one personally clings to and grasps only what has been seen by oneself.
"One who holds firmly" (*ādhānaggāhī*) means one who grasps with tenacity. "One who is difficult to release" (*duppaṭinissaggī*) means it is not possible to make one relinquish what has been grasped.

And here, by the method of referring to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānanaya*) through such phrases as "one who is angry and resentful," unwholesome states such as anger and resentment are shown to be the roots of dispute.
By the phrases "thus with corrupt minds they dispute," and so forth, greed, hatred, and delusion are shown [to be roots of dispute].
And by the phrase "with uncorrupt minds they dispute," and so forth, non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] are shown to be the roots of non-dispute.

217. "Ugly" means having the color of a burnt stump, like a dust-demon (*paṃsupisācaka*). "Unpleasant to behold" means being disagreeable even to look at for one's own mother who has given birth to him.
Okotimakoṭi is a lakkuṇḍaka (a dwarf). "One-eyed" means either one-eyed or two-eyed. "Lame" means either lame in one hand or lame in both hands.
"Lame" means either lame in one foot or lame in both feet. "Winged" means one whose wings are destroyed;
that is, a cripple who moves on a board.

220. Regarding the question, "Is the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), or indeterminate (abyākata)? Is the legal issue of dispute wholesome, unwholesome, or indeed indeterminate?"—this is the inquiry.
The response, beginning with "The legal issue of dispute may be wholesome," and so forth, is the answer.

This same method applies to the remaining [legal issues] as well. He says, "It is called a dispute (vivāda) because they dispute by means of it"; thus, "the mental state (cittuppāda) by which they dispute is the dispute."
But how is that arising of consciousness called a "legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*)? To this he says:
"It is a legal issue because it is to be settled by means of the methods of settling. The meaning is: it is a legal issue because it is to be resolved by means of the methods of settling.

For when the arising of consciousness, which is the cause of dispute, is pacified, there is also the pacification of the sound produced from it; thus, the arising of consciousness is something to be settled by means of the methods of settling.
A method [of classification] is possible.

Regarding the statement that "an offense-dispute (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome (akusala) or indeterminate (abyākata)," this alternative is stated with reference only to what is blameworthy by way of formal rule (paññattivajja), not to what is blameworthy in the world (lokavajja); thus he said, "by way of intentional speech," and so forth. Why?
In this context, the meaning should be understood by way of what was spoken with intentional reference; thus he said, "For in which... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in digging the earth, etc.," the word "etc. includes training rules (sikkhāpada) such as those concerning the destruction of vegetation and other offenses prohibited by formal rule.
When one, through ignorance of the Vinaya, performs acts such as digging the earth under the pretext of performing a duty using a broom or similar tool, the thought that arises in him at that time—
It was said with intentional meaning (sandhāya) that "wholesome consciousness is a factor" (*aṅga*). Regarding the phrase "it is a factor":

even for one who acts under the heading of a formal obligation (*vattasīsa*), such as saying "I am digging this earth," because it proceeds by way of knowing the transgression, that wholesome consciousness constitutes a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*);
the meaning is that wholesome consciousness is the cause of the offense. For [an offense does not occur] for one who does not know the transgression.
An offense may arise in connection with such acts as digging the earth. "When that exists" means when that wholesome consciousness has been apprehended as being of the nature of an offense;

this is the intended meaning. "Therefore" means because, when a wholesome consciousness has been apprehended as being of the nature of an offense, it cannot be said that "there is no legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) that is wholesome"; therefore [this is stated]. This does not refer to a consciousness that is sufficient to constitute a constituent factor (aṅga) of an offense.
As for the statement, "The legal issue of an offense may be unwholesome or indeterminate;
there is no legal issue of an offense that is wholesome," this was not said with reference to the mind that serves as the cause of the offense by way of being a sufficient factor for its origination.
With what, then, was it said? He says: "But this," and so forth. [It refers to] when the bhikkhu’s mind is engaged in his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
If a woman lies down or falls asleep while [the monk] is lying down, at that moment there is an offense consisting of the physical form (rūpa) existing in the mode of lying down;
it is not a state of consciousness proceeding by way of the wholesome and so forth. Therefore, he said: "For one who commits [the offense] unintentionally...

by way of sharing a bed and so forth, it is indeterminate (abyākata). For at that moment, since the duty to rise has arisen and yet one does not rise, the offense is simply the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) proceeding in that mode.

If it is argued that a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) could also be wholesome (*kusala*), on the basis of the statement: "One who commits an offense does so with either a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind"? No.

For the purpose of showing that whoever is said to "commit an offense" does so while possessing one of the three types of minds, and not otherwise, [the text says] "with a wholesome mind," and so forth.

This has been stated. Herein, this is the meaning: because material form arises through such means as transgression during moments of wholesome consciousness while digging the earth and so forth, one who possesses wholesome consciousness incurs an indeterminate offense consisting of the material form that has arisen in that way;
likewise, one who possesses indeterminate consciousness incurs an indeterminate offense consisting of indeterminate material form. [This applies to] killing living beings and so forth.
One with an unwholesome mind incurs an unwholesome offense; however, in this context, matter (*rūpa*) is not subject to conventional designation.

Furthermore, one who commits killing and so forth in a dream, or who incurs an offense that must be incurred through such acts as sharing a bed, incurs an indeterminate offense (*abyākata-āpatti*) while possessing an unwholesome mind.

"One would incur a wholesome state of mind" means that one who, having taken a sheep's wool, travels three *yojanas* while attending to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), or one who recites the Dhamma word by word without knowing the formal rule (*paññatti*), would incur a wholesome state of mind regarding the offense to be incurred.
And therein, even though a wholesome state of mind exists, it is not a factor for the offense; thus, even though a wholesome state of mind exists therein—
"It is not a factor for an offense; the meaning is that it is not itself an offense. Regarding "of those that have moved or proceeded":
"moved" refers to the body, and "proceeded" refers to speech. "One or the other is a factor" means that either the body or the speech constitutes the offense.
By the phrase "and that is indeterminate because it is included within the aggregate of form," he shows that the legal issue of the offense is indeterminate (*avyākata*), and nothing else.

If this is so, would it follow from the statement, "Monks, for one who has committed an offense, I declare [rebirth] in hell or in the animal realm," that even an indeterminate (avyākata) state possesses the quality of being subject to karmic ripening? It does not follow.

For offenses committed unintentionally do not create an obstacle as long as one does not know of them; however, once one knows and yet conceals them, by reason of that concealment, another [obstacle arises].

One incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*), which is classified as an unwholesome legal issue (*akusala-āpattādhikaraṇa*); because it is of an unwholesome nature, it acts as an obstacle to heaven and liberation, and thus it is said that one who possesses such an offense is bound for the states of misery (*apāya*). However, it must be concluded here that an indeterminate (*abyākata*) legal issue of offense is of a nature that does not even have a result of ripening (*avipākadhamma*).
For this very reason, in the ancient *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries as well, it is stated: "An ordinary person (*puthujjana*)..."

Having shown the four types of persons—the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), the trainee (*sekha*), and the arahant—it is stated that among them, for the arahant, an offense-formal act (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is exclusively indeterminate (*abyākata*);
likewise for the trainees; and likewise for the virtuous worldling when he transgresses unintentionally, it is exclusively indeterminate.
For the other [the unvirtuous worldling], however, there is both the unwholesome (*akusala*) and the indeterminate. And because, at the time of his intentional transgression...
"It is exclusively unwholesome; therefore it was said, 'There is no wholesome legal issue arising from an offense.

It was written that 'in all cases it is thus indeterminate,' referring merely to the absence of karmic result (vipāka). And as for that legal issue arising from an offense which is unwholesome, even that, when confessed or cleared, does not act as an obstacle.
For example, the act of reviling the Noble Ones..."

Even though it is unwholesome, by confessing the transgression and obtaining forgiveness, it becomes "ahosi-kamma" (a deed that has become as if it never happened) because its capacity to ripen is warded off by the perfection of the remedy;
