in the same way, this [offense] also, once confessed or cleared, becomes non-obstructive through its state of being *ahosi-kamma* due to the warding off of its ripening by the perfection of the remedy. For that very reason, [it is said]: "For one who possesses an offense..."
“Monks, I speak of hell or the animal realm”—thus it is stated that one who possesses an offense goes to a state of misery (*apāya*).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Settling Methods for the Quelling of Legal Issues (228):
Those who are adversaries regarding a matter characterized by dispute are "adversaries regarding the matter" (*atthapaccatthika*).
229. "In the case of *sammukhāvinaya*" means in the state of *sammukhāvinaya*. 230.
"By way of" means by reason of. 231.
An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for disparaging is not mentioned in the case of a committee (*ubbāhikā*), because there is no giving of consent (*chandadāna*) in that instance.
236. Regarding the phrase *tassa kho taṃ*: here, *kho taṃ* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). 238. In the manuscripts, it is written:

*“Kā ca tattha tassapāpiyasikāyā”* (And what therein is the *tassapāpiyasikā*?). However, the reading to be understood here is simply: *“Kā ca tassapāpiyasikā”* (And what is the *tassapāpiyasikā*?). 242.

Regarding the statement that a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is settled by one means of settlement: herein, the business itself is the legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

This is a designation for formal acts such as the *apalokana-kamma* (act of seeking permission) and so forth. Unlike the *vivādādhikaraṇa* (dispute) and other legal issues, it is not to be settled by means of the methods of reconciliation (*samatha*);
rather, it is accomplished through the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused).
Therefore, in the phrase "it is settled" (*sammati*), the meaning of "it is accomplished" (*sampajjati*) should be understood. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Samathakkhandhaka is finished.
5. The Minor Matters Section (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka):
Commentary on the Discussion of Minor Matters.

243. “In the manner of an eight-padded board” means in the shape of an eight-padded gaming board; it is said to be similar to a gambling board (*jūtaphalaka*). “In the shape of the base of a spittoon” means in the shape of the base of a spittoon for spittle. 245.

Regarding “necklaces, pendants, and so forth,” the word “and so forth” includes earrings and other such items. “A hanging thread” refers to a thread suspended in the form of a sacrificial cord (*yaññopacita*).
246. “With slime” means with phlegm (*silesa*).
248. "Well-sung song" (*sādhugīta*) refers to a song connected with [themes such as] impermanence (*aniccatā*).

249. "By means of a four-cornered turn" (*caturassena vattena*) means by means of a complete method of recitation. The methods of recitation for the "wave-turn" (*taraṅgavatta*) and so forth have fallen into disuse.
"With the hair outside" (*bāhiraloma*) is a statement in the neuter gender; it is like the exterior of that woolen cloak (*uṇṇapāvāra*).
"Hairs are seen" means that for one who wears [them] in such a manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"These are the four royal families of snakes" is said with reference to those whose venom lies in their fangs;
for whatever creatures have venom in their fangs, they are all included within these four royal families of snakes. "For the protection of oneself... refers to one's own...

"For the welfare" means for one's own protection. "For the sake of protecting oneself" means for the purpose of guarding oneself. "I allow you to make a protection for oneself" means I authorize the making of what is called a protection for oneself; this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show how that protection is to be made, he said: "And thus, monks," and so forth.
In this context, "by the Virūpakkhas" means by the Virūpakkha clan of nāgas; the same method applies to the others as well. This instrumental case is used in connection with "together" (*saha*);
what is meant is: "my state of friendship is with these. "By the footless" means by footless beings; the same method applies to the others as well. "All beings":
having thus far described directed loving-kindness (*odissaka-metta*) up to this point, he now describes undirected loving-kindness (*anodissaka-metta*).
This was undertaken in order to speak. In this context, "beings," "living creatures," and "born beings"—all these are merely synonyms for the person (*puggala*).
"May they see auspicious things" means may they see auspicious objects (*ārammaṇa*).
"May no evil come to anyone" means may no evil or wretched thing come to any being.
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha is immeasurable" (*appamāṇo buddho*): here, "Buddha" should be understood as the qualities of a Buddha, for they are indeed called "immeasurable.

The same method applies to the other two [cases]; "possessing measure" (*pamāṇavantāni*) means they are endowed with a measure of qualities. "A spider" (*uṇṇanābhī*) is a hairy-naveled spider. "A *sarabū*" is a house-lizard.
"Protection has been made by me, a safeguard has been made by me" means that protection has been established by me for so many people.
"And protection has been performed. The meaning is: "May all beings retreat"—that is, may all sentient beings for whom protection has been performed by me depart, and not harass me.
"To him" (*sohaṃ*) refers to me, who possesses loving-kindness toward all these [beings];
the connection is: "I pay homage to the Blessed One, and I pay homage to the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones beginning with Vipassī."
"In another thing to be cut" refers to the underlying tendency of lust (*rāgānusaya*). "Or such suffering" refers to the pain produced by striking with the fist and so forth.

252. "Having had nets woven around" means having had nets made in the shape of baskets for the purpose of warding off dangers and protecting ornaments and other items that might fall through negligence. When a ball of sandalwood came into the net...
It is said that there was once a single red sandalwood tree growing on the upper bank of the Ganges;
its roots washed away by the river water, it fell and broke apart against the rocks here and there, scattering in pieces.

From among those fragments, a piece about the size of a water-jar, having been rubbed smooth by the rocks and polished by the spray of the waves, was gradually carried along by the current until it became covered with seaweed.
Having come, it became entangled in that net; it was with reference to this that it was said. *Lekha* means the powder taken up by writing.

*Uḍḍitvā* means having caused it to reach upward by means of a succession of bamboo poles; "having raised it" is what is meant. *Oharatu* means let him take it down by means of psychic power (*iddhi*).
The six teachers were Pūraṇa Kassapa and the others. Therein, *Pūraṇa* is the name of that one who claimed to be a teacher. *Kassapa*...
As for his clan: it is said that he was born as the one who completed a family’s count of ninety-nine servants;

therefore, they gave him the name Pūraṇa (The Completer). Because he was a servant of good omen, there was no one to tell him that what had been done was "badly done," nor that what had not been done was "not done.
He thought, "Why do I live here? and fled. Then thieves stripped him of his clothes.
Thus, not even knowing how to cover himself with leaves or grass, he entered a certain village with his gold.
When people saw him, they thought, "This ascetic is an Arahant of few desires; there is no one like him," and they approached him bringing cakes, alms-food, and other offerings.
He thought, "Because I am without a garment to wear, this has arisen for me," and from that...
Even after receiving a garment, he did not wear it; instead, he took up the life of a renunciant right then and there.
In his presence, five hundred other people—some here, some there—also went forth into homelessness. Thus, having become a teacher of a group, he became renowned in the world as a "Master" (Satthā).
His personal name was Makkhali. Because he was born in Gosālā, his second name was Gosāla. It is said that on a muddy road...
As he was walking along carrying an oil jar on the ground, his master said, "Dear son, do not stumble! He stumbled through negligence and fell;
out of fear of his master, he began to flee. His master ran after him and seized him by the hem of his garment.
He cast off the garment and fled naked. The rest is exactly like the story of Pūraṇa.
“Ajita” is his name. “One who wears a hair-blanket” is *kesakambala*.
Combining these two names, he is called “Ajita Kesakambala. In this context, a “hair-blanket” (*kesakambala*) is a blanket made from the hair of humans;
there is no garment more wretched than that. As it is said: “Just as, monks, whatever... [and so forth].
Of woven garments, a hair-blanket is declared to be the most inferior.
"A hair-blanket, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch.
"Pakudha" is his name; "Kaccāyana" is his clan. Thus, combining both name and clan, he is called "Pakudha Kaccāyana."
He is called one who rejects cold water; even after defecating, he does not perform his ablutions with it, but only does so upon obtaining hot water or sour gruel.

Or, having crossed a river or a puddle by the road, thinking "my virtue (sīla) is broken," he builds a mound of sand, resolves upon his virtue, and proceeds. Such is this one who has attained the acquisition of non-essential qualities (nissirika-laddhi).
“Sañcaya” is his name. “Belaṭṭha’s son” means *belaṭṭhaputta*. He is called a *nigaṇṭha* because he acquired that name by virtue of professing:
“We have no bond of defilement (*kileso*), no fetter of defilement; we are free from the knots of defilement. “Nāṭa’s son” means *nāṭaputta*. *Piṇḍolabhāradvāja*:
he is a *piṇḍola* because he went forth as one who carries and seeks alms (*piṇḍa*). It is said that his wealth had been exhausted.
Having been a brahmin, he saw the great gain and honor received by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
thus, having gone forth from home out of need for alms, he wandered about carrying a large iron bowl as his "alms-bowl.
He drank rice-gruel filling the bowl, ate solid food, and consumed cakes and snacks. Then, [the Teacher] perceived his nature of being of great value.
They reported this matter. The Teacher did not permit him to have a bowl-cloth (pattatthavika). The Elder placed his bowl upside down beneath his bed.
Even when placing it, he would set it down after knocking it; even when taking it up, he would pull it out after knocking it.
As time passed, through that constant knocking, it became worn away until it could hold only the measure of a *nāḷika* of rice.
A bowl was produced. Then they informed the Teacher. Thereupon, the Teacher permitted him an alms-bowl bag (*pattatthavikā*).
At a later time, as the Elder was cultivating the development of the faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*), he established himself in the supreme fruit, Arhatship.

Thus, because he previously went about for alms in a particularly distinguished manner, he was called Piṇḍola; and because of his clan name, Bhāradvāja—combining both together—[he was known as Piṇḍolabhāradvāja].
“He is called Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja.
Why did they speak thus: “Then the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja... said this”?
It is said that the merchant was neither of right view nor of wrong view, but was of a neutral temperament. He thought: “In my house there is sandalwood...”
"Many! What indeed shall I do with this? Then it occurred to him: "In this world there are many who say, 'We are Arahants, we are Arahants,' yet I do not know even a single Arahant.
Having yoked a cart at home, having had an alms-bowl engraved, and having placed it in a carrying-net, I shall suspend it sixty cubits into the air by means of a series of bamboo poles."
“If there is an Arahant, let him come through the air and take it,” he will say. “Whoever takes it, I and my wife and children will go for refuge to him.
Thinking thus, he had the bowl engraved according to his plan, raised it up on a succession of bamboo poles, and said:
“Whoever is an Arahant in this world, let him come through the air and take this bowl.”
Then the teachers said, "He is suitable for us; give him to us alone. He replied, "Come through the air and take him!
On the sixth day, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta sent his disciples, saying, "Go and say this to the merchant:
'He is suitable for our teacher alone; do not [waste] the air for the sake of such a trifle.'"
“Come here and give me back my bowl. They went and spoke thus to the merchant. The merchant said, “Let him take it only if he is capable of coming through the air and taking it.
Nātaputta, wishing to go himself, gave a signal to his disciples:
“I shall act as if I am about to leap up, lifting one hand and one foot.”

"If you were to say to me, 'Teacher, what are you doing? Do not show the quality of Arahantship hidden for the sake of a wooden bowl to the great multitude,' and were to seize me by my hands and feet and drag me down to the ground, you would cause me to fall.
Having gone there, he said to the merchant, "Great merchant, this bowl belongs to others..."
"It is not fitting; do not let it be because of such a trifle that you desire to leap into the air for my sake. Give me my bowl.

"Venerable sir, take it by leaping through the air yourself. Then Nāṭaputta, saying, "In that case, go away, go away," had his pupils removed and raised one hand and one foot, thinking, "I shall leap into the air. Then him—
The pupils said, "Teacher, what is this that you are doing? What is the purpose of showing off a hidden quality for the sake of a mere piece of wooden bark to the great multitude?
Seizing him by his hands and feet, they dragged him and threw him to the ground.
He said to the merchant, "Great merchant, these men will not let me fly up; give me my bowl."
"Venerable sirs, spring up and seize them! Thus, although the sectarians exerted themselves for six days, they did not obtain the bowl at all.

Then, on the seventh day, when the Venerable Moggallāna and the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja had gone to Rājagaha thinking, "We shall wander for alms," and were standing upon a stone slab in the back of a palace while putting on their robes, some ruffians—
How did they raise the issue? "Friends, formerly six teachers wandered about saying, 'We are arahants.

Yet today, for the seventh day, while the merchant of Rājagaha has held up his alms-bowl and said, 'If there be an arahant, let him come through the air and take it,' not even one has leaped into the sky saying, 'I am an arahant!'"
“There are none, friend; it is known that there are no Arahants in our world today.
Having heard those words, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja: “Friend Bhāradvāja, have you heard these words?
They speak as if they were upholding the Buddha’s teaching, yet you possess great psychic power and great majesty; go to them.”
"Go through the air and take the bowl. "Friend Moggallāna, you are renowned as the foremost of those possessing psychic power;
you take it. But if you do not take it, I shall take it," he said. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, "Take it, friend.
Thus they spoke in this way for the purpose of showing that the world was not empty of Arahants.
“He circumambulated Rājagaha three times” means that he went around and wandered about Rājagaha three times. Some, however, say it was seven times.

It is said that the Elder, having entered a jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), arose from it and, delimiting the Back Rock (Piṭṭhipāsāṇa) which was three gāvutas in length, lifted it up into the air like a tuft of cotton-wool; then, over the city of Rājagaha, seven times—
He circled around it. To the inhabitants of the city, which measured three gavutas in extent, he appeared like a lid covering it.
Terrified, thinking, "The rock is seizing us by crushing us," the city-dwellers placed their beds and other belongings upon their heads and hid here and there.
On the seventh round, the Elder broke through the back of the rock and revealed himself. When the great multitude saw the Elder, they...
“Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, grasp the stone firmly; do not destroy us all,” he said.
The Elder kicked the stone with his toe and released it. It went and landed back in its original place.
The Elder stood on the roof of the merchant’s house. Seeing him, the merchant prostrated himself on his chest and cried out, “Descend, Master!”
Having spoken thus, he caused the Elder who had descended from the sky to sit down, took his bowl, filled it with the four sweets, and gave it to the Elder.
The Elder took the bowl and set out toward the monastery.
Then those who had gone into the forest and had not seen the miracle gathered together and followed after the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, show the miracle to us as well."
Thus, displaying various miracles for them, he went to the monastery.
The Teacher, having followed him and heard the noise of the great crowd making a clamor, asked: "Ānanda, whose noise is this? Therefore it was said:
"The Blessed One heard... 'What now, Ānanda, is this loud noise, this great clamor?'"

Regarding the statement, "The miracle of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) is rejected": here, "transformation power" (*vikubbaniddhi*) refers to the supernormal power that functions by means of abandoning one's natural form and undergoing a change, as it is described in such passages as:
"Having abandoned his natural appearance, he displays the form of a youth or the form of a *nāga*, or he displays various military arrays.
On the other hand, "power of resolve" (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) [is described] as "by nature..."
One person adverts to many—whether a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand—and having adverted, resolves with knowledge:
“May I become many. Thus, the supernormal power (iddhi) accomplished by means of resolution is demonstrated through this analysis.
253–254. “Not touched” means they are not well-felt. “Crowded with forms” means crowded with female forms and so forth.

"Bhūmī-ādhāraka" means a bowl-rest with a circular base. "Dāru-ādhāraka-daṇḍa-ādhārakesu" means either a rest made from a single piece of wood or one made with many sticks; however, one made with three sticks is not permitted.
As for the rule that it should be placed on the ground turned upside down, when placing it there, one [should ensure] that the bowl placed on top...

They say it is permissible to place [the bowl] on the ground by making it touch the earth with its rim. Regarding "the *ālindaka*, the *miḍḍhika*, etc.," this refers to the *miḍḍhikas* at the front of the house.
Concerning the phrase "having turned over, it settles right there," it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Having turned over, on the third occasion it settles right there on the *miḍḍhika*.
A *paribhaṇḍa* is that which is outside a house, for the purpose of providing stability to the base of the wall.
"Small-sized" refers to a small *miḍḍhika* (a shallow bowl). "By means of a small-sized [bowl]" means by means of a small *miḍḍhika*.
It is also permissible to place it on a stand (*ādhāraka*) within the *miḍḍhika*.

For, according to the statement, "Monks, I allow a stand," it is permissible to place the bowl wherever among the *miḍḍhikas* and so forth one has placed a stand, provided there is a space for placing the stand.
They say it means "unrestricted. Regarding the term *pattamāḷa*, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points):
"A *pattamāḷa* is a circular or square enclosure made of bricks and so forth, constructed by surrounding [an area] so that bowls do not go beyond it.
255. *Ghaṭika*: a bolt fixed at the top. It is permissible to use [something] for a temporary period; thus, only once...
The intention is that after taking it and consuming that food, it is permissible to discard it. "In a *ghaṭikaṭāha*" means in a vessel or bowl. Regarding the phrase "it was not for me" (*abhū me*):
here, "to be" (*bhū*) means to exist or to increase; "not being" (*abhū*) means non-increase, or lack of growth.
However, out of fear, that woman said "it was not for me" (*abhu*), meaning "there will be destruction for me. "*Chavasīsassa pattaṃ*" means a skull belonging to a corpse.

The bowl (*patta*). This genitive case-ending expresses a relationship between the natural state and its modification; or, even where there is no actual difference, this conventional expression is used by figuratively attributing a distinction, as in such phrases as "the body of a stone statue" (*silāputtakassa sarīraṃ*).
"Having chewed" means having eaten. "Taking up a single mouthful of water" means lifting the bowl with the left hand alone.

"Having taken a mouthful" means having taken a sip with the mouth. "With a soiled hand" means with a hand that has food remnants on it. "By this much" means by the mere act of taking a single mouthful. "Having pulled out" means having extracted the meat from there.
In all these cases, whether one knows the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*) or not, there is indeed an offense.
256. "With yeast-dust" means with the yeast-dust used for brewing liquor. "'Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ' means they do it upon mats and such things."
This is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. "Bidalaka" is a designation for a specific action known as "doubling.
Of what is there doubling? It is of that material, such as reed-matting (*kilañja*), by which a large *kaṭhina* has been spread.
For that [material] must be gathered together at the edges to the size of a staff-*kaṭhina* and then doubled. "Paṭiggaṇha" refers to a finger-glove (*aṅgulikañcuka*).
257–259. A *pāti* (bowl) is a specific type of vessel made in the shape of a receptacle. "It is not permitted" means it is not allowable. 260–262.
"To build with a low base" means to build after having constructed a low foundation all around the exterior wall.
An "arahataghaṭiyanta" (water-wheel) is shaped like the wheel of a cart; it consists of spokes (*ara*) and buckets (*ghaṭikā*) bound together, [operated] by one or two people.
Or it is moving while being turned around. 263.

*Āviddhapakkhapāsa* means having side-walls placed all around the circular center (*kaṇṇikamaṇḍala*). *Maṇḍale* means in the circular center. *Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvā* means having placed the wooden side-wall panels all around.
264. "A *namataka* is like a rug" is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. It should be used with the same care as one would use for a piece of leather.
It should be used without making a formal resolve (*anadhiṭṭhahitvā*). "Included right here" means they are contained within the bowl-washer itself.
Previously, a stand was permitted for the purpose of protecting the bowl; now it is for the purpose of eating. 265.

"It should be turned upside down" means by means of the formal act of turning the bowl upside down (*pattanikkujjanakammavācā*) so that one does not accept the gift of merit (*deyyadhamma*) offered by him.
"It should be overturned," meaning it should not be placed face down. For this very reason, he said: "And furthermore, monks, it should be overturned in this way," and so forth.
"For the sake of non-gain" means for the purpose of not obtaining the four requisites.
"For harm" means for calamity or lack of prosperity. "We shall propitiate" means we shall entreat. He said this: "What I have done is unseemly; but the Blessed One..."
Thinking, "Even if my faults are great, he will accept my transgression," he spoke these words beginning with, "Venerable Sir, I have committed a transgression.
In this context, *accaya* refers to that which proceeds by overstepping the path of right conduct; it is a transgression.
*Accagamā maṃ* means it occurred having passed me by, having overcome me. It was like being crushed or overcome by a man.
For even though an offense has occurred, in its actual nature it is said to have "transcended" or "overcome" the person by prevailing over them. "Paṭiggaṇhātu" means may he forgive.
"Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya" means for the sake of restraint in the future, that is, for the purpose of not committing such an offense, fault, or transgression again.
"Taggha" means certainly. "Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi" means you make amends according to the Dhamma.
"Standing," it is said, means that you act accordingly and ask for forgiveness. "We accept that from you" means we forgive that transgression of yours.

"For this, friend Vaḍḍha, is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline" means, friend Vaḍḍha, this is what is called growth in the Noble One’s Discipline, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One. What is it? It is the acknowledgment of a transgression as a transgression.
Having seen [the transgression], one makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and attains restraint for the future. However, when teaching by way of a specific person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), he said:
"He who, having seen a transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, attains restraint for the future.
268. In the story of Prince Bodhi, *kokanada* refers to the *kokanada* lotus; and that is what the Maṅgala Palace was called.
It was made by displaying the *olokana-padmam* (the lotus for looking at), and therefore it received the designation “Kokanada.

Regarding the phrase “as far as the base of the final flight of stairs,” here “the base of the final flight of stairs” refers to the first step-slab, because it was the very last one to be covered with cloth.
Indeed, the stairway was covered starting from the uppermost step-slab. “He saw” means he saw for the purpose of looking.
Standing at the gate-tower, he saw [the procession].
The Blessed One remained silent; then, reflecting on the matter—“For what purpose has this great honor been performed by the prince?”—he understood that it was done out of a desire for a son.
For that prince was childless, and he had heard [of the Buddha’s power].
He heard, “It is said that by performing service for the Buddhas, one obtains whatever is desired in the mind. He made this aspiration:
“If I shall obtain a son, may the Sammasambuddha step upon this hempen rag-robe; if I shall not obtain him, he will not step upon it.
Having made this prayer, he had it spread out. Then the Blessed One considered: “Will a son be born to him?”
Having reflected, he saw that no son would be born. It is said that formerly, while living on a certain island, he ate young birds together with one who shared his inclinations.
Had his wife been possessed of merit, she might have obtained a son;
however, because they had committed an evil deed together with shared intent, he knew that for this reason no son would be born to him.

But when she has been stepped upon by the oxen, she might fall into a wrong grasp of things, thinking: "There is a worldly tradition that those who have performed service for the Buddhas obtain their aspirations;
yet I have performed great service and do not obtain a son—this saying is empty. The heretics too might think:
"There is nothing indeed that these recluses will not do; they wander about crushing their own rags of cloth."
They would criticize [this]. And nowadays, among those who step on [the footprint], there are many monks who understand the minds of others;

knowing their capacity, they will step on it if they perceive capacity, and they will not step on it if they perceive incapacity. But in the future, the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) will be weak;
they will not know the future, and if they step on it, should their aspiration succeed, that would be well.
If it should not succeed, people will become regretful, thinking: "In the past, having performed services for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they obtained whatever they desired; now they do not obtain it.
It seems those very same bhikkhus were fulfillers of the practice, whereas these [present ones] are unable to fulfill the practice. For these three reasons, the Blessed One...

Not wishing to step forward, he remained silent. As for the statement, "The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations," the Elder spoke this with reference to the third reason among those stated.
"Those desiring good fortune" (*maṅgalikā*) means those who seek auspiciousness. "A fan" (*bījanī*) refers to a square fan.
"A palm-leaf fan" (*tālavaṇṭa*) refers to a handheld circular fan made from palm leaves and the like.
270–275. "The 'single-leaf umbrella' is the palm leaf," so it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
Regarding the phrase "by a hundred acts" (*kamma-satena*), here the word *sata* has the sense of "many"; the meaning is "by many acts," which is to say, "with great effort.
*Rudhi* refers to a minor wound.
278. "In entering a village intentionally or unintentionally with a waist-belt [fastened], there is an offense.
One should enter or turn back having fastened it from the place where the river flows," so it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada.
"Made by wrapping it in the shape of a drum-head" means: having joined many ropes together and wrapped them with threads of various colors, it is made resembling the head of a drum (muraja).

It has been said. For that very reason, it was stated in the commentary on the second *pārājika*: "If many cords are joined together and wrapped around [the waist] continuously with one [cord], it should not be called 'made of many cords';
that is permissible. Regarding this, what ought to be said has already been stated above. A *muddika*-waistband is one that is prepared without being made square. A *pāmaṅga*-girdle...
"Square. "In the shape of a drum" means in the form of a *varaka* (a type of gourd). "The fringe" refers to the base of the hem. 280–282.

"Shavelings" refers to those such as wrestlers (*malla*) and laborers. "By the standard inch" is said with reference to the carpenter’s inch. The rest here is easily understood from the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Minor Section on Matters (*Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka*) is finished.
6. The Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka). Commentary on the Discussion of the Permission for Monasteries (Vihārānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 294.
In the Chapter on Lodgings, the statement "lodgings have not been prescribed" is said with reference to monastic dwellings (vihāra-senāsana).
For there are four kinds of lodgings: the lodging that is a monastery, the lodging that is a bed and chair, the lodging that is a spread, and the lodging that is a space.
In this regard: "A bed is a lodging; a chair, a mattress, and a pillow are lodgings;
a monastery, a gabled house, a mansion, a tower, a cave, a watchtower, a multi-storied building, a rock shelter, a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, and a pavilion are lodgings."

Furthermore, according to the statement, "Or wherever the monks withdraw—that is all 'lodging' (senāsana)"—this refers to the lodging consisting of a vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, or a guhā.
"A bed, a chair, a mattress, and a pillow"—this is called the lodging consisting of beds and chairs.
A felt rug, a skin rug, a grass mat, and a leaf mat...
This is called a "resting-place as a dwelling" (*santhatasenāsana*). Alternatively, "where monks retreat" refers to what is called a "site as a dwelling" (*okāsasenāsana*).
Regarding "at the foot of a tree" and so forth: a "dwelling at the foot of a tree" is any secluded spot at the base of a tree providing shade.
A "mountain" (*pabbata*) is a rocky crag; for there, having performed one's water-related duties by the mountain springs, one may sit in the cool shade of trees.
Seated in various directions, fanned by a cool breeze, they practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Regarding "in a cleft" (*kandare*):
*kaṃ* is said to mean water; a mountain region split or broken by that water is a *kandara*.
This is what some call a "slopes" (*nitamba*) and others a "river-grove" (*nadīkuñja*). For there, the sand is like silver plates, and above it is a canopy of jewels.
Like a dense forest thicket, water flows there resembling a mass of jewels;

having descended into such a cave, drunk the water, cooled their limbs, spread out a layer of sand, and arranged their rag-robes (paṃsukūla-cīvara), those bhikkhus sit there and practice the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). A mountain cave (giriguhā) is the space between two mountains.
Or else, there is a great opening resembling a mountain cave.

According to such statements as, “‘Forest-thicket’ (vanapattha) is a designation for remote lodgings,” it refers to a forest lodging situated beyond the vicinity of human habitation where people neither plow nor sow.
This is called “a forest retreat” (*vanapattha*). An “open space” (*ajjhokāsa*) is a place not covered by anything;
those who so desire may live there after constructing a cloth-hut (*cīvarakuṭi*). “In a heap of straw” means in a pile of straw.
For they take straw out from a large heap of straw and construct a dwelling resembling a mountain cave or a grotto, or they encircle trees, thickets, and the like with straw.
This was said with reference to those sitting below who perform the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). "Five shelters" (*pañca leṇāni*) means five places for hiding.
They are called "shelters" (*leṇāni*) because monks hide within them; this is a designation for monasteries (*vihāra*) and so forth.
"A house curved like a garuḍa" (*supaṇṇavaṅkageha*) is a house constructed in the shape of a garuḍa’s wing.
295. In the verses on rejoicing (*anumodanagāthā*), "cold" refers to the cold that arises either through the disturbance of the internal elements or through the transformation of external seasons.
"Heat" refers to the heat of fire; its occurrence should be understood as arising from forest fires and the like.
"Repels" means it counteracts. It acts in such a way that there is no affliction of body or mind due to those two.
For when the body is afflicted by cold and heat, a monk whose mind is distracted is unable to apply himself with wise attention.
"Wild beasts" refers to wild animals such as lions, tigers, and so forth. Indeed, for one who has entered a well-guarded lodging, closed the door, and sat down, those dangers do not exist.
"Reptiles" refers to any long-bodied creatures that crawl or move about. "Gnats" is mentioned merely as an illustration.
The inclusion of gadflies and other such creatures should be understood by this same principle.
"In the cold" refers to the contact with cold that arises due to the winter season and due to the onset of fevers lasting seven days or more.

"Showers" refers to rains that fall at any time whatsoever. "Fierce wind and heat" refers to the fierce wind and heat—distinguished as dusty or dustless—that prevail by uprooting and breaking trees, shrubs, and so forth.
The wind and the fierce heat of the sun during the summer season of scorching heat are both countered and warded off.

"For the sake of a shelter" means for the purpose of delighting in seclusion by turning the mind away from various objects. "For the sake of comfort" means for the purpose of living at ease due to the absence of the aforementioned dangers.
"To meditate" means to direct the mind to contemplate upon any one among the thirty-eight meditation subjects.
"Vipassituṃ" means to comprehend formations (saṅkhāra) by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Vihāre" means in a dwelling or residence. "Kāraye" means he should have [them] built. "Ramme" means in delightful places that provide the comfort of a dwelling.
"Vāsayettha bahussute" means that after having them built, he should cause those who are learned, virtuous, and of noble character to dwell there in these monasteries.
While residing there, he should provide those learned ones with food,

drink, clothing, and lodgings so that they do not suffer from a lack of requisites; he should do so with a mind made serene through faith in the results of kamma and the qualities of the Triple Gem, directed toward those who are upright and endowed with noble aspiration.
Now, in order to show the mutual assistance between householders and those who have gone forth, he spoke this verse beginning with “Te tassā.
Therein, “te” means those who are learned. “Tassā” means of the lay follower (*upāsaka*).

“Desenti dhamman” means they teach the true Dhamma, which eliminates the entire suffering of saṃsāra. “Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya” means that person, having understood here in this world that true Dhamma...
By practicing rightly in the Dispensation, having understood [the truth], and through the attainment of the supreme path, one becomes free from taints (*anāsava*) and attains *parinibbāna*.
And it is said that "he is a giver of all" because when a gift of a dwelling place is given, it is considered as if every kind of gift has been given.
For instance, even for one who returns from wandering for alms through two or three villages with nothing obtained, [a dwelling] endowed with shade and water...
Having entered a grove, bathed, and lain down for a moment in a shelter, when one rises and sits up, strength returns to the body as if it had been infused.
Furthermore, while wandering outside, the element of beauty (vaṇṇadhātu) in the body is exhausted by the wind and heat;
but for one who has entered a shelter, closed the door, and lain down for a moment, there arises a dissimilar continuity (visabhāga-santati).
It becomes pacified; a homogeneous continuity is established; it is as if a particle of color has been brought and placed there.
For one wandering outside, a thorn pierces the foot, a stump strikes him, and dangers such as reptiles as well as the fear of thieves arise.
But for one who has entered a shelter, closed the door, and lies down, all these dangers [cease].

They do not exist; rather, for one who recites the texts, the joy and happiness of the Dhamma arises, and for one who attends to the meditation subject, the happiness of tranquility arises because there is no outward distraction.

Furthermore, for one who wanders outside, sweat is released, the eyes twitch, and at the moment of entering the lodging, the beds and chairs are no longer visible; however, when he sits down for a moment, the clarity of his eyes returns.

It is as if he has been brought in and placed there; the doors, windows, beds, chairs, and so forth become visible, and seeing him dwelling in that residence, people respectfully attend to him with the four requisites. Therefore it is said:
"He is a giver of all who gives a lodging."
296. "The pulling hole" (*āviñchanacchidda*) is a designation for that [hole] where, having inserted a finger, those who pull the door draw it until it touches the doorpost.

"The pulling rope" (*āviñchanarajju*) is the rope by which, having made a hole in the door itself and inserted [the rope] there, they pull the door until it touches [the post]. Regarding the use of lodgings (*senāsanaparibhoge*).
It is stated, "Even if it is made with a leopard's tail, it is indeed permissible," in order to show that there is no such thing as an "unallowable skin.
"Like a railing on a cetiya" means it is made by displaying bands and so forth on the window frames, just like the railings on a cetiya.
A "pillar-window" (thambhakavātapāna) is one made with bamboo slips and the like standing upright, without placing wooden beams across.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the authorization of monasteries (*vihāra*) is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Authorization of Beds, Chairs, and So Forth (297):
"Poṭakitūla" means the down of *eraka* grass. Here, the mention of "poṭaki" is merely an illustration for various types of grass.
He said: “Of any kind of grass whatsoever. Five kinds of cotton and so forth are also permitted;

here too, the word “for a bolster” (bimbohane) should be brought over and connected. Some say that it is not permitted to use a mattress filled with cotton as a pillow, while others say it is permitted.
“They place” means they set down. “The size of the head” refers to [the space] from the throat...
Starting from the beginning, they provide the entire head; that is the measure of the head.
To show that, according to the maximum limit, it is one fist-cubit (muṭṭhiratana) across, he said: "Of which [the width] at the three corners...
and so forth. "The middle part is one fist-cubit" means that the middle part of the pillow is one fist-cubit in width.
*Masūraka*: a cushion made of leather. *Phusitāni dātuṃ*: to provide drops [of color], meaning to apply dots for the purpose of making a decorative mark.
*Na nibandhati*: it does not adhere; the meaning is that it does not stick. *Paṭibāhetvā*: having smoothed [the surface].
Commentary on the Discussion of the Permission for Brick Piles and Other Structures.
"Having pierced a tree" means having pierced the timber of a tree. "Having driven in stakes" means having driven in two stakes at a time.
This refers specifically to what was made by driving stakes in the manner already described for a "brought-in wall-base.
"To establish it on the ground" means having established it on the ground by its base, in order to provide support for the wall-base.
The intention is that, having raised it, one should place the base of the wall supported by pillars. "Of a space made by carrying out the walls on both sides" means:
having carried out the walls on both sides in such a way that those sitting near the interior door cannot look straight out, one establishes a wall facing [the center] and makes a space therein.
"Encircled all around" means having its front face fixed on every side. "A folding screen for opening" refers to a folding screen that is set up by being lifted with poles.
*Commentary on the Story of Anāthapiṇḍika’s Site*
304. Regarding the story of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, "on some business" refers to trading activities.
It is said that Anāthapiṇḍika and the merchant of Rājagaha were brothers-in-law.
Whenever goods produced in Rājagaha became expensive there, the merchant of Rājagaha would take them and travel to Sāvatthī by means of hundreds of carts.
Having traveled and stopped at a distance of one *yojana*, he makes his arrival known.
Anāthapiṇḍika goes out to meet him, pays him great honor, places him upon a vehicle, and enters Sāvatthī.
If the goods are light to sell, he sells them; if not, he leaves them in his sister’s house and departs. Anāthapiṇḍika also—
He did exactly so. At that time, he had gone out on that very business; it was with reference to this that it was said.
On that day, however, the Rājagaha merchant did not hear the letter sent by Anāthapiṇḍika from a distance of one league for the purpose of informing him of his arrival;
instead, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, he...
Having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha for the sake of his own independence, he had hearths dug, wooden mortars pounded, and other preparations made in his own house.
Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "Now he will come out to meet me;
now he will come," failed to receive a welcome even at the door of his house, and having entered the interior, received no great hospitality.
He received [him]. His greeting was only this much: "What, great merchant? Is all well with your children's health?
Are you not weary on the road? Therefore it is said: "Then it occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika," and so forth.
"'Buddha,' householder, you say"—it is said that upon hearing the word "Buddha" from his mouth, Anāthapiṇḍika [thought]:
He obtained five-colored rapture (*pīti*); it arose from his head and went down as far as the soles of his feet, and from the soles of his feet it rose up as far as his head;
rising from both sides, it moved toward the middle, and rising from the middle, it moved toward both sides.
Being completely suffused with this rapture, he said three times: "Householder, do you say 'Buddha'?"
He asked. [The Buddha replied: "Householder, it is not the right time to approach the Blessed One for an audience at this hour.
Thinking, "Buddhas are indeed difficult to approach, like venomous snakes, and the Teacher dwells near a charnel ground;
it is not possible to go there at this time," he spoke thus. This was said with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha.
"He lay down" means that, without thinking of anything else, he lay down with mindfulness directed solely toward the Buddha.
It is said that on that day, his mind did not even turn toward his merchandise-carts or his attendants, nor did he take his evening meal.
Having ascended the seven-storied palace, while reciting "Buddho, Buddho" upon a well-prepared and exquisitely adorned excellent couch, he fell asleep.
Having lain down, he fell asleep. He woke up three times, thinking it was dawn.
Thus, when the first watch had passed, he rose and recollected the Buddha;
then a powerful faith arose within him, there was a radiance of joy, and all darkness vanished, becoming like the lighting of a thousand lamps or the rising of the moon and the sun.

Thinking, "I have fallen into negligence; I have been deceived; the sun has risen," he rose, stood upon the surface of the sky, and looking at the moon, realized, "Only one watch has passed; two remain. He entered again and lay down.
By this means, he rose three times—at the end of the middle watch and at the end of the last watch. At the end of the last watch...
But rising very early at dawn, he came out onto the open terrace and stood facing the great gate;
the seven-storied gate opened by itself, and descending from the palace, he entered the street.
305. *Amanussā* refers to deities who have attained distinguished spiritual powers (*adhigatavisesā*). For they [perceived] the merchant’s future prosperity directly before their eyes.
Reflecting thus: “This great merchant set out thinking, ‘I will go to attend upon the Buddha.
By his very first sight [of the Buddha], he was established in the fruit of stream-entry;

having become the foremost attendant of the Three Jewels, and having built an incomparable monastery for the Saṅgha, he will be one who leaves the door open for the Noble Saṅgha from the four quarters. It is not fitting to close his door.”
Having reflected thus, they opened the door. "It disappeared" means that Rājagaha was indeed crowded with people;
nine koṭis lived within the city and nine outside the city, making eighteen koṭis of people living in dependence upon it.
Being unable to carry out dead persons at improper times, they would stand on the watchtowers and throw them over the outer gate. The Great Merchant...
As soon as he had stepped outside the city, he stepped with his foot upon a body that was still wet; he struck another with the back of his foot.
Flies swarmed up and scattered about, a foul stench assailed his nostrils, and his devotion to the Buddha grew thin.
Consequently, his light vanished and darkness appeared; as the force of his joy subsided, the material forms produced by it likewise faded away.

"Because of his extreme weakness. "He caused a sound to be proclaimed" means that, thinking "I shall arouse the merchant's enthusiasm," he made a proclamation with a sweet voice, like someone striking a golden bell.
"A hundred thousand maidens"—the preceding words should also be connected with this word "thousand."
"Just as there are a hundred thousand maidens, so too there are a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, and a hundred thousand chariots"—this is the meaning here;
thus, each [category] of one hundred thousand is illustrated. Regarding "the stride of a step" (*padavītihāra*):
it is called a "stride of a step" because one strides a step (*pada*) therein. This refers to walking with even gait, without making it either hurried or slow. Between the two...
"Between the steps, [the distance is] the measure of a fist-sized jewel.
"They do not equal even a sixteenth part"—having divided that single lifting of the foot into sixteen parts, one portion is again divided sixteenfold, and another portion likewise sixteenfold;
thus, when divided sixteen times by sixteen, one portion is called a "sixteenth part" (*soḷasī kalā*). These four [steps] do not equal even that sixteenth part.
They are not worth even a hundred thousand. This is what is meant:

a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots, and a hundred thousand maidens—these being daughters of kings from the entire continent of Jambudīpa, adorned with jeweled earrings—if one goes to a monastery, these many gains are [obtained] by means of leaping over that spot of ground measuring sixteen *kalās*.
"The volitions that have arisen are indeed superior. Or, "That by which one steps upon a footing" is *padavītihāra*;
it refers to the wholesome volition occurring in such a manner. They also say that its fruit is divided sixteenfold.
But with reference to whom is this "going to a monastery" taken? It is with reference to one who, having gone to the monastery, establishes himself in the fruit of stream-entry without obstacle.
It is taken by way of [the intention]: "I will perform worship with perfumes, garlands, and so forth; I will pay homage to the cetiya; I will listen to the Dhamma; I will perform a lamp-offering;
having invited the Saṅgha, I will give a gift; or I will establish myself in the training rules or in the refuges.
It is indeed permissible even for one who goes by way of such an intention.
"The darkness vanished. He thought, "I perceive myself to be alone, yet there are non-human beings following me as my companions;
why should I be afraid? Thus he became courageous.
Then, a powerful faith in the Buddha arose within him, and therefore the darkness vanished. The same principle applies to the remaining sections. "The light appeared."

By virtue of a powerful faith born from long-term cultivation under previous Buddhas, there appeared a preeminent light—arising from the mind-conditioned temperature (utu) and resembling the radiance of insight (vipassanā-obhāsa)—produced by the sublime joy directed toward the Buddha.
Some say this was also created by deities, but the former view alone is more appropriate here. "Come, Sudatta! he said.

It is said that as the merchant was going along, he thought: "In this world there are many sectarians such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others who say, 'We are Buddhas, we are Buddhas. How indeed might I know whether the Teacher is truly a Buddha?
Then it occurred to him: "The great multitude knows my name as it arose from my own virtues; [but what of] the name given by my family?"
"But no one other than myself knows my name; if he is the Buddha, he will address me by my family name.
The Teacher, knowing his thought, spoke thus:
"Parinibbuto" means extinguished by the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*). "Āsattiyo" refers to the state of clinging to form and so forth.

“Attachments” refers to the cravings (*taṇhā*). “Peace” (*santi*) refers to the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*). “Having attained” means having reached it by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*).

The rest here should be understood according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself. As for whatever meaning in this passage is not explicitly explained, that has already been stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
306. Regarding the phrase “the very process of passing away is the weaving,” he says: “‘Weaving’ (*veyyāyika*) is said to be the act of making to pass away (*vaya-karaṇa*).”
The commentary on the account of Anāthapiṇḍika is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning the granting of the foremost seat, etc., 310–311.
“Dakkhiṇodaka” means the water for the offering being presented from the front. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks...
He addressed them: when those bhikkhus had each spoken according to their own preference regarding those worthy of the foremost seat and so forth, [the Buddha said]:
"Bhikkhus, in my teaching, one who has gone forth from a khattiya family is not the measure;
nor one from a brahmin family, nor one from a householder family; nor one who is a master of the Vinaya, nor a master of the Suttantas, nor a master of the Abhidhamma."
"Monks, those who have attained the first jhāna and so forth, nor stream-enterers and so forth, are not the standard;
rather, monks, in this teaching, salutation, rising from one's seat, joining of palms, and respectful service should be performed according to seniority.
The best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food should be received; this is the standard here. Therefore, a more senior monk..."
It is worthy of them. Now, monks, my chief disciple Sāriputta, who sets in motion the wheel of the True Dharma, deserves to receive a dwelling immediately after me.
Yet this night, not obtaining a dwelling, he spent it at the foot of a tree.
If you are now so disrespectful and lacking in deference, what will happen as time goes on?
Having said, "Having done so, you shall dwell," he then spoke for the purpose of giving them exhortation: "In the past, monks, even animals thought:
'It is not fitting for us that we should dwell without mutual respect, without deference, and without living in accordance with our station;
rather, having recognized who among us is more senior, we shall perform salutations and other marks of respect toward him. Thus they practiced diligently."
Having investigated and realized, "This man is an elder," they paid him homage and so forth, and departed filling the path of the gods.
Having said this, he addressed the bhikkhus in order to bring forward and show a past account:
"Those who do not honor the elders"—there are three kinds of elders: the elder by birth, the elder by age, and the elder by virtue. Among these, one endowed with birth...
One who is advanced by birth is called "advanced in birth"; one established in age is called "advanced in age"; one endowed with virtues is called "advanced in virtue.
Among these, it is the one advanced in virtue and advanced in age who is intended here by the term "the elder. "Honoring" means they worship him through the act of honoring the eldest.
"Skilled in the Dhamma" means skilled and proficient in the Dhamma of honoring the eldest. "In this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme) means in this very world.
"In this very life" (*attabhāve*). "Praiseworthy" (*pāsaṃsā*) means worthy of praise. "And a happy destination in the world beyond" (*samparāye ca suggati*):
the meaning is that even in the other world, which must be gone to after passing away and leaving this world, only a happy destination awaits them. This, however, is the summarized meaning here:
"O monks, whether they be khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, or those gone forth..."
Or among those who have gone as animals— whatever beings there may be who are skillful, adept,

and endowed with virtue in performing acts of reverence toward their elders and seniors— they receive praise, eulogy, and acclaim for being "those who perform reverence toward their elders" in this very life,
and upon the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the permission for the foremost seat and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the discussion regarding the refusal of seats, etc. (313–4).

"Made specifically for [the Sangha]" means made by householders with the Sangha in mind. "Householder’s own property" means prepared by householders; it is said to be the possession of householders. "Without going too close" means without going to a place nearer than that of the bhikkhus.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Appointment of the Assigner of Lodgings (Senāsanaggāhāpaka): 318.

"By means of requisites indeed he will obtain that maintenance"—the meaning is that the great elders, for the sake of those requisites, will remain right there in that lodging without going elsewhere and will maintain him. *Ubbhaṇḍikā*.
"They will become" means they will become those who have discarded their belongings; the meaning is that they will wander here and there taking their own requisites with them.
"Long hall" refers to the walking-hall (*caṅkama-sālā*). "Circular pavilion" refers to the attendance hall (*upaṭṭhāna-sālā*). "It consumes" means it oppresses.
"But in Jambudīpa," however, was said with reference to the monks in the Noble Land (Ariyadesa). It is said that they...

They designate [the village]. The phrase "the village of one's range of activity must not be disturbed" clarifies the meaning already stated by the words "no people there should be addressed," and so forth.
"Having cut off thought" means not giving rise to such a thought as: "Seeing him going in this manner, they will stop him and provide requisites. "If one among them" means: if one among those people.
"A wise person. "A covering for goods" means a commodity used for covering; the meaning is that it is a robe (*cīvara*) for covering the body.
"Should be looked after" means they should be maintained by sweeping and so forth. "On the circular railing" refers to the square railing (*hammiyavedikā*) above the shrine (*cetiya*).
"Square railing" is a term for the four-cornered platform atop the shrine. "Having stepped back" means from the monastery (*vihāra*).

"Having stepped aside. "A deposit" means that after handing over a field, a coconut grove or other garden, or kahāpaṇa coins and so forth to the monastery attendants and others, it is given with the instruction:
"Let whatever profit arises from this be for the purpose of the rainy-season residence.
"Having performed the duties" means having performed the duties that must be done in that dwelling place.
"It should be done by way of individuals alone" means that, according to the method to be explained later— such as "The bhikkhus are distressed for robes;
it would be pleasing to the bhikkhus to have this much portion of rice used to make robes"— it must be done by way of the adherence to a person (*puggalaparāmāsa*),
and not by way of the adherence to the Saṅgha (*saṅghaparāmāsa*) such as "The Saṅgha is distressed for robes."
“Requisite of robes” means the requisite known as a robe. “Stated” means stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Why was it stated thus? He says: “For in this way, the junior will receive [it] from the senior, and the senior from the junior.
Since it is not possible for one to cause oneself to obtain [the robe] by oneself, therefore, when two have been appointed, the junior [receives it] from the senior.
The intention is that both the senior and the junior shall take [the lodgings] from one another.
It should be understood that even if the lodgings are taken by someone else at the command of the appointed assigner of lodgings, the taking is still valid.

Regarding the statement "it is permissible to appoint eight or sixteen persons," does it mean they may be appointed individually or collectively? It is permissible even collectively. This is merely a formal act of censure (*niggahakamma*).
For the Saṅgha does not perform [formal acts] for the Saṅgha; however, it is permissible to perform a formal act of authorization (*sammutidāna*) for many people together.
For this very reason, in the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka, eight persons were authorized together in the formal act of appointing officials (*ubbāhika-sammuti*).

"Road" (*magga*) refers to a long hall built along a road. "Lotus pond" (*pokkharaṇī*) refers to a hall built at a lotus pond for those bathing. "At the foot of a tree," etc. [refers to similar structures].
The lodgings were covered and secured with doors. "Having disentangled" means having separated them, that is, having made them distinct from one another.
"In the dwellings" means in the lodgings. "Having placed therein" refers here to the placing of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gift arising from those who reside there.
"Should enter" means that other monks, having stayed in that large monastery complex (*mahālābha*) and performed the duties at the shrine (*cetiya*), [should enter].
The intention is that the gain should be accepted.
"He relinquishes the requisite" means he does not consent to the robe-requisite. "This too" refers even to that requisite which has been relinquished.
"Having bound it, it should be taken" means: "Having stayed under this tree or in this pavilion, and having performed the duties at the cetiya..."
Having thus bound [the mind] with the thought, "Take it," it should be taken up. One who moves about with thoughts that have arisen such as, "Where shall I dwell?
Where will there be comfort for one dwelling there? Or where will there be the necessary conditions? is called a "thought-wanderer" (*vitakkacārika*).
Because five lamps each are required for the purpose of discerning dangers in forest dwellings, [it is said: "five, five lamps..."
"It should be expelled," it is said.
"Vattanti" means the agreed-upon duty (*katikavatta*). "In all three ways" means in the three ways of study (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and penetration (*paṭivedha*).
"Having cleared [them], let them go forth" means: having examined those capable sons of good family regarding their conduct, let them go forth. This concludes the discussion on the ten grounds.

Namely: talk on fewness of wishes, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Controversial speech is that which leads to dispute. "Not letting go of the four protections" refers to the recollection of the Buddha and loving-kindness (*mettā*).

"Without neglecting these four protections—namely, the meditation on the foul (asubha) and the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati)—the rule regarding the use of tooth-sticks (dantakaṭṭha) should be explained.

Herein, regarding the rule for using tooth-sticks: when one enters the midst of the Saṅgha daily, he should place the tooth-sticks brought by the novices (sāmaṇera) and others into the tooth-stick box for the monks to use as they please.
Regarding tooth-sticks, one should take only a single tooth-stick each day. However, for one who does not go out every day—
such as one staying in a meditation hall who appears at a Dhamma discourse or at the Uposatha assembly— he should observe the proper measure,
set aside four or five tooth-sticks in his own dwelling place, and then consume them.
When those have been consumed, if there are still many tooth-sticks remaining in the storeroom, they should be brought back and chewed again.

However, if one brings them without checking the quantity and the store is exhausted even before those previously taken have been finished, then some elders might say, "Let those who took them bring them back," while others might say, "Let them eat them; the novices will bring more."
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding disputes, one should observe the proper measure. However, there is no fault in taking [some food];
even while traveling on the road, one may go after placing one or two portions into a bag.
The conduct regarding the alms-round will be explained in the section on the rules of conduct (*Vattakkhandhaka*) within the rules for those who wander for alms (*Piṇḍacārikavatta*).
"At the place where he has arrived" means at the place where the incoming bhikkhu has arrived according to the length of his rains-residence.
It is said that because their rains-residence is broken, "even if they consent, they are not the owners of the *vassāvāsika* (rains-belonging)";

and it is also said that because the agreement was made first, even if the resident bhikkhus are exhausted [by the work], they are not permitted to refuse to give. "Established as if by hire" means established as if having performed labor for hire.
Regarding "sought after": it is said with reference to what was obtained by performing an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*) for the Saṅgha.
Regarding "obtained by way of requisites": this is said with reference to what was obtained from the donors by way of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) requisites, because of the statement:
"In this case, monks, if a monk who has completed the rains retreat disrobes, this [property] belongs to the Saṅgha alone."
“It belongs to the Saṅgha in the place where [the robe] has been taken,” so it is said. “To the person” means to the person who gives.
“The excellent portion for the novice” is said because he receives the first portion.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the assigner of lodgings is finished.
The Commentary on the Story of Upananda 319.
Regarding the phrase, "The lodging which was taken by you there... it is released here":
that lodging which was taken by you later at that village residence is, for you, released as soon as you take the first lodging here in Sāvatthī.

It is relinquished. Here, when one says, "Now I... [etc. ...there too it is relinquished," by saying, "Friends, I now relinquish the lodging I have taken in this village residence," the lodging taken in that village residence is relinquished. 320.
A long seat (dīghāsana) is anything other than a bed or a chair that is capable of providing comfortable seating for one person.
*Hatthinakha* means "the claw of an elephant. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"The 'claw' of a palace refers to its lower boundary, and that is fixed upon the frontal globes (*kumbha*) of the elephants. They may be used according to the manner of householders' mats;
this means they may be enjoyed according to the manner of householders' mats, for one is permitted to sit only on those [seats] which have been spread out and offered by them.
Neither spread by oneself nor caused to be spread by others.
Commentary on the Discussion of Non-Relinquishable Objects (Avissajjiyavatthu-kathāvaṇṇanā) 321:
*Arañjara* means a large bucket that holds much water. It is called *arañjara* because it is unable to hold [all] the water. "Round bucket" (*vaṭṭacāṭi*).
"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is said: 'Having become as if [two], it was made with a slightly long mouth and a demarcation shown in the middle.
'One with five stainless eyes' means one who has five eyes by way of the flesh-eye, the divine eye, the Dhamma-eye, the Buddha-eye, and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).
Regarding the phrase 'by a stable thing, a stable thing; by a heavy article, a heavy article,' here, among the five categories, the first two..."
The first [offense] is fixed; the latter three should be understood as "valuable goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*). "Having made it known" means having made it known to the Saṅgha of monks.
"Acceptable wooden beds" is said with reference to what has been given saying, "We give this to the Saṅgha.
However, if they say, "We give this to the monastery," it is permissible to accept even unacceptable beds made of gold, silver, or other such materials.
By the phrase "not only... but it is permissible to exchange," he shows that it is permissible to exchange both permanent goods for permanent goods and impermanent goods for impermanent goods.
Indeed, it is not permissible to exchange a permanent good for an impermanent good alone. Regarding the expression "whether unallowable or valuable, or allowable":
here, "unallowable" refers to things such as beds made of gold, as well as unallowable couches and pillows.
"Expensive" refers to items such as beds made of ivory and so forth, as well as allowable coverings such as woolen rugs and the like.
"It is not permitted to carry it about" means that it is not allowed to take possession of it and carry it around as if it were one's own property.

By the statement, "It should be used only through the agency of a householder," it is implied that if monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others store it away and then return it, it is permissible to use it.
It is shown [in this way]. “*Paṇṇasūci* means a writing stylus,” so it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*.
“*Aḍḍhabāhu* means from the elbow up to the shoulder joint,” so it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipadas*.

Some also say that *aḍḍhabāhu* means a span and four finger-breadths (*vidatthicaturaṅgula*). “*Tatthajātakā* means grown on land belonging to the Saṅgha. “The size of a needle-shaft eight finger-breadths long,” so it is said.
In length it is about eight finger-breadths, and in circumference it is about the size of a leaf-needle handle.
Because *muñja* grass and *pabbaja* grass are mentioned separately in the text, it is said: "except for *muñja* and *pabbaja*.
"Measuring eight finger-breadths" means measuring eight finger-breadths in length. A "rubbing-board" (*ghattanaphalaka*) is that upon which one places the dyed robe and rubs it with the hand.

They say that the "stirring mallet" (*ghaṭṭanamuggara*) is made for the purpose of stirring [the dye] with the wind and so forth. "Ambaṇa" refers to a water vessel made of wooden planks resembling a lotus pond.
"Dye-tub" (*rajanadoṇī*) is where they place the boiled dye before setting it aside.

"It is permissible to make a floor-covering" is said with reference to an unallowable skin. By the phrase "it falls under the category of bedspreads" (*paccattharaṇagatika*), [it is implied that this applies to] beds and chairs as well.
This indicates that it is appropriate to spread [it out]. Some say that even coverings such as woolen blankets (*pāvāra*) are "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*); others say they are not;
this should be determined after investigation. "Fist-leaf" (*muṭṭhipaṇṇa*) is said with reference to palm leaves (*tālapaṇṇa*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Assigning Building Work.
323. "Having persuaded someone, he will have it made": the owner himself, having persuaded some bhikkhu, will have it made.
"He is not permitted to refuse during the season": he is not permitted to refuse other bhikkhus who arrive during the winter or summer seasons.
"A third part" means a one-third portion. "If he wishes to give to his co-residents": if he so desires.
The meaning is that he does not wish to give the storage place for the Saṅgha’s requisites or the dwelling place for the novices, but desires to give it only to his own *saddhivihārika*s.
"For this is permitted to be given to the *saddhivihārika*s" means that he is permitted to give this third part or half-share. "In a place where it has not been done" means from the lodging.
"Outside" means in a place where a heap (of refuse) and so forth has not been made. "Outside the wall" means beyond the wall.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of Using [Foot-wipers] Elsewhere (324):
"A wheel-shaped [wiper]" refers to something made suitable for wiping the feet by wrapping it with woolen cloth (*kambala*) and other materials, shaped like a wheel.
“Ground that has been decorated” means ground made with fine clay and colored black or otherwise. “Furniture” refers to beds, chairs, and so forth.
“It is permissible to use it in the same way” means it is permissible to use it in the manner already enjoyed by other resident monks.
“If the residents place [the items] on ground that was not intended for such use as a matter of course, there is no offense for them either.”

This is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. Regarding the phrase "the door as well," etc.: even doors, windows, and so forth that have not been treated with plaster (*aparikammakata*) must not be leaned against.
Regarding the phrase "in the hair": when the hair is being touched.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion concerning the authorization for communal meals and other such matters.
325. Regarding the phrase "having attained the designation ‘uddesabhatta’ and ‘nimantana’”: here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (or "and so forth").
Thus, the meaning here is: "having attained the designations such as ‘uddesabhatta,’ ‘nimantana,’ and so on.
"Including that as well" means including even that *saṅghabhatta* (meal for the Saṅgha) in order to dispel the scruples of the bhikkhus in the future.
Commentary on the Discussion of Designated Alms-food (*Uddesabhattakathāvaṇṇanā*):
"At the door of his own monastery" refers to the vicinity of the gatehouse of the monastery.
"In the dining hall" means in the dining hall that serves as the place for designating the alms-food. Having said, "But it has been given," [it shows] how that donor gives.
To show that procedure, he said, “Venerable sir, from the Saṅgha,” and so forth. “In the interior of a house” means inside a dwelling.
Regarding “those who have come within the precincts”: here, the area within twelve cubits of the village gate, the street, or the crossroads is called the precincts.
To show the specific distinctions found within the precincts of a house, he said, “And herein, the precincts of a house,” and so forth. “A single passage” means...
It should be distributed through a single door. "In various dwellings" means in the dwellings of various families.
He said, "A person who is modest, amiable, and wise should be desired," meaning that such a person, having avoided going on wrong paths and having investigated thoroughly, will give the instruction.
The terms "even though he is sitting" and "even though he is sleeping" are used in a sense of disregard (the genitive case used for the locative). "The requisite of the three robes."

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points): "Just as one who receives a bowl of water, if another person, without receiving a meal by invitation (*uddesabhatta*), should receive various kinds of requisites such as robes and so forth, they belong to that [other] person alone.

It is called a "released messenger" (*vissaṭṭhadūta*) because it has been dispatched to bring whatever [requisites] one desires after stating anything according to one's own preference. "Whatever he desires" refers to requests such as, "Give me a bowl for invitations," and so forth.
They say whatever they wish. Regarding "similar to the question" (*pucchāsabhāgena*), it means resembling the question.
Having stated, "There is one called the *kūṭaṭṭhitikā*," he spoke the words beginning with "or for a king" in order to explain that very *ṭhitikā*.
Because they must be taken separately as a *ṭhitikā*, unmixed with other portions of the recitation (*uddesabhatta*), they are called "single-portion meals" (*ekacārikabhattāni*).
It has been said. "They take by theft" means that the bowl-carriers take them. "There is guilt" means there is guilt for the one who ordered it.
"They go thinking, 'It is permissible to do what people say'" means that they go when told by that bhikkhu, "It is permissible to do what people say.
"An unallotted portion" means a portion for newcomers. "The entire Saṅgha..."

Regarding the statement "let [the Saṅgha] consume it," the *Gaṇṭhipada* states: "In this case, even if one first says, 'Give all the bowls belonging to the Saṅgha,' but subsequently does not say, 'Let the entire Saṅgha consume it,' they should nevertheless consume them after having divided them.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding meals by invitation (*nimantanabhattakathā*).
An invitation belonging to the Saṅgha is one given by saying, “Please take food for so many bhikkhus,” without specifying, “Designate so many bhikkhus from the Saṅgha.

It is permissible even for alms-collectors because it is stated in the context of the alms-round. “In order” means according to the order in which they were received. “Having interrupted” means [saying], “Take food.”
“Without taking a mouthful. For this very reason it says, “by one who does not speak while eating. “By way of a morsel” means by way of each individual lump.

And this method applies only to an invitation meal (*nimantana*), not to a meal given by a formal announcement (*uddesabhatta*). For in that case, only a quantity sufficient for one person should be distributed;
therefore, in a meal given by announcement, there is no such thing as a fixed measure of a morsel. “It remains” means it stays. “One time” means...
"Insofar as the monks reside in that residence, all of them receive [the portion]"—this is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary).
However, the intended meaning here is as follows: "once" (*ekavāra*) is not said with reference to a single day; rather, it refers to all those monks who reside in that residence.
It means that once the monks have been selected on one day, they are not excluded on another day, for as long as it is "once."
"All the bhikkhus have been fed" means that as soon as those who know [the number] have been accounted for, one should depart taking them with one.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion of *salākabhatta*:
"Having tied it up" means having written it down. "Having given by means of compulsion" means having caused even one who is unwilling to accept it through compulsion.
“By way of a single house” means by way of a single enclosure wall. “Having assigned” means having said, “It falls to you and you.
A village that is to be received by turn is a *vāragāma*; even if it is withheld because of its distance, it is still a village to be received by turn.

Those appointed to the turn for the monastery are *vihāravārikā*, those who protect the monastery by turn. “Change of state” means a change in one’s confidence (*pasāda*). “They become merely a counter-action” means...
There are extra gains to be given by the Saṅgha for the purpose of protecting the monastery. At the time when they are received by the junior member of the Saṅgha—
meaning on each day, two or three meals for those traveling alone are brought to him according to that same procedure—
at the time when they are received by the junior member of the Saṅgha, they are to be brought before whoever is present.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points): “If the majority of the monks have gone outside the boundary, the [portion] should be assigned to anyone present;
because they are of like status (*sabhāgattā*), what is received by one belongs to all.
If even that person is absent, it should be given after having assigned it to oneself. *Rasasalākā* means a stick of sugarcane juice.
"Even non-material voting sticks (*salākā*) from the Saṅgha, as well as cooked rice kept in a monastery,
are indeed permissible," because this was stated in the *Visuddhimagga* as a general rule, and because it was not specified that "it should be accepted when taken in this way,

but it should not be accepted when taken in that way," even though voting sticks for medicine and so forth are permissible for alms-collectors (*piṇḍapātika*) as well, since they are taken by means of a voting stick.

However, the underlying intention regarding the phrase "it must not be accepted" should be investigated. For if it were the case that a voting stick (salākā) for medicine and so forth, when taken as a voting stick, could not be accepted, then [the Buddha] would not have stated, "A non-material voting stick from the Saṅgha is indeed permissible.

This is because of such statements as, "An extra gain consists of a meal for the Saṅgha, a designated meal," and so on; and because one might take a voting stick with the thought, "I am refusing an extra gain."

Only food is prohibited from being accepted, not medicine. For it is said that the fourteen types of meals, such as *saṅghabhatta* (meals for the Saṅgha), are precisely what must not be consented to by him;
or else, according to the opinion of the Khandhaka reciters, it should be understood that this is stated here in this manner.
