*Aggabhikkhā* means alms to be given at the head [of the line]. *Laddhā vā aladdhā vā* means whether having received them or not having received them.

Because it is possible that even a very small amount of the best alms-food might arise from what has been set aside, it is said that one may take more on the following day even after having already received some.
For in the phrase "merely the best alms-food" (*aggabhikkhāmatta*), the word *matta* excludes a large quantity.
Regarding "ticket-food" (*salākabhatta*), he says "in the monastery" because it is designated within the monastery itself and is given with reference specifically to the monastery.
“...but it has been removed,” and so forth. Regarding that: “in the assembly hall” means in the assembly hall of that village.

“Having brought it to the monastery, it should be distributed” means that after saying this, the meal given on that day should be brought to the monastery itself and distributed by means of a standing distribution.
“There” means in that direction. “Having taken that” means having taken that voting-ticket (*salāka*) for the village in turn. “By him” means—
As for the one who gave his own bowl or voting-ticket to a traveler: "While he has not yet departed, his ticket must be taken"—
since the ticket reaches only one who is still within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*), therefore,
while that traveler has not yet crossed the boundary of the precinct, the bowl-ticket for that traveler must be obtained by bringing it to oneself.
Regarding the phrase "on the following day," if one asks how the status of those monks as having arrived or not yet arrived is to be understood:
it is because the monks who have come from here and there assemble in that village at the hall for seating; therefore, their status as having arrived or not yet arrived can be known.
"In our alms-village" means in the village of those who provide the *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals). "They come to eat" means...
Thinking, “The Great Elder has remained alone in the monastery; surely he must have taken all the voting sticks for himself,” they come [to check].
Regarding the explanation of the discussion on the fortnightly meal (*pakkhika-bhatta*) and so forth:
a meal to be given on the four specifically marked days of the fortnight is called *pakkhika*. As for the phrase “on the specifically marked [days]”: here—
*Abhi* is merely a prefix; its meaning is simply "in relation to" (*lakkhaṇīyesu*). This means:

in regard to those things that are to be marked, observed, or characterized for the purpose of undertaking the Uposatha, listening to the Dhamma, making offerings, showing respect, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "on the next day" (*sve pakkho*):

it is said because there is no fixed rule for the *pakkhika* (fortnightly) meal, such as "the *pakkhika* meal should not be accepted today. [The thought was: "On the next day, in our house, there will be coarse food..."
They write in the manuscripts, “it will be [the meal]”; however, it should be read as “pakkhabhattaṃ bhavissati” (it will be the fortnightly meal).
*Uposathika* is the meal to be given on the Uposatha day. *Nibandhāpitaṃ* means it has been designated as belonging to “such-and-such monastery.
*Gāhetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ* means that those residing in that dwelling place should receive it according to their standing and then eat.
“They offer rice and so forth…” … “…it is allowable” means it is allowable because it is an offering brought [to the monastery].

“Because it was accepted in that manner” means because it was accepted under the name of alms-food (*bhikkhā*). “Given after filling and covering the bowl” means given with the words, “We give a ball of food (*guḷakabhatta*)”;
even in the case of a lump of sugar, it should be understood here as being the size of a ripe palm fruit.
The rest here is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka is finished.
7. The Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Ordination of Cchāsaka (Chasakyapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā) 330.

In the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka, regarding the passage beginning with "at Anupiyā," where one should have said "Anupiyā nāma" (named Anupiyā), the vowel *ā* was shortened and the nasal augment (*anunāsika*) was added, resulting in the expression "Anupiyaṃ nāma. "Of the Mallas" means of the Malla kings.
"He does not descend from the palace below" means he does not descend from the upper palace to the lower floor; alternatively, they read "the lower palace" (*heṭṭhāpāsāda*).
"Or Anuruddha might go forth" is how it should be construed. "The work appropriate for household life" refers to the duties suitable for a householder.
"Water should be brought in" means water should be fetched. "It should be led out" means the water that has been fetched [should be disposed of].
"It must be cleared out. "It must be weeded" means that the grasses growing here and there must be pulled up and removed.
"It must be harvested" means it must be harvested when it has reached full maturity. "It must be threshed" means the threshing floor must be cleared.
"It must be made straight" means it must be formed into a heap. "The straw must be removed" means the straw must be taken away.
“Bhusikā should be removed” means that the stalks known as *bhusa* (chaff), which have been cut at the tips of the cows’ hooves, should be cleared away.
“It should be winnowed” means that after winnowing it in the wind, the straw should be removed. “It should be brought in” means it should be carried into the inner storehouse.
“Not work” means not tasks. “For the sake of household life” is an instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative.
The prefix *upa-* in the word *upajānāhi* is used merely as a preverb. Therefore, he said, "Know the purpose of the household life.
And here, the meaning of *jānāhi* should be understood as "practice" (*paṭipajja*). *Akāmakā* means "not desiring. 331–332. *Yaṃ na nivatto*:
because he has not turned back. *Suññāgāragato*: "having gone to an empty place," excluding both the village and its precincts.

"Whatever remains is the forest" (Pārā. 92). Thus, excluding the forest and the foot of a tree, any other dwelling place suitable for one gone forth—such as mountain caves and the like—is intended here by the term "empty hut" (*suññāgāra*) because it is free from the crowding of people.
Alternatively, any secluded dwelling whatsoever is called an "empty hut" because it is devoid of sounds, which are the thorns to meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
It should be understood that he had entered that empty dwelling. "Frequently" means repeatedly. "He uttered an inspired utterance" (udānaṃ udānesi):

for that venerable one, whether he had gone to his daytime rest in the forest or had gone to stay there at night, he spent the time for the most part in the bliss of the attainment of fruition and the bliss of the attainment of cessation;
therefore, with reference to that bliss previously experienced by himself—

Having come to loathe the pleasure of sovereignty—which is fraught with fear and feverish distress—he utters an outpouring of rapture born of knowledge accompanied by gladness, exclaiming, “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!

Then those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One; those many bhikkhus, established in a nature inclined toward uplifting others, spoke thus to the Blessed One with the intention of supporting him, and not out of reproach.

"Without doubt" means without uncertainty; the meaning is "certainly. It is said that those monks were worldlings who, not understanding the inspired utterance (udāna) with respect to that venerable one’s bliss of seclusion, spoke thus. "Recalling" means recollecting with a sense of longing.
"A certain one" refers to a single monk whose name and clan were not well-known. "Addressed" means he commanded him, desiring to make those monks understand.
In this way, the meaning of *vacanasampaṭiggahe* (acceptance of the words) is "well said" (*sādhu*). Regarding the phrase *evaṃ bhante*: here the word *evaṃ* (thus) is used in the sense of assent.
Just as those monks say, "He frequently uttered this exclamation: 'O what happiness!
O what happiness!'," he thus acknowledges his own exclamation, saying, "It was exactly so, it was just like that. But why did the Blessed One ask, "But what, Bhaddiya"? [The answer follows:]...
He asks: "Does his mind not know? It is not that it does not know; rather, he asks in order to make those bhikkhus understand by having him state the matter himself.
For this has been said: "The Tathāgatas ask even though they know, and they do not ask even though they know," and so forth.
*Atthavasaṃ* means the reason.

"Inside the inner palace" (*antopi antepure*) means within the royal residence, which serves as the place for the movement of the women's quarters (*itthāgāra*), where the king performs his bathing, eating, sleeping, and other such activities.
"Guarded well" (*rakkhā susaṃvihitā*) means that protection has been thoroughly and completely arranged by guards and other men.
"Outside the inner palace" (*bahipi antepure*) refers to places outside the inner palace, such as the locations of the courts of justice and so forth.

"In the royal palace. Being thus protected and guarded means: being thus protected and guarded for my own sake—out of fearlessness and for the sake of dwelling in comfort—in many hundreds of places, both inside and outside the royal palace, the capital city, and the kingdom, by means of well-arranged defenses, enclosures, and guards.
The words "frightened" (*bhīto*) and so forth are synonyms for one another.
Alternatively, "afraid" (*bhīto*) means fearing other kings. "Agitated" (*ubbiggo*) means shaken by the surge of fear arising from disturbances occurring even within one's own kingdom.

"Suspicious" (*ussaṅkī*) refers to the suspicion that arises when various duties and obligations are neglected, due to a state of mistrust everywhere based on the saying: "A king must indeed always remain vigilant."
And as he was moving higher and higher, he was terrified (*utrāsī*);

that is, he was struck with such terror (*tāsa*)—capable of even causing a trembling of the body—that he thought, "Even while those who dwell near me do not know, some misfortune might perhaps happen to me.
They also read it as *utrasto*. "I dwell" (*viharāmi*) means: having become thus, I dwell.
"Etarahī" means now, from the time of his going forth. "Eko" means alone; by this, he shows the state of having withdrawn the body.
The meaning of the words beginning with "abhīto" should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated [in the previous section].

Because of the absence of the grasping that takes fear and so forth as its sign, and the absence of the thicket of defilements that has those signs as its cause, he is "fearless" and so on; by this, he shows the seclusion of the mind.

"Free from anxiety" (*appossukka*) means being without concern for the protection of the body. "With hair standing on end" (*pannaloma*) means having the hair not bristling due to the absence of that trepidation which causes the hair to stand on end.

By these two phrases, he demonstrates a state of living at ease (*serivihāra*). "Living on what is given by others" (*paradattavutta*) means subsisting on robes and so forth provided by others. By this, through the manner of illustrating the total absence of attachment, he shows the lack of every single cause of fear.
He shows this by means of the phrase "with a mind become like that of a deer. This refers to a mind born of dwelling in confidence, like that of a deer.
For a deer living in a forest on a path frequented by non-human beings dwells, stands, sits, and lies down in confidence, and it departs wherever it wishes with its course unimpeded;
thus he shows: "In this way, I too dwell. For this was said by the Paccekasambuddha:
"Just as a deer in the forest, unbound,
goes wherever it pleases for its grazing,
so does a wise man, looking toward freedom."
“One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Venerable sir, it is for this purpose—that is, for the sake of this supreme bliss of seclusion and the bliss of the attainment of fruition which I now possess—that, seeing this very reason, I exclaim, “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!”

"Having understood this matter"—that is, having understood in every aspect this matter known as the bliss of seclusion, which transcends the domain of ordinary worldlings (puthujjana)—he uttered this *udāna*. "This *udāna*" refers to that utterance which illuminates the power of the disappearance of fear and sorrow along with their causes.
"In whom there is no anger from within"—in whom, that noble person (*ariyapuggala*), there is no anger from within, in his own mind...

Because they cause turbidity of the mind, lust and the other [defilements] are indeed "corruptions of the mind" (*cittappakopa*). Due to the various causes such as the bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), there are many types of these corruptions of hatred (*dosa*).
However, because they have been abandoned by the Path, they do not exist; they are not found.

For although this word *antara* is seen in the sense of "cause" in such phrases as "What is the difference between you and the bed?", it is also seen in such phrases as "during the season of snowfall in the *antaraṭṭhaka*."
In such passages as “in the middle,” it refers to an interval—as in “between the Jeta Grove and Sāvatthī”; in such passages as “fear born from within,” it refers to the mind;
here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to the mind. For this very reason, he said: “In whose mind there is no anger.
Regarding the word *abhava*, he states the reason for its equivalence in meaning with the word *vibhava*: “*Vibhava* and *abhava*...”
“In meaning, it is one. Since the word *iti* expresses a manner, he said: “Thus, in many ways, there is becoming and non-becoming.
“Transcended” (*vītivatto*) means having gone beyond. And here, the phrase “of whom” (*yassā*) should be construed by changing the case-ending as “he who has transcended” (*yo vītivatto*).
“That [state] is free from fear” (*taṃ vigatabhayaṃ*): that which is of such a nature, endowed with the aforementioned qualities, belongs to one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
It is "free from fear" because of the absence of mental agitation and because of the transcendence of both existence and non-existence, thereby removing the cause of fear.
It is "happy" through the bliss of seclusion and the bliss of the supreme fruit; it is "sorrowless" precisely because it is free from fear.

Regarding the phrase "the gods do not come to see [it]," this means that with the exception of those who have attained the Path, all gods born in the realms of rebirth—even if they were to strive—cannot perceive the movements of the mind.
They do not experience, do not attain, and are not able to see him for the sake of seeing, let alone human beings.
For even those in training (*sekkhā*), like worldlings (*puthujjana*), do not know the movement of the mind of an Arahant.
"The sight of him is difficult even for the gods to obtain"—here too, by way of perceiving the movement of his mind, the sight of him is difficult to obtain and unattainable even by the gods.

The meaning should be understood as: "It is not possible to reach that vision. Here, the word *du-* has the sense of "non-existence" (*abhāva*), as in words such as *duppañño* ("one of poor wisdom"). 333.
*Bhattābhihāro* means food that is to be brought forward. To show its measure, [the text says] "and five..."
"Of hundreds of *thālipāka* offerings," it is said. In that context, one *thālipāka* provides food for ten men. Regarding the phrase "by gain, honor, and renown":
here, "gain" (*lābha*) refers to the acquisition of the four requisites. "Honor" (*sakkāra*) is the acquisition of those very things when they have been well-prepared and well-arranged.
"Renown" (*siloka*) is the sound of praise. "The mind-made body" (*manomayaṃ kāyaṃ*) is that which is produced by means of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
The Brahma-body. "Reborn" means having approached [that state]. "Acquisition of a personal existence" means the acquisition of a body. "Two or three Magadhan village-fields":
here, a Magadhan village-field may be small, medium, or large. A small village-field is forty ox-lengths from this side and forty from that side.
"Usabhāni" means one *gāvuta*. "Majjhimaṃ" means half a *yojana*, being one *gāvuta* from here and one *gāvuta* from there.
"Mahantaṃ" means three *gāvutas*, being one and a half *gāvutas* from here and one and a half *gāvutas* from there.
Among these, his personal domain (*attabhāva*) consists of three small village territories, or two village territories consisting of both small and medium sizes.
"His body is four *gāvutas* long. 'I shall carry it,' means I shall attend to it, I shall protect it. 'Guard this' means you must guard it.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Teachers (Pañcasatthuka-kathā-vaṇṇanā): 334. "Teachers" (*satthāro*) means teachers of a group. "There would not be for him" (*nāssassa*) means it would not exist for him. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to that teacher.
“With that” means with what is disagreeable. “I would address him” means I would speak to him. “He honors” means he shows us respect.
Therefore it says “he honors,” or alternatively, the meaning is that he is honored by others.
335. “They might break bile into the nose” means they might put ox-bile or fish-bile into the nostrils.
"Parābhavāya" means for decline, for loss, for destruction. "Assatarī" refers to a mule, born from a female horse (*vaḷavā*) by a donkey;
they mate her with a horse, but when she has conceived and the time to give birth arrives, she is unable to deliver.
She stands striking the ground with her hooves, and then, having bound her four feet to four stakes—
They tear open the womb and pull out the fetus, and she dies right there. Therefore it is said: "She conceives a fetus for her own destruction.
339. *Potthanika* means a small knife, which is also called a *kharanta*.
[End of] The Commentary on the Discourse on the Sending of Nāḷāgiri.
342. "O elephant, do not approach the Nāga," he says: O elephant, do not approach the Buddha-Nāga with a murderous intent.
It is called "suffering" (dukkha) because it is the cause of suffering. To explain how that is suffering, he says, "For [the killing] of one struck by a Nāga," and so forth.
By rejecting a happy rebirth for one who has been struck by a Nāga, he shows that the killing of a Buddha-Nāga is the cause of suffering in an unhappy rebirth.
*Itoti*: from this birth. *Yatoti*: because. *Itoparaṃ yatoti*: or rather, the meaning is "while going beyond this.
*Madoti*: intoxication with pride (*mānamada*). *Pamādoti*: a state of negligence (*pamattabhāva*). *Paṭikuṭitoti*: contracted or shriveled. *Alakkhikoti*: shameless (*ahirika*).
*Yatra hi nāmāti*: indeed, he who... (or "that which is called").
Commentary on the Discourse Requesting the Five Conditions: 343.
"Food for three" means food that is to be eaten by three; the meaning is: "We shall prescribe [the rule] so that one may eat after receiving from three together.
"Kokālika," etc., refers to the four leaders of the factions who were partisans of Devadatta.

The names [of the aeons]. "Ayu-kappāni" (lifespan-aeons) refers to a period of time designated as an *antarakappa* (intermediate aeon), which constitutes one part out of eighty parts of a single *mahākappa* (great aeon).

"He said this to the Venerable Ānanda": having completed all the preliminary stages for the schism of the Saṅgha, Devadatta thought, "Today alone I shall perform the Uposatha and the formal acts of the Saṅgha independently," and thus he spoke these words beginning with "From this day forward."
He said: "Therein, 'apart from the Blessed One' means without the Blessed One, that is, without making that Teacher [one's authority].

'Apart from the community of monks, I shall perform the Uposatha and the formal acts of the community' means: apart from the community of monks who carry out the Blessed One’s instructions, together with those monks who follow me individually, I shall perform the Uposatha and the formal acts of the community."
"And I shall do so. "From this day forward, Bhante, Devadatta will split the Saṅgha"—this was said because Devadatta had prepared all those who cause schism;
thinking, "Devadatta will certainly split the Saṅgha today," he spoke thus.
"He will split" means he will divide into two parts.

"Having understood this matter" means: having understood in all its aspects that act of schism in the Saṅgha being brought about by Devadatta—which leads to rebirth in the great Avīci hell, lasts for an eon, and is incurable.
"This inspired utterance" refers to the fact that, among the wholesome and unwholesome, the practice of good persons and bad persons respectively is easy; however, it is not [easy] for them...
Regarding "among the unwholesome and the wholesome," he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) to clarify its meaning.
In that context, one who accomplishes what is beneficial for oneself and others is called "good" (*sādhu*); thus, a "good person" is one who has entered upon the right practice.
By such a good person—whether a disciple such as Sāriputta and others, a *paccekabuddha*, a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*), or anyone else—[the wholesome is accomplished].
"Good by the worldling is good": that which is beautiful, auspicious, and brings benefit and happiness to oneself and others is easy to perform;
it can be done with ease. "Good by the evil one is difficult": however, that same thing characterized as 'good' is difficult for an evil person such as Devadatta to do;
the meaning is that he is not able to perform it. "Evil by the evil one..."
"Evil is easy for oneself and others": evil, which brings harm to oneself and others, is "easy" (*sukara*)—meaning it can be performed with ease—by the person of evil as previously described.
"But evil is difficult for the Noble Ones": however, for the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others, that evil is "difficult" (*dukkara*), meaning hard to accomplish;
for it is precisely the destruction of the bridge [to rebirth] that characterizes them in that regard. This is what he demonstrates.
Commentary on the Discourse on Schism in the Saṅgha (Saṅghabhedakathāvaṇṇanā) 345.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with “Then the Venerable Sāriputta [performed] the miracle of direct address, the miracle of instruction,” etc.:

the miracle of direct address (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) is speaking after having known the mind of another; and the constant teaching of the Dhamma by both disciples and Buddhas is the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).

The miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*) and the miracle of supernormal power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*). Among these, the miracle of instruction together with the miracle of supernormal power was the habitual practice of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna;

the miracle of instruction together with the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) was that of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). Therefore it was said: "The Venerable Sāriputta, by means of the miracle of mind-reading and the miracle of instruction..."

“...the bhikkhus exhorted them with a discourse on the Dhamma,” and so forth. For at that time, among the two chief disciples, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) taught the Dhamma after knowing the mental disposition of those bhikkhus, while the Elder Mahāmoggallāna taught the Dhamma after displaying his supernormal powers;
and in this passage of the Canon, the acquisition of the Eye of Dhamma occurred through the teaching of both elders.

[The story] has been related. However, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas speak thus: "When the two chief disciples had been sent by the Blessed One, the Dhammasenāpati, having understood the movement of their minds, taught the Dhamma.

Upon hearing the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, five hundred bhikkhus were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then the Elder Mahāmoggallāna displayed his supernormal transformations for them..."
He taught the Dhamma; having heard it, they all became established in the fruit of arahantship.
"He raised Devadatta up" means that he struck him in the middle of the chest with his knee and raised him up.
"Sarasī" means a lake. "Well-washed" means thoroughly washed; the meaning is that it was made perfectly clean.
"Having chewed well" means having thoroughly masticated. "Transforming the earth" refers to one who scratches the earth with his tusks.
"Eating lotus roots in the rivers" should be connected [to the previous phrase]. Here, "river" is intended to mean a great lake.
"Tending" means protecting the herd of elephants. "Like a young elephant" means like a calf-elephant. "Imitating me" means following my example.
347. *Dūteyya* means the work of a messenger. *Gantumarahati* means he is worthy to go; that is, he is worthy to carry and bear the message designated as *dūteyya*.
*Sotā* means one who hears whatever message they give him. *Sāveta* means having learned it, one who reports back, saying, "This is exactly what you said.
*Uggahetā* means one who has grasped it well, having mastered it thoroughly. *Dhāretā* means... [one who retains it].
"Having well-considered," means having reflected upon it. "One who understands" means one who has understood its meaning for oneself.
"One who makes understood" means one who causes another to understand. "Of what is appropriate and inappropriate" means:

being skilled in discerning "this is appropriate" and "this is inappropriate," and being expert regarding what is accepted and what is not accepted, one proclaims the teaching after observing what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
"It does not tremble" means it does not quiver, does not shake. "One who speaks harshly" means one endowed with abusive speech.
"When asked" means asked for the purpose of a formal admission. 348.
Regarding the passage beginning "Bhikkhus, by eight unrighteous qualities," etc.: "unrighteous qualities" (asaddhammehi) means by the qualities of the wicked, by those that are non-existent.
Or by means of unwholesome states (*asobhana-dhamma*). "Overcome" (*abhibhūta*) means overwhelmed. "One whose mind is consumed" (*pariyādinnacitta*) means one whose mind is exhausted;

that is, one whose wholesome mind has been brought to destruction by conduct driven by desire for gain and the like, and by pride, intoxication, and so forth. Alternatively, "one whose mind is consumed" means a mind that is completely seized (*parito ādinnacitta*);
it refers to the opportunity for the arising of a wholesome mind being blocked by the aforementioned categories of unwholesome factors.

The meaning is that his mental continuum has been seized from all sides in such a way that it does not exist [as wholesome]. He is "bound for the states of misery" (*āpāyika*) because he is worthy of being reborn in the realms of misery.
Furthermore, he is "hell-bound" (*nerayika*) because he arises there in the Great Niraya known as Avīci.

He is "one who remains for an eon" (*kappaṭṭha*) because he stays there having fully completed one intermediate eon (*antarakappa*). He is "incurable" (*atekiccha*) because even by the Buddhas he cannot be turned back from the arising in Avīci.
"Beyond cure" (*atekiccha*) means because it cannot be cured; the meaning is that it is not something to be remedied. "By gain" (*lābhena*) means by means of gain acting as a cause.

Alternatively, it refers to pride and so forth caused by gain. For here, some individuals—relying on gain, being of evil desire, overcome by desire, and established in conduct born of desire—resort to various kinds of improper and unsuitable wrong search, thinking, "We shall produce gain."

Having passed away from here, they are reborn in the states of misery. Others, having obtained whatever they might find, fall into negligence by way of pride, arrogance, intoxication, and stinginess on account of that;
having passed away from here, they are reborn in the states of misery, and Devadatta was such a person. Therefore it was said:

"Having seen these qualities" refers to their delight therein, which he expressed thus: "having seen them again and again..."
"The asuras take delight in the great ocean. In this context, "take delight" means they find pleasure;
the meaning is that they dwell there without longing for anything else. "Sloping gradually," and so forth—all these are synonyms for the state of being sloped in successive order.
"Not steep all at once" means it is not a precipice from the very beginning like a great waterfall with a sheer cliff face; rather, it begins from the shore. It is thus: [text continues].
This shows that, having become deep by degrees— starting from one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, a span, a cubit, a fathom, a ratana, a yaṭṭhi, an usabha, half a gāvuta, a gāvuta,
half a yojana, a yojana, and so on— it remains at the foot of Sineru with a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas as it goes further and further down.
"Of stable nature" (*ṭhitadhammo*) means one whose nature is fixed, whose nature is established. "With a corpse" (*kuṇapena*) means with any kind of carcass, such as that of an elephant or a horse.
"He drives away" (*vāheti*) means that, as if grasping it with his hand, he hurls it onto the dry land by means of a wave-like motion. Regarding the Ganges and Yamunā:
at the place where the river flowing from the southern mouth of Lake Anotatta issues forth in five streams, it flows in five ways, being called the Ganges and so forth.
They have reached the ocean. In this context, "river," "stream," and so forth refer to the genus (*gotta*); "Ganges," "Yamunā," and so forth refer to the names (*nāma*).
"Flowing" means those which flow, stream, and go—whether they be great rivers or small streams. "Enter" means they adhere to and flow into it.
"Streams" refers to rain-showers. "Fullness" is the state of being filled. For this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of the great ocean.

It cannot be said, "At this time the rain is light; we shall take our nets and so forth and catch fish and turtles," nor can it be said, "At this time the rain is too heavy; will we find a place to stretch out our backs?
For since the time of the first world-age, the shore has receded until it reached the girdle of Mount Sineru.
The water remains pressed down; from that state, not even a single finger’s breadth of water descends below nor rises above.
"Of one taste" means having an undifferentiated flavor.
"Pearls" refers to the many varieties of pearls, such as small and large, round and long, and so forth. "Jewels" refers to the various kinds such as ruby, sapphire, and so on.
“Mani” is of many kinds. “Veḷuriya” (cat’s-eye) is of many kinds according to its shapes, such as the color of bamboo or the color of the sirīsapuppha flower.

“Saṅkha” (conch) is of many kinds, distinguished by types such as the right-spiraling conch, the kumbha, the kukkhi, and the dhamana. “Sila” (rock crystal) is of many kinds, distinguished by colors such as white or the color of black mung beans.
“Pavāḷa” (coral) is also of many kinds, distinguished by varieties such as small, large, red, or deep red. “Lohitaka” (ruby).
The variety [of gems] is manifold, such as the *padumarāga* (ruby) and others. *Masāragalla* is a *kabara-maṇi* (speckled gem).
Some also call it *cittaphalika*. "Of great beings" means of great creatures. *Timi*, *timiṅgala*, and *timitimiṅgala* are three species of fish.
A *timiṅgala* is one capable of swallowing a *timi*; one capable of swallowing both a *timi* and a *timiṅgala* is a *timitimiṅgala*.
They say: "Nāgas" refers both to those who dwell on the backs of waves and to nāgas residing in celestial palaces (*vimāna*).
This concludes the commentary on the eight wonderful discourses in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
385. "Even so," etc.: although the Teacher [has taught] sixteen, thirty-two, or even more [qualities] in this Dhamma and Vinaya...
He is able to analyze and demonstrate the marvelous and wonderful qualities;
however, by way of providing eight corresponding similes for those [qualities] taken as examples, he analyzes and demonstrates those very eight qualities to be illustrated, saying:
"In this same way, monks, there are eight marvelous and wonderful qualities in this Dhamma and Vinaya. Therein, regarding gradual training...
The three trainings have been undertaken; by way of gradual action, the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) have been undertaken;

by way of gradual practice, the seven contemplations, the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), the thirty-eight classifications of objects, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) have been undertaken.
Full penetration of final knowledge does not come through mere prolixity; it is like a frog leaping across [the water] from the very beginning.

There is no realization of Arahatship without fulfilling the precepts and so forth; rather, the meaning is that one attains Arahatship only after fulfilling virtue, concentration, and wisdom in their proper sequence.
"My disciples" refers to noble persons such as stream-enterers and the rest. "He does not dwell together" means by way of performing the Uposatha ceremony and other such duties.
He does not associate with him. "He casts out" means he removes him. "Far away indeed" means at a great distance.
"Proclaimed by the Tathāgata" means taught, declared, and made manifest by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, among his disciples.

"There is neither deficiency nor fullness in the element of Nibbāna" means that even if Buddhas do not arise for incalculable great aeons, not even a single being is deprived of the opportunity to attain final Nibbāna.
Even then, it cannot be said that "the element of Nibbāna is empty.
Furthermore, during the time of a Buddha, even in a single assembly, incalculable beings attain the Deathless; even then, it cannot be said that "the element of Nibbāna is full.
"The flavor of liberation" means the flavor of being liberated from the defilements. For all the excellence of the Dispensation exists solely for the sake of non-clinging.
The meaning is: "the liberation of the mind from the taints.

As for "jewels," they are called jewels in the sense that they produce delight. For when the foundations of mindfulness and so forth are cultivated, they produce manifold kinds of rapture and gladness even in the prior stage, let alone in the subsequent stage. For this has been said:
"From whatever [aspect] one comprehends The arising and passing away of the aggregates..."
"One who understands that attains rapture and gladness; that is the Deathless.
However, the rapture and gladness caused by worldly jewels do not equal even a fraction of that [rapture]. Moreover:
"It is honored and of great value, incomparable, and difficult to behold;"
That which is enjoyed by beings of incomparable excellence is called a "jewel" (*ratana*).
And if something is called a jewel by virtue of its being honored and so forth, then the true state of being a jewel belongs only to the foundations of mindfulness and the like;
for such is the power of the factors conducive to enlightenment that disciples possess the knowledge of disciple-perfection, and [the same applies to] the Paccekabuddhas.
The knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (individual enlightenment) and the Perfectly Enlightened Ones attain *sammāsambodhi* (perfect enlightenment) because these are the proximate causes.

For the remote cause consists of the necessary conditions such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth. Thus, the status of being a "jewel" (*ratana*) for the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) is preeminent both in the sense of producing delight and in the sense of being honored and esteemed.
Therefore it was said: "In this regard, these are the jewels, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness," and so on.
It is a *paṭṭhāna* (foundation) in the sense of being established by breaking into the object; it is mindfulness itself that is the foundation, thus it is "satipaṭṭhāna.
However, because the object is fourfold—by way of the body and so forth—it is said: "the four foundations of mindfulness.

For, by abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena, one grasps their true nature as foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
And their nature as the contemplation of the body and so forth is analyzed [in detail].
It is called *sammappadhāna* because one strives rightly by means of it, or because it itself strives rightly, or because it is a praiseworthy and beautiful striving;
or else, because it brings about the state of right striving in a person, it is *sammappadhāna*. This is a term for energy (*vīriya*).
This is a designation (*adhivacana*). It is called "the four right endeavors" (*cattāro sammappadhānā*) because it accomplishes four functions:

by way of the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome states that have arisen or have not yet arisen, and by way of the arising and establishing of wholesome states that have not yet arisen or have already arisen.

It is called *iddhi* because it succeeds (*ijjhati*); the meaning is that it is accomplished (*samijjhati*) or brought to fruition (*nipphajjati*). Or else, beings succeed through it; they are successful (*iddhā*) and prosperous (*vuddhā*).
*Iddhi* (success) means that which has reached the highest excellence. In the first sense, *iddhipāda* is "the foot of success," meaning a constituent part of success;
the meaning is a factor of success. In the second sense, it is "the basis for success," meaning the foundation or the means of attainment for success.

For by means of that, one goes to—that is, reaches—success, which consists of successive stages of distinction. And this *iddhipāda* [consists of] the four dominant factors (*adhipatidhamma*), beginning with desire (*chanda*).
Because it arises having placed the foremost in the first place, it is therefore said: "the four bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*).

"The five faculties" (*pañcindriyāni*) refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). Among these, faith is a faculty because, having overcome lack of faith, it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) in the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*).
Having overcome laziness, [energy] exercises lordship in the characteristic of exertion; having overcome negligence...

Wisdom is a faculty because it exercises lordship over the characteristic of establishing by overcoming [distraction], over the characteristic of non-distraction by overcoming distraction, and over the characteristic of seeing by overcoming ignorance.

Those same states should be understood as powers in the sense of being unshakable— because they cannot be overcome by lack of faith and so forth— and in the sense of stability among associated states.
The seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are so called because they are either the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhi*) or the factors for enlightenment.

For this collection of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), when arising at the moment of the supramundane path, serves as the antidote to numerous calamities— such as the foundations of lethargy and agitation, striving, indulgence in sensual pleasure, self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism—
and consists of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Through the harmony of the Dhamma (*dhammasāmaggi*), the noble disciple awakens; he rises from the sleep of the defilements, penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself—thus it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).

The factors of that awakening, which is defined as the harmony of the Dhamma, are the "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*), just like the factors of meditation (*jhānaṅga*) or the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*). And this [harmony] of the aforementioned kind of harmony of the Dhamma...
Because he awakens, the noble disciple is called "Bodhi"; and because they are factors of that Bodhi, they are called "bojjhaṅgas," just as there are "limbs of an army" or "limbs of a chariot.
Therefore, the ancients said: "They are bojjhaṅgas because they are the limbs of the person who awakens.
The meaning of *bojjhaṅga* should also be understood in such ways as: "They are bojjhaṅgas because they conduce to awakening (*bodhāya saṃvattanti*)."

The Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga*): it is "noble" (*ariya*) because it is remote from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it produces the state of a noble one (*ariya-bhāva*), and because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruits (*ariya-phala*). It possesses eight factors such as right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) and so forth;

or rather, it is "eightfold" (*aṭṭhaṅgika*) simply because its factors are eight. It goes along slaying the defilements, or it is sought after (*maggīyati*) by those seeking Nibbāna, or it itself [leads to] Nibbāna.
"It leads (maggati) [to the goal], thus it is the path (magga)"—in this way, the analysis of the meaning of these [terms] such as the foundations of mindfulness should be understood.
"Stream-enterer" (sotāpanna) means one who, having entered and reached the stream known as the path, stands therein;

the sense is "one established in the fruit of stream-entry. "One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry" means for the purpose of making the fruit of stream-entry personally manifest.

One who is practicing and standing at the first path is called the "eighth person" (*aṭṭhamaka*). The "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*) is one whose nature it is to come back to this world only once more by way of rebirth-linking;
he stands at the second fruit. The "non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) is one whose nature it is not to return to the sense-sphere world by way of rebirth-linking;
he stands at the third fruit. Furthermore, there are those who follow by faith (*saddhānusārī*), those who follow by Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*), and the "single-seeded" (*ekabījī*).
This classification of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) begins thus; it is the very distinction among them. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
"Having understood this matter" means having understood this matter, which consists in the non-dwelling together with a person of immoral conduct who is like a corpse in one's own Dhamma and Vinaya.
"This inspired utterance" refers to [the state of] being unworthy of communal living and being worthy of communal living.
He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) as an illumination of the cause.
In that regard, "What is covered the rain will overwhelm" means that one who, having committed an offense, conceals it, commits another new offense;
from that, yet another—thus the rain of offenses and the rain of defilements fall excessively. "What is uncovered the rain will not overwhelm" means...

Having fallen into an offense, one who does not conceal it, but discloses it to his fellow celibates, confessing it according to the Dhamma and according to the Vinaya, making amends, revealing it, and emerging from it, does not incur another new offense.

Because he has disclosed it, the rain of that offense—the rain of defilement—does not fall upon him again. And because this is so, [it is called] "disclosed" (*vivaṭa*). As for the "concealed" (*channa*)...

"Uncover the concealed offense. "In this way it will not rain upon it": when this is the case, having pierced through the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of those individuals who have committed that offense, the rain of the defilements (*kilesa*) does not fall upon or drench them.
Thus, being untainted by defilements and possessing pure virtue, he becomes concentrated; having established insight (*vipassanā*) and practicing comprehension, he gradually reaches *nibbāna*.
The intention is that he attains [it].
The commentary on the Discourse on the Eight Marvels in this Dhamma and Vinaya is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Those Worthy to Hear the Pātimokkha.
386. Then the Blessed One thought: "Now a disturbance has arisen in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; impure persons are coming to the Uposatha.
The Tathāgata does not recite the Uposatha for an impure assembly, and if he does not recite it, the Uposatha of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus will be interrupted.
What if, from now on, I were to [instruct] the bhikkhus themselves..."
“...should authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having reflected thus, he authorized the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the monks themselves.
Therefore it is said: “Then the Blessed One... ‘You should recite the Pātimokkha. In that context, *nadānāhaṃ* means “not now am I.
By means of the negative particle (*na*) applied to each phrase, [it means]: “I will not perform the Uposatha; I will not recite the Pātimokkha.”
The connection. The Pātimokkha is twofold: the Pātimokkha as an injunction (*āṇā-pātimokkha*) and the Pātimokkha as an exhortation (*ovāda-pātimokkha*).

Of these, the one beginning with “Let the venerable saṅgha listen to me” is the Pātimokkha as an injunction; that is recited only by disciples, not by Buddhas, and it is what is recited every half-month.
[The other is: “Patience is supreme… abstaining from all evil… non-reproach and non-injury…” and so forth.
“*Etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ*” (This is the instruction of the Buddhas)—these three verses are known as the *ovāda-pātimokkha* (the exhortation precepts).
Only Buddhas recite them, not disciples. They are recited at the end of six years.

For Buddhas of long lifespan, this is the only recitation of the *pātimokkha* during their lifetime; however, for Buddhas of short lifespan, it is recited only at the time of their first enlightenment.
After that, however, others [recited it], and these were only monks, not Buddhas.
Therefore, our Blessed One also, having recited this *ovāda-pātimokkha* for about twenty years, saw this obstacle and did not recite it thereafter.
"An impossibility" (*aṭṭhāna*) means there is no cause; "no occasion" (*anavakāsa*) is a synonym for the same. For a cause is that wherein the fruit stands.
It is called a "basis" (*ṭhāna*) because it functions in dependence upon that; likewise, it is also called an "occasion" (*avakāsa*).

The word *yaṃ* is a reference to the action. The passage beginning with "And, monks, one who has committed an offense should not listen to the Pātimokkha" is easy to understand from the standpoint of the literal meaning of the words.

As for what ought to be said regarding the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) here, that has already been stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). In that context, "either before or after" means either prior to or subsequent to the formal motion (*ñatti*).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Suspension of the Pātimokkha by One Who Is Both Righteous and Unrighteous (387).

"Taking both what has been done and what has not been done" means: taking both of those—namely, that which for a person has been done exclusively as well as that which has not been done—of one who possesses both.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Suspension of the Righteous Pātimokkha.
389. *Parisā vuṭṭhātīti*: The assembly rises; that is, without having settled the matter upon which the Pātimokkha was suspended, it rises due to some intervening obstacle.
393. *Paccādiyatīti*: It takes up again; the meaning is that one begins once more by saying, "The formal act was not performed," and so forth.
Commentary on the section concerning the factor of taking up oneself.
398. *Attādānaṃ* is a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that one should take up and adopt oneself in order to exhort another. Therefore he said, “desiring to purify the Dispensation,” and so forth.
*Vassāratto* means the rainy season. 399. *Paṭimāsetuṃ* means to reflect upon. “Having severed the obstacles...

having attained a mind of loving-kindness (*mettācitta*)”—by this he shows the development of loving-kindness that has reached absorption (*appanā*). For this very reason he said, “with hostility destroyed by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*”).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Dhamma to be Established by Rebuke (400).
Regarding the phrase "not with a mind full of ill-will": here the word *antara* is a synonym for "mind" (*citta*); thus he says, "not having a corrupted mind.
Commentary on the Discourse Connected with the Rebuker and the Rebuked.

"Compassion" (*karuṇā*) refers to the absorption-jhāna of compassion that has reached full absorption (*appanā*). "The preliminary stage of compassion" (*karuṇā-pubbabhāga*) refers to the compassion proceeding by way of the preparation (*parikamma*) and access (*upacāra*) stages. The same method applies here to "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) and "the preliminary stage of loving-kindness. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha is finished.
10. The Chapter on the Nuns (*Bhikkhunī-khandhaka*).
Commentary on the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (402).
In the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*, the phrase "dwells among the Sakyans" means that she dwelt there after having gone by her first journey.

Regarding the name "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī," here "Gotamī" is a clan name (*gotta*). On the day of her naming, however, the brahmins who had received honors [performed] the examination of her auspicious marks (*lakkhaṇasampatti*).
Having seen her, they prophesied: "If she obtains a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a Wheel-turning Monarch;
if she obtains a son, he will become a Wheel-turning Monarch. In either case, her progeny will indeed be great.
Therefore, because of the greatness of both her offspring of sons and her offspring of daughters, she was given the name "Mahāpajāpatī" (She of Great Progeny).
They did so; however, here, having combined it with her clan name, she is called "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
"She approached the Blessed One" means that after the Blessed One had gone to Kapilavatthu, he first ordained Nanda, and on the seventh day, Rāhula Kumāra.
But during the "pillow-fight," when the inhabitants of both cities were preparing for battle—
When they had departed, the Teacher went and instructed those kings, preaching the *Attadaṇḍa-sutta*.
The kings were filled with faith and gave over two hundred and fifty sons each. Those five hundred princes went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
Then their wives sent messages to them, inciting in them a sense of dissatisfaction. The Teacher—
Knowing that dissatisfaction had arisen in them, he led those five hundred young bhikkhus to the Kuṇāla Lake.

Sitting upon the stone slab where he himself had previously sat during his time as Kuṇāla, he dispelled their dissatisfaction by recounting the Kuṇāla Jātaka, establishing them all in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Then, bringing them back to the Great Forest (*Mahāvana*), he established them in the fruit of arhatship (*arahatta-phala*).
In order to ascertain their state of mind, they sent another message to their sisters-in-law. These women replied with a counter-message, saying, "We are incapable of living the household life.
Upon hearing this, the five hundred women thought, "It is no longer appropriate for us to go to other houses;
we shall go to Mahāpajāpatī and, having obtained her permission to go forth, we will enter the religious life. Thus, the five hundred went to Mahāpajāpatī.
Having approached, they said, "Noble lady, please grant us the going forth.
Mahāpajāpatī took those women and went to where the Blessed One was; some even say she approached him while he was beneath the white parasol at the time of the King’s final passing away.
She departed and re-entered Kapilavatthu once again.
"Having dwelt as long as he desired" means having dwelt according to his inclination while observing the underlying conditions (*upanissaya*) of those beings who were to be awakened.

"He set out on a journey" means that, gathering the great multitude of people, he set out on a journey with unimpeded pace, accompanied by the supreme glory of a Buddha and the incomparable grace of a Buddha.
"Together with many Sākiyan women" means [within] the very confines of the inner residence.
Having taken the robes of one who has gone forth under the One Possessing the Ten Powers, she likewise had those five hundred Sakyan women take the robes of those who have gone forth,
and together with all those many Sakyan women, she departed— that is, she set out on her journey.
At the time of setting out on the journey, however, she thought, "These delicate royal women will not be able to travel on foot."
The Sākiyan and Koliyan kings had golden palanquins prepared;
however, thinking, "If we go mounted on vehicles, disrespect would be shown toward the Teacher," they proceeded on foot for the fifty-one-league journey.
The kings, too, having arranged for protection both in front and behind, filled carts with rice, ghee, oil, and other provisions.
“They have sent men with the instruction: ‘Prepare food at every place they have gone to. Regarding the phrase “with swollen feet”:
because of their extreme delicacy, on their feet one blister arises and another breaks open; both feet become bloated, as if covered with a lattice of bones.
Therefore it is said, “with swollen feet. Regarding the phrase “outside the gatehouse”: it means outside the gatehouse.
But why did she remain thus? It is said that this thought occurred to her: "I have been permitted by the Tathāgata and have myself taken the robes of one gone forth;
moreover, the fact that I have done so has become well known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. If the Teacher grants me permission to go forth, that would be excellent;
but if he does not grant it, there will be great censure. [Thus she remained] in the monastery.
Unable to enter, she stood weeping. "What is it, Gotamī? [he asked. "Has some misfortune befallen the royal family?
For what reason have you come to such a state of pallor, with feet so withered...
standing here? "By another way" means by another cause. "Nurse" means one who has reared them; [the reference is] to your hands and feet.
The meaning is: she was a nurse who looked after [him] by increasing his hands and feet while they were not yet capable of performing the functions of hands and feet.
"She nourished you" means she nourished you by bathing, feeding, and giving you drink two or three times a day. Regarding "she suckled you with milk":
it is said that Prince Nanda was only a few days younger than the Bodhisattva; when he was born, Mahāpajāpatī [suckled him].
Having entrusted the child to the nurses, she herself performed the duties of a nurse for the Bodhisatta and suckled him with her own milk.

Referring to her, the Elder spoke thus. Saying, "Excellent, venerable sir," and praising her virtues with the words "she was very helpful" and so forth, he spoke as follows while again requesting ordination.
The commentary on the account of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Eight Garudhammas: 403.
The Teacher also [thought], "Women, indeed, have limited faith; they would be satisfied with the mere granting of the going-forth upon being requested by a single person."
Thinking, "They will not accept my teaching out of respect for me," he had refused three times;
now, wishing to have them accepted out of respect, he said, "Ānanda, if Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts the eight *garudhammas*, let that be her full ordination (*upasampadā*)," and so forth.
In this context, *sāvassa* means: "let that very thing be both her going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and her full ordination."
"Of one who has been ordained that very day" means: even on the day he was ordained, one must perform salutation, rising from one's seat, joining of palms, and respectful service.
This means: performing salutation by prostrating with the five points of the body without pride or arrogance; rising from one's seat and going forward to meet him;
joining the ten fingernails together in the gesture of reverence (añjali); and providing services such as preparing a seat and fanning him.
And one should perform the appropriate formal duties (sāmīcikamma) consisting of suitable actions. Regarding a "monastery without monks" (abhikkhuka-āvāsa):

a place where there is no teacher to give exhortation, and which is not a location suitable for approaching for the purpose of receiving exhortation without hindrance while residing there—this is called a monastery without monks;
one should not enter the rains residence in such a monastery. "Every half-month" means on each Uposatha day.

"Approaching for exhortation" means approaching for the purpose of receiving exhortation. "By what was seen" means by what was seen with the eye. "By what was heard" means by what was heard with the ear.
"By suspicion" means by that which is suspected on account of what was seen or heard. "A heavy offense" refers to a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
"Probation for a fortnight" means a *mānatta* discipline lasting no fewer than fifteen days. "In the six matters" means...

Regarding the training rules, with the sixth being that concerning untimely eating: "one who has trained in the training" means one who has fulfilled even a single training rule by keeping it unbroken.

"He is not to be reviled nor abused" means he is not to be reviled by any of the ten grounds for reviling, nor is he to be abused by any form of intimidation or threatening speech. [This is] restricted for the bhikkhunīs.
The "path of speech" regarding the bhikkhus refers to the path of speech consisting of exhortation, instruction, and Dhamma-talk;
this is closed and barred for bhikkhunīs toward the bhikkhus. No bhikkhu whatsoever should be exhorted or instructed by a bhikkhunī.
However, she may speak by way of tradition, saying: "Venerable sirs, the ancient elders fulfilled this and that duty."
It is permissible. Regarding the phrase "unrestrained toward the bhikkhunīs for the bhikkhus," the scope of speech for bhikkhus toward bhikkhunīs is unrestricted;
they may exhort, instruct, and deliver Dhamma-talks according to their own preference. This is the summary here;
however, this discourse on the heavy rules (garudhamma) should be understood in detail according to the method set forth in the Mahāvibhaṅga.
Having learned these eight *garudhammas* in the presence of the Teacher, when she heard them being recited by the Elder, Mahāpajāpatī’s immense dejection was instantly allayed.
As if her head had been sprinkled with a hundred jars of cool water brought from Lake Anotatta, her fever subsided; becoming joyful and glad at heart through the acceptance of the *garudhammas*, she—
Manifesting the rapture and gladness that had arisen, she uttered this inspired utterance beginning with, “Just as if, venerable sir.
In this context, *dahara* means young; *yuva* means one established in the state of youth;

*maṇḍanakajātiko* means one whose nature is to adorn. In this regard, someone may be young yet not a youth, such as one who is very immature; and someone may be a youth yet not of a nature to adorn, such as...

One whose nature is tranquil, or one who is overcome by sloth, calamities, and so forth; however, in this context, it is one who is young, youthful, and fond of adornment who is intended, and for that reason he spoke thus. Blue lotuses and the others are mentioned because they are well-known in the world.
Hereafter, whatever remains to be said has already been shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

In this context, the phrase "because women have gone forth" is an indication of the reason for the endurance of the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) for exactly five hundred years, rather than remaining beyond that.
It is stated by way of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who have attained the various analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Here, by the inclusion of "those whose taints are destroyed who have attained the analytical knowledges," the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are also necessarily included. It is not...
"For indeed, for those who contemplate [the truths], success in every way is accomplished"—this is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.

Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding "a thousand years" and so forth by way of a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*) whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), that should be understood as having been stated according to the opinion of the reciters of the *Khandhaka*.
However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated thus:

“It remained for a thousand years with those who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), for a thousand years with those possessing the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), for a thousand years with those possessing the threefold knowledge (tevijja), for a thousand years with those practicing dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka), and it remained for a thousand years with the Pātimokkha.
Also, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*:
“Indeed, for only a thousand years after the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas were they able to produce the analytical knowledges; beyond that—”
Furthermore, when they are unable to produce even those [six] higher knowledges, they produce the three true insights;
and as time goes on, when they are unable to produce even those, they become dry-insight practitioners (sukkha-vipassaka).
By this same method, there are non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers.”
It has been stated. However, in the *Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"At the time of the First Enlightenment, the monks attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Then, as time passed, the analytical knowledges..."

They were unable to attain [the higher stages], yet they became possessors of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Then, being unable to attain the six supernormal powers, they reached the three types of knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*).
Now, as time passes, being unable to reach the three types of knowledge, they will reach the mere destruction of the taints (*āsravakṣaya*);

being unable even to reach that, they will reach the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*); and being unable even to reach that, they will reach the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*). Even that—
"Being unable [to attain] the fruit of stream-entry, as time passes, they will not even be able to attain the fruit of stream-entry"—
so it was said.
And because all of this is mutually contradictory, it is therefore merely the opinion of those respective reciters.
It should be understood that this was shown by the Teacher in various places; otherwise, there would be the consequence of internal contradiction within the Teacher’s own words.

"Those very same" refers to those same five thousand years. He said, "For without the scriptural tradition (pariyatti), there is no penetration (paṭivedha)," and so forth, because when the scriptural tradition disappears, the practice (paṭipatti) also disappears.
When practice disappears, realization disappears. Why is that?
For this scripture is the condition for practice, and practice is the condition for realization; thus, even in relation to practice, the scripture alone is the authority.
In this regard, penetration and practice may both exist or not exist. For at one time, there were monks who attained penetration...
There are many [who are ordinary], such that one must point with a finger and say, "This bhikkhu is a puthujjana.
In this very island, there was not even once a bhikkhu who was a puthujjana. Those who fulfill the practice are sometimes many and sometimes few;
thus, both realization (*paṭivedha*) and practice (*paṭipatti*) may exist or may not exist. However, as for the endurance of the Dispensation (*sāsana*),...
The scriptures alone are the authority. For a wise person, having heard the Tipiṭaka, fulfills both [the theoretical and practical aspects].

Just as our Bodhisatta, having produced the five supernormal powers and the seven meditative attainments in the presence of Āḷāra, asked about the preliminary practice for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he replied, "I do not know," whereupon [the Bodhisatta] went into the presence of Uddaka and [informed him of] the distinction he had attained.
Having joined together, he asked about the preliminary practice for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

the other explained it, and immediately upon hearing his words, the Great Being accomplished it. In the same way, a wise bhikkhu, having heard the scriptures (pariyatti), fulfills both [the letter and the spirit].
Therefore, when the scripture is established, the Dispensation (sāsana) is established. Just as, for example, when the embankment of a great reservoir is firm...
One should not say that there will be no water; nor should one say that when there is water, lotuses and other flowers will not bloom.

In the same way, when the word of the Buddha in its three collections (Tipiṭaka)—which is like the firm embankment of a great lake—exists, one should not say that there are no sons of noble family who fulfill the practice, who are like the water in that great lake; for when they exist, [the lake is full].
Just as it cannot be said that there are no noble persons such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) because there are no lotuses and other flowers, so too,
the scripture alone is the absolute authority.

Regarding the phrase "when the scripture has disappeared," here "scripture" (*pariyatti*) refers to the word of the Buddha in the Three Baskets (*Tipiṭaka*), together with the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The Pāli: As long as that [Pāli] remains, for so long the scripture (*pariyatti*) is said to be complete.
As time passes, the kings of the Kali age become unrighteous; when they are unrighteous, their ministers and others likewise become unrighteous.
Consequently, the inhabitants of the kingdom and the provinces—due to their unrighteousness—the rain does not fall properly, and thus the crops...
They do not succeed; because they do not succeed, those who provide requisites are unable to give requisites to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus, being worn out by a lack of requisites, are unable to support their pupils.
As time passes, the scriptures (pariyatti) decline; they are no longer able to retain them according to their meaning (atthavasena), but only according to the text (pāḷivasena).
They preserve [the teachings]. Then, as time passes, they are no longer able to preserve the entire Canon (pāḷi);
first, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka declines. As it declines, it begins to decline from its very summit. For first the Mahāpakaraṇa declines;
when that has declined, the Yamaka, Kathāvatthu, Puggalapaññatti, Dhātukathā, Vibhaṅga, and Dhammasaṅgaṇī follow.
Thus, when the Abhidhamma Piṭaka has declined from its summit, the Sutta Piṭaka declines.
First, the Aṅguttara Nikāya declines; within that, first the Ekādasaka Nipāta... [and so on] ...down to the Ekaka Nipāta.
Thus, when the Aṅguttara Nikāya has declined from its summit, the Saṃyutta Nikāya declines. First, indeed...
The Mahāvagga is lost, then the Saḷāyatanavagga, the Khandhakavagga, the Nidānavagga, and the Sagāthāvagga.
Thus, when the Saṃyutta Nikāya has been lost, the Majjhima Nikāya begins to be lost from its summit.
First the Upari-panṇāsaka is lost, then the Majjhima-panṇāsaka, and then the Mūla-panṇāsaka. Thus, in the Majjhima Nikāya...
When it has been lost from its beginning, the *Dīghanikāya* disappears. First the *Pāṭhakavagga* is lost, then the *Mahāvagga*, and then the *Sīlakkhandhavagga*.
When the *Dīghanikāya* has thus disappeared, the *Suttantapiṭaka* is said to be lost.
Together with the *Vinayapiṭaka*, they preserve only the *Jātaka*. For the *Vinayapiṭaka*...
Those who are modest retain [the entire canon], but those desiring gain, thinking, "Even when the Suttanta is recited, we do not notice it," retain only the Jātakas.
As time passes, they are no longer able to retain even the Jātakas. Then, first the Vessantara-jātaka is lost to them;
thereafter, in reverse order, the Puṇṇaka-jātaka, the Mahānāradajātaka, and finally, at the end, the Apaṇṇaka-jātaka.
It declines; they retain only the Vinaya Piṭaka.
As time passes, even that declines from its very summit.
First the Parivāra declines, then the Khandhaka, then the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, and then the Mahā-vibhaṅga—in this sequence, until finally only the Uposatha-khandhaka remains.
They preserve it. Even then, the scripture remains unextinguished. As long as even a four-line stanza continues to circulate among human beings, so long does the scripture remain unextinguished.

When a faithful and devoted king, having placed a purse containing a thousand [pieces of gold] in a golden casket upon the back of an elephant, [declares]: "A four-line stanza spoken by the Buddhas..."

“Let whoever knows this take this thousand! Having thus caused the drum to be beaten in the city, and finding no one to take it, [the king thought], “Even when it has been beaten only once, there are those who hear the name and those who do not.

When, after having it beaten for a third time, no one to take it is found, and the royal officers carry the purse containing the thousand back into the royal palace, at that moment the scripture is said to have disappeared.
"It will endure for a long time" means that even when the formal learning (*pariyatti*) has disappeared, the mere outward sign (*liṅgamatta*) will continue to exist for some period.

How so? As time passes, the wearing of robes, the holding of bowls, the bending and stretching of limbs, and the looking ahead and looking aside become ungraceful; monks hold their bowls like gourds, just like the Nigaṇṭha ascetics.
They wander about having wrapped it around their upper arms and carrying it; even at this stage, the outward sign remains unaltered.
But as time passes, they take it down from their upper arms and wander about either holding it by hand or hanging it from a string;
furthermore, they dye the robe not in a manner suitable for dying, but dye it the color of a lip or an elephant’s tusk. As time further passes, even the dye—
It does not exist; having merely made a hem for the fringe and pierced the inner fold, they use it, but they do not pierce the inner fold again or make a hem.
Then, doing neither of these two, they cut off the fringe and wander like wandering mendicants.
As time passes, thinking, "What use have we for this?", they carry a small fragment of saffron cloth on their hand or around their neck.
Or they bind [cattle], or they cause [animals] to be tethered by the hair; maintaining their wives, they wander about making their living by plowing and sowing.
When people give a gift, they give it to these as well, designating it for the Saṅgha.
It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said: "Ananda, in the future there will indeed be those who have reached the lineage (gotrabhū)."

“Those who wear the saffron robe around their necks while being immoral and of evil character—when people give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha for the sake of those immoral ones, even then, Ānanda, I declare that the offering made to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable.
Then, as time passed, people performing various kinds of work thought, “This is a mere distraction; what use have we for this? and they cut off pieces of the saffron robes.
They cast them out into the forest; at that time, it is said that the "mark" (liṅga) is called "disappeared.
From the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa onwards, it is said, the Yonakas developed the custom of wandering about wearing white garments.
Thus, it should be understood that even though the formal study (pariyatti) has disappeared, the mere outward mark will continue to exist for a long time.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Eight Garudhammas is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Permission for the Full Ordination of Bhikkhunīs (404–405).
"From which day" means starting from whichever day. "On that very same day" means on that very day. "By way of permission" means...
Having been granted permission, she said, “Venerable Ānanda, I ask a boon from the Blessed One.
Then, having declared, “In this very way, Venerable Ānanda, I accept these eight *garudhammas* as not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts,” if one asks, “Why does she now ask for a boon?
it is for the purpose of avoiding the censure of others. For some might say: “Mahāpajāpatī... [text truncated]”
"Because it was accepted first, there was no salutation according to seniority among the monks and the nuns;
if she were to ask for a boon, the Blessed One would surely grant it.

406. "For the sake of passion" means for the state of being possessed by passion, for the nourishment of sensual passion and passion for existence. "For the sake of bondage" means for the purpose of binding one to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

"For the sake of accumulation" means for the purpose of increasing the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "For the sake of great desire" means for the state of having great desires. "For the sake of discontent" means for the state of being dissatisfied.

"For the sake of socializing" means for dwelling in the company of the multitude of defilements (*kilesa*). "For the sake of laziness" means for the state of being indolent. "For the sake of being difficult to support" means for the state of being hard to nourish.
"For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of becoming free from passion toward the entire cycle of existence. "For the sake of detachment" means...
For the purpose of dissociating from sensual lust and the like. "For the sake of diminution" means for the sake of the diminution of the entire round of existence (*saṃsāra*);
the meaning is: for the sake of Nibbāna. "For the sake of fewness of wishes" means for the complete departure from wishing by way of fewness of wishes regarding requisites and so forth.

"For the sake of contentment" means for the state of twelvefold contentment. "For the sake of seclusion" means for the state of being secluded, through the accomplishment of physical seclusion and the other types of seclusion that are its factors.
"For the undertaking of energy" means for the purpose of exerting both physical and mental energy. "For being easy to support" means for the purpose of being easily nourished.

Thus, the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma), by way of learning, retaining, inquiring, and reflecting, becomes the cause for one who practices wisely to avoid states such as lust and so forth, and leads toward the state of dispassion (virāga) and so on.

It leads [to that]; this is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, because it is to be upheld by preventing one from falling into the states of deprivation and so forth, and because it disciplines the defilements;

because it constitutes the instruction and admonition of the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, you should bear it in mind as "this is the Teacher’s Dispensation," you should know it, you should understand it—this is the meaning. In this Sutta, by the first section, the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown.
By the second turn, the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) has been explained.
409–410. *Vimānetvā* means having offended. *Kammappattāyopi* means even one who is subject to a formal act (*kamma*). *Āpattigāminiyopīti* means even one who has fallen into an offense.
"They incur the necessity of being dealt with in the manner already stated" because such an action has been prohibited.

They incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). 413–5. "Two or three bhikkhunīs" means by two or three bhikkhunīs. "Do not inform" means they do not inform the reciter of the Pātimokkha. "Do not report back" means they do not report back to the bhikkhunīs. "A distinction" refers to a breach of the proper conduct.
420. "And by that [gift] a bhikkhu should be invited": this is a statement of courtesy; however, there is no offense for one who has not been invited.
425. “Three supports” means, setting aside the support of lodgings, the other three supports. For she does not obtain the lodging of the foot of a tree.
428. “Initiating a censure” means exercising authority. 430.
“Ordaining by means of a messenger-monk” means that a monk himself is the messenger; thus, it is “by means of a messenger-monk. The meaning is: ordaining by having made him a messenger-monk.

431. "It does not agree" means it is not capable [of being used]. "New construction" refers to the gift of land belonging to the Saṅgha after one has performed new construction and requested permission, saying, "May he dwell for so many years.
432. "Women with established embryos" means those whose pregnancy has been confirmed. 434.
"She does not even obtain the going-forth" means that because she has transferred to another religious sect (tīrtha), she has reached a state of incapacity and thus does not obtain it.

"This is permitted specifically for this purpose" means that whether it occurs from one side or from both sides, even if there is an outflow [of semen], it is permissible because it has been specifically permitted for that purpose.
The rest here is easily understood from the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the permission for the full ordination of bhikkhunīs is finished.
The commentary on the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka is finished.
11. The Chapter on the Five Hundred:
Commentary on the Narrative of the Origin of the Council.

437. In the Chapter on the Five Hundred [Monks], regarding the passage from Pāvā to Kusinārā: having wandered for alms in the city of Pāvā, he set out upon the highway with the intention, "I will go to Kusinārā.

"Taking a mandārava flower" means taking a flower the size of a large bowl and holding it like a parasol, fixed upon a long-stemmed stalk. "He saw" means he saw him while he was still far away as he was approaching.

I saw him. Upon seeing him, I thought, "I shall ask him about the Blessed One's well-being," but then I considered, "If I were to ask while he is still seated, it would show a lack of respect toward the Teacher.
Therefore, rising and moving away from my standing place, I took from the Ten-Powered One’s hand the cloud-colored rag-robe given to me—like a jeweled skin—the gift of the Elephant King Chaddanta.

Having clothed himself and placed his hands together in a brilliant añjali with the ten fingernails joined at the head, and out of the reverence he felt for the Teacher, he turned toward the Ājīvaka and asked, "Friend, do you know our Teacher?

Now, did he ask because he did not know of the Teacher’s Parinibbāna, or because he did know it? [The answer is: For those whose taints are destroyed, knowledge is dependent upon a mental advertence (*āvajjanappaṭibaddha*).
[The Elder] knew. However, some say that because he had not adverted [to the object], he asked while not knowing. The Elder was one who frequently entered meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);

in his night-quarters, day-quarters, caves, pavilions, and so forth, he constantly sustained himself by the fruit of attainment alone. Even when entering a village belonging to a lay family, he would enter into attainment at the gate and take alms only after emerging from attainment.
It is said that the Elder thought, "In this, my final physical existence..."
