"I shall perform a great favor for the people; let that which those who give me alms or pay honor with perfumes, garlands, and so forth receive be of great fruit"—it is with this thought that he acts.

Therefore, they say that because of his abundance of meditative attainments (samāpatti), he did not know [the time], and thus he asked while being unaware; however, that should not be accepted. For there is no cause here for such ignorance.
It was so. The Teacher’s Parinibbāna was truly distinguished by signs such as the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system.
Among the Elder’s assembly, some monks had previously seen the Blessed One, while others had not.
In that regard, those who had seen him were still desirous of seeing him again; and those who had not seen him were likewise desirous of seeing him.

In that regard, those who have not seen him before will go out of a desire to see him and, asking "Where is the Blessed One?", upon hearing that he has attained final Nibbāna, they will be unable to sustain themselves.
Discarding their robes, clad in a single garment or poorly dressed, they will weep while beating their breasts. There, people [will say], "Together with Mahākassapa..."
"The alms-collectors who have arrived are themselves weeping like women;
how can they comfort us?"—thus they will point out my fault. But this is a vast, empty forest; here there is no fault in weeping however one may.
"Hearing [the news] earlier indeed makes the grief lighter," thinking thus, he questioned them while knowing full well, for the sake of causing the arising of mindfulness in the bhikkhus.
"Today, seven days after his final passing" means that he passed away on the seventh day counting back from today.

"From there" means from the place where the ascetic Gotama passed away. "Those who are not free from lust" refers to both worldlings (*puthujjana*) and stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*).
For in them, mental grief (*domanassa*) has not been abandoned; therefore, they too, raising their arms...
They wail; placing both hands upon their heads, they weep. "Falling with a severed fall" (*chinnapātaṃ papatanti*):
a "severed fall" (*chinnapāta*) is like the falling of severed [limbs]; this is a neuter compound designation.
The meaning is that, as if cut in the middle, they fall hither and thither. "They whirl" (*āvaṭṭanti*): they turn about facing [forward]. Wherever they have fallen...
Then, having gone a certain distance by way of revolving, they return again by way of revolving to the very place where they fell.
"Revolve" (*vivaṭṭanti*) means that from wherever they have fallen, they turn back;
the meaning is that they go revolving toward the region beyond the place where they fell. Furthermore, revolving forward is *āvaṭṭana*, and revolving backward is *paccavaṭṭana*.

Rolling forward and rolling backward. Therefore, even when they stretch out their two legs and turn around once toward the front, once toward the back, once to the left, and once to the right, they are said to "turn over" and "roll back.
Those free from lust (*vītarāga*) are those who have abandoned mental distress (*domanassa*);
because they are unperturbed by the pleasant and the unpleasant, they are like stone pillars—Non-Returners (*anāgāmi*) whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted. For indeed, as for mental distress...
Even when [lust] is absent, a certain degree of lust still exists; however, when lust is entirely absent, there is simply no possibility for the arising of displeasure (*domanassa*).

For it is said that displeasure is abandoned through the abandonment of lust because they share a common basis (*tadekaṭṭhabhāva*), not because one has become an *āsava*-destroyer (*khīṇāsava*) alone.

Regarding the passage beginning with "from all that is dear" (*piyehi*), they are "dear" (*piya*) because they are objects of affection, and "agreeable" (*manāpa*) because they increase the mind, such as mother, father, brother, sister, and so forth.
“Diversity” (*nānābhāva*) means diversity by way of birth; it is a state of being distinct through proceeding in accordance with one’s birth;

the meaning is a state of being unconnected. “Separation” (*vinābhāva*) means separation by way of death; the meaning is a disjunction because that particular individual existence (*attan-bhāva*) does not proceed again due to passing away.
“Alteration” (*aññathābhāva*) means alteration by way of becoming; through the grasping of another becoming, [the term refers to] a sense-sphere being...
The meaning is that there is a different mode from the previous one, as shown by such passages as "he becomes a being of the form realm" and so forth, and also "a human becomes a deva" and so forth.
"Tat" means "therefore. "Kutettha labbhati" means: where, in what place, in what location—namely, in this occurrence of the aggregates—is it possible to find that which was born...
[and so on] ... "may it not perish"? It is simply not possible for such a thing.
Because of the absence of a cause. This is what is meant:

since there is separation from all that is dear and pleasing, therefore—even after fulfilling the ten perfections, even after attaining full enlightenment, even after setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, even after displaying the Twin Miracle, and even after descending from the heavens—that which is born, become, conditioned, and subject to disintegration [must pass away].
"Even for the body of the Tathāgata, it is impossible that it should not decay;
even by weeping and wailing, that purpose cannot be achieved.

Furthermore, friends, regarding the passage beginning with "At that time, there was an elder who had gone forth as a monk named Subhadda," what is to be said has already been stated according to the method explained in the commentary on the Nidāna.
The commentary on the introductory narrative of the Council (Saṅgītinidānakathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.
Commentary on the discourse regarding the minor and lesser training rules (Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpadakathāvaṇṇanā).
441. “He should abolish”: if he so desires, let him abolish; if he wishes, he may abolish—this is the meaning. Why?
Why did the Blessed One not state categorically, "Uproot it," but instead establish it with a conditional expression, "One who so desires may uproot it"?
It was because he perceived the power of Mahākassapa’s knowledge. For the Blessed One saw that even if he were told, "Uproot it," Kassapa would not uproot it at the time of the recitation;
therefore, he established it by way of a conditional alternative. If...
The non-abandoning has been seen, and that very thing was intended; so why did the Blessed One say, "If he so desires, let him abandon it"?
It was on account of the inclinations of certain individuals. For there are some who are unwilling to undertake and abide by the minor and lesser training rules;
if these had not been spoken of in such a way by the Blessed One, distress would have arisen in them.
That will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. However, when it was spoken thus, no distress arose in them, [thinking]:
"This is our own fault, since some among us themselves do not desire its eradication.
Some say: "But it was stated thus for the purpose of making the entire Dispensation dependent upon the Saṅgha."
Whatever training rule has been laid down by the Teacher, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, receive it with their heads and guard it as they would their own life.

For even when it was said, "Let the Saṅgha abolish the minor and lesser training rules if it so desires," they did not abolish them; on the contrary, they held them even after his passing just as they had before.
"Rakkhiṃsuyeva" (they indeed guarded) should be understood as having been said thus for the purpose of demonstrating the greatness of both the Teacher’s Dispensation and the Saṅgha.
For instance, the Venerable Ānanda or other monks did not ask, "But what, venerable sir, is the minor rule? What is the minor-minor rule?
because they lacked the very intention to abolish them; for that very reason, not even a single training rule...
In order to show that none of them are to be disregarded, they said: "With the exception of the four *pārājika* rules, the rest are minor and lesser rules" (*khuddānukhuddaka*).
For by speaking thus, since it was not determined which ones specifically were "minor and lesser," it was shown that all of them are to be respected.
442. Regarding the statement, "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha," some say:
"Venerable Nāgasena, when King Milinda asked, 'What is the minor, and what is the very minor? the Elder Nāgasena replied, 'The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), Great King, is minor;
the offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita) is very minor. Because of this, the Elder Nāgasena [treated] the minor and very minor [rules as such]."
As for the statement, "But the Elder Mahākassapa, not knowing that, announced the formal act (*kammavācā*) with the words,
'Let the Venerable Ones hear me,' and so forth," it should not be understood in that way. For the Elder Nāgasena, in order to cut off the path of argumentation for others,
took only the final portion from among the sections selected by the Great Elders who compiled the Dhamma at the time of the Council, and [addressed] King Milinda...
The Elder Mahākassapa, however, recited the formal procedure (*kammavācā*) in such a way because he did not wish to abolish even a single training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Regarding this, they say that "belonging to householders" (*gihigata*) means "connected with householders. But here the meaning should be understood as follows: they have gone among the householders, or they are known by them;
thus they are "belonging to householders. That which has smoke as its time is "of the time of smoke" (*dhūmakālika*), from the point when the smoke of the funeral pyre has subsided.

Because it does not proceed further. Regarding the phrases "not laid down" and so forth: when they establish a new, unrighteous formal agreement (*katikavatta*) or a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), they are said to "lay down what has not been laid down," just as the monks did at Sāvatthī in the case of the old rug (*purāṇasanthatavatthu*).
When they proclaim a teaching that is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, they are said to "abolish what has been laid down," as [occurred] one hundred years after the Parinibbāna.

They are like the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī toward the Blessed One. However, those who intentionally transgress even minor and lesser offenses, and do not conduct themselves by undertaking the training rules as they have been prescribed, are said to be like Assaji and Punabbasuka.
But those who do not establish new agreements or training rules, yet illuminate the Teaching according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya—
And by not abolishing even the minor and lesser training rules, they do not prescribe what has not been prescribed,
nor do they abolish what has been prescribed; they undertake and abide by the training rules exactly as they have been prescribed,
like the Venerable Upasena and the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta.
443. "While a gross sign was being made by the Blessed One"—meaning while the Blessed One was dwelling at the Cāpāla Shrine near Vesālī—the Blessed One said:
"Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine;
delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine; delightful is the Sattamba Shrine; delightful is the Bahuputta Shrine; delightful is the Sārandada Shrine."

And the Cāpāla Shrine. "Ānanda, whoever has developed the four bases of psychic power—having cultivated them, made them a vehicle, made them a foundation, established them, consolidated them, and properly undertaken them—that person, if they so desire, could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
Now, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has indeed developed the four bases of psychic power; he has cultivated them, made them a vehicle..."
“Ānanda, if this had been established, practiced, cultivated, and well undertaken by the Tathāgata, he, if he so desired,
could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon”—
thus was it said regarding such a gross sign being made manifest.
"With a mind obsessed by Māra" means with a mind overwhelmed by Māra.

For Māra obsesses the mind of one who has not entirely abandoned all twelve types of perversion (*vipallāsa*). Since the Elder had not yet abandoned four of these perversions, Māra obsessed his mind. As for how he effected that obsession of the mind: what...
How does he do it? He displays a terrifying visual object or makes a terrifying auditory sound heard.
Then, upon seeing or hearing it, beings lose their mindfulness and stand with mouths agape;
thrusting his hand into their mouths, he crushes their hearts, so that they remain there utterly unconscious. But as for this Elder, he thrusts his hand into their mouths—
Was he able to enter? However, he showed him a terrifying object; seeing that, the Elder did not penetrate the manifestation of the sign (*nimittobhāsa*).

The commentary on the discussion of the minor and lesser training rules (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*) is finished. The commentary on the discourse on the "Brahma-punishment" (*brahmadaṇḍa*) follows.
445. *Ujjavanikāya* means "going against the stream. *Rajoharaṇaṃ* means "a dust-remover" (a broom). *Na kulavaṃ gamenti* means they do not lead to useless destruction.
*Kulava* is a contemptible loss (*kucchito lavo*); what is meant is "ruin through misconduct.
Although one should have said "the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya," it is called "the recitation of the Vinaya" because the Vinaya is the primary focus of the recitation.
It has been stated. A recitation centered on the Vinaya is a "Vinaya-recitation" (*vinayasaṅgīti*). The rest here is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Pañcasatikakkhandhaka* is finished.
12. The *Sattasatikakkhandhaka*.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Ten Bases (Dasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 446. Regarding the phrase "jewels and gold" mentioned in the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka: by the very training rule concerning money (*rūpiya*), jewels and gold are already prohibited.

Therein, by the mention of "jewels," all objects involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) are included; by the mention of "gold," all objects involving an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) are included.
It is grasped. "By the number of monks" means by the counting of monks. 447.
"Impurities" (upakkilesā) are so called because they cause a state of being defiled by preventing [the light] from shining forth.
"Mist" (mahikā) is frost. "Smoke and dust" (dhūmarajo) is smoke and dust. Herein, the first three are impurities by way of non-arrival; Rāhu, however—

It should be understood that this is stated by way of the adventitious defilements (upakkilesa). "Ascetics and brahmins do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate" means they do not glow with the heat of their virtues, they do not shine with the luster of their virtues, and they do not radiate with the brilliance of their virtues.
"Not abstaining from the drinking of fermented liquor and spirits" means they have not desisted from drinking the five kinds of *surā* and the four kinds of *meraya*.
"Enveloped by ignorance" means obstructed and shut off by ignorance. "Delighting in pleasant forms" means rejoicing in and being satisfied with what is agreeable and pleasurable.
"Accepting" means grasping. "Unseeing" refers to blind fools. "Dusty" means possessing the dust of defilements. "Deer-like" means resembling deer.
It is called a "guide" (*netti*) because it leads one here and there among sense objects or states of existence; this is a designation for craving (*taṇhā*).
"They proceed together with her" means they are accompanied by her (*sanettikā*).
He said this to that assembly; for it is said that he thought thus:
"When sons of good family go forth, they go forth having abandoned their wives and children as well as gold and silver; yet it is not possible for them to abandon that which they have abandoned."
Having adopted the guiding principle [of the rule], he spoke these words beginning with “Venerable sirs, do not,” with the intent:

“One should grasp this categorically. “This” refers to the practice of the five strands of sensual pleasure; you should hold that this is “not the dhamma of a recluse, not the dhamma of a son of the Sakyan” with absolute certainty.
“Grass” means the grass used for covering the dwelling. “It should be sought” means [grass] for a thatched roof or for a tiled roof.
When the house is collapsing, one should go to those by whom it was built and inform them:
"The lodging built by you is leaking; it is not possible to dwell there. If they are able, they will repair it;
if they are unable, they will say: "You yourselves take carpenters and have it repaired; we shall persuade them for you."
When this has been said, having had [the work] done, it should be explained to them; people will give [the payment] to the carpenters.
If there are no owners of the residence, it is permissible to have it done after announcing it to others as well by means of the conduct of one on alms-round.
It is with reference to this that it is said, "it should be sought."
When the wooden structures of the dwelling, such as the rafters and so forth, are decaying, wood should be sought for that purpose.
A cart should be sought, either belonging to a householder or borrowed for a limited time.
Not only a cart, but other implements such as axes, adzes, spades, and so on, may likewise be sought in this manner. "A man" refers to one who performs manual labor.
A man may be sought after. For if one says to any man, "Friend, will you do manual labor?
and he replies, "I will, venerable sir," it is permissible to have him do whatever one desires, saying, "In this place, do this and that.
But, headman, by no means whatsoever—by no reason at all—do I [permit the acceptance] of gold and silver.
"I do not say it should be sought after.
(449) "An evil deed" means an unwholesome deed.
(450) "Ahogaṅga" is the name of that mountain.
451. “One should go beforehand”: one should go first to that place where the monks assemble to settle that legal matter (*adhikaraṇa*).
“They met”: they arrived. 452. “It will be without salt”: it will be rice or curry that is without salt. “Well-prepared” (*āsutā*): prepared with all the necessary ingredients.
Or there is the reading “*asuttā*” (unmixed). 453. “They went upstream”: having boarded a boat, they traveled against the current. “The Easterners”: those who dwell in the eastern region.
454. "Surely you, friend, are old; surely you, friend, are twenty years of age. You are not bound by dependence [on a teacher];

why then does the Elder expel you?"—thus they explain. "We shall take the Elder as our preceptor": although we are advanced in years, the intention is, "Having made this Elder our preceptor, we shall live under him."
455. Because it consists merely of the fine-material-sphere concentration of loving-kindness (*mettā*), it is called “the raft-like abiding”;
the meaning is “by means of a minor abiding. And because its nature is not profound, he says “by means of a shallow abiding.
“By means of the void abiding” is said with reference to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) reached by way of the door of emptiness (*suññatāmukha*).
457. *Suttavibhaṅge* refers to the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*). *Tena saddhiṃ* means together with the salt previously received.

For here, it is not referring to that which is "for life" (permanently) or "received on that very day," but rather it is stated with reference to the "salt for the corner of the mouth" mentioned in the passage: "The practice of salt for the corner of the mouth is allowable. For that [salt] was received previously and carried in the corner of the mouth; it was not received on that very day.
"Only that which has been received on the same day as it is to be consumed" means it should be eaten mixed with salt and a pinch of salt, referring to food that is not salty.
"Connected with the Uposatha" means connected with the Uposatha; what is meant is "in the Uposatha Khandhaka.

"Transgression" (*atisāra*) means overstepping or exceeding. "A transgression of the Vinaya" (*vinayātisāra*) refers to the exceeding of the Vinaya. "For one who makes that [transgression] a standard" means...
The measurement that has been stated for sitting together with a border-cloth applies to one who makes it while without such a cloth. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka is finished.
"Comprising two sections" means comprised by the two sections known as the Cūḷavagga and Mahāvagga. "Divided into twenty-two parts."
There are ten in the Mahāvagga and twelve in the Cūḷavagga; thus, they are divided into twenty-two types. "In the Sāsana" means in the Teacher’s dispensation (*satthusāsane*).
This should be construed with the words "those Khandhakas which were spoken.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the meaning of the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā.
The commentary on the Cūḷavagga is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Parivāra.
The Sixteenth Major Section: Explanation of the Section on Formulations (*Paññattivāra-vaṇṇanā*).
"Of one whose retinue is purified" means having a retinue that is entirely pure with taints exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "Of the body of the aggregates of the Dhamma" means...
The connection is with the phrase "of the Dispensation," which has as its body the aggregates of Dhamma known as virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"Of that" refers to that which has been entered into the compendium as the "Parivāra. "They lead to what has come before" means they lead to the analysis (vinicchaya) that has already appeared previously.
The word "that" (ta-) is a demonstrative pronoun used as a reference to the words "by the Blessed One" and so forth, standing in grammatical apposition to them.

Showing that the Blessed One declared, emphasized, and made fully manifest that very rule of discipline (vinaya-paññatti) which pertains to the meaning already stated—presenting it together with the formal request as the substance of the matter—he said: “He who... [etc. ...laid down the rule of discipline.
In this context, “rule of discipline” means a formulation that constitutes the discipline.
Regarding the phrases “by one who knows and sees,” since these belong to the Vinaya, one should first apply their meaning according to the method stated therein;
now, however, demonstrating them according to the method of the Suttas, although the terms *ñāṇa* (knowledge) and *dassana* (vision) are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*),

they are presented here by way of the threefold clear vision (*vijjā-ttaya*) and the knowledge of the super-knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the absence of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-ñāṇa*), in order to show the specific range of their respective objects through their various particular distinctions.

Having connected the meaning by way of both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching—through the eye of flesh and the eye of omniscient wisdom—he said, beginning with “Furthermore,” etc.
Therein, “by means of the recollection of past lives, etc. refers to the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

“By means of the wisdom of penetration” refers to the wisdom of the Noble Path. “Beholding by means of the wisdom of teaching” refers to [beholding] the manner in which the phenomena to be taught are to be taught, as well as the persons to be enlightened.

By one who, through the wisdom of teaching (*desanā-paññā*), perceives phenomena as they truly are according to their distinctions—such as latent dispositions (*āsaya*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), temperament (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*).

"By the Arhat": because of the destruction of enemies (*ari*), and because of the destruction of spokes (*ara*), and because of being worthy (*araha*) of conditions and so forth, [he is] "by the Arhat.

"By the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*)": because of having awakened perfectly (*sammā*) and by oneself (*sāma*) to the truths, [he is] "by the Perfectly Enlightened One. Alternatively, [he is so called] because of knowing the obstructive phenomena (*antarāyika-dhamma*) and the liberating phenomena (*niyyānika-dhamma*).

"By the Seer," because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements; "by the Worthy One" (Arahat), because he is worthy; "by the Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha), because he has perfectly and personally awakened to all phenomena—thus should the application here also be understood by way of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*).

Furthermore, [it is so] because he knows the distinction between what is possible and what is impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*), because he sees beings according to their karma, and because of his taints (*āsava*) together with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

By the *Arahat* because of his having severed [the defilements]; by the *Sammāsambuddha* because of his unerring realization of the phenomena classified as "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth, from the perspective of being directly known and so forth.
Alternatively, he is the "Knower" (*jānatā*) due to his unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times;

the "Seer" (*passatā*) due to his correct practice, since his three types of action—bodily, verbal, and mental—proceed in accordance with that knowledge; and [he is endowed] with the perfection of abandonment, which establishes the absence of deceit and the like.

"By the Arahant," "by the Perfectly Enlightened One who possesses omniscience—the cause for the non-decline of zeal and the other [factors] and the basis for inexhaustible eloquence"—in this way, the application should also be made by way of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. 2.
Regarding "the answering of questions": it means in the answering of a question. "In this" means in this answering of questions. Only in the Middle Country.

"Designation" (*paññatti*) refers to the occurrence of an offense when there is a transgression of the aforementioned object in that very place. "Discussion on what has been dealt with" (*vinītakathā*) means a discussion concerning the matter already dealt with;
this is indeed the reading.

However, one incurs an offense by means of the body: having made the mind of pursuit (*sevanacitta*) the factor in the preliminary stage, one [performs] the intimation (*viññatti*) known as the door of the body.
Having produced the offense characterized as the arising of a thought in progress, one incurs it.

For although the intimation (viññatti) is originated by the mind, nevertheless, because the intended purpose is accomplished through bodily intimation, it is said that "one incurs the offense through the door of the body.
It is with reference to this meaning—namely, the bringing about of the state of non-offense for an offense already incurred—that [the text says].
This refers to the meaning designated as "impossibility," not to the pacification of quarrels and the like.
By "the ancient Great Elders" (porāṇakehi mahātherehi) is meant the Great Elders residing on the island of Sīhaḷa. They were "established" at the time of recording them in books;
for the recital of recording in books is indeed similar to the Fourth Council (catutthasaṅgīti). In the two Vibhaṅgas, the thirty-two sections are indeed easy to understand.

Commentary on the Headings for Origination (Samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanā) 257. Regarding the discussion on origination: because they resemble the moon due to their coolness through compassion, they are called "moon-Buddhas" (*buddhacanda*);

because they dispel the darkness of the defilements (*kilesa*), they are called "sun-Buddhas" (*buddhādicca*). As for the phrase "he taught three in the Piṭaka," it is because they teach those [three].
Therefore, he also taught the three Piṭakas to Aṅgīrasa. To the question "Which are these?", he said: "The Suttanta," and so forth.

"Of great virtue" means of great benefit. "Thus is the True Dhamma led forward, provided the Vinaya remains"—if the study of the Vinaya remains, that is, if it is not lost and continues to exist, then, this being the case, the True Dhamma of practice and realization is led forward and continues to exist.
As for how the mastery of the Vinaya (vinayapariyatti) persists, he says: "By both," and so forth. It should be connected [to the phrase] "they persist as they are bound by the Parivāra.
"Of that very Parivāra" means within that very Parivāra.

"Fixed in their performance" (niyatakata) means having their performance fixed; the sense is that they are determined. "Together with others" means together with the remaining training rules (sikkhāpada). "With unmixed origins" (asambhinnasamuṭṭhāna) means having non-confused origins.

"Therefore, one should train": since the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) endures when the Vinaya exists, and the Vinaya endures when it is bound together with the Parivāra, and since the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are seen in the Parivāra, therefore one should train in the Parivāra; the meaning is that one should learn it.

First, regarding the beginning, "in the manner previously stated" refers to the section on the formal rules (*paññattivāra*), which begins: "Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates by one origin; it originates from both body and mind," and so forth.
This was said with reference to the method [of ordination] that has already occurred.
258. "She does not follow the *pavattinī*": this refers to the training rule stated as, "Whatever bhikkhunī does not follow the *pavattinī* who has performed the ordination for two years.
270. "Unmixed" (*akata*): not mixed with others; it is said to be of definite origin (*niyata-samudāna*).
Commentary on the Section of Questions on a Few [Points] within the Intermediate Chapter (Antarapeyyāla) 271.

"He conceals enmity" (*veraṃ maṇati*) means he conceals—that is, destroys—enmity such as lust and so forth. "By this" (*etāya*) refers to by this abstinence (*virati*). "The outlet" (*niyyāna*) refers to the Path (*magga*). "Bodily corruption" (*kāyapāgabbiya*) refers to bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) occurring by way of bodily corruption.
274. *Sāraṇīya* means "worthy of being remembered," fit for recollection, and not to be forgotten even when a long period of time has passed.

*Mettā* is so called because one is moistened (*mijjati*) and refreshed (*siniyhati*) by it; it is the state of a friend (*mittabhāva*). Since this bodily action possesses loving-kindness, it is called "loving-kindness"; moreover, because it is originated by a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, it is said: "bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness."
*Āvi* means manifest. And here, "manifestness" refers to the state of being in the presence of the person for whose sake that bodily action is performed;
thus he said "in the presence" (*sammukhā*). *Raho* means unmanifest. And "unmanifestness" refers to the state of not being in the presence of the person for whose sake that action is performed;
thus he said "in the absence" (*parammukhā*). "By both" means by the novices and by the elders. "Pleasant" (*piyaṃ*)...
One who acts in a way that is endearing is "one who creates affection" (*piyakaraṇo*). One who treats what is venerable as venerable is "one who shows respect" (*garukaraṇo*).

"For the sake of gathering" (*saṅgahāya*) means for the purpose of gathering fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*), by virtue of being a specific basis for gathering (*saṅgahavatthu*). "For the sake of non-dispute" (*avivādāya*) means precisely because it is a basis for gathering, it is not for the sake of dispute.
And when there is the state of being a basis for gathering that serves as a cause for non-dispute, by means of those [bases], [the welfare] of fellow practitioners of the holy life [is achieved].
Since the state of being united—the absence of division—is already established, he said, “for the sake of unity,” and so forth.
“Elevated speech” means speaking by emphasizing [the title] not merely as “Devathera,” but by highlighting the stability of his qualities through such designations as “Devathera.
“Speech that makes one aware of possessiveness” is speech that expresses the sense of ownership. Of that which is exclusively hidden...

The "presence" (*sammukhatā*) of mental action occurs solely by way of generating a manifestation (*viññatti*); and yet, without referring to what is well-known and recognized in the world as bodily action—such as the movement of the hands and so forth—he said, "having opened his eyes," and so on, in order to show that very thing.
In this context, it should be understood that the opening of eyes moistened with the affection of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the gazing with a serene face [constitute this presence].

Loving bodily action is simply that; however, with reference to that state of mind by virtue of which the eyes are moistened with the oiliness of loving-kindness and the face is bright, it is said: "This is called loving mental action.
And these types of loving bodily action and so forth, though presented in the Canon in relation to monks, are certainly found among laypeople as well.

For monks, the fulfillment of the duties pertaining to proper conduct—such as the duties toward teachers and preceptors—by means of a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is called "loving-kindness bodily action" (*mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ*).
It should be understood that all blameless bodily action is indeed included within the category of actions pertaining to proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika-kamma*).
For laypeople, it includes going for the purpose of worshipping a *cetiya*, for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi tree, for the purpose of inviting the Saṅgha, or [going] to a village...
Furthermore, when seeing monks who have entered for alms, going out to meet them, receiving their bowls, preparing seats, following them as they leave, and so forth—
this is called loving-kindness in bodily action (*mettā-kāyakamma*). That which proceeds by way of instructing monks in the rules of conduct with a mind of loving-kindness,
teaching meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), preaching the Dhamma, answering questions, and explaining the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is likewise [loving-kindness in verbal action].
Even the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas is called loving verbal action. For laypeople, it includes: "We shall go for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya;
we shall go for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi tree; we shall listen to the Dhamma; we shall perform offerings of lamps, garlands, and flowers;
we shall conduct ourselves by undertaking the three types of good conduct; we shall give alms-food by lot and so forth; we shall give the rains-retreat gift."
Vocal action of loving-kindness occurs at the time of saying such things as: "Today we shall provide the four requisites for the Saṅgha;

having invited the Saṅgha, prepare the various kinds of food, arrange the seats, set out drinking water, go out to meet the Saṅgha and lead them in, seat them on the prepared seats, and perform services with a joyful heart and a spirit of enthusiasm."

As for the name: when monks, having risen early in the morning, attend to their physical needs, perform the duties of the shrine courtyard (*cetiyangana*), and so forth, and then sit in a secluded place thinking, "May the monks in this monastery be happy, free from enmity and free from affliction"—this is called loving-kindness as mental action (*mettā manokamma*).
When laypeople think, "May the noble ones be happy, free from enmity and free from affliction"—this is called loving-kindness as mental action.

"Gains" (*lābhā*) refers to requisites such as robes that have been obtained. "Righteous" (*dhammikā*) means arisen through the practice of alms-gathering in accordance with the Dhamma and justice, having abandoned wrong livelihoods such as hypocrisy and the like.

"At least as much as what has fallen into the bowl" (*antamaso pattapariyāpannamattam-pi*) means, at the very minimum, even just two or three spoonfuls of alms-food that has fallen into the bowl and is contained within it.
"One who enjoys without making a division" (*appaṭivibhattabhogī*) means one who consumes after having made no distinction between the gift and the recipient worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
Here, there are two kinds of "divisions": the division of material goods (*āmisa-paṭivibhatta*) and the division of persons (*puggala-paṭivibhatta*).
Among these, "division of material goods" refers to a mental differentiation such as, "I will give this much, I will not give that much. "Of such-and-such a person... [and so forth].
"‘I will give to such-and-such, I will not give to such-and-such’—this kind of mental differentiation is called ‘differentiation by person.
One who eats without performing either of these two is called ‘one who enjoys what is undifferentiated.

Therefore he said: ‘He does not eat after having differentiated the alms-food,’ and so forth. By the word ‘also’ (*pi*) in the phrase ‘even when not giving,’ it is implied that [he eats] even when giving."

This shows that it is appropriate. Indeed, giving is not prohibited for anyone; therefore, when there is the possibility, one should give even to an immoral person who has need, provided it is done out of compassion and not for the sake of fulfilling a formal obligation.
Because one who fulfills the "conducive to remembrance" (sāraṇīya) qualities shares their enjoyments without partiality, it is said: "It must indeed be given to all.
However, for those who are ill and so forth, there is a specific [allocation].
Having given a gift that is not subject to partiality—that is, because there is no exclusion such as "I will not give to so-and-so"—for partiality consists primarily in making distinctions.
Therefore he said: "It is even permissible to give after discriminating between the sick and those attending the sick... [and so on]... it is fitting to give after having discerned.
Regarding the phrase "one who shares enjoyments," this is the characteristic of one who shares enjoyments: whatever excellent thing one receives, [one gives it away].
Protecting his own purity of livelihood, he does not give various gains to householders under the pretext of seeking gain for gain,
nor does he consume them himself, thinking, "May there not be a state of exclusive consumption on my part. And when receiving such things, one should accept them with the thought,
"Let this be common property of the Saṅgha," and having struck the gong, they should be consumed as belonging to the Saṅgha.
He sees it as if it were [already] so. By this, the establishment of that gain as common to all three times is shown.
By the words, “And while receiving it, let it be shared with the Saṅgha,” the time of receiving is shown; by the words, “Having received...
[and] he sees,” the time of having received is shown. Both of these, however, are preceded by such a preliminary stage.
The prior time is established by the fact that [the object] does not exist without it. This too occurs before the acceptance: "I shall accept it so that it becomes common property of the Saṅgha";
while accepting it, [the thought occurs]: "I am accepting it so that it becomes common property of the Saṅgha";
and after having accepted it, [the thought occurs]: "It has been accepted by me so that it becomes common property of the Saṅgha."

Having thus endowed it with the three characteristics, one who enjoys what has been obtained without violating the characteristic of completion is a sharer of enjoyments and one whose enjoyments are not divided.
Now, who fulfills this duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) and who does not fulfill it? First of all, the immoral person does not fulfill it; for indeed...
Those possessed of virtue take what belongs to him. However, one who is pure in virtue fulfills the duties (*vatta*) without breaking them.
Herein, this is the duty: if someone gives [food] specifically intended for his mother, father, teacher, preceptor, or others, he may give what ought to be given;
yet for him, there is no "duty of remembrance" (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), but rather it is called "tending to an impediment. This is the duty of remembrance.

Indeed, it is appropriate only for one who has no impediments to [receive] them. However, when distributing them specifically, they should be given to the sick, those attending the sick, newcomers, those departing, and the newly ordained who do not know how to take up the outer robe and bowl.
Having given these, the remainder should be distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder; rather than giving little by little to everyone, one should give as much as each person takes.
If there is nothing remaining, one should go out again for alms; then, starting from the senior’s seat, whatever is choice should be given, and the remainder should be eaten.
This duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), however, is well fulfilled by an assembly that has been thoroughly trained in the method of fulfilling the duties of courtesy.
This occurs. For when a community is well-trained, one who receives [alms] from elsewhere does not take it;
even if one does not receive it from elsewhere, one takes only what is moderate, not more than that.
Furthermore, this quality of courtesy (*sāraṇīyadhamma*) is fulfilled in twelve years by one who gives whatever is obtained after wandering for alms again and again, and not before then.

For if, even in the twelfth year, one who fulfills the duties of courtesy (sāraṇīyadhamma) goes to bathe after placing his bowl full of alms-food in the sitting hall, the senior of the Saṅgha asks, "Whose bowl is this?
When it is replied, "It belongs to the one fulfilling the duties of courtesy," he says, "Bring it here! and having examined and eaten all the alms-food, he leaves the bowl empty.
Then, if that bhikkhu, seeing the bowl empty, gives rise to dejection, thinking, "They have consumed [the food] without leaving anything for me," the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* is broken;
it must be fulfilled again for twelve years. For this is similar to the probation (*parivāsa*) for one belonging to another sect (*titthiya*):
once a breach has occurred, it must indeed be fulfilled anew. But he who thinks, "It is a gain for me! It is well-gained by me!"...
When he generates joy, thinking, “My fellow celibates enjoy what has come into my bowl without even asking for permission,” that is called *puṇṇa*.
For one who has thus fulfilled the quality of conciliation (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), however, there is neither envy nor avarice; such a person is beloved by human beings.
Conditions are easily obtained; even when what is placed in his bowl is given to him, it is never exhausted;
he receives the finest goods in the place where the communal property is kept; and when danger or famine arises, the deities exert themselves on his behalf.
Here are some examples: it is said that the Elder Tissa, who dwelt at Leṇagiri, lived near Mahākhīragāma.
About fifty elders, while traveling to Nāgadīpa to pay homage at the cetiya, entered the village of Khīra for alms;
having received nothing, they departed. As the senior elder was entering the village, he saw them and asked, "Venerable sirs, have you received anything?
"We wandered about, friend," they replied. Knowing that they had received nothing, he said, "Venerable sirs, please remain right here until I return."
"Friends, we fifty people have not even received so much as the oil for our bowls. "Venerable sir, the resident monks are capable;
even if they do not receive anything, they know the path to the village where alms are gathered. The elders arrived.
The elder entered the village. At the very house where he was staying, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and was looking out for the elder.
Standing there, she filled the bowl of the elder who had just arrived at the door and gave it to him.
Taking it, he went into the presence of the elders and said to the senior of the Saṅgha, "Take this, venerable sir. The elder thought, "With so many of us, nothing has been obtained;
yet this man has come back so quickly after taking it—what could it be? With this very look on his face, the elder looked toward the others. By that very manner of looking, the elder [understood].
Knowing this, he said, "Venerable sirs, this alms-food has been obtained righteously and justly;
please accept it without hesitation," and starting from the beginning, he gave as much as they required to everyone, and then he himself ate as much as he required.
Then, at the conclusion of his meal, the elders asked him, "Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma? He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have not."
"Supramundane Dhamma. "Friend, have you attained the jhānas? "I do not have that either, venerable sir.
"Is there not, friend, the miracle? "Venerable sir, I have fulfilled the qualities conducive to harmony;
from the time they were fulfilled, even if there were a hundred thousand bhikkhus, what is in my bowl does not diminish. "Excellent, excellent, good man! This is worthy of you."
"Tuyhanti" (They belong to you). This, first of all, is the story regarding the bowl that does not run out.
Furthermore, this same elder, having gone to the place of almsgiving for the Great Offering of Giribhaṇḍa at Cetiyapabbata, asked:
"What is the most excellent gift in this offering? "Two robes, venerable sir. "These shall come to me," he said.
Having heard this, the minister informed the king, "A certain young man spoke thus. The king said, "The mind of that youth is such;
however, fine robes are suitable for the great elders," and saying, "I shall give them to the great elders," he set them aside.
When the community of monks was standing in order and he was giving [the gifts], those robes placed upon the head reached his hand.
They did not mount [the elephant]; others mounted instead. However, when it was the youth’s turn to give the gift, he had already mounted the elephant’s hand.

Having placed the youth on the hand, the king looked at the face of his minister, seated the youth, gave the gift, dismissed the Saṅgha, and sat down beside the youth, asking: "Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma? He—
“Even by way of a figurative expression, when speaking of what does not exist, he said: ‘Great King, I have no supramundane Dhamma.
But, Bhante, did you not say so even before? “Yes, Great King. I am one who fulfills the qualities that create affinity.
From the time I began fulfilling that Dhamma, the best portion of the goods to be distributed has come to me. “Excellent, excellent, Bhante!”

"This is appropriate for you," she said, and having paid homage, she departed. This is the story regarding the rule that the best portion of goods should fall to the one in the place of distribution (*bhājanīya-ṭṭhāna*).
However, out of fear of Caṇḍālatissa, the inhabitants of the brother-village fled without informing the Elder Nun Nāgā.
At dawn, the Elder Nun [thought], "The village is exceedingly quiet; wait and observe," and addressed the junior nuns.
She said: "Having gone there and learned that they had all departed, they returned and reported it to the Elder Nun.
Having heard this, she said, 'Do not worry about their departure; apply yourselves solely to your own study, questioning, and wise reflection.
Then, at the time for the alms-round, having put on her robes, she went to the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate, accompanied by twelve others."
She stood there. A deity dwelling in the tree, having given almsfood to all twelve bhikkhunīs, said:
"Noble ladies, do not go elsewhere; come here always. The Elder’s younger brother, however, was a monk named Nāgatthera;
he thought, "There is great danger; it is not possible to survive here. We shall go to the other shore," and accompanied by eleven others, he set out.
Having departed from his own dwelling place, he came to his brother’s village thinking, “I shall go after seeing the Elder Nun.
Hearing that the Elders had arrived, the nun went into their presence and asked, “What is it, Noble Sirs? He related the circumstances to her.
She said, “Stay in the monastery for one day today; you may depart tomorrow. The Elders then returned to the monastery.
On the following day, the elder nun, having wandered for alms at the foot of a tree, approached the elder and said, "Please partake of this alms-food.
The elder replied, "It will suffice, elder nun," and remained silent. She said, "Venerable sir, this alms-food is lawful;
please partake of it without anxiety. He replied, "It will suffice, elder nun. She then took his bowl.
He threw it into the air. The bowl remained suspended in the sky. The Elder said, "Even though it remains at the height of seventy palm trees, this is still the alms-food of the nuns, Elder.

Then he thought, "Fear does not exist at all times; when fear has subsided, while I am preaching the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa), if I am mentally reproached by [someone] saying, 'O alms-collecting monk, you spent your time eating the food of the nuns!'"
“I shall not be able to steady myself; be heedful, O Elder Sisters,” he said, and ascended the path.
A tree deity, standing there thinking, “If the Elder eats the alms-food from the hand of the Elder Sister, I will not turn him back;
if he does not eat it, I will turn him back,” saw the Elder’s departure from the tree.
Having descended, she said, "Venerable sir, give me your bowl," and taking the bowl, she led the Elder to the very foot of the tree.
She prepared a seat, gave him alms-food, and having ensured that he had finished his meal, she made a promise [to serve him].
For seven years, she attended upon twelve bhikkhunīs and twelve bhikkhus. This is what is meant by "the deity applied herself with zeal" in this context.
The *vatthu* (narrative). For therein, the Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*).
They are "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*) because there is no breach (*khaṇḍa*) in them; however, in order to show that breach of theirs, the words beginning with "of whom" (*yassā*) were spoken.
Therein, for those whose virtue is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), the beginning and end should be understood according to the sequence of the recitation. Therefore he said, "In seven," and so forth.
However, for those who have not received full ordination (*anupasampanna*), the beginning and end of the precepts are obtained through the sequence of their undertaking.
It is "like a garment with its hem cut," meaning like a cloth whose edge or fringe has been severed. This is a dissimilar illustration because of the addition of the term "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍāni*).
The remaining illustrations are to be understood in the same way. "Broken" (*khaṇḍa*) means possessing a break, or that which is shattered.
The same method applies to the terms *chidda* (hole) and so forth as well. The connection is: "like a cow with a dissimilar color.
That which has half or a third part mixed with a dissimilar color is *sambhinnavanna* (of mixed color) or *sabala* (spotted).
However, that which is interspersed here and there with drops of a dissimilar color is *kammāsa* (dappled). This is the distinction between these.
"By making one free" means by releasing one from the slavery of craving and establishing the state of freedom.
And the release of virtue from the slavery of craving consists in bringing it to a state that serves as a necessary condition for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*);

thus its status as a necessary condition for the turning away is shown. Furthermore, by the phrase "by making one free," [virtues] are called "freedom-makers" or "freedoms" through the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).

He shows that this is the exposition (*niddesa*). Furthermore, because the person who possesses them is called independent (*serī*), self-mastering (*sayaṃvasī*), and free (*bhujisso*), they are therefore "free" (*bhujissāni*).
Because they are praiseworthy due to their state of extreme purity, they are "praised by the wise" (*viññupasatthāni*).
The mention of "the wise" is made because the praise of the ignorant is not authoritative. Because they are not clung to by craving or views, [it is said]: "By this virtue..."

It is because it is not clung to through the clinging of craving— thinking, "By means of this virtue, having become a deva, I shall be permanent, stable, and eternal there"— and because it is not clung to through the clinging of views— thinking, "I shall become a deva or some other kind of deva. Alternatively,
it is because one has pointed out some failure among the four failures, saying, "This slave of yours is in his virtues," and then [said], "This...

The meaning here should be understood as follows: because it is impossible for anyone to touch upon or accuse one of having previously fallen into [such an offense], they are "untouchable" (aparāmaṭṭhāni).
As for "virtue" (sīla), it is for the purpose of bringing about concentration through the succession of states beginning with non-remorse;
thus he said, "conducive to concentration" (samādhisaṃvattanikāni). Those whose function is to lead to the attainment of concentration are "conducive to concentration."

“Sāmāñña” means the state of being the same (samānabhāva). Because there is no division—just as there is none in gold that has been melted down—due to the state of the four purifications being complete, there is a commonality with virtue;
thus it is “sīlasāmañña. One who has gone to, or approached, that is “sīlasāmaññagata. Therefore he said: “one whose virtue has attained the state of being the same.
This means one whose virtue has attained the state of being the same through the perfection of virtue, and who thus lives in commonality.

The meaning is as follows: For the virtue (sīla) of those who have attained the stream-entry (sotāpanna) and so forth remains exactly the same as the virtue of other stream-enterers and so forth, even when they dwell in the midst of the ocean or in the world of the gods;

there is no diversity in the virtue of the Path (maggasīla). Granted, there might also be no diversity in the virtue of the fourfold purification (catupārisuddhisīla) among ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), but that is not absolute and is therefore not intended here; the virtue of the Path, however, is absolute.
Regarding "of certain nature," it was said with reference to that very thing: "Those virtues which... and so forth.
"By which" means by this [view] which is directly evident to both me and you. "View" means the right view of the Path. "Faultless" means having removed faults;
the meaning is that the evil states such as lust and so on have been utterly severed. "Leads out" means from the suffering of saṃsāra.
It "escapes" (nissarati) means it goes forth (nigacchati). For it is said that, by itself leading the person who possesses that path, it causes them to emerge from the suffering of saṃsāra.
"One who acts accordingly" (takkaro) means one who performs what has been instructed by the Teacher; the meaning is: of one who practices exactly as instructed.
"Having attained commonality of view" (diṭṭhisāmaññagato) means having reached the state of possessing a shared view through the penetration of the Truths.
The commentary on the section on questions and answers is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Sixfold Origin of Offenses (Cha-āpatti-samudāna-vāra-kathā-vaṇṇanā): 276.

Regarding the phrase "by the first origin of offense" and so forth, everything can be understood by following the canonical text as it proceeds through its sections of enumeration, exposition, and so on.

293. Regarding the section on the classification of *samatha* (tranquility) within the discourse on the methods for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇapariyāya*), it is said that "greed is the precursor" because they dispute with greed as the cause. Thus, it is stated: "Greed is the precursor."
The same applies to the remaining cases. "Points" (*ṭhānāni*) means causes (*kāraṇāni*). It is called a "point" (*ṭhāna*) because things stand (*tiṭṭhanti*) therein.

What stands there? Disputes, legal issues, and so forth. It is called a "basis" (*vatthu*) because they dwell (*vasanti*) therein; it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*) because they arise (*bhavanti*) therein.

Because those possessing wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate minds dispute [over these], it is said that there are "nine roots. The "twelve roots" refer to the twelve roots beginning with "he is angry and resentful," and so on.
294–295. These same twelve, together with [the offenses of] body and speech, are called the "fourteen roots.

Regarding the phrase "the seven classes of offenses are the grounds," it should be understood that for one who conceals an offense after having committed it, the offenses previously committed are the "grounds" for that [concealment].
This is because of the statement: "There is no wholesome legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). In the case of a legal issue arising from an offense...
Six roots are mentioned by way of the unwholesome and the indeterminate. However, a wholesome consciousness is a factor (*aṅga*), not a root (*hetu*).

296. Regarding the phrase "the four kinds of action are the bases": here, "action" (*kamma*) refers to the textual passage that proceeds by way of showing what is to be done, such as "it should be done thus.
For those who perform [the rite] according to the established textual sequence, the performance is called the "matter of duty" (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

The formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattiñattidutiya*), a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), and the formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) arise from the motion;
thus it is said, "either from a motion or from seeking permission. The legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is settled by one method of settlement;
the meaning is that it is accomplished. It is stated that they are "common to the legal issue concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*)" because they must be settled by those same methods.
Commentary on the Section on "Belonging to That" (Tabbhāgiyavāra): 298.

Regarding "belonging to that" (*tabbhāgiya*) of a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*): they belong to its side by virtue of being the settling of that very legal issue arising from a dispute.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the commonality of the methods of settlement (*samatha*).

299. Asking whether all methods of settling (*samatha*) can settle a single legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) together or not, he said: "Are the methods of settling common to one another, or are the methods of settling not common to one another?
He further stated: "The majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) is common to the presence rule (*sammukhāvinaya*)," because a settlement by majority decision does not occur without the presence rule.
Because one who possesses the *sativinaya* and so forth has no need for a *yebhuyyasika* (decision by majority), it is said: "The *sativinaya*... [etc. ...are not shared.
The same applies to the remaining cases. This same method applies to the section on their respective categories (*tabbhāgiyavāra*) as well.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the section on the *vinaya*.

302. Since the method of the Vinaya is applicable to all modes of settling disputes (*samatha*), the section on the Vinaya has been set forth beginning with the words, "The Vinaya is the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).

In the phrase "it might not be a *sammukhā-vinaya*," the remaining modes of settling—such as the *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection) and so forth—are intended, excluding the *sammukhā-vinaya*. This same principle applies to the others as well.
Commentary on the Section on the Wholesome (Kusalavārakathāvaṇṇanā) 303.
When a confession is made in the presence of the Saṅgha, that admission is called "being in the presence of the Saṅgha" (saṅghasammukhatā).

It is said that the statement beginning with "Skilled in resolution in the presence" (*sammukhāvinayo kusalo*) was spoken with reference to the mind of that confession. There is no resolution in the presence that is unwholesome.
The *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) consists of three factors—the presence of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the persons—and it does not exist without these.
In that regard, when it is performed by those with wholesome minds (*kusalacitta*), it is wholesome; when it is performed by Arahants, it is indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Because these factors, such as the presence of the Saṅgha, are the opposites of unwholesomeness, there is no possibility of unwholesomeness therein; therefore, it is said: "There is no unwholesome *sammukhāvinaya*."

It is said: "The majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) is unwholesome at the time of settling a dispute by those who speak contrary to the Dhamma, when even among those speaking according to the Dhamma, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma becomes the distributor of voting sticks.
The resolution through recollection (*sativinaya*) is unwholesome when it is granted for intentional [offenses] to one who is not an arahant.

The resolution because of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) is unwholesome when granted to one who is not insane. Acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) is unwholesome when acting upon the admission of one who is insane or ignorant."

"The *tassapāpiyasikā* (proceeding for the worse) is unwholesome when applied to one who is pure; the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) is unwholesome when applied intentionally during a great quarrel.
In all cases, it is indeterminate (*abyākata*) by way of an Arahant. All this has been stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the resolution of disputes (*samathavāra-vissajjanāvāra-kathāvaṇṇanā*).
304–305. "Where *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority) is applicable, there *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) is also applicable," and so forth—this is the question.
"At whatever time, by means of *sammukhāvinaya*... and so forth—this is its answer.
At whatever time a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) is settled both by *sammukhāvinaya* and by *yebhuyyasikā*, at that time, wherever *yebhuyyasikā* is applicable...

In this context, the phrase "the resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) is obtained" is to be connected in every instance. Wherever the "acting according to what is admitted" (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) is applicable, there the "resolution face-to-face" is also applicable;

for example, when one, two, or many monks are asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense? and they admit it by saying "Yes," both the "acting according to what is admitted" and the "resolution face-to-face" apply.
They are obtained. In that regard, concerning the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) described as "presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and presence of the person":
if it is confessed in the presence of the Saṅgha, there is "presence of the Saṅgha. If it is confessed in that very place, there is also "presence of the Dhamma and Vinaya" obtained.
Then, if those disputing acknowledge one another [as witnesses], there is "presence of the person. Of that very...

If it is confessed in the presence [of the Sangha], it is obtained through face-to-face confrontation with both the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Or, when one person confesses an offense to another alone, and the latter says, "Do you see it?

and the former replies, "I see it," then in that instance, both the *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) and the *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what is admitted)—which are designated as face-to-face confrontation with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person—are obtained.
Commentary on the Section on Association (Saṃsaṭṭhavārakathāvaṇṇanā) 306.

The settling of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) is called "method of settlement" (*samatha*); therefore, since there are no methods of settlement without legal issues, it is said: "He should not be addressed thus... [etc. ...having analyzed them, one should point out their distinction.
Commentary on the Section on Methods of Settlement and Legal Issues (Samathādhikaraṇavārakathāvaṇṇanā).

309–310. “Are the methods of settling (samatha) settled by means of methods of settling? and so forth is the question. “It may be that the methods of settling are settled by means of methods of settling” and so forth is the answer.

In this context, regarding the phrase “the methods of settling are settled by means of methods of settling”: here, *sammanti* means they succeed (*sampajjanti*), or alternatively, legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) are settled, meaning they reach pacification (*vūpasama*).
Therefore, it is said that the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) is settled by means of the presence rule (*sammukhāvinaya*).

In this context, it should be understood that *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority) occurs together with *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of), but not with *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection) and the others, because those [latter] do not assist it. 311.
The reading is: “*Sammukhāvinayo* is settled by means of a legal question involving a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). “*Sammukhāvinayo* is not [settled] by anything else...”

Because it is stated at the conclusion, "it is settled," *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) is not something that must itself be settled by another means of settlement (*samatha*) or by another legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "A legal issue arising from a dispute... is settled by a legal issue arising from business": here it should be understood that the legal issue arising from a dispute is settled by a legal issue arising from business in this manner: "Let the venerable ones hear me... [the formal motion]... first I cast the voting ticket.
Commentary on the Section on Origination.

314. Regarding the question, "Which legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) does the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) give rise to?"—the meaning is that no legal issue whatsoever is not given rise to by the mere statement, "This is not the Dhamma.
Commentary on the Section on Grouping (Bhajativārakathāvaṇṇanā) 318–9:
"Which legal issue is included? means which of the legal issues it is included in; or rather, this very [dispute] itself.

The recitation (*pāṭha*). A legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) "partakes of" a legal issue arising from a dispute means that a dispute which arises later partakes of a dispute that arose earlier.
A legal issue arising from a dispute "partakes of" two methods of settlement (*samatha*) means it partakes [of them] as if saying, "You are capable of settling me.
It is "comprised by" the two methods of settlement by those who say, "We shall settle it."
It is comprised by two methods of tranquility (samatha).
The Section on Questions from the Khandhaka;
Commentary on the Exposition of Questions.

"320. 'Together with the introduction (nidāna) and the exposition (niddesa)': here, 'by the introduction' means by the introduction consisting of the place where the training rule (sikkhāpada) was promulgated.
'By the exposition' means by the exposition of the individuals (puggala) and so forth. By both of these, the basis (vatthu) for each respective training rule is shown;
therefore, the meaning here is: 'We shall ask about the Khandhaka together with the basis. In that regard..."
In that *Upasampadakkhandhaka*, the "supreme words" were spoken; by the method beginning with, "Monks, a person less than twenty years of age is not to be ordained," the supreme words were spoken.
In the *Cammasaṃyutta*, that is, in the *Cammakkhandhaka*, there is the *Ekuttarikanaya* (the Numerical Method).
321. Explanation of the Single Occurrence:

"An intermediate offense regarding purification from the root" refers to that committed by one who, having committed an intermediate offense, has undergone a sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana) and remains there.
"An intermediate offense regarding purification by value" refers to when, after having committed several offenses, among those...
"By one who dwells having taken the calculation of the duration based on the longest period of concealment, an offense is incurred"—this is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
"With a mind full of zeal" means with a mind full of zeal [thinking], "I shall incur it again.
This was said with reference to the eight rules for bhikkhunīs. For that very reason he said: "In the eighth rule, for a bhikkhunī, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense."
[It] occurs. Because it is stated, “In order not to falsify a legitimate promise,” there is no *dukkaṭa* offense for failing to fulfill an illegitimate promise.
For instance, if one says, “You may disrobe,” and having been addressed with a pure mind, one agrees saying “Very well,” yet does not subsequently disrobe, there is no offense.
This applies in all such cases. Regarding the “fifteen matters”: “I shall speak at the proper time...”
Regarding the fifteen qualities stated in the passage beginning with “not at an improper time,” those who are capable of committing an offense are called "capable of falling into an offense.
The commentary on the section on single items is finished.
The commentary on the section on pairs begins.
322. Regarding "in pairs": it refers to storing after having left [the salt] in the sun for too long. One incurs [an offense] by confessing while teaching what is similar to the substance;
one incurs [an offense] by not confessing while laying down the burden, thinking, "I will not confess the offense I have committed.
"Romaka" means that which is produced in the country of Roma. "Pakkālaka" means barley-alkali. Since salts are permitted, salts are also mentioned in the pairs.
The commentary on the section on dyads is finished.
Commentary on the section on triads (323).
Regarding the triads: "Having performed bodily action associated with speech" means having performed an act of homage with the body. "Distinguished by such acts as uncovering the head," and so forth.
It is divided into types such as the sounding of a drum at the mouth [of a vessel].

A training rule (*sikkhāpada*) for the transgression of which there are offenses originating from the body is a training rule prescribed for the door of the body. "To destroy" means to ruin. "It should not be accepted" means:
"Do not even go out from this monastery; rather, come into the presence of those who uphold the Vinaya to provide a formal decision."
The meaning is that his word should not be accepted when it has been spoken.

They are both "unwholesome" (*akusala*) and "roots" (*mūla*): they are called "unwholesome" in the sense of being produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*) because they are exclusively unwholesome in nature;
they are called "roots" because they effect the state of firm establishment for the states associated with themselves, not because they effect an unwholesome state.
For there is no unwholesome nature in unwholesome states from their very root, nor a wholesome nature in wholesome states and so forth.
If that were the case, then delusion (*moha*) within the two types of bewildered consciousness (*momūha-citta*) would not be unwholesome.
"Bad conduct" (*duccarita*) means that, by way of condition, associated phenomena, and mode of occurrence, they have not been well or correctly conducted.

"Ugly" (*virūpāni*) means repulsive, because they are undesirable in both the present and the future. In phrases such as "well-practiced," the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated above.
Both of these triads may be explained either by way of their designation (*paññatti*) or by way of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*).
First, by way of designation: transgression of a training rule prescribed for the door of the body is bodily misconduct (*kāya-duccarita*); non-transgression is bodily good conduct (*kāya-sucarita*).
The transgression of a training rule prescribed for the door of speech is verbal misconduct; its non-transgression is verbal good conduct.
The transgression of a training rule prescribed for both [doors] is mental misconduct, because there is no training rule prescribed specifically for the door of mind.
This should be understood by way of an offense originating from non-action in respect of these two doors, as has been stated.
The non-transgression regarding offenses is itself mental good conduct. This is the explanation according to the formal designation (*paṇṇatti*).

However, the three volitions beginning with killing living beings—whether they arise at the door of the body or the door of speech—are bodily misconduct because the name of the kamma is not abandoned even when it arises at another door, due to its general occurrence and its frequent occurrence. Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said:
“Kamma operates through the doors; the doors themselves do not operate through the doors.
Therefore, by way of the doors, kamma-acts are established as distinct from one another.

Likewise, the four volitions beginning with false speech, whether they arise at the door of the body or the door of speech, constitute verbal misconduct (*vācī-duccarita*); [as does] covetousness (*abhijjhā*).
Ill will and wrong view—these three factors associated with volition that constitutes mental action (*manokamma*) are mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*).
However, covetousness and the rest, which are associated with volition that constitutes bodily and verbal action, are either partial to one side or indeterminate (*abbohārika*).

Furthermore, the three types of volition and the three types of abstention (*virati*) that arise in one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth constitute bodily good conduct (*kāyasucarita*).

Because it proceeds by way of the non-performance of bodily transgression. However, when the training rules are undertaken by means of the body, there is nothing at all that needs to be said regarding the nature of virtue as bodily good conduct.

For one who abstains from false speech and so forth, the four volitions and the four abstinences constitute verbal good conduct, because they proceed by way of the non-performance of verbal transgression.
Non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—these three factors associated with volition constitute mental good conduct. This concludes the discussion on the courses of kamma.
The commentary on the section of threes is finished.
The commentary on the section of fours follows.

324. Regarding the tetrads: "Noble speech" (*ariya-vohāra*) refers to the transactions, dealings, and verbal expressions of the noble ones (*ariya*), that is, of the true persons (*sappurisa*). "Ignoble speech" (*anariya-vohāra*) refers to the transactions, dealings, and verbal expressions of the ignoble, the base. "Speaking what has been seen" (*diṭṭha-vāditā*) means speaking thus: "I have seen it.
In this context, the meaning should be understood by way of the volition (*cetanā*) that originates each respective [act].
He says, "by way of what first arose," because among those belonging to the first eon, the male characteristic itself arose first.
"He abandons the former male characteristic" means that he abandons the male characteristic reckoned as "former" because of its state of being the precursor in the sense already stated.
"One hundred and thirty training rules" means one hundred training rules plus thirty.
"Regarding the four *pārājika* offenses for a monk and a nun" refers specifically to the four *pārājika* offenses that are common to both.
"The first question" refers to the question: "Is there a difference in the objective basis (*vatthu*), but not a difference in the offense (*āpatti*)?
"There is a similarity in the offense, but not a similarity in the objective basis"—this is what is called the second [question] here.
“Non-offense regarding the interruption of the rains-retreat”: there is no offense in this interruption of the rains-retreat; thus it is “non-offense regarding the interruption of the rains-retreat.
The meaning is: of that interruption of the rains-retreat which is without offense. “Speech with wisdom” (*mantābhāsā*):
because it is spoken after having investigated with the intellect (*mati*), speech that is not idle chatter is here called “speech with wisdom.”
From the time of the ninth bhikkhunī onwards, even preceptors are worthy of being saluted but not worthy of rising from one's seat;

for the Blessed One, by saying, "Bhikkhus, I allow that in the dining hall, of the eight bhikkhunīs [at the head] it shall be according to seniority, and of the rest according to the order of their arrival," has established that in the dining hall, starting from the beginning, it is only for the first eight bhikkhunīs that precedence is according to seniority.
It has been permitted for the remainder [of the nuns] according to the order of their arrival;
therefore, starting from the ninth nun onwards, even if the preceptor is a nun who arrives later, she is not one to whom rising is due.

She is merely one to whom salutation is due, because she must be saluted by those already seated simply by raising her head. However, among the eight [nuns] seated at the beginning, whichever one is more senior...
If one who is senior arrives, she is permitted to sit after having had a junior nun ordained by her.

Therefore, she is worthy of being stood up for by those eight nuns. But as for one who is junior even to those eight—even if she is sixty years old—she is permitted to sit according to the order of arrival.

"Speaking thus while standing in a border region: 'It is not allowable here'—one who speaks thus while standing in a border region incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for transgressing the Vinaya.
For one who says that what is allowable is 'not allowable' is said to abolish what has been prescribed.
The same principle applies to such statements as 'it is allowable here,' and so forth."
The commentary on the section of four [cases] is finished.
Commentary on the section of five [cases]: 325.
Regarding the five [cases], because of the statement, "Being invited and having already partaken of a meal, without having asked a monk who is present," this refers to an improper invitation.
"Going uninvited while one is already eating is not permitted"; therefore, it is said, "they are allowable for a forest-dweller (*piṇḍapātika*).

The same principle applies to group meals (*gaṇabhojana*) and so forth. "Eating after having resolved" means eating after forming an intention (*ābhoga*) such as, "This is the time for the sick," and so on.
"Non-designation" (*avikappanā*) means not designating [the food] in this way: "I give my share of alms-food to such-and-such a person."

Regarding the phrase "disrepute or blame": here, disrepute (*ayasa*) is the speaking of faults in one's absence; blame (*garahā*) is [speaking of faults] in one's presence. "It scatters" (*viyasati*) thus it is "calamity" (*byasana*);
