the meaning is that it scatters and destroys welfare and happiness. Calamity of relatives is "relative calamity" (*ñātibyasana*);

the meaning is the destruction of relatives through thieves, disease, fear, and so forth. Calamity of wealth is "wealth calamity" (*bhogabyasana*); [this occurs] by way of kings, thieves, and so forth.
The meaning is the destruction of wealth. Illness itself is the calamity; thus, "the calamity of illness. For illness is a calamity because it ruins—that is, destroys—health.
The calamity of virtue is "virtue-calamity" (*sīlabyasana*); this is a name for immorality. A view that arises destroying right view is itself the calamity;
thus, "view-calamity" (*diṭṭhibyasana*). "Perfection of kinsmen" means the excellence or fulfillment of kinsmen.
The state of having much. The same method applies to the perfection of enjoyments. The perfection of health is the attainment of health;
its fulfillment is being free from illness for a long time. The same method applies to the perfections of virtue and view as well.
"He delimited his duties" means he brought to completion the duties to be performed on that day. "He recollected eight eons," and so forth.
This indicates that having produced jhāna at that moment, he then produced the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).

"Having reached the stage of formal action by means of a motion" (*ñattiyā kammappatto*) means that once the motion (*ñatti*) had been established, he reached the stage of the formal act consisting of the proclamation (*anussāvana*).
"Through dullness and delusion" means that because of his own dullness and delusion, he neither understood the undertaking nor the benefit; rather, it was due to his own dullness and delusion.
One becomes a forest-dweller through ignorance alone. One who is of evil desire and overcome by desire does so by standing upon such evil desire and being dominated by it, thinking:

"While I am dwelling in the forest, they will show me honor with the four requisites, saying 'This one is a forest-dweller,' and they will esteem me for qualities such as 'this monk is modest' and 'he is secluded.
Thus, being overcome by that very desire, he becomes a forest-dweller.
The meaning is "it happens. Therefore he said: "one who, desiring the acquisition of requisites through dwelling in the forest.
One who enters and dwells in the forest due to insanity is called a forest-dweller because of that insanity and mental derangement.
Regarding the phrase "praised": this factor of forest-dwelling is praised and commended by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas; thus, one is a forest-dweller.
The commentary on the section of five is finished.
Commentary on the Section of Six (Chakkavāra): 326. Regarding the six [rules], the word-commentary shows that they should be carried for a maximum of six years. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the section of sixes is finished.
Commentary on the section of sevens (327):

Regarding the sevens, those very factors stated in the section of sixes should be applied according to the sevens; thus, having divided the fourteen maximums stated in the section of sixes into two groups, they should be applied by way of two sets of seven.
“He knows an offense” means he knows an offense simply as “an offense. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Regarding the phrase *ābhicetasikānaṃ*:
here, *abhiceto* refers to a preeminent, purified mind because it is beautiful, opposed to, and purer than ordinary sense-sphere minds (*kāmāvacara-citta*);
this is a designation for the mind of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*). [The term] *abhicetasi*...
"Born of the higher mind" (*ābhicetasika*) means either "born from the higher mind" or "dependent upon the higher mind.

"Dwellings in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) means dwellings that are happy in this very life. "This very life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the manifest personal existence; the meaning is "those which constitute a dwelling in happiness therein.
This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhānas. For when meditators have entered those [jhānas] and are seated, right here in this very [life]...
They experience the bliss of renunciation, which is undefiled within their own person; therefore, they are called "those who dwell in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā*).
"Obtaining at will" (*nikāmalābhī*) means obtaining according to one's wish;
it means being capable of entering [the attainment] at whatever moment one desires. "Obtaining without difficulty" (*akicchalābhī*) means having easily suppressed the opposing states.
This means he is capable of attaining [the attainment]. "One who gains it without difficulty" means one who gains it abundantly;
that is to say, he is capable of emerging exactly according to his predetermined limit. For some are indeed gainers, yet they are unable to attain it at whatever moment they desire.
Some are able to attain it in such a manner, but they suppress obstacles only with difficulty.
A certain person enters [jhāna] in such a way that he suppresses the obstacles with ease, yet he is unable to emerge at the exact predetermined time, like a water-clock mechanism.
"The destruction of the taints" means the destruction of all defilements by means of the path of Arahatship. "Taintless" means free from the taints.
Regarding the phrase "liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom": here, by the word "mind" (ceto), the concentration associated with the fruit of Arhatship is meant;
and by the word "wisdom" (paññā), the wisdom associated with that same fruit is meant.

Furthermore, it should be understood that concentration is called "liberation of mind" because it is liberated from lust, while wisdom is called "liberation by wisdom" because it is liberated from ignorance. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, whatever concentration he has, that is his faculty of concentration. Whatever wisdom he has, that is his faculty of wisdom.
Thus, bhikkhus, through the fading away of lust comes liberation of mind; through the fading away of ignorance comes liberation by wisdom.
Furthermore, it should be understood here that liberation of mind is the fruit of serenity, and liberation by wisdom is the fruit of insight.

"In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāve*). "Having realized by direct knowledge for oneself" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having made it manifest through one's own wisdom;

the sense is that one has known it independently of others. Having abandoned dependence on others and the grasping of mere logic—as is the case with knowledge consisting of what is heard and so forth—one has made it manifest through one's own wisdom, which is the attainment of meditation following the voice of another.
The intention is that he does not [attain it] by means of self-originated knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*). "Having attained and dwelling" means having reached and having accomplished, he dwells.
The commentary on the section of seven is finished.
The commentary on the section of eight.
328. "By seeing eight benefits in the eight [cases]" means:
"But here, monks, a monk has committed an offense; he regards that offense as no offense, while other monks regard that offense as an offense. If those monks..."

They know of that bhikkhu thus: "This venerable one is indeed learned, one who has mastered the tradition, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training;
if we were to suspend this bhikkhu for not seeing an offense, we would not perform the Uposatha together with this bhikkhu."
“Monks, if [the monks] think, ‘We will perform the Uposatha without this monk; because of that, there will arise for the Saṅgha quarreling,
strife, contention, dispute, schism in the Saṅgha, fracture of the Saṅgha, division of the Saṅgha, and separation of the Saṅgha,’ then, monks,
out of respect for the gravity of causing a schism, those monks should not suspend that monk for his refusal to see an offense.”

By one who perceives the eight benefits stated by the opening words. For, together with him, the non-performance of the Uposatha and other duties is a disadvantage because it leads to schism; their performance is a benefit because it leads to harmony.
Therefore, the meaning is that this monk should not be suspended by one who perceives these eight benefits.
In the second group of eight as well, it says: "By seeing eight benefits...
Here, monks, a monk has committed an offense, yet he regards that offense as no offense;
other monks regard that offense as an offense. If, monks, that monk..."
Those monks know thus: “These venerable ones are learned, masters of the tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, bearers of the Mātikā;
they are wise, competent, intelligent, modest, conscientious, and desirous of training;
they are not capable—whether for my sake or for the sake of others—of going astray through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; if these monks [should act] toward me...”
“They will suspend me for not seeing an offense; they will not perform the Uposatha together with me; they will perform the Uposatha without me;

on that account there will arise for the Saṅgha quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute, as well as schism in the Saṅgha, fracture in the Saṅgha, division in the Saṅgha, and separation in the Saṅgha. Monks, one who values harmony...
The meaning is: "by one who perceives the eight benefits stated beginning with, 'The bhikkhu should confess that offense even out of faith in others.
Regarding the phrase "by the seven [factors] mentioned in the Pāḷi": "First, he thinks, 'I will speak falsely'; while speaking, he thinks, 'I am speaking falsely'..."

"I am speaking," and after having spoken, he thinks, "I have spoken falsely," while setting aside his view, setting aside his preference, setting aside his inclination, and setting aside his disposition—by these seven [factors] thus arrived at. "Unholy conduct" means conduct that is not noble.
"One should not eat at night, which is eating at the improper time," refers to one who has observed the Uposatha.
One should not eat at night nor eat at an improper time during the day.

"One should lie on a bed or on the ground" means one should lie either on a permissible bed or on a prepared surface made of earth treated with plaster and the like, or on a mat made by spreading grass, leaves, straw, and so forth.
This is called the eightfold Uposatha; that is, [the abstention from] killing living beings and the other [precepts].
Because it is observed with eight factors by one who does not act improperly, they call it "eightfold" (*aṭṭhaṅgika*).
There are eight things called "not left over" (*anatiritta*), beginning with "that which has been made unallowable" and "that which has not been formally accepted.
Ghee and so forth become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) at the rising of the sun on the eighth day. These first eight should be understood by applying them according to the number eight.
The meaning is that other sets of eight should also be constructed by this method: taking one from the first set of eight, and then adding one to each of the remaining sets, and so forth.
The commentary on the section on the sets of eight is finished.
Commentary on the Ninefold [Set]: 329.

Regarding the "bases for resentment" (*āghātavatthu*) among the ninefold set, these are the causes of resentment. Regarding the "ways of removing resentment" (*āghātapaṭivinaya*), these are the means for the removal of resentment.
As for the phrase "How can this be obtained here?": it means, "How can this practice of harmfulness be avoided with regard to this person? (i.e., "May such harm not occur").
"For what reason is it possible to obtain [this]? Thinking, 'Another indeed does harm to another according to his own mental inclination,' one dispels resentment.
Or alternatively: 'If I were to harbor anger, from where could that act of anger be obtained in this person?
For what reason should it be obtained?'—the meaning is that it is because it is purposeless. [They are] owners of their own karma.
For beings, by whose will could they become either suffering or happy? Therefore, the intention is that it is merely my own anger toward him.
Alternatively, from where can such a cause for anger be found in this person?
For, in the ultimate sense, there is an absence of both one who should be angry and one who is angry; this is merely a conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*).
The five aggregates, which are called a "being," are formations that are short-lived and momentary; what person could be angry with whom? This is the meaning.
There is also the reading “kuto lābhā,” which means: if I were to harbor anger here, what profit would there be in my acting thus?
For what could be considered a profit other than the arising of harm? And in this...
In this context, *taṃ* is merely a particle.
"Dependent on craving" (*taṇhaṃ paṭicca*) refers to two types of craving: the craving for seeking (*esanatāṇhā*) and the craving for what is sought (*esitatāṇhā*).

That craving by which one seeks and searches for wealth after setting out upon paths such as those of the goat-tracks or the cart-tracks is called the craving for seeking. [That which exists] in those things sought and searched for...
Craving for what has been acquired is called craving for what has been sought after (*esita-taṇhā*); here, craving for what has been sought after is to be understood.

"Seeking" (*pariyesanā*) is the seeking of objects such as forms; for that exists when there is craving for seeking. "Gain" (*lābha*) is the acquisition of objects such as forms; for that exists when there is seeking.
"Decision" (*vinicchaya*), however, is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and applied thought.

In this context, “One should know the discrimination of pleasure; having known the discrimination of pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal pleasure”—this is the discrimination by knowledge (*ñāṇa-vinicchaya*).
As for the statement, “Discrimination means two kinds of discrimination:

the discrimination of craving (*taṇhā-vinicchaya*) and the discrimination of views (*diṭṭhi-vinicchaya*),” the eight hundred types of the wanderings of craving (*taṇhā-vicariya*) that have been handed down are the discrimination of craving. The sixty-two views are the discrimination of views.

In this sutta, however, regarding the statement, “Desire, O Lord of Devas, has its source in thought,” it is precisely *vitakka* (thought) that is presented as the "determination" (*vinicchaya*) here.
For after obtaining a gain, one determines what is desirable or undesirable, and what is beautiful or ugly, by means of thought:
“This much will be for the sake of the object of form; this much for the sake of the object of sound; this much for me...”
“There will be this much for another; I will enjoy this much; I will store away this much.
Therefore it is said: “In dependence on gain, there is discrimination.
“Lustful desire” (chandarāga) refers to both weak lust and strong lust toward an object that has been thought over by such unwholesome thinking.
And it arises. "Clinging" (*ajjhosa*) is a strong determination [in the form] of "I" and "mine. "Possession" (*pariggaha*) is the act of grasping by way of craving and views.
"Avarice" (*macchariya*) is the inability to endure sharing with others.
For this very reason, the ancients explain its etymological meaning thus: "May this wonder be mine alone; let it not be a wonder for another."
“Because it causes [the mind] to proceed, it is called ‘avarice. *Ārakkho*:
guarding well by means of locking doors, securing chests, and so forth. *Adhikaroti*: it makes something its basis; this is a name for a cause (*kāraṇa*). *Ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ*:
this is a neuter abstract noun (bhāva-napumsaka), meaning “for the sake of guarding. In the taking up of sticks and so forth, there is the taking up of a stick for the purpose of restraining others.
Taking up a staff is *daṇḍādāna*. Taking up a weapon such as a single-edged blade is *satthādāna*. A quarrel (*kalaha*) is both a quarrel of body and a quarrel of speech.
The former instances are opposition (*virodha*) or conflict (*viggha*), while the latter instances are disputes (*vivāda*).
Saying "you, you" out of a lack of respect is the expression *tuvaṃ tuvaṃ*.

"From the time they have been determined, they must not be transferred"—this means that one who wishes to transfer them must do so either before the determination, or after the determination has been relinquished.
The intention is that what has not had its determination relinquished must not be transferred.
They are stated with reference to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the passage: "If [one] perceives the Saṅgha of nuns as incomplete... and so forth.
By way of the method beginning with “he admonishes,” two sets of nine [cases] regarding illegal formal acts (*adhammakamma*) are stated as offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The commentary on the section of nines is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section of tens.
330. It should be understood by way of the passage beginning with "In the ten [views], there is no giving," etc.: "There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no oblation;
there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done; there is no this world, there is no other world;
there is no mother, there is no father; there are no beings of spontaneous birth; there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who..."

This was said with reference to what has been handed down thus: "Those who have gone rightly, who have practiced rightly, and who, having personally realized through direct knowledge this world and the other world, proclaim them.
It is by way of [the views] such as "the world is eternal" and so forth;
that is, "the world is eternal," or "the world is non-eternal," or "the world is finite," or "the world is infinite," or "the soul and the body are the same," and so on.

or "the soul is one thing and the body another," or "the Tathāgata exists after death," or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
it includes all that has come down [in the scriptures] in this manner.
"Wrong view and so forth, ending with wrong liberation"—this is said with reference to what has been handed down thus:
"wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation.
In this context, "wrong knowledge" refers to that which is evil by way of thinking up means for performing evil deeds.
Delusion that arises in the manner of reviewing, thinking, "It was well done by me.

Wrong liberation (*micchā-vimutti*) is the perception of being liberated while one is actually not liberated. These are specified in the *Samathakkhandhaka* by such passages as, "The legal issue is trivial;
it has not been fully resolved, nor has it been properly investigated and settled. [These] are stated in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.

"He is endowed with" is the connection [to the following]. There are ten types of women, beginning with those protected by their mothers (*māturakkhitā*). There are ten types of wives, beginning with those purchased with wealth (*dhanakkītā*).
The commentary on the section of tens is finished.
The commentary on the section of elevens begins.
331. "In the sets of eleven, they do not purify" means they do not shine forth.
"Made like a well-yoked vehicle" means it is made like a yoked vehicle because it can be operated with ease at whatever time one desires.
"As a foundation" means as the foundation for the attainments. "Occurring repeatedly" means occurring repeatedly through the practice of frequent cultivation (*bhāvanā-bahulīkāra*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "He sleeps happily": whereas other people sleep in pain, tossing and turning and scratching themselves, he does not sleep in such a manner but sleeps happily;
even when falling asleep, he is as if one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Regarding "He awakens happily":
whereas others awaken in pain, yawning, stretching, and tossing about, [he does not].
Thus, without waking up, he wakes up happily and without agitation, like a lotus blossoming.
Because of his previous experiences and because of the assistance provided by deities, his dreams are auspicious and not evil; thus it is said, "He sees nothing but what is auspicious," and so forth.
Furthermore, even those dreams caused by disturbances of the elements are for the most part generally auspicious.
This is because the temperature-born and nutriment-born material qualities conform to the mind-born material qualities.

In this regard, "he sees only auspicious things" means that he does not see an evil dream in the way that others see themselves as if surrounded by thieves, as if afflicted by wild beasts, or as if falling over a precipice; rather, he sees only what is auspicious, which serves as a cause for prosperity.
He is as if paying homage to a *cetiya*, as if making an offering, and as if listening to the Dhamma.
He is dear to human beings: like a necklace of pearls worn upon the breast or a garland bound upon the head, he is dear and pleasing to human beings.
He is dear to non-human beings (*amanussa*): just as he is dear to human beings, so too is he dear to non-human beings.

He becomes beloved, like the Elder Visākha. Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons affect him; for one who dwells in loving-kindness, fire does not affect his body—as with the laywoman Uttarā—nor does poison, as with the Elder Cūḷasīva, the reciter of the Saṃyutta Nikāya;
nor do weapons, as with the novice Saṅkicca. It is said that they do not affect him, they do not enter him, and they do not harm his body.
There is. In this regard, they also tell the story of the cow: it is said that once a cow stood letting her milk flow for her calf.
A hunter, thinking, "I shall pierce her," whirled a long-staffed spear with his hand and released it.
It struck her body and passed through, turning away like a palm leaf; yet, by the power of her proximity [to the calf], she did not die.
It is not by the power of absorption (*appanā*), but solely through the state of having a mind firmly fixed on the calf. Such is the great majesty of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"He quickly attains concentration" means that because ill-will (*byāpāda*) has been kept at a distance, one who has fallen away from jhāna due to some obstacle quickly attains concentration again.
"The complexion of his face brightens" means like a palm fruit released from its bond.
His face becomes serene in color. "He passes away undeluded" means that for one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no such thing as a death in delusion;

The meaning should be understood as follows: when the *yojanā* (method of arrangement) is performed, one hundred words are stated together with the words spoken in the *saṅkhalika-naya* (chain-method).
Otherwise, it would not be possible to obtain one hundred words within the *ekamūlaka-naya* (single-root method) alone.
By combining the preceding and following words from the *ekamūlaka-nayas*, nine words are stated in each turn; thus, through ten such turns, there are ninety [words].

Only the words themselves are obtained. Therefore, when those ninety words are joined according to the method of linked chains (*saṅkhalika-naya*) by way of combined wheels (*baddha-cakka*), ten words are obtained;

However, otherwise, as for how a hundred meanings and a hundred phenomena are obtained separately in both methods, that has already been explained in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.

**Commentary on the Concluding Statement:** Regarding the final verses, this is their meaning. "The analysis of the teaching" (*vibhattadesanaṃ*) should be construed with "the Vinaya Piṭaka," which is the teaching analyzed by means of the two *Vibhaṅgas*, the *Khandhaka*, and the *Parivāra*. "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to that Vinaya.
The passage beginning with "Among these" (*tatridaṃ*) and so forth follows the same method as explained in the commentary on the first *Pārājika* offense.
"Adorned with the Great Bodhi tree of the Teacher" means it was beautified and decorated by the Great Bodhi tree used by the Teacher;

the connection is that "the supreme meditation hall" refers to that which is on the southern side of that Mahāvihāra. Therein, "meditation hall" (padhānaghara) refers to the courtyard (pariveṇa) bearing that name.
"Served by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus of pure conduct and virtue" is also an epithet qualifying the meditation hall.
*Therein*: in that house of striving (*padhānaghara*). *Encircled by a beautiful rampart*: surrounded by a pleasing wall.

*Endowed with trees of cool shade*: endowed with trees possessing cool shade because their branches and sub-branches are covered with thick, dense foliage. Because it is filled with sweet, cool water covered by blooming lotuses, blue lilies, white lotuses, fragrant water-lilies, and so forth.
"Abounding in water-reservoirs" means having abundant reservoirs of water. "Having designated" means by depending upon the elder named Buddhasiri;
that is to say, by depending upon his request. "Prosperous" means successful, flourishing, and complete through the analysis of meaning and so forth.
"Of the abode of glory" means of that which has become the dwelling place of glory. "In the year of victory" means in the year in which victory was attained.
This is the commentary on the Vinaya that was undertaken for the sake of the Elder Buddhasīri. "Connected with the Dhamma" means dependent upon what is wholesome (*kusala*).
Now, dedicating his own merit for the attainment of ultimate happiness by the world together with its devas, he said, "For the long endurance of the Dhamma," and so forth.
In that context, "accumulated" (*samācita*) means built up (*upacita*). "By the power of all... [is the phrase].
By the power of all that merit. "All living beings" refers to all sentient beings, including those of the sense-sphere realm and other divisions.

"May they partake of the essence of the True Dhamma" means may they become partakers of the essence of the True Dhamma by attaining, as appropriate, the three types of enlightenment. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the concluding statement is finished.
The Conclusion:
And to this extent—
for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya and for the growth of the Dispensation—
The commentary that has been undertaken here is that of the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*.
This work, named *Sāratthadīpanī*, is now entirely completed;
it measures approximately thirty thousand units of text in extent.
I have been appointed by that lord of men, Parakkamabāhu,
who desires the establishment of the True Dhamma and who causes the Dispensation to shine forth.
In this delightful monastery built by him, adorned with hundreds of palaces;
In this Jeta Grove, filled with various multitudes of trees, a dwelling-place for those delighting in meditation, endowed with cool water—
I have composed this well-determined exposition, perfect in both meaning and phrasing.
Whatever merit has been accomplished by this [act], and whatever else has been performed by me—
by this meritorious deed, in my second existence as a self,
may I rejoice in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, delighting in virtue, conduct, and good qualities.
Attached to the five sensual pleasures, having attained the first fruit [of the path],
in my final existence, I shall see Metteyya, the bull among sages, the supreme person in the world,
the Protector who delights in the welfare of all beings.
Having seen that wise one and having heard his teaching of the True Dhamma,
and having attained the supreme fruit, may I bring glory to the Conqueror’s dispensation.
May kings always protect these people by means of the Dhamma alone.
Devoted to meritorious deeds, may they illuminate the teaching of the Conqueror.
And may all these living beings, forever free from affliction and always possessed of noble intentions, attain the state of the Deathless.
The Vinaya commentary named Sāratthadīpanī is completed.
